Article 2 of the convention for the protection of industrial property signed at Washington, June 2, 1911, states:

The subjects or citizens of each of the contracting countries shall enjoy, in all the other countries of the Union, with regard to patents of invention, models of utility, industrial designs or models, trade-marks, trade names, the statements of place of origin, suppression of unfair competition, the advantages which the respective laws now grant or may hereafter grant to the citizens of that country.

The same article also provides that these subjects and citizens shall have the same legal remedies against infringement of their rights "provided they comply with the formalities and requirements imposed by the National laws of each State upon its own citizens" and that the "obligation of domicile or of establishment in the country where the protection is claimed shall not be imposed on those enjoying the benefits of the Union". 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2953, 2956.

The Department of State instructed the Embassy in Mexico City, on November 7, 1929, that it was clearly of the opinion that under the Corporations provisions of article 2 of the convention any corporation organized under the laws of a country party to that convention and owning a trade-mark registered in the United States would be permitted to sue in the United States courts for infringement of such trade-mark, citing the cases of the French Republic v. Saratoga Vichy Spring Co., 

191 U.S. (1903) 427, and Baglin, Superior General of the Order of 

Carthusian Monks v. Cusenier Company, 221 U.S. (1911) 580. 

Secretary Stimson to the Embassy in Mexico City, telegram 505, Nov. 7, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 812.543 Palmolive Co./5.

In response to a letter regarding the apprehension of a certain American company that its trade-mark might be registered in Cuba by a local Cuban firm, the Department of State wrote thatthe Department does not understand that, in the absence of treaty stipulations to the contrary, the registration of a trade mark in the United States operates to confer upon the owner of such trade mark a right to the exclusive use thereof in Cuba. In the absence of such a right under Cuban law, there would appear to be no illegality in the registration in Cuba by a citizen of that country of a trade mark identical with that registered in the United States 15 12

by an American citizen. Therefore, while fully aware of the hardships which may in many cases result to American trade mark owners under these conditions, the Department regrets to say that it does not consider that it would be justified in making any representations to the Cuban Government with a view to prevent its citizens from exercising a privilege to which they are undoubtedly entitled by the laws of their own country. 

Counselor Lansing to Senator Penrose, Apr. 30, 1915, MS. Department of 

State, file 837.543 Am 3/1.

In 1924 the Department of State addressed the Minister of the Netherlands concerning the registration of a certain trade-mark by the Commissioner of Patents of the United States, stating that by the provisions of the act approved March 19, 1920 (41 Stat. 533), ante, page 23, under which the registration was effected, it was incumbent on the Commissioner of Patents to register the trade-mark presented but that the registration of the mark was not a grant to the registrant of the right to use the mark but merely a registration of his claim of Unfair comuse. Under section 2 of the act it was said, provision was made that petition the registration of a mark in the United States Patent Office might be canceled in a proper proceeding instituted by any person deeming himself injured by such registration. It was further stated that if any person believed that the use of the trade-mark in question constituted unfair competition affecting his interests he might institute proceedings for an injunction to prevent the further use of the mark. 

The belief was expressed that the mere registration of the mark in question could not be regarded as constituting unfair competition likely to affect the interests of subjects of the Netherlands and that the legal remedies above mentioned constituted full compliance on the part of the United States with the provisions of article 10bis of the convention for the protection of industrial property as revised at Washington in 1911, relating to unfair competition. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Harrison) to Minister de Graeff, Sept. 

12, 1924, MS. Department of State, file 811.543H71/1. Article 10bis of the convention of 1911 provides: "All the contracting countries agree to assure to the members of the 

Union an effective protection against unfair competition." 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2953, 2959; 38 Stat. 1645, 1652.

In January 1909 the American Ambassador protested to the Austro- Hungarian Foreign Office against the refusal of its Government to register an American trade-mark under certain provisions of the Austrian trade-mark law. The Ambassador was of the opinion that the trade-mark convention concluded November 25, 1871 between the

Treaties and municipal law

United States and Austria-Hungary (1 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 

47; 17 Stat. 917) provided for the registration of any trade-mark in Austria which had been registered in the United States Patent 

Office. The United States Commissioner of Patents, to whom the question was referred, stated that the force and effect of that convention as applied in the United States did not extend to all trade-marks sought to be registered in this country and that it was believed, for equally cogent reasons, that the Austrian Patent Office might refuse to register trade-marks which were in contravention of its own trademark law; that it had been the practice of the United States Patent 

Office to refuse the registration of trade-marks registered in foreign countries where it was found that the registration of such marks would conflict with laws prohibiting the registration of similar marks by citizens of the United States; that under the construction placed by his office on "the reciprocal convention relating to the registration of trade-marks between the United States and foreign countries registration is not permitted within the United States where the mark presented is prohibited from registration under the terms of the trade-mark law of this country, upon the ground that the convention is not self-executing"; and that under these circumstances it was not believed that the Government of the United States could well contend that a mark should be registered in Austria merely because it had been previously registered in the United States, if the registration of such mark would be in contravention of the trademark law of Austria. The protest of the American Ambassador was consequently formally withdrawn. 

Ambassador Francis to Secretary Root, no. 761, Jan. 21, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 17830; the Assistant Secretary of the Interior (Wilson) to the Secretary of State (Bacon), Feb. 15, 1909, ibid. 17830/1; Mr. Francis to Mr. Bacon, no. 804, Mar. 5, 1909, ibid. 17830/2.

Articles I and II of the convention of 1871 read as follows: 

"Every reproduction of trade-marks which in the countries or territories of the one of the contracting parties are affixed to certain mer chandize to prove its origin and quality is forbidden in the countries or territories of the other of the contracting parties, and shall give to the injured party ground for such action or proceedings to prevent such reproduction, and to recover damages for the same, as may be authorized by the laws of the country in which the counterfeit is proven, just as if the plaintiff were a citizen of that country. "If the owners of trade marks, residing in the countries or territories of the one of the contracting parties, wish to secure their rights in the countries or territories of the other of the contracting parties, they must deposit duplicate copies of those marks in the Patent Office at Washington and in the Chambers of Commerce and Trade in Vienna and Pesth." 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 47, 48; 17 Stat. 917-918.

Article VI of the convention for international protection of industrial property signed at Paris in 1883, as amended at Brussels in 1900, reads: 

Every trade or commercial mark regularly deposited in the country of origin shall be admitted to deposit and so protected in all the other countries of the Union. 

Shall be considered as country of origin, the country where the depositor has his principal establishment.

If this principal establishment is not situated in one of the countries of the Union, shall be considered as country of origin that to which the depositor belongs. 

The deposit may be refused, if the object, for which it is asked, is considered contrary to morals and to public order. 

Article VIII of the same convention reads: 

The commercial name shall be protected in all the countries of the Union without obligation of deposit, whether it forms part or not, of a trade or commercial mark. [2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1935, 1938, 1945; 25 Stat. 1372, 1376.]

Section 3 of the Food and Drugs Act approved June 30, 1906 (34 

Stat. 768) directed the Secretaries of the Treasury, Agriculture, and Commerce and Labor to make uniform rules and regulations for carrying out the provisions of the act. Pursuant thereto certain regulations were adopted in 1906. Regulation 17 required that the principal label on food or drug products be printed in English and include certain information in respect to compound or mixed products. Regulation 18 required that the name of the manufacturer or producer or the place of manufacture, if given, be the true name or place. On May 9, 1908 the French Ambassador protested to the 

Secretary of State that these regulations contravened the international convention of 1883 for the protection of industrial property. He enclosed a memorandum prepared by the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs in which attention was called, inter alia, to article VI of the convention providing for admission to deposit and protection as such in all the countries members of the Union for the Protection of Industrial Property, of every trade-mark duly registered in the country of origin, and to article VIII providing for the protection of brands in every country of the Union without necessity of registration, whether or not they formed part of a trade-mark. 

It was asserted that the regulations in question were equivalent to a refusal of protection to the trade-marks and brands such as French citizens had a right to use, and it was alleged that the spirit of the convention was violated since its principal object was to insure uniformity of trade-marks in all countries. 

---

The Department of Agriculture, to which the matter was referred, expressed the opinion: 

1. That under the Industrial Property Convention the United 

States owes to the trade marks registered in France no greater rights and privileges than it accords to trade marks registered in the United States. 

2. That under the laws of the United States trade marks which are misleading and deceptive will not be registered or protected. 

3. That inasmuch as Regulations 17 and 18 affect only those trade marks which, when applied to food and drug products, are misleading and deceptive as to the nature or qualities of those products, they do not in any way violate the obligations assumed by the United States in adhering to the Industrial Property Convention.

The Department of Agriculture stated that if the United States were obligated by the convention to register and protect marks registered in France, whether or not they were misleading and deceptive, the trade-mark laws of the United States would be nullified to that extent and that it was not conceivable that such a result could have been contemplated by the contracting states in adhering to the convention. Attention was called to the case of French Republic v. 

Saratoga Vichy Spring Co., 191 U.S. (1903) 427, in which the

Supreme Court of the United States in considering article VIII of the convention stated that the rights of the French Republic were the same and no greater under that article than those of the United States would be. The right of the United States, the Department of 

Agriculture said, to determine according to its own laws questions relating to the registration and protection of trade-marks, whether or not they were registered in France, was not affected by the convention except as to questions concerning solely the form of the marks. As to these section 4 of the final protocol of the convention provided that no trade or commercial mark should be excluded from protection in any of the states of the Union simply because it might not satisfy in respect to the signs composing it the conditions of the laws of that state, provided that it satisfied in this regard the laws of the country of origin and had been duly deposited in the latter. 

The French Ambassador again addressed the Secretary of State on December 3, 1908, calling his attention, inter alia, to the fact that, with reference to regulation 18, French law permitted a merchant who had acquired the right to utilize a trade-mark or brand to put on the labels only the well-known name of the founder of the firm, although it required the firm at every change of ownership to put its own name on all billheads and business papers. 

A memorandum by the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs in respect to the position taken by the Department of Agriculture discussed

above, stated that the assertion that the United States did not owe any greater rights or privileges to trade-marks registered in France than to those granted to trade-marks registered in the United States was entirely erroneous; that the question as to whether a trade-mark was deceptive and fallacious was intimately connected with the signs composing it and that, since everything concerning such signs was decided by the country of origin, the question of the deceptive and fallacious nature of a trade-mark should be decided exclusively by the country of origin and the law of that country; and that to place a series of statements in English on French trade-marks would inevitably result in distorting and destroying those trade-marks, which was the opposite of the protection to which they were entitled. If all the countries signing the convention were to adopt similar provisions, it was said, an end would be put to all uniformity in trade-marks, which was the principal object of the convention. 

The Department of State, on January 29, 1910, transmitted to the Ambassador a communication from the Secretary of Agriculture dated April 26, 1909, in which it was stated that that Department did not and could not legally attempt to prescribe a particular form of label for a particular product and that any form of labeling which clearly conveyed to purchasers of a product a correct conclusion regarding the article and did not convey a false and misleading impression was satisfactory. It was added: 

Two reasons exist why an exception cannot be made to Regulation 18 permitting French manufacturers to place on their labels, without qualification, firm names under which they do not do business. First, a regulation authorizing the use on French labels of fictitious firm names which are forbidden in domestic and other labels, effects a discrimination in favor of French articles of commerce, and is illegal. Second, the law plainly prohibits the admission into the United States of articles, the labels of which are misleading and deceptive. The Department of 

Agriculture does not doubt that a label which bears, without qualification, the name of an individual or firm which is not the manufacturer or producer is misleading and deceptive. Even if there existed in law some color of authority for the purpose, the wisdom of making an exception in favor of French products in this particular must be regarded as questionable, now that a very large number of French manufacturers and producers have changed their labels to conform to the requirements of Regulation 18. 

Ambassador Jusserand to Secretary Root, May 9, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 12601/4-5; the Acting Secretary of Agriculture (Hays) to 

Mr. Root, Sept. 25, 1908, ibid. 12601/13; Mr. Jusserand to Mr. Root, Dec. 3, 1908, ibid. 12601/14-18; Secretary of Agriculture (Wilson) to the Secre- 'tary of State (Knox), Apr. 26, 1909, ibid. 12601/27-34; Mr. Jusserand to 

Mr. Knox, May 7, 1909, ibid. 12601/35-36; Mr. Knox to Mr. Jusserand, no. 779, Jan. 29, 1910, ibid. 12601/27-34.

Extraterri- torial effect of cancela- tion In 1912 the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce complained of the refusal of the United States Patent Office to register a trademark registered in Great Britain on the ground that the firm named on the mark was not written in a distinctive form and its requirement that that name should either be removed from the mark or specifically disclaimed. This was alleged to violate article VI of the international convention for the protection of industrial property signed at Paris in 1883 and amended in Brussels in 1900, providing that "Every trade or commercial mark regularly deposited in the country of origin shall be admitted to deposit and so protected in all the other countries of the Union." It was contended that under this article applicants were entitled to registration in the United States identical with Great Britain. The United States Patent Office took the position that the act approved February 20, 1905 (33 Stat. 

724), which was controlling on it, made no distinction, in regard to registration, between a citizen of the United States and a resident of a foreign country which adhered to the international convention; that it had no authority in law to treat applications of foreigners differently from those of citizens of the United States; and that the application of the trade-mark laws of this country in respect to the matter in question was substantially identical with the enforcement of the British Trade Mark Act. 

The Commissioner of Patents (Moore) to Secretary Knox, June 28, 1912, 

MS. Department of State, file 811.543/2.

The case of Baglin, Superior General of the Order of Carthusian 

Monks v. Cusenier Company involved a bill in equity to restrain the infringement of trade-marks and unfair competition. The order of 

Carthusian monks in 1876 and 1884 had registered two trade-marks in the Patent Office of the United States for the liqueur manufactured by them in France and known as "chartreuse". In 1903 the congregation of these monks in France was dissolved by operation of French law, and possession was taken of their properties in that country by a "sequestrating administrator and liquidator" appointed by the French court. The monks thereafter set up a factory in Spain and continued to manufacture the liqueur according to their ancient process. The French liquidator placed upon the market a product—a liqueur either identical with or resembling as closely as possible the old "chartreuse"-under the old name which was shipped to and sold in the United States in bottles of precisely the same description and under the same marks and symbols that had been used by the monks. 

Meanwhile the monks, debarred in France from the use of their old marks and symbols, devised a new designation for their liqueur and in the suit in question sought to prevent the use of the word "chartreuse" as designation of the liqueur made in France subsequent to

their expulsion. The defendant was the representative in the United 

States of the French company to whom the liquidator had sold the property. The Supreme Court of the United States held that the 

French law could not have the effect of detaching the trade-marks in the United States from the product of the monks, which they were still manufacturing. The Court stated that the decree of the circuit court adjudging the defendant guilty of infringement of trade-marks and unfair competition was plainly right and ordered that an amendment of the decree of the lower court in that portion containing an injunction against unfair trade include a provision restraining the use of the word "chartreuse" in connection with the sale of liqueur not made by the monks as the name of or as descriptive of the liqueur or without clearly distinguishing it from the monks' product. 

221 U.S. (1911) 580.

The In the case of Ingenohl v. Olsen & Company, Inc., suit was brought to recover costs allowed the plaintiff in an action by him against the defendant in the British colony of Hong Kong. The judgment declared the plaintiff to be the owner of certain trademarks and trade names and entitled to the exclusive use thereof in his business. It restrained the defendants from selling cigars under those trade-marks and awarded the costs in question. The Supreme 

Court of the Philippine Islands reversed the decision of the lower court for the plaintiff on the ground that by §311(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure a judgment against a person "may be repelled by evidence of a want of jurisdiction, want of notice to the party, collusion, fraud or clear mistake of law or fact" and that the judgment of the Hong Kong court showed such a clear mistake. supposed mistake consisted of denial of effect in Hong Kong of a sale of business- and trade-marks by the Alien Property Custodian of the United States to the defendant in 1918. At that time the 

Alien Property Custodian seized and sold all the property of the plaintiff "wheresoever situate in the Philippine Islands". The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the judgment of the 

Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands, stating that "A trademark started elsewhere would depend for its protection in Hongkong upon the law prevailing in Hongkong and would confer no rights except by the consent of that law." The Court said further that it did not see how it was possible for a foreign court to pronounce as wrong the decision of the Hong Kong court that the acts of the Alien Property Custodian would not be allowed to affect the rights of the plaintiff in Hong Kong. In regard to §311(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court stated that "whatever scope may be given to the section it is far from warranting the refusal to enforce

Good offices this English judgment for costs, obtained after a fair trial before a court having jurisdiction of the parties, when the judgment is unquestionably valid and in other respects will be enforced". 

273 U.S. (1927) 541, 543, 544. In its opinion in this case the Supreme

Court said that a foreign state might accept the transfer by the Alien Property Custodian as good within its jurisdiction if there were no opposing local jurisdiction or right and suggested that this might be the fact for China outside of Hong Kong, as seemed to have been held in another case not finally disposed of at that time. In an instruction to the Legation in Peiping on June 28, 1930 the Department of State declared that the case referred to might be the case of Ingenohl v. Wing 

On Company decided by the British Supreme Court at Shanghai in 1925, in which it was held that so far as British subjects in China were concerned the sale by the Alien Property Custodian of the United States gave the purchaser the exclusive right to use the trade-marks in question in China. The Department said that, in view of that decision and the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in the case of Ingenohl v. Olsen & Company, Inc., the legal and equitable basis of the claim of the assignee of the purchaser to the exclusive right to use the trademarks in China appeared to warrant the Government of the United States in supporting the assignee's efforts to establish its claim before the Chinese authorities. The Legation was authorized to take such action in behalf of the assignee as might be appropriate. Secretary Stimson to the Legation in Peiping, telegram 218, June 28, 1930, MS. Department of State, file 893.543 Olsen and Co./16.

A Mexican national in 1910 was manufacturing and selling in Mexico a product purporting to be that of a well-known American firm, and using its trade-mark. A representative of the American firm informed the American Consul in San Luis Potosi that the person was clearly punishable under Mexican law for the infringement and urged the Consul to enter a complaint. The Department of State on July 12, 1910 wrote to the Consul saying:

There appears to be no convention in force between this country and the Mexican Government covering the protection of trade marks.

In the absence of a trade mark convention with Mexico it is not seen what action you could properly take in the matter, as no act seems to have been committed in this case requiring an official of this Government to become a complainant. However, the Department sees no objection, as a protectionary measure, to your using your good offices with the local officials with a view to bringing about the punishment, under the Mexican laws, of the offender in this case. 

Consul Bucklin to Secretary Knox, no. 90, June 18, 1910, and the Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Mr. Bucklin, no. 35, July 12, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 25123.

The case of A. Bourjois & Company, Inc. v. Katzel involved an action to restrain the infringement of trade-marks registered in the

United States Patent Office which the plaintiff had purchased from a French company, together with its business in the United States. 

The defendant had bought a large quantity of powder manufactured by the French company in France and was selling it in the United States in boxes with labels closely resembling the labels used by the plaintiff under its trade-mark. The Supreme Court of the United 

States reversed a decree of the circuit court of appeals reversing an order of the district court granting a preliminary injunction to the plaintiff. The Court held that the fact that the defendant's boxes and powder were a genuine product of the French concern did not give her a right to sell them in the form which she was using in the 

United States, saying: "Ownership of the goods does not carry the right to sell them with a specific mark." 

260 U.S. (1923) 689, 692. trade-marks A decree of the Guatemalan Government provided in part that a trade-mark should be considered distinct from another mark although the two were designated by the same word or class named if they were differentiated by an adjective or the name of the dealer and had distinctive markings and designs. In response to an inquiry by the 

American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in that country as to the Similar notice to be given owners of a registered trade-mark before a mark which they considered to conflict therewith should be registered, the Guatemalan Foreign Office, on July 27, 1923, stated that the notice in question should be the publication for one month in the official newspaper of the proposed registration and that persons having acquired rights might protest within the period which the law fixed against every application for registration of a trade-mark which might directly or indirectly be confused with a mark registered prior to the issuance of the decree. The Department of State, on September 17, 1923, instructed the Chargé d'Affaires to point out to the Guatemalan Foreign Office the apparent opportunity afforded by the decree for the substantial appropriation by others of American trade-marks and to urge, "in the interest of justice and in line with the essential purpose of trade-mark laws as existing generally throughout the civilized world", the amendment of the decree so as to obviate the danger of working injustice on persons who had conducted business in Guatemala under the protection of duly registered trade-marks. The Chargé d'Affaires was instructed further to point out that, although the Guatemalan authorities appeared to recognize that owners of trademarks were entitled to protection against the apparent purport of the decree, it would be more equitable to amend the decree removing the menace to their lawfully acquired rights rather than to subject them to the necessity of watching closely the official newspaper for

Misleading labels China the notice of proposed registration injuriously affecting them and of entering protests against such registration. 

On August 23, 1924 the Guatemalan Foreign Office wrote to the Chargé d'Affaires quoting an interpretation by its Secretary of the Interior of the provisions of the decree, holding that "no trade mark can be registered legally, if said mark is of such nature or character that it can produce, directly or indirectly, confusion of products on the part of the public". The Department stated that this interpretation appeared to be satisfactory from the standpoint of American manufacturers.

The Department of State, on June 23, 1916, informed the Legation in Peking that it was not satisfied that a certain American company was entitled to American protection for its products since their labels indicated that they were British products manufactured by a British concern, since the trade-marks were registered in British Consulates in China, and since the United States Government was without control of products so manufactured.

The Department informed the company that consular protection would be given to such of its goods as might be wholly manufactured in the United States, provided that they were marketed and labeled as American goods and that their labels showed compliance with the 

Pure Food and Drugs Act of the United States. The Government of the United States, it was said, could not be a party to any mislabeling of goods nor could it consent to give protection to goods the manufacturers of which had not conformed to the laws of the United States. The Department stated that, if the company would assure it that in the future it would conform to the requirements set forth above, the American Consul General would be instructed to extend protection to such of its products as should be manufactured in the 

United States and properly labeled. 

Secretary Lansing to the Legation in Peking, June 23, 1916 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 893.543F81/1; the Acting Secretary of State (Polk) to Edwin McClellan, July 8, 1916, ibid. 893.543F81/9.

The Government of China undertook, under article IX of its treaty of October 8, 1903 with the United States, to protect American trademarks in China and to issue proclamations forbidding Chinese subjects from infringing on or imitating the trade-marks belonging to American citizens registered by the proper authorities of the United States at Chinese offices after payment of a reasonable fee and investiga-

tion by the Chinese authorities and in compliance with reasonable regulations.

No regulations for the protection of trade-marks having been in force in China prior to 1923 (with the exception of regulations promulgated by the Chinese Government in 1904 and withdrawn within a few days), it became the custom for consular officers, at the instance of American manufacturers, to request the native authorities to issue proclamations protecting American trade-marks against infringement by Chinese subjects. Also, the Commissioners of Customs at Tientsin and Shanghai were instructed by the Chinese Government to open provisional offices for registration of trade-marks. 

On May 3, 1923 the Chinese Government at Peking promulgated a trade-mark law, to the application of which to American trade-marks as from September 1, 1926 “subject to the general provisions of the treaties", the American Legation assented on May 29, 1926.

The Nationalist Government at Nanking in 1927 promulgated regulations relating, inter alia, to the registration of trade-marks previously registered with the Bureau of Trade-Marks at Peking. The American 

Legation on March 6, 1929 informed the Chinese Minister of Industries, Commerce, and Labor that in view of certain assurances from the Director of the Trade-Mark Bureau in Nanking he was taking steps to advise American trade-mark owners to register their trademarks with that bureau.

A new trade-mark law was promulgated by the Nationalist Government on May 6, 1930 to take effect on January 1, 1931.

The Chesebrough Manufacturing Company, an American corporation, registered the company's trade-mark for vaseline at the appropriate office at Shanghai in pursuance of article IX of the treaty of October 8, 1903 between the United States and China. Imitations of Japanese manufacture bearing the company's trade-mark were thereafter sold in China by certain Chinese. Criminal proceedings were instituted by the company in the Mixed Court at Shanghai 

---

against the sellers for the purpose of having them penalized for infringement of the trade-mark and enjoined from further dealing in imitation goods bearing the mark. The Japanese Consul General at 

Shanghai represented to the local Chinese authorities that the company having failed to obtain, by appropriate action in Japan, annulment of the Japanese registration of its trade-mark was not entitled to proceed, even in a Chinese court, against Chinese who, contrary to the laws of China, were dealing in an infringement. He contended that the fact of infringement should first be established in a Japanese court.

The American Minister in China was authorized by the Department of State on February 27, 1915 to instruct the Consul General at Shanghai that, so far as prosecutions by Americans against Chinese were concerned, the rights of industrial property in China were determinable by local law as based upon priority of use and registration and proclamation and that Japanese registration could not interfere with the right of an American company to seek redress in a Chinese court for violations by Chinese citizens of its rights under Chinese law. The American Chargé d'Affaires informed the 

Chinese Foreign Office that, should the prosecution be dismissed, such action would not only be detrimental to the rights of the American firm but would also establish a precedent under which the rights and duties of even Chinese nationals in respect to the use of trade-marks in China would be subjected to the test not of Chinese law alone but also of the law of any country whose nationals might register in their home state the marks already registered in China and entitled to Chinese protection.

The magistrate of the Mixed Court at first declared himself in favor of dismissing the case on the ground that the fact of infringement must first be established in a Japanese court. However, he later assumed jurisdiction and on August 19, 1915 rendered a judgment stating:

Inasmuch as the defendant's goods now held in court bear a mark somewhat resembling that of the plaintiff's, the goods are to be detained for examination and consideration.

The present case being a criminal action, this court does not deem it fit to grant the application of the plaintiff for an injunction against the sale of the defendant's goods. 

Should the plaintiff file any further suits against the defendants, we will institute further inquiries and deal with the cases according to their merits.

The defendants are hereby released and the case closed. 

With reference to the judgment, the American Chargé d'Affaires stated that, since it released the defendants but detained, under circumstances which were tantamount to confiscation, the stock of goods

bearing the infringing trade-mark, it was not wholly unsatisfactory in as much as it implied "a recognition of the trade-mark rights of the American owners, and of the jurisdiction of the Chinese court in enforcing those rights as against Chinese dealers in the infringement". He considered that the judgment was unsatisfactory, however, in that it left those principles to inference and could not but appear inconclusive by reason of that fact and of the further fact that no definite penalty was imposed upon the defendants, nor was there even a direct statement of their guilt. 

Minister Reinsch to Secretary Bryan, Feb. 15, 1915 (telegram), MS. 

Department of State, file 893.54/310; Chargé MacMurray to Secretary 

Lansing, nos. 695 and 761, July 20 and Sept. 22, 1915, ibid. files 893.54/322 and 893.543C42/5; Mr. Reinsch to Mr. Lansing, no. 826, Nov. 18, 1915, ibid. file 893.543C42/7. See also 1915 For. Rel. 231-256.

Between 1905 and 1907 agreements were concluded by the United States through exchanges of notes with certain other countries for the protection in China of trade-marks registered in the United States by nationals of those countries and registered in those countries by nationals of the United States. The agreements provided that actions by nationals of one country against nationals of the other for infringement of trade-marks should be brought in the consular courts of the defendant's country. Such agreements were concluded with Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Netherlands, and Russia.

Special treaties were concluded by the United States with Japan on May 19, 1908 in regard to the reciprocal protection of inventions, designs, trade-marks, and copyrights in Korea and China. 

The treaty with respect to Korea provided (art. II) that in case of the infringement by American citizens of inventions, designs, trademarks, or copyrights entitled to protection in Korea they should "in these respects be under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Japanese courts in Korea, the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the United States being waived in these particulars".

Article III of the treaty with respect to China provided for recourse by aggrieved Japanese and American nationals to their respective territorial or consular courts. 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1041, 1042, 1043; 35 Stat. 2041, 2044.

Act of 1905, as amended Upon inquiry as to whether the treaty concluded with Japan on May 19, 1908, relative to the reciprocal protection of Japanese and American trade-marks in China, obviated the necessity, to which owners of American trade-marks registered in Japan were then subject under Japanese law in order to receive protection, of continuously transacting business in Japan in the article covered by the trade-mark, the Department of State replied:

So far as the Department is at present advised it believes that the provisions of the recent treaty between the United States and Japan for the reciprocal protection in China of the inventions, designs, trade-marks and copyrights of the citizens and subjects of the two countries, are drawn upon the theory that each country shall give to patents, trade-marks, et cetera, properly registered by citizens of the other country, the same protection to [in] China which it gives at home. That is to say, the protection which American citizens receive for their patents, designs, trade-marks, et cetera, in Japan, is the measure of the protection to which they are entitled in China under the terms of the recent treaty with Japan. Forfeiture of the right of protection in Japan, therefore, would seem to forfeit the right of protection, in accordance with the terms of the treaty, in China.

The Acting Secretary of State (Bacon) to the China and Japan Trading 

Co., Ltd., July 16, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 406/189.

Section 4 of the act approved February 20, 1905, as amended by the Act approved June 20, 1936, provides that an application for registration in the United States of a trade-mark previously filed in any foreign country affording by treaty, convention, or law similar privileges to citizens of the United States shall be treated as if filed in the United States, provided that the application is filed within six months from the date on which the application was first filed in such foreign country.

Section 5 of the act approved Feb. 20, 1905 prohibits the registration of a trade-mark consisting of or including the flag, coat of arms, or other insignia, or simulation thereof, of the United States or any State or municipality or any foreign nation. 33 Stat. 724, 725; 15 U.S.C. §85.

According to the United States Commissioner of Patents trade-marks including in their design the letters "U.S.A." would not be regarded as registrable in the United States. The Department of State on Nov. 3, 1920 informed the American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Buenos Aires that the registration of designs consisting of or including as a prominent feature the letters "U.S.A." in Argentina would be contrary to the spirit of article V of the convention for the protection of trade-marks signed at Buenos Aires in 1910, prohibiting the adoption of flags, coats of arms, etc., as trade-marks. There was no objection, the Department said, to having goods or the packages in which they were contained marked to show that they were made in the United States, although the words "United States" or the letters "U.S.A." should not appear as a part of the trade-mark itself. The Chargé d'Affaires was instructed to bring the matter to the attention of the Argentine Government and to say that, in view of the prohibition in the laws of the United States against the registration of insignia of foreign governments, the Government of the United States would appreciate similar consideration in cases arising in Argentina involving the letters "U.S.A." The Chargé d'Affaires informed the Department on Sept. 22, 1921 that a petition for the registration of the trade-mark containing the letters "U.S.A." had been definitely refused in Argentina on June 10, 1921. The United States Patent Office in 1934 rejected an application for a design patent filed by a French citizen and based on a prior application filed in France in that year, on the ground that it had not been submitted before the expiration of four months from the date of the foreign application, as required by section 4887 of the Revised Statutes. The French Embassy, in a note of August 7, 1934 to the Department of State, observed that this decision disregarded the provisions of article 4 (a) (c) of the industrial-property convention of 1925 establishing a priority period of six months. As to this, the Commissioner of Patents expressed the opinion that the provision of the convention was not self-executing and could not properly be observed in the absence of legislation by Congress. 

Chargé Henry to Secretary Hull, Aug. 7, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 811.542 Vernin, Louis/1; the Secretary of Commerce (Roper) to Mr. 

Hull, Nov. 3, 1934, ibid. 811.542 Vernin, Louis/5.

Section 4887 of the Revised Statutes was amended by act of Congress approved June 19, 1936 to provide a six months' priority period in the case of foreign applications for design patents. 49 Stat. 1529.

Section 4887 of the Revised Statutes of the United States, as amended March 3, 1897, March 3, 1903, and June 19, 1936, provides that no person otherwise entitled thereto shall be debarred from receiving a patent for his invention or discovery nor shall any patent be declared invalid by reason of its having first been patented in a foreign country, unless the application for the foreign patent was filed more than 12 months, in the case of patentable inventions and discoveries, and 6 months, in the case of designs, prior to the filing of the application in the United States, in which case no patent shall be granted in this country. It further provides that an application for patent for an invention or discovery or design filed in the United States for which an application for a patent has been previously regularly filed in a foreign country affording by treaty, convention, or law similar privileges to citizens of the United States shall have the same force and effect as if filed in the United States on the date on which the application was first filed in such foreign country, provided the application in the United States is filed within 12 months in the case of patentable inventions and discoveries and within 6 months in the case of designs from the earliest date on which any such foreign application was filed. It also provides that no patent shall be granted on an application for a patent for an invention or discovery or design which has been patented or described in a printed publication in the United States or any foreign country more than two years before the date of the actual filing of the application in the United States or which has been in public use or on sale in this country for more than two years prior to such filing. 

Rev. Stat., sec. 4887; 29 Stat. 692, 693; 32 Stat. 1225; 49 Stat. 1529; 

35 U.S.C. §32. 

The case of Cameron Septic Tank Company v. City of Knoxville, Iowa involved a bill in equity praying for an injunction to restrain the defendant from the use of a certain invention patented in the United States on October 3, 1899. The invention had previously been patented in Great Britain on November 8, 1895, and that patent had expired on or before November 8, 1909. When the patent was issued in the United States the term of a patent, as now, was 17 years (Rev. Expiration of patents Stat., sec. 4884), and section 4887 of the Revised Statutes provided that every patent granted which had been previously patented in a foreign country should be limited so as to expire at the same time with the foreign patent. The complainant alleged that the patent in question had not expired in the United States since, by article 4bis inserted in the convention for the protection of industrial property of 1883 un der article I, paragraph III, of the Act of Brussels of December 

14, 1900 proclaimed by the President (on August 25, 1902) to take effect September 14, 1902, it was provided that patents applied for

Patentabil in the different contracting states should be independent of the patents obtained for the same invention in the other states. It was also provided that such provision should apply to patents existing at the time of its going into effect. The Supreme Court of the United States held that the article was not self-executing and that in the absence of a statute putting that article into effect the provisions of section 4887 of the Revised Statutes applied to the patent in question and affirmed the decree of the circuit court of appeals holding that the patent had expired. 227 U.S. (1913) 39. 

In Leeds and Catlin Company v. Victor Talking Machine Company the defendant was enjoined from manufacturing, using, or selling apparatus or devices embodied in certain claims of letters patent issued in the United States in 1895. The defendant had alleged that the invention had previously been patented in certain foreign countries, that the foreign patents had expired, and that consequently under section 4887 of the Revised Statutes the United States patent had also expired. The Court stated that, if limited at all, the patent in the United States would be limited only by a prior foreign patent identical with it and found that certain of the foreign patents were not identical with the United States patent and that, therefore, the latter had not expired with those foreign patents. 213 U.S. (1909) 301. 

The recognition by a government of the patentability of an invenity, a munici- tion does not afford a basis for questioning the refusal of another pal question government to admit its patentability.

Scope of rights con- ferred

The Assistant Secretary of State (Welles) to the Minister to Sweden 

(Steinhardt), no. 68, Aug. 13, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 858.542 

Masonite Corporation/6.

The right conferred by a patent under our law is confined to the United States and its Territories (Rev. Stat., §4884) and infringement of this right cannot be predicated of acts wholly done in a foreign country. See United Dictionary Co. v. Merriam Co., 208 U.S. 260, 265. The case of Manufacturing Co. v.

Cowing, 105 U.S. 253, is cited as holding otherwise but is not in point. There the defendant made the infringing articles in the 

United States. Here, while they were made in the United States, they were not made by the defendants. The latter's infringement consisted only in selling the drills after they passed out of the makers' hands. The place of sale [Canada] is therefore of controlling importance here.

Dowagiac Manufacturing Company v. Minnesota Moline Plow Company and Dowagiac Manufacturing Company v. Smith, 235 U.S. (1915) 641, 650.

The monopoly of a patent does not "extend beyond the jurisdiction of the government granting it. . . . Whatever effect a patent granted by one country has in another depends upon the status given to it by the laws of the latter."

Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Rubber Tire Wheel Co. et al., 164 Fed. 

869, 872-873 (C.C.S.D. Ohio, 1908).

When a patent has been granted in any country, any action looking to its invalidation must be taken in accordance with the applicable laws of the particular country by the person or company alleging infringement.

The Acting Solicitor for the Department of State (Baker) to the General 

Printing Ink Corporation, Feb. 19, 1930, MS. Department of State, file 

894.542 General Printing Ink Corp./2.

With reference to the annual taxation by certain foreign countries of patents owned by citizens of the United States, the Department Taxation of of State stated that, while the United States does not impose any patents annual tax on patents, the tax laws of the foreign countries to which reference was made applied to the citizens of such countries and to all other owners of patents in exactly the same way as to citizens of the United States and that therefore the United States could not question the right of those countries to grant patents on such conditions as they deemed proper. Since the tax did not discriminate against citizens of the United States, it was said, no basis for complaint existed. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Johnson) to Julian W. Fretwell, Sept. 1, 1927, MS. Department of State, file 811.54200/3.

In September 1914 the Mexican Government issued a decree invalidating all patents of invention from February 19, 1913 to August 21, 1914 but providing that the legal dates would stand and new patents would be issued upon application to the Patent Office and re-payment Succeeding of full fees. The regulations were also made applicable to trade- governments marks. The Department of State objected to the application of the requirements to American citizens who had been granted patents or trade-marks or who had instituted or carried on proceedings toward such grants during the Huerta regime in strict conformance with and under regularly established and applicable, previously existing proceedings or requirements. It stated that such persons should not be obliged again to make payment of the amounts required by Mexican law during that period and that those whose patents or trade-marks had thus been incepted or acquired should have a reasonable opportunity to prove that their titles thereto were in conformance with the then-existing law.

Nolan act 

The same position was taken by the Department in 1928 in an instruction to the Legation at Peking to inform the Nationalist Government that the United States expected that that Government, having succeeded the government which promulgated the trade-mark law of 1923, would assume and carry out the duty imposed by that law to give protection throughout China to rights acquired thereunder by American nationals. The Department stated that American citizens who had registered their trade-marks in accordance with the law of 1923 or who had filed applications for registration and had paid the fees prescribed by the law, had complied with all the requirements thereof and were entitled to receive from the Chinese Government the protection afforded thereby without the payment of any additional fee and without being required to re-register or renew their application for registration in cases where registration had not been completed.

Section 1 of the act of Congress approved March 3, 1921, known as the "Nolan act", provided for the rights of priority acquired under section 4887 of the Revised Statutes which had not expired on August 1, 1914 or which had arisen since that date to be extended until the expiration of a period of six months from March 3, 1921 in favor of the citizens of the United States or citizens or subjects of all countries extending substantially reciprocal privileges to citizens of the United States. Section 2 of the act extended the time then fixed by law for the payment of any fee or for the taking of any action with respect to an application for a patent which had not expired on August 1, 1914, or which commenced after August 1, 1914, until the expiration of one year from March 3, 1921 without the payment of extension fees or other penalty in favor of the citizens or subjects of countries extending substantially reciprocal privileges to

citizens of the United States, provided that no extension should confer such privileges on the citizens or subjects of the foreign country for a longer term than that during which such privileges were conferred by such foreign country on the citizens of the United States. 

41 Stat. 1313; 35 U.S.C. §§ 80, 81. 

The proviso in section 1 of the act approved Mar. 3, 1921, that the extension of the priority rights granted therein shall in no way furnish a basis of claim against the Government of the United States, has been held to preclude a British subject who, on Mar. 28, 1922, had obtained patent rights in the United States under the act, from suing in the Court of Claims for alleged acts of infringement by the Government of the United States alleged to have taken place on June 30, 1930, it being conceded that during the six months' period allowed foreign inventors under the act the Government was not in possession of and did not use the invention. Chessborough James Henry Mackenzie-Kennedy v. The 

United States, 85 Ct. Cls. (1937) 405; certiorari denied, 303 U.S. (1938) 646. the object of the Nolan Act is to confer upon citizens and subjects of those countries which grant reciprocal privileges to citizens of the United States the same benefits as are accorded by 

Articles 307 and 308 of the Treaty of Versailles. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Harrison) to the British Chargé d'Affaires (Chilton), Aug. 9, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 811.54247h/6.

In 1910 the Italian Ambassador to the United States pointed out that by article II of the international convention for the protection of industrial property of 1883, as amended in 1900, there was imposed on the states parties to the Union for the Protection of Industrial Interna- Property the obligation of reciprocally granting temporary protec- tional tion to the inventions, industrial designs, models, and trade-marks of expositions products exhibited at the official international expositions held on the territory of one of those states and that a decree had been prepared for submission to His Majesty the King of Italy to meet the obligations assumed under the convention with respect to the exposition to be held at Turin (Torina) in 1911. He inquired as to the practice of the United States and was informed that it was the custom of Congress to pass special acts putting in force the provisions of the convention with respect to the temporary protection of inventions exhibited at official international expositions held within the territory of the United States, as, for example, the act approved April 6, 1892 with reference to the World's Columbian Exposition at Chi-

Inter-Ameri- can copyright conventions cago (27 Stat. 14) and the act approved March 3, 1901 with reference to the Louisiana Purchase Exposition (sec. 22; 31 Stat. 1440, 1445).

The Commissioner of Patents of the United States stated that it was the uniform custom of the states which were adherents to the convention to promulgate special legislation for each official international exposition and that the United States had fully complied with its obligations in that respect. The Italian Ambassador was informed, therefore, that American citizens who might be exhibitors at Turin should be accorded the protection provided for by article II of the convention. 

Secretary Knox to Marchese Confalonieri, no. 11, Nov. 12, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 811.541/1.

Article 6(1) of the Rome convention of 1928 provides: 

"Authors who are not nationals of one of the countries of the Union, and who first publish their works in one of those countries, shall enjoy in that country the same rights as native authors, and in the other countries of the Union the rights granted by the present Convention." 

On Jan. 21, 1931 President Hoover transmitted to the Senate, for its advice and consent to adherence thereto by the United States, the convention of 1908 signed at Berlin. On Feb. 19, 1934 President Roosevelt transmitted to the Senate the convention of 1928 signed at Rome for its consideration in lieu of the convention of 1908 on which the Senate had taken no action. No action has thus far been taken by the Senate on the Rome convention. See S. Ex. Rept., 76th Cong., 1st sess.

By section 8 of the Copyright Act approved by the President 

March 4, 1909 privileges of copyright are extendedto the work of an author or proprietor who is a citizen or subject of a foreign state or nation, only: (a) When an alien author or proprietor shall be domiciled Act approved within the United States at the time of the first publication of 1909 his work; or (b) When the foreign state or nation of which such author or proprietor is a citizen or subject grants, either by treaty, convention, agreement, or law, to citizens of the United States the benefit of copyright on substantially the same basis as to its own citizens, or copyright protection substantially equal to the protection secured to such foreign author under this Act or by treaty; or when such foreign state or nation is a party to an international agreement which provides for reciprocity in the

Mechanical reproduction granting of copyright, by the terms of which agreement the United States may, at its pleasure, become a party thereto. 

It provides that the existence of such reciprocal conditions shall be determined by the President of the United States by proclamation. 

35 Stat. 1075, 1077; 17 U.S.C. §8. 

The Act of March 3, 1891 [26 Stat. 1106], which extended copyright in the United States to foreign authors, provided (section 13) that the Act should only apply to a citizen or subject of a foreign state when such foreign state permits to citizens of the United States the benefit of copyright on substantially the same basis as to its own citizens. The Act of March 4, 1909, amends this by adding "or copyright protection substantially equal to the protection secured to the foreign author under this Act or by treaty," and provides that the grant of reciprocal rights may be "either by treaty, convention, agreement, or law." 

The new Act, therefore, establishes another additional basis of copyright relations. The Act of March 3, 1891, requires substantially equal national treatment, and the new Act adds the alternative of copyright protection to American authors in the foreign country substantially equal to the protection secured to foreign authors in the United States.

The Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to the German Chargé d'Affaires 

(von Wedel), Aug. 9, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 11682/13–14.

The case of Bong, Plaintiff in Error v. Alfred S. Campbell Art 

Company involved an action to recover for the infringement of the copyright of a painting. The plaintiff was a German national, Germany being a country whose nationals had been declared entitled to the benefit of the copyright laws of the United States by presidential proclamation. He had become the sole proprietor of a painting made by a citizen of Peru, as to which country the President had issued no copyright proclamation, and had applied for a copyright of the picture in conformity with the laws of the United States. The Supreme 

Court of the United States affirmed a judgment for the defendant on the ground that the plaintiff's rights were determined by those of the maker of the picture and that a citizen of Peru was not entitled to statutory copyright since there was no presidential proclamation to that effect. 214 U. S. (1909) 236. 

It is provided in subdivision (e) of section 1 of the act approved March 4, 1909 that the provisions of the act, so far as they secure copyright controlling the parts of instruments serving to reproduce mechanically musical works, shall not include the works of a foreign author or composer unless the foreign state of which he is a citizen or subject grants similar rights to citizens of the United States.

35 Stat. 1075. Assistant Attorney General Fowler informed the Secre tary of State on May 6, 1911 that it was "the duty of the President to determine and proclaim what foreign countries grant to the citizens of the United States rights similar to those specified in the provisions of section 

1(e)". 29 Op. Att. Gen. (1913) 64, 69. 

In the case of G. Ricordi & Co., Inc. v. Columbia Graphophone Co., a suit for infringement of copyright in a musical composition, the music of which was written by a British composer who at the time of its first publication resided in New York city, the United States District Court, speaking through Circuit Judge Manton, expressed the opinion that domiciled foreigners were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of subdivision (e) 

of section 1 of the Copyright Act of Mar. 4, 1909. With reference to the possible ambiguity between this section and section 8(a) of the act of 1909, Judge Manton expressed the opinion that "Congress intended that domiciled foreigners are entitled to the benefit of the provisions of subdivision (e) section 1, of the act, and that it intended only to exclude subjects or citizens of countries denying similar protection to our citizens" and that "In other words, it intended that domiciled foreigners should receive the same protection and have the same rights as American citizens." 

258 Fed. 72, 76 (S.D.N.Y., 1919). Contra, on preliminary injunction in the same case, 256 Fed. 699 (S.D.N.Y., 1919).

In the case of Leibowitz v. Columbia Graphophone Co. et al., which involved a bill for infringement of a musical copyright for mechanical reproduction, the work having been copyrighted as an unpublished work under section 

11 of the act approved Mar. 4, 1909 (35 Stat. 1075, 1078), the United States 

District Court, speaking through Judge Learned Hand declared that, assuming that Judge Manton was right in regarding section 8(a) as applying equally to copyrights for mechanical reproduction, that section refers only to aliens domiciled in the United States when the work is first published. 

Judge Hand said: 66 • · · 

I hold only this: That a domiciled alien can protect an unpublished work under the statute only in case his sovereign extends reciprocal rights to Americans." 298 Fed. 342, 343 (S.D.N.Y., 1923).

The United States and Germany entered into a copyright agreement on January 15, 1892 by virtue of which the United States engaged that the President should, in pursuance of section 13 of the act approved March 3, 1891, issue the proclamation therein provided for in regard to the extension of the provisions of that act to German subjects. 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 557; 27 Stat. 1021, 1022.

While Germany in 1909 did not afford protection to composers against mechanical reproduction of their work, the German Ambassador on June 5, 1909 wrote to the Department of State that he supposed that- the Reciprocity Proclamation to be issued by the President of the United States in accordance with section 8(b) [of the Copyright Act approved Mar. 4, 1909] will also include protection to the authors of musical works against reproduction by mechanical instruments, as provided in sec. 1(e) of the law of 

March 4, without the necessity of a special guarantee of reciprocity in this particular point.

The Department replied that the President's proclamation of April 15, 1892, issued pursuant to the agreement of January 15, 1892 with respect to copyright for German subjects, simply proclaimed that those subjects had access to the copyright legislation of the United States and might secure the rights and benefits accorded by the copyright laws of this country upon compliance with their stipulations and requirements; that if German authors claimed copyright under the act approved March 4, 1909 it would of necessity seem to be with such reservations and under such stipulations as were included in the act; and that a German composer's copyright in his music would not include the control of the reproduction of his copyright music upon instruments reproducing music mechanically, unless and until the stipulations of the proviso to section 1(e) had been complied with, namely, when Germany had granted either by treaty, convention, agreement, or law similar rights to citizens of the United States.

Suit was brought in the case of Ferris v. Frohman to restrain the production of a play copyrighted in the United States by the de- Common-law fendant which had been adapted from a play performed in England right and subsequently registered under the British statutes. The rights to the production of the latter play in the United States were acquired by the complainants after its production in England. This playwas not copyrighted in the United States or published anywhere. The 

Supreme Court of the United States affirmed the judgment of the Supreme Court of Illinois affirming a decree of the lower court restraining the defendant from producing his play. The Court said that it might be assumed that after the original play had been performed in England the right of its owner to protection against its unauthorized production in England was only that given by statutes. "At common law", the Court declared, "the public performance of the play is not an abandonment of it to the public use." The public representation of a dramatic production not printed and published, the Court continued, did not deprive the owner of his common-law right save by operation of statute, and there was no statute in the United States by virtue of which the common-law right was lost through the performance of the unpublished play. The Court stated that as the British statutes did not affect the common-law right of representation in the United States, it was not material that the first performance of the original play took place in England. 223 U.S. (1912) 424, 435.

By the terms of article XI of the treaty as to commercial relations concluded on October 8, 1903 between the United States and China, the United States undertook to give the benefits of its copyright

laws to the subjects of China on an equal basis with its own citizens, and China, in order to secure such benefits, agreed to give full protection to American "authors, designers or proprietors of any book, map, print or engraving especially prepared for the use and education of the Chinese people, or translation into Chinese of any book, in the exclusive right to print and sell such book, map, print, engraving or translation in the Empire of China during ten years from the date of registration".

Article 14 of the regulations issued by the Government of China for the enforcement of the Chinese Copyright Law of May 14, 1928 contained provision that foreigners who produced "works useful to the Chinese" might apply for registration under the law, on condition of reciprocity. It limited the period of copyright on such works to 

10 years from the date of registration. The United States objected to the regulation on the ground that it provided for less favorable treatment for foreigners than for natives and was contrary to article XI of the treaty of 1903, under the terms of which the copyright protection accorded in China to the works of American citizens was to be "on an equal basis with its own (China's) citizens". 

On December 30, 1932 the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs informed the American Legation that, prior to the revision of the regulations for the enforcement of the copyright law, the provision of article 14 in regard to a 10-year limitation on copyrights for foreigners would not apply to the literary work of American citizens.

CUSTOMS LAWS 

$119 Subject to such international undertakings as may circumscribe its freedom of action, a state may prohibit or regulate the importation into and the exportation from its territories of goods and commodities in such manner and to such extent as in its judgment may best serve its nterests. The treatment to be accorded by a state to another state and its nationals in these respects is frequently covered by a treaty or other form of international agreement. Some of these treaties and agreements prescribe specific rates of duty on specified articles or classes of articles; others accord to articles the benefits of specified tariff schedules (when more than one tariff schedule is in force); and still others provide for national and most-favored-nation treatment. 

Treaties and other agreements between the United States and foreign countries with respect to commerce and navigation contain varying

National treatment types of most-favored-nation clauses as well as clauses with respect to national treatment. Examples of such clauses are found in articles 

IV, V, VIII, and XIV of the commercial treaty of 1911 with Japan, article IV of which read: 

There shall be between the territories of the two High Contracting Parties reciprocal freedom of commerce and navigation. The citizens or subjects of each of the Contracting Parties, equally with the citizens or subjects of the most favored nation, shall have liberty freely to come with their ships and cargoes to all places, ports and rivers in the territories of the other which are or may be opened to foreign commerce, subject always to the laws of the country to which they thus come. 

Article V of this treaty, after stating that the import duties to be charged on articles produced or manufactured in one country upon their importation into the other should thereafter be regulated by treaty between the two countries or by the internal legislation of each, stated: 

Neither Contracting Party shall impose any other or higher duties or charges on the exportation of any article to the territories of the other than are or may be payable on the exportation of the like article to any other foreign country. 

Nor shall any prohibition be imposed by either country on the importation or exportation of any article from or to the territories of the other which shall not equally extend to the like article imported from or exported to any other country. The last provision is not, however, applicable to prohibitions or restrictions maintained or imposed as sanitary measures or for purposes of protecting animals and useful plants.

Article VIII stipulated, on the basis of reciprocity, that all articles that might be imported into either country from foreign countries in national vessels might likewise be imported in the vessels of the other country without being liable to any other or higher duties or charges than if such articles were imported in national vessels, and provided like treatment for exportations. Article XIV provided thatin all that concerns commerce and navigation, any privilege, favor or immunity which either Contracting Party has actually granted, or may hereafter grant, to the citizens or subjects of any other State shall be extended to the citizens or subjects of the other Contracting Party gratuitously, if the concession in favor of that other State shall have been gratuitous, and on the same or equivalent conditions, if the concession shall have been conditional. 

37 Stat. 1504, 1505-1506, 1507; 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2712, 2713-2714, 2716. Following notice of abrogation given by the United States on July 26, 1939, the treaty ceased to exist at midnight of Jan. 26, 1940.

Favored-nation clauses in treaties and agreements may be either of two types, i.e. conditional or unconditional. Most of the treaties concluded by the United States prior to 1923 contained the so-called "conditional" most-favored-nation provisions. In 1923 the United 

States embarked upon a new treaty-making policy by embodying in its treaties subsequently concluded the unconditional most-favored-nation provisions. In a letter addressed by Secretary Hughes to President

Harding on January 15, 1923 the two types of provisions and the effect thereof were explained as follows: .. Under the conditional clause favors which either party to the treaty grant to a third country accrue to the other party to the treaty when the favor to the third country is granted freely, but do not accrue if the favor be granted for a consideration unless the other party to the treaty proffer an equivalent consideration: under the unconditional clause all favors granted by either party to third countries accrue to the other party irrespective of questions of consideration or equivalents. 

In a circular instruction to American diplomatic officers on August 

18, 1923 the Secretary of State said:

Most of the treaties to which the United States has been or is a party, for example, the Treaty of February 6, 1778, with 

France [8 Stat. 12; 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 468, 469-470] and the Treaty of February 21, 1911, with Japan [ante], contain most-favored-nation clauses that are in this respect expressly conditional. Others, such as the Treaty of July 3, 1815, with 

Great Britain [8 Stat. 228; 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 624, 625], in which the most-favored-nation clause is not expressly conditional, have nevertheless been interpreted as though the condition were specified. In connection with the negotiation of new commercial treaties the Department of State has decided to propose a most-favored-nation clause under which the United States will guarantee and expect to be guaranteed unconditional equality of treatment. The United States, in making this proposal, will offer nothing more than a guarantee of the treatment which, in practice, it already accords to the commerce of other countries. 

Concerning the reduced duties which the United States, under the Treaty of 1902, levies upon the products of Cuba, the relations between which country and the United States, both political and economic, are exceptional, and also concerning the free importation of goods from American dependencies, it is proposed to make specific exception. It is not considered that the exception of Cuba is inconsistent with or a deviation from the general principle adopted. 

Secretary Hughes to President Harding, Jan. 15, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 611.0031/163; Mr. Hughes to the American diplomatic officers, Diplomatic Serial No. 211, Aug. 18, 1923, ibid. 611.0031/162.

The first treaty embodying this new policy was that concluded with Germany on December 8, 1923 under article VII of which each country bound itself "unconditionally to impose no higher or other duties or conditions and no prohibition on the importation of any article, the growth, produce or manufacture, of the territories of the other than are or shall be imposed on the importation of any like article, the growth, produce or manufacture of any other foreign country". It was further provided in that article: 

Any advantage of whatsoever kind which either High Contracting Party may extend to any article, the growth, produce, or manufacture of any other foreign country shall simultaneously and unconditionally, without request and without_compensation, be extended to the like article the growth, produce or manu facture of the other High Contracting Party. 

With respect to the amount and collection of duties on imports and exports of every kind, each of the two High Contracting Parties binds itself to give to the nationals, vessels and goods of the other the advantage of every favor, privilege, or immunity which it shall have accorded to the nationals, vessels and goods of a third State, and regardless of whether such favored State shall have been accorded such treatment gratuitously or in return for reciprocal compensatory treatment. Every such favor, privilege or immunity which shall hereafter be granted the nationals, vessels or goods of a third State shall simultaneously and unconditionally, without request and without compensation, be extended to the other High Contracting Party, for the benefit of itself, its nationals and vessels.

The stipulations of this Article shall apply to the importation of goods into and the exportation of goods from all areas within the German customs lines, but shall not extend to the treatment which either Contracting Party shall accord to purely border traffic within a zone not exceeding ten miles (15 kilometers) wide on either side of its customs frontier, or to the treatment which is accorded by the United States to the commerce of Cuba under the provisions of the Commercial Convention concluded by the United States and Cuba on December 11, 1902, or any other commercial convention which hereafter may be concluded by the United States with Cuba, or to the commerce of the United States with any of its dependencies and the Panama Canal Zone under existing or future laws.

But these provisions of article VII, together with others, were abrogated as from October 14, 1935 by an agreement between the two 

Governments on June 3, 1935. 4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4191, 4193, 4194, 4221; 44 Stat. 2132, 2137-2139, 3258. The treaty was, however, followed by 10 other treaties containing similar provisions.

The conclusion of such agreements was made possible by the fact that the tariff legislation of the United States has been non-discriminatory in character in respect to imports and the further fact that certain provisions in this legislation were designed to discourage discrimination against American products in foreign countries. The 

Tariff Act of 1922 (42 Stat. 858, 941-946) gave the President the power in sections 315-317 by proclamation to raise or lower, within a range of 50 percent above or below the existing tariff, the duty on imported goods for the purpose of equalizing the cost of production of articles grown or produced in the United States and like or similar articles, the growth or produce of competing foreign countries. He was also authorized to impose additional import duties not exceeding 50 nor less than 10 percent of the value of the articles, or in certain cases to exclude them from the United States altogether, in order to prevent unfair methods of competition and unfair acts having the effect of or tending to destroy or substantially injure an industry or to prevent the establishment of such an industry or restrain or monopolize trade and commerce in the United States. He was directed to specify and to declare by proclamation new or additional rates of duties not exceeding 50 percent ad valorem upon articles wholly or in part the growth or produce of any foreign country whenever he should find that such country was imposing unreasonable charges upon the disposition in, transportation through, or reexportation from
