590, 701-706.

The Trade Agreements Act of 1934 states as its purpose the expanding of— foreign markets for the products of the United States by regulating the admission of foreign goods into the United States in accordance with the characteristics and needs of various branches of American production so that foreign markets will be made available to those branches of American production which require and are capable of developing such outlets by affording corresponding market opportunities for foreign products in the United States. 

And it authorizes the Presidentwhenever he finds as a fact that any existing duties or other import restrictions of the United States or any foreign country are unduly burdening and restricting the foreign trade of the United States and that the purpose above declared will be promoted by the means hereinafter specified from time to time- (1) To enter into foreign trade agreements with foreign governments or instrumentalities thereof; and (2) To proclaim such modifications of existing duties and other import restrictions, or such additional import restrictions, or such continuance, and for such minimum periods, of existing customs or excise treatment of any article covered by foreign trade agreements, as are required or appropriate to carry out any foreign trade agreement that the President has entered into hereunder.

It limits the authority of the President by providing: 

No proclamation shall be made increasing or decreasing by more than 50 per centum any existing rate of duty or transferring any article between the dutiable and free lists. 

The act further provides that the proclaimed duties and other import restrictions shall apply to articles from all foreign countries whether imported directly or indirectly. The President is authorized, however, to suspend their application to articles of any country "because of its discriminatory treatment of American commerce or because of other acts or policies which in his opinion tend to defeat the purposes" of the act (48 Stat. 943–944).

It is provided in the reciprocal-trade agreements (with the exception of that with Cuba) that the contracting countries shall grant each other unconditional and unrestricted most-favored-nation treatment in respect to customs duties and subsidiary charges and that any advantage, favor, preference, or immunity granted by either of the two contracting countries to any product originating in any third country or consigned to the territory of any third country (with the exception of advantages accorded by the United States to Cuba) shall be accorded immediately and without compensation to the like product originating in or consigned to the territory of the other contracting country. Annexed to each trade agreement are schedules of the products of the two contracting countries which if dutiable are to be exempt from ordinary customs duties in excess of those set forth in the schedules.

The President notified the Secretary of the Treasury on September 

15, 1935 "that on October 15, 1935 the United States will cease to be bound" by the provisions of article VII of the treaty with Germany of 1923 (ante, p. 58). The duties proclaimed in the trade agreements concluded prior to the date of his letter ceased in consequence to be applicable to products of Germany imported directly or indirectly (T.D. 47865). As subsequent trade agreements were concluded, the President informed the Secretary of the Treasury that he had found as a fact that the treatment of American commerce by Germany was discriminatory and directed that the duties proclaimed in connection therewith should not be applied to products of Germany. Similarly in 1936 he found that the treatment of American commerce by Australia was discriminatory and directed that the duties proclaimed in connection with the trade agreements should cease to apply to products of Australia (T.D. 48405). Subsequently, however, in 1938 he informed the Secretary of the Treasury that Australia no longer applied to American commerce the treatment which caused him to suspend the application of the above-mentioned duties to products of that country and directed that such duties should be applied to Australian products on and after February 1, 1938, with the exception of duties proclaimed in connection with the trade agreement with Cuba (T.D. 49368).

MONOPOLIES 

$120 The general attitude of the Department of State concerning na- National and tional or provincial petroleum monopolies and monopolistic pipe-line concessions in foreign countries, was thus explained in an instruction to the Chargé d'Affaires in Argentina on November 13, 1920: 

petroleum monopolies 

Import monopoly The Department does not take the position that it will make representations with respect to any monopoly of natural resources or transportation established or proposed in any foreign country. It is believed that government monopolies or monopolies granted by a government to its own nationals are, generally speaking, matters of domestic jurisdiction. Monopolistic concessions granted by a foreign government to nationals of another country other than the United States would probably in many cases be considered objectionable on grounds of discrimination. 

The Department desires its representatives in foreign countries to endeavor to prevent the adoption of discriminatory measures directed at or injuriously affecting American interests. 

To this end it might be urged informally and discreetly whenever there is an appropriate opportunity that monopolistic measures tend to restrict freedom of commerce and increase the possibility of misunderstandings, friction, and entanglements, leading to possible movements for retaliation and consequent ill feeling. 

In the case of Argentina, a monopolistic concession relating to petroleum production would violate the principle of reciprocity and it might have injurious effects on trade between Argentina and the United States. If the Argentine Government, however, after giving careful consideration to the American point of view, decides to grant a monopolistic concession, you should impress upon the Argentine Government the feeling of this Government that citizens of the United States should have the same opportunity to participate in such a concession as the citizens of any other country.

The Under Secretary of State (Davis) to Chargé Wadsworth, no. 601, 

Nov. 13, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 835.6363/36. See also 1920 

For. Rel., vol. I, pp. 369-370.

Having been informed of the possibility of the establishment of a Government petroleum import monopoly in France, the Department of State in 1933 instructed the Embassy in Paris as follows: 

As far back as 1919, when a monopoly was first proposed following the War, you will find from your archives that the Embassy made representations to the French Government. The latter replied to the effect that the establishment of an oil monopoly was a question of internal policy in which foreign Governments might only find grounds to intervene if (a) the monopoly should jeopardize any rights acquired by their nationals or (b) if the monopoly should deliberately favor the exporters of certain nationalities to the prejudice of other na-

oreig a) the eir vor th ther of T6 tionalities. The contention of the American companies is that through their license authorizations and by virtue of the obligations which they have incurred thereunder, they have acquired rights for 20 years, that is, for the period of the licenses in question. Approximately 50 million dollars has been expended by 

American interests in establishing import facilities and refineries, and this investment was made on the basis of the licenses in question. Should an import monopoly and/or a refining monopoly be established in France, the rights acquired by virtue of these licenses would be jeopardized; it would seem moreover from the tenor of your telegram No. 428 of September 26 that the French are considering the possibility of obtaining a large percentage of their petroleum needs from Russia. If so, both of the points raised by the French in 1919 become applicable. If imports of 

Russian oil should be deliberately favored, the result would be very important to the American interests inasmuch as they have so developed crude oil production in the United States as to meet the requirements of their French refineries. All things considered the French should not consider that representations of the Embassy would be in the nature of an interference with internal policy. [Paraphrase.] 

The Embassy was instructed to take up the matter with the French authorities, indicating that the Government of the United States viewed with concern reports indicating the possibility of the establishment of an oil monopoly which would undoubtedly result in seriously jeopardizing existing American licenses and investments. 

Secretary Hull to the Embassy in Paris, telegram 287, Sept. 28, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 851.6363/157.

Upon being informed that an oil monopoly might be established in Spain and that certain properties might be expropriated in connection therewith, the Department of State instructed the Embassy in Madrid to inform the Spanish Government that, while the Government of the United States had no thought of objecting in principle to the establishment of such monopoly, it expected that the Government of Spain would grant fair and full compensation to all the American interests concerned. Such compensation was defined as the fair value of the property taken over and such damages as might be considered reasonably to have resulted to other property by virtue of the taking. Secretary Kellogg to the Embassy in 

Madrid, telegram 85, Nov. 8, 1927, ibid. 852.6363/75.

In 1923 the Albanian Government was considering the granting of a certain oil concession which appeared to be monopolistic. The Minister in Albania was authorized by the Department of State to point out to the Albanian Government that the Department would regret any action tending to deny the principle of the open door in the development of the natural resources of Albania, that the Government of the United States expected the Albanian Government to treat the granting of an oil concession on its merits and to afford an equal opportunity to American companies and to the companies of any other nationality, and that it expected that there would be no concession granted of a monopolistic character or of a nature to exclude the possibility of participation by American nationals.

The Afghan Government in 1923 granted a monopoly to a French professor for archeological exploration in that country. The French 

Foreign Office informed the American Ambassador in France that the French Government was opposed to monopolies of this character. The 

Department of State instructed the Ambassador to say to the Foreign Office that the American Government was "likewise opposed to the granting of privileges of this nature to the nationals of one country calculated to exclude the nationals of other countries". The Department felt, it was said, that to allow this would be contrary to the true interests of international scholarship and research, and it therefore considered it essential that American individuals or institutions, if they desired in the future to enter the field with the consent of the Afghan authorities, should enjoy an equality of opportunity with the nationals of any other country. Open door 

Article XV of the treaty of July 3, 1844 between the United States and China provides that citizens of the United States "are admitted to trade with any and all subjects of China without distinction" in China and that they shall not be "impeded in their business by monopolies or other injurious restrictions". 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 196, 200. 

In article III of the so-called "Nine Power Treaty of 1922" relating to the application of the principles of the open door in China the contracting powers, other than China, agree not to seek, nor to support their respective nationals in seeking, inter aliaany such monopoly or preference as would deprive the nationals of any other Power of the right of undertaking any legitimate trade or industry in China, or of participating with the Chinese Government, or with any local authority, in any category of public enterprise, or which by reason of its scope, duration or geographical extent is calculated to frustrate the practical application of the principle of equal opportunity. [3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 3120, 3122.]

In an instruction to the Minister in Peiping on September 4, 1935, the Department stated that in its opinion and notwithstanding assertions by the Chinese Government to the contrarythe creation of Chinese private and government trade monopolies, as well as foreign trade monopolies, would, in whole or in part, contravene the provisions of Article 15 of the Chinese-American 

Treaty of 1844, Article 14 of the Chinese-French Treaty of 1858 

and Article 3 of the Nine Power Treaty of 1922. 

The Department had previously instructed the Legation in Peiping on February 19, 1934 that in its opinion article III of the nine-power treaty did not preclude a protest against the establishment of a Government trade monopoly and that the above-cited provisions of the French and American treaties, in effect, prohibited Chinese private and Government as well as foreign trade monopolies. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Moore) to Minister Johnson, no. 1745, Sept. 4, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 893.6359 Antimony/20; Secretary 

Hall to the Legation in Peiping, telegram 44, Feb. 19, 1934, ibid. 893.6359

Wolfram Ore/30; 51 Br. & For. St. Paps. 636 (Chinese-French treaty of 1858). 

In an instruction to the Ambassador in China in 1936 the Department of State said that "the Embassy should continue to oppose actively not only monopoly agreements which accord to foreign interests an exclusive or preferential trade position but also unreasonable restrictions on international trade". The Under Secretary of State (Phillips) to Ambassador 

Johnson, no. 182, May 20, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 893.602/45.

Article VIII of the reciprocal-trade agreement with Sweden provides: 

In the event that the United States of America or Sweden establishes or maintains a monopoly for the importation, pro- གྲྭ་

der ments duction or sale of a particular commodity or grants exclusive Reciprocal privileges, formally or in effect, to one or more agencies to im- trade agreeport, produce or sell a particular commodity, the Government of the country establishing or maintaining such monopoly, or granting such monopoly privileges, agrees that in respect of the foreign purchases of such monopoly or agency the commerce of the other country shall receive fair and equitable treatment. 

To this end it is agreed that in making its foreign purchases of any product such monopoly or agency will be influenced solely by those considerations, such as price, quality, marketability, and terms of sale, which would ordinarily be taken into account by a private commercial enterprise interested solely in purchasing such product on the most favorable terms.

FOREIGN EXCHANGE 

$121 In response to a request that it protest against foreign-exchange regulations then in force in Chile, the Department of State in 1932 wrote: 

The Department understands that the Chilean exchange control decrees are general legislative acts applicable to foreign transactions irrespective of the nationality of the foreign interest affected. 

Such legislation does not ordinarily afford grounds for protest by foreign governments in the absence of discrimination against their respective nationals. The establishment of priorities of right to such foreign exchange as becomes available is usually considered within the right of the government exercising control; and provided these priorities do not form a discrimination against American interest the Department cannot ordinarily seek to modify them.

The Economic Adviser of the Department of State (Feis) to the General 

Printing Ink Corporation, Sept. 7, 1932, MS.

Department of State, file 825.5151/63. "Some thirty governments at present have in force measures of exchange control similar in general type to those in force in Uruguay. As long as such measures have been applied irrespective of the nationality of the interests affected, they have generally been held to afford no ground for protest by foreign governments." The Assistant Secretary of State (Bundy) to the 

New Home Sewing Machine Company, Dec. 19, 1932, ibid. 833.5151/91.

Complaint was made to the Department of State in 1936 by an American corporation in regard to Spanish exchange-control measures affecting its credit in a French bank in Barcelona. The Department replied:

It is not believed, however, that the fact that the credit is deposited with a French bank in Barcelona would have the effect of preventing the application of Spanish Exchange Control measures. A foreign bank doing business in Spain or in 

Spanish territory is subject to the jurisdiction of the government of that country.

The Legal Adviser of the Department of State (Hackworth) to Columbia 

Smelting & Refining Works, Inc., Dec. 10, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 852.5151/241. Frozen commercial credits constitute a practical problem for which no general solution has been found anywhere. 

Exchange control authorities are generally charged with the duty of restricting payments abroad to correspond to the amounts of foreign exchange available and within those amounts must naturally provide first for payments for necessary goods which can be obtained only by importation. The question of allowing exchange for the payment of existing debts, and of priorities

wing

Drit among such debts, appears to be a less obvious matter. The 

Department of State has no jurisdiction to pass on the propriety of payments for current imports or of the treatment of commercial debts unless the interests of American citizens appear to be discriminated against.

As to the complaint regarding failure to give fair notice before Discriminaestablishing an exchange control, it is a matter of current ob- tion; notice servation that such acts are usually drastic emergency measures not taken until the stability of banks and currency is threatened by lack of confidence and consequent withdrawal of funds from the country.

Corporation, Apr. 26, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 825.5151/89.

The Uruguayan exchange-control authorities failed to assign an import quota to the United States for the month of January 1938, explaining that dollar-exchange purchases and sales, including debt service, left the United States with an approximately balanced account for 1937 and that no import quota would be granted until Uruguay obtained a favorable balance with the United States. 

The Government of the United States stated that, if the Government of Uruguay intended to permit the importation into that country of goods from certain foreign countries while at the same time preventing importation of similar goods from the United States, it was reluctantly obliged to protest. It was pointed out to the Uruguayan Minister of Foreign Affairs that Uruguayan exports of all categories were accorded access to the markets of the United States under conditions as favorable as those accorded to goods from any foreign country, except Cuba, and the hope was expressed that such official action as the Government of Uruguay might take in regulating its foreign trade would be directed toward furthering, rather than discouraging, trade between the two countries.

An American citizen resident in New York city wrote in 1933 to the Department of State in regard to the German law restricting foreignexchange transactions affecting remittances to him from Germany of interest payments on a trust fund in Berlin. The Department replied that- "while it is regretted that American citizens have been inconvenienced by the German emergency decree laws forbidding the transfer of money from that country for the time being, it must be remembered that investments or funds within the jurisdiction of a foreign country are subject to the laws of that country. In the absence of specific treaty provisions to the contrary, there is no way in which a private person may secure immunity from the local law for his investments or property held within the jurisdiction of a particular state." The Acting Chief of the Division of Western European Affairs (Hickerson) to Ernst Wolf, Aug. 12, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 862.5151/1192.

The Department of State, while striving to obtain a general improvement of exchange conditions, does not undertake to press for special consideration for specific commodities where only a limited amount of controlled dollar exchange is made available, since such action might be at the expense of other American interests.

The assistance of the Department of State was requested in 1935 in obtaining the release of $1,659.85 deposited in Spain to the credit of an American corporation in payment for certain nuts which were

Nationality of products External debt shipped by that company from its stocks in New York and which were of Ecuadoran origin. The Spanish Exchange Control Board, in conformity with restrictions which it had placed on payments for imports of Ecuadoran origin, was willing to release the money only in payment for Spanish exports to Ecuador. The Department stated: 

The question of the nationality of goods frequently arises in international trade. There is no universally accepted standard for determining the nationality of products but it is generally held that a raw material product moving through a second country to a third country is not treated as a product of the second country unless it undergoes some transformation therein by processing. National laws and international agreements contain divers stipulations as to the percentage of transformation necessary for change of nationality. As it does not appear from your letter that the nuts in question, which you state are of Ecuadoran origin, have been subjected in the United States to any form of working-up or processing, it is not felt that there exists any basis for a request for the release by the Spanish authorities of the payment for these nuts on the ground that they are not Ecuadoran but American products.

The Chief of the Division of Western European Affairs (Moffat) to 

A. E. Whitehouse, Mar. 7, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 852.5151/103.

The Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Uruguay was instructed in May 1935 that, if officials of the Uruguayan Government expressed the view that payments on dollar bonds were in any way contingent upon the amount of dollar exchange available, he should make it clear that the Government of the United States did not agree that payments on a country's external debt were contingent on the state of the balance of payments between the lending and the borrowing country. No such provision, it was said, was made when Uruguayan borrowings in the United States occurred, nor would it have been possible to have interested American or other investors if the bond payments had been made subject to such a condition. The Chargé d'Affaires was further instructed, in June following, in his discretion to express to the Uruguayan Minister of Foreign Affairs the view of his Government that "the service of national debts is a matter of national interest and exchange for that purpose should be taken from the general fund of foreign exchange" and that "any reduction in the purchases of foreign goods by Uruguay, due to the withholding of exchange by the Government to meet debt service, should be applied proportionately to all nations and that the entire burden should not be imposed on the trade of those countries which have lent money for the development of Uruguay". 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Welles) to Chargé Dominian, nos.

The Argentine Control Commission, on May 31, 1933, officially informed all banks that, effective on that date, all permits granted for purchases of dollars must be covered by dollars derived from exports to the United States. The Department of State, on June 3, purchases- 

1933, instructed the Embassy in Buenos Aires that it assumed this exports to order covered purchases of all foreign currencies and did not refer only to the dollar. It pointed out that nevertheless the order would occasion grave difficulties to American exporters to Argentina and instructed the Embassy to express to the Argentine officials the profound regret of the Government of the United States that they had adopted a measure constituting a serious impediment to trade between the United States and Argentina, and one not in harmony with the objectives of the World Economic Conference or the proposed tariff truce. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Phillips) to the Embassy in Buenos 

Aires, telegram 30, June 3, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 835.5151/116A.

Chargé White to Secretary Hull, no. 2105, June 9, 1933, ibid. 835.5151/129. this Department, after careful consideration, has deemed it wise, on grounds of general policy, not to seek to obligate any country to give preferential treatment in the application of exchange restrictions to our trade or other interests. 

The Economic Adviser of the Department of State (Feis) to Ad. Auriema, 

Incorporated, May 8, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 832.5151/341.

The reason for this policy has been explained as follows: "As the struggle to sell exports in world markets becomes more and more intense, nations launch into practices known as 'bilateralistic balancing.' In simplest form this means the insistence that each nation with which the country trades buy as much from it as it buys from the other nation. Thus are born clearing agreements and compensation agreements, frequently involving governmental sequestration and control of funds payable by one country's citizens to those of another. A country whose imports from another exceed its exports to the other by such an agreement is in a position to force the other to spend part or all of the proceeds from its export balance in the purchase of the former country's goods. 

Compensation and clearing agreements are for the most part highly unsatisfactory. Experience has usually shown them to result in formidable administrative difficulties and burdens and diminished trade. "With bilateralistic balancing goes trading in exclusive preferences and the discard of the policy of equality of treatment embodied in the mostfavored-nation policy. Exclusive preferences granted to one nation mean discriminations against every other nation, and discriminations involve retaliations and counterdiscriminations. Trading in exclusive preferences thus means constantly rising trade barriers, arbitrary and uneconomic diversions of trade and shiftings of trade channels, unceasing and mounting economic conflict."

U.S. opposed to preferen- tial agree- ments

Bounty or grant

Address by Assistant Secretary Sayre, Department of State, XX Press 

Releases, weekly issue 501, pp. 386, 388 (May 5, 1939). "In most of the countries of the world the supply of dollar exchange granted by American purchases falls short of the obligations of these countries to us arising out of the purchases of American goods and previous American loans. Assuming that Brazil would be willing to conclude a preferential exchange agreement with the United States similar to that between Argentina and Great Britain, other countries whom we have been criticizing for the same practice would derive justification for continuing and extending it. Likewise, the resentment that would be caused in other countries whose sales to Brazil would be curtailed through such action would stimulate the tendency on their part to extend their own special advantages wherever it might be possible with resulting disadvantage to competing American interests. Out of our fifteen principal markets as measured by the value of exports in 1934 which together bought some three-fourths of our total exports, with only three, namely, the Philippine Islands, Brazil and Cuba, did we not have a markedly favorable trade balance. In such a situation, the dangers and disadvantages to our whole trade of adopting measures such as you suggest designed to further our trade with one market are obvious." The Chief of the Division of Latin 

American Affairs (Wilson) to the General Printing Ink Corporation, May 

20, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 832.5151/622.

Article X of the reciprocal-trade agreement with Ecuador provides in part: "In the event that the Government of the United States of America or the Government of the Republic of Ecuador establishes or maintains, directly

or indirectly, any form of control of the means of international payment, it shall, in the administration of such control: "(a) Impose no prohibition, restriction, nor delay on the transfer of payment for imported articles the growth, produce, or manufacture of the other country, or of payments necessary for and incidental to the importation of such articles; "(b) Accord unconditionally, with respect to rates of exchange and taxes or surcharges on exchange transactions in connection with payments for or payments necessary and incidental to the importation of articles the growth, produce, or manufacture of the other country, treatment no less favorable than that accorded in connection with the importation of any article whatsoever the growth, produce, or manufacture of any third country; and "(c) Accord unconditionally, with respect to all rules and formalities applying to exchange transactions in connection with payments for or payments necessary and incidental to the importation of articles the growth, produce, or manufacture of the other country, treatment no less favorable than that accorded in connection with the importation of the like articles the growth, produce, or manufacture of any third country." 

Aug. 6, 1938, Ex. Agree. Ser. 133.

A substantially similar provision was embodied in an exchange of notes with Italy on Dec. 16, 1937, establishing a temporary commercial arrangement between the United States and that country. Ex. Agree. Ser. 116. 

It is provided in article IX of the reciprocal-trade agreement with 

Sweden: 

"The tariff advantages and other benefits provided for in this Agreement are granted by the United States of America and Sweden to each other subject to the condition that if the Government of either country shall establish or maintain, directly or indirectly, any form of control of foreign exchange, it shall administer such control so as to insure that the nationals and commerce of the other country will be granted a fair and equitable share in the allotment of exchange. "With respect to the exchange made available for commercial transactions, it is agreed that the Government of each country shall be guided in the administration of any form of control of foreign exchange by the principle that, as nearly as may be determined, the share of the total available exchange which is allotted to the other country shall not be less than the share employed in a previous representative period prior to the establishment of any exchange control for the settlement of commercial obligations to the nationals of such other country." 

May 25, 1935, Ex. Agree. Ser. 79.

A substantially similar provision is found in the reciprocal-trade agreements with the following countries: El Salvador (art. IX, ibid. 101, Feb. 

19, 1937); Finland (art. X, ibid. 97, May 18, 1936); Honduras (art. VIII, ibid. 86, Dec. 18, 1935); Nicaragua (art. IX, ibid. 95, Mar. 11, 1936). The reciprocal-trade agreements with Costa Rica and Guatemala contain a similar provision and in addition provide: "With respect to non-commercial transactions it is agreed that the Government of each country shall apply any form of control of foreign exchange in a non-discriminatory manner as between the nationals of the other country and the nationals of any third country." Costa Rica (art. 

IX, ibid. 102, Nov. 28, 1936); Guatemala (art. IX, ibid. 92, Apr. 24, 1936).

It is provided in article VII of the reciprocal-trade agreement with Haiti: "If either the United States of America or the Republic of Haiti establishes or maintains any system of control of foreign exchange or enters directly or indirectly into any arrangement which affects in fact the provision of foreign exchange or the regulation or control of the transfer or disposition of means of payment, or employs any other system of control or any other arrangement with respect to the settlement of international obligations, any advantage, favor, privilege, or immunity which may be granted in connection with any such system or arrangement or the administration thereof to the nationals or commerce of any third country shall be accorded immediately and unconditionally to the nationals or commerce of the Republic of Haiti or the United States of America, respectively." 

Mar. 28, 1935, Ex. Agree. Ser. 78.

The reciprocal-trade agreement with Cuba provides in article XI: "The customs preferences and other benefits provided for in this Agreement are granted by the United States of America and the Republic of Cuba to each other subject to the condition that the Government of each country will refrain from subjecting payments or the transfer of means of payment or the disposition thereof to any regulation, restriction, charge or exaction, other or higher than was in force on April 1, 1934, which results in (one) impairing or circumventing any provision of this Agreement, (two) placing an undue burden on trade between the nationals or residents of the respective countries, or (three) preventing or hindering nationals of either country residing, doing business, or traveling in the territory of the other country from securing and transferring in or to either country the funds reasonably necessary for, or arising from, such residence, business, or travel." 

Aug. 24, 1934, Ex. Agree. Ser. 67.

In article VI of the reciprocal-trade agreement with Brazil the two Governments agree "that if they shall establish or maintain a control of the foreign exchanges, they will accord to the nationals and commerce of each other the most general and complete application of the unconditional most-favored-nation principle". Ex. Agree. Ser. 82. 

In an exchange of notes on the day when the agreement with Brazil was signed, Feb. 2, 1935, the Brazilian Ambassador informed the Secretary of State that his Government interpreted the promise contained in article VI above quoted as follows: 

"I. The Bank of Brazil will furnish sufficient exchange for the payments, as they become due, for all future importations of American products into Brazil; moreover, the Bank of Brazil will provide sufficient foreign exchange for the gradual liquidation of the American commercial debts now in arrears, it being understood that the Bank of Brazil will establish a system of payment under which the amount of foreign exchange required for the purposes mentioned shall not be less than a percentage calculated in accordance with the share represented by American goods in total Brazilian imports during the past 10 years, but slightly increased in order that the purposes contemplated by the new trade agreement may be accomplished; "II. With respect to transfers of profits and dividends of American companies operating in Brazil, my Government cannot, until the situation becomes normal, do more than promise that such companies will receive 2

12 treatment never less favorable than that which is enjoyed or which may be enjoyed by any foreign companies established in the country; "III. My Government suggests the cooperation of the Bank of Brazil with the Federal Reserve Board of New York (or any other institution which the Government of the United States of America may indicate), in the sense of inaugurating a foreign exchange information service, affording greater knowledge of the situation of each of the two countries with relation to the other and, in this way, intensifying the exchange of products between them; "IV. If, as it hopes, the negotiations in progress for obtaining banking credits should come to a happy conclusion, the Brazilian Government will reserve from the foreign exchange at its disposal that necessary to meet the payment, to the holders of bonds of loans negotiated in the United States of America, of the sums fixed by the plan of February 5, 1934, for payment of debts."

Ibid. 

In an instruction to the Embassy in Rio de Janeiro the Department of State expressed the opinion that the undertaking of the Brazilian Government, stated in the Brazilian Ambassador's note of Feb. 2, 1935, entitled the Government of the United States to expect that the advantages contemplated in the agreement would not be impaired through the operation of exchange control and that the necessary exchange would be made available for payments, when due, for all imports from the United 

States. Secretary Hull to the Embassy in Rio de Janeiro, telegram 100, Dec. 30, 1937, MS. Department of State, file 832.5151/944. 

A Brazilian decree of Dec. 24, 1937 imposed a tax of 3 percent on purchases of foreign exchange. The Department of State thereupon informed the Embassy in Rio de Janeiro that, in its opinion, in the administration of the decree, or any regulations issued pursuant thereto, the provisions of the trade agreement of 1935 between Brazil and the United States required that no tax be imposed on exchange sold for payment for imports from the United States which was not imposed in connection with payment for imports from every other country, including countries with which trade was conducted on a compensation basis.

The Department declared on Feb. 8, 1938 that this tax was not regarded as "imposed on or in connection with importation", and therefore as violating article III of the trade agreement with Brazil which provided that articles enumerated in schedule I attached thereto should be exempt from ordinary customs duties in excess of those set forth in the schedules and other duties, taxes, fees, charges, or exactions "imposed on or in connection with importation" in excess of those imposed or required to be imposed by the Brazilian laws in effect on the date of the signature of the agreement. 

Secretary Hull to the Embassy in Rio de Janeiro, telegram 100, Dec. 30, 1937, MS: Department of State, file 832.5151/944; the Chief of the Division of the American Republics (Duggan) to Mr. Elwin Walker, of Walker, Goulard, Plehn Company, Inc., Feb. 8, 1938, ibid. 832.5151/953.

LEGAL REMEDIES COMPETENCE OF TRIBUNALS 

In the case of Charter Shipping Company, Ltd. v.

Bowring, Jones & Tidy, Ltd. the United States Supreme Court said: 

The retention of jurisdiction of a suit in admiralty between foreigners is within the discretion of the District Court. The exercise of its discretion may not be disturbed unless abused. 

281 U.S. (1930) 515, 517.

In the case of Cunard S.S. Company, Limited v. Smith the circuit court of appeals reversed without prejudice a judgment of the United States District Court in favor of the plaintiff below, a subject of the Provisional Government of Russia and a resident of New York State, against the defendant below, a British corporation. The court stated that no jurisdiction is conferred on Federal courts in cases in which both parties are aliens and that a United States court cannot obtain jurisdiction to hear and decide a case by consent of the parties. It did not follow, it said however, that, because the district court as such had no jurisdiction of the case on account of the alienage of the parties, the plaintiff was unable to bring suit in any of the courts of the United States to determine the merits of the action. It has been held, it was said, that one alien may sue another in the State courts even on contracts made abroad or for tort committed in a foreign country. It was also pointed out that, while an admiralty court of the United States is under no obligation to entertain jurisdiction where all the parties are foreigners, it may entertain jurisdiction of a suit between aliens in civil causes of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction and is inclined to do so when it is necessary to prevent a failure of justice and if the rights of the parties will thereby be best promoted. 

255 Fed. 846 (C.C.A. 2d, 1918).

In the Sagamore, case nos. 1158 and 1159, libels in personam were filed against the owners of the Sagamore, a British steamer, raising the question whether a State statute of Massachusetts, creating a right of action to recover for death by wrongful act, applied to the deaths resulting from a collision on the high seas between the British steamer and a vessel owned by a Massachusetts corporation. 

The circuit court of appeals declared that, while the statute in question created liability on the part of Massachusetts owners to those injured, it did not follow that it might impose a liability upon citizens of another state who were without its territorial jurisdiction. 

The court said: "Its authority over its own ships and citizens does not extend to the ships and citizens of another nation." The court held that the Massachusetts statute imposed no obligation on the owners of the Sagamore to make compensation or to pay a penalty for causing death and that, as the general maritime law offered no recovery for death thus occurring on the high seas, the libels, so far as they sought damages for death, should be dismissed. The court stated, however, that so far as they sought recovery for personal effects lost through the disaster the libels might be maintained. 

247 Fed. 743, 757 (C.C.A. 1st, 1917).

Pursuant to affidavits of the plaintiffs, owners of an American vessel which had collided with the defendant American vessel in American waters, warrants were issued and the latter vessel was arrested by Canadian authorities while it was in innocent passage through Canadian waters. The Supreme Court of Canada held that the Toronto 

Admiralty District Court had no jurisdiction of the case.

The Ship "D. C. Whitney" v. The St. Clair Navigation Company and The Southern Coal and Transportation Company, 38 Can. Sup. Ct. (1907) 303. 

For a fuller account of this case, see §94, vol. I. 

Jurisdiction by United States courts over a controversy arising out of a collision between two vessels, each registered under the laws of a foreign country and each owned by a foreign corporation, is not obligatory where the collision occurs within United States territorial waters, but it lies within the discretion of the court to decline to assume jurisdiction. 

Canada Malting Co., Ltd. v. Paterson Steamships, Ltd., 285 U.S. (1932) 

413. 

In the following cases United States District Courts assumed jurisdiction in respect to collisions between foreign vessels in foreign territorial waters: 

The Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse, 175 Fed. 215 (S.D.N.Y., 1909); The Kongsli, 252 Fed. 267 (D. Me., 1918); Royal Mail Steam Packet Co. v. Companhia de

The British merchant ship Sidra and the tugboat Potomac, belonging to the Government of the United States, collided in the Patapsco River in Maryland in 1905. In the award in the case of a claim by the British Government against that of the United States on account of the collision, the tribunal said:

According to the well settled rule of international law, the collision having occurred in the territorial waters of the United States, the law applicable to the liability is the law of the United States Nielsen's Report (1926) 452, 457. In accord, see the award of the same tribunal in the case of The Canadienne (Great Britain v. United States), in which it was said: "According to the generally recognized rule of international law in the United States (Story, Conflict of Laws, ch. 14, sec. 558) and in Great 

Britain (Marsden, Collisions at Sea, 6th ed., p. 198), in such a case as this the lex loci delicti commissi must apply." Ibid. 427, 430. 

The case of George W. Johnson, Arthur P. White, Executor, and Martha

J. McFadden, Administratrix (United States v. Mexico), decided by the 

General Claims Commission established under the convention of Sept. 8, 1923, involved a collision between an American vessel and a Mexican gunboat in Mexican territorial waters. The presiding commissioner, Mr. van Vollenhoven, in his opinion, said: 66 

There would seem to be no doubt but that with reference to the present collision the law of Mexico is applicable. 

In 1888, at its session of Lausanne, the Institut de droit international considering the problem of collisions both from the viewpoint of existing law and from 2

that of a future uniform law, resolved in its drafts covering both viewpoints (under the guidance of such experts as Messrs. Lyon-Caen and 

Renault from Paris) that the law applicable is the law of the land where the collision took place a solution qualified by Mr. Renault as required even by 'ordre public'—and the Institute identified collisions within territorial waters with collisions in the interior of a country. If Mexican law in this matter were in open conflict with a universally recognized provision of international law the Commission should take such conflict into account; 99 In a separate opinion Commissioner Nielsen, in reference to the rule laid down in the cases of the Sidra and the Canadienne, said: 

This rule would appear to be sound as a general principle. But the recognition of the proper application of the rule in any given case would, I think, not necessitate the conclusion that an international tribunal would be impotent to determine liability based on the general rule of international law and the facts in a case in which it may appear that there is no applicable local admiralty law or is a law the effect of which may be to deny responsibility for a clearly wrongful act. In situations of that kind an international tribunal should, I think, determine the question of responsibility in the light of facts and general, applicable principles of law, as responsibility is determined, for example, in the case of wanton, negligent, or unnecessary destruction of property by some other agency for which the government is responsible." 

Opinions of the Commissioners (1927) 241, 245, 246, 250.

In the case Molina v. Comision Reguladora del Mercado de 

Henequen, involving an action by a Mexican citizen in respect to Civil suits certain property alleged to have been sequestered by revolutionary authorities in Yucatán, Mexico, in 1915, the Supreme Court of New 

Jersey said:

The motion to dismiss the complaint must be denied unless I am required to grant it because both plaintiff and defendant are citizens of Yucatan and the wrong complained of was committed there. I know of no such rule in New Jersey; and the cases cited by counsel from the New York courts, to which I have had access, do not sustain his position. 

Even the case of Dewitt v. Buchanan, 54 Barb. 31, cited in defendant's brief, implies that special reasons may justify an action by a non-resident plaintiff against a non-resident defendant for an injury happening abroad. Such a special reason exists in this case, where the proceeding is in rem to reach property attached in our jurisdiction. 

92 N.J.L. (1918) 38, 42, 43, 104 Atl. 450, 452.

There is no legal provision or principle of international law which says that the defendant who is resident in Austria is not

Suits by foreign sovereigns subject to Austrian jurisdiction on the ground that the object of the suit is immovable property situated abroad. 

Entscheidungen des österr. Obersten Gerichtshofes in Zivil- und Justizverwaltungssachen (1927), vol. IX, no. 53, pp. 134, 135; Annual Digest, 1927-28, Case No. 120. 

It is claimed that the plaintiff has not capacity to sue and that the action should be brought by the ambassador of the republic of Mexico, when appointed, in plaintiff's behalf. It was early settled in this state in the case of Republic of Mexico v. De Arangois, 11 How. Pr. 1, affd., 5 Duer. 634, that a foreign government may maintain an action in the New York state courts in the name of the state as an aggregate body. The court said: "In my opinion, the action can be maintained in the name of the republic as an aggregate body; and the modes of proceeding in cases of foreign corporations, and of other states of the Union may be resorted to for the regulations of the practice." In adopting this rule the court departed from the earlier 

English precedent as established by the case of the Columbian Government v. Rothschild, 1 Sim. 103. In the case of The 

Sapphire, 11 Wall. 164, the United States Circuit Court not only held that a suit could be maintained in our courts by the emperor of France to recover damages for an injury to a vessel which was the public property of the state, but that the right to recover was not affected by the deposition of the emperor during the pendency of the appeal. This was on the theory that the continuity of the state itself and its title to the property of the state is not affected by changes in the personnel of the government. The English law is now to the same effect. United 

States v. Wagner, L.R. (2 Ch. App. 582). 

State of Yucatan v. Argumedo et al., 92 Misc. (Sup. Ct., N.Y. Cy., spec. term, 1915) 547, 555-556, 157 N.Y. Supp. 219, 225-226.

In the course of his opinion in the case of Russian Socialist Federated Soviet Republic v. Cibrario, Judge Andrews of the New York

Court of Appeals said, in considering the question as to whether an existing foreign government might become a plaintiff in the New 

York courts: 

If recognized, undoubtedly it may. (Republic of Honduras v. De Soto, 112 N.Y. 310; United States of America v. Wagner, L.R. 2 Ch. App. 582; King of Spain v. Machado, 4 Russ. 560; 

King of Prussia v. Kuepper, 22 Mo. 550.) Conceivably this right may depend on treaty. But if no treaty to that effect exists the privilege rests upon the theory of international comity. 

This is so with regard to all foreign corporations. (Hollis v. 

Drew Theological Seminary, 95 N.Y. 166; Bank of Augusta v.

Earle, 13 Pet. 519; National Telephone Mfg. Co. v. DuBois, 165 

Mass. 117.

) Their power to sue may be regulated as is done by section 15 of our General Corporation Law (Cons. Laws, ch. 23). 

(Paul v. Virginia, 75 U.S. [8 Wall.] 168.) And except as limited by constitutional provisions the same thing is true of

those not citizens of our state. Much more true is it that the right of a foreign government to sue is likewise based upon the same consideration. Neither a natural person nor a corporation, ordinarily we would not recognize it as a proper party plaintiff. 

(W. & A. R.R. Co. v. Dalton Marble Works, 122 Ga. 774.) It represents, however, the general interests of the nation over which it has authority. We permit it to appear and protect those interests as a body analogous to one possessing corporate rights, but solely because of comity. (Republic of Honduras v. 

De Soto, 112 N.Y. 310; Hullet & Co. v. King of Spain, 1 Dow & 

Clark, 169, 175; Duke of Brunswick v. King of Hanover, 6 

Beav. 1, 37; The Sapphire, 78 U.S. [11 Wall.] 164.)

We reach the conclusion, therefore, that a foreign power brings an action in our courts not as a matter of right. Its power to do so is the creature of comity. 

235 N.Y. (1923) 255, 257, 262, 139 N.E. 259, 260, 262. 

That a foreign government may sue in our courts is elementary. That its ambassador, on its behalf, has authority to instruct that suit shall be begun, seems one of the simplest incidents of the ambassadorial office. Such authority has nowhere been doubted as matter of law, and it has long since become effective by practical construction in addition to other reasons. 

Russian Government v. Lehigh Valley R. Co., 293 Fed. 133, 135 (S.D.N.Y., 1919).

The Chancery Division of the British Supreme Court of Judicature dis missed an action brought by Her Majesty the Queen of Holland claiming a declaration that she was a creditor of the estate of one Visser who died at Amsterdam while domiciled in Holland. The court stated its opinion that there was a recognized rule that the British courts would not collect the taxes of foreign states for the benefit of the sovereigns of those states. 

In re Visser, H.M. the Queen of Holland (Married Woman) v. Drukker and Others, [1928] Ch. 877.

Supp. 782 (S.D.N.Y., 1937), in which the district judge defined the plaintiff as a "sovereign state, being the Upper Province of the Republic of Austria".

See the Harvard draft convention on "Competence of Courts in regard to Foreign States", part II of which relates to "States as Complainants in the Courts of Other States". Research in International Law, Harvard 

Law School (1932) 455, 493; 26 A.J.I.L. Supp. (1932) 455, 493.

Local law and proce- dure 

REGULATION OF PROCEDURE §123 

When the nationals of one state enter the territory of another state, whether for business or pleasure, they subject themselves to the laws of the latter state and although those laws and the rules of procedure in the courts may be wholly different from those which obtain in their home state, so long as such laws and rules are not below the standard generally obtaining in well-ordered states and are administered fairly and impartially, neither the aliens nor their governments have a right to complain.

In 1935 the Department of State wrote to the Governor of Maryland with reference to the trial of a German national in Leipzig, Germany, stating that "under international practice the officials of a foreign government may not with propriety intercede with another government in connection with judicial proceedings involving the latter and one of its own nationals". It was stated further that "Intercession by American officials is necessarily restricted to those cases in which American citizens or direct American interests are involved." 

The Acting Secretary of State (Carr) to Governor Nice, Dec. 21, 1935, MS. 

Department of State, file 862.00/3559. 

Christopher Stephano, a native American citizen of Greek parentage, was held for a short time in Greece in 1935 for court martial, the Greek Government having, it was alleged, grounds for suspecting him of complicity in a revolution. The American Legation in Athens was informed that the Department of State did not feel that it could properly intervene in behalf of American citizens who had contravened Greek law in respect to rebellion unless a grave miscarriage of justice would otherwise result. Later the Legation was instructed to make formal inquiry as to the charges against Stephano, bearing in mind that the Supreme Court of the United States had held that aliens domiciled in the United States owed this Government a local and temporary allegiance during the period of their residence and that they might become liable for prosecution for treason like a citizen. (Stephano was released by the Greek authorities on March 29, 1935.) 

Secretary Hull to the Legation in Greece, telegrams 12 and 15, Mar. 11 and 22, 1935, MS. Department of State, files 368.1121 Stephano, Christopher/2 and /7.

In the case of Ricaud et al. v. American Metal Company, Limited the Supreme Court said:

It is settled that the courts will take judicial notice of such recognition, as we have here of the Carranza Government, by the political department of our Government (Jones v. United States, 137 U.S. 202), and that the courts of one independent government will not sit in judgment on the validity of the acts of another done within its own territory (Underhill v. Hernandez, 168 U.S. 250, 253; American Banana Co. v. United Fruit Co., 213 U.S. 347; 

Oetjen v. Central Leather Co., ante, 297). This last rule, however, does not deprive the courts of jurisdiction once acquired over a case. It requires only that, when it is made to appear that the foreign government has acted in a given way on the subjectmatter of the litigation, the details of such action or the merit of the result cannot be questioned but must be accepted by our courts as a rule for their decision. To accept a ruling authority and to decide accordingly is not a surrender or abandonment of jurisdiction but is an exercise of it. It results that the title to the property in this case must be determined by the result of the action taken by the military authorities of Mexico 

246 U.S. (1918) 304, 309.

In the course of its opinion in the Salem claim (United States v. 

Egypt) the arbitral tribunal said: 

The American Government take it indeed already as a culpable violation of the rights of Salem that, according to Egyptian law, the public prosecutor who was charged with the investigation was likewise entitled to open the trial, combining thereby in his person the role of accuser, investigating magistrate and judge deciding on the opening of the trial; they assert that such a method of jurisdiction does not procure the accused with sufficient guarantees against a frivolous injury done to his reputation by public criminal proceedings due to an indictment for which no sufficient grounds of suspicion exist. The American Government relies [sic] upon principles of the Anglo- Saxon law according to which a special jury other than that judging the crime is charged with the decision if the accused shall be brought to trial or not. But in the different codes of criminal procedure in force with civilized nations this sort of guarantee is not so general that another method of preparing the trial could be designated as being below the standard of international law. The system whereby the trial is preceded by an investigation executed by a judge is under most codes of procedure an exception and only carried out when grave crimes are at stake; generally the investigation is left to the Parquet so that the accusing and the investigating magistrate coincide. 

It is true that even under the law of such countries where the rules of criminal procedure are based on the French system the result of the investigation is mostly examined by a judge before the trial is opened, but each lawyer conversant with the socalled continental system of criminal procedure knows well

that the examination of the file, in the case of minor delinquencies, is more or less formal. According to Egyptian law forgery of private documents is not regarded as a grave crime but as a minor offence (délit). Besides, with regard to the vast material which Ibrashy Bey gathered during the investigation, there is no reason to assume that a judge of the court at Mehalla would have refused a motion of the Parquet if this material had been presented for the purpose of a formal decision to open the trial. It cannot therefore be admitted that Salem was damaged by the absence of a rule purporting that a judge and not a member of the Parquet is competent to summon the accused for trial. 

Department of State, Salem Claim: Award of the Arbitral Tribunal 

(Arbitration Ser. 4(6), 1933) 56-57.

EXECUTION OF FOREIGN JUDGMENTS 

Freeman says in regard to the law of the United States in respect to foreign judgments:

The decisions in the United States upon the subject of foreign judgments are infrequent. The law on that subject must therefore be regarded as not well settled. 

Freeman, Treatise of the Law of Judgments (5th ed., by Tuttle, 1925), vol. III, p. 3047, §1484.

On the general subject of foreign judgments, see ibid., pp. 3040-3108, §§1482-1516; Beale, Treatise on the Conflict of Laws (1935), vol. II, pp. 1363-1440, §§429.1-462.2 On the effect of foreign judgments in England, see Dicey, Digest of the Law of England with Reference to the Conflict of Laws (5th ed., by Keith, London, 1932) 443-494.

Title X of the Code of Private International Law (the Bustamante 

Code), annexed to the convention on private international law adopted by the Sixth International Conference of American States at Habana in 1928, relates to the execution of judgments rendered by foreign courts. Articles 423 and 424 of chapter I of title X provide:

ARTICLE 423 

Every civil or contentious administrative judgment rendered in one of the contracting States shall have force and may be executed in the others if it combines the following conditions: 

1. That the judge or the court which has rendered it have competence to take cognizance of the matter and to pass judgment upon it, in accordance with the rules of this Code. 

2. That the parties have been summoned for the trial either personally or through their legal representative; 

3. That the judgment does not conflict with the public policy or the public laws of the country in which its execution is sought; 

4. That it is executory in the State in which it was rendered. 

5. That it be authoritatively translated by an official functionary or interpreter of the State in which it is to be executed, if the language employed in the latter is different. 

6. That the document in which it is contained fulfils the requirements necessary in order to be considered as authentic in the State from which it proceeds, and those which the legislation of the State in which the execution of the judgment is sought requires for authenticity. 

ARTICLE 424 

The execution of the judgment should be requested from a competent judge or tribunal in order to carry it into effect, after complying with the formalities required by the internal legislation.

Articles 436 and 437 of chapter III of the same title provide: 

ARTICLE 436 

No contracting State shall execute the judgments rendered in one of the others in penal matters in respect to the sanctions of that class which they impose. 

ARTICLE 437 

They may, however, execute the said judgments in respect to civil liability and the effects thereof upon the property of the convicted person if they have been rendered by a competent judge or tribunal in accordance with this Code and upon a hearing of the interested party and if the other conditions of form and procedure established by the first chapter of this title have been complied with.

Sixth International Conference of American States: Final Act (Habana, 

1928) 79, 81. The convention on private international law of 1928 has been ratified by the following countries: Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Costa 

Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, and Venezuela.

In 1907 the Department of State said thatthere is no provision in the treaties between the United States and Mexico which requires the latter to accept as binding and conclusive the judgments of the courts of the United States. 

Questions of this nature are governed by international comity and are dependent upon the view taken by the Mexican courts of the comity existing between the United States and Mexico. 

The general principle of international private law applicable to your case is that a foreign state claims and exercises the right to examine judgments for three causes: (1) to see if the court has jurisdiction; (2) to see if defendant was summoned; (3) to see if the proceedings were vitiated by fraud. For fuller information you are referred to Hilton v. Guyot, 159 U.S., 113.

In this connection it may not be improper to direct to your attention the fact that it would appear that the laws of Germany and the United States are not in accord in other particulars than the one to which you have referred. As an illustration of this, there might be cited the recent suit instituted in the German courts by American policyholders against certain German insurance companies, which had issued large policies in San Francisco prior to the destruction of that city by earthquake and fire. The extent to which foreign judgments are given faith and credit in the United States is determined by decisions of the courts, which apply the principle of the comity of nations. There are no statutes governing the matter in this country. Courts in the 

United States allow judgments rendered in a foreign country the same effect as the courts of that country allow judgments rendered in the United States. One of the leading cases on the subject is the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in Hilton v. Guyot, 159 U.S. 113 [202-203]. The opinion in that case summarizes the applicable rule as follows: " we are satisfied that, where there has been opportunity for a full and fair trial abroad before a court of competent jurisdiction, conducting the trial upon regular proceedings, after due citation or voluntary appearance of the defendant, and under a system of jurisprudence likely to secure an impartial administration of justice between the citizens of its own country and those of other countries, and there is nothing to show either prejudice in the court, or in the system of laws under which it was sitting, or fraud in procuring the judgment, or any other special reason why the comity of this nation should not allow it full effect, the merits of the case should not, in an action brought in this country upon the judgment, be tried afresh, as on a new trial or an appeal, upon the mere assertion of the party that the judgment was erroneous in law or in fact. The defendants, therefore, cannot be permitted, upon that general ground, to contest the validity or the effect of the judgment sued on." 

Attorney General Cummings to Secretary Hull, Nov. 30, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 844D.04600/2.

In the case of Ingenohl v. Olsen & Company, Inc., summarized ante $116, the Supreme Court of the United States reversed a judgment of the Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands refusing to enforce a judgment for costs obtained in the British colony of Hong Kong on the ground that §311(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure provided that a judgment against a person might "be repelled by evidence of a clear mistake of law or fact" and that the judgment in question showed such a mistake. In reversing the decision the Court pointed out that the judgment was "obtained after a fair trial before a court

In the case of Robert D. Johnston v. Compagnie Générale Transatlantique the defendant set up as a defense an adjudication in a French court in favor of it upon the same cause of action, in a suit brought by the plaintiff, and established on trial that the French judgment was the final judgment on the merits of a court of competent jurisdiction. The New York Court of Appeals reversed a judgment for the plaintiff and refused to follow the doctrine expressed in the case of Hilton v. Guyot, 159 U.S. (1895) 113, that on principles of comity a French judgment is not conclusive when sued on in the United States, since by French law no foreign judgment can be rendered executory in that country without a review of the judgment on the merits. The court of appeals said:

When the whole of the facts appear to have been inquired into by the French courts, judicially, honestly and with full jurisdiction and with the intention to arrive at the right conclusion, and when they have heard the facts and come to a conclusion, it should no longer be open to the party invoking the foreign court against a resident of France to ask the American court to sit as a court of appeal from that which gave the judgment. 

The court pointed out however that the instant case could be distinguished from the case of Hilton v. Guyot on the ground that, in the former, the judgment in the French court had been for the defendant, whereas, in the latter, the judgment in the French court had been for the plaintiff. The court said:

The law of the State of New York remains unchanged, and the French judgment should be given full faith and credit. 

242 N.Y. (1926) 381, 387, 388, 152 N.E. 121, 123, 124.

In an action on a money judgment recovered by the plaintiffs in the Province of Quebec, Canada, against the defendants, the appellate division of the Supreme Court of New York (3d Dept.) reversed the order of the lower court and granted the plaintiffs' motion for judgment on the pleadings, saying:

The general rule in this State is settled as follows: A judgment recovered in a foreign country, when sued upon in the courts of this State, is conclusive so far as to preclude a retrial of the merits of the case, subject, however, to certain well-recognized exceptions, namely, where the judgment is tainted with fraud, or with an offense against the public policy of the State, or the foreign court had not jurisdiction. (Lazier v. Westcott, 26 N.Y. 

146 [82 Am. Dec. 404]; Dunstan v. Higgins, 138 id. 70 [33 N.E. 

729; 20 L.R.A. 668; 34 Am. St. Rep. 431].)

The court expressed the opinion that this rule must be applied to the case in question and that, on the authority of Robert D. Johnston v. Compagnie Générale Transatlantique, the proposition of the defendant that the judgment was only prima facie evidence because the courts of Quebec did not reciprocate as to judgments of the State of New York, was in conflict with the policy and law of the latter State. 

This judgment was affirmed by the New York Court of Appeals.

In the case of Traders' Trust Co. v. Davidson the plaintiff, a Manitoba corporation, brought an action against a citizen and resident of the city of St. Paul, Minnesota, on a personal judgment obtained by it against the defendant in a court in Manitoba. The plaintiff had been appointed liquidator of an insolvent Manitoba corporation by a court in that Province. The defendant was a shareholder in the insolvent corporation. The judgment in question had been obtained in winding up proceedings in which the defendant was never served with a summons or other process within Manitoba and had never voluntarily appeared in the action. The plaintiff contended that the defendant had appeared in those proceedings by giving a proxy to one Fisher to vote at a shareholders' meeting against contesting the winding-up proceedings and that such appearance gave the court jurisdiction to render a personal judgment against him for the amount claimed to be due from him as a "contributory" to the assets of the company. The Supreme Court of Minnesota rejected this contention. 

It also held that the appointment by the Manitoba court of counsel to represent the shareholders of the insolvent corporation did not give one Hamilton authority to make a personal appearance for a shareholder over whose person it had no jurisdiction; that the plaintiff had failed to prove the existence of any law in the Province of Manitoba making the act of becoming a shareholder therein operate as a consent that the courts, by service on the corporation or on some designated public official, might acquire jurisdiction to render a judgment in personam against such shareholder; and that the plaintiff had failed to prove any law authorizing a judgment in personam against a non-resident who did not appear in the action and upon whom no process was served within the jurisdiction of the court. The court therefore, on the ground that the Manitoba court was without jurisdiction to render a judgment in personam against the defendant, reversed the judgment of the lower court for the plaintiff. 

146 Minn. (1920) 224, 178 N.W. 735.

In an action brought on a judgment recovered by the plaintiffs against the defendant in a court in Jalisco, Mexico, it appeared that summons in the Mexican action had been served on the defendant personally in Pennsylvania, and that he had appeared in that action through his attorney and presented a counter claim. The United 

States District Court gave judgment for the plaintiffs saying that the Mexican court had jurisdiction of the subject-matter involved (certain waters in the State of Jalisco); that it also acquired jurisdiction of the defendant by his own voluntary act; and that there being no fraud alleged in respect to the Mexican judgment, except in particulars contested in and considered by the Mexican courts, the defense was insufficient. 

Cruz et al. v. O'Boyle, 197 Fed. 824 (M.D. Pa., 1912).

In Skandinaviska Granit Aktiebolaget v. Weiss a Swedish corpo ration had instituted arbitration proceedings in Sweden against the defendant in which it had prevailed, and upon the arbitration report a judgment had been entered in a court of general jurisdiction in Sweden in favor of the plaintiff. The contract under which the dispute arose had been entered into in Sweden and provided that any dispute arising thereunder was to be settled by arbitration and without appeal. The plaintiff had served notice on the defendant, demanding arbitration, appointing its arbitrator, and demanding that

at t oft atr ng the defendant select an arbitrator. This the defendant had failed to do, and an officer of the Swedish Government had appointed an arbitrator to act in his behalf. The plaintiff brought action on the 

Swedish judgment in the courts of New York. When the agreement was made, during the time of the arbitration proceedings, and when the notice was served on the defendant, an American citizen, he was a resident of New York State. The appellate division of the Supreme 

Court of New York (2d Dept.) affirmed the judgment and order granting defendant's motion for judgment on the pleadings. The court said thatpersonal liability as against this defendant cannot be recognized in this State upon a judgment of a court of Sweden, founded upon a report of an arbitration tribunal in Sweden, even though the laws of Sweden authorize service in arbitration proceedings to be made without Sweden and in the city of New York by the mere serving of a notice upon the defendant that the arbitration proceeding is about to proceed to pass judgment upon the matters in controversy, and that, therefore, an arbitrator should be appointed by the one upon whom notice is thus served. 

The question herein involved is not whether the agreement to arbitrate in Sweden is enforcible as against this defendant or whether the defendant could be compelled to proceed to Sweden to arbitrate. There is no claim of jurisdiction in rem. 

The only question is whether the court of Sweden, directly or through the arbitration proceedings, acquired jurisdiction in personam over the defendant. Neither the process of the Swedish arbitration tribunal nor the court of Sweden had any such extra-territorial effect. 

226 App. Div. 56, 60 (1929), 234 N.Y. Supp. 202, 208.

In the case of Harrison et al. v. Triplex Gold Mines, Limited et al., the court said: fault In any case to justify setting aside a decree for fraud, it must appear that the fraud practised, unmixed with any Fraud or negligence of the party complaining, prevented him from making a full and fair defense, and that the fraud complained of was not involved in, or presented to, the court of first instance either at the original' trial or in a petition for review. This rule is universal.

The court in this case found that the plaintiffs had already, through a petition for review in Canadian courts, set forth the fraud, perjury, etc., on the basis of which United States courts had been asked to intervene and that the petition for review had been contested and denied.
