CHAPTER VI—NATIONAL JURISDICTION 

Judgments in personam In the cases of The W. Talbot Dodge and United States v. 789 

Packages of Whisky et al., involving libels in rem by the United 

States, the United States District Court held that a decree of the Supreme Court of the Bahama Islands and the pretended sale thereunder of the schooner W. Talbot Dodge to the claimant were void and of no effect by reason of the fraud and deception practiced on the court in the proceedings. The court said that, although the general rule was that an in rem decree of a foreign court in admiralty, having jurisdiction, was binding and conclusive upon all persons and in all countries, such a decree was open to collateral attack by a stranger to the record if it could be shown that fraud was practiced on the court in obtaining it. 

15 F. (2d) 459 (S.D.N.Y., 1926).

In Swift et al. v. David an effort was made to recover the sum of $77,500 on a contract of sale of certain shares of stock. Plaintiffs in error asked leave to file a supplemental answer showing that, in an action instituted by them in the courts of British Columbia against defendant in error, the latter had recovered judgment against them on a counter claim for the sum of $77,500, for the payment of which they had given security to the satisfaction of the registrar. The circuit court of appeals affirmed the judgment of the lower court denying the application for leave to file the supplemental answer, saying that a judgment in personam in a foreign court, while it constitutes a good cause of action in a domestic court, does not merge the original cause of action or extinguish the original contract debt and is no bar to an action thereon in a domestic court unless it has been paid or satisfied. The fact that security had been given for the payment of the judgment of the Canadian court, it was said, created no exception to the rule, since that undertaking was merely a supersedeas bond on appeal and was not security for or satisfaction of the judgment. 

181 Fed. 828 (C.C.A. 9th, 1910).

In the case of Banco Minero v. Ross et al. the plaintiffs (defendants in error) brought action in Texas against the defendant bank of Chihuahua, Mexico (plaintiff in error) for the conversion of a deposit made by them with the bank to be delivered to one Terrazas upon transfer by the latter of certain land which he had contracted to sell to the plaintiffs. After the contract had been concluded it was discovered that Terrazas did not have title to the land in question. Prior to the institution of the suit in Texas Terrazas brought suit in the State of Chihuahua, Mexico, against the plaintiffs for specific performance of the contract. One of the plaintiffs was

51 fe Sed Tis Is fis served by publication and did not appear. A default judgment was taken against him. The other plaintiff appeared by attorney and attempted to defend the action. Judgment was rendered by the 

Mexican court against both of the plaintiffs in the American suit. 

The defendant bank was not a party to the suit or the judgment rendered, but subsequent to the judgment the judge issued an order to that bank that it pay over to Terrazas the money on deposit which had been delivered to it by the plaintiffs. The Supreme Court of 

Texas affirmed a judgment for the plaintiffs. It held that, since the 

Mexican action was essentially in personam, the judgment as to the plaintiff on whom service was rendered by publication was void. 

The court further held that, although the Mexican court had jurisdiction over the plaintiff who appeared as defendant in the suit, it was necessary for the recognition of a foreign judgment that an opportunity for a full and fair trial be afforded and that this meant not a summary proceeding, though sanctioned by the law of the forum, but an opportunity to be heard upon the proof where questions of fact were involved and to have the case considered by an unprejudiced court. The court found that the trial in the Mexican court was wanting in these essential elements on the ground that the defendant in that suit was denied the right to present his defense and that he was denied an appeal on what seemed to it a frivolous ground, namely, the omission to affix a stamp to the document of appeal. 

106 Tex. (1915) 522, 172 S.W. 711.

LETTERS ROGATORY 

$125 The question of the validity of the execution and the legal sufficiency of documents executed in foreign countries for use in judicial In general proceedings in the United States is one for the determination by the competent judicial authorities of the jurisdiction where the proceedings are held, subject to applicable laws and proceedings of that jurisdiction. The functions of the Department of State with respect to such documents are limited to the notarial acts performed by American diplomatic and consular representatives in connection with the execution or transmission thereof. The functions of the Department with respect to documents issued in the United States for use in judicial proceedings in foreign countries are usually limited to the attesting of the seals of Federal or State authorities affixed to the documents.

In 1925 certain attorneys in Chicago having forwarded to the Department of State a certified copy of a "Commission to take testi-

Letters roga- mony orally, by depositions or by letters rogatory in England and the British Empire" for transmission to the American Ambassador in London, the Department pointed out the differences between commissions to take testimony and letters rogatory, as follows: tory; com- missions to take testi- mony

Authority of consuls

It appears that you may contemplate that the document transmitted with your letter can be used as a commission and as letters rogatory under the authority of which testimony may be taken. The Department understands that it is not permissible to provide in one document for the taking of testimony by both methods. It would seem that the document should be issued either as a commission to take testimony or as letters rogatory. 

Your attention is invited to the differences which exist between commissions to take testimony and letters rogatory. It is understood that commissions to take testimony in a foreign country are usually addressed by a court in the United States to the appropriate American consular officer at the place where the testimony is to be taken and are executed by him. Letters rogatory are addressed by the courts of the United States to the appropriate judicial authority in the country in which the testimony is to be taken, and are executed by the appropriate court or under its direction. The question as to which of these methods of obtaining testimony should be used is a matter for determination by the court desiring to have the testimony taken, having in mind that consular officers of the United States have no authority to compel witnesses to appear and give testimony, or to produce documents which they may have in their possession. 

It is believed that commissions to take testimony and letters rogatory should state definitely the place at which they are to be executed as it is understood that it is not in accord with the usual practice to have them executed in part in one place and completed in another. In this connection you are referred to the following authorities: Moore's International Law Digest, Vol. 

2, pages 104-133; Revised Statutes of the United States, Secs. 

866 and 875; Bouvier's Law Dictionary, Rawles' Third Revision, Vol. 2, page 1935; 13 Cyc. 847 (note), 892; 6 Encyclopedia Pleading and Practice, 497; Union Square Bank v. Reichmann, 9 App. 

Div. (N.Y.) 596, 41 N.Y. Supp. 602; The Westminister, 96 Fed. 766. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Messrs. Parkinson and Lane, Aug. 13, 1925, MS. Department of State, file 081.41/329. 66 It is understood that a commission to take testimony in a foreign country is usually addressed by the court in the United States to the appropriate American consular officer or officers, usually at the place where the testimony is to be taken and is executed by the designated officer, provided there is no objection thereto by the authorities of the country where the officer is stationed. Letters rogatory are usually addressed by a competent court in the United States 'to the appropriate judicial authority' in the country in which the testimony is to be taken, and are executed by the court or under its direction. "If such a commission or letters rogatory is accompanied by a list of interrogatories or cross interrogatories, the commissioner or the court,

Ta as the case may be, will (presumably in accordance with the usual procedure) propound to the witnesses the questions contained therein. If, on the other hand, the commission or the letters rogatory is unaccompanied by a list of interrogatories, it is presumed that the interrogatories or cross interrogatories, et cetera, will be propounded orally either by the parties to the action or by the attorneys in the case, since it might not be known in advance what information or testimony it may be necessary to bring or to be brought out. The printed instructions in the commission or in the letters rogatory, or any special instructions of the issuing court, will doubtless be observed by the executing authority. "If the court's instructions as contained (in printed form generally) either in a commission or in letters rogatory, are deemed by the executing court or the commissioner to be insufficient in any particular case, it is believed that such court or authority, i.e., the court or the commissioner, will endeavor, in so far as possible, to follow such additional instructions as the issuing court may deem it appropriate to insert." 

The Chief of the Division of Foreign Service Administration (Hengstler) 

to Mr. N. Roy Beller, Feb. 18, 1932, MS. Department of State, file 811.04500/23.

On March 25, 1924 the following circular note was addressed by the Department of State to the chiefs of missions in Washington: 

While the Department of State understands that certain for- Circular to eign countries require the presentation of letters rogatory Diplomatic through the foreign office, this practice does not obtain in the Corps, 1924 United States. No duty or authority to have letters rogatory executed is by law imposed on the Executive Branch of the Government of the United States. In some States of the Union laws have been enacted requiring letters rogatory to be presented to the State court by the appropriate consular officer of the country in which the testimony is to be used. The Department of State is of the opinion that this practice, if followed generally with respect to both Federal and State courts, will cause letters rogatory issuing from foreign courts to be more expeditiously executed.

On July 15, 1937 the Department of State made the following observations in respect to certain letters rogatory received from the Commissioner of Patents to be forwarded to the appropriate judicial authority in Germany to take testimony in connection with cancelation proceedings pending in the United States Patent Office:

It has been noted that there is included under the seal of the United States Patent Office a certificate in blank to be executed by an American consular officer, which provides that the direct interrogatories are to be reduced to writing by the consular officer or in his presence. When forwarded to the Department, letters rogatory are sent and received through the diplomatic channel and they do not, therefore, ordinarily come to the attention of any consular officer. As in the case in question, they are usually addressed to the appropriate judicial authority of the country from which testimony is desired. This would seem to preclude any participation by consular officers in the proceedings.

en ding The Department suggested that the blank certificate in question as well as any other references to consular participation in the proceedings should be deleted.

On May 6, 1922 the Department of State transmitted to the Amer- Consular ican Consul General in Tientsin the following memorandum prepared by the Office of the Solicitor for the Department concerning fees chargeable for the taking of depositions and the execution of letters rogatory by American consular officers:

It is evident that since by letters rogatory is meant a formal communication from a court in which an action is pending to a foreign court requesting that the testimony of a witness residing in such foreign jurisdiction be taken under the direction of the court addressed and transmitted to the court making the request, a consular officer is without authority to execute them except in those countries where by treaty and by statute he is permitted to exercise judicial powers and it is evident that such a construction should be placed upon the language used in Section 8 of the Act of April 5, 1906 [34 Stat. 99, 101]. It would seem, therefore, that as stated by the Consulate General, item 39 of the Consular Tariff would have no application but the Tariff Consular Court fees would govern the charges to be made in executing letters rogatory. Considering the request of the Consulate General that the Department rule that in the taking of depositions de bene esse and in the execution of letters rogatory, item 39 should apply, it may be stated that there is apparently no authority for the 

Department to make such a ruling.

In the course of its opinion in the case of Decauville Auto. Co. v. 

Metropolitan Bank, the appellate division of the Supreme Court of 

New York (1st Dept.) said:

It would seem from the decision in Froude v. Froude, (3 T. & C. 79) that the rule was formerly that the courts of France will not enforce the execution of commissions to take the depositions of witnesses in that country, but that they probably do act under letters rogatory; and it appears by affidavit, and is not controverted, that the courts of France are still without authority to compel witnesses to testify under a commission issued from a foreign jurisdiction. In such cases courts have inherent power to issue letters rogatory, and we now have express statutory authority under section 913 of the Code of Civil Procedure to thus obtain the testimony of witnesses where their testimony cannot be obtained by commission; but owing to the fact that the law of the foreign jurisdiction then governs with respect to the taking of the testimony, the remedy is only resorted to in cases of necessity. (Union Square Bank v. Reichmann, 9 App. Div. 596 [41 N.Y. Supp. 602]; 6 Ency. Pl. & Pr. supra [497, 498]; 13 

Cyc. supra [892].)

With respect to the procedure in the matter of letters rogatory to take the testimony of witnesses in Mexico and as to whether the Department of State would transmit letters rogatory without written interrogatories annexed, the Department stated:

This Department, as an act of courtesy to the courts in the United States, transmits through the diplomatic officers of the United States, letters rogatory issued by such courts to foreign courts. Such letters rogatory are sent by the American diplomatic officers to the ministers for foreign affairs unofficially or informally, for such action thereon as the laws of the foreign countries will permit. Such letters rogatory are not examined by the Department. Therefore, if a letter rogatory issued by a court in the United States to a court in Mexico without written interrogatories annexed, were sent to this Department, it would forward the letter rogatory to the American Ambassador at Mexico City and instruct him to request the Mexican Foreign Office to obtain such action thereon as would be permissible under the law and procedure in Mexico. The Department is unable to say whether such a letter rogatory would be executed by the Mexican court or not.

I may add that while American consuls in Mexico cannot execute letters rogatory, the Department has no record that the Mexican Government has ever objected to their taking depositions in Mexico in civil cases. The question of the acceptability of such testimony in this country would, however, depend upon the laws of the State in which the testimony is to be used. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Wilson) to Messrs. Hyman and Campbell, Apr. 27, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 13670/1.

In the case of In re Smith the Surrogate's Court of New York County granted an application for letters rogatory to take the testimony of the District Court Judge of the Royal Court at Berlin, who was alleged to have approved the adoption by an intestate of a young German girl who was making certain claims to the intestate's estate. 

In granting the application the court remarked that it ought not to be held at that stage that none of the desired testimony of the German judge was material or competent and that it could not assume that the latter would allow himself to be interrogated as to matters of law or matters irrelevant to the issue before the American court or incompetent under the New York laws of evidence. The court also remarked that the German judge might regard the letters rogatory as extra modum and that, if he so thought, he was not obliged ex comitate to violate his own conception of the judicial proprieties or to compro-

mise his judicial dignity. The court stated further that, though some of the interrogatories to be propounded to the German judge might relate to matters not evidentiary under the lex fori, this was not a reason to deny the application altogether, since the German judge might testify to matters competent or material under the lex fori. 

79 Misc. (1913) 77, 139 N.Y. Supp. 522.

In De Villeneuve v. Morning Journal Assn. a motion for letters rogatory was granted by the United States District Court. The court stated that the statutes of the United States conferred no general power upon the courts to issue letters rogatory and that section 875 of the Revised Statutes treated of letters issued in cases in which the United States was a party or had an interest and, while this had been thought evidence of an intention on the part of Congress to restrict the inherent power of the court, it was of the opinion that, since the courts executed letters rogatory from foreign countries and since this method of obtaining testimony was most necessary in countries which refused to compel the attendance of witnesses under commissions, it ought not to be supposed that Congress intended to limit the power of the court. 

In granting the motion the court stated further that the case in question was one in which a number of witnesses were likely to be unwilling and that the examination should be oral and not upon written interrogatories. 

206 Fed. 70 (S.D.N.Y., 1913).

In the case of Martinelli, petitioner, the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts sustained exceptions to the granting of a petition for letters rogatory by the superior court for taking the testimony of witnesses in Italy, to be used in hearings on proceedings brought and pending before the Industrial Accident Board of Massachusetts for the recovery of payments under the Workmen's Compensation Act.

The court stated that it had always been recognized that the power to issue letters rogatory could be exercised only in aid of a cause actually pending in the court issuing the letters. The court thus defined the nature of the issuance of letters rogatory: 

It is in form a request to a court of a foreign jurisdiction asking as matter of comity that that court will take the testimony of a witness or witnesses within its jurisdiction and transmit the same to the court making the request, for its aid in the doing of justice as to a cause before it. The matter is not dependent upon statute, but rests upon the international good will toward each other by which courts of civil countries are actuated. Anonymous, 59 N.Y. 313, 314. State v. Bourne, 21 Ore. 218 [27 Pac. 

1048]. Nelson v. United States, Pet. C.C. 235 [Fed. Cas. No. 10, 116]. 1 Greenl. Ev. §320.

It declared that it was not within the power of a court, even of general jurisdiction, to issue letters rogatory to obtain testimony to be used before a tribunal over whose procedure and trials it was given no authority until the case itself might be brought before it for review and that, therefore, it was not within the authority of the superior court to procure evidence for use before a tribunal over whose proceedings it had no more intimate supervisory power than it had over the 

Industrial Accident Board. The court added: 

It is urged that power is conferred by that part of St. 1912, c. 571, §8, which provides that, "The board or any member thereof shall have the power to subpoena witnesses, administer oaths, and to examine such parts of the books and records of the parties to a proceeding as relate to questions in dispute. The Superior 

Court shall have power to enforce by proper proceedings the provisions of this section relating to the attendance and testimony of witnesses and the examination of books and records." These words confer no power to issue letters rogatory or to issue commissions to take depositions. It plainly goes no further than to authorize the court to compel the attendance of witnesses within its jurisdiction and to deal with those who refuse to appear and testify. It would have been a simple matter for the Legislature to have conferred upon the Superior Court the additional power here invoked. 

219 Mass. (1914) 58, 59, 60, 106 N.E. 557, 558.

The Supreme Court of Michigan set aside an award of the commission of the Department of Labor and Industry pursuant to the Workmen's Compensation Act, it appearing that the commission had issued letters rogatory to the American Consul General at Lisbon, Portugal, authorizing and requesting him to take the responses of certain witnesses to interrogatories and that the letters rogatory had been returned with the responses of the witnesses taken and were followed by hearing, appeal, and award. The Supreme Court held that the commission had no authority to issue letters rogatory since it was not a court.

Carvalho et al. v. Cass Putnam Hotel Company, et al., 239 Mich. (1927) 

508, 215 N.W. 21.

Rule 28(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, adopted by the Supreme Court pursuant to the act of Congress of June 19, 1934 Federal rules (48 Stat. 1064), provides:

A commission or letters rogatory shall be issued only when necessary or convenient, on application and notice, and on such terms and with such directions as are just and appropriate. 

Officers may be designated in notices or commissions either by name or descriptive title and letters rogatory may be addressed 

"To the Appropriate Judicial Authority in [here name the country]". 

On November 22, 1935 notes were exchanged between the United States and the Soviet Government relating to the execution of letters Agreement rogatory. The American Ambassador in Russia in his note said in part: 

Letters rogatory issuing out of courts in foreign countries are executed in the United States in accordance with the pertinent provisions of the laws of the United States, or of the State or Territory thereof in which resides the person whose testimony is desired, and in compliance with the rules of the executing court. 

The Government of the United States is, accordingly, not in a position to set forth with precision what may be the requirements of a particular court in the United States at a given time in respect of the execution of letters rogatory issuing out of a court in a foreign country.

It is understood that it is the practice of American courts of appropriate jurisdiction to execute letters rogatory issuing out of foreign courts, if properly prepared and presented, and that no difficulty is likely to be encountered by Soviet courts in obtaining the execution of letters rogatory by American courts. However, should a Soviet court encounter such difficulty, my Government would, it is understood, upon its attention being drawn thereto through the diplomatic channel, consider what steps it might appropriately take with a view to eliminating the difficulty. 

After a reference to the fact that the executive branch of the United States Government does not make it a practice to act as a channel for the transmission of letters rogatory issuing out of courts in foreign with Soviet

Government

countries and addressed to courts in the United States, the Ambassador made the following suggestions which he stated the Soviet courts might find it advantageous to observe in preparing letters rogatory for execution in the United States: (a) The letters rogatory should be addressed by name to the court in the United States which is to execute them, if that is known; or they may be addressed "To any court of competent jurisdiction in the United States". (b) Requests for the execution of letters rogatory should specify the name of the court out of which they issue, as well as the names of the parties to the action in which the testimony called for by the letters rogatory is desired. (c) Requests for the execution of letters rogatory should be accompanied by English translations thereof and of accompanying documents such as exhibits and any instructions to the executing court.

Enclosed with the Ambassador's note were excerpts from sections 653, 701-704, title 28, of the United States Code. 

The People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs in his note outlined as follows the procedure according to which the Soviet courts will accept for execution letters rogatory of United States courts: 

1. Letters rogatory issuing out of courts in the United States for execution in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics should be delivered through the diplomatic channel, i.e., through the 

American Embassy in Moscow, and the People's Commissariat for Foreign Affairs, to the appropriate court in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and, when executed, they will be returned through the same channel. 

2. Letters rogatory issued out of a court in the United States forwarded for execution in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics should be addressed to the Supreme Court of that constituent republic which is competent to execute such letters rogatory. In case the exact title of the Soviet court is unknown to the court which issues the letters rogatory, the letters rogatory may be addressed "to the competent court of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics". 

3. Requests of courts in the United States for the execution of letters rogatory addressed to courts in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics should specify the name of the court out of which they issue, as well as the names of the parties to the action in which the testimony called for by the letters rogatory is desired. 

4. Requests for the execution of letters rogatory should be accompanied by Russian translations of all the basic documents, such as the interrogatories themselves and any accompanying instructions to the executing court. It will be sufficient in the case of documents of secondary importance to forward short summaries of their contents in the Russian language. 

5. Depending upon the nature of the letters rogatory, a fee varying from five to ten dollars ($5 to $10) will be charged for the execution of letters rogatory issued out of courts in the United

States. In addition to this fee, remuneration for the services of experts as well as for the travelling expenses and expenditure of time by witnesses may be requested in individual cases, such remuneration to be based on rates current at the time as fixed by law or regulation then existing. Payment of fees and other possible expenses of the nature referred to above will be effected in dollars by the American Embassy at Moscow upon receipt from the People's Commissariat for Foreign Affairs of the executed letters rogatory and an appropriate statement setting forth the amount due, and the fees and services covered thereby. 

6. The court in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics by which the letters rogatory are executed shall give effect to them in accordance with the procedural rules obtaining in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

7. The court issuing the letters rogatory shall, if it so desires, be informed of the date and place where the proceedings will take place, in order that the interested parties or their legal representatives may, if they desire, be present. 

8. The execution of letters rogatory issuing out of a court in the United States may be refused in whole or in part, if the appropriate authorities in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics consider that the execution thereof would affect its sovereignty or safety. In returning letters rogatory unexecuted in whole or in part, the authorities refusing such execution shall affix under seal to the letters rogatory a written statement of the reasons for such refusal. 

9. Any difficulties which may arise in connection with a request by a court in the United States for the execution of letters rogatory in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics shall be settled through the diplomatic channel.

While letters rogatory must be transmitted through the diplomatic channel, American diplomatic and consular institutions may, in connection with cases pending in the United States courts, serve juridical documents on American nationals within the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, without the application of coercion. 

Ex. Agree. Ser. 83. 

In 1909 United States Circuit Judge William W. Morrow transmitted to the Department a copy of a reply which he had made to an application by the Consul General of Mexico to take the testimony of a witness in California for use in a criminal case in Mexico. Judge 

Morrow said:

As at present advised I do not think I have authority to direct the Commissioner to require the attendance of a witness to give his deposition in a criminal case.

After a reference to sections 4071 and 875 of the Revised Statutes he said: Issued in foreign countries 

Furthermore, Article 6 of the Amendments to the Constitution Criminal pro of the United States provides that: "In all criminal prosecutions ceedings the accused shall enjoy the right .. to be confronted with the

Netherlands; convention of 

1905 on civil procedure witnesses against him." Testimony obtained by letters rogatory in foreign countries would not therefore be admitted in evidence against the accused in a criminal case in this country, and it would seem to follow that the courts of the United States would not authorize the taking of a deposition to be used in a criminal case in a foreign country unless such authority was expressly conferred by a statute.

He referred to a case discussed in II Moore's Digest 111, and said: 

This action of our Department of State in this case indicates that it approved the opinion of the Attorney General of Pennsylvania in the case mentioned, and while such action is not binding upon the courts it is of persuasive force. I am, therefore, of the opinion that it is not competent for a court of the United States to direct a United States Commissioner to take the testimony of witnesses by letters rogatory where the testimony is to be used in a criminal case in a foreign country. 

If, however, you are of the opinion that I am in error in this view of the law, I would be pleased to hear from you further upon the subject. 

Judge William W. Morrow to Secretary Knox, Apr. 12, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 19147/-1.

The American representative at the Conference on Counterfeiting held in Geneva in 1929 requested instructions with regard to the exemption of letters rogatory from the payment of taxes or expenses in the convention for the suppression of counterfeiting currency which was being drafted. The Department of State replied that it was not clear that statutes of the United States made provision for the execution of letters rogatory in criminal proceedings and that, moreover, the provisions of the sixth amendment to the Constitution prevented the use in criminal proceedings in the United States of testimony obtained by letters rogatory. The Government of the United 

States would not therefore desire, it was stated, to agree to commitments by treaty for the execution of letters rogatory on the question of fees and expenses or otherwise. 

Secretary Stimson to Mr. Hugh Wilson, telegram 5, Apr. 18, 1929, MS. 

Department of State, file 551.58B1/47.

It is stated in the note from the Netherlands Foreign Office, dated February 7, 1922, a copy of which is enclosed in the Legation's despatch of February 10, that under the Netherlands statutes witnesses cannot be compelled to appear before the local courts in response to letters rogatory issued in a foreign country unless the foreign country is a party to the convention concluded at The Hague on July 17, 1905, which deals in part with the execution of letters rogatory and that, as the United States is not a party to this convention, the Netherlands Government has been unable to compel the appearance of the witnesses whose testimony was desired by the District Court of Wisconsin.

From a translation of the convention concluded at The Hague on July 17, 1905, it appears that Chapters I, III, IV and V deal, respectively, with the communication of judicial and non-judicial papers; with the filing by alien litigants having no domicile or residence in the country, of bonds as security for the payment of the expenses and the execution of a judgment; with suits in forma pauperis; and with imprisonment as a method of execution in civil or commercial cases.

These matters are dealt with very largely by the state courts in the United States and the legislation concerning these subjects is not uniform. Furthermore, it may be observed that Congress has not undertaken to pass legislation dealing with these matters, whereas sections 875 and 4071 to 4074, inclusive, of the Revised Statutes as amended have been passed dealing with letters rogatory. 

Under the circumstances this Government does not consider that it is in a position to adhere to the provisions of the convention concluded at The Hague on July 17, 1905, and thereby be in a position to take advantage of the Dutch law of June 12, 1909, the Netherlands statute carrying the convention into effect. 

It may be observed that letters rogatory received from the Netherlands in cases in which the Government of the Netherlands is a party or has an interest are executed by the courts in the United States, but that under the Netherlands statutes witnesses cannot be compelled to appear before the local courts in response to letters rogatory issued in the United States.

You are instructed to inform the Foreign Office of the reasons which render it impracticable for the United States to become a party to the Convention concluded at The Hague on July 17, 1905. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Phillips) to Chargé Sussdorff, no. 371, Apr. 28, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 081.59/19; 99 Br. & For. St. 

Paps. 990 (convention of 1905). 

In 1938 the Department of Justice said thatthe power of the District Courts of the United States to execute letters rogatory in private cases is questionable and at best illdefined. They have express jurisdiction in cases where a foreign government is a party or has an interest, but it is doubtful whether their power extends to private cases. 

Assistant Attorney General Whitaker to Secretary Hull. Apr. 11, 1938, MS. Department of State, file 811.04556/13.

In the case of In re Letters Rogatory of Republic of Colombia the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York denied without prejudice a petition for an order designating a commissioner to execute certain letters rogatory issued out of the customs court of Bogotá. The court stated that to found any jurisdiction by it in such circumstances it was necessary under section 701

Case of 

Martin

De Mott of title 28 of the United States Code that the following facts affirmatively appear: 

1. That there be a suit pending in a foreign court out of which the letters rogatory issue, 2. That the government of the country of that court be a party to said suit or interested therein, and 

3. That the suit be for the recovery of money or property.

The court declared that in this case, while it appeared that the Colombian Government was interested in some kind of a summary proceeding in the customs court of Bogotá, it did not appear that there was a suit pending in that court or that if there were a suit pending it was one for the recovery of money or property. 

4 F. Supp. 165 (S.D.N.Y., 1933).

In 1923 the clerk of the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia informed the Secretary of State that that court did not find it in its power under section 4071 of the Revised Statutes to take any action under certain letters rogatory issued by the court of first instance of the Department of the Seine, France, in connection with proceedings on a charge of theft and obtaining money by false pretenses, and addressed to the proper judicial authorities of the United States. The clerk said:

That section in substance limits the action of the Court to suits for the recovery of money or property in which the foreign government is a party or has an interest, and it moreover requires that there be specific interrogatories accompanying the letters addressed to the witnesses, and that the testimony should be shown to be material by due proof. There should also be a commissioner named to execute, although I fancy the Court might designate one of its own officers where this was lacking in the letters themselves.

I have endeavored to devise some means whereby the request might be honored without the Court assuming unwarranted jurisdiction, but I regret that such quest has been unsuccessful. 

Mr. Beach to Secretary Hughes, Nov. 5, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 082.51/30. 

The American Embassy in Rome informed the Department of State in 1934 that the Italian authorities would address letters rogatory to the competent American authorities to obtain the necessary evidence in connection with the trial of one Martin De Mott who was charged with the killing of the chief officer of the American steamship Exchange on board that vessel in the port of Messina. The Department informed the American Embassy that the Federal statute regarding testimony for use in foreign countries, 28 U.S.C. §701,

provides for the use of letters rogatory only in cases involving the recovery of money or property and that the Federal courts had held that they had no authority to execute letters rogatory or to issue summonses for witnesses to appear before foreign consuls in criminal cases. 

Secretary Hull to the Embassy in Rome, telegram 106, Dec. 18, 1934, MS. 

Department of State, file 195.8 De Mott, Martin/9.

In 1920 the Department of State transmitted to the Governor of Illinois, for such action as might be possible under the laws of that State, letters rogatory addressed by the second numerary district judge of the Federal District of Mexico to the competent authorities of Chicago. The Governor returned these letters unexecuted, stating that the Attorney General of Illinois had called to his attention "the fact that sections 7619-7622 of the United States Compiled Statutes of 1918 clearly contemplate that such letters should be produced before the United States District Judge of the district wherein the witness resides or shall be found". The Department returned the papers to the Governor with the following comment:

In reply your attention is invited to the fact that as indicated in Section 7619, action under the sections of the Statutes to which you refer seems to be limited to testimony "to be used in any suit for the recovery of money or property". It appears that the action brought against Mario Banuet y Palascios is upon the charge of the crime of rebellion, and, therefore, that under this Statute the District Judge at Chicago does not have the authority to act in this case.

The papers are, therefore, returned to you in the hope that you may find that the letters rogatory may be executed under the laws of the State of Illinois, and that thus there may be compliance with the expressed desire of the Chargé d'Affaires ad interim of Mexico.

It is suggested that authority may be found in appropriate State legislation relating to the subject, or that, pursuant to the generally established law of nations concerning the execution of letters rogatory, you may consider that the appropriate court of your State may furnish assistance to the Mexican courts in the case under consideration. In this relation, your attention is invited to the statements made on pages 256 and 257 of Volume 

32 of the Federal Reporter and in Section 456 of the Fourth Edition of Benedict's Treatise on The American Admiralty. 

Governor Lowden to Secretary Colby, Mar. 31, 1920, and Mr. Colby to 

Mr. Lowden, Apr. 15, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 082.12/124.

In the case of In re Romero, Mexican Consul General, the Supreme Court of New York granted a motion to vacate an order entered in that court directing the service upon the Manhattan Trust Company of New York city of certain so-called "letters rogatory" issuing out of the Second Civil Court of Mexico City. The court stated that the papers issued by the Mexican court were not in the nature of letters rogatory but appeared to be a summons and complaint in an action instituted therein by a resident of Mexico for legal services alleged to have been rendered in Mexico to the trust company. It was clear, the court said, that the New York courts possessed no power to order the service of such a summons and complaint and that by statute the New York courts would assist in the execution of foreign letters rogatory for the examination of witnesses within their jurisdiction, but that even as to such process there was no inherent or

implied power in the court and the authority must be found in the statute. 

56 Misc. (1907) 319, 107 N.Y. Supp. 621.

In the case of In re Letters Rogatory out of First Civil Court of City of Mexico the United States District Court granted a motion to vacate an order for service of summons upon a resident of the southern district of New York, issued pursuant to a request from the Mexican court. It appeared that the defendant had entered into a contract of lease in Mexico City and that suit had been brought against him in the Republic of Mexico for the payment of rent and redelivery of certain property claimed under the contract. The judge of the United States District Court stated that the judicial request was said to come within the definition of letters rogatory in civil law and that under the provisions of the Mexican Civil Code it was apparently possible, through the aid of the United States District Court, to render the person sought to be served subject to a personal judgment in Mexico, because the contract sued upon was to be performed there. Such a result, he said, was contrary to the American system of jurisprudence, which treats the legal jurisdiction of a court as limited to persons and property within its territorial jurisdiction. 

It was undesirable, he said, to aid a process which might require residents of the southern district of New York to defend suits brought in distant countries where they had no property or, as an alternative, to suffer a personal judgment by default, which would be enforceable against them personally whenever they might enter the foreign territory. He stated further that, so far as he was aware, no American or English court had ever "by an order directing the service of process aided a foreign tribunal to acquire jurisdiction over a party within the United States". Letters rogatory, he said, had been so long familiar to American courts and so exclusively limited to proceedings in the nature of commissions to take depositions of witnesses at the request of a foreign court, that he hardly felt inclined to assume such a novel jurisdiction as was proposed, without statutory authority, even if the case were one where as a matter of sound policy aid should be given to the foreign tribunal. 

261 Fed. 652 (S.D.N.Y., 1919).

In response to an inquiry from the Spanish Ambassador as to whether the proper authorities of the United States would have any objection to executing a letter rogatory dealing with a legal notice from a foreign judge to an officer of the United States Navy, the 

Department of State replied:

A letter has been received from the Secretary of the Navy stating that if the letter rogatory in question concerns only the

Mandamus private affairs of an officer of the United States Navy his status relative thereto is deemed not to be different from that of any other citizen of the United States, but that if the letter rogatory concerns a matter arising from performance of official duties it is thought that the said letter should first be submitted to the Navy Department for its consideration and determination as to whether or not the subject matter thereof is of a character to which reply may properly be made.

Memorandum from the Department of State to the Spanish Embassy, Apr. 29, 1924, MS. Department of State, file 852.04511/2

The case of Christ v. Superior Court in and for City and County of San Francisco et al. involved a proceeding in mandamus to require a California court to issue a commission for the taking of testimony of witnesses upon letters rogatory issued out of a court of record of Guatemala. In the course of its opinion granting a preliminary writ, the Supreme Court of California said:

It is insisted that the letters rogatory were not properly authenticated. It appears that the affidavit of the petitioner attached to the letters was verified before the consul-general of the United States at Guatemala and these documents were transmitted to the respondent court by the consul-general of Guatemala located at San Francisco by a communication which recited that they were so transmitted pursuant to instructions of the Guatemalan minister at Washington, D. C. The letters rogatory, the accompanying affidavit, and the letters of transmittal were original documents and their genuineness was not denied in the answer to the petition herein. In addition there is much force in the contention of the petitioner that the original documents prove themselves. (See Wickersham v. Johnston, 104 Cal. 407, 413 [43 Am. St. Rep. 118; 38 Pac. 89].) 

211 Cal. (1931) 593, 600-601, 296 Pac. 612, 615.

Revised Statutes of the United States] is limited to obtaining testimony of witnesses residing in the United States for use in suits, in which the government of the foreign country shall be a party or shall have an interest, for the recovery of money or property. 

Secretary Knox to the Minister of Peru, no. 7, June 14, 1912, MS. Department of State, file 800.04511/14.

cation or alternative personal service upon absent defendants, "wherever found"; that a number of the States of the Union also provide for personal service upon absent defendants; that, in some instances, the consuls of the United States have been instructed to serve such processes upon persons in their consular districts; and that it is understood that Germany accords to foreign consuls the privilege of serving, in her territory, the processes of courts of their nationality, the Department does not believe that this Government would be justified in objecting to the action of the German Consul at St. Louis in serving a process of the German court on Mr. Pape.

In the case of Jacques Gilbert v. Henry C. Burnstine et al. the plaintiff demanded judgment for the amount of an award against the defendants by an arbitrator appointed in London, allegedly pursuant to the English Arbitration Act of 1889. In a contract concluded between the plaintiff and the defendants in New York the parties had agreed that all differences arising thereunder should be "arbitrated at London pursuant to the Arbitration Law of Great Britain". Differences arose under the contract, and the defendants failed to comply with a notice served upon them in New York requesting them to concur in the nomination of an arbitrator. The plaintiff thereupon obtained from the King's Bench Division an order permitting him to issue a form of process described in the complaint as an originating

Service in foreign countries summons, and this process was served on the defendants in New York directing them to appear in London before a master in chambers so that an arbitrator might be appointed. Upon failure of the defendants to appear the master appointed an arbitrator who issued a notice served on the defendants in New York requiring them to furnish him in London with all documents relevant to the matters in dispute. The defendants ignored the notice. After service of a peremptory notice on them in New York the arbitration was proceeded with and the award against them rendered.

The New York Court of Appeals reversed the judgment of the lower courts dismissing the complaint on the merits, saying:

Generally, extraterritorial jurisdiction of alien tribunals, however vigorously asserted, is denied by us. Of its own force, process issued from the court of a foreign state against our citizen and served upon him here is void. Without his consent he cannot be made subject to it, but whenever he agrees to be bound by its service, his conduct presents a problem.

The court said further that, since public policy did not forbid defendants to appoint an agent to accept service or to confess judgment in their behalf or to acknowledge in person receipt of service, the same policy ought to prevail if it were clear that in advance of any litigation or arbitration they actually intended to contract that in the event of such a proceeding they would render themselves subject to foreign process. It declared that there was an implied submission to the terms of the British Arbitration Act and to any rules of procedural machinery adopted by competent authority in aid of its provisions. 

Merely as a pleading, the court said, the complaint stated a good cause of action, and whether its allegations could be sustained would have to be determined on trial. 

255 N.Y. (1931) 348, 354, 174 N.E. 706, 707.

Officers and employees of the Foreign Service are hereby forbidden to serve subpenas, citations, complaints, or other forms of legal process, in connection with cases pending in Federal or 

State courts of the United States.

Three exceptions to this rule are noted, namely, the service of subpenas and orders to show cause under the act of July 3, 1926 (44 Stat. 835) and the delivery of documents in connection with fraudulent naturalization. 

For. Ser. Reg. U.S. X-6, Feb. 1940; Ex. Or. 8292, Nov. 30, 1939.

It was suggested that the matter be brought to the attention of the 

Italian Ambassador in the United States. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Wright) to Miss Helena A. Ivory, Nov. 4, 1925, MS. Department of State, file 081.65/184.

POLICE AND OTHER REGULATIONS DISPLAY OF FLAGS 

$127 The following circular instructions in regard to the use of the American flag were issued to American consular officers in 1907: 

It has been reported to the Department that the proper use of the American flag is not understood by all consular officers and that the flag has been used as an article of furniture, a curtain for a door and a cover for a box. 

The flag should never be used for such purposes and should never be employed in a manner which would lead visitors to think that a consular officer was lacking in respect for it. 

The flag which is used for public display, when not in use should be carefully laid away. A flag which has become unserviceable may, however, be displayed partly unfurled, on the wall of the consulate, in such a manner that all who see it may know that it is exhibited as the national emblem. 

The Third Assistant Secretary of State (Wilson) to American consular officers, Jan. 25, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 697/5. In March 1912 the Mexican Ambassador wrote to the Secretary of State setting forth the views of his Government in regard to the right of a consul in Mexico to display the flag of his nation and

10. requesting that the American Consul at Ensenada be instructed not Mexico to display unduly the American flag over his consular premises. The 

Secretary replied that the request had been received with surprise and that the Department was at a loss to understand why the Mexican Government should perceive any objection to the display of the American flag above the Consulate at Ensenada, especially under the conditions prevailing in Mexico at that time. The Secretary said: 

Concerning the flying of the national flag as a question of right, the Department, after very careful consideration, feels quite sure that a reexamination of the authorities upon international law by the proper Mexican officers will convince your excellency's

Government that the display by a consul of the flag of his country is a thing which may be properly claimed as a right under international law and that the Mexican Government, by its practice in permitting the consul to display the flag on the national holiday of his country, and the legal adviser of the Mexican Foreign Office in the present instance by so recommending, appear to recognize this, notwithstanding the Mexican municipal law of 1859 cited by your excellency, which provides that commercial agents residing in Mexico may display the flags of their countries only when the town where they reside is besieged, or when a riot or sedition breaks out therein.

This Department is aware that the extent to which the right to display the flag can be exercised is variously stated; that some authorities limit it to solemn occasions and some to national holidays, while others merely state the right without limiting it. 

But since the reason for displaying the flag above the consular premises as recognized in international law is, as expressed in the consular treaties of the United States with other countries, "in order that the consular office or dwelling may be easily and generally known for the convenience of those who may have resort to them," it would seem that the flag of the consul's nation might be displayed at all times and not merely on certain holidays. And indeed this is the course that has been followed by 

American consuls at various places throughout the world, who, basing their action upon this ground, do now, as they have done in the past, daily display the national flag. This is likewise, it would appear, the practice of other nations.

He said further that it had been learned from the Consul at Ensenada that when he first arrived there conditions throughout northern Lower California were such as to make it highly desirable to display the American flag daily, that nothing had since occurred to suggest the possibility of discontinuing the practice, and that no opposition to the appearance of the flag over the Consulate from either official or private sources had ever come to the knowledge of the Consul. The Secretary expressed the hope that the Mexican

Government would see fit "fully to recognize the rules and principles of international law governing this matter and to refrain from insisting upon a strict compliance by American consuls with the provisions

Sweden El 

Salvador of the Mexican law of 1859 with regard to the matter, thus permitting them to display the American flag in such manner and at such times as their discretion dictates, unless in particular cases some good reason exists and can be shown why this should not be done". 

Secretary Knox to Ambassador Calero, no. 33, June 21, 1912, MS. 

Department of State, file 812.0151/1. See also 1912 For. Rel. 903-905.

In view of the probability of air raids by Federal forces, the American Consul at Guaymas, Mexico, displayed the American flag daily over his Consulate during an insurrection in 1929 and advised American citizens in that place to display the flag until the Federals had recovered control of the port. His action met with the approval of the Department of State.

Article V of the consular convention signed by the United States and Sweden on June 1, 1910 forbade the display by consular officers of the flag of their country on their offices in the capital of the country when there was a Legation there, 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2846, 2848. In 1923 the Department of State instructed the

Minister in Sweden to inquire of the Swedish Foreign Office whether, in view of the fact that the British Consulate as well as the British 

Legation at Stockholm and the Finnish Consulate and Legation were permitted to fly their national colors, there was any objection to the flying of the American flag by the American Consulate General in that place. The Swedish Government immediately granted the requested permission.

As to the official display of the American flag by consular and diplomatic officers of the United States, section IV-15 (6) of the Foreign 

Service Regulations of the United States (June 1940) provides: 

Display of flag. The flag shall be flown over an American mission or consulate between the hours of sunrise and sunset on all American national holidays and flag days, on all holidays in the country in which the mission or consulate is located, and on such other occasions as the officer in charge may deem appropriate. 

When necessary, the flag may also be flown for purposes of protection. 

A Salvadoran Executive order of February 1, 1908 announced that foreigners residing in that Republic could fly the flag of their nation only by special permit from the district governor and that this per-

mit could in no way imply a privilege or immunity in the person or the residence of the foreigner. The Acting Secretary of State thereupon instructed the Chargé d'Affaires in San Salvador as follows: 

Referring to the recent Salvadorian executive order prohibiting the flying of foreign flags, you express the opinion, after discussing the matter with the Minister for Foreign Affairs, that there will be no trouble for Americans who may desire to display their national colors.

As to the display of foreign flags, international usage confers a quasi-right upon consuls to display their national flag. In some countries, as in Mexico, display of their national flag by private foreigners or of foreign flags by natives, is prohibited. 

The Salvadorian requirement of a permit from the local authorities is reasonable, it being expressed or understood that foreign consuls have such permission in virtue of their office and that foreign ships are necessarily entitled to fly their national flags. 

Chargé Gregory to Secretary Root, no. 66, Salvadoran series, Apr. 7, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 4598/47-48; 1908 For. Rel. 705; the Acting 

Secretary of State (Bacon) to Chargé Gregory, no. 19, Mar. 19, 1908, MS. 

Department of State, file 4598/29. in U.S. 

In reply to an inquiry as to whether "international etiquette and American usage prescribe that when a foreign consulate in the Foreign flags United States wishes to display its flag, it must, as a matter of courtesy, display the American flag above its own", the Department of State said thatthe Department knows of no such rule. American consuls in foreign countries are expected to display the flag of the United States on their consulates on suitable occasions, and the similar privilege of flying their national flags is accorded to foreign consuls in the United States. 

Secretary Knox to Mr. Ernest A. Spongberg, June 26, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 20277. 

In 1906 the Department of State said thatthere is no federal law of the United States forbidding the flying of foreign flags in this country, and so far as this Department is aware no such law is in force in the State of New Hampshire. 

In answer to your second enquiry [whether it would be a breach of etiquette to hoist his national flag], the Department would say that it knows of no code of etiquette which covers your question. It is rather a matter of propriety in the determination of which the general sentiment of the local community should be well considered. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to Mr. John Williams, Sept. 

24, 1906, MS. Department of State, minor file, vol. 61.

Protection 

The Portuguese Minister to the United States brought to the attention of the Secretary of State the fact that, on February 22, 1922, the Portuguese flag over the Portuguese Vice Consulate office at Providence, Rhode Island, had been hauled down by a policeman. 

The Secretary informed him that he had been told by the Governor of Rhode Island that the police officer's action, which was very unfortunate, was the result of the officer's failure to understand that the Vice Consulate had a right to display the national flag of Portugal on the Consulate. The Governor had told him further, he said, that he would send his secretary accompanied by his military aides to call on the Portuguese Vice Consul to express sincere regret on behalf of the State of Rhode Island. 

Secretary Hughes to Minister d'Alte, Mar. 30, 1922, MS. Department of

State, file 853.015311/1. 

Demonstrators in New York city in 1935 tore down the flag flying from the bow of the German steamship Bremen. The German Chargé d'Affaires ad interim protested against the acts which he termed a "serious insult to the German national emblem". The Department of State wrote to the Chargé d'Affaires enclosing a report from the appropriate authorities in New York on the matter and stating that it was "unfortunate that, in spite of the sincere efforts of the police to prevent any disorder whatever, the German national emblem should, during the disturbance which took place, not have received that respect to which it is entitled."

The Under Secretary of State (Phillips) to the German Chargé d'Affaires 

(Leitner), Aug. 1, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 862.015311/6; Department of State, XIII Press Releases, weekly issue 305, pp. 100, 101 (Aug. 2, 1935).

15, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 5931/240.

With reference to a decree of the Government of Guatemala regulating the flying of foreign flags, the Department of State stated that "the display of a foreign flag is a matter which may be regulated by the municipal laws of the country". Referring to its statement that "the display of a flag, not as denoting extraterritorial jurisdiction, but as indicating the foreign ownership of property, had become so far a usage, in certain countries liable to domestic dis-

turbances as to warrant its continuance", the Department said that this rule was inapplicable in countries where specific laws regulate the display of a foreign flag.

In answer to an inquiry by a private individual whether it would be a violation of international law for him to display the American flag over a hotel in Montego Bay, Jamaica, the Department of State said: 

In reply you are informed that this is a matter of local regulation. International law only takes cognizance of the representative display of flags, as on diplomatic missions, consulates and vessels, and for legitimate protection in extra territorial countries and in times of civil disturbance involving injury to actual citizens.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Mr. J. B. White, Dec. 

18, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 697/64.

In 1910 certain Chinese subjects, whose interests in Ecuador were represented by American consular and diplomatic officers, expressed the desire to place over the doors of their stores and warehouses a placard bearing a representation of the flag of the United States with the statement that the property was Chinese and was under the protection of the United States. The Department of State informed the American Consul General at Guayaquil that it did not feel justified in authorizing the proposed use of the flag, since such use would be liable to serious abuse, and that, while perhaps no serious legal objection could be urged to the inscription which the merchants proposed to put over their doors, he should carefully refrain from expressing any sanction thereof and from saying or doing anything that would lead either the Chinese or the local inhabitants to believe that the placing of such inscription would give to the Chinese any greater or further rights and protection than that which was then extended to them.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul General Diet rich, Oct. 1, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 704.9322/109.

In reply to a letter stating that an American citizen wished to display the American flag on his house in Palestine and inquiring whether there would be any objection on the part of the local authorities or the British Government, the Department of State said thatthe display of a national flag is not customary except on buildings of diplomatic, consular, or other official representatives. In several Oriental countries, however, foreigners have been permitted to display their own national flags over private residences.

The Department is not in a position to assure Mr. Faber whether the Palestine authorities or the British Government would permit his using an American flag on his house. This question lies within the province of the local authorities and he would have to comply with the customs usually observed in this respect by other foreigners. 

The Third Assistant Secretary of State (Bliss) to Shreve Steamship 

Agency, Mar. 28, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 811.0151/327.

In 1937 the Department of State informed the American Embassy in Nanking that there was no United States statute forbidding the display of the American flag over American-owned property or by American citizens over their residences. American diplomatic and consular officers, therefore, it was said, could only issue advice designed to discourage the display of the American flag in inappropriate cases, such as where it was displayed to protect a purely Chinese interest or where the display would add to rather than lessen the danger to American residents or American property. 

Secretary Hull to the Embassy in China, telegram 134, Aug. 7, 1937, MS.

QUARANTINE 

§128 Every sovereign state has the right to establish, in the interest of its public health, quarantine regulations designed to prevent the introduction into its country of infectious or contagious diseases deleterious to human, animal, or plant life. Consuls stationed in foreign ports are usually authorized to issue bills of health to vessels bound from the foreign ports at which they are stationed to ports in their respective countries. They are not expected and cannot be required to issue bills of health to vessels if, in their opinion, the sanitary conditions aboard are such as to render the entrance of the vessels into the ports of the consuls' home state unsafe from the point of view of sanitation and health. To facilitate the work of consuls in these respects, health officers of the states represented by the consuls are sometimes stationed in foreign ports. Such an arrangement, of course, must be made with the consent of the foreign state in which the officer is stationed. If the foreign state refuses to allow inspection of vessels departing from its ports the authorities of the port of destination may refuse to allow such vessels to enter prior to an inspection and, if necessary, fumigation by the local authorities. 

These matters are sometimes covered by conventional arrangements. 

The United States is a party to the following multilateral sanitary conventions: International sanitary convention signed at Paris, Jan. 17, 1912, 42 Stat. 1823, 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2972; convention revising the international sanitary convention of Jan. 17, 1912 signed at 

Paris, June 21, 1926, 45 Stat. 2492, 4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4962; international sanitary convention signed by certain American republics at Washington, Oct. 14, 1905, 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 2144; sanitary convention between the United States and other American republics signed at Habana, Nov. 14, 1924, 44 Stat. 2031, 4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4700; additional protocol between the United States and other American republics signed at Lima, Oct. 19, 1927, 45 Stat. 2613, 4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4720.

tine laws 

The act of Congress approved April 29, 1878 forbids the entrance into any port of the United States, or the crossing of the boundary between the United States and any foreign country, of any vessel or State quaranvehicle coming from a foreign port or country where any contagious or infectious disease exists, or conveying any persons, merchandise, or animals affected with any infectious or contagious disease, contrary to the quarantine laws of any State of the United States into or through the jurisdiction of which such vessel or vehicle may pass or to which it is destined. 

20 Stat. 37; 42 U.S.C. §86. 

The quarantine of vessels from foreign ports and the issuance of bills of health thereto are governed in the United States by the acts of Congress approved February 15, 1893, as amended, and June 19, 1906. Provision is made in section 3 of the former for the posting of the act and the rules and regulations made in pursuance thereof in American consular offices. 

27 Stat. 449; 34 Stat. 299; 42 U.S.C. §§ 82, 85, 92.

The Mexican Chargé d'Affaires ad interim brought to the attention of the Department of State the fact that the Mexican vessel Nicaragua had, allegedly, been unduly detained in quarantine at Mobile,

Alabama, for fumigation on the ground that it had not been fumigated before sailing from Tampico, although its bill of health was countersigned by the American Consul and examined by the American health officer at that port, neither of whom informed the master that fumigation would be required. The Department replied that it was informed by the Treasury Department that fumigation had been recommended by the representative of the United States Public Health Service at Tampico before the Nicaragua sailed but that the agent would not incur the expense, thinking it unnecessary; that the fumigation at Mobile was not only proper from a quarantine standpoint but was demanded by the quarantine regulations; and that a representative of the Treasury Department in the office of an American Consul in a foreign port could only recommend quarantine measures. 

Secretary Knox to Ambassador Don Manuel Calero, Dec. 10, 1912, MS. 

Department of State, file 192/579. Vessels

The Treasury Department has for a number of years maintained officers of the Public Health Service in the offices of the Public-health American Consuls in foreign ports, to sign bills of health in conjunction with the latter in accordance with national law, the object being to furnish protection to United States ports by utilizing in every way possible any preventive work which might be officers in foreign ports

done in foreign ports by the foreign quarantine authorities, or by the steamship companies themselves. 

The duty of the Department's representatives in foreign ports has not been to enforce measures of this kind, but simply to suggest or advise that certain measures applying to certain ports, if taken prior to the departure of vessels, would mitigate the quarantine treatment called for in the United States quarantine regulations, upon arrival of the vessels at United States ports. 

The Acting Secretary of the Treasury (Malburn) to the Secretary of 

State (Lansing), Sept. 24, 1915, MS. Department of State, file 158.941/34.

The representative in the United States of the administration then (February 10, 1923) functioning in Mexico addressed a note to the 

Department of State stating that the Mexican Health Department had complained that several steamship companies had experienced difficulties with the representative of the United States Public Health Service at Tampico, Mexico, because he insisted on the fumigation of vessels clearing Mexico for American ports regardless of whether or not they had been fumigated by Mexican health authorities, to which the Department replied by submitting a report by the appropriate branch of the Government, reading as follows:

It appears that the Mexican authorities do not quite understand Dr. Gruver's detail.

The quarantine laws of the United States and the regulations made in accordance therewith require that officers of the United States Government be held directly responsible for the fumigation of those vessels which may require such treatment. 

Accordingly a trained medical officer has been detailed to assist and advise the American Consul in effecting such fumigation at Tampico, in the case of those vessels whose owners or agents desire this service at the port of departure rather than at the port of arrival. The latter procedure would necessarily involve detention as well as fumigation.

The Surgeon General of the Public Health Service has no intention to duplicate the work of the Mexican authorities. If the Mexican Health Delegation is already fumigating the vessels in question the Surgeon General will consider accepting these fumigations provided that his representative is permitted to be present and to observe the procedure in detail so that he may certify that the fumigations have been conducted in accordance with the quarantine laws and regulations of the United States. 

The direct effect of fumigation at the port of departure is to facilitate commerce. Since the arrival of Dr. Gruver at Tampico, the attitude of certain of the steamship companies has definitely changed from that of opposition to cooperation. 

The Chief of the Division of Mexican Affairs (Hanna) to Señor Manuel 

Téllez, Mar. 31, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 158.1208/21.

In 1911 complaint was made by certain Americans, passengers on the British steamship Tennyson, against the American Consul at

Trinidad in connection with the refusal of the health authorities at Port-of-Spain to permit the removal from the Tennyson of passengers suffering from smallpox. The Department of State replied: 

The duty of the American Consul at Trinidad in connection Function of with this vessel, which was bound for an American port, was to American see that it complied with the Quarantine Regulations of the Consul United States, and to issue a bill of health accordingly. He had no authority whatever over the vessel, which is of British registry, and, of course, he had no jurisdiction over the health officials at Port of Spain and could not interfere with their enforcement of the local health regulations. 

The question as to whether the persons who were ill could be landed at Port of Spain was one for the determination of the port authorities, and you will of course readily perceive that they would doubtless be as anxious to keep a quarantinable disease out of Trinidad as the passengers on the vessel were to have the persons suffering therefrom removed to the shore, especially in view of the health conditions then existing at Trinidad, as shown by the Consul's report. 

Secretary Knox to Mr. James Stewart, June 27, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 158.44g5/6.

The Acting Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Wasson, Feb. 7, 1931 

(telegram), MS. Department of State, file 195.3/1091.

The British Ambassador, in March 1914, addressed a note to the Department of State in regard to the treatment accorded by the quarantine authorities at Mobile, Alabama, to the British vessel

Newlands which had been subjected to fumigation and had been consequently delayed for a day and a half in discharging her cargo. The 

Treasury Department explained—and the explanation was transmitted to the British Ambassador-that the vessel had arrived from the port of Rosario where the presence of plague infection had been reported and that:

The points involved in the treatment of this vessel from a quarantine standpoint are first, the regulations governing a group of ports in which Rosario is included, and second, the proved necessity for extraordinary precautions against the escape of rats from grain-carrying vessels from plague suspected ports. The difficulties encountered in the carrying out of these precautions are an entirely different matter, and will not be discussed in connection with the policy of operating quarantine regulations under Delays

State fumigation national law for the prevention of the introduction of the quarantinable diseases.

The delay of one and one-half days resulting from the quarantine treatment of a vessel of this kind is a matter of small importance compared with the monetary loss which would follow the entrance of one plague infected rat into an important port. 

Ambassador Spring Rice to Secretary Bryan, no. 82, Mar. 17, 1914, MS. 

Department of State, file 158.008/4; the Secretary of the Treasury (McAdoo) to Mr. Bryan, Mar. 31, 1914, ibid. 158.008/5.

In response to a complaint from the Spanish Minister, in 1913, regarding the removal to quarantine at San Juan, Puerto Rico, and the detention in the lazaretto for 5 days of 94 passengers bound to that port from Spain, the Department of State transmitted a copy of a letter from the Secretary of the Treasury in which it was explained that the detention of passengers was due to the presence on board the ship of a suspected case of bubonic plague; that every attempt had been made to provide for the necessities and comfort of the passengers; and that while "Detention at quarantine is invariably a hardship it is only by the scientific determination of the diagnoses of just such cases as the one under consideration that communities can be protected from the infection of such a disease as bubonic plague, with its consequent loss of life, and damage to commercial activity." 

The Secretary of the Treasury (McAdoo) to the Secretary of State 

(Bryan), Dec. 5, 1913, MS. Department of State, file 158.008/3.

The British vessel Trecarne was subjected to fumigation by both 

Federal and State quarantine officials in Galveston, Texas, in October 1916, the State authorities insisting that the previous fumigation Federal and by the Federal authorities did not fulfil all the requirements of the 

Texas Department of Health. A note in regard to the incident having been received in the Department of State from the British Ambassador and referred to the Treasury Department, the latter replied that the Federal maritime quarantine laws were not intended to prevent States from imposing additional restrictions on vessels in accordance with any existing local sanitary laws and that the issue was not one for adjustment by the Federal Government since it was a matter of obligation on the part of vessels to comply with local sanitary regulations after the national quarantine inspection had been made and a certificate given therefor. 

The Assistant Secretary of the Treasury (Newton) to the Secretary of State (Lansing), Feb. 3, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 158.008/8.
