The German Foreign Office addressed a note verbale to the American Embassy in Berlin in 1909 with regard to one Max Runge who was being sought by New York police upon a charge of theft and whose arrest with a view to extradition by the New York police department had been requested of the police president of Berlin. 

The note verbale pointed out that the individual in question would not seem to be extraditable as the offense against him was not included in the extradition treaty of June 16, 1852 but that if he was a German subject he might be prosecuted before the German courts, if this was requested by the United States Government and the assurance given of reciprocal treatment on the part of the United States in similar cases. The Department of State instructed the 

Ambassador as follows: 

Inasmuch as, under Anglo-Saxon legal theory, crime is territorial, not personal, and therefore the criminal jurisdiction of the United States does not, as a general rule, extend to crimes committed outside of its jurisdiction, whether by American citizens or aliens, it is not possible to meet the suggestion of the German note verbale that this Government guarantee, in cases the reverse of Max Runge's case, the criminal prosecution in this country of an American citizen charged with the commission of a crime in Germany. 

Chargé Hitt to Secretary Knox, no. 527, Dec. 6, 1909, and Assistant 

Secretary Wilson to Ambassador Hill, no. 299, Jan. 11, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 22867. See also 1910 For. Rel. 517-518.

The French Ambassador in Washington submitted an aidemémoire to the Department of State pointing out that, since the United States Government considered itself as without authority to surrender its citizens to France under article 5 of the extradition treaty of January 6, 1909, American citizens committing crimes in France and fleeing to the United States would go unpunished and that, though the French law prohibited the surrender of French citizens in extradition cases, it made provision for their trial in France for offenses committed abroad. It was suggested that the practical operation of article 5 was disadvantageous to France and

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

181 that the treaty be amended either by inserting a provision whereby the United States would undertake to surrender all persons, while France would undertake to surrender all persons except her nationals, or by adding to article 5, as then in force, the following clause: "Provided their law permits of their trying and punishing offenses committed by their nationals abroad." The Secretary of State replied: 

Since, generally speaking, the law of the United States does not provide for the trial and punishment of its nationals for offenses committed abroad, the second alternative suggested by your Embassy would appear to be identical for all practical purposes with the first suggestion.

The Department recognizes that it is an undesirable condition of affairs under which American citizens committing crimes abroad can escape punishment by fleeing to this country, but its experience with relation to the practical working out of the system of law under which citizens of a country are placed upon trial in their own land for offenses committed abroad would seem to indicate that the inequality existing as a result of the provisions of Article 5 of the Extradition Treaty between the United States and France is not perhaps so great as your 

Embassy appears to suppose.

It seems to the Department from its information as to the results of the trials in their home countries of persons who are charged with the commission of offenses in the United States that the theory of the law under which such persons thereby meet their just deserts is not largely borne out in practice. The 

Department's information on this point would appear to indicate that juries in foreign countries are not as a rule thoroughly in sympathy with the idea of punishing their fellow countrymen for offenses committed abroad, and their reluctance in this respect may perhaps be due to the fact that ordinarily witnesses to the offense are not sent abroad to give their testimony in court, but the evidence for the prosecution is made up in writing which as a natural consequence does not appeal so strongly to jurymen as would the appearances of witnesses in person. 

Your Embassy calls attention to the fact that in some of its extradition treaties Great Britain agrees to surrender all persons while the other contracting parties undertake to surrender all persons except their nationals. However, the following quotation from a British writer would seem to indicate that this arrangement is not entirely satisfactory from the standpoint of 

Great Britain: "The territorial sovereign has the strongest interest, the greatest facilities, and the most powerful instruments for repressing crimes, whether committed by native-born subjects or by domiciled aliens in his territory. But a sovereign government which pursues its subjects into foreign countries, and keeps its criminal law suspended over them, attempts a task in which, even if undertaken with earnestness, it is sure to fail; but which will

probably be performed in a careless, indifferent, and intermitting manner. A government has no substantial interest in punishing crimes in the territory of another state; it has not on the spot officers of justice to discover and arrest the criminal; the transport of witnesses to a distance is a troublesome and costly operation; the difference of language, law, and customs creates further impediments. A failure of justice, and an acquittal, is therefore likely to occur, even if the utmost diligence is used; but it may be assumed as certain that, unless some special motive exists, little diligence will be used. A government would feel, with respect to offences committed abroad in a civilized country, that it was, at the best, undertaking a work of supererogation; perhaps that it was interfering in a matter which, as the law of the place provided for it, would most properly be left alone. 

The experience of this and other countries shows that a criminal law applicable to offences committed in foreign lands (such as the act of 33 Hen. 8 and 9 Geo. 4) is for the most part a brutum fulmen, and that it is rarely carried into execution." Lewis on 

Foreign Jurisdiction, etc., Page 29, et seq.)

The views above quoted appear to be shared by one of your own jurists, who is understood to be an authority on matters of extradition. He has written as follows: "Without doubt it may be said that the penal law is not exclusively territorial, and that it is possessed also, to a certain degree, of a personal character. It follows that the judges of the country of refuge may be competent, ratione personae, to take cognizance of the offence committed abroad. In that case, it is unnecessary to have recourse to extradition. The largest part of states have admitted this reasoning and promulgated laws which attribute to local justice the competence to judge citizens accused of offences committed abroad. Supported by these provisions and driven by an exaggerated notion of their sovereignty and of the protection due to their citizens, they have erected it into a principle that extradition is not applicable to these latter. We come, further on, to what it is necessary to say of this principle. Nevertheless, we may now show that the personal competence does not satisfy the interests of repressive justice as well as the territorial competence." (Billot, Traité, etc., pp. 10-11).

Reference may also be made to the following statement contained in Moore on Extradition (Volume I, p. 154) as indicating the American viewpoint on this matter, which accords with that of the British and French writers cited: "The practice of extradition is in itself a recognition not only of the principle that crime should be punished, but also of the fact that it can best be punished at the place of its commission. Nowhere else can it be so conveniently and so successfully prosecuted."

It is believed that while the present treaty arrangement relative to the surrender of citizens, theoretically at least, works 3.

183 adu the to the disadvantage of France, the arrangement proposed by your Embassy, for the reasons above indicated, would operate to the disadvantage of the United States.

In the case of the American Banana Company v. United Fruit 

Company the plaintiff brought action to recover threefold damages under section 7 of the so-called "Sherman Act" of 1890 (26 Stat. 209, 210). The plaintiff alleged that, by the acts of the defendant in territory occupied by Costa Rica, the title to which was in dispute between Costa Rica and Panama, it had been deprived of the use of its plantation and that the defendant by outbidding had driven purchasers out of the market and had compelled producers to come to its terms, also preventing the plaintiff from buying for export and sale. The Supreme Court held that the Sherman act did not govern acts done outside of the jurisdiction of the United States and within that of other states, saying: acts No doubt in regions subject to no sovereign, like the high seas, or to no law that civilized countries would recognize as adequate, such countries may treat some relations between their citizens as governed by their own law, and keep to some extent Punishable the old notion of personal sovereignty alive. See The Hamilton, 207 U.S. 398, 403; Hart v. Gumpach, L.R. 4 P.C. 439, 463, 464;

British South Africa Co. v. Companhia de Moçambique [1893], 

A.C. 602. They go further, at times, and declare that they will punish any one, subject or not, who shall do certain things, if they can catch him, as in the case of pirates on the high seas. 

In cases immediately affecting national interests they may go further still and may make, and, if they get the chance, execute similar threats as to acts done within another recognized jurisdiction. An illustration from our statutes is found with regard to criminal correspondence with foreign governments. Rev. 

Stat., §5335. See further Commonwealth v. Macloon, 101 Massachusetts, 1; The Sussex Peerage, 11 Cl. & Fin. 85, 146. And the notion that English statutes bind British subjects everywhere has found expression in modern times and has had some startling applications. Rex v. Sawyer, 2 C. & K. 101; The Zollverein, Swabey, 96, 98. But the general and almost universal rule is that the character of an act as lawful or unlawful must be determined wholly by the law of the country where the act is done. Slater v. Mexican National R. R. Co., 194 U.S. 120, 126.

This principle was carried to an extreme in Milliken v. Pratt, 125 Massachusetts, 374. For another jurisdiction, if it should happen to lay hold of the actor, to treat him according to its own notions rather than those of the place where he did the acts, not only would be unjust, but would be an interference with the authority of another sovereign, contrary to the comity of nations, which the other state concerned justly might resent.

Legislation, prima facie territorial 

Phillips v. Eyre, L.R. 4 Q.B. 225, 239; L.R. 6 Q.B. 1, 28; Dicey, Conflict of Laws (2d ed.), 647. See also Appendix, 724, 726, Note 2, ibid.

The foregoing considerations would lead in case of doubt to a construction of any statute as intended to be confined in its operation and effect to the territorial limits over which the lawmaker has general and legitimate power. "All_legislation_is prima facie territorial." Ex parte Blain, In re Sawers, 12 Ch. 

Div. 522, 528; State v. Carter, 27 N.J. (3 Dutcher) 499; People v. Merrill, 2 Parker, Crim. Rep. 590, 596. Words having universal scope, such as "Every contract in restraint of trade," "Every person who shall monopolize," etc., will be taken as a matter of course to mean only every one subject to such legislation, not all that the legislator subsequently may be able to catch. In the case of the present statute the improbability of the United States attempting to make acts done in Panama or Costa Rica criminal is obvious, yet the law begins by making criminal the acts for which it gives a right to sue. We think it entirely plain that what the defendant did in Panama or Costa Rica is not within the scope of the statute so far as the present suit is concerned. 

213 U.S. (1909) 347, 355–357.

The Department of Justice, on April 2, 1935, wrote to the Department of State regarding the killing of B. W. Lindberg, a member of the crew of the S.S. President Grant, by a shipmate. It appeared that Lindberg had been killed while on shore in Hong Kong. 

The Department of Justice concluded, therefore, that the homicide was not within the jurisdiction of the United States Court for China or of any court in the United States. If the conspiracy to commit such an assault was formed on shore, it was said, such conspiracy was likewise out of the jurisdiction of the United States court, but if it was formed, or any act in pursuance thereof was committed, on shipboard it was within the jurisdiction of the United States. 

The Department of Justice wrote further to the Department of State in regard to the subject on May 9, 1935, enclosing a letter from the United States Attorney at Seattle, Washington, and concurring in the latter's view that, in order to give jurisdiction to the courts of the United States, it would be necessary that the conspiracy should have been a conspiracy to commit some offense against the United States and that a conspiracy to commit an assault in Hong 

Kong would not be such an offense. 

Assistant Attorney General Keenan to Secretary Hull, Apr. 2 and May

Henry Werblow was convicted of grand larceny in the first degree in New York. He and two brothers were charged with the crime of grand larceny in obtaining money under false pretenses. The false pretenses were made in London, England, and the money was paid by the London branch of the Guaranty Trust Company of New 

York. At that time Henry was in China, one brother was in New

York, and the other brother was in London. Upon appeal, the Court of Appeals of New York reversed the conviction of Henry, stating:

The plan was laid here. The execution was in other lands. The question is whether our courts have jurisdiction of the crime.

Section 1930 of the Penal Law of New York subjects to punishment within the State "a person who commits within the state any crime, in whole or in part". In construing this statute the court said: 

We think a crime is not committed either wholly or partly in this State, unless the act within this State is so related

to the crime that if nothing more had followed, it would amount to an attempt.

It held that the plans laid in New York for the obtaining of money by false pretenses in London did not reach the stage of an attempt. 

With reference to a count in the indictment alleging that the principal office of the Guaranty Trust Company of New York was in New York County, that its business in London was a branch of the business conducted in New York, and that all losses sustained in the operation of the latter were in truth losses of the company in New York, the court said that such allegations did not bring the offense within section 1933 of the Penal Law of New York, which declares thata person who commits an act without this State which affects persons or property within this State and which, if committed within this State, would be a crime, is punishable as if the act were committed within this State. 

In this connection the court said: 

The larceny at London was not an act affecting any property in New York. The property, pounds sterling, was in 

London, and from London was transmitted to China. It was not an act affecting any person in New York, for it was not a crime against or injuring the person at all, but one directed against property (cf. Penal Law, §43) The court concluded: 

• • The defendant should answer for his crime to the courts of the sovereignty within whose territorial dominion it was committed in all its parts. 

People v. Werblow, 241 N.Y. (1925) 55, 58-59, 61, 67-68, 71, 148 N.E. 

786, 789, 791, 792, 793.

In Yenkichi Ito v. United States the circuit court of appeals reversed a judgment of conviction for bringing into and attempting to bring into the United States certain Japanese aliens. It appeared that the persons whom Yenkichi Ito was charged with aiding and abetting transported the aliens in question from a point in Mexico to a point some 40 miles off the mainland of the coast of California where they were intercepted by the United States Coast Guard. 

The court held that these acts did not constitute an attempt to bring in or land aliens not lawfully entitled to enter the United States within the jurisdiction of the United States or of the District Court thereof of the Southern District of California; that no illegal act was committed by them within the jurisdiction of the United States; that the act committed was legal where committed and was wrong

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

187 Sold da only because coupled with an intent to consummate the act of landing the aliens within the United States; and that since no substantive offense was committed by them the defendant could not properly be convicted as their aider and abetter. The court also held that certain remarks made by the defendant in the United States did not carry the project far enough forward to come within the domain of an attempt. 

64 F. (2d) 73 (C.C.A. 9th, 1933).

In the case of Juana Fernandez Gamboa v. The State the defendant had been convicted of slander. It appeared that while in Mexico she had uttered allegedly defamatory language and that she had also uttered such language in the city of El Paso, Texas. The Court of 

Criminal Appeals of Texas reversed the judgment of conviction on the ground that there was a fatal variance between the averment and the proof. The court said: 

The offense can rest alone upon the language used in El Paso. That used in Juarez was admissible upon the issue of intent, but not as a basis for the prosecution. 

94 Tex. Cr. R. (1923) 451, 452, 252 S.W. 167.

With regard to crimes as defined by international law, that law has no means of trying or punishing them. The recognition of them as constituting crimes, and the trial and punishment of the criminals, are left to the municipal law of each country. 

But whereas according to international law the criminal jurisdiction of municipal law is ordinarily restricted to crimes com- Piracy mitted on its terra firma or territorial waters or its own ships, and to crimes by its own nationals wherever committed, it is also recognized as extending to piracy committed on the high seas by any national on any ship, because a person guilty of such piracy has placed himself beyond the protection of any State. He is no longer a national, but "hostis humani generis" and as such he is justiciable by any State anywhere: Grotius (1583-1645) "De 

Jure Belli ac Pacis," vol. 2, cap. 20, §40."

In re Piracy Jure Gentium, [1934] A.C. 586, 589.

In the case of Ford et al. v. United States the Supreme Court affirmed a conviction of conspiracy to import liquor into the United States in violation of the Prohibition Law. The defendants below were charged with a conspiracy, "at the bay of San Francisco", illegally to import liquor into the United States and with overt acts of smuggling and attempting to smuggle. They objected that they had been corporeally at all times during the alleged conspiracy out

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

189 1年 ​of the jurisdiction of the United States and so could commit no offense against it. The Supreme Court said: 

The conspiracy was continuously in operation between. the defendants in the United States and those on the high seas adjacent thereto, and of the four overt acts committed in pursuance thereof, three were completed and took effect within the United States and the fourth failed of its effect only by reason of the intervention of the federal officers. In other words, the conspiring was directed to violation of the United States law within the United States by men within and without it, and everything done was at the procuration and by the agency of each for the other in pursuance of the conspiracy and the intended illegal importation. In such a case all are guilty of the offense of conspiring to violate the United States law whether they are in or out of the country. 273 U.S. (1927) 593, 620. it is in my opinion a crime under section 37 of the Criminal Code (Comp. St. §10201) for two or more persons on an 

American vessel on the high seas to conspire together to smuggle dutiable or prohibited merchandise into this country. 

United States v. Tello et al., 6 F. (2d) 579, 580 (D. Mass., 1925).

Downing and Downey were convicted by a district court of the United States of a conspiracy to import a cargo of intoxicating liquor into the United States from Canada. The facts of the case were thus summarized by the circuit court of appeals: 

The evidence of the prosecution was that one, Devine, met Downing in Hamilton, Ontario, and agreed with him to bring a thousand cases of ale into the United States. Later he had a telephone talk with Downing, and arranged to have the ale brought in by some one else, as Devine was leaving Buffalo for a time. He thereupon posted a letter to one, Cullen, giving 

Downing's name and address in Buffalo, and Cullen undertook the job, writing Downing when he would reach Hamilton with his barge to load the ale. He took her to Hamilton, and after some delay received the cargo at Port Colborne, whence he carried it to Buffalo, and delivered it with the help of Devine, who had returned. Downey helped to load the barge at Port Colborne and to discharge her at Buffalo.

In affirming the conviction of Downing the circuit court of appeals said: 

On this evidence Downing argues that there was no proof of any conspiracy within the United States, and that the indictment should have been dismissed. If Downing was in Buffalo when Devine agreed on the telephone to get a substitute, this would alone have been enough. Possibly the evidence is not entirely clear as to where he was at that time, though Devine

Bringing in of alien gave Cullen a Buffalo address. However, when the barge came in, Devine advised Downing at Downing's request, who was then at any rate in Buffalo. But all this is quite beside the point, since it was not necessary that Downing should have come to the United States at all. Conspirators are considered by a fiction as repeating their agreement wherever any part of it is executed. 

Thus, when Cullen brought the laden barge to Buffalo, and

Devine and Downey discharged her, under an arrangement with Downing to that effect, all the parties to the original agreement could be treated as conspiring_afresh. Ford v. U.S., 273 

U.S. 593, 47 S. Ct. 531, 71 L. Ed. 793, is precisely on all fours with the case at bar and lays all doubts, if any could arise. 

Again, it is true that in those cases the indictment laid, and the evidence proved, an overt act within the jurisdiction, and that it was upon this that the court relied. That was not true here, because while the indictment laid overt acts in Buffalo, the proof broke down as to them, being sufficient only as to an overt act laid in Ontario. However, the conspiracy is the crime (Hyde v. Shine, 199 U.S. 62, 25 S. Ct. 760, 50 L. Ed. 90); the overt act is necessary only to show that performance has begun, and it may be laid outside the jurisdiction [Dealy v. U.S., 152 

U.S. 539, 547; 14 S. Ct. 680, 38 L. Ed. 545. Chew v. U.S., 9 

F. (2d) 346, 353 (C.C.A. 8)]. Since jurisdiction depends upon where the crime is committed, and it is committed wherever any part of the agreement is performed, the act of performance relied upon need not be an overt act laid in the indictment. We can see nothing in Downing's appeal to warrant a reversal. 

United States v. Downing et al., 51 F. (2d) 1030-1031 (C.C.A. 2d, 1931).

Danton Claramont was convicted of unlawfully counseling and procuring the bringing into and landing in the United States from Cuba of an alien not entitled to enter. Upon appeal from his conviction he alleged that the lower court should have directed a verdict of not guilty, on the ground that the only evidence of his participation in the transactions alleged was as to what he did while he was in Cuba. The evidence showed that he arranged in Cuba with other accused to bring the alien in question into the United States and was there paid for so doing, the bringing of such alien into the United States being effected by other accused. The circuit court. of appeals held that the defendant, for his participation in the criminal offense charged, amounting to the counseling and procuring alleged, "was criminally liable, though he was not physically present in the United States when the alleged unlawful transaction was begun and consummated", and affirmed the judgment of the lower court.

Claramont v. United States, 26 F. (2d) 797 (C.C.A. 5th, 1928).

In the case of Ex parte Hammond the circuit court of appeals affirmed an order remanding the petitioner in habeas corpus proceedings to the custody of a United States marshal to be held for extradition to Canada. 

The petitioner was charged with obtaining money by false pretenses from a company in Canada through a draft deposited to his credit in California which was forwarded to Canada and there paid. 59 F. (2d) 683 (C.C.A. 

9th, 1932). mails Defendants Horwitz and Guerra were charged with conspiring Conspiring with others within the jurisdiction of the District Court of the in use of United States for the Southern District of Texas to deliver and cause to be delivered by United States mail, newspapers, circulars, letters, and instruments concerning a lottery, and to bring and cause to be brought into the United States from Mexico, papers, certificates, and instruments purporting to represent a ticket, share, and interest in the lottery. It appeared that they operated a radio station in 

Mexico in connection with their lottery, from which they solicited participation therein; that they caused a letter concerning a lottery to be delivered by United States mail to certain persons in the United States; and that funds out of which winners in the lottery were paid were deposited in a bank at McAllen, Texas. In affirming a judgment of conviction the circuit court of appeals, speaking through 

Circuit Judge Bryan, said:

It makes no difference whether the conspiracy was originally entered into in Houston, within the jurisdiction of the trial court, or in Mexico outside that jurisdiction. If it be conceded that in the beginning it was formed in Mexico, appellants and their associates brought it into the jurisdiction of the trial court, by depositing and withdrawing funds from the bank at McAllen, by causing letters and checks to be delivered by the United States

mail, and by performing other acts in pursuance of it and to effect its object. Hyde v. United States, 225 U.S. 347, 32 S. Ct. 

793, 56 L. Ed. 1114, Ann. Cas. 1914A, 614; Brown v. Elliott, 225 

U.S. 392, 32 S. Ct. 812, 56 L. Ed. 1136; People v. Mather, 4 Wend. (N.Y.) 229, 21 Am. Dec. 122; Wing v. United States (C.C.A.) 280 F. 112. 

There can be no doubt that the operation of the radio station constituted an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. A lottery could not be and was not conducted without the radio station; it was the broadcasting from Reynosa that brought forth the use of the mails. And so there was sufficient averment and proof of an essential overt act. We have then a case in which, according to the undisputed evidence, a conspiracy was in existence within the jurisdiction of the trial court and an overt act was committed in furtherance of it in a foreign country. It is settled that "if the conspiracy be entered into within the jurisdiction of the trial court, the indictment will lie there, though the overt act is shown to have been committed in another jurisdiction, or even in a foreign country." 

Hyde v. Shine, 199 U.S. 62, 25 S. Ct. 760, 761, 50 L. Ed. 90. 

See, also, United States v. Britton, 108 U.S. 199, 2 S. Ct. 531, 27 L. Ed. 698; Dealy v. United States, supra [152 U.S. 539; 14 

S. Ct. 680; 38 L. Ed. 545]. 

In a concurring opinion Circuit Judge Sibley said:

But as to an overt act that is alleged, constructive presence thereby is justly sustained. That act completes the crime of conspiracy where it was done, no matter where the conspiracy was previously made or carried on. It is authorized by all because it is to effect the object of the conspiracy. That it is done across an international line does not differentiate conspiracy from any other offense. If pistol or poison takes intended criminal effect from Mexico in the United States, the United States may punish if it can catch the criminals. The effect in the United States of the act done in Mexico draws to it jurisdiction to punish those who are responsible for it. It may properly be alleged as done in the United States. These mailed lottery receipts and checks are like bullets that hit their mark. In re Palliser, 136 U.S. 257, 10 S. Ct. 1034, 34 L. Ed. 514. They are clearly acts done in pursuance of this conspiracy and by authority of the conspirators. 

The radio communications in English were also clearly solicitations to misuse the United States mail intended to reach the people of the United States, and, although more like poison gas than bullets, I think their intended effect when accomplished in the United States constitutes an overt act there. Jurisdiction exists from the standpoint of international law. Venue in the 

Southern District of Texas exists under the Federal Constitution (Amendment 6), which requires prosecution where the crime was committed, not where the criminal was when he committed it. 

I concur in the affirmance. 

Horwitz et al. v. United States, 63 F. (2d) 706, 708, 709 (C.C.A. 5th, 1933).

The defendants demurred to the indictment on the ground that the conspiracy charged was the gist of the action; that under the sixth amendment to the 

Constitution all criminal prosecutions must be had in the "district wherein the crime shall have been committed"; that the conspiracy, if any, took place in the Province of British Columbia; and that, consequently, the District Court of the United States had no jurisdiction of the action. In overruling the demurrer the court said: 

The unlawful conspiracy, being entered into in British Columbia to commit an offense against the United States, continued with the parties on entering the jurisdiction of this court, and the doing of the overt act in furtherance of this conspiracy, within this district, vitalizes the conspiracy in this jurisdiction as fully as though it had originally been entered into here.

These parties cannot be prosecuted in British Columbia. 

Can it be said that parties living on the border line of the United States could go across into Canada or Mexico and enter into a conspiracy to defraud the United States, and then come into the United States and proceed to carry out the unlawful confederation, and not be subject to the jurisdiction of the courts of the United States? The courts will not subscribe to such a doctrine.

On August 2, 1926 a collision occurred between the French vessel Collision on Lotus and the Turkish vessel Boz-Kourt on the high seas, resulting high seas in the death of eight Turkish nationals on board the latter vessel. 

Subsequently, the officer of the watch on board the Lotus at the time of the collision, who was a French citizen, and the captain of the 

Boz-Kourt were arrested in Constantinople (Istanbul), criminal proceedings were instituted against them in the Turkish courts pursuant to Turkish legislation, and sentence was pronounced against them.

On October 12, 1926 the French and Turkish Governments signed a special agreement submitting to the Permanent Court of International Justice the question of judicial jurisdiction which had arisen between them as the result of the diplomatic protests of the French Government against the arrest and prosecution of the French officer. 

The Court was requested to decide whether Turkey, contrary to article 15 of the Convention of Lausanne of July 24, 1923, had acted in conflict with the principles of international law by the institution of the joint criminal proceedings and, if so, what reparation was due the French officer.

The French Government alleged that the Turkish criminal court claimed jurisdiction under article 6 of the Turkish Penal Code. 

This was not denied by the Turkish Government, but it did not appear whether the prosecution in question was based solely on that article providing for the punishment under the Turkish Penal Code of any foreigner arrested in Turkey, guilty of an offense abroad to the prejudice of Turkey or of any Turkish subject for which Turkish law prescribed a penalty of not less than a specified amount. 

Article 15 of the Convention of Lausanne above referred to, respecting conditions of residence, business, and jurisdiction, provided that all questions of jurisdiction between Turkey and the other contracting powers should "be decided in accordance with the principles of international law". 28 League of Nations Treaty Series (1924) 151. 

The Court rendered judgment on September 7, 1927, declaring that neither the conformity of article 6 of the Turkish Penal Code with the principles of international law nor the application of that article were at issue. It rejected the argument of the French Government that Turkey should be able to cite some rule of international law authorizing her to exercise jurisdiction but stated that it was necessary to determine whether any rule of international law limited the freedom of states to assume criminal jurisdiction in a situation such as the one under consideration. In this connection the Court said: 

International law governs relations between independent States. ... Restrictions upon the independence of States cannot therefore be presumed. Now the first and foremost restriction imposed by international law upon a State is that failing the existence of a permissive rule to the contrary-it may not exercise its power in any form in the territory of another State. In this sense jurisdiction is certainly territorial; it cannot be exercised by a State outside its territory except by virtue of a permissive rule derived from international custom or from a convention. 

Far from laying down a general prohibition to the effect that States may not extend the application of their laws and the jurisdiction of their courts to persons, property and acts outside their territory, it leaves them in this respect a wide measure

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

195 ts sp Inte da of discretion which is only limited in certain cases by prohibitive rules; as regards other cases, every State remains free to adopt the principles which it regards as best and most suitable. 

In these circumstances, all that can be required of a State is that it should not overstep the limits which international law places upon its jurisdiction; within these limits, its title to exercise jurisdiction rests in its sovereignty.

Though it is true that in all systems of law the principle of the territorial character of criminal law is fundamental, it is equally true that all or nearly all these systems of law extend their action to offences committed outside the territory of the State which adopts them, and they do so in ways which vary from State to State. The territoriality of criminal law, therefore, is not an absolute principle of international law and by no means coincides with territorial sovereignty. 

In determining whether general international law prohibited Turkey from prosecuting the French officer, the Court considered three arguments advanced by the French Government: First, that international law does not allow a state to take proceedings with regard to offenses committed by foreigners abroad, simply by reason of the nationality of the victim, and that in the case under consideration the offense was committed on board the French vessel; second, that international law recognizes the exclusive jurisdiction of the state whose flag is flown as regards everything occurring on board a ship on the high seas; and third, that this principle is especially applicable in a collision case. 

The Court rejected the first argument saying thatit is certain that the courts of many countries, even of countries which have given their criminal legislation a strictly territorial character, interpret criminal law in the sense that offences, the authors of which at the moment of commission are in the territory of another State, are nevertheless to be regarded as having been committed in the national territory, if one of the constituent elements of the offence, and more especially its effects, have taken place there.

As to the second argument, the Court concluded that "there is no rule of international law prohibiting the State to which the ship on which the effects of the offence have taken place belongs, from regarding the offence as having been committed in its territory and prosecuting, accordingly, the delinquent". In regard to the third argument, the court concluded that "there is no rule of international law in regard to collision cases to the effect that criminal proceedings are exclusively within the jurisdiction of the State whose flag is flown" and that this was a case of concurrent jurisdiction.

On the judgment as a whole the vote of the Court stood six to six, and the President gave a casting vote. Six dissenting opinions were 

---

filed. Mr. John Bassett Moore, in his dissenting opinion, stated that he concurred in the judgment of the Court that there is no rule of international law giving exclusive criminal jurisdiction in case of a collision at sea, resulting in loss of life, to the country of the ship by or by means of which the wrong was done. He declared, however, that he was unable to concur in the view that the international validity of article 6 of the Turkish Penal Code was not before the Court under the terms of the compromis and expressed the opinion that the jurisdictional claim of that article, that Turkey has a right to try and to. punish foreigners for acts committed in foreign countries not only against Turkey herself but also against Turks, if such foreigners are afterward found on Turkish territory, is contrary to well-settled principles of international law. He said:

No one disputes the right of a State to subject its citizens abroad to the operations of its own penal laws, if it sees fit to do so. This concerns simply the citizen and his own government, and no other government can properly interfere. But the case is fundamentally different where a country claims either that its penal laws apply to other countries and to what takes place wholly within such countries or, if it does not claim this, that it may punish foreigners for alleged violations, even in their own country, of laws to which they were not subject. 

He concluded thatthe criminal proceedings in the case now before the Court, so far as they rested on Article 6 of the Turkish Penal Code, were in conflict with the following principles of international law: (1) that the jurisdiction of a State over the national territory is exclusive; (2) that foreigners visiting a country are subject to the local law, and must look to the courts of that country for their judicial protection; (3) that a State cannot rightfully assume to punish foreigners for alleged infractions of laws to which they were not, at the time of the alleged offense, in any wise subject. 

Per. Ct. Int. Jus., Judgment 9, Sept. 7, 1927, Ser. A, No. 10, pp. 18, 19, 20, 23, 25, 30, 92-93, 94; II Hudson, World Court Reports (1935) 20, 35, 36, 38, 40, 44, 82, 83.

ACTS COMMITTED OUTSIDE OF THE TERRITORIAL JURISDIC- TION PUNISHABLE BY THE LAWS THEREOF 

$137 The case of United States v. Bowman was brought to the Supreme 

Court of the United States on writ of error for a review of the ruling of the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York sustaining a demurrer to an indictment for conspiracy to defraud the United States Shipping Board Emergency 

Fleet Corporation, under an act of Congress approved on October 23, 1918 (40 Stat. 1015). This act, which amended paragraph 35 of the United States Criminal Code, prescribes a penalty for the presentation of a false claim against the Government of the United States, knowingly, to any officer of the civil, military, or naval service or to any department thereof or any corporation in which the United States is a stockholder. It also penalizes connivance at such presentation by the use of any cheating device, as well as a conspiracy to these ends. The defendant, engineer of the steamship Dio belonging to the 

United States and operated by the National Shipping Corporation for the Emergency Fleet Corporation, together with others, was charged with conspiracy to defraud the Fleet Corporation by obtaining and aiding to obtain the payment and allowance of a false and fraudulent claim against it. The offense was laid in the first count the high seas; in the second, on the high seas and at the port of 

Rio de Janeiro as well as in that city; in the third, in the city of 

Rio de Janeiro; in the fourth, in the harbor of Rio de Janeiro on board the Dio; in the fifth, in that city; and in the sixth, at the port and in that city. Objection was made to the indictment on the ground that the crime was committed outside of the jurisdiction of the United States or any State thereof and on the high seas or within the jurisdiction of Brazil. The district court considered the first count and having held it bad for lack of jurisdiction sustained the demurrer to the other counts. In reversing the decision of the district court, the Supreme Court, Chief Justice Taft speaking, said: on We have in this case a question of statutory construction. 

The necessary locus, when not specially defined, depends upon the purpose of Congress as evinced by the description and nature of the crime and upon the territorial limitations upon the power and jurisdiction of a government to punish crime under the law of nations. Crimes against private individuals or their property, like assaults, murder, burglary, larceny, robbery, arson, embezzlement and frauds of all kinds, which affect the peace and good order of the community, must of course be committed within the territorial jurisdiction of the government where it may properly exercise it. If punishment of them is

Statutes not dependent on locality to be extended to include those committed outside of the strict territorial jurisdiction, it is natural for Congress to say so in the statute, and failure to do so will negative the purpose of Congress in this regard. We have an example of this in the attempted application of the prohibitions of the Anti-Trust Law to acts done by citizens of the United States against other such citizens in a foreign country. American Banana Co. v. United 

Fruit Co., 213 U.S. 347. That was a civil case, but as the statute is criminal as well as civil, it presents an analogy. 

But the same rule of interpretation should not be applied to criminal statutes which are, as a class, not logically dependent on their locality for the Government's jurisdiction, but are enacted because of the right of the Government to defend itself against obstruction, or fraud wherever perpetrated, especially if committed by its own citizens, officers or agents. Some such offenses can only be committed within the territorial jurisdiction of the Government because of the local acts required to constitute them. 

Others are such that to limit their locus to the strictly territorial jurisdiction would be greatly to curtail the scope and usefulness of the statute and leave open a large immunity for frauds as easily committed by citizens on the high seas and in foreign countries as at home. In such cases, Congress has not thought it necessary to make specific provision in the law that the locus shall include the high seas and foreign countries, but allows it to be inferred from the nature of the offense. Many of these occur in c. 4, which bears the title "Offenses against the operations of the Government". Section 70 of that chapter punishes whoever as consul knowingly certifies a false invoice. Clearly the locus of this crime as intended by Congress is in a foreign country and certainly the foreign country in which he discharges his official duty could not object to the trial in a United States court of a United States consul for crime of this sort committed within its borders. Forging or altering ship's papers is made a crime by $72 of c. 4. It would be going too far to say that because Congress does not fix any locus it intended to exclude the high seas in respect of this crime. The natural inference from the character of the offense is that the sea would be a probable place for its commission. Section 42 of c. 4 punishes enticing desertions from the naval service. Is it possible that

Congress did not intend by this to include such enticing done aboard ship on the high seas or in a foreign port, where it would be most likely to be done? Section 39 punishes bribing a United

States officer of the civil, military or naval service to violate his duty or to aid in committing a fraud on the United States. It is hardly reasonable to construe this not to include such offenses when the bribe is offered to a consul, ambassador, an army or a naval officer in a foreign country or on the high seas, whose duties are being performed there and when his connivance at much fraud must occur there. So, too, §38 of c. 4 punishes the wilfully doing or aiding to do any act relating to the bringing in, custody, sale or other disposition of property captured as prize, with intent to defraud, delay or injure the United States or any captor or claimant of such property. This would

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

199 naturally often occur at sea, and Congress could not have meant to confine it to the land of the United States. Again, in §36 of c. 4, it is made a crime to steal, embezzle, or knowingly apply to his own use ordnance, arms, ammunition, clothing, subsistence, stores, money or other property of the United States furnished or to be used for military or naval service. It would hardly be reasonable to hold that if any one, certainly if a citizen of the United States, were to steal or embezzle such property which may properly and lawfully be in the custody of army or naval officers either in foreign countries, in foreign ports or on the high seas, it would not be in such places an offense which Congress intended to punish by this section. 

We can not suppose that when Congress enacted the statute or amended it [40 Stat. 1015], it did not have in mind that a wide field for such frauds upon the Government was in private and public vessels of the United States on the high seas and in foreign ports and beyond the land jurisdiction of the United States, and therefore intend to include them in the section.

Section 41 of the Judicial Code provides that "the trial of all offenses committed upon the high seas, or elsewhere out of the jurisdiction of any particular State or district, shall be in the district where the offender is found, or into which he is first brought." The three defendants who were found in New 

York were citizens of the United States and were certainly subject to such laws as it might pass to protect itself and its property. Clearly it is no offense to the dignity or right of 

Sovereignty of Brazil to hold them for this crime against the government to which they owe allegiance. The other defendant is a subject of Great Britain. He has never been apprehended, and it will be time enough to consider what, if any, jurisdiction the District Court below has to punish him when he is brought to trial.

Harry M. Blackmer, an American citizen resident in France, was adjudged guilty of contempt of the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia for failure to respond to subpenas served upon him in France, requiring him to appear as a witness on behalf of the United States at a criminal trial in that court. A fine was imposed on him for failure to respond to the subpenas to be satisfied out of his property which had been seized by the court. The subpenas were issued and served and the contempt proceedings taken under the act approved July 3, 1926 (44 Stat. 835), providing that whenever the attendance at a criminal trial of a witness abroad who is an American citizen or domiciled in the United States is desired by the Attorney General, or any assistant or district attorney acting under him, the 

Subpena as witness in U.S. of citizen abroad

judge of the court in which the action is pending may order a subpena to issue, to be addressed to an American Consul and to be served by him personally upon the witness with a tender of traveling expenses. Upon proof of such service and of the failure of the witness to appear, an order may issue requiring the witness to show cause why he should not be punished for contempt, and upon the issue of such an order property belonging to the witness and within the United States may be seized and held to satisfy any judgment which may be rendered against him. If the charge is sustained, the witness may be adjudged guilty of contempt, and a fine not exceeding $100,000 may be imposed upon him to be satisfied by a sale of the property seized.

The Supreme Court of the United States affirmed the decrees of the Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia which had affirmed the decision of the Supreme Court of the District. The Court said: 

While it appears that the petitioner removed his residence to France in the year 1924, it is undisputed that he was, and continued to be, a citizen of the United States. He continued to owe allegiance to the United States. By virtue of the obligations of citizenship, the United States retained its authority over him, and he was bound by its laws made applicable to him in a foreign country. While the legislation of the Congress, unless the contrary intent appears, is construed to apply only within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States, the question of its application, so far as citizens of the United States in foreign countries are concerned, is one of construction, not of legislative power. American Banana Co. v. United Fruit Co., 213 U.S. 347, 357; United States v. Bowman, supra [260 U.S. 

94]; Robertson v. Labor Board, 268 U.S. 619, 622. Nor can it be doubted that the United States possesses the power inherent in sovereignty to require the return to this country of a citizen, resident elsewhere, whenever the public interest requires it, and to penalize him in case of refusal. Compare Bartue and the 

Duchess of Suffolk's Case, 2 Dyer's Rep. 176b, 73 Eng. Rep. 388; 

Knowles v. Luce, Moore 109, 72 Eng. Rep. 473. It is also beyond controversy that one of the duties which the citizen owes to his government is to support the administration of justice by attending its courts and giving his testimony whenever he is properly summoned. Blair v. United States, 250 U.S. 273, 281.

And the Congress may provide for the performance of this duty and prescribe penalties for disobedience.

In the present instance, the question concerns only the method of enforcing the obligation. The jurisdiction of the United 

States over its absent citizen, so far as the binding effect of its legislation is concerned, is a jurisdiction in personam, as he is personally bound to take notice of the laws that are applicable to him and to obey them. The question of the validity of the provision for actual service of the subpoena in a foreign country is one that arises solely between the Government of the United States and the citizen. The mere giving of such a

EXTRATERRITORIAL CRIME 

201 notice to the citizen in the foreign country of the requirement of his government that he shall return is in no sense an invasion of any right of the foreign government; and the citizen has no standing to invoke any such supposed right. While consular privileges in foreign countries are the appropriate subjects of treaties, it does not follow that every act of a consul, as e.g., in communicating with citizens of his own country, must be predicated upon a specific provision of a treaty. 

Blackmer v. United States, 284 U.S. (1932) 421, 436, 437, 438, 439.

In the case of United States ex rel. Majka v. Palmer an appeal was taken from an order dismissing a petition for habeas corpus. 

The relator, one Stanislaus Majka, had made certain false statements in respect to his application for a passport before the American Consul in Warsaw, Poland. He admitted before an immigrantinspector that he had made these statements and that he understood that that constituted the crime of perjury, and he had been consequently ordered deported on the ground that he had committed a crime involving moral turpitude. He thereupon filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. outside of U.S. 

The circuit court of appeals, in affirming the dismissal of the peti- "Perjury" tion, refused to sustain the contention of the relator that the definition of perjury in the United States was not applicable where the act was committed outside of its own territorial boundaries. The court relied on section 1750 of the Revised Statutes giving to every notarial act done before any consular officer within the limits of his consulate the same force and effect as if done in the United States and providing that, in the case of perjury, the offender may be proceeded against in any district of the United States in the same manner as if the offense had been committed within the United States. 

The court said thatit seems clear to us that when he did enter the United States, thereby making use of the fraudulent passport for the very purpose for which the crime was committed, he placed himself within the control of its laws and subjected himself to whatever proceedings it might see fit to bring as the result of his criminal act. It therefore becomes immaterial to determine whether or not perjury is held to be a crime in Poland, since the crime admitted was committed against the United States. Being a crime involving moral turpitude it may be the basis for deportation proceedings. 

In regard to the relator's contention that the crime was not complete until he set foot upon United States territory and therefore was not committed prior to his entry into the United States, the court said: 

The crime was completed when he made the false statements concerning a material matter under oath administered by

Accepting bribe in foreign country "Committed an officer of the United States empowered by it to administer that oath. ... A crime against the United States committed outside its territorial boundaries but within the limits of its consular jurisdiction may also be reason for deporting the alien, particularly where, as in this case, the act made it possible for him to enter and it might otherwise have been impossible for him to do so. 

67 F. (2d) 146 (C.C.A. 7th, 1933).

Sir Roger Casement was convicted of treason against the British King in the King's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice. 

The indictment charged him with "adhering to the King's enemies elsewhere than in the King's realm, to wit, in the Empire of Germany, contrary to the Treason Act, 1351 (25 Edw. 3, stat. 5, c. 2)". The words of that statute were thus paraphrased by the court: 

It shall be treason if a man do levy war against our Lord the King in his realm or be adherent to the King's enemies in his realm, giving to them aid and comfort in the realm or elsewhere.

203 

Lord Reading, C.J., said: Treason

But I have no hesitation myself in stating that if a man adhere to the King's enemies without the realm he is com- "without the mitting the offence of treason; and that he is committing the realm" offence of treason at common law, notwithstanding that the offence is committed without the realm. 

My view is that it is an offence to adhere within the realm or without the realm to the King's enemies, and it is equally an offence to adhere within the realm to the King's enemies by giving them aid and comfort without the realm. 

The court of criminal appeal, on July 17, 1917, dismissed an appeal from the judgment. Darling, J., said:

We think that the meaning of these words is this: "giving aid and comfort to the King's enemies" are words in apposition; they are words to explain what is meant by being adherent to, and we think that if a man be adherent to the King's enemies in his realm by giving to them aid or comfort in his realm, or if he be adherent to the King's enemies elsewhere, that is by giving them aid or comfort elsewhere, he is equally adherent to the King's enemies, and if he is adherent to the King's enemies, then he commits the treason which the statute of Edward III. defines. 

The King v. Casement, [1917] 1 K.B. 98, 122, 123, 129, 137.

§138 of Italians for crimes in U.S. 

The Government of Italy refuses to surrender its subjects for Prosecution prosecution in the United States for crimes committed in the United States. It has been willing, however, to try and to punish Italian subjects, fugitives from justice in the United States, under its penal

laws, which give Italian courts jurisdiction over crimes of a certain category committed by Italian subjects outside of Italy. Penal Code (1889), art. 5; ibid. (1930) art. 9. The procedure in such cases was explained to the Governor of Illinois by the Acting Secretary of State as follows in a letter written in response to a request for the extradition from Italy of one Antonio Minella, who was charged with murder in Illinois:

In a case occurring more than fifteen years ago, the Italian Government refused, on the ground of nationality, to surrender certain of its subjects charged with a murder in this country, but accompanied its refusal with an offer to try and punish the fugitives under Italian law. Since then this Department has not requested of Italy the surrender of Italian subjects, but in many cases their punishment in Italy has been secured at its suggestion. 

If you desire to endeavor to secure the punishment of this fugitive in the manner suggested, and will so indicate to the Department, it will be glad to telegraph the Embassy at Rome to request the Italian Government provisionally to arrest the fugitive with a view to his trial and punishment in that country. 

You should then furnish the Department, as soon as possible, for presentation to that Government, with properly authenticated evidence sufficient to obtain the conviction of the fugitive. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to Governor Deneen, Mar. 22, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 5240.

$139 The first paragraph of article VII of the treaty of friendship, commerce, and consular rights of 1923 between the United States and 

Germany provides: 

Between the territories of the High Contracting Parties there shall be freedom of commerce and navigation. The nationals of each of the High Contracting Parties equally with those of the most favored nation, shall have liberty freely to come with their vessels and cargoes to all places, ports and waters of every kind within the territorial limits of the other which are or may be open to foreign commerce and navigation. Nothing in this treaty shall be construed to restrict the right of either High Contracting Party to impose, on such terms as it may see fit, prohibitions or restrictions of a sanitary character designed to protect human, animal or plant life, or regulations for the enforcement of police or revenue laws.

Britain on July 3, 1815. 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 624; 8 Stat. 228.

Cf. article 2 of the statute on the international régime of maritime ports annexed to the convention signed at Geneva on December 9, 1923, to which

Although a neutral may grant asylum to belligerent men-ofwar in his ports, he has no duty to do so. He may prohibit all belligerent men-of-war from entering any of his ports, whether these vessels are pursued by the enemy, or desire to enter for other reasons. However, his duty of impartiality must prevent him from denying to one party what he grants to the other; he may not, therefore, allow men-of-war of one belligerent to enter his ports and exclude men-of-war of the other belligerent (Article 9 of Convention XIII [signed at The Hague in 1907]).

With regard to documents issued by "Manchukuo" and vessels which may carry a "Manchukuoan" flag, it is believed that, inasmuch as the American Government has not recognized "Manchukuo", and because of various other political factors and of undesirable developments which might ensue upon and follow from such an entry into our ports of a tanker operating under "Manchukuoan" documents and flying a "Manchukuoan" flag, the entry of such a vessel into our ports should be discouraged by all legitimate means.

JURISDICTION OVER MERCHANT VESSELS CRIMINAL JURISDICTION 

$140 In the case of Cunard Steamship Company, Ltd., et al. v. Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, et al. the Supreme Court of the United 

States held that the eighteenth amendment to the Constitution and the National Prohibition Act (41 Stat. 305) were applicable to foreign and domestic ships within the territorial waters of the United States and that neither the amendment nor the act was intended to apply to domestic vessels when outside of the territorial waters of this country. The Court said:

A merchant ship of one country voluntarily entering the territorial limits of another subjects herself to the jurisdiction of the latter. The jurisdiction attaches in virtue of her presence, just as with other objects within those limits. During her stay she is entitled to the protection of the laws of that place and correlatively is bound to yield obedience to them. Of course, the local sovereign may out of considerations of public policy choose to forego the exertion of its jurisdiction or to exert the same in only a limited way, but this is a matter resting solely in its discretion. 

262 U.S. (1923) 100, 124. On Nov. 1, 1920 the Acting Attorney General had expressed the opinion that the National Prohibition Act applied to persons "on board American ships, whether in American waters, on the high seas, or in foreign waters equally with those in any of the States of the United States". 32 Op. Att. Gen. (1919-21) 332, 336.

On March 23, 1914 the British Ambassador addressed an inquiry to the Department of State requesting information as to "the law and practice of the United States in regard to the exercise of criminal and civil jurisdiction (a) by the United States over foreign ships and

persons on board them in United States waters, and (b) in foreign territorial waters over members of the crew by the master of a private ship, sailing under the United States flag, or by any other person acting under the authority of the United States". The Counselor for the Department, in reply, cited Wildenhus's Case, 120 U.S. (1887) 

1, in the matter of criminal jurisdiction exercised by American courts over foreign ships in American territorial waters and over persons on board such vessels, and with respect to civil jurisdiction in cases involving the rights of foreign vessels or persons connected with them he cited the case of The Carolina, 14 Fed. 424 (D. La., 1876), and the cases cited in the opinion of the court in the case of The Ester, 190 Fed. 216, 220-221 (E.D.S.C., 1911). 

The Counselor said further:

With reference to the question of the jurisdiction over American merchant vessels in foreign territorial waters, it may be stated that the Government of the United States in the past has asserted in behalf of its vessels the right which, as indicated by the judicial decisions to which attention has been called, are accorded to foreign vessels in waters of the United States. This Government, while conceding on the one hand that, when one of its vessels visits the port of another country for the purposes of trade, it is amenable to the jurisdiction of that country and is subject to the laws which govern the port it visits so long as it remains unless it is otherwise provided by treaty, has, on the other hand, on a number of occasions, made clear its views to the effect that, by comity, matters of discipline and all things done on board which affect only the vessel or those belonging to her and do not involve the peace or dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port should be left by the local government to be dealt with by the authorities of the nation to which the vessel belongs, as the laws of that nation or the interests of its commerce may require. 

Private vessels belonging to this country are deemed parts of its territory. They are accordingly regarded as subject to the jurisdiction of this country, on the high seas, and in foreign ports, even though they admittedly are also temporarily subject generally to the laws of such ports. 

In this connection he cited the case of United States v. Rodgers, 150 U.S. (1893) 249. 

The Ambassador's attention was invited to treaties concluded by the Government of the United States in respect to consular jurisdiction over questions of wages, shipment, and discharge of seamen and over all transactions occurring on board vessels lying in foreign ports, whether in the nature of contracts, torts, or crimes, so far as they concerned only the vessels or their cargoes and the persons on board and did not concern the public peace of the country or the rights of persons not belonging on board, and to the following cases:

Counselor Lansing to Ambassador Spring Rice, no. 355, May 19, 1914, MS. Department of State, file 800.858/3. See also 1914 For. Rel. 307-316 and article XXIII of the commercial treaty of 1923 between the United

Paragraph 2 of article 12 of the consular convention between the United States and Germany of 1871 provided that no examination or search of merchant vessels by judicial authorities and customhouse officials should be made without previous notice to the consular officers of the nation to which such vessels belonged. Paragraph 

3 provided for the giving of "due notice to the said consular officers, in order to enable them to be present at any depositions or statements to be made in courts of law or before local magistrates, by officers or persons belonging to the crew, thus preventing errors or false interpretations which might impede correct administration of justice". 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 550, 554.

In 1914 two seamen from the German steamship Hornsund were sentenced on a charge of disorderly conduct to 30 days in jail or a $25 fine by the police court of Baltimore. On June 12 and December 

29, 1914 the German Ambassador wrote to the Secretary of State complaining that notice of the proceedings against the seamen was not given to the appropriate consular officers in accordance with paragraph 3 of article 12 of the convention of 1871. The Ambassador said:

In the Imperial Government's opinion paragraphs 2 and 3 of Article 12, of which the first deals with the examination and search of vessels and the other with the examination of members of the crew are regarded as independent of each other. On the one hand paragraph 3 directs that previous notice [of the examination] be given to Consuls expressly in every case [in order to enable them to be present] "(at any statements or depositions)" of the officers or persons belonging to the crew of the vessel concerned in courts of law or before other local magistrates. On the other hand the treaty does not either in its wording, its spirit or its substance [afford] any ground whatever to assume that such notice is required in such cases only as are involved in the examination and search of vessels as contemplated in paragraph 2.

The declared purpose of the notice to the Consuls as expressed in paragraph 3, "to prevent errors or false interpretations which might impede the correct administration of justice" rather indicates that no such limitation was intended. The intent of the requirement that timely notice be given to the Consular Officer was rather to secure, in the interest of a correct administration of justice, that officer in the exercise of his right to intervene in behalf of the seafaring class, which is guaranteed to him by paragraph 1, in all cases of judicial examination of seamen. 

The Secretary replied on February 19, 1915 thatwithout particular reference to the case set forth in Your Excellency's note of June 12, 1914, this Government, in the absence of any judicial decision directly applicable to the question under consideration, is not disposed to disagree with your Government's interpretation of the treaty as set forth in Your Excellency's note under acknowledgment.

The German Ambassador, Count von Bernstorff, to Secretary Bryan, 

Dec. 29, 1914, and Mr. Bryan to Count von Bernstorff, no. 1251, Feb. 19, 1915, MS. Department of State, file 711.6221/108.

On April 27, 1907, while the Spanish vessel Viviana was anchored in the harbor of Pensacola, Florida, the cook killed a steward on Breach of board ship. The Spanish Vice Consul ordered the cook delivered peace, etc. into the custody of the examining magistrate of Pensacola at the request of the magistrate. He later asked that he be brought back to the vessel to be taken to Spain and was informed by the magistrate that he had already been tried, found "not guilty" by an American jury, and released. The matter was brought to the attention of the Department of State by the Spanish Minister on November 29, 1910, with the statement that the failure to return the accused to the Vice Consul was a manifest misinterpretation of the provisions of article 23 of the treaty of friendship and general relations of 1902 between the United States and Spain, providing for consular jurisdiction over the internal order of merchant vessels and over differences between officers and crews. The Department replied that article 23 of the treaty provided that the local authorities might interfere when disorder on board a vessel was of such a nature as to cause or be likely to cause a breach of the peace or serious trouble in the port or on shore. It stated that there would appear to be no question but that the killing of one human being by another was "a disorder of such a nature as to cause, or be likely to cause a breach of the peace or serious trouble in the port or on shore". The Department cited 

Wildenhus's Case, 120 U. S. (1887) 1, and expressed the opinion that the case under discussion came clearly within the cognizance of the

local authorities and that there was no infringement of the treaty provisions. 

Secretary Knox to Minister Riaño, no. 22, Dec. 7, 1910, MS. Department of State, fille 711.5211/-. See also 1910 For. Rel. 851-855.

On Nov. 2, 1920 the Department of State informed the American 

Minister in Cuba that, in its opinion, "while American merchant vessels in Cuban ports are amenable to the jurisdiction of that country and subject to the laws thereof, acts committed thereon which do not involve the peace and dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port should by comity be left to be dealt with by the authorities of the United States". 

The Minister was instructed to endeavor to adjust with the Cuban authorities questions relating to jurisdiction over offenses committed on American vessels in Cuban waters, in the light of these suggestions and in the light of the principle set forth in the Department's instruction to the Consul at

In response to representations made by the Minister the Cuban Foreign Office stated that it was desirous of having all cases connected with acts committed on board American vessels in Cuban ports not involving the peace and dignity of the country or the tranquility of the port left to the jurisdiction of the American authorities but that it had not been the practice theretofore for Cuba to surrender jurisdiction in such cases and, further, that the Cuban Department of Justice was apparently unwilling to surrender jurisdiction to foreign authorities in such cases in the absence of treaty provisions to

that effect. The Department of State instructed the Minister on Dec. 6, 1920 to bring the facts to the attention of the Cuban President and to say that, while his Government recognized that when a merchant vessel visited a foreign port for the purpose of trade it was, generally speaking, amenable to the local jurisdiction and subject to the laws governing the port it visited so long as it remained unless it was otherwise provided by treaty, it was of the opinion that by the recognized comity of nations matters of discipline and all things done on board affecting only the vessel or those belonging to her and not involving the peace or dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port should be left by the local government to be dealt with by the authorities of the nation to which the vessel belonged, as the laws of that nation or the interests of its commerce might require.

In all other cases, not expressly provided for by the laws of foreigners (Ley de extranjeria), the Fiscal of the Supreme Court instructed the judges to declare that they were brought in error and to place them within the knowledge of the consuls of the nations to which the ships belonged.
