Concurrent jurisdiction A writ of error was sued out in the Supreme Court of the United States from a judgment and sentence of death for a murder committed on board the steamer Rosecrans, an American vessel, while lying in the harbor of Honolulu in the Territory of Hawaii. That Court held that the second paragraph of section 5339 of the Revised Statutes of the United States relating to murder committed". upon the high seas, or in any arm of the sea, or in any river, haven, creek, basin, or bay within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States, and out of the jurisdiction of any particular State", conferred jurisdiction in the case under consideration upon the District Court of the United States for the Territory of Hawaii and that the harbor of Honolulu was "out of the jurisdiction of any particular 

State". The Court said:

If it be true, as claimed, that the territorial courts exercise jurisdiction over homicides in the harbor of Honolulu, under and by virtue of the laws of Hawaii thus continued in force, it only establishes that there may be concurrent jurisdiction in respect of certain crimes when committed in certain places, and is far from establishing that the courts of the Union have been deprived of a jurisdiction which they have at all times claimed and exercised over certain offenses when committed upon the high seas, or in any arm of the sea, or in any river, basin, haven, creek or bay within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States and out of the jurisdiction of any particular State. 

Wynne v. United States, 217 U.S. (1910) 234, 245.

In May 1930 two American seamen on board the American steamship Winding Gulf, which was moored alongside the wharf at Georgetown, Prince Edward Island, were reported to have assaulted another seaman on board the steamship. The Department of State informed the Consul at 

Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, on May 28, 1930, that the Department of Justice held that the United States courts would have jurisdiction to try the case if the accused were returned to this country. Such return was usually advisable, it was said, for the sake of convenience to witnesses and to avoid interference with the itinerary of the ship. It was stated, however, that, since the Canadian authorities desired to try the case and this was agreeable to the master of the ship, the Department withdrew a proposal previously made by it that the trial should be held in the United States. 

The Secretary of State (Stimson) to the Consul at Charlottetown, May 28, 1930 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 195.8 Winding Gulf.

In the case of United States v. Flores, an American citizen had been indicted in the United States District Court for the murder of another American citizen on board the American vessel Padnsay, while at anchor in the port of Matadi in the Belgian Congo and attached to the shore by cables, at a point 250 miles inland from the mouth of the 

Congo River. Section 272 of the Criminal Code makes punishable

offenses defined by other sections thereof, among other circumstances "when committed within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States and out of the jurisdiction of any particular state, on board any vessel belonging in whole or in part to the United States" or any of its nationals. The district court, following its decision in 

United States ex rel. Maro v. Mathues, 21 F. (2d) 533 (E. D. Pa., 

1927), affirmed, 27 F. (2d) 518 (C.C.A. 3d, 1928), sustained a demurrer to the indictment and discharged the prisoner on the ground that the court was without jurisdiction to try the offense charged. Upon appeal the Supreme Court of the United States considered two questions, first, whether the extension of the judicial power of the Federal Government "to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction" by article III, section 2, of the Constitution conferred on Congress power to define and punish offenses perpetrated by a citizen of the United States on board one of its merchant vessels lying in navigable waters within the territorial limits of another sovereignty; and, secondly, whether Congress had exercised that power by the enactment of section 

272 of the Criminal Code. The Court said: 

The appellee insists that even though Congress has power to define and punish crimes on American vessels in foreign waters, it has not done so by the present statute since the criminal jurisdiction of the United States is based upon the territorial principle and the statute cannot rightly be interpreted to be à departure from that principle. But the language of the statute making it applicable to offenses committed on an American vessel outside the jurisdiction of a State "within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States" is broad enough to include crimes in the territorial waters of a foreign sovereignty.

It is true that the criminal jurisdiction of the United States is in general based on the territorial principle, and criminal statutes of the United States are not by implication given an extra-territorial effect. United States v. Bowman, 260 U.S. 94, 98; compare Blackmer v. United States, 284 U.S. 421. But that prínciple has never been thought to be applicable to a merchant vessel which, for purposes of the jurisdiction of the courts of the sovereignty whose flag it flies to punish crimes committed upon it, is deemed to be a part of the territory of that Sovereignty, and not to lose that character when in navigable waters within the territorial limits of another sovereignty. 

United States v. Rodgers, supra [150 U.S. (1893) 249]; compare 

Thomas v. Lane, 2 Sumner 1; Queen v. Anderson, supra [L. R. 1

Crown Cases Reserved 161]; Queen v. Carr & Wilson,_supra [10 Q.B.D. 76]; Rex. v. Allen, supra [1 Moody C.C. 494] Rex. v. 

Jemot, supra [1 Russell on Crimes, 4th ed. 153]. This qualification of the territorial principle in the case of vessels of the flag was urged by Mr. Webster while Secretary of State, in his letter to Lord Ashburton of August 1, 1842, quoted with approval in 

United States v. Rodgers, supra, 264, 265. Subject to the right

of the territorial sovereignty to assert jurisdiction over offenses disturbing the peace of the port, it has been supported by writers on international law, and has been recognized by France, Belgium, and other continental countries, as well as by England and the United States. See Moore, International Law Digest, Vol. 

2, 287, 297; Fiore, International Law Codified, translated by E. 

M. Borchard, 192, 193; Wheaton, International Law, Vol. I, 245; 

Hall, International Law, 8th ed. 253-258; Jessup, The Law of 

Territorial Waters, 144-193.

In view of the wide recognition of this principle of extraterritorial jurisdiction over crimes committed on merchant vessels and its explicit adoption in United States v. Rodgers, supra, we cannot say that the language of the present statute punishing offenses on United States vessels out of the jurisdiction of a State, "when committed within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States," was not intended to give effect to it. 

A related but different question, not presented here, may arise when jurisdiction over an offense committed on a foreign vessel is asserted by the sovereignty in whose waters it was lying at the time of its commission, since for some purposes the jurisdiction may be regarded as concurrent, in that the courts of either sovereignty may try the offense.

The Court concluded: 

In the absence of any controlling treaty provision, and any assertion of jurisdiction by the territorial sovereign, it is the duty of the courts of the United States to apply to offenses committed by its citizens on vessels flying its flag, its own statutes, interpretated in the light of recognized principles of international law. So applied the indictment here sufficiently charges an offense within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States and the judgment below must be Reversed. 

289 U.S. (1933) 137, 155-157, 159.

In the case of In re Eduardo Henke the accused, a Brazilian member of the crew of the Brazilian merchant vessel Guandú, killed another member of the crew, also a Brazilian, in the port of Marseilles. Proceedings were instituted against him in France, but upon the request of the Brazilian Consul he was turned over to the Brazilian authorities. In criminal proceedings against him in Brazil the Supreme Federal Tribunal upheld the jurisdiction of the Brazilian courts, under article 14 of law 2416, June 28, 1911, making punishable crimes committed abroad by a Brazilian against Brazilians where the penalty is at least two years imprisonment. 

Diario oficial (Sept. 4, 1921) 17078; Annual Digest, 1919-22, Case No. 108. 

In 1934 it was reported that the chief officer of the American ship Exchange was killed on board that ship by the chief engineer, Martin De Mott, while the vessel was in the port of Messina, Italy. The 

Department of Justice, on December 8, 1934, informed the Secretary of State that, under the authority of the case of United States v. 

Flores, 289 U.S. (1933) 137, it had no doubt of the jurisdiction of the 

United States District Court of the district into which the offender

was first brought, or in which he was found, of his person and of the subject matter. On the other hand, it was said, under Wildenhus's Case, 120 U.S. (1887) 1, that the right of the Italian authorities to hold and to try the offender was clearly established. The 

Department of State informed the American Embassy in Rome that the American Export Line, to which the steamship Exchange belonged, desired the return of De Mott to the United States for trial and that there was concurrent jurisdiction in the case. The Embassy was instructed to ascertain whether the Italian Government would be willing to surrender De Mott if arrangements could be made for his trial in the United States. Subsequently the Embassy informed the Department that the Italian Foreign Office had informed it that, as the crime took place in Italian territorial waters and on board a merchant vessel, the judicial authorities of Italy had jurisdiction of the case under article 6 of the Italian Penal Code and that, consequently, De Mott must be tried in Italy and undergo sentence there if found guilty. 

Assistant Attorney General Keenan to Secretary Hull, Dec. 8, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 195.8 De Mott, Martin/3; the Under Secretary of State (Phillips) to the Embassy in Rome, telegram 103, Dec. 11, 1934, ibid. 195.8 De Mott, Martin/7; the Counselor of Embassy (Kirk) to

In the case of Johnson Plazen the defendant, an American citizen and a member of the crew of a British steamer, had killed another member of the crew of that vessel, a British subject, on board the vessel in the port of Limón, Costa Rica. Paragraph 4 of article 219 of the Penal Code of Costa Rica gives jurisdiction to the Costa Rican courts in respect to offenses on board a foreign merchant vessel in the waters of Costa Rica "when the offender, the victim or both do not belong to the personnel of the crew, or when, both being members of it, the offence has affected the port or littoral". The Court of Cassation of Costa Rica upheld the 

Jurisdiction of the Costa Rican courts in this case, stating that the public authorities of Limón had to take cognizance of the act since the vessel was moored to one of the piers in that port and the deceased was transferred to a hospital there. Sentencias de la Corte de Casacion (2d sess., 1928) 711; Annual Digest, 1927-28, Case No. 99.

The police authorities at Rio de Janeiro arrested and imprisoned two American seamen on account of minor offenses committed by them on the American vessel Margaret Thomas on December 25, 1908.

The arrests of the seamen were made at the instance of a Brazilian revenue officer who was on board the vessel at the time and who did not approve of the action of the captain in placing in irons one of the seamen who was in such a state of intoxication as to be dangerous. 

However, the men were subsequently released at the request of the Arrest of American foreign port seamen in a

Internal discipline Consul General. In an instruction to the Ambassador the Department of State said:

No treaty or agreement of any character appears to have been entered into by the United States and Brazil governing the matter of the jurisdiction over offenses committed on board a vessel of either country in a port of the other, and the question, therefore, seems to be a much disputed one. A decree of November 

8, 1851, as cited in Moore's International Law Digest, regulates the jurisdictional rights of consuls in Brazil and concedes to them cognizance in certain civil and criminal matters arising between members of crews of vessels of their respective countries, 

"When a foreign merchant vessel shall be lying within any of the ports of Brazil the criminal and police jurisdiction of the respective consular agents shall not extend to high crimes or to those that may in any manner disturb public tranquil [1]ity or particularly affect any inhabitant of the country.' 

Whether this concession might be construed as a partial or complete surrender of jurisdiction to consular officers by the local authorities seems not to be well settled, but when the seamen mentioned herein were turned over to the consul general upon his demand that they be released the local officers appear to have recognized the authority of the consular officer in such cases, in accordance with the decree hereinbefore cited. The consul general's action, therefore, appears to have been proper under the circumstances.

It is desired that this matter be brought to the attention of the Brazilian foreign office, in order that an undesirable precedent may not be claimed for the arbitrary act of the revenue officer in forbidding the captain of the vessel to place the dangerous seamen in irons. There appears not to have been any pretense of exercise of local jurisdiction. The seamen were arbitrarily taken from the captain's jurisdiction by the police on the revenue officer's order, without judicial process, and were promptly returned to the ship when the circumstances were made known to the competent authorities. The department considers that this was sufficient amends and you are further requested to advise the Brazilian Government that it is so accepted, but that the arbitrary interference of the revenue and police authorities with the internal discipline of a vessel and with the rights of the master thereof, as generally recognized by international law and usage, having been disavowed and corrected by the return of the men to the captain's jurisdiction, the incident is satisfactorily ended, and the case can not, from any point of view, be deemed to create a precedent for similar unwarranted interference in the future.

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Ambassador Dudley, Nov. 4, 

1909, MS. Department of State, file 17753/3. See also 1909 For. Rel. 41.

The Mexican Ambassador inquired of the Department of State, in August 1911, whether the Government of the United States would promise reciprocity to the Government of Mexico in cases in which the Mexican courts declined to exercise their jurisdiction of offenses committed on board American vessels in Mexican ports when both the offender and the sufferer belonged to the crew and the peace of the port had not been disturbed, it being provided in section 3 of article 189 of the Penal Code of the United Mexican States that action in such cases should be determined by the rule of reciprocity. 

The Department replied that "in the absence of a treaty stipulation, the jurisdiction over offenses against the peace of a port is, under the laws of the United States, lodged in the local authorities, to exercise their jurisdiction without, as a rule, any constraint by the Federal Executive". Under these circumstances, it was said, any arrangements of lower dignity than a treaty would not be binding on local officers and would not, as such, be enforcible by the Federal Executive. However, the Department continued, it seemed that the stipulation which the Ambassador desired was rendered unnecessary so far as the United States was concerned, in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Wildenhus's Case, 120 U.S. (1887) 1, which recognized the jurisdiction of the nation to which a vessel belonged over matters affecting only the vessel or those belonging to her and not involving the peace or dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port in which the vessel was found. It was suggested that, waiving what might be regarded as the international right in the matter and looking at the question solely from the standpoint of reciprocity, it would seem that vessels of the United States would, while in Mexican ports, be entitled to enjoy freedom from local jurisdiction in the matters named in Wildenhus's Case, since Mexican vessels in American ports would enjoy the exemption indicated in that case.

The Mexican Ambassador wrote to the Department on October 18, 1911 informing it that the Attorney General of Mexico accepted the proposition of the Department and, consequently, would cause the dismissal of judicial proceedings against the perpetrator of manslaughter committed on board an American merchant vessel in the port of Salina Cruz. The Department replied on October 26, 1911 that, though it was not advised of the details of that incident, it would appear from the Ambassador's description that the manslaughter was committed on board an American merchant vessel while that vessel was in the port of Salina Cruz and that in all probability the port authorities of the United States, in a reciprocal case, would insist upon taking jurisdiction of the offender and punishing him according to local law, since this would most likely be regarded as a crime "of a character to disturb the peace and tranquillity of the 157511-41-15

country to which the vessel has been brought". The Department stated that it made this announcement in order that the position of the United States Government might be entirely clear beforehand. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to the Mexican Ambassador 

(Crespo), no. 29, Aug. 31, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 812.858; the 

Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to Señor Crespo, no. 53, Oct. 26, 1911, ibid. 812.858/1. 

In May 1923 the American Vice Consul at Manzanillo, Mexico, refused to deliver to the captain of the port an American seaman, a citizen of Mexico, who was reported to have assaulted another American seamen aboard an American vessel in that port, on the ground that the assault was committed on an American vessel and that it in no way affected the peace and dignity of the port. The 

Mexican authorities did not insist upon their request for custody of the seaman, and the captain of the port considered the matter closed upon learning that the Vice Consul had settled the affair on board the vessel. The Department of State informed the Vice Consul on 

June 19, 1923 that, in cases of offenses on American vessels involving only members of the crew of the vessel, the settlement of the matter was usually left to the American authorities by comity of nations. 

However, it was said, if in spite of this practice the Mexican authorities should insist on jurisdiction in such cases there seemed to be no authority to justify the Vice Consul in refusing their demand. The 

Vice Consul was instructed that if, in the future, a similar case should arise in which the competent Mexican authorities requested the delivery to them of an offender against Mexican law where the offense had been committed within Mexican territorial waters on an American vessel, he should inform the appropriate Mexican authorities of the circumstances and of his understanding that the settlement of the matter should be left to American authorities, urging at the same time that the latter be permitted to assume jurisdiction. He was instructed that he should not make a formal refusal to deliver an offender but that if the Mexican authorities persisted in their attitude he should consult the Department of State by telegraph and inform the Mexican authorities that he had taken up the matter with his Government and must await instructions. 

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Vice Consul Aguirre, June 19, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 195.8/655.

In 1919 the Department of State instructed the Ambassador in Buenos Aires, with reference to the arrest of three American seamen on board an American schooner in that port by the Argentine authorities, that if the offense affected only the interior discipline of the ship without disturbing the tranquillity of the port, he should insist

on recognition by the Argentine authorities of consular jurisdiction in accordance with international practice on the ground of comity and convenience in commercial intercourse and that he should pursue this course in other cases that might arise.

In a note addressed to the American Ambassador on November 21, 1919 the Argentine Minister of Foreign Affairs reviewed certain instances where seamen on American vessels had been arrested by Argentine authorities and asserted that these had occurred as the result of denouncements by officers of the vessels. The Department of State instructed the Ambassador as follows: 

In his note of November 21, 1919, the Argentine Foreign 

Minister makes the following statement: "In conclusion I take pleasure in expressing to Your Excellency that the principles to which your Excellency_refers-of leaving to the authority on board and to the consular officials of the nation to which the vessel belongs the vigilance and control of matters which affect the internal discipline of the vessels are those which inspire the Argentine Government, and which it applies in the waters and ports of its jurisdiction; always providing, as I have stated, that the disturbances do not affect the peace or public order, or that the intervention of the authorities is not solicited." 

In your reply of November 26, 1919, you make the following statement: "I am in some doubt as to whether the mere invitation of a member of a crew of a ship to the police authorities to intervene is of itself sufficient justification, at least against the objection of the Consul General. Your Excellency will see that in such case the result may be that the Argentine police would have to intervene whenever there was any dispute between a ship's captain and a member of the crew. The Consul General is naturally desirous of obtaining full authority over the American seamen, who are now coming down here in such great numbers, and in the interest of the peace of the port; and Your Excellency will also note that neither the Consul General nor the captain of the vessel can maintain this authority if any disorderly member of the ship's crew can at any moment invoke the intervention of the shore police. I trust, therefore, that this matter will be considered when the police are carrying out their instructions." 

The principal question involved in the correspondence mentioned above is whether the Argentine authorities are always justified in arresting and trying American seamen when their intervention is requested by the Master, one of the other officers, or a member of the crew. It is the Department's opinion that such a request does not necessarily warrant the Argentine official to whom it is addressed in making an arrest, although it doubtless does warrant him in making an investigation. If, after such investigation as seems necessary, it appears that there has

In the case of In re Jorge Alejandro Jackson the Federal Court of Appeal of Argentina affirmed a judgment of the court of first instance holding, in the trial for homicide of a member of the crew of an English merchant vessel in the port of Buenos Aires who had subsequently fled ashore, that the Argentine court had jurisdiction over the crime as soon as the criminal came of his own accord into their control on shore. Gaceta del foro (Jan. 16, 1920), no. 1158, p. 95; Annual Digest, 1919-22, Case No. 69.

The Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands affirmed the convic tion of H. N. Bull, master of a Norwegian vessel, under an act of the 

Philippine legislature establishing certain regulations for the transportation of cattle in vessels and penalizing the violation thereof. 

The vessel sailed from the port at Ampieng, Formosa, to the port of 

Manila. The court said:

The offense, assuming that it originated at the port of departure in Formosa, was a continuing one, and every element necessary to constitute it existed during the voyage across the territorial waters. The completed forbidden act was done within 

American waters, and the court therefore had jurisdiction over the subject-matter of the offense and the person of the offender. 

The United States has adhered consistently to the view that when a merchant vessel enters a foreign port it is subject to the jurisdiction of the local authorities, unless the local sovereignty has by act of acquiescence or through treaty arrangements consented to waive a portion of such jurisdiction. (15 Op. Attys. 

Gen., U.S., 178; 2 Moore, Int. Law Dig., sec. 204; article by Dean 

Gregory, Mich. Law Review, Vol. II, No. 5.) 

United States v. H. N. Bull, 15 Phil. (1910) 7, 13, 15, 18.

The Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands held that the Philippine courts had jurisdiction over Look Chaw who, while on board an English vessel bound from Hong Kong for Mexico and calling at the ports of Manila and Cebu, had in his possession certain sacks of opium and who sold some of their contents in the Philippines. The court said thatalthough the mere possession of a thing of prohibited use in these Islands, aboard a foreign vessel in transit, in any of their

ports, does not, as a general rule, constitute a crime triable by the courts of this country, on account of such vessel being considered as an extension of its own nationality, the same rule does not apply when the article, whose use is prohibited within the Philippine Islands, in the present case a can of opium, is landed from the vessel upon Philippine soil, thus committing an open violation of the laws of the land, with respect to which, as it is a violation of the penal law in force at the place of the commission of the crime, only the court established in the said place itself has competent jurisdiction, in the absence of an agreement under an international treaty. 

United States v. Look Chaw, 18 Phil. (1910) 573, 577-578.

In the case of People v. Wong Cheng the Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands held that the Philippine courts had jurisdiction over the defendant who was charged with illegally smoking opium on board the English vessel Changsa while anchored in Manila Bay. The court declared that the smoking of opium within the territorial limits of the Philippines, even on board a foreign merchant ship, was a breach of the public order of the Philippines because of its pernicious effects within the territory of the Philippines. 46 Phil. (1922) 729.

In 1922 the German Embassy brought to the attention of the Department of State the fact that two members of the crew of the German vessel Selma had been arrested on board the vessel in the port of New Orleans by agents of the United States Government without the German Consul's having been advised, because cocain was found in their possession. The 

Embassy stated that, according to the principles of international law observed by its Government, the jurisdiction of a country over German vessels in its ports could only become effective if persons not belonging to the crew of those vessels were the victims of criminal offenses committed on board, if the help of the authorities of the country to which the port belonged was asked by a member of the crew of the vessel who was a citizen of that country, or if the peace of the port was violated by a criminal offense, and that none of these circumstances applied to the case in question. The Department replied that, in its opinion, wher a vessel visited the ports of a foreign country it was amenable to the jurisdiction of that country and subject to the laws which governed the port it visited so long as it remained there, unless it was otherwise provided by treaty; that it was probably true that by comity matters of discipline and all things done on board affecting only the vessel or things belonging to it and not involving the peace or dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port were in accordance with general international practice, left by the foreign government to be dealt with by the authorities of the nation to which the vessel belonged; but that it did not consider "that there is any rule of international law or comity under which a member of the crew of a foreign vessel in an American port should be exempt from arrest for a violation of penal statutes relating to the importation of narcotics". Subsequently, the Department informed the Embassy that on trial the court had directed a verdict for the defendants on the ground that they had been entrapped into the alleged commission of an offense by a narcotic agent and a paid informer and that what they had done was without any unlawful intent whatever. Memoranda from the Department of State to the German Embassy, June 8 and July 1, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 311.6221 Selma/-, /1.

ARREST AND SEARCH ON BOARD

In November 1910 the authorities of Corinto, Nicaragua, requested the captain of the American steamship City of Panama to have removed to the German steamer Serak one Dr. Sebastian Salinas.

The American Consul in that port informed the captain of the American vessel that he (the captain) was not bound or authorized to surrender Dr. Salinas; he also informed the Commandante at 

Corinto that, as Consul, he had no authority to surrender Dr. Salinas or to prevent his arrest but that if an attempt were made forcibly to remove him from the ship he would protest against such action. The 

Department of State in this connection instructed the Consul as 

1. Nations have, in general, the right to exercise, if they choose, civil and criminal jurisdiction over foreign merchant vessels entering their ports. 

2. In practice, however, according to the so-called French modification of this rule, such jurisdiction is not generally exercised over matters which do not involve the "dignity of the country" or "the peace and tranquillity of the port". In the words of the United States Supreme Court in Wildenhus' Case: 

"Disputes which disturb only the peace of the ship or of those on board, are to be dealt with exclusively by the sovereignty of the home of the ship, but those which disturb the public peace may be suppressed and, if need be, the offenders punished by the proper authorities of the local jurisdiction". This, however, is a matter of comity or of treaty stipulation and it is not generally regarded as a settled principle of international law. 

3. Any country, consequently, may cause the arrest, by due process of law of any person of whatever nationality on board foreign merchant ships within its ports. The duty of the ship's master is not to resist the proper arrest of persons in such cases. 

4. Conversely, a country must not so arrest such persons without due process of law. Thus, in the case of the Creole, the arbitrator held that the magistrate was not authorized "to violate the law of nations by invading with an armed force the vessel of a friendly nation that has committed no offense and forcibly dissolve the relations which, by the laws of his country, the captain is bound to preserve and enforce on board". 

5. When an arrest is made in accordance with law, an American diplomatic or consular officer has no authority to approve or disapprove of, or aid in the same. (See cases of Gomez and 

Barundia, Op. Cit.) [II Moore's Dig. 867, 871]. A custom, however, appears to have grown up in Latin American countries not to cause an arrest on shipboard without first obtaining the consent of the Minister or Consul, and if this consent is refused, the arrest is rarely made. 

6. Where an arrest is about to be made in an arbitrary or forcible manner in contradistinction to proper arrest under legal

process, an American diplomatic or consular officer should protest with a vigor commensurate with the threatened unnecessary danger to lives and property and report the matter fully to his Government. How far the ship's master is bound to submit to such arbitrary and extra-legal treatment, is a question for the master to decide. 

7. Finally the action of the local authorities does not become illegal because some ill advised person, such as the master of the ship, resists arrest under due process of law. 

The above general rules may, of course, be modified by treaty provisions or other understanding between the two countries or be affected by mitigating circumstances, such as a ship's putting into port under stress of weather, urgent distress or other grave necessity. 

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Johnson, no. 30, Jan. 24, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 815.00/911. 

In November 1911 Esther Moreno, a daughter of a Mexican father and an American mother, who had embarked upon the American steamer Mexico in the harbor of Veracruz, was removed from the vessel by a Mexican revenue officer acting under an order of the captain of the port. The Department of State informed the American Consul in Veracruz that this case did not come within the exceptions to the general rule of local jurisdiction over foreign merchant vessels in a port and that there did not appear to be any treaty provisions between the United States and Mexico modifying that rule. It said:

It would seem, therefore, that the captain of the Mexico acted in accordance with the law of nations when he refrained from opposing the action of the Mexican police or customs guards in taking a passenger from the steamer in the harbor of Vera Cruz upon presentation of an order for the detention of such passenger, made by the captain of the port upon the apparent instructions of the chief civil magistrate of the county. That the captain of the steamer doubted the legal capacity of the captain of the port to take the action in question could hardly be considered sufficient justification for opposing such action. It would seem clear that by the laws of Mexico such authority might well be vested in the captain of the port, and any person denying such authority and opposing its exercise, would of course do so at his peril, and should, it would seem, be very certain of his ground before taking such a stand.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Canada, no. 439. 

Feb. 17, 1912, MS. Department of State, file 312.112M81. 

On June 28, 1921 the American vessel Lake Farley was preparing to leave Saloniki, Greece, for Constantinople (Istanbul) when a police captain presented a written request to the American Consul

to board the ship for the purpose of finding an alleged criminal. 

The police officer, accompanied by the American Vice Consul, boarded and searched the vessel. The American Consul, however, protested against the arrest of the man in question since no proof of the charges against him or of his identity had been presented. After receipt of the Consul's protest, and without notice to him, the Governor General ordered his agents to board the vessel. The captain refused to deliver up the man without the consent of the Consul, and the authorities searched the vessel without finding him. The vessel finally sailed, obliging the authorities to leave it. On July 5, 1921 the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs addressed a note to the American Chargé d'Affaires in Athens in which it was said: 

It is quite unnecessary to bring up the particularly grave character of these actions. International law does not recognize the right of asylum on board merchant ships which happen to be in territorial waters of foreign states. The action of the foreign public authority thereby exercises itself freely when it is a question of arresting a delinquent who has taken refuge on board a ship and the Consular authority and the Captain who saw fit to hinder this action, exercised under the responsibility of the state in the waters of which the ship in question was anchored, rendered themselves guilty of the most flagrant infraction of treaties and conventions. 

On November 7, 1921 the Department of State instructed the

Chargé d'Affaires as follows: 

It is the understanding of the Department that no written warrant of arrest or statement of charges was exhibited to the Consul at Saloniki at the time permission was asked to make the desired arrest. If this understanding is correct, you may reply to the note of the Greek Government along the following lines:

This Government recognizes the principle that when a merchant vessel visits the port of a foreign country for the purpose of trade, it is in general amenable to the jurisdiction of that country and is subject to the laws which govern the port it visits so long as it remains. This principle does not, of course, mean that the local authorities are warranted in making an arbitrary, unlawful, or forcible invasion of a foreign vessel or taking any action against any one on board that is not authorized by provisions of the local law.

Where in a proper case the local authorities desire to apprehend a person on board a foreign vessel and request permission of the Consul of the country whose flag the vessel flies to board the vessel and make the arrest, the Consul is justified in satisfying himself that all due forms of arrest according to the local law have been observed before granting such permission. Otherwise there would be no protection for foreign vessels against arbitrary action by individual local officials acting outside of their authority and without warrant of law.

In the present case it does not appear that any duly executed warrant of arrest was exhibited to the Consul at the time permission was requested to make the arrest, and the Consul was accordingly not in a position to grant the desired permission. 

It appears that in a written communication to the Chief of Police at Saloniki the Consul stated that he had no jurisdiction or authority to consent to or refuse to consent to the arrest of the man in question but that since no evidence of identity or statement of charges had been submitted to him he found it necessary to protest against the entry on board the vessel for the purpose of effecting the arrest. The Consul also instructed the Captain of the vessel at the same time that if the authorities persisted in making the arrest, only verbal protest was to be made and that no resistance was to be offered. The subsequent action of the Captain in ordering the departure of the vessel from the port while the authorities were still on board, was contrary to the instructions of the Consul. At the same time this Government feels that the course pursued by the local authorities in forcibly boarding the vessel and attempting to make the arrest without producing any written warrant from the appropriate authorities for doing so is contrary to the precepts of international law and that the Consul was justified in protesting against such action.

In April 1922 the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in response to the representations of the Chargé d'Affaires made in accordance with the Department's instructions, wrote to the Chargé d'Affaires that his Government was unable to accept the American point of view. He declared:

According to international law merchant vessels visiting the ports of a foreign country are generally amenable to the jurisdiction of that country. Also, for questions which come within the jurisdiction of the local authorities, these have the right of police. In consequence the local authorities can board a vessel in order to pursue and arrest a person charged with an act for which he is amenable to the tribunals of the country. 

The local authorities act, in this case, on their own responsibility and are not bound, in order to make the visit and the arrest, to ask the permission of the foreign consular authority, still less to assure him that the arrest is in conformity with the laws of the country. Only, previous notice should be given to the foreign consul in order that he may, if he so desires, be present during these operations.

This rule of international law was also admitted in practice. 

Thus the consular convention between the United States and 

Greece of December 19/January 2, 1902, in Article 16, prescribes that the judicial authorities of the two countries cannot make visits on board vessels without previous notice to the consular authorities.

Under these conditions the conduct of the authorities at Saloniki who desired to arrest a Greek subject, accused of a common law crime, on board the vessel "Lake Farley", after 157511-40VOL. II— -16

Use of soldiers giving notice to the American Consul, was regular and in conformity with the treaties in force and with international law. 

Also the protest of the American Consul is not justified. The action of the police was hindered only by the arbitrary conduct of the Captain of the boat in question. 

Chargé Hall to Secretary Hughes, telegram 104, July 8, 1921, MS. 

Department of State, file 811.0144/128; Consul Morris to Mr. Hughes, no. 

178, June 29, 1921, ibid. 811.0144/131; Mr. Baltazzi, Greek Ministry of

Foreign Affairs, to Mr. Hall, July 5, 1921 (enclosure to despatch 741 from the Legation in Athens, Aug. 9, 1921), ibid. 811.0144/133; the Second

On October 2, 1907 the American mail steamship City of Sydney anchored in the harbor of Acajutla, El Salvador, and was boarded by military officers and soldiers of the Salvadoran Army who presented the captain with a warrant for the arrest of one John Moisant, alleged to be a passenger on board the ship. The commander of the U.S.S. Chicago, stationed off El Salvador, immediately informed the captain of the Salvadoran gunboat Presidente that he would not permit armed soldiers to be placed on board the City of Sydney. 

The latter replied that he would not send soldiers on board. The commander reported to the Secretary of the Navy that he refrained from advising the captain of the City of Sydney in regard to delivering up Moisant in case he should be found on board and also refrained from interfering with the search for Moisant by Salvadoran officers. When the search was made, the Salvadoran officers removed their arms at the request of the captain. No attempt was made again by the Salvadoran authorities to place soldiers on board the ship, but they remained alongside in two boats. Moisant was not found.

The Secretary of State, in a letter addressed to the Secretary of the Navy, approved the action of the commander of the Chicago, saying: 

The action of Commander Doyle in remonstrating against the forcible boarding of the City of Sydney by an armed force in order to institute a search for a passenger supposed to be an offender against Salvador, is to be commended, not alone because of the grave peril in which innocent passengers were placed, but because of the apparent absence of the regular and orderly processes of law in seeking to effect the arrest.

The nationality of the passenger is not material to the question of lawful exercise of jurisdiction. 

Commander Doyle to the Secretary of the Navy, Oct. 7, 1907, and Secretary Root to the Secretary of the Navy, Nov. 13, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 6775/181-183.

In reply to a despatch from the Minister in Cuba with regard to the action of Cuban courts in serving warrants on and making arrests Members of of American seamen on American ships in the harbor of Habana crew without previous notification to the Consul General, the Department of State wrote thatwhile it appears that a custom of notifying American consular officers and obtaining their consent before arrests are made on American vessels has grown up in Latin American countries, such custom apparently is not based on any principle of international law, and the Department therefore would not be in a position to insist on its observance by the Cuban authorities. 

Such being the case, in the absence of any treaty provisions between this Government and Cuba governing the matter, the rights of the Cuban authorities of course must be determined in accordance with the general principles of international law relating to jurisdiction over merchant vessels in foreign ports.

On July 5, 1922 the Consul General in Athens, Greece, requested Seamen liable instructions from the Department of State on the subject of the for military removal from American ships in Greek ports of seamen of foreign nationality who might be liable for military service in Greece. He stated that agents of certain American steamship lines had reported to him that the captain of the port at Piraeus had warned them that all their crews would be inspected on arrival there and that such members thereof as appeared to be liable for military service under the Greek Government would be removed. The Department replied: 

Since there appears to be no existing treaty provision between the United States and Greece exempting American merchant vessels from the local jurisdiction while in Greek territorial waters, the Department believes that you should avoid raising the question of the right of the Greek authorities to remove from an American merchant vessel, while it is in a Greek port, seamen of Greek nationality who may be liable for military service under the Greek Government. 

However, should the Greek authorities remove from an American merchant vessel any members of the crew of foreign nationality on the ground that they are liable for military service, it is suggested that you or a subordinate American consular officer render to these seamen the aid to which they appear to be entitled under Article XVI of the Consular Convention of 

November 19, 1902, between the United States and Greece, 

---

Search for contraband You will observe that under Article XVI of the convention referred to an American consular officer has a right to be present when an American merchant vessel in a Greek port is examined or searched by the judicial authorities or by the customs officials, and to accompany any officers of the ship or members of the crew before the judicial or administrative authorities, in order to assist them in presenting their cases before these authorities. This 

Government considers, therefore, that under Article XVI a seaman of foreign nationality who may be removed from an American merchant vessel in a Greek port on the ground that he is liable for military service has the right to be accorded a hearing before the appropriate Greek authorities in order to establish any legal right which he may have to exemption from such service, and that an American consular officer is entitled to be present at the hearing.

The Chief of the Consular Bureau (Hengstler) to Consul General Lowrie, 

Sept. 20, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 196/450.
