CIVIL JURISDICTION PERSONAL INJURY 

$142 The Baker, a vessel flying the German flag and registered in Germany, was libeled for damages alleged to have been sustained by the libelant, who was not an American citizen, while the vessel was on the high seas and as the result of negligence of the owners, agents, servants, and crew of the vessel. An exception was taken to the libel on the ground that, under the consular convention of December 11, 1871 between the United States and Germany, the exclusive power to take cognizance of such a case was vested in the German consular department. Article XIII of the convention provided for consular jurisdiction over the internal order of the merchant vessels of each nation

and exclusive power over differences of every kind arising at sea or at port between the captains, officers, and crews, and especially in reference to wages and the execution of mutual contracts, 1 Treaties, etc. 

(Malloy, 1910) 550, 554. The United States District Court stated that it was difficult to see how this article could have been intended to include suits against the owners of the vessel or the vessel itself on the ground of negligence, since such a cause of action is not a difference between the captain, officers, or crew. The court overruled the exception based upon the proposition that the German Consul had exclusive jurisdiction, saying that it did so without finally precluding itself from exercising its discretion upon a further knowledge of the facts. 

157 Fed. 485 (E.D.N.Y., 1907).

A libel in rem was brought against a Swedish vessel, the Ester, by a seaman thereon to recover unpaid wages and damages for personal injuries incurred by him while the vessel was in the port of 

Charleston, South Carolina. The respondents, owners of the ship, appeared especially and raised the question of jurisdiction, alleging that the libelant, although a German subject, became a Swedish subject during his service on the Swedish vessel; that, under treaty stipulations between the United States and Sweden, the United States District Court did not have jurisdiction as the matter involved a difference between the master of the Swedish vessel and a Swedish subject as a seaman on that vessel; and that even if the district court had jurisdiction, as a matter of comity it would not exercise it where the Swedish Consul protested against the exercise by the court of any jurisdiction in the case. The Swedish Consul in New York certified to the court that the matter of the adjustment of the controversy and the performance of the treaty provisions between Germany and Sweden was in course of correspondence between the consuls of those countries and that his Consulate desired that the libelant be returned to Germany according to the requirements of the declaration between Sweden and Germany in respect to destitute seamen. 

There was also presented to the court a letter from the Swedish Minister in Washington asking that the request of the Swedish Consul be granted.

The United States District Court made an exhaustive review of the authorities in respect to jurisdiction over merchant vessels. With reference to the decisions of the United States Supreme Court it said: Internal order: "dif- ferences" 

In Ex parte Newman, 14 Wall. 150, 20 L. Ed. 877, the court, in the course of the delivery of its opinion (although the point was not involved in the question actually decided), states, on Foreign the question of a libel by a Prussian seaman against a Prussian consul vessel for wages, that admiralty courts, it is said, will not take

3 Treaty case. jurisdiction in such a case except where it is manifestly necessary to do so to prevent a failure of justice; but the better opinion is that, independent of treaty stipulations, there is no constitutional or legal impediment to the exercise of jurisdiction in such a Such courts, may, if they see fit, take jurisdiction in such a case; but they will not do so as a general rule without the consent of the representative of the country to which the vessel belongs, where it is practicable that the representative should be consulted. His consent, however, is not a condition of jurisdiction, but is regarded as a material fact to aid the court in determining the question of discretion whether jurisdiction in the case ought or ought not to be exercised. This and the succeeding cases in which the subject has come up for an opinion in the Supreme Court of the United States appear to have established the following rules: (1) The merchant vessels of one country visiting the ports of another for the purposes of trade subject themselves to the laws which govern the port they visit, so long as they remain. 

United States v. Diekelman, 92 U.S. 520, 23 L. Ed. 742; Wildenhus' Case, 120 U.S. 11, 7 Sup. Ct. 385, 30 L. Ed. 565. (2) In the absence of treaty stipulations, the courts of admiralty have civil jurisdiction in all matters appertaining to the foreign ship while in port, and also in certain cases when the court has the vessel in its territorial jurisdiction, although the cause of action arose on the high seas. The Belgenland, 114 

U.S. 355, 5 Sup. Ct. 860, 29 L. Ed. 152; Wildenhus' Case, 120 

U.S. 1, 7 Sup. Ct. 385, 30 L. Ed. 565. (3) The exercise of this civil jurisdiction, where those who are concerned are all citizens of the same foreign state and the cause of action occurred on or with regard to the ship, is not imperative, but discretionary, and the courts from motives of convenience or international comity will not take jurisdiction without the assent of the consul of the country to which the ship belongs, where the controversy involves matters arising beyond the territorial jurisdiction of this country, or relates to differences between the master and the crew, or the crew and the shipowners. In such cases on such general principles of comity, the admiralty courts of this country will not interfere between the parties, unless there is special reason for doing so, and will require the foreign consul to be notified, and although not absolutely bound by, will always pay respect to, his wishes_as_to taking jurisdiction. Ex parte Newman, 14 Wall. 152, 20 L. Ed. 

877; The Belgenland, 114 U.S. 355, 5 Sup. Ct. 860, 29 L. Ed. 152; 

Patterson v. Eudora, 190 U.S. 169, 23 Sup. Ct. 821, 47 L. Ed. 1002. (4) Where, however, special circumstances exist, such as where the voyage is ended, or the seamen have been dismissed or treated with great cruelty, the courts, in the absence of treaty stipulations, will entertain jurisdiction, even against the protest of the consul. The Belgenland, 114 U.S. 355, 5 Sup. Ct. 860, 29 L. Ed. 

152. (5) Where treaty stipulations exist, however, with regard to the right of the consul of a foreign country to adjudge controversies arising between the master and the crew, or other mat-

ters occurring on the ship exclusively subject to the foreign law, such stipulations are the law of the land, and must be fairly and faithfully observed. The Belgenland, 114 U.S. 355, 5 Sup. Ct. 

860, 29 L. Ed. 152; Wildenhus Case, 120 U.S. 17, 7 Sup. Ct. 385, 

(6) Congress has power by legislation to regulate matters affecting foreign seamen and foreign vessels and foreigners generally when within the ports of this country by making their entrance subject to such conditions, as Congress may seek to impose or withdrawing its consent to permit them to enter wholly, if it see fit. Patterson v. Eudora, 190 U.S. 169, 23 Sup. Ct. 821, 47 L. Ed. 1002. (7) Where Congress has passed an act which may conflict with prior treaty stipulations, it is the duty of the court to uphold the later statute if clear and explicit, even in contravention of express stipulations in an earlier treaty. Fong Yue Ting v. 

United States, 149 U.S. 720, 13 Sup. Ct. 1016, 37 L. Ed. 905; 

Patterson v. Eudora, 190 U.S. 178, 23 Sup. Ct. 821, 47 L. Ed. 1002.

The court also made the following review of the decisions of the lower Federal courts:

Consideration of these cases shows that they may be said to fall within the following four classes or categories:

First. This class includes cases in which it has been held that the courts of admiralty have the right to take jurisdiction in the absence of special treaty stipulations in controversies between foreign seamen and foreign vessels, whether arising on the high seas or in the port, and whether based on tort or for wages. 

That this jurisdiction is not compulsory, but is discretionary.

That this discretion will not be exercised against the protest of the consul of the country to which the vessel belongs, except under special circumstances. Where these special circumstances exist, however, the jurisdiction will be exercised, notwithstanding such protest. The Becherdass, 1 Low. 569, Fed. Cas. No. 

1,203; The Lilian M. Vigus, 10 Ben. 385, Fed. Cas. No. 8,346; 

Boult v. Ship Naval Reserve (D.C.) 5 Fed. 209; The Carolina (D.C.) 14 Fed. 424; Fry v. Cook, Id.; The Montapedia (D.C.) 

14 Fed. 427; The City of Carlisle (D.C.) 39 Fed. 807, 5 L.R.A. 

52; Camille v. Couch (D.C.) 40 Fed. 176; The Topsy (D.C.) 44 

Fed. 651; The Sirius (D.C.) 47 Fed. 825; The Karoo (D.C.) 49 

Fed. 651; The Walter D. Wallet (D.C.) 66 Fed. 1011; Bolden v. 

Jensen (D.C.) 70 Fed. 505; The Lamington (D.C.) 87 Fed. 752;

The Eudora (D.C.) 110 Fed. 430; The Kestor (D.C.) 110 Fed. 

432; The Troop (D.C.) 118 Fed. 769; The Alnwick (D.C.) 132 

Fed. 117; The Ucayali (D.C.) 164 Fed. 897.

Second. The second class of cases are cases in which the courts have held that notwithstanding there are treaty stipulations, apparently excluding the jurisdiction of the court, yet that the court is at liberty to ignore these stipulations and take jurisdiction where there are special circumstances. The Elwin Kreplin,

Right of 

American seamen 

4 Ben. 413, Fed. Cas. No. 4,427; The Amalia (D.C.) 3 Fed. 652;

The Salomoni (D.C.) 29 Fed. 534. 

Third. The third class is that of cases in which it is held that, where the existing treaty stipulations upon the face of them exclude the jurisdiction of the court, such treaty stipulations are to receive faithful observation, and the court cannot take jurisdiction. The Elwin Kreplin, 9 Blatchf. 438, Fed. Cas. No. 4, 426; The Burchard (D.C.) 42 Fed. 608; The Marie (D.C.) 49 

Fed. 286; The Welhaven (D.C.) 55 Fed. 80; The Bound Brook (D.C.) 146 Fed. 160; Tellefsen v. Fee, 168 Mass. 188, 46 N.E. 

562, 45 L.R.A. 481, 60 Am. St. Rep. 379. 

Fourth. There are also cases which have gone to the length of holding that where the proceedings are brought on behalf of an American citizen, although they may be brought against a foreign vessel, and brought by reason of libelant's having served as an enlisted seaman on that vessel, yet that under the Constitution of the United States he has a constitutional right to invoke the jurisdiction of the court, of which he cannot be deprived either by treaty stipulation or act of Congress. Bolden v. Jensen (D.C.) 70 Fed. 505; The Falls of Keltie (D.C.) 114 Fed. 

357; The Troop (D.C.) 117 Fed. 557; The Neck (D.C.) 138 Fed. 

144. All these last four decisions are by the District Court for the District of Washington. The conclusion arrived at in these later cases appears to be in direct conflict with the principle that a seaman duly enrolled upon a foreign vessel is for the time being, and with regard to his employment on that vessel, a citizen of the same country as that to which the vessel belongs. 

The court said:

From a consideration of the decisions in all these cases in connection with the conclusions reached by the Supreme Court of the United States, it would appear to be the better rule of law that, where special treaty stipulations exist which would upon the face of them exclude this court from jurisdiction in a cause such as the present one, it is not empowered to proceed and take jurisdiction because of any special circumstances in the particular case, as the absence from the district of South Carolina, in which the court is sitting, of a consul or consular agent or officer of the country to which the vessel belongs (and a fortiori not where a consul of the country actually appears and protests, although not resident in the district), or of any other special circumstances, such as brutality exercised towards the seamen, and the fact that if jurisdiction were not taken, and relief given by the court, it might leave the applicant practically penniless.

The court cited article XI of the consular convention of June 1, 1910 between Sweden and the United States conferring jurisdiction "Differences" on consuls over differences arising at sea or in port between the include torts captains, officers, and crews. 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2846, 2849; 37 Stat. 1479, 1485. It concluded that the word differences

Discretion; included controversies based on torts in the sense of personal injuries occurring through the master's negligence and stated that under this view its jurisdiction would be excluded by the terms of the convention. Assuming, however, the court said, that it had the discretionary power in exceptional cases of taking jurisdiction or assuming that the word differences did not include a controversy such as was where set forth in the libel, under the general rule of comity, in the face foreign sovereign of the request of the Kingdom of Sweden itself as transmitted by intercedes its minister and the circumstances of the case, even if it had discretionary power to take jurisdiction, such discretion should not be exercised. The libel was dismissed. 

190 Fed. 216, 220-221, 222, 224, 225-226 (E.D.S.C., 1911).

A libel in admiralty was brought by a Norwegian subject, an infant, through his guardian ad litem, against the Hanna Nielsen, a Norwegian vessel, and the claimant to the vessel, a Norwegian corporation, for injuries sustained by the libelant while he was a sailor on the vessel and while that vessel was taking cargo at Port Angeles, Washington, as the result of its unseaworthiness. The United States District Court overruled the exceptions taken to the libel. It stated that article XIII of the treaty of July 24, 1827 between the United States and Norway and Sweden, giving jurisdiction to consuls over differences arising between the captains and crews of vessels, 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1748, 1752, antedating as it did the recognition of the existence of the right of seamen to recover for injuries suffered through the unseaworthiness of a vessel, could not have been intended to include cases of that kind. 25 F. (2d) 984 (W.D. 

Wash., 1928).

In the case of The Thorgerd a Norwegian member of the crew of that vessel, which was also Norwegian, filed a libel against the vessel on account of an accident which he had suffered while the vessel was in the British port of St. John's, Newfoundland. The claimant owners and the 

Norwegian Consul General in New York moved to dismiss the libel. The motion was sustained by the United States District Court, which said that there seemed to be no good reason for assumption of jurisdiction against the protest of the Kingdom of Norway. 11 F. (2d) 971 (E.D.N.Y., 1926).

In the cases of the Fern and the Boheme suits in admiralty were brought by a Swedish and an Italian seaman, respectively, against the Swedish and Italian vessels upon which each was serving. Each seaman brought action for personal injuries claimed to have been sustained by him on the high seas, and in each case the Consul General of Sweden and Italy, respectively, appeared and requested the court to decline jurisdiction, averring that under the laws of their respective countries the libelants were entitled to obtain relief under insurance laws and could apply therefor in their respective consulates. The United States District Court dismissed the libels on the ground that it would not exercise jurisdiction against the protest of the Consul of the country to which the vessel belonged except under special circumstances of extraordinary hardship and that these cases did not fall within that rule. 15 F. (2d) 887 (E. D. N. Y., 1926).

Heredia, a Peruvian citizen, filed a libel against the Peruvian vessel 

Apurina and G. F. Davies, her master, to recover damages for personal

Where libel- ant and ship are foreign injuries sustained by him, as the result of a defect in the stairway of the vessel, while she was at the dock in New York city. Libelant was employed as a messman on the Apurina. The respondent appealed from a decree for the libelant, and the libelant cross-appealed. The circuit court of appeals stated that in the absence of treaty stipulation courts of admiralty of the United States have jurisdiction of all matters appertaining to a foreign ship while in the ports of this country. 

It stated also that, while an admiralty court of the United States is under no obligation to entertain jurisdiction of a libel to recover for personal injuries where the libelant and the ship are foreign, when the district court does exercise its discretion in favor of assuming jurisdiction, this discretion will not be refused on appeal in the absence of a showing that it was exercised on wrong principles or that the district judge has acted "so absolutely differently from the view which the court of appeals holds that they are justified in saying he has exercised it wrongly", The Belgenland, 114 U.S. (1885) 355. The circuit court decided that the district court had properly taken jurisdiction of the case. It stated that as the injuries occured in American waters the district-court judge had properly held the rights of the parties to be determined by the law of the lex loci delicti. In regard to proof offered that under Peruvian law there was no right to attach a vessel except in certain cases among which claims for personal injuries were not included, the court said that this proof related to a matter of procedure as to which the law of the forum and not that of a foreign nation governed. The circuit court found the award of the district court to the libelant insufficient and stated that he should be awarded a larger sum. 

Heredia v. Davies, 12 F. (2d) 500, 501 (C.C.A. 4th, 1926).

A libel was filed in a United States District Court against the Gloria de Larrinaga by a duly-articled seaman thereon, under the provisions of the British Merchant Shipping Act of 1894. The court declined to take jurisdiction of the case and dismissed the libel, holding that any recovery for short allowance or bad provisions was of the nature of a penalty and was awarded by way of punishment for wrong and that no instance was shown of courts of admiralty having accepted jurisdiction of claims such as that arising on foreign vessels in foreign places and presented by foreigners. 

The court stated, considering the provisions of section 198 of the British Merchant Shipping Act for rectifying complaints of that nature, that no consideration, even of charity, would move it to accept jurisdiction. 196 

Fed. 590 (S.D.N.Y., 1911).

A libel was filed against the Swedish steamship Bifrost by four seamen thereon claiming damages for breach of contract in shipping articles, by the unlawful arrest and jailing of two on shore at Georgetown, British Guiana, and of two at McKenzie, about 70 miles from Georgetown, at the instance of the master of the vessel. A protest was filed by the Royal 

Swedish Vice Consul on the ground that the controversy was between foreign owners and officers of the vessel and certain members of the crew, none of whom was a citizen of the United States, and concerned matters

occurring outside of the territorial jurisdiction of the United States which he, as Vice Consul, pursuant to authority vested in him by the Kingdom of Sweden, must investigate and adjust; and that such an investigation was then going forward. The master of the vessel, as bailee for the owner, excepted and objected to the exercise of jurisdiction by the United States District Court. That court stated that certain testimony taken prior to the hearing on the exception strongly indicated that the alien libelants had no intention of returning to the country of their allegiance but intended to remain in the United States, which suggested that they might be in the United States unlawfully and in violation of the immigration laws. The court also said that there was a suggestion that the case arose out of a tort rather than from contract but that that point need not be decided. It stated that the dispute could far better be settled by the courts of the country to which the libelants belonged, notwithstanding the fact that they insisted that, since the shipping articles for the voyage were signed in New Orleans, the law of the forum (the District Court of the United 

States for the Eastern District of Louisiana) should govern. There appeared to be no special circumstances, the court declared, such as would work hardship or injustice on the libelants and thereby justify it in assuming jurisdiction by detaining the vessel and proceeding with the case over the protest of the foreign sovereign to which the parties on both sides belonged. The libel was dismissed. 8 F. (2d) 361 (E.D. La., 1925).

A libel was brought by an American citizen, through his guardian, against the Cuzco, a vessel owned by a Norwegian corporation, based on injuries sustained by him while he was employed as a stevedore in discharging cargo in the harbor of Victoria, British Columbia.

It was alleged in the plea and answer that under the law of British Columbia no maritime lien against the vessel existed for the tort set forth in the libel and also that the United States District Court had no jurisdiction of the case. The United States District Court stated that the issue was not as to its jurisdiction but rather as to the Lew loci law which should govern. The court held that the lex loci delicti determined the rights and liabilities of the parties; that the act complained of took place in the territorial waters of British Columbia; and that under that law no maritime lien was given for personal injuries suffered by a stevedore. 

225 Fed. 169 (W.D. Wash., 1915).

A libel in rem was brought against the Oriskany, a British vessel, by a seaman, an American citizen, for injuries, and maintenance and care in connection therewith, sustained by him because of the alleged unseaworthiness of the vessel during a voyage from Kingston, Jamaica, to St. John, New Brunswick. The United States District

Court assumed jurisdiction of the case. It appeared from the court's analysis of the British law that under that law a seaman has an action in rem in respect to an injury resulting from the ship's unseaworthiness only if such injury occurs in British waters upon a foreign delicti

Suit in rem; equitable policy ship and that otherwise he must proceed in personam either under the British workmen's compensation laws or under the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876. The court stated that the existence of a lien under foreign law against a vessel is not necessarily a prerequisite to the jurisdiction of an American court. To assume jurisdiction of the proceeding in rem under consideration, the court declared, seemed but part of an equitable policy entirely consistent with admiralty jurisdiction. It stated that, since such a remedy was allowed to seamen injured on an American vessel and since it was likely that a proceeding in personam against the American owners of the vessel could be pressed more rapidly by a seaman within an American jurisdiction than it could be against an owner in England, not to assume jurisdiction in the suit before it would be tantamount to discrimination both against American seamen who would be compelled to sue in Great Britain and also against American ship-owners who could be sued in rem by American seamen while their English competitors could not. The court, however, found that the charge that the vessel was unseaworthy was not sustained and that the libelant was not entitled to recover damages for his injuries nor for maintenance and care. The libel was therefore dismissed. 

3 F. Supp. 805 (D. Md., 1933).

A suit in admiralty was brought by one Braga, a Brazilian, against the Swedish steamship Falco lying in the port of New York. Braga asked damages for injuries sustained when he fell into an open and unlighted coalhatch while the vessel was in the port of New York. 

He claimed that the ship was unseaworthy. The owner of the ship moved to dismiss the libel because it involved a controversy between a foreign ship and an alien seaman over which the United States District Court should not take jurisdiction. The Swedish Consul 

General filed an affidavit in support of the motion, alleging that under Swedish law Braga was entitled, as his only remedy, to workmen's compensation, which he could receive through the Consul General without going to Sweden. The circuit court of appeals in affirming a decree dismissing the libel declared that it seemed to be proved that Braga was a member of the crew. Normally, it said, disputes arising out of a seaman's employment are referred to the tribunals of the flag, but courts of admiralty will in such cases satisfy themselves that there are no special circumstances which will leave the seaman without adequate remedy. The court stated that Braga's suit, being in rem, was not good in law under the Jones act (41 Stat. 

988) and that, if the suit lay, it would have to be under general maritime law; and it declared that to leave the covers off a coalhatch

was not a defect in seaworthiness and that under maritime law no liability arose from it. 

20 F. (2d) 362 (C.C.A. 2d, 1927).

Section 33 of the Jones act (the Merchant Marine Act of 1920) 

reads: 

Sec. 33. That section 20 of such Act of March 4, 1915, be, and is, amended to read as follows: "Sec. 20. That any seaman who shall suffer personal injury in the course of his employment may, at his election, maintain an action for damages at law, with the right of trial by jury, and in such action all statutes of the United States modifying or extending the common-law right or remedy in cases of personal injury to railway employees shall apply; and in case of the death of any seaman as a result of any such personal injury the personal representative of such seaman may maintain an action for damages at law with the right of trial by jury, and in such action all statutes of the United States conferring or regulating the right of action for death in the case of railway employees shall be applicable. Jurisdiction in such actions shall be under the court of the district in which the defendant employer resides or in which his principal office is located." 

41 Stat. 988, 1007.

It was held by the United States Supreme Court in the case of the 

International Stevedoring Co. v. Haverty that section 33 of the Jones act was applicable to stevedores employed in maritime work on navigable waters. 272 U.S. (1926) 50. 

In the case of Plamals v. S.S. "Pinar Del Rio", etc., a libel was filed against the British ship Pinar Del Rio by Plamals, a Spanish subject, and a member of the crew of the vessel, for an accident suffered by him while the vessel was anchored at Philadelphia. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the circuit court of appeals dismissing the libel, holding that section 33 of the Jones act invoked by the petitioner conferred no lien against the vessel in favor of the injured seaman. The Court said: 66 The section under consideration does not undertake to impose liability upon the ship itself, but by positive words indicates a contrary purpose. Seamen may invoke, at their election, the relief accorded by the old rules against the ship, or that provided by the new against the employer. But they may not have the benefit of both."

The Court stated that it found it unnecessary to consider whether the provisions of section 33 were applicable when a foreign seaman employed on a foreign ship suffers injuries while in American waters. 277 U.S. (1928) 151, 156-157. 

In the case of the Paula a libel in rem against a Danish vessel and in personam against its owner, a Danish corporation, was brought by a German seaman on the vessel, who had signed shipping articles in a 

Chilean port, for personal injuries suffered in the harbor at Jacksonville,

Florida, claiming under maritime law and under section 33 of the Jones act. The circuit court of appeals affirmed a decree declining to take jurisdiction of the case. The court said that it was not clear "that a Jones act

foreign seaman who had signed on at a foreign port should have the benefit of the Act" and that "the intention to legislate for alien seamen who have signed articles abroad on a foreign ship ought to be clearly expressed before the courts extend the statute to them". 91 F. (2d) 1001 (C.C.A. 2d, 1937); certiorari denied, 302 U.S. (1937) 750.

In the case of Wenzler v. Robin Line S.S. Co., in which an American seaman had been injured on board an American vessel in the harbor of Habana, Cuba, it was held that the law of the flag (sec. 33 of the Jones act), and not the law of Cuba, was applicable. 277 Fed. 812 (W.D. Wash., 1921). 

In the case of Gerradin v. United Fruit Co. it was held that an American seaman employed in New York by an American corporation who was injured on the high seas upon a vessel of Honduran registry was entitled to the benefit of section 33 of the Jones act. 51 F. (2d) 417 (E.D.N.Y., 1931).

The case of Uravic, Administratrix v. F. Jarka Company, Incorporated, et al. involved an action for the death of the plaintiff's intestate, an 

American citizen employed as a stevedore by the defendant. The injury resulting in death was caused on July 13, 1926, while the deceased was helping to unload, in the harbor of New York, a vessel flying the German flag. The applicability of section 33 of the Jones act was involved. The 

New York Court of Appeals on the authority of Resigno v. F. Jarka Co., 

Inc., et al., 248 N.Y. (1928) 225, 162 N.E. 13, affirmed a decision dismissing the complaint. In the latter case it had held that section 33 was limited to seamen who work upon domestic vessels. The Supreme Court of the 

United States reversed the judgment of the court of appeals stating that section 33 "is construed to give the rights of seamen to stevedores" and that "as they are American workmen, they have the rights of American seamen as well on German as on American ships." 282 U.S. (1931) 234, 239.

An action was brought to recover damages for personal injuries sustained by the plaintiff while he was working as a pumpman on board a 

British steamship at a wharf in Jersey City, New Jersey. Upon appeal to the appellate division of the Supreme Court of New York (2d Dept.) from a judgment for the plaintiff the question was presented whether section 33 of the Jones act was applicable. The appellate division, pointing out that the plaintiff had alleged his employment as a seaman on a British ship, stated that the fact that he had signed no articles did not appear to change his status for the purpose of the case and held that the plaintiff being injured upon a British ship was subject to British law and that the Jones act was applicable only to seamen employed upon American vessels. 

Clark v. Montezuma Transportation Co. Ltd. et al., 217 App. Div. (1926) 

172, 216 N.Y. Supp. 295.

The act of Congress approved Mar. 30, 1920 provides for the recovery of damages in the admiralty courts of the United States for wrongful death on the high seas. 41 Stat. 537. The Longshoremen's and Harbor 

Workers' Compensation Act of Mar. 4, 1927 provides compensation for disability or death of an employee resulting from an injury occurring upon the navigable waters of the United States (including any drydock). 

The term employee is defined as not including "a master or member of a crew of any vessel nor any person engaged by the master to load or unload or repair any small vessel under eighteen tons net". 44 Stat. 1424, 1425.

A suit in admiralty was brought by a Norwegian subject against the Seirstad, a vessel of Norwegian registry, claiming that as a seaman engaged in removing hatch-covers and strongbacks thereon he had received injuries while the vessel was proceeding up the Delaware River, because of the negligence and carelessness of the respondent. A motion, in which the Norwegian Consul General in 

New York joined, was made, requesting that the United States District Court decline jurisdiction and dismiss the libel. The Consul 

General made affidavit that the libelant was entitled to compensation for his injuries from the Royal Accident Insurance Office of Norway under Norwegian laws. The district court in granting the motion stated that this was a case in which jurisdiction was discretionary and that discretion would not be exercised against the protest of the consul of the country to which the vessel belonged except under special circumstances and extraordinary hardship. The court declared that no circumstances existed whereby the libelant would be deprived of any rights by reason of its declining jurisdiction.

A motion to reargue was granted and the original motion denied, new facts having been presented showing that the libelant was a subject of Norway, that he had filed a declaration of intention to become a citizen of the United States, that it was not unlikely that he would have difficulty in returning to the United States, and that in order to obtain compensation under the Norwegian laws it was essential that he return to Norway. The court stated that it would be a hardship if the libelant went to Norway and was unable to return to the United States, that it was possible that his return might not be permitted by reason of his serious injuries, that this was an extreme case, and that it was only for that reason that the court would assume jurisdiction. 

Upon a subsequent hearing the district court, relying on Clark v.

Montezuma Transportation Co., 217 App. Div. (1926) 172, 216 N.Y. 

Supp. 295, and Resigno v. F. Jarka Co., Inc., et al., 248 N. Y. (1928) 

225, 162 N.E. 13, held that the provisions of section 33 of the Jones act were limited to seamen at work upon domestic vessels and that it could not make an award under the Norwegian compensation law. 

The court, however, granted a decree for the libelant covering certain expenses. 

12 F. (2d) 133 (E.D.N.Y., 1926); 27 F. (2d) 982 (E.D.N.Y., 1928). See the case of Uravic v. Jarka Co., summarized ante, p. 240.

In the case of Elman et al. v. Moller et al. the circuit court of appeals reversed that part of a decree of the district court declining jurisdiction in respect to one Elman, who had joined in the libel of a Swedish steamship and who had asked for his discharge from the

Enforced employment ship while it was at Panama and declared his intention to become an American citizen. The master had promised to discharge him when the ship put in at Newport News. Upon her arrival there she was boarded by an immigration officer who was asked whether Elman could be discharged and who had replied that he could not say until the following day. On that day he told the captain that Elman might be paid off. Meanwhile a petition for habeas corpus had been filed. The circuit court stated that when the master had produced 

Elman in response to the writ of habeas corpus he should at once have told the court that he made no further claim to detain petitioner. 

The court said:

Even a foreign ship cannot, when in an American port, forcibly compel one of its crew, albeit an alien, to serve against his will. If he alleges that such attempt has been made, we believe that an American court is bound to hear his complaint and give him such redress, if any, as he may show he should have. 

The circuit court made an award of $100 in favor of Elman. 

11 F. (2d) 55, 57 (C.C.A. 4th, 1926); certiorari denied, 271 U.S. (1926) 675.

WAGES 

$143 In 1907 a libel in rem was brought by a seaman, an American citizen, against a British steamship, August Belmont, for wages. The

Prior to 1915 libelant had signed the articles on board the vessel at Pensacola, Florida. He alleged that he had been wrongfully discharged from the vessel at Bremen, Germany. The respondent urged that, since the contract was entered into on board a British steamship before the British Consul at a time when the vessel was not within the jurisdiction of the Southern District of Georgia and since the contract terminated in Bremen, Germany, the United States District Court was without jurisdiction of the subject-matter. The district court stated that it had no doubt of its jurisdiction to determine the merits of the controversy. It pointed out that the libelant was an American citizen; that the parties on the vessel were within the reach of its processes; that the voyage was ended; and that the libelant, as contended, was wrongfully dismissed. The case of The Amalia, 3 Fed. 

652 (D. Me., 1880) was cited for the proposition that the jurisdiction of the United States District Court is discretionary in a case for wages against a foreign vessel unless restricted by treaty. It was obvious, the court said, that though the libelant might have signed shipping articles aboard a British ship the conditions of his agree- Discretion- ary jurisdic- tion

ment were subject to the regulations established by Congress and to the remedial cognizance of the United States admiralty courts. 

In the case of The Albani the United States District Court dismissed a libel by three Norwegian seamen against a British schooner to recover wages on the ground that there was no evidence that an injustice would be done the claimants by a refusal of the court to take jurisdiction. 169 

Fed. 220 (E.D. Pa., 1909).

A libel in admiralty was filed against the Ucayali, a British vessel, by a British seaman thereon for wages allegedly due him. It appeared that the libelant had had a disagreement with the mate and captain of the vessel while in the port of New York; that he had been told by the latter that he could be paid off at a certain rate which he refused; and that he had left the vessel and later appeared before the British Consul who upheld the decision of the captain. The United States District Court dismissed the libel, stating that the libelant was a British seaman; that the occurrences were upon a British ship; that his contract and his remedies, so far as they related to contract rights, were governed by the British law; and that it could not question the disposition of the matter already made by the British Consul. 164 Fed. 897 (E.D.N.Y., 1908). 

A libel was filed by a citizen of the United States and three subjects of Greece against the Epsom, a vessel of British registry, for wages as seamen. They had previously presented their claim to the 

British Vice Consul at Seattle, who had refused to order their discharge from the ship or the payment of their wages. In the answer it was alleged, inter alia, that, under the laws of Great Britain under which the contract of the libelants' employment was made, seamen were not entitled under articles such as those in issue to sue in any foreign court for wages unless discharged with the sanction of the laws and written consent of the master or unless they had proven ill usage, that such was the common maritime law of the world, and that none of the libelants had been so discharged. The United States 

District Court in rendering a decree for the libelants said: ... An American citizen, when he signs shipping articles and steps upon a British ship, flying the British flag, becomes entitled to the protection and the benefit of the British law as fully as a British subject; but he does not thereby forfeit his citizenship, nor his right to redress wrongs in the courts of his own country. 

The right to invoke the jurisdiction of the federal courts by a citizen of the United States for the purpose of determining a Right of dispute under shipping articles with a foreign vessel is a consti- American tutional right, which the courts cannot deny. The people have citizen ordained by the Constitution that judicial power shall be vested in the national courts, and that the judicial power shall extend to all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction. These provisions without doubt are for the purpose of creating a tribunal where a citizen of the United States may as a matter of right seek redress of wrongs cognizable in adn iralty, and enforce legal rights.

It stated that having taken cognizance of one libelant because of his American citizenship it would not dismiss the others but would inquire into the grievances of all and declared that the issue was governed by English law, under which they were justified in refusing to serve on the ground that the commercial risk was not that contemplated in their contract. It was held that they were entitled to recover wages. 

227 Fed. 158, 161 (W.D. Wash., 1915).

Section 4 of the Seamen's Act of March 4, 1915, as amended June 

5, 1920, amending section 4530 of the Revised Statutes, gives to every seaman on a vessel of the United States the right to demand one half of the unpaid wages he has earned, at every port where such vessel, after the commencement of the voyage, loads or delivers cargo before the end thereof and provides that stipulations in the contract to the contrary are void. The section also provides that "Such a demand shall not be made before the expiration of, nor oftener than once in, five days" and that failure on the part of the master to comply with the demand releases the seaman from his contract and entitles him to full payment of wages earned. The section provides further that it shall apply to seamen on foreign vessels while in the harbors of the United States and that the courts of the United States shall be open to such seamen for its enforcement. 

38 Stat. 1164, 1165; 41 Stat. 988, 1006.

In Strathearn S.S. Co., Ltd., v. Dillon a libel had been filed against a British vessel by a British subject, who had shipped thereon at Liverpool, for the wages allegedly earned by him. He had demanded one half of his wages while the vessel was in the port of Pensacola, Florida, and payment was refused. Under the libelant's shipping articles wages were made payable at the end of the voyage, no cash was to be advanced to him abroad or liberty granted other than at the pleasure of the master, and his voyage was to end at a port in the United Kingdom. The libelant's demand was made within less than five days after the vessel's arrival in Pensacola. The United States

Supreme Court held that section 4 of the Seamen's Act of 1915 conferred equality of right on American and foreign seamen in respect to the privileges thereof, with equal opportunity to resort to American courts for the enforcement of the act. It upheld the right of 

Congress to pass such a statute applicable to foreign vessels in American ports and controlling the employment and payment of seamen as a condition of the right of such foreign vessels to enter and use the ports of the United States and, further, held that the

libelant's demand for wages was not premature, stating that the section permitted no demand until five days after the voyage had begun and that to require that a vessel be in an American port for five days before demand could be made "would run counter to the manifest purpose of Congress to prevent a seaman from being without means while in a port of the United States". The Court affirmed the decree of the circuit court of appeals holding the libelant entitled to recover. 252 U.S. (1920) 348, 357. 

In the case of Transportes Maritimos Do Estado v. Almeido, Almeido, the plaintiff below, sought to recover wages allegedly due him as a waiter on the Portuguese steamer Goa, owned by the defendant. The circuit court of appeals stated that Almeido was "a foreign seaman", that it was solely upon his contractual relations with the Goa that his cause of action depended, and that it remained uncontroverted that when the action was begun, and at all times since, the Goa was not in New York or elsewhere in the United States. The plaintiff's right of action was asserted under sections 4529 and 4530 of the Revised Statutes. In view of the proviso in the latter section that it shall apply to seamen on foreign vessels while in the harbors of the United States (ante, this section), the cause was remanded with directions to dismiss the complaint. 5 F. (2d) 151 (C.C.A. 

2d, 1925).

In The Strathlorne, Van Der Liet et al. v. Burrell & Sons a libel against the steamship Strathlorne, a foreign vessel, was brought by four foreign seamen, charging a breach of contracts in that the vessel was unseaworthy and seeking to recover the balance of wages due thereunder. The respondent excepted to the libel on the ground that the suit was between foreigners and that the court should not exercise jurisdiction in the case. 

The action was brought under section 8322 of the United States Compiled Statutes relating to the time and manner of the payment of seamen's wages (sec. 4530 of the Rev. Stat.) The United States District Court, in sustaining the exception and dismissing the libel, stated that that statute was exclusively a wage statute and was not intended to extend to foreign seamen other relief than the payment of their stipulated wages. 

Since the action sought not merely to show a failure to pay wages but also a breach in the contracts on the ground that the ship was unseaworthy and since the contracts were between foreigners, the court declared that the action was outside of the purview of section 8322. 15 

F. (2d) 210 (D. Ore., 1926).

In the case of The Sneland I the libelant brought an action for wages against the vessel claiming the benefit of shipping articles signed in Norway under Norwegian law and double wages under the laws of the United States. He alleged that he had become ill in 

Gulfport, Mississippi, where he had consulted a doctor and that he had later consulted doctors at New Orleans. The claimant master, as bailee for the owner, excepted and objected to the exercise of jurisdiction by the court. A protest was also filed by the Norwegian Consul at New Orleans, on the ground that the controversy was between for-

Exception to the rule Advance payment of wages eign owners and officers of the vessel and a seaman who was not a citizen of the United States but a Norwegian subject concerning a contract of shipping articles made in Norway over which the Norwegian Consul was given authority to decide disputes under the contract and the laws of Norway and which was justiciable in the courts of that Kingdom. The District Court of the United States for the 

Eastern District of Louisiana in dismissing the plea to the jurisdiction stated that the allegations of the libel and the attached exhibits inclined it to the opinion that since discharge and failure of payment of wages due occurred in New Orleans and since the alleged failure of the master to give the seaman necessary medical attention necessitated a surgical operation there where all the witnesses resided, the case should be considered as coming within the exception to the rule that jurisdiction would ordinarily not be exercised over such cases between foreign seamen and foreign owners under foreign shipping articles because a hardship might otherwise be unjustly imposed on the seaman. 

19 Fed. (2d) 528 (E.D. La., 1927).

Section 11 of the Seamen's Act of March 4, 1915 forbids the pay ment to seamen of wages in advance and penalizes any violation of the provision. It provides that payment of advance wages shall not absolve the vessel or master or owner thereof from the full payment of wages when they shall have been actually earned and also that that section shall apply to foreign vessels while in waters of the United States, and that the master, owner, or consignee or agent thereof shall be liable to the same penalties as the master, owner, or agent of a vessel of the United States. 

38 Stat. 1164, 1168. See the amendment to the section, post p. 247.

The Commissioner of Navigation instructed the collectors of customs, shipping commissioners, and others concerned that on and after Mar. 4, 1916 section 11 of the Seamen's Act of Mar. 4, 1915 would apply "to seamen engaged in the United States for vessels of every foreign nation". Counselor Polk to the diplomatic officers of the United States in certain countries, Mar. 9, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 196.6/86. See also 

1916 For. Rel. 5. 

In the case of Sandberg et al. v. McDonald, Claimant of the British Ship "Talus", a libel was filed by seamen, who were not alleged to be American citizens, against the British vessel Talus to recover wages allegedly due them. It appeared that the seamen had boarded the ship in Ireland and had received certain advance wages from the master thereof at Liverpool, England. When the ship was in the harbor of Mobile, Alabama, the libelants demanded of the master one half of the wages already earned by them. The master paid them a certain sum deducting therefrom the advances made to them in Liverpool. The United States Supreme Court

held that section 11 of the Seamen's Act of 1915 did not control such matters otherwise than in the ports of the United States and said: "Legislation is presumptively territorial and confined to limits over which the law-making power has jurisdiction . . "... Congress certainly did not intend to punish criminally acts done within a foreign jurisdiction; a purpose so wholly futile as not to be attributed to Congress.". 

The Court affirmed the decision of the circuit court of appeals holding that the advance payments made to the seamen in Liverpool should be deducted from their half-wages. Justices McKenna, Holmes, Brandeis, and Clarke dissented. 248 U.S. (1918) 185, 195, 196.

In the cases of Neilson et al. v. Rhine Shipping Co., Claimant of the 

Sailing Ship “Rhine" and Hardy et al. v. Shephard & Morse Lumber Co., Claimant of the Barkentine "Windrush", the libelants were seamen on

American vessels who had shipped at Buenos Aires and had received in that port advance wages. When the vessel arrived in New York the libelants were paid the wages earned less the sums advanced. They sought to recover the sums thus deducted under section 11 of the Seamen's Act of 1915. The United States Supreme Court affirmed a decree of the circuit court of appeals reversing a decree of the district court in favor of the libelants. The Court said that the same general considerations as to the interpretation of the statute which controlled in the decision of the case of Sandberg v. McDonald were applicable in this case. The 

Court stated that it might be conceded that American vessels might be controlled by Congressional legislation as to contracts made in foreign ports but declared that it appeared that Congress intended to legislate as to advances made in ports of the United States. Justices McKenna, Holmes, Brandeis, and Clarke dissented. 248 U.S. (1918) 205.

Following the decisions in the two cases last cited, Congress by Jones act, section 32 of the Jones act (the Merchant Marine Act of 1920) 1920, sec. 32 amended that clause of section 11 of the Seamen's Act, approved March 4, 1915, providing that the payment of advance wages shall not absolve the master or owner thereof from the full payment of wages, to read as follows:

The payment of such advance wages whether made within or without the United States or territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof, shall in no case except as herein provided absolve the vessel or the master or the owner thereof from the full payment of wages after the same shall have been actually earned, and shall be no defense to a libel suit or action for the recovery of such wages. 

41 Stat. 988, 1006–1007.

The Supreme Court of the United States held in 1928 that the amendment to section 11 of the Seamen's Act of 1915 contained in section 32 of the Jones act "expressed no intention to extend the provisions of the statute to advance payments made by foreign vessels while in foreign ports" and that the phrase "whether made within

or without the United States or territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof" contained in the act of 1920, when read in the light of the context, was given full effect when applied to American vessels and indicated no intention to extend the prohibition of the statute to advance wages paid by foreign vessels while in foreign ports. 

Jackson et al. v. S.S. “Archimedes”, 275 U.S. (1928) 463, 470.

DESERTION OF SEAMEN 

$144 Section 5280 of the Revised Statutes of the United States contained provision that, on application in writing of a consul or vice consul of any foreign government having a treaty with the United States stipulating for the restoration of deserting seamen, stating that a Prior to 1915 seaman had deserted from a vessel of that government while in a port of the United States, and on proof by the exhibition of the register of the vessel, ship's roll, or other official document that the person named belonged to the crew of the vessel, it should be the duty of any court, judge, commissioner of any circuit court, justice, or other magistrate, having competent power, to issue warrants to cause the seaman to be arrested for examination; and that if, on examination, the facts stated were found to be true, the seaman (not being a citizen of the United States) should be delivered up to the consul or vice consul making the request.

The German Ambassador wrote to the Secretary of State in 1903 contending that under article XIV of the consular convention of 

December 11, 1871 between the United States and Germany, 1 

Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 550, a person charged with desertion should be turned over to the German Consul upon his written request supported only by the documents mentioned in the convention. The convention provided that German Consuls in the United States might apply to the Federal, State, or municipal courts or authorities in writing for deserters, supporting the request "by an official extract of the register of the vessel and the list of the crew, or by other official documents, to show that the men whom they claim belong to said crew" and that, upon such request thus supported, the deserters "shall be given up to the Consuls". The Attorney General to whom the question was referred informed the Secretary of State on November 2, 1903 that the question whether deserters should be given up without the examination authorized in section 5280 of the Revised Statutes upon the written request of a German Consul and the filing of the papers mentioned in article XIV of the convention was a question to be determined by an appropriate court. He pointed out that under both the statute and convention a method for judicial determination of the question was provided, since provision was made

in both for application to the proper court for the restoration of deserting seamen. 

25 Op. Att. Gen. (1906) 77.

The Norwegian Minister on Feb. 23, 1907 wrote to the Department of 

State complaining of the passage of a bill by the California Senate on Jan. 30, 1907 repealing an article of the Penal Code of that State making it a misdemeanor to entice seamen to desert their ships. The Secretary of Commerce and Labor on Mar. 16, 1907 wrote to the Secretary of State in this regard, saying: "While the repeal of this State law would doubtless render easier the desertion of seamen the Norwegian Minister may be advised that such repeal would not affect the duties of the State and local officers of California under acts of Congress relating to deserters."

He added that, under section 5280 of the Revised Statutes, the State and local authorities of California "must at the request of Consuls undertake to reclaim deserters from foreign ships in ports of California, whatever the laws of the State may be”. A copy of this letter was transmitted to the Norwegian Minister. Minister Hauge to Secretary Root, Feb. 23, 1907, MS. As the result of protests by the French Ambassador in respect to the crimping of deserters from French vessels on the Pacific coast, the United 

States Commissioner of Navigation, on July 12, 1907, issued the following instructions to the shipping commissioners at Port Townsend, Washington, and San Francisco, California, outlining measures to check the practice in which the French Government had indicated its willingness to cooperate: "When a seaman applies to you for shipment on an American vessel, who is, in your opinion, a deserter from a French vessel, you will at once communicate the fact, by telephone if practicable, to the French Consul. 

If the French Consul states that steps have been taken for the apprehension of the deserter, you will decline to ship the seaman before the expiration of twenty-four hours from the time he applies for shipment. "You will please confer with the French Consul on these instructions. 

The Bureau is advised that that officer will be instructed by his government."

The French Consul General at San Francisco had previously been instructed by the French Ambassador in Washington to consult with the competent American authorities when the measures outlined above had been put into effect and to issue suitable instructions when the occasion arose to the consular agents concerned within his district.

In an informal memorandum of Feb. 12, 1908 the German Embassy brought to the attention of the Department of State the alleged practice of discharged and deserting seamen in Honolulu of bringing into court claims against the captains of their ships, which claims, even when based on the slightest evidence, were on principle, the Embassy said, always taken up by the Federal court in that port. The memorandum stated that the chief advantage derived from this practice went to various solicitors

Seamen's 

Act, 1915 and that the captains of the vessels usually preferred to accept a compromise even when the decision of the court would probably be in their favor, so as to protect the owners of the vessels from the heavy costs of a lawsuit which they would in any case be unable to recover from the penniless claimants. This course, it was said, appeared the more advisable as the solicitors generally enforced their demands for an agreement by the threat of appealing to the superior court at San Francisco, by which the cost of the suit would be increased still further. It was asked, therefore, whether the judge in similar cases could not first ask the consul of the foreign claimant for the necessary information before admitting the case to court. Ibid. 14648.

This matter was referred to the Attorney General by the Department of State. The substance of his reply was transmitted to the German Embassy on Sept. 23, 1908 in a memorandum in which it was said that the Department of Justice ". . . has caused an investigation to be made by the United States District Attorney for the District of Hawaii. The 

District Attorney has reported to the Department of Justice that the correspondence in regard to the matter has been brought to the attention of the Judge of the United States Court. The Statutes of the United States provide for suits in forma pauperis in proper cases at the discretion of the Court, and it would not be possible under our law for the Judge in such cases to take the opinion of a foreign consular officer. It is, of course, possible that the courts may have been imposed upon in some cases and permission to sue in forma pauperis secured by persons who would not have secured it had not the court been misled as to the facts of the case. "It is believed by the Department of Justice that the attention of the court having been called to the matter, special care will be taken in the examination of applications for suit in such cases of in forma pauperis. 

There would seem to be no further action which can be taken by the Department of Justice at present but should any specific case hereafter arise in which it is believed injustice has been done, this Department will be glad, upon the matter being brought to its attention, to request the Department of Justice to make such investigation as may be proper, with a view to doing whatever can properly be done to correct any evils which may be found to exist." 

Ibid. 14648/2.

The prior situation with respect to deserting seamen was changed by the so-called "La Follette Seamen's Act" approved March 4, 1915. 

Section 16 of the act contained provision that the President should, within 90 days after the passage of the act, give notice to the foreign governments concerned of the termination of articles in treaties and conventions "of the United States in so far as they provided for the arrest and imprisonment of officers and seamen deserting or charged with desertion from merchant vessels of the United States in foreign countries, and . . . of officers and seamen deserting or charged with desertion from merchant vessels of foreign nations in the United States and the Territories and possessions thereof, . . ." and of any other treaty provision in conflict with the provisions of the act,

the termination to take effect on the expiration of such periods after notices had been given as required in the treaties and conventions. 

Section 17 contained provision that upon the termination of such periods, the above-described provisions in treaties and conventions should be held to have expired and section 5280 of the Revised Statutes and so much of section 4081 as related to deserting seamen should be and was thereby repealed. 

38 Stat. 1164, 1184. See Van der Weyde v. Ocean Transport Co., Ltd., et al., 297 U.S. (1936) 114, and The Sinaloa, 292 Fed. 640 (N.D. Cal., S. Div., 1923).

In regard to the termination of treaty provisions pursuant to the act, see chapter on "Treaties".

In 1917 the Department of State wrote to the American Consul at Le Havre, France, in regard to the effect of the Seamen's Act approved March 4, 1915 on the convention of navigation and commerce of June 24, 1822 and the consular convention of February 23, 1853 concluded between the United States and France, as follows:

You are correct in your understanding that Article VI of the Treaty of June 24, 1822, and Articles VIII and IX of the Treaty of February 23, 1853, were abrogated in accordance with an understanding between the two Governments, made necessary by certain provisions contained in the so-called Seamen's Act, approved March 4, 1915.

Article VI of the Treaty of 1822, and Article IX of the Treaty of 1853 were affected by section 16 of the act which directed the President within ninety days of the enactment thereof to notify all foreign governments concerned of the termination of articles of all treaties providing for the arrest and imprisonment of seamen deserting or charged with desertion from vessels of the United States or from foreign vessels in American waters. 

Article VIII of the Treaty of 1853 was inconsistent with section 4 of the act which provides among other things for the enforcement of certain specified rights of foreign seamen respecting their wages and further provides that the "courts of the United States shall be open to such seamen for its enforcement." article was also affected by section 16 of the act. This It appears to be well recognized that when a merchant vessel visits the port of a foreign country for the purpose of trade, it is amenable to the jurisdiction of that country and is subject to the laws which govern the port it visits so long as it remains, unless it is otherwise provided by treaty. This Government, while conceding on the one hand such amenability of vessels to local jurisdiction, has made clear its views in the past to the effect that by comity matters of discipline and all things done on board which affect only the vessel or those belonging to her and do not involve the peace or dignity of the country or the tranquillity of the port should be left by the local govern- 157511-40-VOL. II-17

ment to be dealt with by the authorities of the nation to which the vessel belongs, as the laws of that nation or the interests of its commerce may require. Numerous excerpts from diplomatic correspondence indicating the position of this Government on this subject may be found in Moore's Digest of International 

Law, Vol. II, pp. 272 to 362. However, it must apparently be considered that this general rule of comity has been set aside in a measure by section 4 of the Seamen's Act which confers jurisdiction on courts of the United States in suits of seamen for wages. 

After quoting from Wildenhus's Case, 120 U.S. (1887) 1, 11-12, the

You are, therefore, instructed that, in connection with matters affecting the relations of masters and crews of vessels, your activities should be limited to such acts as, on the one hand, are consistent with laws and regulations of this Government and, on the other hand, are permissible under the laws of France. 

Touching your inquiry as to whether you would be justified in applying to the local police authorities for the arrest and detention of drunken or obstreperous sailors whom the Captain of the vessel is unable to manage, it may be stated that no action should be taken by you in matters of this kind not in harmony with the letter and the spirit of section 16 of the act abolishing "the arrest and imprisonment of officers and seamen deserting or charged with desertion from merchant vessels." It may be observed, however, that in certain cases it may not be improper for you to call the attention of local authorities to misconduct such as that referred to in your despatch which may be contrary to local law. 

A similar answer would appear to be pertinent to your second inquiry as to whether you would be justified hereafter "in requesting the Gendarmerie Maritime to detail to an American ship one or more gendarmes, in order to prevent desertions from the ship just before the time of sailing." It may be possible that local laws or regulations may forbid the departure of a seaman under the circumstances indicated in your despatch, and should such be the case, the French authorities would doubtless be within their rights in preventing seamen from leaving a vessel under such circumstances. 

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Osborne, no. 185, July 17, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 711.5121/5.

The Department of State instructed the Consul General at Buenos Aires in 1917 in regard to the arrest of deserting seamen as follows: 

The view which you apparently entertain to the effect that the local Argentine authorities should arrest deserting seamen on your request seems to be based on the supposition that, since it appears that treaty stipulations between Italy and the Argentine Republic obligate authorities of the latter country to arrest deserting Italian seamen on the request of Italian consular officers, American seamen should be arrested on the request of

American consular officers in view of the favored nation clause contained in Article III of the treaty concluded July 27, 1853, between the United States and the Argentine Republic. 

Without entering into a discussion of the question as to whether the favored nation clause just mentioned could properly be construed as having the effect of carrying the benefits of treaty stipulations such as those in force between Italy and Argentina to which you call attention, the Department may point out to you that, in view of the provisions of Section 16 of the so-called Seamen's Act, approved March 4, 1915, which abolished the arrest of deserting seamen and authorized the President to take steps to terminate treaty stipulations providing for the arrest and imprisonment of seamen deserting from vessels of the United States abroad, or from foreign vessels in American waters, no request for the arrest of American deserters by Argentine authorities, should be made by you.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul General Robertson, no. 320, Nov. 7, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 196.3/29.

In a circular instruction of Aug. 15, 1917 to American consular officers, the Department of State, after referring to the Seamen's Act approved Mar. 4, 1915 and listing the articles of treaties at variance with the provisions of the act, said: "Provisions of treaties relating to the arrest of deserting seamen and to the adjudication of disputes between masters and crews regarding wages found in the articles above referred to should therefore no longer be invoked by American consular officers, and your activities in relation to these matters should be limited to such acts as, on the one hand, are consistent with the laws and regulations of this Government and, on the other hand, are permissible under the laws of the country in which you are stationed." Ibid. 196.5/51a.

On May 11, 1917 the Portuguese Minister addressed a memorandum to the Department of State pointing out that Portuguese steamers arriving in New York and Baltimore had been greatly hampered in their movements through the desertion of members of their crews and suggesting that the United States immigration law might be used to prevent such desertion, especially in view of the fact that their abandonment of the vessels amounted practically to desertion from the Portuguese military forces which were then an ally of the United States in the war with Germany. The Department replied that the Secretary of Labor had pointed out thatin view of the provisions of the Act of Congress, approved 

March 4, 1915, (38 Statutes at Large, 1164) known as the "Seamen's Act", his Department is compelled to enforce the immigration law so far as it applies to the cases of seamen in such manner as not to interfere with the provisions of the Statute which annuls the remedy which theretofore existed to prevent the desertion of alien seamen in ports of the United States. 

Memorandum from the Secretary of State to the Portuguese Minister, May 22, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 853.865/4.
