In August 1927 a strike of firemen occurred on board the British vessel Firpark in the harbor of New Orleans. The master of the vessel appealed to the police authorities of the State of Louisiana who referred him to the British Consul General in New Orleans, on the ground that as the ship flew a foreign flag it was not within their competence to intervene in the dispute. The Consul General was unable to persuade the firemen to return to work, and he then invoked the aid of the United States District Attorney who expressed the opinon that the matter was one with which the Consul General himself was fully competent to deal under section 4081 of the Revised Statutes of the United States, to the exclusion of any authority and jurisdiction of the United States. Under British law the British consular officers were not authorized to proceed in disputes of that nature beyond an effort to bring about an amicable settlement. Failing the success of their efforts, the only course open to them was to summon a naval court to deal with the matter under sections 480-486 of the British Merchant Shipping Act of 1894 and sections 

67 and 68 of the British Merchant Shipping Act of 1906. The 

British Consul General, however, hesitated to summon such a court and subsequently advised the master of the Firpark to discharge the striking seamen without penalties and to engage substitutes. The master accepted this advice, and on August 16, 1927 the Firpark cleared from New Orleans.

On November 3, 1927 the British Ambassador submitted a memorandum to the Department of State reciting these facts and inquiring whether the United States would be prepared to express its willingness to permit British Consuls in the United States, in case of necessity, to summon a naval court in accordance with the relevant provisions of the British Merchant Shipping Acts and to recognize and give effect to the findings of such a court, thereby obviating the recurrence of similar incidents. The Department replied:

The Congress of the United States, by the Act of March 4, 1915, commonly known as the Seaman's Act, requested and directed the President to abrogate all treaties or parts thereof insofar as they provide for the arrest and imprisonment of officers and seamen deserting or charged or charged with desertion from merchant vessels of the United States in foreign countries and for the arrest and imprisonment of officers and seamen deserting or charged with desertion from foreign merchant vessels in the United States and for the cooperation, aid and protection of competent legal authorities in effecting such arrest or imprisonment. Pursuant to this Act notice of abrogation of the treaty between Great Britain and the United 

States concluded June 3, 1892, providing for the recovery of deserters from merchant vessels was sent to your Government, the abrogation to be effective July 1, 1916. .. You will note that Section 17 specifically repeals Section 5280 of the Revised 

---

Statutes of the United States providing for the restoration by authorities of the United States of deserting seamen on the application of a consul or vice consul of any foreign government having a treaty with the United States stipulating for such action. It also repeals that part of Section 4081 of the Revised 

Statutes of the United States relied upon by the United States District Attorney in New Orleans in expressing the views referred to on page one of your memorandum. There appears to be no other provision of law authorizing the authorities of the United States to give assistance in such matters. 

In these circumstances you will readily appreciate that a decision by a Naval Court convoked in the United States by a 

British consul pursuant to the British Merchant Shipping Acts could not be accorded recognition or support by the authorities of the United States. 

The Under Secretary of State (Olds) to Sir Esme Howard, Nov. 14, 1927, MS. Department of State, file 841.303/2.

SALVAGE $145 

In December 1926 the Cuban Embassy in Washington requested permission for Cuban vessels to salvage the Cuban fishing vessel Rita 

Maria then stranded at the entrance to the port of Tampa, Florida.

The Department of State replied that section 4241 of the Revised Statutes of the United States forbade the regular employment of a vessel or its master in the business of wrecking on the coast of Florida without the license of the judge of the District Court for the District of Florida. It was assumed, however, it was said, that in the instant case the vessels employed would not be regularly engaged in such business, so that the Department of Commerce would interpose no objection to the salvaging of the vessel by foreign vessels provided that a report was made to the customhouse at Tampa before the work was begun. 

The Under Secretary of State (Grew) to Ambassador Ferrara, Jan. 28, 1927, MS. Department of State, file 837.857/26.

In 1908 the Department of State, in reply to an inquiry from the 

German Ambassador regarding the navigation of salvage-wrecking vessels in the United States, stated that such navigation was governed by the rules, laws, and regulations generally applicable to ocean navigation on the seacoasts of the United States and that special rules had been made governing the operation of Canadian salvagewrecking vessels on the northern frontier in the waters of the United States contiguous to the Dominion of Canada, including the Great

Remunera tion for services Lakes, the privileges accorded in the last-mentioned case being dependent upon reciprocity by Canada. 

Secretary Root to the Chargé d'Affaires, Count Von Hatzfeldt-Wilden burg, no. 761, May 26, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 13380/1.

On the question of remuneration for services for the salvaging of vessels in distress, the Legal Adviser of the Department of State on November 28, 1934 stated:

It is important in considering this subject to bear in mind that remuneration for salvage services, unlike that for most other services rendered voluntarily, is not determined on a quantum meruit basis, nor is it necessarily governed by the contractwhen there is a contract-between the salvors and the salvaged vessel. Remuneration for salvage service, generally speaking, has two aspects, namely, (1) compensation for services rendered and (2) reward designed to encourage prompt, energetic and efficient service in the relief of vessels in peril. Steamer Avalon 

Co. v. Hubbard S.S. Co., 255 Fed. 854, 856 (C.C.A. 9th, 1919); 

Hughes on Admiralty (1920) 143.

The matter is not governed by international law, except in so far as international agreements on the subject may be regarded as international law. The subject is one controlled primarily by the municipal law of the various countries. In some countries the amount to be paid for salvage services is fixed by law. In the United States, however, and this apparently is also true in Great Britain, the rate of compensation is largely a matter within the discretion of the court. 271 Fed. 202, 203 (C.C.A. 2d, 1921). 

Article III, section 2, clause 1, of the Constitution of the 

United States provides that "The judicial Power shall extend to all Cases of admiralty and maritime Jurisdiction." 

By title 28, sections 41 and 371 of the United States Code, the Federal courts of the United States are given exclusive jurisdiction, in admiralty cases, and hence in salvage cases. These courts, in determining the amount to be allowed for salvage services look to the circumstances of the individual case. When the risk is inconsiderable and the service slight, the award is generally little more than the remuneration for the work and labor involved. When the service is attended with unusual danger and difficulty, the award is proportionately higher. 

While the rule has been variously stated, the elements generally considered by the court in any case are the danger to the ship, actual or apprehended, the degree of danger from which the property was rescued, the labor expended and the promptitude, energy and skill displayed by the salvors, whether the property is saved, the value of the property employed in the service, and the risks and damage to which it was exposed. The Neshaminy, 228 Fed. 285, 289 (C.C.A. 3d, 1915). 

The act of Congress approved March 3, 1800, made provision for the payment, in lieu of salvage, on the turning over to the owners in the United States of recaptured vessels or goods which

had been taken as prize by enemies of the United States, oneeighth part, if retaken by a public vessel of the United States, and one-sixth part, if retaken by a private vessel of the United States, of the true value of the vessel or goods so restored. If the vessel or goods previously belonged to aliens, nationals of a friendly Power, the aliens were required by the act to pay such portion of the value of the property restored as by the law or usage of that country "shall be required on the restoration of any vessel or goods of a citizen of the United States, under like circumstances of recapture, made by the authority of such foreign prince, government or state". 2 Stat. 16, 17.

A somewhat similar practice was followed in England, Portugal, Denmark, Sweden, Holland, and Spain. Hall's International Law (8th ed., by Higgins, 1924) 584, 585.

The act of 1864 (13 Stat. 314), amended by the act of 1899 (30 

Stat. 1007), now embodied in title 34, sec. 1158 of the U.S. Code, provides that in cases of recaptured property from any hostile force "the court shall award a meet and competent sum as salvage, according to the circumstances of each case". 

These provisions of law do not have a direct bearing on the subject under consideration, which relates only to the salvage of vessels in distress, but they are referred to as of possible interest in showing the legislative trend in salvage matters. The Congress does not appear to have laid down any rule as to the remuneration to be paid in the ordinary case of salvage of vessels and property. The matter, as stated above, seems to have been left to the discretion of the Federal courts in the exercise of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction. In the older cases the percentage rule seems to have been followed. Thus, Kent in his 

Commentaries on American Law states, with reference to salvage, that "the allowance fluctuates between one-half, one-third, and one-fourth of the gross or net proceeds of the property saved, but one-third has been the most usual rate". Vol. III, op. cit. (12th ed., by Holmes, 1873) 245. Recent cases indicate that the courts do not follow any fixed rate or share of the value of the salvaged property. They allow such amounts as in their judgment seem to be just and fair. In the case of The Kia Ora, 252 Fed. 507, 509 (C.Č.A. 4th, 1918), the court said: "Examination of the many cases with their varying facts gives a general sense of the proportion which the award ought to bear to the risk and expense incurred, the skill employed, the value of the property saved and the property lost, the peril of the vessel and cargo, the investment and enterprise of the salvor, the liberality of the allowance for profit in order to encourage enterprise in assisting and saving vessels in peril. But no formula can be derived which will meet the justice of every case. The per cent. basis is no longer followed, because its application to the large values of modern times would lead to obvious injustice. 

Post v. Jones, 19 How. 150, 15 L. Ed. 618. In view of these rules, we consider the strong and perspicuous opinion of the 

District Judge."

Convention of 1910 In this case $150,000 was allowed for the rescue from a coral reef near the Bahamas of a ship and cargo worth $3,900,000. 

In the case of The George Hawley et al., 242 Fed. 473 (C.C.A. 

5th, 1917), a salvage award of $17,500 was allowed on a ship and cargo worth $215,000. The vessel was sinking at a wharf in 

New Orleans. 

Where a vessel was valued at $70,000, $9,000 was allowed two tugs and a revenue_cutter for salvage aid. United States v. 

Central Wharf Towboat Co. et al., 3 F. (2d) 250 (C.C.A. 1st, 1924).

In the case of Bullard et al., v. 230,263 Feet of Lumber, 267 

Fed. 860 (S.D. Fla., 1920), an award of 75 percent of the net proceeds was made for the salvaging of a cargo of lumber of a wrecked and abandoned schooner, which lay in an exposed position, the work being difficult. 

In another case, that of The High Cliff, 271 Fed. 202 (C.C.A. 

2d, 1921), $2,500 was allowed for towing a drifting barge having on board a cargo worth $200,000, and berthing it to a pier, the barge being in a protected place and the service requiring less than an hour's labor and being unattended with danger to the tug. 

The only international convention bearing on this subject is the convention for the unification of certain rules of law with respect to assistance and salvage at sea, signed at Brussels, September 23, 1910, and proclaimed by the President, February 13, 1913. 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2943; 37 Stat. 1658. The leading maritime nations of the world, some twenty-five or thirty countries in all, including Great Britain, France, Germany, Japan, Norway and Sweden, are parties to this Convention. 

The underlying theme of the convention is that, in the absence of an agreement between the parties, the remuneration is fixed by the court according to the circumstances of each case. 

Articles 2, 6, 7, and 8 provide that: 

"ARTICLE 2. 

"Every act of assistance or salvage which has had a useful result gives a right to equitable remuneration. "No remuneration is due if the services rendered have no beneficial result. "In no case shall the sum to be paid exceed the value of the property salved. 

"ARTICLE 6. 

"The amount of remuneration is fixed by agreement between the parties, and, failing agreement, by the court. "The proportion in which the remuneration is to be distributed among the salvors is fixed in the same manner. "The apportionment of the remuneration among the owner, master, and other persons in the service of each salving vessel is determined by the law of the vessel's flag. 

"ARTICLE 7. 

"Every agreement as to assistance or salvage entered into at the moment and under the influence of danger can, at the request

of either party, be annulled or modified by the court if it considers that the conditions agreed upon are not equitable. "In all cases, when it is proved that the consent of one of the parties is vitiated by fraud or concealment, or when the remuneration is, in proportion to the services rendered, in an excessive degree too large or too small, the agreement may be annulled or modified by the court at the request of the party affected. 

"ARTICLE 8. 

"The remuneration is fixed by the court, according to the circumstances of each case, on the basis of the following considerations: (a) First, the measure of success obtained, the efforts and the deserts of the salvors, the danger run by the salved vessel, by her passengers, crew and cargo, by the salvors and by the salving vessel, the time expended, the expenses incurred and losses suffered, and the risks of liability and other risks run by the salvors, and also the value of the property exposed to such risks, due regard being had, the case arising, to the special adaptation of the salvor's vessel: (b) second, the value of the property salved. "The same provisions apply to the apportionment provided for by the second paragraph of article 6. "The court may reduce or deny remuneration if it appears that the salvors have by their fault rendered the salvage or assistance necessary, or have been guilty of theft, receiving stolen goods, or other acts of fraud."

It will be seen from article 7 that agreements entered into at the moment of danger may, under certain specified circumstances, be annulled by the court, and from article 8 that the court, in fixing remuneration for salvage service, is to take into consideration all the circumstances of the case. That is, in fact, what the courts in the United States and Great Britain have been doing. 

Article 12 of the convention reads: 

"ARTICLE 12. 

"The High Contracting Parties whose legislation does not forbid infringements of the preceding article bind themselves to take or to propose to their respective legislatures the measures necessary for the prevention of such infringements. "The High Contracting Parties will communicate to one another, as soon as possible, the laws or regulations which have already been or may be hereafter promulgated in their States for the purpose of giving effect to the above undertakings." Subsequent It will be seen that this article requires of the contracting parties to undertake to obtain legislation to prevent infringement of the provisions of the convention. Great Britain enacted legislation to give effect to the convention December 16, 1911. legislation 

49 L.R., 1 and 2, Geo. V, ch. 57. Our Congress enacted legislation, approved August 1, 1912, to give effect to the convention. 

The act, entitled "An Act To harmonize the national law of salvage with the provisions of the international convention for 

---

the unification of certain rules with respect to assistance and salvage at sea, and for other purposes" provides, in part, as 

"Sec. 2. That the master or person in charge of a vessel shall, so far as he can do so without serious danger to his own vessel, crew, or passengers, render assistance to every person who is found at sea in danger of being lost; and if he fails to do so, he shall, upon conviction, be liable to a penalty of not exceeding one thousand dollars or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. "Sec. 3. That salvors of human life, who have taken part in the services rendered on the occasion of the accident giving rise to salvage, are entitled to a fair share of the remuneration awarded to the salvors of the vessel, her cargo, and accessories. "Sec. 4. That a suit for the recovery of remuneration for rendering assistance or salvage services shall not be maintainable if brought later than two years from the date when such assistance or salvage was rendered, unless the court in which the suit is brought shall be satisfied that during such period there had not been any reasonable opportunity of arresting the assisted or salved vessel within the jurisdiction of the court or within the territorial waters of the country in which the libelant resides or has his principal place of business. "Sec. 5. That nothing in this Act shall be construed as applying to ships of war or to Government ships appropriated exclusively to a public service." 

37 Stat. 242; U.S. Code, title 46, secs. 728-731.

It will be seen that this act, which follows very closely the provisions of the convention, does not undertake to fix the amount to be paid for salvage services, nor does it lay down any yardstick by which that amount is to be determined. It leaves the matter in the hands of the courts as theretofore. 

It would seem that the convention referred to above was framed largely along the lines of the practice obtaining in the United States and Great Britain in salvage matters. It leaves with the courts the question of determining the amount to be awarded, without any maximum or minimum limitations. While we could amend our law in such a way as to lay down a criterion to be followed by the courts, it would be binding only as to cases brought in our courts. it might be regarded as contravening the convention which leaves the matter to the discretion of the court, subject only to the limitation contained in article 2, namely, that the remuneration shall not exceed the value of the property salved.

The Legal Adviser of the Department of State (Hackworth) to the Under 

Secretary of State (Phillips), MS. Department of State, file 585.7A2a/2.

In the case of Creighton v. Samos Navigation Company and Others a claim was made for salvage by the captain of an English man-of-war which came to the assistance of a Greek vessel on the high seas and brought the vessel to Port Said. The Mixed Tribunal of Port Said held

that the claim must be determined according to the international convention of Brussels of 1910. 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2943. It stated that although Egypt was not a party to the convention the latter was applicable by the Mixed Courts of Egypt as a rule of international law and that where the vessel which carries out the salvage has a different nationality from that of the vessel assisted the national law is not applicable. 17 Gazette des Tribunaux Mixtes d'Egypte (July 1927) 211; 

Annual Digest, 1925-26, Case No. 1.

Upon the subsequent enactment of a law by the Norwegian Government for the recognition by it of certificates of inspection of foreign passenger steamers, the Department of Commerce and Labor on November 4, 1909 informed the Department of State that the necessary instructions had been given for the recognition by the United States of Norwegian certificates of inspection of passenger steamers of that nation.

On March 24, 1911 the Attorney General informed the Secretary of Commerce and Labor that an Italian vessel carrying passengers between American ports and European ports, which sailed from New York with a certificate of inspection and would arrive back there more than 30 days after the expiration of the certificate, would not thereby violate the provisions of sections 4393-4500 of the Revised Statutes, since foreign vessels were subject to inspection only when carrying passengers from the United States. 

29 Op. Att. Gen. 19 (1913).

In a letter addressed to the President on August 25, 1915 the Attorney General expressed the opinion that when not actually carrying passengers neither foreign-cargo nor foreign-passenger steam vessels leaving ports of the United States are subject to the regulations prescribed by section 14 of the Seamen's Act approved March 4, 1915 regarding life-saving appliances and equipment (38 

Stat. 1164, 1170; 30 Op. Att. Gen. (1913-16) 441). The French Ambassador on February 14, 1916 expressed the desire of his Government that the construction thus put on the act of 1915 by the Attorney General, as well as the parity of the French and American safety laws, be officially made of record. The matter was referred to the 

Secretary of Commerce who replied to the Secretary of State that in conformity with the Attorney General's opinion his Department, on September 24, 1915, had issued a circular specifically stating that section 14 of the act would "not apply to foreign steamers carrying passengers from the United States under the flags of those countries whose inspection laws approximate those of the United States and that have entered into reciprocal relations with the United States". 

The circular listed Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Canada, New South Wales, New Zealand, Japan, Netherlands, and Norway as countries having such approximate laws which had entered into such relations. This information was communicated to the 

French Ambassador with the comment that apparently a satisfactory arrangement had been effected so far as French vessels were concerned. 

Secretary Lansing to Ambassador Jusserand, no. 1680, Apr. 12, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 711.5121/1.

PILOTAGE, TONNAGE DUTIES, LIGHT FEES, ETC. 

$147 In many countries the laws require that a vessel entering into or departing from a port thereof, and in some instances in navigating certain territorial waters, canals, etc., shall take on board a local official pilot for the purpose of navigating the vessel while it is within those waters, for which a charge for pilotage service is made.

Questions of pilotage, tonnage duties, light fees, etc., are frequently regulated by agreements between states. 

Section 4219 of the Revised Statutes of the United States, as amended, which prescribes the amount of tonnage duties on foreign vessels entering the United States from any foreign port or place, provides that none of the duties on tonnage "shall be levied on the vessels of any foreign nation if the President of the United States shall be satisfied that the discriminating or countervailing duties of such foreign nations, so far as they operate to the disadvantage of the United States, have been abolished". 46 U.S.C. §121.

Section 4225 of the Revised Statutes, as amended, provides for the levying on foreign vessels entering ports of the United States of a duty denominated "light money" in the same manner and under the same regulations as the tonnage duties. 46 U.S.C. §128. 

Section 4228 of the Revised Statutes, as amended, provides that, upon receipt of satisfactory proof that no discriminating duties of tonnage or imposts are imposed in the ports of a foreign nation upon American vessels, or upon the cargo imported therein, the President may issue a proclamation declaring that "the foreign discriminating duties of tonnage and impost within the United States are suspended" in respect to the vessels of such foreign nation, and the produce, manufactures, or merchandise imported into the United States from such foreign nation, or for any other foreign country, the suspension to take effect from the time of such notification being given to the 

President. 46 U.S.C. §141. 

Certain German steamships were compelled to pay a tax and duty on their tonnage under sections 4219 and 4225 of the Revised Statutes between July 14, 1919 and November 11, 1921. Section 4229 of the 

Revised Statutes provides that no higher rate of duties shall be imposed on vessels of Prussia or their cargoes than are payable on vessels of the United States or their cargoes, and section 4230 provides that the preceding section shall continue in force as long as the equality provided for therein is reciprocated in Prussian ports. On 

July 14, 1919 a general license for trade with Germany was issued by the War Trade Board. War Trade Board Regulation 802, 1919 

For. Rel., vol. II, p. 239. On March 22, 1922 the President, by proclamation, exempted German vessels from the payment of discriminating tonnage duties and imposts under section 4228 of the Revised 

Statutes, the exemption being made effective as from November 11, 1921 (42 Stat. 2267). The plaintiff, owner of the German vessels, sought to recover in the Court of Claims the duties and taxes paid under protest during the period above mentioned. 

The court ordered judgment for the plaintiff. It found that section 4229 of the Revised Statutes was intended to carry into effect.

article II of the treaty of May 1, 1828 between the United States and Prussia providing for reciprocal national treatment in respect to tonnage duties and lighthouse, pilotage, salvage, and port charges of

Prussian and American vessels and that the Government of the United States had recognized this article as applicable to Germany subsequent to the formation of the North German Union in 1866 and the German Empire in 1871. It found also that "under the terms of the treaty of peace with Germany of 1921 [42 Stat. 1939; 3 

Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2596], the provision was made for the manner of the termination of the treaty of 1828 and its termination was effected six months later, after the date of the exchange of ratification of November 11, 1921, the date from which the President's exemption order of March 22, 1922, was made to apply". The court stated that the defendant was in error in insisting that exemption from duties imposed under section 4219 of the Revised Statutes could be claimed only by presidential proclamation under section 4228. It stated that the purpose of the general trade license of July 

14, 1919 "was to make it possible to resume the former commercial dealings between the nationals of the two countries upon and in accord with existing treaties and laws". In regard to the argument that, since sections 4229 and 4230 of the Revised Statutes were omitted from the United States Code of 1926, they are obsolete, the court said that the adoption of the code did not serve to repeal a law and added: 

While a subsequent change of political status may operate to render ineffective a statutory provision in reference to the status quo existing on the date of its enactment, nevertheless it is obviously a delicate matter for a judicial tribunal to hold such a law invalid in the face of long-continued recognition of its validity as applicable to the changed conditions, and the failure of Congress to repeal the law involving important relations with a foreign government adds to the difficulty of so doing. The reciprocal trade relations established by the law continued and each nation involved recognized the legality of the procedure. 

Flensburger Dampfercompagnie v. U.S., 73 Ct. Cls. (1932) 646, 660, 661, 59 F. (2d) 464, 471; certiorari denied, 286 U.S. (1932) 564.

In the case of Standard Oil Company, a Corporation of the State of New Jersey v. The United States claim was made for the refund or remission of certain tonnage taxes and light-moneys paid under protest between August 15, 1920 and April 22, 1921 in respect to vessels owned by a limited-liability company organized under the laws of the Free City of Danzig, of which the plaintiff was the sole beneficial owner. On May 6, 1921 the President of the United States, under the authority vested in him by section 4228 of the Revised Statutes, issued a proclamation discontinuing and suspending the

imposition and collection of the tonnage duties and imposts against the vessels of Poland and the vessels of the Free City of Danzig entering the ports of the United States, such suspension to be effective on and after the date of the proclamation. The Court of Claims held: 

The duties and imposts on foreign vessels imposed by sections 4219 and 4225 can only be suspended by a proclamation of the President issued pursuant to section 4228. Until such proclamation has been issued the taxes provided in these sections are legally imposed and collected. From the effective date of such proclamation the discriminating taxes may no longer be imposed. 

The controlling date as to the suspension and discontinuance of the imposition of the taxes is the effective date of the President's proclamation, in this case May 6, 1921. The taxes involved having all been imposed and collected prior to that date were legally assessed and collected. 

77 Ct. Cls. (1933) 205, 218, 2 F. Supp. 922, 928; certiorari denied, 290

U.S. (1933) 632. 

In accord, see the opinion of the Acting Attorney General rendered to the Secretary of Commerce on Oct. 30, 1925, in which he said: "Sections 4219 and 4228 of the Revised Statutes must be construed together. They pertain to the same subject matter and from their very wording must be considered as parts of one law relating to tonnage duties and imposts on vessels coming into United States ports from foreign ports. Assuming that the underlying purpose of section 4219 was to impose retaliatory duties upon countries discriminating against American vessels, the statute accomplishes this purpose, first by imposing a flat duty upon all vessels entering the United States from foreign countries, and in the same section provides that such vessels may be relieved of paying these duties if the President of the United States shall be satisfied that the country from which the vessels came imposed no duties to the disadvantage of the United States. Nondiscriminatory countries fall into two classes, first those which never have discriminated against vessels of the United States; and, second, those which have imposed such discrimination but have ceased to do so. Under the terms of section 4219 and 

4228, Revised Statutes, the countries falling within either class, by compliance with the terms of the sections may escape the duties imposed by the United States. "Section 4219 deals with the second class by providing that whenever the President shall be satisfied that the discriminating duties have been abolished, the duties provided in that section shall be imposed no longer. 

Section 4228 deals with the first class of countries by providing that whenever the foreign government furnishes to the President satisfactory proof that no discriminating duties are imposed or levied he may issue his proclamation suspending the discriminating duties of the United States. "Under section 4219, the controlling factor in whether duties shall be imposed by the United States is not whether foreign countries have had discriminating duties against the United States and have abolished them but rather it is when the discontinuance of those duties has been determined by the President. Likewise, the controlling factor under section

4228, as to the United States discontinuing the collection of duties is when satisfactory proof has been furnished to the President. Under section 4219, the tonnage duty is imposed and if such duty is levied on vessels from foreign countries which have ceased to discriminate against vessels of the United States, the imposition of the duties under this section can not be suspended until the President shall be satisfied that the discriminating duties of such foreign nation have been discontinued. 

Under both sections 4219 and 4225 this power rests solely with him. "Under section 4228, it is immaterial with regard to the collection of tonnage duties by the United States from foreign vessels coming into our ports that the nation from which that vessel came imposes no tonnage duties on United States vessels unless satisfactory proof of such is given to the President. The section clearly provides that upon satisfactory proof being given to the President by the government of any foreign nation that no discriminating duties of tonnage or imposts are levied in the ports of such nation upon vessels wholly belonging to citizens of the United States, the President may issue his proclamation declaring that the foreign discriminating duties of tonnage and imposts within the United States are suspended." 

34 Op. Att. Gen. (1923-25) 577, 581-582. 

A proclamation by the President, dated Jan. 16, 1934, suspended discriminating duties of tonnage and imposts within the United States on vessels of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the suspension to take effect from Nov. 21, 1933. 48 Stat. 1729. The Attorney General wrote to the Secretary of State on Jan. 12, 1934 expressing the opinion that "As an original proposition the provision of section 4228 of the Revised

Statutes providing that the suspension of discriminatory tonnage dues shall take effect 'from the time' of the notification being given to the President that no discriminating duties of tonnage or imposts are imposed or levied in the ports of the particular foreign State upon vessels wholly belonging to the citizens of the United States, etc., would require an interpretation that the suspension takes place from the time of the day when such notification is received." The Attorney General said, however, that since the notification was actually received at 9 a.m., Nov. 21, 1933, the question as to the proper interpretation of the term time in the statute would appear to be immaterial. 37 Op. Att. Gen. (1932-34) 402.

Article IX of the treaty of friendship, commerce, and consular rights concluded by the United States and Germany on December 8, 1923 is typical of provisions commonly found in treaties relating to pilotage, tonnage duties, light fees, etc. It stipulates: 

No duties of tonnage, harbor, pilotage, lighthouse, quarantine, or other similar or corresponding duties or charges of whatever denomination, levied in the name or for the profit of the Government, public functionaries, private individuals, corporations or establishments of any kind shall be imposed in the ports of the territories of either country upon the vessels of the other, which shall not equally under the same conditions, be imposed on national vessels.

The same article states that the equality of treatment provided for shall apply "reciprocally" to the vessels of the two countries, from

whatever place they may arrive and whatever may be their destination. 

4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4191, 4194; 44 Stat. 2132, 2139-2140.

By notes exchanged in 1894 and 1895 between the United States and Sweden the United States agreed that, for the purpose of computing tonnage dues of Swedish steam vessels having an appendix to their certificates of registry stating their measurement according to the so-called "English system", it would take the tonnage figure indicated in the appendix rather than the tonnage computed according to the Swedish system of measurement and contained in their certificates of registry. In 1922 the Swedish Legation informed the 

Department of State that the San Francisco bar pilots computed pilot charges for Swedish steam vessels on the tonnage computed according to the English system of measurement contained in the appendixes of their certificates of registry but based the pilotage fees on Swedish motor vessels on the tonnage computed according to the Swedish system of measurement indicated in their certificates of registry. The California authorities, to whom the matter was referred, stated that they construed the words "registered measurement" as used in the California statutes dealing with pilotage rates into and out of the harbor of San Francisco to mean the tonnage of vessels indicated in their certificates of registry but that because of the exchange of notes mentioned above they made an exception in the case of Swedish steam vessels but would not be able to extend this exception to Swedish motor vessels. The Swedish Legation upon being informed of this inquired of the Department if it “would consider the conclusion of an agreement supplementing the conditions contained in the notes of 1894 and 1895, providing for the reciprocal treatment of motor vessels on the same basis as steam vessels". The 

Secretary of State replied:

Under the Constitution and Statutes of the United States tonnage charges, which are assessed against a vessel according to its tonnage as an instrument of commerce for entering or leaving a port, or navigating the public waters of this country, are subject to regulation by Congress. On the other hand, fees and charges for pilotage, which are charges of an essentially different kind, are subject to regulation by the several States until such time as Congress deems it advisable to undertake their regulation. 

The notes exchanged between the two governments in 1894 and 1895, which were based on the Act of Congress approved August 5, 1882, (22 Stat. L. 300), relate to the tonnage fees to be charged 

Swedish steam vessels and accordingly need not have been considered by the California authorities as applicable to the question of pilotage fees to be assessed against Swedish steam vessels under the California pilotage regulations; and the fact that they

have considered these notes applicable to the pilotage fees charged Swedish steam vessels would not, so far as the Federal authorities are concerned, obligate them to consider the notes applicable to the pilotage fees charged Swedish motor vessels. 

In the absence of applicable legislation by Congress on the subject, I am of the opinion that a modification of the decision of the California authorities with respect to the pilotage fees charged Swedish motor vessels cannot properly be arranged by an exchange of notes between the United States and Sweden. 

Such a modification can be effected through the negotiation of a treaty or through appropriate legislation by Congress or by the State of California.

The Department of State on August 31, 1927 instructed the Embassy in Chile in respect to a proposed Chilean law containing a provision allowing a 10-percent reduction in the customs duties on imports into Chile on Chilean vessels, to point out that the same duties and charges in American ports were paid by American and

British light dues Chilean vessels and their cargoes and that the Government of the United States would greatly regret the failure on the part of Chile to accord reciprocal treatment to American vessels. It was instructed also to state that the policy of national treatment of shipping was then almost universally followed and was subsequently instructed to call the attention of the Chilean Government to the provisions of section 2502, as amended, and section 4228 of the Revised Statutes of the United States. The former section provides for a discriminating duty of 10 percent on merchandise imported into the United States on foreign vessels, but the latter section authorizes the President to suspend the application of the "foreign discriminating duties of tonnage and impost" in favor of vessels of any country which gives satisfactory proof that it does not impose discriminating duties of tonnage or impost on American vessels or their cargoes. In accordance with the latter provision, it was said, the President, on 

November 1, 1850, issued a proclamation suspending the application of such discriminating duties so far as Chilean vessels were concerned, the suspension to remain effective so long as American vessels were reciprocally exempted from discriminatory treatment in Chile. The 

Ambassador was instructed to point out that the intent of the laws of the United States was that the vessels and merchandise of each foreign country should enjoy in American ports privileges identical with those which American vessels and merchandise enjoyed in that country. The Chilean law in question, as enacted, did not contain the provision against which the United States protested.

A British Order in Council, dated December 17, 1931, fixed dues to be levied after April 1, 1932 at one English penny a ton for every occasion on which a ship passed and derived benefit from certain lighthouses and buoys situated on or near the coast of the Bahamas and the Leeward Islands (Statutory Rules and Orders, 1931, p. 803). 

The Department of State in an instruction to the Ambassador in London on February 2, 1933 pointed out that this Order in Council would apply to United States Shipping Board vessels and other vessels operating between Gulf and United Kingdom ports and that the charge on Shipping Board vessels would approximate $83 a vessel a voyage, in addition to the customary light dues then paid by such vessels when entering a Britsh port. It was explained:

In order to make the situation clear the following actual case is set forth by the Acting Secretary of Commerce: "The motor ship California sailed from San Pedro March 26th last for London and while enroute from the Canal set a course by way of the Inagua Island. As a result following this course the vessel upon her arrival in London was compelled to pay these recently imposed light dues and in addition had to pay the customary United Kingdom dues. The vessel therefore was burdened with the expense of double light dues on a single voyage." 

This Government does not impose light dues except under exceptional conditions; see sections 4219 R.S. as amended and 

4225 R.S. It has been held that the light dues under 4225 R.S. are imposed only under the conditions and in a like manner with those imposed under 4219 R.S. Tonnage duties of two cents per ton, not to exceed ten cents per ton, per annum from vessels of all nationalities, including our own, are collected on entries into our ports from nearby foreign ports; a duty of six cents per ton, not to exceed thirty cents per ton, per annum is collected from vessels of all nationalities, including our own, entering from other foreign ports. Treaties of reciprocity have in some instances restricted light dues or tonnage dues. 

You will appreciate that the new dues are an extra burden to ship owners. Inasmuch as the Shipping Board vessels do not enter any of the ports in the Bahamas or Leeward Islands, but merely pass through the territorial waters on their westbound passage to Gulf ports from United Kingdom ports, you may readily appreciate that the assessment is not reasonable. 

The Ambassador was instructed to confirm the understanding of the Department that the dues in question were imposed upon vessels of all nations, including the British, which passed through the waters in question and entered United Kingdom ports. The Department added: "It would appear that vessels passing near the lights named on voyages to other than United Kingdom or other British ports would enjoy benefit therefrom without payment, and that, accordingly, the dues are not uniformly applicable." 99 The British Foreign Office thereafter informed the Ambassador that the dues were payable in the United Kingdom and certain other ports by shipping which had derived benefit from the lighthouses named in the Order in Council, any other arrangement having been found impracticable. It was explained: 

The effect is that vessels are charged at one port for two different sets of lights from both of which they have derived benefit. It is, of course, the case, as stated in your note, that vessels passing near the Bahamas lights on voyages to other than United Kingdom ports would enjoy benefit from them without payment. This is unfortunately unavoidable; but, since the dues in question are payable in respect of services rendered and are, as the Department of State correctly assumes, levied

without distinction upon vessels of all nations, including British vessels, which pass through the waters in question and enter United Kingdom and certain other British ports, His Majesty's Government do not feel that the arrangement can be considered unreasonable. It is the policy of His Majesty's Government, as the United States Government are aware, to treat shipping of all flags on a perfect equality, and the principle underlying the Order-in-Council is, they feel, in full accord with that policy. 

On June 5, 1933 the Department instructed the Ambassador to draw to the attention of the British Government the case of three vessels of the Dollar Steamship Line passing the British lights on or near the Bahamas and the Leeward Islands, two of them at 20 miles offshore and one at 15 miles offshore. None of the vessels was in a position to observe the lights nor to receive assistance from them, yet light dues were collected at Singapore in the course of world cruises by the three boats. The Department said: "It thus appears that the British Government in these cases charged light dues against American vessels navigating the high seas, at no time in British waters, and a very considerable distance beyond the point at which the lights are visible." The collection of dues in those instances, it was said, could not be defended on the ground that the vessels had derived any benefit from the lights mentioned. 

The British Foreign Office replied that when the Order in Council was issued notices were published stating that the question whether or not any particular ship passing the lights derived benefit from them would be decided with reference to lines marked on a chart, thus following the analogous practice in force for many years in connection with the levy of light dues in respect to certain lighthouses on or near the coast of Ceylon and on the Island of Minicoy, and it was said:

The fact that a ship passes on a course out of sight of a lighthouse or a lighted buoy, is not conclusive evidence that no benefit was derived by that ship from the lighthouse or buoy. Within limits greater than those of visibility ships may be said to have derived potential benefit from the sea mark,. 

The Under Secretary of State (Castle) to Ambassador Mellon, no. 382, Feb. 2, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 844E.842/3; Mr. R. L. Craigie, of the British Foreign Office, to Mr. Mellon, Mar. 13, 1933 (enclosure to despatch 735 from the Embassy at London, Mar. 14, 1933), ibid. 844E.842/4; the Acting Secretary of State (Phillips) to Ambassador Bingham, no. 9, June 5, 1933, ibid. 844E.842/5; Mr. Craigie to Mr. Bingham, Aug. 3, 1933 (enclosure to despatch 138 from the Embassy in London, Aug. 4, 1933), ibid. 844.842/8.

SHIPS' PAPERS 

$148 The customs officers at Paita, Peru, in 1912, required the master of an American schooner to surrender to them the certified copy of his crew list together with all his manifests. The Department of Commerce and Labor pointed out to the Department of State that section 4576 of the Revised Statutes of the United States specifically Crew list required, under heavy penalty, that the master of a vessel exhibit the certified copy of his crew list, required by section 4574, at the first port of arrival in the United States on his return from a foreign voyage. The action of the Peruvian Government, it was stated, nullified those laws and rendered difficult, if not impossible, the effort of the American Government to furnish a means to identify the crew on entry of the vessel with the crew on board at the time of clearance. 

The Department of Commerce and Labor stated further: 

In the opinion of this Department the requirement by Congress that vessels of the United States shall produce certified copies of their crew lists is within its powers and should be recognized by South American countries. The right of our 

Consuls in Peru to the custody of the papers of American vessels while in ports of that country should be upheld. The custom of maritime nations recognizes the Consul of the vessel's nationality as the sole guardian of all national rights pertaining thereto, and it cannot be expected that an American Consul can exhibit the crew list of an American vessel in proceedings to secure the rights of seamen if he is not permitted to have possession of the crew list. To all intents and purposes, the papers of the vessel are part of the vessel itself and are properly within the continuous jurisdiction of the vessel's nation, and therefore in a foreign port within the jurisdiction of the Consul of that nation. This custody of the ship's crew list by the Consul of her nation is a protection to the rights of seamen, and proper action by the Consuls in matters concerning those rights is rendered almost impossible by the passage of the papers out of the control of the nation to which the vessel belongs. The Department does not seek to take from Peru or other South American countries a recognized right, but wishes to retain for the masters of our vessels and for our Consuls a right which is deemed to pertain to them as the representatives of our national sovereignty and one which is claimed and recognized as just among maritime nations.

Representations along this line were made to the Peruvian Government, and on July 12, 1912 the Minister informed the Department that an instruction had been issued by the Peruvian Government to the captains of the principal ports of Peru not to deprive American ships of their certified crew lists in the future.

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Minister Howard, no. 50, Apr. 5, 1912, MS. Department of State, file 195.3/61, enclosing letter of 

Mar. 25, 1912 from the Acting Secretary of Commerce and Labor (Cable) to 

Secretary Knox; Mr. Howard to Mr. Knox, no. 132, July 12, 1912, ibid. 

The customs authorities at Taltal, Chile, in 1914, required the masters of American vessels to deliver to them their crew lists, and when the vessels cleared they refused to surrender them to the masters. The Department of Commerce and Labor requested that the attention of the Chilean Government be called to the matter, stating that the crew list was a paper intended for the protection of the crew and was of no direct interest to any foreign country. There was no objection, it said, to copies thereof being made by the Chilean customs authorities, but it was necessary that the copy furnished at the customhouse be presented at the arrival of the vessel in the United States in order that there might be authentic evidence that members of the crew taken out at the beginning of the voyage were safely returned to an American port. A copy of this letter was forwarded to the American Minister in Chile with instructions to bring the matter informally to the attention of the appropriate authorities. The Chilean Foreign Office informed the American 

Minister on Sept. 15, 1914 that the Marine Department had been asked to issue general instructions to the maritime authorities along the lines of a report of the Director of the Maritime Territory of Mar. 7, 1910 in which it had been stated that the Chilean law required the surrender to the maritime authority of a copy of the crew list and not the original list. The harbor master at Belawan-Deli, Sumatra, in 1921, claimed that he was entitled to hold the papers of an American ship until Ships' papers the ship had duly entered the port and to hold such papers pending the receipt of a guaranty or bond from the American vessel that she would be responsible for damages caused to a Netherland vessel. The

entitled to obtain such information from them as might be required for official reference.

The Department of State subsequently transmitted to the Consul a letter from the Department of Commerce in regard to this matter, in which it was stated that under section 4309 of the Revised Statutes it was essential to the proper control of American vessels by consular officers that the latter should have the custody of the vessel's papers. Reference was made to section 4209 of the Revised 

Statutes providing that foreign vessels coming into American ports shall, previous to entry, produce to the Collector of Customs, with whom such entry is made, the vessel's register or other documents in lieu thereof, together with the clearance and other papers granted at the port of departure, and providing further that the master within 48 hours after such entry shall deposit these papers with the consul or vice consul of the nation to which the vessel belongs and deliver to the Collector of Customs a certificate of the consul or vice consul that this has been done. The law and practice, it was said, seemed to contemplate a possible presentation of a vessel's papers to officers other than the consul and the eventual delivery of such papers to the consular officer. The period fixed in American courts, the Department of Commerce stated, was 48 hours after entry before such delivery to the consul, and it was suggested that arrangements might be made in Sumatra to have a similar time fixed there.

INVOLUNTARY ENTRANCE 

$149

In regard to entrance of foreign vessels into territorial waters on account of force majeure, Jessup says:

There is one condition under which a foreign vessel in territorial waters may claim as of right an entire immunity from Distress the local jurisdiction. The condition is that such presence in territorial waters be due to force majeure. If a ship is driven in by storm, carried in by mutineers, or seeks refuge for vital repairs or provisioning, international customary law declares that the local state shall not take advantage of its necessity. 

Jessup, Law of Territorial Waters and Maritime Jurisdiction (1927) 194. 

In its award in the North Atlantic Coast Fisheries case, the arbitral tribunal said:

The Tribunal is of opinion that the provision in the first 

Article of the Treaty of October 20th, 1818, admitting American fishermen to enter certain bays or harbors for shelter, repairs, wood and water, and for no other purpose whatever, is an exercise in large measure of those duties of hospitality and humanity which all civilized nations impose upon themselves and expect the performance of from others.. To impose restrictions making the exercise of such privileges conditional upon the payment of light, harbor or other dues, or entering and reporting at custom-houses, or any similar conditions would be inconsistent with the grounds upon which such privileges rest and therefore is not permissible. 

Per. Ct. Arb., North Atlantic Coast Fisheries Tribunal of Arbitration 

(The Hague, 1910) 133-134; Scott, Hague Court Reports (1916) 146, 180.

Under the Tariff Act of September 21, 1922 (42 Stat. 858, 952) vessels arriving in ports of the United States in distress or for the purpose of taking on necessary ship stores or sea stores are not required to make entry at a customhouse if they depart within 24 Entry at hours after arrival without having landed or taken on board any merchandise other than stores, but they are required to report to the collector of customs the dates of arrival and departure and the quantity of stores taken on board. (A similar provision is found in art. 

441 of the Tariff Act approved June 17, 1930, as amended August

the time of clearing from the foreign port. 27 Stat. 449; 28 Stat.

In the case of United States v. Eagle Indemnity Company it was held that a Cuban vessel which had arrived in an American port in distress and had been forced to remain more than 24 hours in order to make necessary repairs, was obliged to make formal entry at the customhouse and to give bond, conditioned that the merchandise should not be landed in the United States, under section 442 of the Tariff Act of 1922. 42 Stat. 858, 952; 18 F. (2d) 135 (E.D. Va., 1926).

In the case of United States v. Sullivan et al. a British vessel in distress had been brought by a United States revenue cutter into a port in Florida and her master required to give bond for a sum which was the estimated duty on the cargo. Action was subsequently brought, alleging a breach of one of the provisions of the bond on the ground that the cargo of the vessel had not been delivered to the port to which it was destined. The circuit court of appeals held that a reasonable interpretation of section 442 of the Tariff Act of 1922, permitting the Secretary of the Treasury to require a bond in the case of a foreign vessel proceeding to a foreign port, that no merchandise should be landed in the United States (42 Stat. 858, 952), was that it was not intended to apply to vessels not required to make entry and that a regulation requiring a penal bond, with the condition that the cargo be actually delivered at the port of destination shown in the manifest, went beyond the requirements of the statute and was unreasonable. The court also held that the bond if valid at all must be considered one for indemnity to protect the fisc and that as no tariff duties were due in this case there could be no recovery. 

26 F. (2d) 606 (C.C.A. 5th, 1928). Contra: Eagle Indemnity Company v. 

United States, 22 F. (2d) 388 (C.C.A. 4th, 1927); certiorari denied, 276 U.S. (1928) 624. 

Article 3 of the international convention for safety of life at sea signed at London on May 31, 1929 reads:

Cases of "Force Majeure".—No ship, which is not subject to the provisions of the present Convention at the time of its departure on any voyage, shall become subject to the provisions of the

present Convention on account of any deviation from its intended voyage due to stress of weather or any other cause of force majeure. 

Persons who are on board a ship by reason of force majeure or in consequence of the obligation laid upon the master to carry shipwrecked or other persons shall not be taken into account for the purpose of ascertaining the application to a ship of any provisions of the present Convention.

A provision similar to that contained in the first paragraph of article 3 quoted above appears in article 4 of the international loadline convention signed at London on July 5, 1930. 

4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 5134, 5138; ibid. 5287, 5291; 50 Stat. 

1121, 1130; 47 Stat. 2228, 2240.

In August 1920 the Naiwa, a vessel belonging to the United States 

Shipping Board, was stranded on Stranger Cay, North Bahamas.

The customs authorities of the Bahamas demanded the payment of $5,000 as duty upon the cargo of the Naiwa, which was transferred to two American ships. The claim was based upon the provisions of the second schedule of the Bahamas' Tariff Act of 1919, which provided for a 5 percent customs duty on exports of "wrecked goods”. 

The Department of State, on November 5, 1921, informed the

American Consul at Nassau that it appeared that goods transferred from the Naiwa were never in fact landed on Bahaman shores and that- Before goods can properly be regarded as exported from Exportation; a country, they must first be imported or produced in the coun- importation try itself. To constitute importation the goods must be voluntarily brought within the country with the intention of unloading them. This rule has been followed in the United States and 

Great Britain.

Under generally accepted principles, it is usually held that a vessel which is driven into waters by stress of weather or other causes beyond the master's control, does not thereby become subject to the foreign jurisdiction.

Under the circumstances, the Department has considered it desirable to advise the Shipping Board to withhold payment of the export duty demanded by the Bahaman authorities.

The Acting Colonial Secretary of the Bahamas on March 6, 1922 

informed the American Consul that "in view of all the circumstances of the case" his Government did not desire to press the claim for the payment of duty in respect to the disembarked cargo.

In the case of The Squanto, involving a libel by the United States against the schooner and her cargo of intoxicating liquor based on a violation of the Tariff Act of 1922 and the National Prohibition Act, the circuit court of appeals rejected the contention of the claimant that the schooner had entered New York harbor in distress, pointing out that "the vessel was seaworthy, and the supply on board was sufficient to carry out her voyage according to the captain". 

13 F. (2d) 548, 549 (C.C.A. 2d, 1926).

In the case of Kate A. Hoff, Administratrix, etc. (United States v. 

Mexico) it was alleged by the claimant that the Rebecca, an American vessel, while en route for Brazos Santiago, Texas, had entered the port of Tampico, Mexico, in distress, having on board a cargo destined for both of those places. The master of the vessel was arrested in Tampico, charged with bringing goods into a Mexican port without proper papers. He was subsequently released from bail but was assessed treble damages against the merchandise on the vessel which had been seized, and, because of his refusal and inability to pay these damages and other penalties, the Rebecca and her cargo were sold by order of court. The General Claims Commission, established under the convention of September 8, 1923, made an award in favor of the claimant, finding as a matter of fact that the vessel when it sailed into Tampico was in a crippled condition and that the captain had no intent to perpetrate a fraud on Mexican customs laws. The Commission said:

The principles with respect to the status of a vessel in "distress" find recognition both in domestic laws and in international law. The enlightened principle of comity which exempts a merchant vessel, at least to a certain extent, from the operation of local laws has been generally stated to apply to vessels forced into port by storm, or compelled to seek refuge for vital repairs or for provisioning, or carried into port by mutineers. It has also been asserted in defense of a charge of attempted breech [sic] of blockade. It was asserted by as early a writer as Vattel. The Law of

Nations, p. 128. In the instant case we are concerned simply with distress said to have been occasioned by violent weather. 

Opinions of the Commissioners (1929) 174, 177. 

The Louise F., a British schooner, was seized by the United

States customs authorities four or five miles off the coast of Florida and libeled by the United States, charged with a violation of the 

National Prohibition Act and unlawful unloading of intoxicating liquor. The evidence showed that the vessel, which had sailed from 

Nassau for Halifax, had been seized while on the high seas by one of the members of the crew and two persons not connected with the vessel and had been brought into American waters where the liquor was landed without the consent of the officers and crew. The United States 

District Court held that under these circumstances neither the vessel nor her officers incurred any penalty under the Tariff Act of 1922 nor forfeiture under the National Prohibition Act. The libel was dismissed. 

293 Fed. 933 (S.D. Fla., 1923). "SEC. 5. The National Prohibition Act does not apply to merchant vessels which are forced into port by stress of weather, or by inevitable necessity. 

The involuntary entrance furnishes a ground of exemption, and, under international law, it is improper to impose fines upon vessels compelled to put into port for such reason. This rule also applies to goods on board vessels so circumstanced. These exemptions depend, however, upon proof of the fact of the urgency of the distress." 

United States Treasury Decision 3484 approved June 2, 1923, 25 Treasury 

Decisions, Internal Revenue (1923) 144, 145.

In the case of The Ship “May" v. His Majesty the King, the Supreme Court of Canada affirmed a judgment declaring forfeited an American fishing vessel arrested within three miles of the coast of 

British Columbia. Section 1 of the Canadian Customs and Fisheries 

Protection Act of 1927 excepted from forfeiture vessels entering Canadian waters in distress. It was alleged on behalf of the vessel that it had entered Canadian waters on account of "stress of weather", "Stress of since it was necessary to renew the packing of the oil pump which had weather" become worn. The court found that the usefulness of the pump had been affected but that navigation had not become dangerous. The court said thatan entry by a foreign vessel into Canadian waters cannot be justified on the ground of "stress of weather" unless the weather is such as to produce in the mind of a reasonably competent and skillful master, possessing courage and firmness, a well grounded bona fide apprehension that if he remains outside the territorial waters he will put in jeopardy his vessel and cargo.

In every case the questions whether the master fairly and honestly on reasonable ground believed it necessary to take

Firing across boundary shelter, and whether he exercised reasonable skill, competence and courage in the circumstances, are questions of fact for the tribunal whose duty it is to find the facts. 

1931 Can. Sup. Ct. 374, 382–383; [1931] 3 D.L.R., 15, 23; Annual Digest, 1931-32, Case No. 81. 

 BREACHES BY MILITARY AND NAVAL AUTHORITIES 

$150 On March 9, 1911 the Department of State wrote to the Mexican Ambassador calling his attention to the fact that during a battle between Mexican troops and insurgents at El Mulato, on February 

7 and 8, 1911, the Mexican troops deliberately fired on American troops, who were patrolling the American side of the river in order to prevent any violation of the neutrality laws, and wounded a boy and a packhorse. The Department said thatit is unnecessary to point out to your excellency that the firing upon American troops on the American side of the border by the Mexican troops on the Mexican side constitutes a most grave violation not only of the principles of international law and of the sovereignty of the United States, but also of that traditional friendliness which exists between the Governments of the United States and Mexico. While the Government of the United States must assume that the soldiers in question acted in this case not only without authority, but in disobedience and defiance of what must have been their positive orders, yet it feels that it can not overlook the incident and that it must expect that the Government of Mexico will at once disavow the action and take all steps necessary to make certain that no further acts of this sort shall occur, since, if repeated, they would inevitably lead to collisions between the troops of the two countries, which there would be the strongest reasons to deplore. 

On March 14 the Mexican Ambassador replied that the President of

Mexico deplored these events and that, although he was inclined to believe that the missiles which fell in American territory and injured a boy were spent bullets, he had ordered a thorough investigation so as to elucidate the point fully and punish the guilty, if any. The 

Ambassador wrote again on May 3 that General Gonzalo Luque had reported that El Mulato lay in a well-marked bend of the Rio Grande, so that from whatever part of the Mexican side an attack might be made on it, the shots were sure to go to the other side, and in no case could the man firing the gun be charged with intentionally so firing, as his target was so near the bank of the river and the conditions were such that the only way out of it would have been not to fire. He

wrote further on May 5 that General Luque stated that the shots were fired by rebels at Mexican Federal forces near the river; that he accordingly supposed that some shots reached the point occupied by the American patrol; and that his soldiers not only were under orders not to make the mistake of harming American soldiers but that such an error would be impossible since they daily saw American soldiers on duty.

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Ambassador de la Barra, Mar. 9, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 812.00/843; Señor de la Barra to 

Secretary Knox, no. 1052, Mar. 14, 1911, ibid. 812.00/964; Ambassador de 

Zamacona to Mr. Knox, nos. 1325 and 1340, May 3 and 5, 1911, ibid. files 

812.00/1629, 812.00/1676. See also 1911 For. Rel. 419, 423, 473, 476. 

On March 16, 1911 the Mexican Ambassador informed the Department of State that, from certain official reports made to it, the Mexican Government had learned that several groups of persons on the American bank of the Rio Grande had fired at Mexican soldiers, west of Ciudad Juárez, on February 7 of that year.

The Secretary of State replied that it seemed clearly established that the shots which were thought by the Mexican troops to have been fired upon them from the American side of the river were, in reality, fired from the Mexican side by certain insurrecto scouts who suddenly appeared upon the hills directly opposite the point occupied by the Mexican soldiers, who, apparently, were more or less directly in line with the crowd collected upon the American side of the river. The Secretary concluded that the United States Government would in the future, as it had in the past, make every effort to secure strict enforcement of the so-called "neutrality" statutes of the United States, to the end that no hostile act should be carried on from American territory. 

Ambassador de la Barra to Secretary Knox, no. 1058, Mar. 16, 1911, MS. 

Department of State, file 812.00/980; Mr. Knox to Ambassador de Zamacona, no. 3, Apr. 22, 1911, ibid. 812.00/1348. See also 1911 For. Rel. 426, 467.

The Department finds itself under the necessity of again asserting that, the facts in this case being as stated, the firing upon American troops on the American side of the border by the Mexican troops on the Mexican side constitutes a most grave violation not only of the principles of international law and of the sovereignty of the United States, but also of that traditional friendliness which exists between the Governments of the United States and Mexico. Moreover, as this Government has been compelled 157511-40-VOL. II-19

I must emphasize the great potentiality of danger which lies in these seeming repetitions of this offense, and urge upon you the imperative necessity that the Mexican Government immediately take all requisite steps to prevent acts so inconsistent with good will and friendliness.

During a battle on April 13, 1911 at Agua Prieta, Mexico, many bullets struck houses in Douglas, Arizona, killing two American citizens, wounding eleven, and jeopardizing the life and property of others. The American Ambassador in Mexico was instructed on the following day to inform the Mexican Government that the President felt that urgent and express instructions should be given to prevent further jeopardy of American life and property on American territory. This was the third time that regularly organized Mexican troops had fired into American territory, thereby threatening human life, it was said. The Ambassador was instructed to point out that, while the difficulties under which the Mexican Government was acting were appreciated by the President, the latter would be compelled, "in self-defense, so to speak, of American lives on American soil", if such incidents recurred, to take action which he would desire to avoid by the use of every proper effort. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Ambassador Wilson, Apr. 14, 1911 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 812.00/1333A; 1911 For. 

Rel. 456.

On April 17 as a result of fighting across the international line, within gunshot range of the heart of Douglas, five Americans were wounded on the American side. The Governor of Arizona telegraphed to the President of the United States on the same day that everything pointed to a repetition of casualties on the following day, and, while the armies of the Federal Mexican Government seemed

disposed to keep their agreement not to fire into Douglas, the position of the insurrectionists was such that when fighting occurred on the east and southeast of the intrenchments people living in Douglas were put in danger of their lives. It was impossible, he said, to safeguard the people of Douglas unless the town was vacated. 

The President informed the Governor that he had made urgent demand upon the Mexican Government to issue instructions to prevent firing across the border by Mexican Federal troops and that in the meantime he had sent direct warning to the Mexican and insurgent forces near Douglas. The situation might justify him, he said, in ordering American troops to cross the border and attempt to stop the fighting, or to fire upon both combatants from the American side; but, if he took this step, he must face the possibility of resistance and greater bloodshed, as well as the danger of having American motives misconstrued and misrepresented and of thus inflaming Mexican popular indignation against many thousands of Americans then in Mexico, jeopardizing their lives and property. It might not be practicable to resist the pressure for general intervention under such conditions, he said, and, it being impossible to foresee or reckon the consequences of such a course, the United States must use the greatest self-restraint to avoid it. He therefore declared that he could not order the troops at Douglas to cross the border but must ask the Governor and the local authorities, in case the same danger recurred, to direct the people of Douglas to place themselves where bullets could not reach them. 

On April 17 the Mexican Foreign Minister wrote to the American 

Ambassador that it was not the Federal soldiers who on April 13 had fired at the citizens of Douglas but the revolutionists. Even if it had been the Federal soldiers who had fired toward Douglas, he said, such an act would have been unintentional and such fatal accidents might be placed among those which the United States Government, with sufficient reason, counted as inevitable in the case of an armed conflict, and which, for one reason or another, could not form the grounds for claims of any character. The Minister informed the Ambassador that immediately upon learning that shots had reached American territory, his Department had informed the War Department so that it might give the commanders of the Federal forces orders that all engagements near the border which might result in damage to the interests, lives, and property of American citizens, should be avoided. 

On December 11, 1911 the Secretary of State transmitted to the

American Ambassador a memorandum in refutation of the note of the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs of April 17, 1911. The 

Ambassador was instructed to bear in mind, in presenting the memo-

randum, that, while the Department desired to refrain from reviving a discussion the elements of which doubtless arose from misinformation as to the happenings incident to the abnormal and turbulent conditions existing at the time, the Government of the United States felt constrained to request the Government of Mexico to take due note of its absolute dissent from the allegations made and the views expressed in the Mexican note of April 17, 1911.

Minister de la Barra to Ambassador Wilson, Apr. 17, 1911 (enclosure to despatch 479 from the Embassy in Mexico City, Apr. 19, 1911), and Secretary Knox to Mr. Wilson, no. 672, Dec. 11, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 812.00/1458. See also 1911 For. Rel. 459, 460, 462-463, 523.

During the course of insurrectionary disturbances in Mexico in Feb. 

1912, the Department of State telegraphed to the American Ambassador in Mexico that the President felt that his duty and public opinion absolutely forbade toleration of any repetition of injury to Americans on American soil, as was then threatened at Ciudad Juárez, and that he was disposed to give public warning that in such emergency he would be obliged to order troops to cross the line, as a police measure, to disarm or drive away from Ciudad Juárez any fighting forces threatening life in El Paso, thereafter returning.
