On Jan. 30, 1913 the Governor of Texas telegraphed to the President of the United States that 1,000 rebels were surrounding Ciudad Juárez and that there would probably be a battle in 48 hours. He requested the President to direct that the necessary steps be taken to prevent firing into El Paso. 

The Department of State telegraphed to the Governor on the following day that the War Department had been requested to renew to the General in command at El Paso the general precautionary instructions relative to notifying the leaders of the Federal and insurrectionary forces at Ciudad Juárez that in any engagements which might occur between them there must not be any firing which would result in the passage of bullets across the international boundary line and that such orders were sent by the War Department on the previous night. The attention of the Mexican Government, the 

Department said, had already been called to the situation. The Acting 

Secretary of State (Wilson) to Governor Colquitt, Jan. 31, 1913 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 812.00/6019. See also 1913 For. Rel. 695.

On March 3, 1913 the Department of State telegraphed to the American Ambassador in Mexico City that an American officer and three men patrolling two miles west of Douglas, Arizona, had been fired on by some Mexicans from a point across the border; that the officer immediately rode toward the Mexicans to investigate which side of the boundary line they had fired from and, although he made no hostile demonstration, they fired about five shots at him from about ten yards away, before he had an opportunity to speak; that sixteen other patrols having heard the shots then came to his support and the officer returned the fire and held his position; and that in the interchange of shots at least six Mexicans were killed, although

there were no American casualties. The Ambassador was instructed to say to the Mexican Government that it appeared that the aggressors were the Mexican troops and that the action of the United States troops was "the perfectly justifiable action of repelling what is known in international law as foreign invasion of national territory". For any discreet use that might seem necessary, the Ambassador was informed that the following instruction had been sent to Colonel Guilfoyle by General Bliss, who was in command of the army headquarters at San Antonio, Texas:

In case of intentional firing from Mexican side upon persons on the American side your proposed action in using rifle fire when necessary to stop such shooting is approved. If the firing from 

Mexican side consists of random shots accidentally reaching our side you will use every proper means to induce citizens to temporarily withdraw from zone of fire but you will not in any event send or allow any armed American troops to cross the border without specific instructions to that effect from these headquarters or the War Department. Keep these headquarters fully advised of the situation and report any important action taken by you. 

Secretary Knox to Ambassador Wilson, Mar. 3, 1913 (telegram), MS. 

Department of State, file 812.00/6498B. See also 1913 For. Rel. 754.

On December 9, 1914 the American Consul at Veracruz, Mexico, was instructed to call upon General Carranza and to say that a considerable number of Americans had been wounded by shots fired across the boundary line at Naco, Sonora, and that several had died. The Consul was instructed to urge General Carranza to send instructions to those acknowledging allegiance to him, warning them against any further violations of the rights of American citizens, and to say that unless the firing of shots across the border could be prevented it would become the duty of the United States, much to its regret, to take the steps necessary to protect American lives, by the employment of such forces as might be required. These would be employed, it was said, not for aggression but purely for defense and with no intention of invading the territory of Mexico or in any way interfering with its sovereignty or the rights of its people to settle their disputes among themselves. 

The American Vice Consul at Mexico City was instructed to make similar representations to General Gutiérrez, the Provisional Conventionist President of Mexico. 

General Gutiérrez, on December 10, 1914, instructed Governor

Maytorena at Naco to make every effort to prevent bullets from his forces from passing to American territory and, if it were necessary, even to suspend attack pending new orders, to prevent difficulties with the United States.

General Carranza replied to the American Consul at Veracruz on December 12, 1914 that, although it was impossible for shots fired by the Constitutionalist forces occupying Naco to wound American citizens on the other side of the line, since the line was behind them, he was sending special instructions to avoid any accident as the result of the shots fired. He declared that any use whatsoever of force attempted by the United States on Mexican territory, although it had the object of protecting American lives, would have to be considered by his Government as an act of hostility and as an attack against the sovereignty of Mexico. 

Secretary Bryan to Consul Canada, Dec. 9, 1914 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 812.00/13984a; General Gutiérrez to Governor Maytorena,

Dec. 10, 1914 (quoted in telegram from Vice Consul Silliman, Dec. 11, 1914), ibid. 812.00/13994; General Carranza to Mr. Canada, Dec. 12, 1914 (enclosure to despatch 1085 from the American Consulate, Veracruz, Dec. 13, 1914), ibid. 812.00/14089. See also 1914 For. Rel. 649-652.

An agreement was concluded between the Constitutional Governor and Military Commandant of the State of Sonora, Governor Maytorena, and General Calles, Commandant of the Constitutionalist forces in Naco and Agua Prieta, Sonora, on Jan. 11, 1915, providing for the evacuation of Naco by the Constitutionalist forces, that port to remain neutral and closed to traffic and commerce until the constituted government of Mexico, recognized by the United States, should take possession or until one of the contending factions completely dominated the other. It was also agreed that the contending factions would respect the occupation of Nogales by the forces under the command of General Maytorena and the occupation of Agua Prieta by the forces under the command of General Calles, these two places not to be attacked for any reason in order to avoid a struggle on the frontier, "with the object of avoiding damage on American territory". 

MS. Department of State, file 812.00/14612. See also 1915 For. Rel. 789. 

On Apr. 17, 1918 the Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of War informing him that President Carranza had caused strict orders to be issued to Mexican troops not to fire upon persons on the American side of the boundary and that he had expressed the hope that similar orders might be given to American troops along the Rio Grande. On May 15, 1918 the 

Department informed the American Ambassador to Mexico that the Secre tary of War had issued the following instructions to the United States military authorities: "No American troops shall fire upon any person on the Mexican side of the international boundary, unless such troops shall first have been fired upon from the Mexican side and a return of fire is made necessary as a measure of self-defense."

On July 10, 1918 the Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of War that the Department was embarrassed by the number of complaints made to it by the Mexican Ambassador in respect to the invasion of Mexican territory by American soldiers and of their firing across the border. He suggested that orders given to officers in command of the forces along the Mexican border "be so modified as to prevent American soldiers from entering Mexico or firing across the border into Mexico, without specific orders in each case from the War Department".

The Secretary of War replied: 

"I agree with you wholly as to the necessity of our having no avoidable friction with the Mexicans who live along the border, but if Mexicans cross our border and commit raids, I can not agree that they should not be pursued by our patrols even if they flee across the Mexican border. With regard to the question of preventing soldiers firing across the border into Mexico without specific orders in each case from the War Department, it would be most undesirable from a military standpoint to instruct our men that when they are being shot at themselves from the Mexican border they were not to return the fire, but to ask the War Department for permission to do so."

The commission appointed by the Secretary of War, on August 30, 1912, pursuant to the terms of a joint resolution of Congress approved on August 9, 1912, "to investigate the claims of American citizens for damages suffered within American territory and growing out of the late insurrection in Mexico", in its report of November 29, 1912, with particular reference to the cases that arose in El Paso, Texas, and Douglas, Arizona, on account of gunshot wounds inflicted from the Mexican side of the border during the then recent disturbances in 

Mexico, stated:

If the situation as between Mexico and the United States were reversed and this Government found itself assailed by armed rebels avowing the purpose of overthrowing the established order of things, and its border cities were besieged, nobody can doubt that attack would be met by defense, let the bullets fall where they might. What we should undoubtedly claim for ourselves as right we must admit as right in our neighboring States. But when a State in the exercise of its sovereign rights of self-defense has been compelled to inflict injuries as incidental thereto upon a neighboring and friendly power, prompt expressions of regret and prompt atonement in so far as money indemnity can atone are to be expected.

The ground upon which this position rests is simply that the right of self-defense rose superior in the particular circumstances Self-defense; to the right of territorial inviolability. territorial The duty of Governments to see that their citizens when inviolability damaged by foreign governments should be given justice is too well established in our own diplomatic history and through the long list of international claims commissions to be now questioned.

In response to oral inquiries by the Mexican Ambassador as to the disposition to be made of Mexican Federal troops detained in the United States since their crossing the frontier under arms on the occasion of fighting at Agua Prieta, the Secretary of State wrote:

Upon the assurance of your excellency's Government that such technical invasion of American territory will not again occur in respect to the troops in question, and without prejudice to the course which this Government might find it necessary to take in any future case of the kind, I am happy to inform you that next week the necessary orders will be issued for the release of the troops now detained, who will then doubtless be enabled to return to Mexico in the course of a few days.

On February 15, 1912 a lieutenant in the American Army and 19 soldiers were ordered to proceed to the Santa Fé Street Bridge in El Paso to relieve a detachment already stationed there. In carrying out these orders the lieutenant started for his destination in a street car, the route of which crossed into Ciudad Juárez, thence back to the American side of the Rio Grande. Being ignorant of the topography of El Paso and of the route of the street car and assuming that he was entitled to ride all the way to his destination, the lieutenant did not heed the notice of the corporal at the Stanton Street Bridge that he should dismount and walk to the Santa Fé Bridge and so remained in the car and thus crossed into Mexico. 

The Mexican Ambassador, on February 16, addressed a note to the Secretary of State requesting the Government of the United States to give a precise explanation as to the passage of those American soldiers across the frontier at Ciudad Juárez and into Mexican territory. 

The Acting Secretary of State replied on February 26 expressing the sincere regret of the United States Government for the unfortunate occurrence. He recounted to the Ambassador the facts of the case as outlined above and said that the colonel who was in command of the United States forces in El Paso had made an appropriate apology to the Mexican Consul in that city for the error of the lieu-

tenant who had been subjected to the action of court martial and would be suitably punished. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Ambassador Crespo, no. 121, Feb. 26, 1912, MS. Department of State, file 812.00/2825; 1912 For. Rel. 726.

On Oct. 1, 1915 the Department of State telegraphed the American Special 

Agent near General Carranza, that on Sept. 23 a Carrancista officer had crossed the Rio Grande at Los Pelados Crossing with a detachment of troops and had attacked a small detachment of American soldiers on American soil, killing two of them, badly mutilating the body of one of the soldiers so killed, and taking horses and arms from the soldiers to the cuartel of the Carrancista soldiers. The Special Agent was instructed to state to General 

Carranza that the Government of the United States could not view these outrages other than as acts in which the Carrancista troops participated either because of instructions from headquarters or of their own volition. 

In either case, it was said, the responsibility appeared to rest upon General Carranza. The Special Agent was also instructed to say to the Carrancista authorities that the United States Government expected them immediately to issue orders which would definitely stop these reprehensible acts. 

On Oct. 5 the Carrancista authorities replied that General Carranza had issued orders to the general in chief of the zone in question, for the necessary investigation of the matter so that he might take proper measures for the severe punishment of those found guilty, if the deed should be confirmed. 

They also replied that the supposition that the soldiers had acted under orders was deemed unjustified.

Rel. 812, 814. 1916-17 On March 9, 1916 the town of Columbus, New Mexico, was attacked Punitive by Francisco Villa and his troops. Several American soldiers and expedition, civilians were killed, and a number of buildings in Columbus were burned. President Wilson at once directed that an armed force be sent into Mexico with the sole object of capturing Villa and preventing any further raids by his bandits, this to be done with scrupulous regard to the sovereignty of Mexico. American troops immediately crossed the Mexican border in pursuit of Villa.

On March 10 the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the de facto 

Mexican government addressed a note to the American Special Agent recalling the agreement reached between the United States and Mexico at the time of Indian raids onto Mexican territory during the years 1880 through 1886 providing that the armed forces of either country might freely cross into the territory of the other to pursue and chastise the bandits. He asked that Mexican forces be permitted to cross into American territory in pursuit of Villa and his followers "upon the understanding that, reciprocally, the forces of the United States may cross into Mexican territory, if the raid effected at Columbus should unfortunately be repeated at any other point on the border". 

---

On March 11 General Carranza instructed the Confidential Agent of the de facto Mexican government in the United States, Mr. Arredondo, that if the United States Government did not take into consideration the mutual permission for American and Mexican forces to cross into each other's territory in pursuit of bandits and insisted on sending an operating army onto Mexican soil, the Government of Mexico would consider this act as an invasion of national territory. 

He declared that there was no justification for an invasion of Mexican territory by an armed force of the United States. This instruction was read to the Secretary of State on March 12 by Mr. Arredondo. 

The Secretary of State instructed the Special Agent to the de facto government in Mexico on March 13 to reply to the Mexican note of 

March 10 saying:

The Government of the United States, in view of the unusual state of affairs which has existed for some time along the international boundary and earnestly desiring to cooperate with the de facto Government of Mexico to suppress this state of lawlessness, of which the attack on Columbus, New Mexico, is a deplorable example, and to insure peace and order in the regions contiguous to the boundary between the two Republics, readily grants permission for military forces of the de facto Government of Mexico to cross the international boundary in pursuit of lawless bands of armed men who have entered Mexico from the United States, committed outrages on Mexican soil, and fled into the United States, on the understanding that the de facto Government of Mexico grants the reciprocal privilege that the military forces of the United States may pursue across the international boundary into Mexican territory lawless bands of armed men who have entered the United States from Mexico, committed outrages on American soil, and fled into Mexico.

The Government of the United States understands that in view of its agreement to this reciprocal arrangement proposed by the de facto Government the arrangement is now complete and in force and the reciprocal privileges thereunder may accordingly be exercised by either Government without further interchange of views. 

On the same day the Secretary of State communicated to Mr. 

Arredondo the following statement:

In order to remove any apprehension that may exist either in the United States or in Mexico, the President has authorized me to give in his name the public assurance that the military operations now in contemplation by this Government will be scrupulously confined to the object already announced, and that in no circumstances will they be suffered to trench in any degree upon the sovereignty of Mexico or develop into intervention of any kind in the internal affairs of our sister Republic. On the contrary, what is now being done is deliberately intended to preclude the possibility of intervention.

resolution On March 17 the United States Senate adopted a concurrent resolution approving the use of the armed forces of the United States for Senate the apprehension and punishment of Villa and his band and declared that the pursuit of these men across the international boundary line into Mexico was "for the single purpose of arresting and punishing the fugitive band of outlaws" and also that such military expedition should "not be permitted to encroach in any degree upon the sovereignty of Mexico or to interfere in any manner with the domestic affairs of the Mexican people". Cong. Rec., vol. 53, pt. 5, p. 4274. 

The following day Mr. Arredondo transmitted to the Department a note from the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs in which it was explained that the de facto Mexican government was of the opinion that the terms and conditions of the agreement which should be formally entered into between Mexico and the United States had not been fixed regarding the crossing of troops and that the consent expressed by that government in regard to the crossing of armed troops over the frontier was being erroneously understood in taking for granted that the crossing of a military expedition in pursuit of Villa had been permitted. The note stated that it had already been declared that Mexico was disposed to act within the terms of strict reciprocity should any incursion similar to that at Columbus occur. 

It was also stated that the Mexican note of March 10 should not be understood as permitting any expeditions into Mexico and that the de facto Mexican government could not authorize the crossing into Mexican territory of American troops before a mutual agreement was reached. The Acting Secretary of State replied on March 19 that it had been the impression of the Department of State that the de facto government of Mexico fully understood and acquiesced in the arrangement proposed by the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs on March 10 and accepted by the Government of the United States in its note of 

March 13. With that understanding, he said, American troops were directed to pursue the common enemy, as it was realized that no time was to be lost if the pursuit was to be effective. While American military commanders had been given explicit instructions scrupulously to respect Mexican sovereignty, the United States would be glad, he concluded, to receive any suggestions from the de facto Mexican government as to the terms of a definite agreement to cover operation of troops either in Mexico or the United States, under the particular conditions.

Mr. Arredondo, on March 19, submitted to the Department a draft of an agreement in regard to the crossing of troops of both countries over the boundary line. (The Governments of the two countries however, were never able to reach an accord upon the terms of such an agreement.) On the same day, he informed the Secretary of State

that so long as there was no agreement concerning pursuit of bandits, the Government of Mexico could not permit the occupation of Mexican towns by American forces, much less such towns as were occupied by Mexican troops.

The Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs, on April 12, 1916, ad dressed a note to the Secretary of State which was handed to him on the following day by Mr. Arredondo, in which he declared that the Mexican Government believed it advisable to suspend all discussion of negotiations in regard to the reciprocal passage of troops and also that General Carranza considered that it was time to discuss with the United States the question of the withdrawal of American forces from Mexican territory. The Secretary of State instructed 

Special Representative Rodgers on April 14 to state orally to Gen eral Carranza or the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs that the Government of the United States desired to repeat again to the de facto Mexican government that it had no intention of violating in any way the sovereignty of Mexico and intended to withdraw immediately as soon as the object of the expedition-the capture of Villawas accomplished.

The American Consul at Chihuahua informed the Department on 

April 17 that the municipal president at Santa Cruz had delivered an ultimatum to an American officer in writing from the military commander at Chihuahua, forbidding his troops to advance without orders from him or the Mexican Secretary of War. The Secretary of State on the same day instructed Special Representative Rodgers to communicate this information to General Carranza and to express the earnest hope of the Government of the United States that the local authorities would be restrained from negotiating in regard to a matter which should be treated only by their Governments. 

Adjutant General McCain instructed Generals Scott and Funston on April 26, 1916 to meet with General Obregón and to discuss with him the future military operations of American forces in Mexico.

The three Generals met but were unable to arrive at an understanding. 

On May 5, 1916 Mexican bandits raided Glen Springs, Texas, killing three soldiers and one nine-year-old boy. American troops were immediately dispatched in pursuit of the raiders and crossed into 

Mexican territory. The Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs on 

May 22 addressed a note to the Secretary of State declaring that this passage of American troops onto Mexican territory violated the sovereignty of Mexico. He requested that the new forces be immediately withdrawn and that the United States abstain from sending any further expedition of a similar nature. He declared that his Government understood its obligation to guard the frontier but

that this obligation was not exclusively Mexican and that it was hoped that the American, Government, on which a similar obligation fell, would appreciate the material difficulties to be met with in the protection of the frontier. He also requested the withdrawal of the troops sent into Mexico after the raid on Columbus and stated that his Government requested of the American Government "a more categorical definition of its true intentions toward Mexico". 

On the following June 17 General Funston telegraphed to the 

Secretary of War that he had been informed by General Pershing that General Treviño had informed him that he had orders from the de facto Mexican government to prevent by use of arms new invasions of his country by American forces and also to prevent the American forces from moving from positions which they then occupied. General Pershing replied to General Treviño, it was stated, that he would use his own judgment as to when and in what direction he should move his forces in pursuit of the bandits or in seeking information regarding them.

There was a clash between the Mexican and American troops at 

Carrizal on June 22, in which both American and Mexican soldiers were killed and 17 American soldiers made prisoners. On June 24

Mr. Arredondo wrote to the Secretary of State, calling to his attention the correspondence between General Treviño and General 

Pershing, outlined above. On June 25 the Department instructed 

Special Representative Rodgers to say to the Mexican Minister of

Foreign Affairs that the United States could put no other construction on Mr. Arredondo's note of June 24 than that it was intended as a formal avowal of deliberately hostile action against American forces in Mexico. Mr. Rodgers was instructed to demand the immediate release of the American prisoners taken at Carrizal, together with any property of the United States taken with them. He was also instructed to say that the United States expected an early statement as to the course of action determined upon by Mexico and that the United States expected that such a statement should be made through the usual diplomatic channels and not through subordinate military commanders. 

Meanwhile, on June 20, the Secretary of State had addressed a note to the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs pointing out the numerous depredations upon American persons and property by Mexicans, in both Mexico and the United States, and saying that the United States, because of the fact that the perpetrators thereof were neither apprehended nor punished, "had no recourse other than to employ force to disperse the bands of Mexican outlaws who were with increasing boldness systematically raiding across the international boundary". He stated that "as immediate action alone could avail,

there was no opportunity to reach an agreement (other than that of March 10-13 now repudiated by General Carranza) prior to the entrance of such an expedition into Mexico if the expedition was to be effective". He stated that it was well known that the forces of the de facto government in Mexico had not carried on a vigorous pursuit of the remaining bandits and that no proper distribution of forces had been made to prevent the invasion of American territory. 

He declared that American troops had crossed into Mexico on May 10 "upon notification to the local military authorities, under the repudiated agreement of March 10-13, or in any event in accordance with the practice adopted over forty years ago, when there was no agreement regarding pursuit of marauders across the international boundary". He emphatically denied that the Government of the United 

States had had ulterior and improper motives in its diplomatic representations or had countenanced the activities of American sympathizers and the American press opposed to the de facto government in Mexico. He said:

It is admitted that American troops have crossed the international boundary in hot pursuit of the Columbus raiders and without notice to or the consent of your Government; but the several protestations on the part of this Government by the President, by this Department, and by other American authorities, that the object of the expedition was to capture, destroy, or completely disperse the Villa bands of outlaws or to turn this duty over to the Mexican authorities when assured that it would be effectively fulfilled, have been carried out in perfect good faith by the United States. Its efforts, however, have been obstructed at every point; first, by insistence on a palpably useless agreement which you admit was either not to apply to the present expedition or was to contain impracticable restrictions on its organization and operation; then by actual opposition, encouraged and fostered by the de facto Government, to the further advance of the expedition into Villa territory, which was followed by the sudden suspension of all negotiations for an arrangement for the pursuit of Villa and his followers and the protection of the frontier; and finally by a demand for the immediate withdrawal of the American troops. Meantime, conditions of anarchy in the border States of Mexico were continually growing worse. Incursions into American territory were plotted and perpetrated; the Glen Springs raid was successfully executed, while no effective efforts were being made by General Carranza to improve the conditions and to protect American territory from constant threat of invasion. In view of this increasing menace, of the inactivity of the Carranza forces, of the lack of cooperation in the apprehension of the Villa bands, and of the known encouragement and aid given to bandit leaders, it is unreasonable to expect the United States to withdraw its forces from Mexican territory or to prevent their entry again when their presence is the only check upon further bandit outrages and the only efficient means of protecting

American lives and homes-safeguards which General Carranza, though internationally obligated to supply, is manifestly unable or unwilling to give.

The Secretary also declared that, if the Mexican Government was unwilling or unable to prevent its territory from being the rendezvous and refuge of murderers and plunderers, that did not relieve the Government of the United States from its duty to take all the steps necessary to safeguard American citizens on American soil. He said further: 

The United States Government can not and will not allow bands of lawless men to establish themselves upon its borders with liberty to invade and plunder American territory with impunity and, when pursued, to seek safety across the Rio Grande, relying upon the plea of their Government that the integrity of the soil of the Mexican Republic must not be violated.

The de facto Government finally argues that "if the frontier were duly protected from incursions from Mexico there would be no reason for the existing difficulty"; thus the de facto Government attempts to absolve itself from the first duty of any Government, namely, the protection of life and property. This is the paramount obligation for which governments are instituted, and governments neglecting or failing to perform it are not worthy of the name. This is the duty for which General Carranza, it must be assumed, initiated his revolution in Mexico and organized the present government and for which the United States Government recognized his government as the de facto Government of Mexico. Protection of American lives and property, then, in the United States is first the obligation of this Government, and in Mexico is, first, the obligation of Mexico, and second, the obligation of the United States. In securing this protection along the common boundary the United States has a right to expect the cooperation of its neighboring Republic; and yet, instead of taking steps to check or punish the raiders, the de facto Government demurs and objects to measures taken by the United States. The Government of the United 

States does not wish to believe that the de facto Government approves these marauding attacks, yet as they continue to be made, they show that the Mexican Government is unable to repress them. This inability, as this Government has had occasion in the past to say, may excuse the failure to check the outrages complained of, but it only makes stronger the duty of the United States to prevent them, for if the Government of Mexico can not protect the lives and property of Americans exposed to attack from Mexicans, the Government of the United States is in duty bound, so far as it can, to do so. 

An American-Mexican Joint Commission was constituted in August 1916 to study the settlement of the questions arising out of the

situation in Mexico. This Commission adjourned in January 1917 without having been able to reach any understanding. A protocol of agreement, ad referendum, drawn up by them in respect to the withdrawal of American troops from Mexican territory and the protection of the American-Mexican international boundary, on November 24, 1916, was rejected by General Carranza. The American Commissioners refused to agree to changes in this protocol subsequently proposed by the Mexican Commissioners.

On February 6, 1917 the last troops of the American expeditionary force in Mexico returned to the United States.

In the case of Jose Antonio Arce et al. v. The State, Jose Arce and others were convicted of murdering a corporal in the United States Federal Army during a fight between American and Mexican troops at 

San Ignacio, Texas. Upon appeal the Court of Criminal Appeals of 

Texas reversed the judgment on the ground that the trouble occurred at the time of the Pershing punitive expedition in Mexico and that this expedition brought about a condition of "war" between the two countries. 

The court said: 66 Whatever may have been the rights of these Mexicans, the authority to punish, the writer feels, is within the jurisdiction of the United States and not the courts of Texas. If there was a state of war between the two countries, actual and complete, or inchoate and incomplete, then it became an international or Federal question and not a 

State matter." 

83 Tex. Cr. R. (1918), 292, 296, 202 S.W. 951, 953.

In September 1918 the Mexican Ambassador informed the Secre- Other tary of State that on August 11 a party of seven American soldiers crossed the boundary line and entered the town of El Mulato, Mexico, where they were challenged by the revenue officers and inhabitants. 

On hearing the challenge, they fired and the exchange of shots resulted in the killing of an American and the wounding of a revenue officer. The Ambassador protested against this violation of Mexican territory and asked that the guilty soldiers be punished. The Secretary of State replied that, since the action of those soldiers was without authority and in direct violation of orders, they had been tried by court martial, the trials resulting in their being dishonorably discharged from the Army and confined at disciplinary barracks. 

Ambassador Bonillas to Secretary Lansing, Sept. 10, 1918, MS. Department of State, file 812.0144/119; Mr. Lansing to Mr. Bonillas, no. 675, Nov. 2, 1918, ibid. 812.0144/127. See also 1918 For. Rel. 572, 573. 

On June 15, 1919 during the course of skirmishes between Mexican 

Federal troops and rebel troops at Ciudad Juárez, several shots from the Mexican side of the border resulted in casualties on American soil. Late in the evening of that day 1,600 American soldiers were sent into Ciudad Juárez and its environs. On June 16 the Department of State telegraphed to the American Chargé d'Affaires in Mexico that the dispatch of troops into Ciudad Juárez should not be considered in any manner as unfriendly to the Mexican Government, being necessitated solely by the fact that rebel forces had been so situated that their shots crossed the border and endangered the lives of American citizens. The troops had been ordered across the line, it was said, in order to drive the rebels away, and for no other purpose. The forces in question returned to the United States early in the evening of June 16.

The Mexican Ambassador addressed a protest to the Department of State on August 21, 1919 against the entrance of American forces on Mexican territory in pursuit of the captors of two American aviators, Davis and Patterson, who had landed in the State of Chihuahua and who had been captured by bandits. The Secretary of State replied that the Mexican Government had been immediately notified of the capture of the aviators and had been requested to take steps to obtain their prompt release but that, as it seemed evident that the Mexican Government was unable to accomplish this, it had been

necessary to pay a ransom to the captors to save the lives of the Americans, and that since it appeared that the Mexican Government had taken no effective measures to hunt down the bandits a detach-. ment of American troops had entered Mexico in pursuit of them. 

The Secretary said further: 

The attention of the Mexican Government has been repeatedly called to the menace to the lives of American citizens growing out of the lawless conditions existing in many parts of Mexico, and especially along our border. The Mexican Government has had ample time and warning to adopt adequate measures to restore orderly conditions. The Government of the United States cannot be expected to suffer the indefinite continuance of existing lawless conditions along its border, which expose its citizens to maltreatment at the hands of ruffianly elements of the Mexican population, which their Government seems unable to control, and which have undoubtedly been encouraged to continue their acts of aggression against citizens of the United States by reason of the immunity from punishment for such acts which they have enjoyed. 

No violation of the national sovereignty of Mexico was intended by this expedition. It was despatched upon the hot trail of the bandits in question with the sole object of punishing them for their mistreatment of officers of the American Army, and of preventing future activities of a similar nature upon our frontier. This object, having been accomplished as far as was possible in the circumstances, orders have been issued for the return of the troops to American territory. 

The Mexican Ambassador replied that his Government did not accept the criterion set forth in the Secretary's reply "as no foreign force has any right to enter Mexican territory on any excuse without the permission of the Mexican authorities, and to do so without meeting that requisite, no matter what cause is invoked, constitutes a violation of the Sovereignty of Mexico." 

Secretary Lansing to Ambassador Bonillas, Aug. 26, 1919, MS. Department of State, file 812.0144/151; Señor Bonillas to Mr. Lansing, Sept. 23, 1919, ibid. 812.0144/184. See also 1919 For. Rel., vol. II, pp. 560-561, 563.

With respect to a complaint of the Chargé d'Affaires ad interim of Panama regarding field operations of American troops in the Province of Coclé which were allegedly made without any request for permission from the Panamanian Government, the Department U.S. Army of State informed the Chargé d'Affaires that it had received a report Panama to the effect that at no time had the army headquarters or the American Legation requested authority from the Panamanian Government to enter its territory, as the right to enter such territory in connection with the defense of the Canal and of the Republic of Panama was clearly set forth in articles 1, 2, and 23 of the convention for the construction of a ship canal of 1903. 33 Stat. 2234; 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1349. It was stated, however, that in deference to the 

Republic of Panama it had been the practice of army headquarters in the Canal Zone before sending troops into the field in Panamanian territory to address a formal letter to the American Minister requesting him to notify the Panamanian Government of intended troop movements and to obtain assistance in securing such aid from the local authorities as the troop commanders might need. No advance notice had been given, it was said, with reference to the reconnaissance in Coclé Province as no assistance had been needed from the local authorities, and the reconnaissance was but an extension of the work then in progress there concerning which notice had been given. Instructions had been issued, it was declared, to the commanding general, Panama Canal Department, to take the greatest care in the future to assure the conveying of due notice to the proper local authorities when it was intended to send American troops into Panamanian territory under the provisions of the existing convention. 

In a note dated November 12, 1921 the Panamanian Chargé d'Affaires explained at some length the position of the Panamanian Government, that it could not accept the theories expressed by the 

Department of State in its note of August 31, 1921.

In the case of Ex parte Toscano, et al., the following facts were stipulated: that a state of civil war had existed in Mexico since early in March 1913; that the United States was not a party thereto and occupied the position of a neutral; and that the petitioners, members of the Federalist troops, had fled from the Constitutionalist Army into the United States on April 13, 1913 where they had voluntarily surrendered to the armed forces of the United States which, acting under authority of the President of the United States, had disarmed and interned them. The case came before the court on a petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The court dismissed the petition. In its opinion the court quoted article XI of the convention respecting the rights and duties of neutral powers and persons in war on land, obliging a neutral power to intern belligerent troops received on its territory. 36 Stat. 2310, 2324; 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 2290, 2298. The court, in holding that the petitioners were not deprived of their liberty without due process of law in violation of the fifth amendment of the Constitution, stated that internment was "not a punishment for crime, but simply an appropriate means agreed upon for the temporary care of alien forces who seek asylum in neutral territory". The court said further:

Internment, in many respects, closely resembles the temporary confinement necessary to the exclusion or deportation of aliens, both being means respectively employed for the execution of laws a treaty in the one case, and an act of Congress in the other.

Except in its statement of some general principles, about which there is no controversy, Ex parte Orozco, 201 Fed. 106, has no

application here. The Hague Treaty, upon which the government justifies its detention of the petitioners herein, was not even referred to by the learned judge who decided the latter case. I agree with him that the power to deprive an individual of his liberty without due process of law has no existence in this country, but here "due process of law" is found in the Hague Treaty, its execution by the President, and the admitted facts which bring petitioners under its operation. 

The court also declared that the view that, since the United States had not accorded official recognition to either party to the civil war in Mexico, neither of the parties was a nation within the meaning of international law and that therefore the principles of international law did not apply, was unsustained by authority. It concluded:

First, that the petitioners are completely within the provisions of chapter 2, art. 11, of the Hague Treaty; second, that said article violates no provision of the Constitution of the United States, requires no legislation to render it effective, and is accordingly the law of the land; and third, that the President has full authority, and it was and is his duty to execute said treaty provisions. 

208 Fed. 938, 941, 943, 944 (S.D. Cal., 1913).

Pascual Orozco, an officer in the army opposed to the administration of President Madero in Mexico in 1912, escaped after a conflict between the Government and revolutionary forces and entered the United States where he was arrested by American troops and by them delivered to the civil authorities to answer an indictment in the Federal Court at El Paso, Texas, charging him and others with a conspiracy to export arms and ammunition to Mexico. He was acquitted on this charge and ordered discharged. Subsequently, on Nov. 10, 1912, pursuant to orders issuing from the War Department by direction of the President, he was arrested in El Paso by the military authorities who continued to hold him in custody under instructions from the President. The District Court of the United States for the Western 

District of Texas on Dec. 14, 1912 granted his petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The court held that the "President was without lawful power to order the arrest and imprisonment of the relator". Ex parte Orozco, 201 

Fed. 106, 118 (W.D. Tex., 1912).

Habana convention Military planes; vessels

In 1929 the Departments of State, Justice, Labor, and War reached the following informal understanding concerning the disposition to be made of Mexican Federal and rebel troops entering the United 

States: 

(1) Unarmed rebels admissible under the immigration laws and not having maltreated American citizens or property in Mexico shall be permitted to enter the United States, it being understood of course that should evidence be developed of any violation of law on the part of the applicants while previously in the United States which would subject them to prosecution, proper action looking to such prosecution would be taken by representatives of the Department of Justice. (2) Armed rebel combatants seeking or effecting admission into the United States either at a regular port of entry or otherwise shall be taken into custody by the Army. (3) Individual Federal soldiers officers or privates-are to be permitted to come to and go from the United States freely as heretofore. (4) Should any large detachment of Federal soldiers come into the United States to be moved across the territory of the United States, it would be necessary to secure the consent of the States through which they pass for such movement, subject to the approval of the Secretary of Labor. (5) Should any detachment of Federal troops seek refuge in the United States they shall be disarmed and taken into custody by the Army and turned over to the appropriate Mexican Consul for disposition, subject to the approval of the Secretary of Labor. The arms shall be similarly and separately disposed of.

The Acting Secretary of State (Clark) to the Attorney General (Mitch ell), May 4, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 812.00 Detention/68.

By article 1 of the convention in regard to the duties and rights of states in the event of civil strife, signed at Habana, February 20, 1928, to which the United States is a party, the contracting states bound themselves:

To disarm and intern every rebel force crossing their boundaries, the expenses of internment to be borne by the state where public order may have been disturbed. The arms found in the hands of the rebels may be seized and withdrawn by the government of the country granting asylum, to be returned, once the struggle has ended, to the state in civil strife.

Having been informed that an aeroplane belonging to General Calles had invaded American territory near Nogales, Arizona, on July 31, 1915, the Department of State instructed the American Consul at Nogales to inform General Calles that a repetition of such acts might have disastrous results since the commander of the American

forces along the border had been instructed by the War Department to repel such invasions. The Consul replied that General Calles declared that this was the first notice he had had of the crossing of his aeroplane onto American territory and that this act was probably due to the error of the aviator as he had no intention to commit such an invasion, which would not be repeated.

The American Consul at the city of Chihuahua, Mexico, telegraphed to the Department of State in August 1919 that the presence of American planes on the preceding day over the city had caused more ill-feeling there than the recent crossing of the border by American troops in pursuit of bandits. The Mexican Ambassador brought the matter to the attention of the Secretary of State on September 1 and again on September 5, requesting an investigation of the facts and the punishment of the guilty persons. The War Department promised to issue strict orders against repetitions of such flights.

The Mexican Ambassador on February 11, 1918 protested to the Secretary of State because of the fact that the U.S.S. Iroquois had recently seized the American vessel North Fork and forced it to leave the port of Ensenada, Lower California, Mexico. The Secretary of

State explained that the incident had occurred because of the mistaken idea of the commander of the Iroquois that he was within his rights in making the seizure on account of the apparent violation by the captain of the North Fork of the provisions of the act of Congress known as the "Trading with the Enemy Act" and that as a disciplinary measure the commander of the Iroquois had been detached from his command; also that measures had been taken to prevent any repetition by American war vessels of the violation of Mexican territorial waters.

Pursuant to a joint resolution of Congress of June 25, 1910, appropriating $1,000,000 to protect property in the Imperial Valley within the United States against injury through changes in the channels of the Colorado River and for expenditure within Mexican territory in accordance with such agreements as might be made with Mexico (36 Stat. 883), J. A. Ockerson was designated to investigate and make recommendations in the matter. As a result of his surveys, Mr. Ockerson recommended the erection of a levee on Mexican territory. The 

Mexican Foreign Office stated that President Díaz had no authority to permit the erection of levees and suggested the negotiation of a treaty. The Department of State instructed the American Ambassador on November 26, 1910 that the United States did not desire to secure for itself any rights on Mexican territory and only desired that American settlers be protected from the losses which would follow from the failure to erect a levee; also that the United States was willing that the money should be expended by the Mexican company which owned the land where the levee was to be built and that if such an arrangement were adopted it would probably be unnecessary to negotiate a treaty as the United States would have no legal interest in the levee.

An agreement between the two Governments was embodied in an exchange of notes, that of the Mexican Embassy being dated Decem- Exchange of ber 20, 1910 and that of the Department of State, December 24, 1910. notes 

In the latter note, the bases of the agreement were enumerated as follows: That the works should be constructed by the Colorado River

Land Co., owner of the land on which they were to be constructed; that they should be made in accordance with the surveys and plans approved by the inspector appointed by the Mexican Department of Fomento; that in the construction of the works the rights of the riparian owners on both banks and of the persons to whom the Government of Mexico might have granted permits or concessions for the use of the water of the Colorado River should stand unimpaired; that the 

Mexican Government did not guarantee the result of the work nor assume any responsibility to private persons or to the Government of the United States; that the Government of the United States, even though it might aid the Colorado River Land Co. pecuniarily or otherwise, should not acquire any right of ownership or servitude, or any

other, over any part of the territory, or over the works that might be erected in Mexican territory, whose rights, real or of any other nature, should reside in the jurisdiction and sovereignty of the Mexican Government; that the Mexican President should propose to the Mexican

Congress the free entry of the machinery, etc., necessary for the construction of the works, as soon as the Colorado River Land Co., in the capacity of a Mexican company, applied therefor. It was added that the Government of the United States accepted these bases and that the Secretary of State would be glad to take up with the Mexican Ambassador the arrangement of various details in the practical carrying out of the work and also to undertake with him the negotiation of a treaty providing for the maintenance of the levee after it was completed. 

The Mexican Ambassador in a note dated January 4, 1911 stated that his Government did not consider the maintenance of the defensive works a proper subject for a treaty since the agreements relative thereto were to be embodied in the contract to be made by the Mexican Government with the Mexican company; that the exchange of notes fixing the general bases for the execution of the works having been effected, all other agreements should be arranged between the building company and the Department of the Mexican Government concerned. 

Later, on January 9, 1911, the Ambassador informed the Secretary of State that he had reached an agreement with a representative of the Secretary of the Interior concerning modifications of the printed specifications prepared by J. A. Ockerson, the attorney for the Colorado 

River Land Co., to which the Mexican Government had objected. 

He expressed the belief that the negotiations between the two Governments on the matter ended with his conferences with the representative of the Secretary of the Interior since the defensive works were to be exclusively the subject of agreements between his Government and the Mexican company about to build them and were without any international character and since consequently the adjustment of all questions thereafter arising would be subject exclusively to the concessions granted to the company and to the pertinent provisions of law. The 

Secretary of State replied that it was never intended to create by the contracts in question any rights in favor of the Government of the United States to the ownership of the land or to sovereignty; nor any other rights to any portion of the Mexican territory or to the works to be built on it.

The Department of State addressed a note to the Mexican Ambassador on March 14, 1911 stating that two young American citizens, Lawrence F. Converse and Edward M. Blatt, on the preceding February 21 or 22, had been kidnapped on American territory by Mexican citizens and conveyed across the Rio Grande to Mexican territory where, apparently awaiting the kidnappers' return, were Mexican soldiers whose commanding officer appeared to be directing the kidnappers' work. The note stated that the Americans had been placed in jail at Ciudad Juárez and were being held on the charge of sedition, awaiting trial in the Federal court. It was stated that the matter was being investigated in order to determine the actual facts in the case, in as much as the kidnapping of American citizens from American territory would constitute under the circumstances "a grave violation of the sovereignty of the United States by officials of the Mexican Government"; that, should it be established that the Americans were actually kidnapped on American territory and taken into Mexican territory, the United States Government would be obliged to request that they be immediately returned, with appropriate explanations; that, if it were established that they had committed an offense properly extraditable under the existing extradition treaty between the United States and Mexico, the Mexican Government would naturally possess the right to institute, in accordance with the treaty, regular proceedings for their return to Mexico and trial and punishment.

In a note of March 17 the Mexican Ambassador stated that his Government held documentary proof that the boys in question were arrested on Mexican territory.

The Department informed the Ambassador in Mexico on April 10 that the Government of the United States was of the opinion that the question of violation of sovereignty should be held in abeyance and that the boys should be released at once. Reference was made, as a precedent, to the Banco de Vala case, in which Mexico had suggested that parties arrested by both Governments on territory under dispute should be released and the question of violation of territory left for later determination and the Government of the United States had acquiesced in that suggestion. MS. Department of State, 23 Instructions, Mexico, 416, 418, 420; ibid. 118 Despatches, Mexico, no. 110,

Sept. 9, 1893. It was further pointed out that the evidence submitted to the Department clearly showed that, admitting that the

Blatt and Converse

Kidnapping of Samuel

Cantú arrest took place on disputed territory, the captors passed over Amer ican territory after making the arrest, which seemed to be a clear violation of American sovereignty. This fact alone, it was said, would be sufficient ground for the release of Converse and Blatt. 

The Mexican Government declared that it could not release the boys until a mutual agreement could be made in accordance with the following proposals: that the Banco de Vala case was not analogous to the case under discussion because in the former both Governments made arrests on disputed territories; that the question of sovereignty of the territory in which the boys were arrested might be left for further settlement but that they could not be released until the exact spot of their capture was determined; that it was reported that the capture took place in the Chamizal tract which was claimed to be, under the agreement between Mexico and the United States for the preservation of the status quo, under Mexican jurisdiction; and that the judicial status of the place of arrest under that agreement must be ascertained. The Mexican Government proposed that the Boundary Commission proceed at once to determine the exact place of arrest and, if it was on a banco, when and how the banco was formed and which country had jurisdiction over it, the release of the prisoners to depend upon which country exercised jurisdiction over the banco. 

It considered that the passage over American territory of the captors of Blatt and Converse, with the prisoners, was only a secondary incident in connection with the capture, but it agreed to have it included in the discussion if the above-mentioned proposals were accepted. 

On April 22 President Díaz ordered the release of Converse and

Blatt, stating that he was doing this without authority but that he was a father and understood the grief of the father of young Converse. 

On May 10, 1911, the Mexican Minister of Foreign Affairs informed the American Ambassador that in accordance with article 190 of the Penal Code of the Federal District, it had been decided to expel 

Converse and Blatt from Mexico.

On March 24, 1915 Ricardo Bermudez, a Panamanian citizen, was Bermudez arrested by Canal Zone police at Las Sabanas in the Republic of case Panama and brought back to the Canal Zone charged with conspiracy to defraud the United States Government under section 37 of the United States Criminal Code. The territory on which he was arrested had been transferred to Panama by the boundary convention of September 2, 1914. Ratifications of this convention had been exchanged on February 11, 1915, and it had been proclaimed by the 

President on February 18 of that year. 38 Stat. 1893; 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2770. However, the Panamanian authorities did not take physical possession of the territory in question until May 1, 1915 and up until that date Canal Zone authorities continued to police the region.

In the District Court in the Canal Zone Bermudez agreed to appear in the Southern District of New York to plead to the indictment, giving bond for $10,000. It did not appear at the time of his appearance in the Canal Zone court that he questioned the jurisdiction of that court in any way.

The Panamanian Minister in Washington, on April 20, addressed a note to the Secretary of State protesting against Bermudez's arrest on the ground that Las Sabanas was under the jurisdiction of Panama and asking that the indictment be dismissed. The Department of State replied that it concurred in the opinion of the Attorney General that it was proper that Bermudez should present the question of jurisdiction to the United States District Court in New York since he had voluntarily agreed to come to New York for trial and had made no protest whatsoever as to the jurisdiction of the court in the Canal Zone.

In a note dated June 8 the Panamanian Minister, after alleging that Panamanian sovereignty had been violated by the entrance of Canal Zone police onto its territory, by the arrest made, by the fact that the prisoner had been conducted across Panamanian territory to the Canal Zone, and by the assumption of jurisdiction by a court in

New York City over acts committed by a Panamanian citizen in Panamanian territory, stated that his Government agreed to order that the acts imputed to Bermudez should be investigated and punished by the Panamanian courts.

On June 7 United States Circuit Court Judge William H. Hunt heard Bermudez's plea to the jurisdiction and held that the United States having asserted and exercised jurisdiction over Las Sabanas between the time of the execution of the above-mentioned boundary convention and the physical transfer of possession, such acts through the political authorities were binding on the judicial department and that the court was bound to recognize the jurisdiction of the United States and that of the Canal Zone District Court over the place where the arrest occurred.

The Secretary of State informed the Panamanian Minister on September 3 that considering the peculiar circumstances of the case and in view of the technical discussion of the point of sovereignty into which it had turned, he had concluded to recommend to the Attorney General the discontinuance of legal proceedings and the discharge of Bermudez as an act of comity "on the understanding that neither Government waives its contentions as to principle, and that the Government of Panama will not, at any time hereafter, present a claim against the United States Government, arising out of this case". 

The Minister replied that such disposition of the case met with his Government's approval. The Attorney General acceded to the request for Bermudez's release on condition that the Panamanian Government would agree to designate officers to take him into custody upon delivery by United States officers and give assurances that he would be prosecuted under Panamanian laws for any crime which he might have committed. The Panamanian Minister stated on September 18 that Bermudez was not in custody, but that he had been arrested and was then in Panama under bail, and that assurance had already been given that he would be prosecuted.

claim In the case of Guillermo Colunje (Panama v. United States) the Colunje 

American-Panamanian Claims Commission on June 27, 1933 allowed a claim based on the fact that after criminal charges were preferred in the tribunals of the Canal Zone against Colunje for the use of the United States mails for fraudulent purposes, a Canal Zone detective had gone to the offices of Colunje in the Republic of Panama and had induced the latter to accompany him to the Zone where he had informed him that he was under arrest and had taken him to the Ancon police station. Colunje was brought before the district judge, detained for several hours, and released on a bond of $200. 

Subsequently proceedings against him were nolle-prossed, Colunje was released, and his bond was returned to him. The Commission said: 

It is evident that the police agent of the Zone by inducing Colunje by false pretenses to come with him to the Zone with the intent of arresting him there unduly exercised authority within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Panama to the prejudice of a Panaman citizen, who, as a result thereof, suffered the humiliation incident to a criminal proceeding. For this act of a police agent in the performance of his functions, the United States of America should be held liable. 

Hunt's Report (1934) 733, 748.

In 1907 Robert Kuehnert, an American attorney, resident in Berlin, was commissioned by the Governor of the State of New York as commissioner of deeds in Germany. He took his oath of office as such before the American Consul General in Berlin. By a note Commis- deeds in sioner of foreign country

Administra tors in foreign country verbale of March 1, 1908 the German Ministry for Foreign Affairs informed the American Ambassador of the inadmissibility under German law of Kuehnert's acting in such capacity. It was said: 

According to the statutes of the State of New York (The Executive Law, chapter 9 of the General Laws, secs. 87-89, in 

Birdseye's Revised Statutes, Codes and General Laws of the 

State of New York, 1901, vol. 1 S. 1346-1348), commissioners of deeds abroad are officials whose duty it is to take the acknowledgment of and to authenticate legal transactions, to administer oaths, and to draw up legal documents. Such duties, however, lie exclusively within the authority of a public official and can be performed in Germany only in conformity with the statutes which govern such public offices. If the commissioner should perform such public acts in Germany he would run the risk of trespassing upon the territory of the German courts and notaries, and would consequently be in danger of legal punishment, under Paragraph 132 of the German criminal law. The Imperial Ambassador in Washington has therefore been instructed to bring this subject to the attention of the United States Government and to request that the appointment of Mr. Kuehnert as a commissioner of deeds, if it has actually taken place, be withdrawn as speedily as possible, and that he be requested in the meantime to desist from the performance of the duties of his office. 

Ambassador Tower to Secretary Root, no. 1309, Mar. 5, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 12547/-1.

Replying to an inquiry as to the legal status in Germany of an administrator appointed in the United States, the Department of 

State, in March 1909, said thatthere appears to be no treaty provision between the United States and Germany conferring extraterritorial powers upon administrators appointed in either country. 

It seems to be a well-settled principle of international law that letters of administration have no such force. In the absence of statute, then, an administrator is not entitled, as a matter of

right, to administer upon property outside of the country of his appointment. Any recognition which he may receive beyond his own jurisdiction may be extended only upon a principle of international comity, to be given or withheld according to pleasure or policy. 

However, ancillary letters of administration may undoubtedly be taken out in the German jurisdiction where the property referred to is located.

The Assistant Secretary of State (Wilson) to Messrs. Forman and Forman, Mar. 29, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 18604. See article X of the consular convention concluded between the United States and Germany, Dec. 11, 1871, 17 Stat. 921, 926; 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 550, 553.

On August 31, 1937 the President of Mexico issued a decree, amending article XIV of a decree of March 18, 1925 establishing an income tax, providing that persons sending goods to Mexico should pay a tax on their annual gross income less a deduction of 65 percent, and providing that such tax should never in any case exceed 3 percent of the total income and that, as an advance against the income tax accruing, such exporters should pay to Mexican consulates 3 percent of the value of the goods sent to Mexico. The Department of State instructed the Ambassador in Mexico to discuss the matter informally with the Mexican Foreign Office and to bring to its attention the following considerations: 

1. Other countries having an income tax law are confronted with the problem of collection of taxes imposed on profits incident to the shipment of goods into the country, but, as far as is known, it is unprecedented for one country to attempt to collect such taxes in the territory of the other country through its own agents operating in that country. 

---

Delivery of mail pouches to foreign consul 2. The action of the Mexican Government amounts in effect to the establishment of a part of its fiscal system in the United 

States. 

3. The right to lay and collect taxes in a country appertains to the local sovereign and any assertion of such a right by a foreign power is in derogation of that sovereignty. 

4. The taxing power of the state does not extend beyond its limits and it is essential to the validity of a tax on property that the property taxed shall have a situs within the territorial jurisdiction of the taxing power. In the case of an income tax the recipient of the income must have a domicile within the state or the property or business out of which the income issues must be within the state. 

5. Moreover, it is by no means certain that the collection of these taxes in the manner contemplated by the Mexican decree would not be in violation of the Constitutional inhibition with respect to the laying of a tax on articles exported from the 

United States. 

The Ambassador informed the Department on April 13, 1938 that he was advised that the Finance Minister would on that day present to the Mexican Congress a decree signed by the President canceling the decree creating the 3-percent advance income tax in question. 

Counselor Moore to Ambassador Daniels, no. 1747, Oct. 13, 1937, MS. Department of State, file 812.5123/87; Mr. Daniels to Secretary Hull, telegram 116, Apr. 13, 1938, ibid. 812.6363/3465.
