In 1912 the Mexican Government inquired whether Mexican mails routed through Ciudad Juárez (a center of revolutionary disturbances) could be delivered to the Mexican Consul at El Paso for distribution. The Department said thatunder the rules of international law a foreign port in the hands of insurgents (except where ingress or egress from such port is physically prevented by blockade or otherwise by the parent government) is regarded as if it were still in the hands of the parent government and so open to the intercourse and commerce of other nations. 

This Government does not feel, therefore, that it has any legal basis for prohibiting the routing of mail through Ciudad Juárez when that is the only point through which mails destined to that section of the country can be dispatched. Moreover, as it would be manifestly improper for a postmaster of a foreign country to exercise his functions within the territory of the United States, still more would it be improper for such functions to be exercised by a foreign consul; and accordingly mail pouches can not properly be delivered to a consul. I may add, however, that official mail adressed to officials of the established government can probably be delivered to a consul, and that if mail can reach its desti-

nation through any other point than Ciudad Juárez it may be so routed. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Ambassador Crespo y Martinez, Mar. 4, 1912, MS. Department of State, file 812.71/8a. See also 1912 For.

Rel. 736. in transit In consequence of the theory of English and American juris- Prisoners prudence regarding the territoriality of crime, no person can lawfully be arrested or held in custody in this country for a crime committeed outside of its jurisdiction, except as provided by statute or by treaty. 

The laws of the United States contain no provision authorizing the detention or custody of a fugitive in transit between two foreign countries from which and to which he is being extradited, and the only authority for such detention would, therefore, be a provision of treaty. The only treaty to which the United States is a party which provides for the question of transit is the treaty with Mexico. In other cases, even though the government to which the fugitive is being returned may have a treaty in force with the United States covering the crime for which the fugitive is being surrendered, this Government is bound to surrender such person only upon compliance with the treaty requirements, which are not fulfilled in the ordinary case of transit across its territory. Therefore, the only way a prisoner under such circumstances can, in the full strictness of the law, be conveyed across United States territory is for the demanding government to institute formal extradition proceedings in this country in accordance with treaty requirements. 

The existence of this rule in other countries has sometimes necessitated the making of special arrangements for the return of a fugitive where the vessel conveying him must stop at an intermediate port. In one case the department applied, through the diplomatic channel to the Government of the authorities of such port, for the provisional detention of the fugitive, in case he should attempt to secure his release upon habeas corpus or analogous proceeding. Once in a case of transit across the Isthmus of Panama in 1888 [1878], the fugitive was permitted to escape altogether. (For. Rels., 1878, p. 151.)

Many of the States of Europe and South America have enacted laws so as to permit transit through their territory upon more or less liberal conditions. Some provisions stipulate that the request shall be made through the diplomatic channel, and some require the presentation of the documents forming the basis of the demand for the extradition. In England the practice is the same as in the United States. In 1878 the American minister at London was told by the British foreign office, regarding the contemplated transit through British jurisdiction of an American fugitive surrendered by Portugal to the United States, that if he were landed in England he would be "entitled to apply for a habeas corpus, and if the judge decided he was not in lawful custody, he would be set at liberty". 

The question of the amendment of our extradition statutes so as adequately to cover the situation under discussion has twice.

been made the subject of recommendations to Congress by the President. In his second annual message of December 6, 1886, President Cleveland said: "Experience suggests that our statutes regulating extradition might be advantageously amended by a provision for the transit across our territory, now a convenient thoroughfare of travel from one foreign country to another, of fugitives surrendered by a foreign Government to a third State. Such provisions are not unusual in the legislation of other countries, and tend to prevent the miscarriage of justice."

And President McKinley, in his second annual message of December 5, 1898, renewed the recommendation of his predecessor (Rich. Messages, vol. 10, p. 187), but no legislative action resulted in either case.

The foregoing observations, it will be noted, have been addressed to the strict question of law, as to whether or not the Government has a right to demand that a fugitive, under the circumstances stated, be set at liberty. A distinction is, however, made in practice between the existence of this right and its exercise by the United States. This department, as a matter of practice, does not in these cases interfere to secure liberty for a prisoner by reason of a technical violation of its jurisdiction, but leaves the prisoner to avail himself of the remedy afforded by the laws, without any interference or suggestion upon its part. 

As an instance of the department's attitude it may be stated that twice in recent years, when application has been made by the British ambassador, on behalf of Canadian authorities, for leave to take prisoners through United States jurisdiction from one part of Canada to another, the department has stated that it was not disposed to object to such transit, but that it reserved entire freedom of action in the event of an appeal being made to it on behalf of the prisoners, and that, moreover, its failure to object was not be regarded as a precedent.

The department's conclusion upon the question propounded is, therefore, that although the United States reserves at any time a right to object to the transit of fugitives in course of transportation between third States, this is a right which is in practice left to be invoked by the party in appropriate judicial proceedings, and not by this Government in the first instance. 

Memorandum from the Department of State to the Japanese Embassy, Mar. 2, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 4904. See also 1907 For. Rel., pt. II, pp. 759-761.

The Japanese Government on Apr. 9, 1915 informed the American Ambassador that its consent was required whenever a foreign prisoner passed through Japanese territory, that during such transit he should be under the control of the imperial authorities, and that it was desired that whenever an American prisoner was to pass through Japanese territory the consent of the Japanese Government should be formally obtained. On Nov. 18, 1916 that Government informed the Ambassador that the control of the Japanese Government over foreign prisoners was equally applicable to those who remained on board a vessel and those who were permitted to land but that vessels used exclusively for military purposes belonging to and commanded

by officers of the United States Navy would be treated like warships and that prisoners remaining on such vessels would not be placed under Japanese control. Ambassador Guthrie to Secretary Lansing, no. 657, Nov. 18, 1916,

MS. Department of State, file 894.0144/8. The Japanese Government informed the American Embassy on Sept. 10, 1924 that it was desired that its consent be obtained before calls were made in Japanese ports by United States Army transports with military prisoners on board. Chargé Caffery to Secretary Hughes, no. 702-E, Sept. 16, 1924, ibid. 811.2394/15. 

On June 29, 1910 the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police in

London informed the police in Paris that the British-Indian, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, was to be sent to India for prosecution for abetment of murder, etc., on board the vessel Morea touching at Marseilles. 

The Morea arrived at Marseilles on July 7, and on the following day Savarkar escaped therefrom and swam ashore. He was arrested by a brigadier of the French maritime gendarmerie and taken back to the vessel. The brigadier was assisted by three persons who had come ashore from the vessel. The Morea left Marseilles with Savarkar on board on July 9.

The French Government subsequently demanded that Savarkar be restored to its custody. The question was submitted to a special arbitral tribunal chosen from members of the Permanent Court at The Hague, by an agreement entered into by France and Great Britain on October 25, 1910. The tribunal, in a decision dated February 

24, 1911, found that the case wasnot one of recourse to fraud or force in order to obtain possession of a person who had taken refuge in foreign territory, and that there was not, in the circumstances of the arrest and delivery of Savarkar to the British Authorities and of his removal to India, anything in the nature of a violation of the sovereignty of France, and that all those who took part in the matter certainly acted in good faith and had no thought of doing anything unlawful.

The tribunal held further that the conduct of the French brigadier not having been disclaimed by his chiefs before the Morea left Marseilles, the British police "might naturally have believed that the brigadier had acted in accordance with his instructions, or that his conduct had been approved". The tribunal, while admitting that an irregularity was committed by Savarkar's arrest and by his being handed over to the British police, held also that there was no rule of international law imposing in such circumstances "any obligation on the Power which has in its custody a prisoner, to restore him because of a mistake committed by the foreign agent who delivered him up to that Power". 

Per. Ct. Arb., official report (The Hague, 1911) 58; Scott, Hague Court 

Reports (1916) 275, 279.

Wrongful arrest in foreign countries Article I of the treaty concluded between Great Britain and the United States on May 18, 1908 provides for reciprocal rights for officers of the United States and Canada in respect to the conveyance of prisoners charged with or convicted of certain specified crimes and arrested in one country through any part of the other country. It is provided that during such conveyance the officers of each country may keep the prisoner in custody and in case of escape may recapture him. 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 830; 35 Stat. 2035.

In 1920 the British Government protested against the alleged arrest of Charles Vincenti at Bimini in the Bahamas by United States officials on board the Aquaria who had invited Vincenti to board the vessel and had then seized him and informed him that he was under arrest by the United States Government. (A warrant for his arrest had been issued in Baltimore, Maryland, charging him with the illegal sale of intoxicating liquors.) After the arrest the 

Aquaria immediately left the harbor of Bimini.

The persons who made the arrest acted on their own initiative and without knowledge or approval of the United States Government and they were subsequently reprimanded and indefinitely suspended for their participation in the affair. Vincenti's bail was exonerated and all proceedings subsequent to his unlawful arrest were revoked. 

Chargé Lindsay to Secretary Colby, no. 230, Apr. 12, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 611.44e244/5; Mr. Colby to Sir Auckland Geddes, June 

10, 1920, ibid. 611.44e244/10.

In the case of United States v. Unverzagt, the defendant, who was charged with using the mails to defraud, alleged that he had been kidnapped from the city of Vancouver, British Columbia, by purported officials of the United States. He was subsequently arrested in the United States upon the basis of an indictment returned in the Western District of New York. The district court, in discharging a writ of habeas corpus, said that there appeared to be no question as to the legality of his arrest in the United States or as to the regularity of the proceedings in the United States courts. It stated: 

The defendant states he is a citizen of the United States. He is now before the courts of the United States. Canada is not making any application to this court in his behalf or its behalf, because of any unlawful acts charged, and if Canada or British Columbia desires to protest, the question undoubtedly is a political matter, which must be conducted through diplomatic channels. The defendant cannot before the court invoke the right of asylum in British Columbia. 

299 Fed. 1015, 1017 (W.D. Wash., 1924).

BREACHES BY PRIVATE PERSONS §152 

In 1905 Antonio Martinez was kidnapped from Mexican soil by Antonio Felix and delivered to American authorities in the United States to stand trial for an offense against the laws of California. 

The United States subsequently granted the extradition to Mexico of Antonio Felix. Upon learning that Martinez was undergoing trial in the United States, the Mexican Embassy, in a note to the Department of State, stated that the Mexican Government considered it selfevident that the action against him could not rest on any legal foundation, since the United States by the extradition of Felix recognized that the means used to bring Martinez onto American territory was unlawful and requested that Martinez be returned to Mexican territory. The Department of State was of the opinion that the question presented in this case had been decided by the Supreme Court of the United States in 1886 in the case of Ker v. Illinois, wherein it was held that the irregularity in bringing the defendant Ker within the jurisdiction of Illinois was not a defense which could be presented as a valid bar to trial for a crime under a regular indictment, 119 U.S. (1886) 436. The Department declared that it was unable to comply with the Mexican request, adding further that the trial of Martinez was proceeding in the courts of California which were independent of the Federal Executive. 

Chargé Davalos to Secretary Root, no. 159, June 11, 1906, MS. Department of State, 53 Notes from Mexico; the Acting Secretary of State (Bacon) to Mr. Davalos, no. 78, June 22, 1906, ibid. 11 Notes to Mexico 355. See also 1906 For. Rel., pt. II, pp. 1121–1122.

In 1923 the British Chargé d'Affaires ad interim wrote to the Department of State with reference to the flight of an American airplane over Canadian territory which had resulted in an accident and the death of both occupants of the plane. The Chargé d'Affaires pointed out that no application had been received for permission for the plane to cross into Canadian territory or to operate on the Canadian side of the international border, that the plane was engaged in commercial operations without permission from the Department of National Defence, and that it was not registered or marked in accordance with the Canadian regulations, nor had it reported to the customs on entering Canada. The Department of State expressed regret that the plane should have flown into Canadian territory without observing the Canadian regulations and stated that steps

aircraft were being taken to prevent any such unauthorized flights in the future. 

The Under Secretary of State (Phillips) to Chargé Chilton, Oct. 5, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 842.0144/1.

52 Stat. 973, 979, 991.

By article 2 of the international convention for the regulation of aerial navigation signed at Paris, Oct. 13, 1919 (signed but not ratified by the 

United States), each contracting state undertakes in time of peace to accord freedom of innocent passage over its territory to the aircraft of the other contracting states under certain specified conditions. It is provided that regulations as to the admission of aircraft over each contracting state shall be applied without distinction of nationality. Article 3 entitles the contracting states to prohibit the flight of aircraft over certain areas of their territory for military reasons or in the interests of public safety. 

11 League of Nations Treaty Series (1922) 173; 3 Treaties, etc. 

(Redmond, 1923) 3768.

In the convention signed at Habana, on Feb. 20, 1928, by the United States and other American republics relating to commercial aviation it is provided in article IV tha: "Each contracting state undertakes in time of peace to accord freedom of innocent passage above its territory to the private aircraft of the other contracting states", under conditions laid down in the

convention. It is also provided in that article that regulations established by a contracting state in regard to the admission of aircraft shall be applied without distinction of nationality. It is further provided in article V that each contracting state has the right to prohibit in the public interest the flight over fixed zones of its territory by the aircraft of the other contracting states and privately owned national aircraft employed in the service of international commercial aviation, with the reservation that no distinction shall be made between its own private aircraft engaged in international commerce and those of the other contracting states likewise engaged. 

4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4729, 4730; 47 Stat. 1901, 1902.

PERMISSION FOR PASSAGE OF FOREIGN FORCES 

Upon receipt of an inquiry from the president of the San Antonio International Fair asking whether permission could be granted for the entry of a Mexican band and a contingent from the Mexican Army to participate in the fair, the Department of State replied: 

Before the band and troops can enter the United States, the Mexican Government should, through its Embassy at this capital, request permission. This Department will then transmit the request to enter Texas to the Governor of that State, and, on receiving a favorable reply, will accord permission for them to enter the United States, advising the Treasury Department of the place of entry.

Such procedure was in fact followed, the permission was granted, and the appropriate customs officers at the frontier were instructed to extend the usual courtesies to the troops upon their arrival. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to Mr. Wahrmund, president of the 

San Antonio International Fair Association, Sept. 1, 1906, MS. Department of State, file 302/1.

In 1915 permission was granted to General Ricaut (Mexican) to transport wounded soldiers to Matamoros over Texas soil, the State of Texas having consented. On Mar. 30 General Funston, at Brownsville, Texas, telegraphed to the Adjutant General of the United States that General Ricaut, who had not yet availed himself of the permission just referred to, desired to send 15 men to Matamoros. In view of the fact, he said, that the latter city was then being attacked by Villa troops and that Nuevo Laredo would probably soon be attacked also, he had given orders to the commanding officer at Laredo not to permit any wounded to be sent to the American side from Nuevo Laredo until further orders. Such wounded, if sent over, he said, would probably become a public charge for an indefinite time. On account of the situation at Matamoros, the permission previously granted was withdrawn. On February 12, 1911 the Department of State addressed a memo- Protection of randum to the Mexican Embassy in regard to protecting the work then in progress on the Colorado River levees in Mexico against molestation by insurgents and inquiring whether the military cooperation of the United States was needed. The Embassy replied that though the Mexican Government appreciated the offer of cooperation, it did not deem it necessary to have recourse to the aid of the United States. 

On the same day the Department addressed an aide-mémoire to the Embassy, saying that it was in receipt of information from the Mexican Government that it proposed to send an officer of the Mexican Army, Colonel Vega, with 200 men to the place of the works to protect them and that he would be instructed to purchase arms, ammunitions, and provisions in Yuma. It was stated that on the understanding that 

Colonel Vega's activities would be wholly confined to the protection of the levee rights, the United States would not object to the proposed commercial purchase of arms, etc., in Yuma, and that if it were desired to transport them over American territory it would be pleased, acting with the Governor of Arizona, to grant facilities for such transportation, it being understood that the men should be used only to protect the Colorado River works.

On February 17, 1911 the Department instructed the American Ambassador in Mexico to repeat the suggestion of effective cooperation of the two Governments, if not with regular military forces, then by an un-uniformed force acting as a police constabulary under the direction of the Secretary of the Interior of the United States. The Ambassa dor replied that at an interview with the Mexican President and the Minister of Foreign Affairs it had been agreed that in view of the urgent necessity, the Department of the Interior might employ as many un-uniformed guards as were necessary to afford adequate protection to the Colorado River works, the guards to be placed upon the roll of the Colorado River Land and Irrigation Company nominally as employees thereof.

The Mexican Ambassador wrote to the Secretary of State that Mexican troops to protect the Colorado River works and in general

all interests in the lower part of California would arrive on March 10 at Ensenada de Todos Santos where they would join Colonel Vega's forces; and that, so as not to lose any time, the Mexican Government was disposed to request that the troops be allowed to pass by rail through San Diego, California. The Department replied that it would be preferable to have the troops reach their destination over Mexican territory since it would hardly be compatible with the circumstances and principles involved for the United States to permit their passage over American territory for the avowed purpose of engaging in general hostilities. 

Memorandum from the Department of State, Feb. 12, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 711.1216M/218c; note verbale from the Mexican Embassy, Feb. 14, 1911, ibid. 711.1216M/221; aide-mémoire from the Department of 

State, Feb. 14, 1911, ibid. 711.1216M/224a; aide-mémoire of Feb. 17, 1911, ibid. 711.1216M/227A; Ambassador Wilson to Secretary Knox, Feb. 17, 1911 (telegram), ibid. 711.1216M/229; Ambassador de la Barra to Mr. Knox, no. 1056, Mar. 6, 1911; the Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Señor de la Barra, Mar. 7, 1911, ibid. 711.1216M/256. LANDING OF FORCES 

$154 During the course of the political disturbance in Cuba in September Cuba, 1906 1906 when American vessels had been sent to that country under the orders of President Roosevelt, the American Chargé d'Affaires in 

Habana, on September 13, at the request of the President of Cuba ordered the landing of a battalion of 100 men from two vessels, with three fieldpieces, in a central position in Habana, the force to be used only in case of disorders within the city menacing the lives and property of American citizens. The order was issued by the Chargé d'Affaires prior to receiving an instruction from the Department of State that he was, under no circumstances, to request the landing of marines or of any armed force except under orders of the Department. 

Immediately upon receipt of this instruction the battalion was withdrawn. In explaining his action to the Department, the Chargé d'Affaires said in a despatch dated September 15, 1906 that he had acted according to his best judgment in the emergency, convinced that rioting would occur and that American interests and property might be endangered. 

Chargé Sleeper to Secretary Root, telegram of Sept. 13, 1906 and no. 188 of Sept. 15, 1906, MS. Department of State, files 244/147, 244/182-183. See also 1906 For. Rel., pt. I, pp. 478, 482.

Nicaragua, 1910 Cuba, 1912 In 1907, during hostilities between Honduras and Nicaragua, the U.S.S. Marietta was detailed to protect American interests. On 

March 18 the commanding officer of the vessel, which was anchored at Truxillo, Honduras, upon learning that that town, occupied by the Nicaraguans, was likely to be attacked at any time by Honduran troops, landed a force of 10 men as a guard for the American Consulate. He instructed the ensign in command of the guard "to extend protection to the citizens of other neutral powers if asked to do so by their consular representatives", and to call officially upon the general commanding the Nicaraguan forces, inform him of his orders, and assure him that he would not intervene except for the proper protection of American interests. He also instructed him not to permit the guard to go beyond the limits of the Consulate unless necessary to give the protection specified above.

During the course of uprisings in Cuba in 1912 the American Minister in that country was informed on May 25 that the S.S. 

Nebraska would arrive in Habana on the following day, that a large naval force would be assembled at a convenient point, probably Key West, and that a gunboat would be ordered to Nipe Bay. He was instructed to inform the Cuban Government that in the event of its inability or failure to protect American lives or property the Government of the United States would land forces to accord the necessary protection. It was emphasized that this was not intervention. 

President Taft, on May 27, telegraphed to the President of Cuba that the sending of ships to Key West and to the Guantanamo Naval

Station was "merely to be able to act promptly in case it should unfortunately become necessary to protect American life and property by rendering moral support or assistance to the Cuban Government". These "ordinary measures of precaution", he said, "were entirely disassociated from any question of intervention". Subsequently the American commander at Guantanamo Naval Station landed four companies of marines. This action was taken, the Secretary of State informed the American Minister in Cuba, as a measure of protection only and not for the purpose of putting down the insurrection, which was clearly the duty of Cuba. 

The Minister reported on June 6 that, although the Cuban Government had not requested the landing of marines to protect foreign property, the President of Cuba had expressed his gratification on learning of their landing and had informed him that as rapidly as American forces arrived for the protection of different foreign properties, the Cuban troops would be promptly withdrawn and devoted to active operation against the rebels.

A résumé of the following incidents relating to the use of the armed forces of the United States during the years 1912-27 for the protection of the lives and property of American citizens in foreign countries or in the fulfilment of its treaty obligations with respect to certain countries, was submitted to Representative Strong by the 

Department of State on February 28, 1928.

In March 1917 a detachment of marines was landed at Santiago to prevent the destruction of the city and to protect American and foreign lives and property. They were withdrawn as soon as sufficient Government forces arrived to maintain order. Later in the same year, with the consent of the President of Cuba, American troops were sent to Cuba for training purposes and to protect the sugarcane fields in their vicinity from injury by such revolutionists as were still in the field. The last of these forces were withdrawn in 

1922. By the provisions of the treaty of May 22, 1903 between the 

United States and Cuba, Cuba granted to the United States the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life, property, and individual liberty and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris. 33 Stat. 2248; 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 362. This treaty was abrogated by a treaty signed by the two countries on May 29, 1934. 48 Stat. 1682; 

4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4054.

In 1905 the Dominican Republic failed to meet its financial obligations to foreign governments and their nationals, and threats of occupation were made by various European powers. In order to prevent such occupation the Government of the United States induced the Government of the Dominican Republic to accept a plan for receivership of the customs and the eventual settlement of the public debt. This was effected by a convention concluded by the two Governments, on February 8, 1907, which authorized the United States

to appoint a General Receiver of Customs and necessary assistants and to exercise certain control over the customs collection and obligated it to accord such protection as was necessary to accomplish the purpose of the convention. 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 418; 35

Stat. 1880. In 1916 serious disorders occurred; and in order to prevent loss of life and destruction of property and to fulfil the obligations of the United States under the convention of 1907, American troops were landed and remained in the country until 1924. 

As a result of disturbances in 1920 threatening the safety of the Guatemala American Legation in Guatemala, a Legation guard was sent to the capital but was withdrawn after about 10 days. 

United States marines were landed for brief periods during local Honduras disturbances for the protection of American and foreign lives and property in certain Honduran ports, on September 8, 1919, February 

2, 1924, March 5, 1924, and March 9, 1924. They were withdrawn immediately after the disturbances subsided. During the revolution of 1924 United States marines were sent to guard the American Legation at Tegucigalpa and remained there during the siege of that city but did not participate in any fighting. The guard was withdrawn immediately after the capture of the city by the attacking forces. 

Marines were sent to Nicaragua in 1912 on the invitation of the Nicaragua, Government of that country, and a small guard was maintained at Managua continuously until 1925 to protect the American Legation. 

Shortly thereafter on the recurrence of local disturbances and at the request of the Nicaraguan Government, marines were stationed in several places in the country. 1912 1918-19, 1925 In 1918 and 1919 American forces were used to police the Province Panama, of Chiriqui. In 1925 at the request of the Panamanian Government troops were used to police the city of Panamá for a few days during a period of strike riots. These acts were considered to be in conformity with the convention between the United States and Panama of November 18, 1903. 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1349.

Under the provisions of the protocol entered into on September 7, 1901 between China and other countries, including the United States, generally referred to as the Boxer Protocol, China conceded to the United States the right to maintain a guard at Peking for the defense of its Legation and to occupy certain points in Chinese territory with military forces to maintain open communication between Peking and the sea.

On December 3 and 4, 1917 during hostilities between two Chinese factions, an armed guard was landed from an American gunboat in the harbor of Chungking and stationed at the American Consulate at that place. The guard was withdrawn within a few days. On March 14, 1920 the commander of the U.S.S. Elcano sent a landing force ashore to protect lives endangered by a disturbance at Kiukiang. It returned to the ship within a few hours. On August 25, 1920 a detachment of 12 marines was sent from the Legation Guard at Peking to Tungchow to protect the American Board Mission during riots and looting participated in by Chinese soldiers. The detachment returned to Peking within a few days. 

On May 4, 1922 a similar detachment was sent to Tungchow for the same purpose. On November 15, 1923 a detachment of eight marines was sent to Tungshan, a suburb of Canton, to protect American missionaries during fighting between Chinese forces. The guard was withdrawn within a few days. In September 1924 hostilities occurred in the vicinity of Shanghai between two rival Chinese factions, and, as a precautionary measure, the United States and other countries con-

centrated naval forces at Shanghai. Small detachments of marines were landed to assist local volunteer companies to protect Americans and other foreigners in the city. In January 1925 fighting occurred between rival Chinese forces near Shanghai and a large body of one of the forces was interned in the foreign settlement of Shanghai. The 

United States and other powers landed sailors on January 15, and the Americans in conjunction with the French guarded the interned Chinese soldiers in order to protect the foreign lives in the settlement. On 

May 30, 1925 disorders again occurred in Shanghai resulting in the killing and wounding of Chinese by the police of the International Settlement. Strikes and demonstrations followed, necessitating the landing of a force of American sailors, on June 2, 1925, to guard, in cooperation with other foreign forces, the water and light supplies of the International Settlement. The American forces remained on shore until August 29, 1925. In August 1926 the Nationalist forces attacked 

Hankow, and American naval forces were landed to protect American citizens. They were withdrawn, with the exception of a small guard at the Consulate General, on September 16, 1926. On November 4, 1926 American, British, and Japanese naval forces were landed for the protection of foreigners in Kiukiang following the capture of that city by Nationalist forces. They were withdrawn two days later. 

In February 1927 the naval forces and marines at Shanghai were augmented because of fighting in and around the city. After the capture of the native city by Nationalist forces on March 21, 1927, a small naval guard was established at the American Consulate at Nanking, and, as a result of an attack on an American Consul, a Vice Consul, and others by Nationalist soldiers, American and British destroyers dropped shells around the house in which more than 40 Americans and other foreigners had sought protection. The firing which lasted about 20 minutes enabled the beleaguered party to escape. Following this incident additional forces of marines and naval vessels were ordered to China and stationed in the vicinity of Shanghai and Tientsin. 1922 In September 1922 American sailors were landed in Smyrna to Turkey, protect American lives and property during the retreat and evacuation by Greek forces and the entrance into the city of Turkish forces. 

The landing of the American forces was made with the approval of the Greek authorities in charge at the time, and they remained in the territory with the consent of the Turkish authorities who supplanted the Greek authorities.

The Department stated that, while it had no objection to the Denver's visit to Ceiba, it did not desire that the marines be landed without previous consultation with it, unless danger to American lives and property was so imminent as to make previous consultation impossible. Sale of arms

 REPRESSION OF CRIMINAL OR HOSTILE ACTS 

$155 In order to cooperate with the Mexican Government to suppress the smuggling of arms from Arizona across the international boundary line to hostile Yaqui Indians in Mexico, the War Department of the United States, on August 25, 1906, directed the commanding general, department of the Colorado, to patrol the Mexican border. 

The officer in charge of this patrol was instructed that, while he and his command could not lawfully make or participate in making arrests, seizures, or forcible examinations of suspected persons or property, they could be of material service by obtaining and promptly furnishing to the proper officials on either side of the boundary line information that would enable those officials to make such arrests, seizures, or examinations. He was expressly charged, however, "that his detachment must confine its operations to American territory, and must not be permitted to cross the boundary line between the two countries".

In July of that year the Department of State had telegraphed the Governor of Arizona bringing to his attention the smuggling of arms and ammunition into Mexico for use there by hostile Yaquis. 

The Governor immediately issued a proclamation directing the various county officers to be diligent in preventing the sale of arms and in punishing any violations of the law. (Sec. 362 of the Penal Code of Arizona, 1901, made the sale of firearms or ammunition to Indians a misdemeanor.) He also requested the Arizona Rangers to be especially alert in preventing the sale of arms to Indians and in preventing the setting on foot of any hostile military expedition into Mexico.

In March 1907 the Mexican Ambassador informed the Secretary of State that the smuggling of arms and ammunition from Arizona for the use of the Yaqui Indians had been resumed. The Acting 

Attorney General pointed out to the Secretary of State that, apparently, the purchases of arms were made in the United States not by persons acting as agents for the Indians but on their own account for re-sale in Mexico, so that the case did not seem to fall within the prohibition of section 362 of the Penal Code of Arizona cited above; he pointed out further that there was no provision in the neutrality laws or other federal statutes forbidding the exportation of arms or ammunition from the United States to any foreign country for any purpose whatsoever when dissociated from the fitting out in this country of an armed expedition against another country or the fitting out of a warship, or other similar cases contemplated by the neutrality laws, so that even if the arms purchased in the United States were sold to Indians in Mexico, "there would be no offense for which they could be legally arrested or convicted in this country".

The Acting Secretary of War to the Secretary of State (Root), Aug. 

25, 1906, MS. Department of State, file 283/6-7; Governor Kibbey to the 

Acting Secretary of State (Bacon), Aug. 18 and 22, 1906, ibid. files 283/1-3, 283/8-9; Ambassador Creel to Mr. Root, Mar. 13, 1907, and Mr. Root to Mr. 

Creel, Mar. 20, 1907, ibid. file 283/61-64; the Acting Attorney General (Purdy) to Mr. Root, Mar. 27, 1907, ibid. 283/66. See also 1907 For. Rel., pt. 2, pp. 846 et seq.

In the case of Daeche v. United States, Daeche was convicted in a United States District Court of a conspiracy to violate section 298 of the United States Criminal Code and of a violation of section 296 thereof. It appeared that he and certain others planned in 1915 to prepare metal boxes to be filled with high explosives and attached to the sterns of ships leaving the port of New York loaded with munitions for the Allied Powers in the Great War. The bombs were intended to explode and to injure or sink the ships. The scheme was frustrated by the police. The circuit court of appeals upon appeal affirmed the judgment of conviction under section 298 of the Criminal Code penalizing an attack on a vessel "upon the high seas or any other waters within the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States". Daeche argued that, as his plan was to blow up the vessels outside of the three-mile limit of the United States Place of waters and as the vessels were not shown to be of United States registry, his offense was to be committed outside of the United States upon a foreign vessel and that consequently the United States had no jurisdiction over such a crime. The court held that in the case of a crime covering only the conscious act of the wrongdoer, regardless commission ARB =

Plots against foreign country of its consequences, "the crime takes place only where he acts"; that under section 298 of the Criminal Code the attack took place where the wrongdoer performed the last conscious act in whose train in the course of things he expected the loss to follow. 

250 Fed. 566, 570 (C.C.A. 2d, 1918).

In accord, see the case of the Tennyson decided by the Supreme Federal Tribunal of Brazil in 1917. In that case the Brazilian court assumed jurisdiction over a crime resulting from the explosion on the English vessel Tennyson on the high seas of an infernal machine placed aboard it in the port of Bahia, Brazil. 46 Revista de direito civil commercial e criminal (Rio de Janeiro, 1917) 327.

After the assassination of the King of Yugoslavia in Marseilles in 1934 by a group of terrorists who had allegedly been previously active on Hungarian territory, the Council of the League of Nations on December 10, 1934 adopted a resolution statingthat it is the duty of every State neither to encourage nor tolerate on its territory any terrorist activity with a political purpose; 

That every State must do all in its power to prevent and repress acts of this nature and must for this purpose lend its assistance to Governments which request it . . 

The resolution also stated that the Council was of the opinion that certain Hungarian authorities might "have assumed, at any rate through negligence, certain responsibilities relative to acts having a connection with the preparation of the crime", and that it was “incumbent on the Hungarian Government . . to take at once appropriate punitive action in the case of any of its authorities whose culpability" might be established. The Hungarian Government was requested to communicate to the Council the measures it took to that effect. 

League of Nations, Official Journal (July-Dec., 1934) 1759. 

It is well settled that a State is bound to use due diligence to prevent the commission within its dominions of criminal acts against another nation or its people (United States v. Arjona (1887), 120 U. S. 479)

Dissenting opinion of Judge Moore in the case of the S. S. Lotus, Per. Ct. Int. Jus., Judgment 9, Sept. 7, 1927, Ser. A, No. 10, pp. 88-89;

II Hudson, World Court Reports (1935) 20, 80. 

UNNEUTRAL ACTS 

§156 

On September 5, 1906, seventeen members of a Mexican revolutionary junta were arrested at Douglas, Arizona, under section 5286 of the Revised Statutes of the United States forbidding military

expeditions from within the United States against a people at peace with the United States. Through their arrest, there came into the possession of the United States District Attorney at Phoenix, Arizona, a large amount of correspondence between the president of a revolutionary junta in St. Louis, Missouri, and the officers of a junta in 

Douglas, containing directions and commissions to such officers to execute the plans of the junta at St. Louis relative to an invasion of 

Mexico from points in Arizona.

Upon receipt of notice of a threatened movement of a body of armed men across the border directed against the Government of Mexico, the President directed that the several branches of the Government having cognizance of the situation should use all possible efforts toward checking the matter. On September 7 the Acting 

Secretary of War telegraphed to the Commanding General of the Southwestern Division to take, under sections 5286 and 5287 of the Revised Statutes, prompt and effective measures, including such use of troops as might be necessary to prevent the carrying out of any military expedition or enterprise from within the limits of his command against Mexican territory. The Governor of Arizona instructed the officers of the Rangers and sheriffs of border counties to be constantly on the alert to prevent and intercept all revolutionary movements on this side of the international line. The United States 

Attorney in Phoenix, Arizona, issued warrants for the arrest of all 

Mexicans found with arms traveling toward Sonora, Mexico. The immigration officers also took steps to prevent any armed force of persons from proceeding into Mexico. Whatever revolutionary organizations may have existed in Arizona were promptly broken up. 

United States Attorney at Phoenix, Arizona, to the Attorney General, Sept. 8, 1936 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 100/32-34; the 

Acting Secretary of State (Bacon) to Ambassador Thompson, Sept. 11, 1906 (telegram), ibid. 100/28-29; the Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to 

Mr. Thompson, no. 113, Sept. 20, 1906, ibid. 100/71. 

In a note of March 4, 1907 the Mexican Embassy at Washington brought to the attention of the Department of State certain alleged plots which, it was thought, were being fomented along the border between the United States and Mexico on American territory, having for their purpose the launching of attacks in Mexican territory.

The Ambassador requested that the necessary steps be taken to prevent the violation of the neutrality laws of the United States. In submitting the matter to the Attorney General the Secretary of 

State said:

To have its territory used as a base of operations for men plotting not only revolution but assassination against President

Diaz is a serious injury to this country which should be pre-

Violation of neu- trality laws vented if it is practicable to take legal proceedings against the offenders.

The Attorney General reported that while there was ample evidence of the publication in this country by citizens of Mexico temporarily residing in the United States of newspapers, circulars, et cetera, directed against the administration of President Díaz and intended to excite uprisings and foment revolutionary movements in Mexico, the District Attorney had thus far been unable to obtain any evidence connecting any of these parties with acts and conduct constituting a violation of the neutrality laws of the United States, "there being no evidence yet obtained showing acceptance by a citizen of the United States of a military commission to serve against the Republic of Mexico or of the beginning or setting on foot or providing means for any military expedition to be carried on from the United States against Mexico". 

In a memorandum of November 14, 1907 the Mexican Ambassador informed the Department that some of the Mexicans who were endeavoring to cause trouble on the frontier had collected some arms at a place near the city of Brownsville, Texas. With reference thereto the Attorney General wrote to the Secretary of State as follows: 

The difficulty with the case, from our present information, seems to be that it is not clear that these arms have been prepared for any military expedition of the above mentioned character, and if they have been simply stored for the purpose of being sent to Mexico to aid insurgents there, and not in connection with any military expedition starting from this country, I am unable to see that there would be any violation of our neutrality laws, which, as you know, are distinctly limited in their character. Furthermore, even if furnished for such military expedition, I doubt if there is any right of seizure under our laws other than the authority vested in the President by the Revised Statutes, section 5287, to employ any part of the land or naval forces or militia for the purpose of preventing the carrying on of any military expedition from our territory against the territories of a foreign state. It appears that under the Act of March 10, 1838, c. 31 (5 Stat. 212) collectors, marshals and other officers were authorized to seize any arms or munitions of war provided for such military expedition, provision being made for trials in the Federal courts upon such seizure, but this act expired by its own limitation in 1840 (sec. 9), and I have not as yet been able to find any subsequent provision of a like character.

Subsequently convictions were obtained for violation of the provisions of sections 5440 and 5286 of the Revised Statutes, the one penalizing conspiracy, and the other penalizing the setting on foot of military expeditions. On March 25, 1909 Colonel Encarna-

cion Díaz Guerra, chief of the third military zone of Mexico, pleaded guilty in the District Court of Texas to a charge of beginning and setting on foot a military expedition against Mexico, consisting of an attack on the city of Las Vacas, Mexico. The American military forces along the border continued to exert every effort to prevent the territory of the United States from being used as a base for attack upon Mexico, and commanding generals in Texas and Colorado were directed to use the utmost vigilance to prevent any revolutionary movement from recrossing from Mexico into American territory.

In reply to a request made by the Mexican Ambassador in May 1911 that the Department of State obtain the necessary orders to have judicial proceedings brought against one Ricardo Flores Magón and his associates who were allegedly principals in "the many scandalous filibustering attempts organized in territory of the United States Filibusters against Lower California", the Department said:

The Department can not, however, fail to observe your statement (with which it must disagree) that there have been many scandalous filibustering attempts organized on territory of the 

United States against Lower California. As your excellency is well aware, the Government of the United States has been most vigilant in the measures which it has taken to insure the most complete observance not only of its international duties but also the strict enforcement of its own so-called neutrality statutes. 

These measures have involved an elaborate policing of the American side of the border, which has been maintained with marked efficiency, notwithstanding the conspicuous absence of similar measures upon the part of the Government of Mexico on its own

territory, upon whom rests primarily the responsibility of prohibiting the taking of arms and ammunition to Mexico or the landing of them at particular times or places, or the prevention of incursions of marauding or other bands of men. The absence of proper policing on the Mexican side of the border has been the more conspicuous because these matters of protection relate to the revenue and police regulations of the Government of Mexico, and it has never been recognized by international law that such regulations come within the rules regulating the conduct of other nations. 

Secretary Knox to Ambassador de Zamacona, no. 45, June 6, 1911, MS. 

Department of State, file 812.00/1963. See also 1911 For. Rel. 498-499.

In May 1911 the Mexican Ambassador informed the Department of State that a company of Mexicans at San Diego, California, having resolved to go to Ensenada, Lower California, to assist in the maintenance of order against raids of filibusters, had tried to put to sea on the Mexican steamer General Reyes at San Diego, California, and had been arrested by the authorities of that city, some of them having been maltreated in spite of their being unarmed. The Ambassador said that he did not need to call the attention of the Secretary of State to the gravity of the occurrence "for not only did those that effected the arrest board a boat flying the Mexican flag and arrest these gentlemen without just cause, but they detained them as if they belonged to an irregular band acting in contempt of the neutrality laws and not to a company of citizens lawfully engaged in defending their country against piratical attacks". He stated that besides the arrest on board the General Reyes, two others, members of the "junta mexicana", were arrested on the ground of having relations with the others. These acts, he said, stood in contrast with the ease with which the filibusters could cross the boundary line. He expressed the hope that the facts would be thoroughly investigated and that the persons arrested would be immediately released. The Secretary of 

State replied thatobviously the Government of the United States can scarcely undertake, as you seem to desire, to discriminate between the various more or less independent insurrectionary movements which from your note would seem to exist within the Republic of Mexico. Obviously this Department is not in a position to determine which, if any, of these movements are to be regarded as recognized insurrections and which, if any, are to be regarded as filibusters operating for ends and principles which the Government of Mexico can not approve. It is quite clear that these are questions concerning the Government of Mexico only, and that the Government of the United States, obviously able to entertain neither disfavor, sympathy, nor interest for any such movements, must treat and consider all upon identic basis.

This being the legal status of the present situation, it is unnecessary to say that the Government of the United States will continue in the future, as in the past, to observe a strict impartiality, at the same time using its utmost endeavors to the end that there shall be no violation either of its obligations under the principles of international law, or of the proper observance of its own so-called "neutrality statutes." 

Again I should call your excellency's attention to the fact that in international law and under the Federal statutes of this Government a very wide difference exists on the one hand between the passage of men singly and in small groups across our frontier and into another country, or the sailing of individuals or small groups in the ordinary course of events from one of our ports and on the other hand the departure from our territory of organized groups of men avowing the purpose of undertaking belligerent activities in foreign territory.

It would appear from the information furnished by you to the Attorney General that the men of whose arrest you complain were more or less regularly enlisted for the Mexican service within the jurisdiction of the United States-that is, in San Diego, Cal.; and, being so enlisted, constituted an expedition organized within American territory. Whether or not the organization of such an expedition, under the circumstances of this case, constitutes a violation of the so-called "neutrality statutes" of the United States is a question the determination of which is, by the Constitution of the United States, placed in our courts. It is not improbable that such an organization will be found to be not within the statute, and I raise the point merely to indicate to your excellency that prima facie and in absence of a judicial determination there seems to have been reasonable grounds for making the arrest complained of. 

In this connection I must again repeat to your excellency that not only is there no rule of international law requiring, and no local Federal statute that would permit, the Federal officials of this Government to prevent the passage into foreign territory of unarmed and unorganized men either singly or in groups; but, on the contrary, it is an express provision of international law that the responsibility of a neutral power is not engaged even in time of recognized war by the fact of persons crossing the frontier separately to offer their services to one of the belligerents; and as to the mandates of municipal law, the courts of the United States have repeatedly declared that our neutrality statutes do not forbid one or more individuals singly or in unarmed, unorganized groups from leaving the United States for the purpose of joining in any military operations which are being carried on between other countries or between different parties in the same country. 

Ambassador de Zamacona to Secretary Knox, no. 1466, May 27, 1911, and Mr. Knox to Señor de Zamacona, no. 47, June 7, 1911, MS. Department of State, file 812.00/1984. See also 1911 For. Rel. 494, 501-502.

Article 1 of the convention signed by certain American republics at Habana in 1928 in respect to the duties and rights of states in the event of civil strife provides:

The contracting states bind themselves to observe the following rules with regard to civil strife in another one of them: 

1. To use all means at their disposal to prevent the inhabitants of their territory, nationals or aliens, from participating in, gathering elements, crossing the boundary or sailing from their territory for the purpose of starting or promoting civil strife. 

2. To disarm and intern every rebel force crossing their boundaries, the expenses of internment to be borne by the state where public order may have been disturbed. The arms found in the hands of the rebels may be seized and withdrawn by the government of the country granting asylum, to be returned, once the struggle has ended, to the state in civil strife. 

3. To forbid the traffic in arms and war material, except when intended for the government, while the belligerency of the rebels has not been recognized, in which latter case the rules of neutrality shall be applied. 

4. To prevent that within their jurisdiction there be equipped, armed or adapted for warlike purposes any vessel intended to operate in favor of the rebellion. 

46 Stat. 2749, 2750; 4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4725, 4727.

POLLUTION OF WATER AND AIR 

$157 

Article IV of the convention concluded January 11, 1909 between of 1909, U.S.- the United States and Great Britain, concerning the boundary waters Gt.Br. between the United States and Canada, provides in part that "the waters herein defined as boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other."

On August 2, 1912 the Governments of the United States and Canada referred the subject of the extent and manner of pollution of boundary waters between the two countries and the possibility of remedial or preventive works to insure the purity of the waters, to the International Joint Commission (provided for in the convention) for investigation and report. The Commission adopted a report in August 1918 containing findings and recommendations for remedial and protective works. The Commission's experts agreed that, while in certain cases where the ratio of boundary waters to sewage discharged therein was unusually large, there was no danger to the public health but that "effective sanitary administration requires the adoption of the general policy that no untreated sewage from cities

or towns should be discharged into boundary waters." It was found that neither country polluted the waters to the detriment of the other and that, in general, the waters of the lakes were pure but that the Detroit and Niagara Rivers were grossly polluted mostly by the discharge of sewage from nearby cities and towns. At the request of the two Governments the Commission submitted on October 6, 1920 a draft treaty designed to carry out its recommendations. A treaty, however, has not been concluded. 

The Secretary of the Commission (Kluttz) to the Department of State, Apr. 16, 1919, MS. Department of State, file 711.42155/358; Mr. George 

Turner to Solicitor Woolsey, Dec. 12, 1919, ibid. 711.42155/432. For an official list of documents regarding the investigation and report of the Commission, see the Papers Relating to the Work of the International Joint Commission (1929) 162. For the treaty of 1909, see 36 Stat. 2448, 2450; 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2607, 2609.

In the case of New Jersey v. City of New York suit was brought to enjoin the city from dumping garbage into the ocean, it being alleged that garbage was carried by the water and cast upon the beaches and shores of New Jersey, thereby creating a nuisance and causing damage. The city of New York contended that as it dumped the garbage into the ocean and not within the waters of the United States or of New Jersey, the court was without jurisdiction to grant the injunction. The Supreme Court held that "The situs of the acts creating the nuisance, whether within or without the United States, is of no importance", and issued an injunction.

Noxious gases 

Trail Smelter case

In 1907 the Supreme Court of the United States granted an injunction to the State of Georgia restraining the defendant company from discharging noxious gases from its works in Tennessee over the plaintiff's territory. The Court said: This is a suit by a State for an injury to it in its capacity of quasi-sovereign. In that capacity the State has an interest independent of and behind the titles of its citizens, in all the earth and air within its domain. It has the last word as to whether its mountains shall be stripped of their forests and its inhabitants shall breathe pure air. It might have to pay individuals before it could utter that word, but with it remains the final power.

It is a fair and reasonable demand on the part of a sovereign that the air over its territory should not be polluted on a great scale by sulphurous acid gas, that the forests on its mountains, be they better or worse, and whatever domestic destruction they have suffered, should not be further destroyed or threatened by the act of persons beyond its control, that the crops and orchards on its hills should not be endangered from the same source. 

Georgia v. Tennessee Copper Co., 206 U.S. (1907) 230, 237, 238.

The Governments of the United States and Canada, on August 7, 1928, pursuant to the terms of article IX of the convention of January 11, 1909 between the United States and Great Britain, transmitted to the International Joint Commission a reference relating to the damage in the State of Washington caused by fumes from the smelter at Trail, British Columbia, operated by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada, Limited. The Commission's report dated February 28, 1931 (which according to art. IX of the above-mentioned convention did not have the character of an arbitral award) contained a finding in respect to the extent to which property in Washington had been damaged by the fumes from the Trail smelter and concluded that the amount of indemnity which would compensate the American interests in Washington for damages up to and including January 1, 1932 was $350,000. The Commission recommended, inter alia, that the smelting company proceed as expeditiously as might be reasonably possible with works already erected for the purpose of reducing fumes from the smelter and also erect such further works as might be necessary until the fumes drifting into the United States were reduced to a point where no damage would be done in the United States. The United States was unwilling to accept the Commission's report. 

3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 2607; 36 Stat. 2448; the Secretary of the International Joint Commission (Smith) to the Secretary of State

(Stimson), Mar. 4, 1931, MS. Department of State, file 711.4215 Air Pollution/183; Secretary Hull to Minister Robbins, no. 194, Jan. 27, 1934, ibid. 

711.4215 Air Pollution/458.

On April 15, 1935 the United States and Canada signed a convention establishing an arbitral tribunal to decide the following questions: (1) Whether damage caused by the Trail Smelter in the State of Washington has occurred since the first day of January, 1932, and, if so, what indemnity should be paid therefor? (2) In the event of the answer to the first part of the preceding Question being in the affirmative, whether the Trail Smelter should be required to refrain from causing damage in the State of Washington in the future and, if so, to what extent? (3) In the light of the answer to the preceding Question, what measures or regime, if any, should be adopted or maintained by the Trail Smelter? 

(4) What indemnity or compensation, if any, should be paid on account of any decision or decisions rendered by the Tribunal pursuant to the next two preceding Questions? (Article III.)

Article I of this convention provided for the payment to the Government of the United States by the Government of Canada of $350,000 in settlement of all damage which had occurred in the United States prior to January 1, 1932 as a result of the operation of the 

Trail smelter. 

4 Treaties, etc. (Trenwith, 1938) 4009, 4010-4011; 49 Stat. 3245, 3246.

On April 16, 1938 the arbitral tribunal established under the convention of 1935 rendered an interim decision in which it reported its final decision on question 1, awarding to the United States as damages up to October 1, 1937, an indemnity of $78,000 with interest at the rate of 6 percent from the date of the filing of the report and decision until the date of payment. The question of the existence of damage occurring after October 1, 1937, and the indemnity to be paid therefor was left for later determination by the tribunal in its final decision. The tribunal rendered a temporary decision on questions 2 and 3 and provided for a temporary regime thereunder and for a final decision on these questions and on question 4 within three months from October 1, 1940. With respect to question 2 the tribunal decided that until the date of the final decision the Trail smelter should refrain from causing damage in Washington to the extent set forth under the temporary regime until October 1, 1940, and thereafter to such extent as the tribunal should require in the final decision. 

The tribunal said:

The controversy is between two Governments involving damage occurring in the territory of one of them (the United States

of America) and alleged to be due to an agency situated in the territory of the other (the Dominion of Canada), for which damage the latter has assumed by the Convention an international responsibility. In this controversy, the tribunal is not sitting to pass upon claims presented by individuals or on behalf of one or more individuals by their Government. 

In considering question 1 it declared thatthe Tribunal finds it unnecessary to decide whether the facts proven did or did not constitute an infringement or violation of Sovereignty of the United States under International Law independently of the Convention, for the following reason. By the 

Convention, the High Contracting Parties have submitted to this Tribunal the questions of the existence of damage caused by the Trail Smelter in the State of Washington, and of the indemnity to be paid therefor, and the Dominion of Canada has assumed under Article XII, such undertakings as will ensure due compliance with the decision of this Tribunal. The Tribunal finds that the only question to be decided on this point is the interpretation of the Convention itself. The United States in its Statement (page 59) itemizes under the claim of damage for "violation of sovereignty" only money expended "for the investigation undertaken by the United States Government of the problems created in the United States by the operation of the Smelter at Trail." The Tribunal is of opinion that it was not within the intention of the parties, as expressed in the words "damage caused by the Trail Smelter" in Article III of the Convention, to include such moneys expended. 

Since the United States has not specified any other damage based on an alleged violation of its sovereignty, the Tribunal does not feel that it is incumbent upon it to decide, whether, in law and in fact, indemnity for such damage could have been awarded if specifically alleged. · The Tribunal is, therefore, of opinion that neither as a separable item of damage nor as an incident to other damages should any award be made for that which the United States terms "violation of sovereignty."

Decision Reported on April 16, 1938 to the Government of the United States of America and to the Government of the Dominion of Canada by the Trail Smelter Arbitral Tribunal, under the Convention signed April 15, 1935, pp. 4, 41-42, 43, MS. Department of State, file 711.4215 Air Pollution/941.

The $350,000 covering damages occurring prior to Jan. 1, 1932 and the $78,000 covering damages occurring between the latter date and Oct. 1, 1937, paid by Canada to the United States, were distributed by the United States to claimants in the affected area in Stevens County, Washington.

AGENCIES VIOLATIVE OF MUNICIPAL LAW 

$158 In May 1912 suit was instituted by the Department of Justice against Brazilian certain members of the committee on coffee valorization of the State valorization plan of São Paulo, Brazil, controlling the sale in New York of coffee from that state. It was alleged that in furtherance of the valorization plan, as embodied in the laws of Brazil and the State of São Paulo, the object of which was to sustain the price of coffee at a certain level, the committee both withheld certain coffee from the market and required, upon making any sale, a promise that the coffee would not be resold on the Coffee Exchange. It was sought, inter alia, to have the valorization plan, so far as it affected the interstate and foreign commerce of the United States, declared violative of the anti-trust act approved July 2, 1890 (26 Stat. 209); to have the conspiracies, contracts, and agreements of the committee declared unlawful; and to have the withholding of coffee from the market and its sale upon condition that there should be no re-sale enjoined. The Brazilian Ambassador thereupon wrote to the Secretary of State as follows:

It is not for me here to enter upon an examination of the merits of the case since, be those what they may, the jurisdiction of an American tribunal over the acts of a foreign sovereign State can not be admitted. The doctrine alleged by a representative of the 

Department of Justice before the court that by placing merchandise on the market of the world a State loses its sovereignty, can not be defended before the Department of State, where it is well known that sovereignty is never lost or relinquished automatically but always through a formal and express instrument, whether voluntarily or under compulsion. With a refusal to consider the international aspect of the question, the matter assumes more importance, as the initial proceedings of the suit were instituted without due warning to the foreign and friendly Government interested therein. The court has already denied that part of the Attorney-General's petition which relates to the previous delivery of the coffee owned by the State of São Paulo to a depositary (for sale) in the market, but the suit continues. 

This state of things, which has lasted for weeks and which, I fear, may not continue without detriment to the moral and material interests of both countries, is that which I wish to submit to your excellency's consideration in order that you will, if you deem it proper, bring it to the knowledge of the President of the Republic with a view to its discontinuance and proper reparation. 

On October 17, 1912 the American Ambassador in Brazil, at the request of the Brazilian Minister of Foreign Affairs, informed the Department of State that the Governor of the State of São Paulo had assured the Minister that at its annual meeting in January following, the 

---

Combinations in restraint of trade valorization committee would vote to dispose of the entire stock of valorized coffee in New York. The Brazilian Minister, he said, was anxious to learn whether in view of this assurance it would be possible to defer the proposed suit against the international coffee syndicate until the cause of action should have disappeared, and had also expressed the hope that the proposed liquidation might check any contemplated Federal legislation against the valorized coffee. The Brazilian Minister had stated emphatically, the Ambassador said, that his Government did not wish the action of a sovereign state of the Republic of Brazil, which had been endorsed by a Federal law, to be reviewed by a foreign legislative body or court, and was anxious that further newspaper controversy regarding valorized coffee should, if possible, be avoided.

The Department informed the Ambassador that the Attorney General had agreed to postpone action provided the proposition related to the entire stock of valorized coffee then in New York, and that if it was proposed to sell it in the open market free from any restrictions on or before April 1, 1913, he was willing to abandon further proceedings. The sale of the valorized coffee was subsequently carried out in accordance with an understanding between the Governments of the United States and Brazil, and the suit was accordingly withdrawn.

In 1906 the attention of the Mexican authorities was brought to the fact that many aliens afflicted with trachoma were entering Mexico and thence making an illegal entry into the United States. The mere enforcement of quarantine regulations promised by the Superior Board of Health of Mexico offered no means of relief as trachoma was not a quarantinable disease. On account of the frequency with which trachoma was found to afflict Asiatic immigrants, the Superior Board of Health of Mexico was authorized in August 1907 to direct that such immigrants when suffering from trachoma should not be allowed to land either at the ports on the Gulf of Mexico or those on the Pacific.

Pure Food 

A protest having been received from the British Government, the Attorney General and the Secretary of the Treasury were instructed by the President of the United States on April 25, 1908 as follows: 

At the present time the question whether certain brands of whiskey are properly labeled within the purview of the food and drugs act of 1906 is pending in the courts of this country. With and Drugs respect to domestic merchandise of this character, the seizure Act guarantees a judicial proceeding and gives the defendant his day in court, whereas with respect to imported merchandise, under the provisions of section 11 of said act, the merchandise must either be exported or destroyed if the same be held adulterated or misbranded by an administrative officer, and thus the foreigner is denied his day in court.

If it shall be decided that the treaty relations existing between Great Britain and this country are of such a character as to guarantee to British subjects the right to enjoy the privileges of the courts of this country on the same terms as citizens of this country, then it would appear that the administrative procedure under section 11 results in a denial to the British subject of rights guaranteed to him under such treaty. 93

Without determining the merits of that question, it is suggested that pending the judicial determination of the question all imported whiskey held to be merely misbranded shall be allowed to pass the customs without in any wise restricting the right of the Secretary of Agriculture to proceed against such whiskey after it shall have entered into the commerce of this country in identically the same manner that domestic whiskey is proceeded against. 

Memorandum from the British Embassy, Apr. 9, 1908, MS. Department of State, file 12194/4; memorandum of the Department of State, ibid. 12194/7. Foreign se- curities, etc.

COUNTERFEITING 

$159 

Sections 156-165 of the United States Criminal Code penalize the counterfeiting of foreign securities and the uttering of counterfeit foreign securities, the counterfeiting of notes of foreign banks, and the uttering of counterfeit notes of foreign banks, the possession of counterfeit foreign securities or counterfeit plates of foreign securities and the counterfeiting or falsifying, mutilating, or lightening of foreign gold or silver coin current in the United States or in actual use as money within the United States. 

18 U.S.C. 88270-279.

Section 160 of the United States Criminal Code making it a crime to have possession of certain enumerated false documents, naming inter alia bills "issued by a bank or corporation of any foreign country", has been held to include the possession of counterfeit obligations of a foreign government. Forlini v. United States, 12 F. (2d) 631 (C.C.A. 2d, 1926); 

18 U.S.C. $274.

In the case of Biddle, Warden v. Luvisch, the circuit court of appeals held that, by entering a plea of guilty, Luvisch had admitted the allegation in the indictment that the inland excise stamps were "obligations and securities" of the Canadian Government within the meaning of section 161 of the United States Penal Code, penalizing the possession or making of a plate for the purpose of counterfeiting the obligations and securities of any foreign government. 287 Fed. 699 (C.C.A. 8th, 1923). In accord, see Biddle, Warden v. Lieberman, 8 F. (2d) 870 (C.C.A. 8th, 1925).

The act of Congress approved May 26, 1926 amended section 220 of the Criminal Code which penalizes the counterfeiting of foreign postage stamps, by making likewise criminal the counterfeiting of revenue stamps of foreign governments. 44 Stat. 653; 18 U.S.C. §349. 

In 1913 the Brazilian Ambassador pointed out to the Secretary of State that counterfeiters of Brazilian money, securities, and paper credit who were out of Brazil were immune from judicial process and inquired whether there was any general or special law in the United States for the prosecution and trial of counterfeiters of foreign money and credit papers, including seals and adhesive stamps,

and whether, even should such laws exist, the United States Government would be disposed to enter into a special agreement regulating the prosecution and trial of such counterfeiters when not subject to extradition. The Department replied that provision is made in the laws of the United States for the prosecution and punishment of any person who "within the United States or any place subject to the jurisdiction thereof, with intent to defraud”, counterfeits bonds, certificates, obligations, or other securities of any foreign government, or any Treasury note, bill, or promise to pay issued by such foreign government intended to circulate as money. The Ambassador's attention was invited to sections 156 to 161 of the Revised 

Penal Code of the United States approved March 4, 1909. No treaty agreement, it was stated, would be required to secure the prosecution and trial of Brazilian or other foreigners violating the provisions of those laws. The Department concluded: 

As the territorial theory of crime obtains in the United States, it would not be practicable for this Government to enter into a treaty arrangement with the Brazilian Government providing for the prosecution of persons for committing in Brazil the crimes of counterfeiting Brazilian money, securities, etc. 

Counselor Moore to Ambassador da Gama, no. 36, Nov. 8, 1913, MS. 

Department of State, file 211.32/7. See also 1913 For. Rel. 38.

At that time the United States had not recognized the 

Constitutionalist Government.

On December 18, 1908 under instructions from the Department of State, the Embassy at Berlin brought to the attention of the German Foreign Office certain advertisements being circulated in Germany on which was imprinted a facsimile reproduction of American onedollar silver certificates.
