In 1920 the Treasury Department was in possession of a facsimile onedollar bill in imitation of a United States Federal Reserve Bank note then being circulated in Paris as an advertisement for a French theater. The 

Treasury Department wrote to the Department of State, pointing out that sections 150 and 161 of the United States Penal Code forbade, with penalties, the making or executing of any such print or impressions with intent to sell or otherwise use the same, and that it was, therefore, unlawful to bring these facsimiles into the United States or in any way to circulate them. The matter was brought to the attention of the French Foreign

 MARRIAGE IN THE UNITED STATES 

$160 The fact that petitioner had been married in England in 1911 and had not been divorced was held-in the absence of a showing that her first husband was living when she married the second time-not to show that the second marriage was bigamous, since there was a presumption in favor of the validity of the formal ceremony of her marriage to an American citizen, in 1921, in the United States. 

Prentis, District Director of Immigration v. McCormick, 23 F. (2d.) 

802 (C.C.A. 6th, 1928). 

In 1937 the Department of State said:

It is the view of the Department that in general the validity of a marriage is determined by the laws of the place where it is contracted and that if valid in such place it should be considered valid everywhere. An exception to the general rule, however, is ordinarily made where the marriage is repugnant to the public policy of the domicile of the parties, in respect to polygamy, incest, or miscegenation, or is otherwise contrary to its positive laws. While it appears from your despatch that the marriage of an Aryan to a non-Aryan is prohibited under the Nuremberg law of September 15, 1935, the Department does not consider that such law would have application to an Aryan woman who changed her domicile from Germany to the United

States and thereafter married a non-Aryan in this country. The 

Department is of the opinion that in any such case Germany would not have jurisdiction over the marital status and consequently could not invoke its laws with a view to the annulment of such a marriage.

She should not, in the opinion of the Department, be regarded as having evaded the laws of Germany by marrying a non-Aryan.

The Assistant Secretary of State (Messersmith) to Consul General 

Hathaway, Aug. 25, 1937, MS. Department of State, file 362.1121 Strauss, Maria/2.

According to Belgian law a Belgian subject marrying in the

United States is subject to the restrictions of the laws of his own country. In order to determine the validity of such marriage in Belgium it is therefore necessary to know the Belgian law on the subject.

In 1933 an alien man resident in the State of Michigan was married by telephone to an alien woman resident in Sweden. The

American Consul General in Stockholm informed the Department of State that the woman intended to apply at his office for a secondpreference immigration visa as the wife of an alien lawfully admitted to the United States for permanent residence. The Department instructed the Consul General that the woman was not considered a wife for immigration purposes and was therefore not entitled to preference. The laws of Michigan where the purported marriage took place, it was said, required the parties to declare in the "presence" of a magistrate or minister and attending witnesses that they took each other as husband and wife, and, since she was not present in Michigan, the purported marriage was of doubtful validity in that State, the Department declared, and no legal obligation apparently rested on the alleged husband to support her. 

It was stated however that, if the woman in question applied for a non-preference visa and established that she was coming to the United States to contract a valid marriage and would be dependent on him for support, consideration might properly be given to evidence regarding his ability and willingness to support her.

MARRIAGE ABROAD 

§161 In 1907 the British Ambassador communicated to the Department of State the text of the marriage-with-foreigners act of 1906 enabling the British Government to conclude agreements with foreign countries by which persons subject to the marriage laws of those countries who proposed to marry British subjects in the United Kingdom should produce a certificate, issued by the proper officers of their country, stating that after proper notice had been given no impediment according to the laws of that country existed to the marriage. He inquired whether the United States Government was willing to conclude an agreement with the British Government similar to one already concluded between the British and French Governments in this regard. The Department replied that so far as it was aware there was no Federal, State, or Territorial law providing for the issuance by any officer of any certificate stating that after proper notice had been given no impediment existed according to the laws of the United States to a specified marriage. 

The Department said, therefore, that it would seem to be practically impossible for the Government of the United States to enter into an agreement of the kind contemplated by the British Ambassador's note. 

Ambassador Bryce to the Acting Secretary of State, no. 222, Oct. 10, 1907, and Secretary Root to Mr. Bryce, no. 180, Oct. 29, 1907, MS. Department of 

State, file 9143/2; 1907 For. Rel., pt. I, pp. 538-541.

In 1907 the Department of State instructed the Ambassador in Germany informally to bring to the attention of the German Government the difficulties arising in the case of American citizens desiring to marry in Germany, in view of the requirement of German law that aliens must exhibit a certificate stating that no impediment existed to their marriage under the laws of their country. The German Minister of Foreign Affairs suggested as a remedy that officials be appointed in the United States duly authorized to issue such certificates. The Acting Secretary of State (Bacon) to Ambassador Tower, no. 731, Oct. 23, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 6878/5; 

Mr. Tower to Secretary Root, no. 1288, Jan. 24, 1908, ibid. 6878/6–7. See also 1907 For. Rel., pt. I, p. 525; 1908 For. Rel. 360.

Section XIII-5 of the Foreign Service Regulations of the United States (June 1939) provides: 

Although a consular officer may have knowledge respecting the laws of marriage, he shall not issue any official certificate as to such laws. (E.O. April 11, 1939.) 

Note 1... A consular officer shall not certify officially relative to the status or capacity to marry of persons domiciled in the United States who propose to be married abroad; or to the laws of the United States, or of the States or Territories, touching capacity for marriage or the solemnization thereof. 

Note 2. A consular officer is not legally competent to give an authoritative opinion to parties proposing to be married abroad upon matters of local law and fact. 

The American Consul in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, brought to the attention of the Department of State on December 2, 1932 the provision of article 103 of the Honduran Civil Code that a foreigner desiring to be married in Honduras must prove by a certificate from his consular or diplomatic agent or by a legal certificate from any qualified authority in his country that, according to the pertinent provisions of law, there is no obstacle to the projected marriage. 

The Consul pointed out that under section 422 of the Consular Regulations, consular officers were prohibited from issuing such certificates. 

The Department instructed the Consul that, when a somewhat similar matter arose in Turkey in 1927, it had invited attention to the act approved April 5, 1906 (34 Stat. 101) which provides for the Alternative administration or taking by consular officers of the United States of any oath, affirmation, affidavit, or deposition and suggested that perhaps the Honduran authorities would accept as complying with the pertinent provisions of the Civil Code, an affidavit of an interested American citizen sworn to before the Consul on the above-quoted statutory authority setting forth that there is no obstacle in the United States laws to the projected marriage of such citizen and containing such information concerning the status of the affiant as the place and date of birth, citizenship, and previous marriages and divorces, if any. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Smith, Feb. 23, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 133/2698.

The American Consul in Tsingtau, China, in 1908, inquired of the Department of State whether he was authorized to issue a certificate stating that "according to the terms of the American laws, the consent of parents, or other persons, is not necessary to a marriage of persons 

21 years of age" and whether he was authorized to issue a certificate stating that, so far as was known, there were no impediments to the proposed marriage (of an American citizen or citizens) in the place of suggestion

Certification of facts of own knowledge 

Where marif performed in U.S. previous residence in his district. It appeared that under the law of the German colony of Kiaochow, China, American citizens wishing to be married in that colony were obliged to produce evidence showing that if they were of age, the consent of their parents or other persons to their marriage was unnecessary and also to show, if for six months previous to the proposed marriage they had lived outside of the German colony, that there was no impediment to their marriage so far as was known in the place of their residence. The Department of State transmitted to the Consul an opinion of its Solicitor holding that an American Consul is not entitled to issue such a certificate as was contemplated by the Consul's first question above mentioned. In regard to the second question the Solicitor said: 

As to the second inquiry, some interesting questions arise. It is believed that the certificate here called for, since it is in addition to the statement already covered in regard to the "consent of the persons whose consent is necessary according to the laws of their country", merely refers to possible impediments arising out of matters of law and fact within the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the Consul making certification. That is, the matters of law which are to be covered by this certification are simply the questions of American extraterritorial law which the consul administers, not the law of the States of the United States in which the parties in question may, perhaps, have their domicil. (But see 

Judge Willey's recent decision in the matter of Young John

Allen, holding that it is possible for an American to acquire legal domicil in China.)

Under these circumstances it is believed that such a certificate as is here suggested is not within the prohibition which the Department has so often made against consuls certifying to the laws of the various States and Territories or even of the United States. The certificate here called for covers only matters of fact, so far as known to the consul, and the law of his district which he administers, and it would seem that a consul exercising extraterritorial jurisdiction should be permitted and instructed to give this certificate in a proper case. 

Consul Gracey to the Assistant Secretary of State, no. 43, Feb. 5, 1908, and the Chief Clerk (Carr) to Mr. Gracey, July 24, 1908, MS. Department of 

State, file 6878/8-10. See also 1908 For. Rel. 362–365.

It was held in the case of State v. Fenn that the law of the State riage invalid of Washington forbidding the marriage of any divorced person within six months from the date of the entry of the judgment or decree granting the divorce, was directed solely against marriages within the State or by persons domiciled within the State but contracted in other States for the purpose of evading Washington laws, and that if the parties to a marriage in British Columbia were domiciled in Washington at the time that the marriage was contracted and went to that Province in order to avoid Washington laws (having mar-

ried within 10 days after the divorce was procured) such marriage was null and void, but that if the parties to the marriage in British Columbia were domiciled there at the time the marriage was contracted such marriage did not fall within the provision of the Washington statute and was valid. 

47 Wash. (1907) 561, 92 Pac. 417.

In 1925 the Supreme Court of Oregon granted a decree of annulment of a marriage performed in British Columbia within two months and a half of a divorce procured by one of the parties in the State of Washington, on the ground that the marriage was invalid by the law of British Columbia and that common-law marriages were not valid in Oregon. Huard v. 

McTeigh, 113 Ore. (1925) 279, 232 Pac. 658.

An action for the annulment of marriage was brought in New York by Susanna Simmons, then 17 years old, who had been married in the British West Indies when she was 14 years old. No evidence was introduced to show that the marriage was invalid under the law of British West Indies. The Appellate Division of the Supreme 

Court of New York (1st Dept.) held that, though under the New 

York statutes a marriage where either party is under 18 years of age is voidable, the New York courts have no power to annul and declare invalid ab initio a marriage contracted in another country between two actual bona-fide residents and citizens and subjects thereof when the marriage was valid by the laws of that country. 

Simmons v. Simmons, 208 App. Div. (1924) 195, 203 N.Y. Supp. 215.

To the same effect, see Donohue v. Donohue, where a marriage of minors in Canada and valid in Canada, was held valid in New York on the ground that it was a valid Canadian contract. 63 Misc. (1909) 111, 116 

N.Y. Supp. 241.

A Pennsylvania court has held that a California court has no power or capacity to annul a Mexican marriage ab initio by virtue of California statutes on the ground of fraud, as fraud is not a ground for annulment under Mexican law, and that, since the marriage was valid under Mexican law and had not been annulled in accordance therewith, it was still an existing fact in Pennsylvania. Dodds v. Pittsburgh, Mars & Butler 

Railways Company, 107 Pa. Super. Ct. (1932) 20, 162 Atl. 486.

On November 7, 1933, the Secretary of State instructed the Consul 

General at Montreal thata marriage which had been entered into for the purpose of facilitating the entry of an alien into the United States does not in and of itself invalidate the marriage, since the motive for entering into a marriage is not material if the marriage is bona fide. In view of the legal presumption of the validity of marriages, a marriage should be accepted as being bona fide unless it is established by the admission of one or both parties thereto or by other evidence that it is not bona fide. 

MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Katonah, Paul.

Inasmuch as it is uniformly held that in spite of the prohibition against remarriage in a divorce decree, if a lawful and legal marriage is performed elsewhere, it will be recognized also in the state in which the divorce was granted, and the consular report indicates that the second marriage in Poland is valid in so far as Polish law is concerned, no action is contemplated at this time to disturb the authorization of nonquota status under Section 4(a) of the Immigration Act of 1924 accorded Hodes Nadel- Topale on the basis of the visa petition filed by Joe Topale, April 11, 1935.

POLYGAMOUS MARRIAGES 

§162 The Department of State instructed the Consul at Bangkok, Siam, that as a general rule the validity of a marriage was determined by the law of the place where the ceremony was performed but that an exception was made in the case of the marriage of one having a consort living and undivorced, though the subsequent marriage was contracted in a state where dual marriages were valid. Such a marriage, it was stated, being contra bonos mores, would probably not be upheld in the United States. Consequently, it was said, an Italian woman, who, the Consul had reported, had married an American citizen in Siam knowing that he already had a Siamese wife and children, could not upon the assumption of the validity and subsistence of the first marriage be regarded as having acquired Amer-

ican citizenship by going through the ceremony of marriage with the American citizen in question.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Dunlap, Dec. 6, 

1922, MS. Department of State, file 133/2385.

In 1926 the American Consul in Bombay, India, informed the 

Department of State that Raja Narendra Shah, the ruling Prince of the Tehri Garhwal State, desired a visa as a temporary visitor and that he was a polygamist accompanied by two wives. The 

Consul inquired whether he was admissible under section 3 of the act approved February 5, 1917 (39 Stat. 874, 875). The Department replied that while Raja Narendra Shah would not be subject to the exclusion provisions of the act cited by the Consul if he came as an accredited diplomatic representative of his country, it was believed that as a visitor with visas under section 3 (1) of the act of 1924 (43 Stat. 153, 154) he would, under the circumstances, be subject to exclusion. 

Consul Keblinger to Secretary Kellogg, Nov. 17, 1926 (telegram), and 

Mr. Kellogg to Mr. Keblinger, Nov. 19, 1926 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Shah, Raja Narendra.

In the case of Earle v. Earle the Appellate Division of the Supreme 

Court of New York (1st Dept.) held that the law of the matrimonial domicil governs in an action for the annulment of a marriage but that in the absence of a statute of the state of domicil of the parties expressly regulating marriages abroad the lex loci contractus governs (in this case, Italy) as to the validity of the marriage unless it were odious by common consent of nations; and that the marriage in question being polygamous if celebrated in New York (remarriage before all formalities of a divorce had been complied with) would have been void and that an action to annul it on the ground that it was void was expressly authorized by New York statutes. 

141 App. Div. (1910) 611, 126 N.Y. Supp. 317. 

See also Royal v. Cudahy Packing Co., 195 Iowa (1922) 759, 190 N.W. 427.

INCESTUOUS AND RITUAL MARRIAGES 

$163 The following circular instructions were sent by the Department of State to American consular officers regarding the validity of marriages in connection with immigration cases: 

While it is a generally recognized rule of law that the validity of a marriage, at least so far as formalities are concerned, is to be determined by the law of the place where it is contracted, the courts in the United States in determining questions of this

nature, are inclined to rely on the presumption in favor of the validity of a marriage and to assume that the formalities of that law had been complied with, apparently for the reason that to require strict proof of compliance in this respect would cause unnecessary hardships and difficulties in many cases where the marital union has evidently been entered into in entire good faith by the parties concerned. 

In determining whether a woman is entitled to be regarded as the wife of an American citizen, or whether a man may have the status of a husband of an American wife, it would be proper to apply the tests ordinarily applied by the courts in the United States. The Department, therefore, considers that in any case where persons have entered into marital relations in a foreign country apparently in good faith, have lived together thereafter, have consistently held themselves out, and have generally been regarded in the community in which they have resided, as husband and wife, they should be recognized as such, and it will not be necessary in such cases to inquire of the local authorities whether all the formalities of local municipal law have been complied with.

Of course, where the facts and circumstances in any particular case cast doubt upon the good faith of the individuals in holding themselves out as married, or where it appears that there may have been some impediment to the assumption of marital relations, such as blood relationship within a prohibited degree of consanguinity, or a previous marriage of one of the parties which has not been terminated, all reasonable inquiries should be made to ascertain the facts in such cases. Any peculiar circumstances surrounding marriages within your jurisdiction should be brought to the Department's attention and the local authorities may be appealed to for information in such cases. Cases involving marriages between uncles and nieces should be reported fully to the Department before final action is taken. The consul's report should indicate the husband's domicile at the time of the application, the place where he expects to reside in the United States, and, if the husband is domiciled in the United States, whether he left the United States with the intention of marrying his niece, and also whether the marriage is valid under the laws of the place where contracted. If the husband is abroad and calls at the consulate, he should be requested to make an affidavit covering the points referred to. The affidavit should be forwarded with the consul's report. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to American consular officers, July 28, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Regulations/1631.

The American Consul General in Berlin, Germany, inquired of the Department on January 5, 1933 whether a non-quota visa could be given to an alien woman who had married an American citizen, she being his sister's daughter. The Department replied on January 

6, 1933 that, since the courts in the United States generally hold a

marriage between an uncle and niece to be incestuous and void, a visa should not be issued in such cases. 

Secretary Stimson to Consul General Messersmith, Jan. 6, 1933 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Quota 62/399. "Persons who are parties to a marriage between first cousins, if such marriage is valid where performed, are not generally regarded as being subject to criminal prosecution for incestuous cohabitation in the various States of the Union where such marriages could not be legally performed. 

An alien, party to such a marriage, therefore, would not be regarded as inadmissible into the United States under the public charge clause of the immigration laws because of such marriage." 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Messersmith, Apr. 24, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Dressler, Anna K. S.

The case of Incuria v. Incuria was a proceeding by Laura Incuria against her alleged husband for support and maintenance. The parties had been married in Italy in 1927. The petitioner at that time was on a visit to Italy and the respondent was a resident and subject thereof. Petitioner was the aunt of the respondent. The 

Domestic Relations Court of the City of New York, Family Court, Borough of Manhattan, held that the marriage was void as incestuous not only under the law of New York but also under Italian law and dismissed the petition. 

155 Misc. (1935) 755, 280 N.Y. Supp. 716.

A citizen of the United States and a resident of the State of Virginia married his alien niece in Poland in 1931 and subsequently petitioned the Secretary of Labor for approval of an immigration visa for his wife under section 4 (a) of the Immigration Act approved 

May 26, 1924 (43 Stat. 153, 155). The Department of Labor ap proved the petition, and a non-quota status was accorded the wife. 

Attorney General Mitchell advised the Secretary of State, on March 2, 1933, that a consular officer might lawfully issue an immigration visa to the wife since in the opinion of the Attorney General of Virginia the marriage between uncle and niece was lawful in Poland and since the uncle and niece might maintain the relation of husband and wife at the place of his residence in Virginia provided the uncle left 

Virginia for Poland without any intention of marrying his niece. 

Attorney General Mitchell said: 

Of course, if the State of the residence of the husband prohibits cohabitation between uncle and niece who had contracted marriage abroad, the wife might well be excluded on the ground that she is likely to become a public charge because faced with prosecution and punishment at the place where she proposes to reside. 

37 Op. Att. Gen. (1932-34) 102, 111.

Ritual marriages 

One Marie Brummer, born in Germany, was married to an American citizen in that country by a ceremony performed in a Catholic Church. A civil ceremony was not performed. In 1921 Mrs. Brummer applied to the American Consul at Cologne for an emergency passport. The American Consul General in Berlin referred the matter to the Department of State. The Department informed him that- it appears that the marriage, if contracted in the United States, would constitute a valid marriage under the laws in force in this country. There is no evidence of fraud or bad faith on the part of either of the parties and the Department sees no reason for questioning the validity of the marriage. 

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul General Coffin, 

May 16, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 130B8384.

The American Consulate General in Warsaw, Poland, in 1925 forwarded to the Department of State the passport application of one Mrs. Liba Zam who was born in Poland and who in 1902 was married to Harry Zam by a religious ceremony. Mr. Zam was naturalized as an American citizen on May 23, 1922. According to the consular officer taking the application, the marriage in Poland was not valid until it had been duly recorded by the civil authorities. Mrs. Zam's marriage was not so recorded until January 10, 1925. The Department instructed the Consul General as follows: 

With reference to the validity of marriages performed in a foreign country, it may be stated that the statutes requiring marriages to be solemnized in a particular manner, although they may impose penalties for non-observance, are generally construed as directory only in so far as this, that a marriage valid at common law but not celebrated in accordance with the requirements of the statute, will be held valid and binding unless expressly declared void by statute. (Matthewson vs. Phoenix Iron Foundry, 20 Fed. 

281; Meister vs. Moore, 96 U. S. 76). In the latter case, the Supreme Court held that a common law marriage in Michigan was valid notwithstanding the statutory provisions of that State. In the course of the opinion the court stated: "As before remarked, the statutes are held merely directory; because marriage is a thing of common right, because it is the policy of the State to encourage it, and because, as has sometimes been said, any other construction would compel holding illegitimate the offspring of many parents conscious of no violation of law."

Consequently, if it is shown that an American citizen and an alien woman agreed to become man and wife and a religious ceremony was publicly performed ostensibly in celebration of such tract, and that the parties regarded themselves as then married con-

and thereafter assumed the duties and obligations of the marital status, there would appear to be, in the absence of fraud or bad faith, no reason for questioning the validity of the marriage. 

If, therefore, after a further investigation of the present case, you are of the opinion that Mrs. Liba Zam was married under conditions similar to those stated above, you are directed to obtain for her an emergency passport to be valid for her journey to the United States.

The Assistant Secretary of State (MacMurray) to Consul General 

Jaeckel, May 20, 1925, MS. Department of State, file 130 Zam, Liba.

In response to an inquiry by the

She, of course, did not acquire American citizenship by virtue of the civil ceremony performed on August 3, 1929.

In determining whether the status of husband and wife exists between a man and a woman, the Department employs the tests ordinarily applied by the courts in the United States. The Department, therefore, usually considers that in any case in which it appears that persons have entered into marital relations in a foreign country in good faith, have lived together thereafter, having consistently held themselves out and have been regarded generally in the community in which they have resided as husband and wife, they should be recognized as such. 

The Department of State to the American Consul General in Warsaw, Poland, Dec. 18, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 130 Blumenfeld, Sabina.

The father of a decedent petitioned for appointment as administrator of the estate of his son, and Ida Lando objected, claiming to be the widow of the deceased. She and the deceased, residents of the State of Minnesota, had been married in Hamburg, Germany, in 1907 by a person whom she believed to be a minister of the gospel. 

The trial court found that the marriage was not performed by any person authorized by German law to perform marriage ceremonies and concluded that Ida Lando never was the wife of the deceased. 

The Supreme Court of Minnesota reversed the judgment, stating that the evidence showed a marriage valid under the laws of Minnesota and that it was not justifiable to impute an uncertain construction upon the German law which would render the marriage invalid. 

In re Lando's Estate, 112 Minn. (1910) 257, 127 N.W. 1125.

Parties were married in Galicia, Austria, in 1906 by a ceremony performed by a Jewish rabbi. The bans were not published nor the registration of the marriage made as required by Austrian law. 

Within one year after the marriage ceremony the husband emigrated to the United States and became naturalized as an American citizen. 

His wife, the plaintiff, and their daughter arrived in New York in 1913, and he, at the time of her arrival and thereafter, repudiated her. In a suit for maintenance the Court of Chancery of New Jersey directed a decree in favor of the wife stating that the husband had not met the burden of proving that under the law of Galicia the

marriage was void or even voidable and held that the marriage was valid. 

Sturm v. Sturm, 111 N.J. Eq. (1932) 579, 163 Atl. 5.

The court stated that even if the marriage were void in Galicia it became valid as a continuing contract upon the transfer of the matrimonial domicil to New Jersey, the fact of continuing consent having been proved. 

Frederick Manzella entered into a religious marriage ceremony with Teresa Buttino in Italy in 1878, performed by an authorized priest of the Roman Catholic Church and under the rules of the Church. In 1881 he emigrated to the United States, leaving his wife and child in Italy. He never returned to Italy. His child joined him in the United States in 1902. The Supreme Judicial Court of 

Massachusetts, in a case involving a petition for instructions as to the disposition of the residue of his estate, held that the validity of the marriage must be determined by the law of Italy where it was solemnized and that since the parties thereto never lived together in Massachusetts the law of that jurisdiction could not be invoked to establish its validity. The court stated that the evidence showed that a marriage solemnized as was the one in question, was not recognized in Italy in 1878 as legal and that it was not justified in reversing the findings of the trial judge that the marriage was not valid. 

Gorrasi v. Manzella et al., 287 Mass. (1934) 165, 191 N.E. 676.

PROXY MARRIAGES 

§164 

Section 28(n) of the Immigration Act approved May 26, 1924 Immigration provides that as used in the act "The terms 'wife' and 'husband' do Act, 1924 not include a wife or husband by reason of a proxy or picture marriage." 

43 Stat. 153, 169.

In an instruction to the Consul in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, the Department of State said that— "it would appear that in including Section 28(n) in the Act of 1924 the intent of Congress was not to declare proxy or picture marriages invalid but to make it clear that an alien who may be a husband or a wife by reason of such a marriage shall not be entitled to any preference or other privileged status provided by the Act in the case of the husbands or the wives of certain persons." The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to 

Consul Clark, Apr. 12, 1932, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 

Englander, Erna E. "While the provision in Section 28(n) of the Immigration Act of 1924, as amended, precludes the consideration of Mrs. da Silva's case as that of a wife, for the purposes of that Act, this provision apparently relates to

her classification and not to her admissibility under the immigration laws. 

For the purpose of the Immigration Act of 1917, Section 3 of which contains the clause providing for the exclusion of 'persons likely to become a public charge,' it would seem that in view of the decisions of the courts in the United States, Mrs. da Silva may be regarded as a wife, provided the proxy marriage to which she is a party was valid under the laws of the place where it was contracted." Assistant Secretary of State Moore to Vice Consul Lightner (Pará, Brazil), Aug. 31, 1934, ibid. 811.111 Silva, Luiza M. da.

In response to an inquiry from the American Consul in Oporto, Portugal, as to the effect under the American immigration laws of a proxy marriage between a resident of Portugal and an alien residing in the State of Pennsylvania, the Department said: 

Answering your inquiries categorically you are informed that (1) an alien woman who was married abroad by proxy, such marriage being valid in the foreign country in which the proxy marriage occurred, may be considered a wife within the meaning of the clause in Section 3 of the Immigration Act of 1917, providing certain exemptions from the literacy test, and it will not be necessary to inquire into the validity of the marriage in the place of the proxy husband's domicile in the United States. (2) Although proxy marriages are not valid for the purposes of the provisions of the Immigration Act of 1924, the Department considers that, in a case where the parties to such a marriage have subsequently cohabited and held themselves out as husband and wife, the proxy character of the marriage would be thereby removed, and the alien wife in such a case would be entitled to preference status under Section 6 (a) (2) of the Immigration Act of 1924, provided it is established that the husband was lawfully admitted into the United States for permanent residence. (3) As stated above, if the proxy marriage was valid in the foreign country where it was performed, it would not be necessary to inquire into the validity of the marriage at the place of the domicile of the party in the United States, it being a generally accepted rule of law that a marriage which is valid where performed will be considered as valid everywhere, unless the marriage is repugnant to the public policy of the place where the parties undertake to reside. As proxy marriages are not generally regarded under the laws of the various States in this country as falling within this exception, it is considered that, except where Section 28 (n) of the Immigration Act of 1924 is applicable, they should uniformly be held valid for the purposes of the immigration laws. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Davis, Dec. 4, 1935, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Barros, Maria da Silva. 

Manuel Gomez, domiciled in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, contracted a marriage with Sabina Suzanna, a Portuguese woman, by proxy. 

The law of Portugal allowed such proxy marriages, and the required

forms were properly carried out. The immigration authorities of the United States refused to allow her to land as Gomez's wife, taking the position that the proxy marriage was invalid under the laws of the United States. The United States District Court held that the question must be decided in accordance with the law of Pennsylvania as Gomez was domiciled there, that that law recognized the validity of a "common law" marriage, and that it appeared that there was nothing therein requiring the personal presence of the parties at a marriage ceremony. 

Ex parte Suzanna, 295 Fed. 713 (D. Mass., 1924). On the same point, see also: Kane v. Johnson, Commissioner of Immigration, 13 F. (2d) 432 (D. Mass., 1926); and Silva v. Tillinghast, Commissioner, etc., 36 F. (2d) 

801 (D. Mass., 1929).

While in Spain, on October 9, 1922, Elodia Gisbert Lledo was married by proxy to an alien resident in the United States. The 

United States District Court declared that the Spanish law seemed to recognize a marriage by proxy and that the contract was therefore valid in Spain and should be recognized as valid in the United States. 

United States ex rel. Aznar v. Commissioner of Immigration at port of 

New York, 298 Fed. 103 (S.D.N.Y., 1924).

In a case where the husband, a Turkish subject, naturalized in the United States and domiciled in the State of Louisiana, was married by proxy to a Turkish national in Constantinople (Istanbul), on Mar. 17, 1922, the court held that the law of Louisiana prohibiting marriages by proxy was only intended to prohibit marriages contracted within the state and that the marriage was valid. United States ex rel. Modianos v. Tuttle, Immigration Commissioner, 12 F. (2d) 927 (E.D. La., 1925).

The United States Circuit Court of Appeals, in considering the admissibility to the United States of an alien woman who had been excluded on the ground of illiteracy and who had been married in Italy by proxy to an American citizen domiciled in New Jersey, stated that the Italian law was not in evidence and, unless it could presume what it was, the alien woman had not proved a valid marriage since it is the lex loci celebrationis which controls. The court stated that it had no reason to assume what the law of Italy was on the subject and that it would be a violent presumption that it corresponded with the American law. 

Cosulich Societa Triestina Di Navigazione v. Elting, Collector of Customs, 

66 F. (2d) 534 (C.C.A. 2d, 1933). brides" In 1917 the question of the immigration of Japanese "picture brides" into the United States was a matter of correspondence between "Picture the Department of Labor, the Department of State, and the Japanese Embassy. The question arose in connection with the provision of the immigration laws, which became effective May 5, 1917, that the wife of an alien resident in the United States might be admitted to this country though illiterate if not otherwise inadmissible. The question

was raised as to whether a picture bride whose marriage, while she was resident in Japan, to a Japanese subject resident in the United States, took place in Japan through the notification and registration of the marriage before the appropriate Japanese authorities, was in fact a wife for the purposes of admission to the United States; and also as to what evidence such a wife should be required to present to establish her marriage. The Japanese Embassy informed the Secretary of State that under Japanese law a marriage took effect immediately upon its being notified either in writing or orally to the registrar by both parties with at least two witnesses. A Japanese man resident in the United States, it was said, could marry a Japanese woman resident in Japan by affixing his seal to the notification, and the validity of such a marriage was amply attested by the issuance of a certified copy of the family registry bearing the official seal of the registrar. 

The Ambassador explained further that under Japanese law a Japanese man, resident in the United States, could send his registered personal seal to anyone in Japan to be affixed to the notification on his behalf. The Secretary of Labor informed the Secretary of State, on

August 20, 1917, that thereafter all women applying for admission to the United States as the wives of Japanese men would be required to furnish the immigration officers at ports of entry, as evidence of their marriage, a certified copy of so much of the family record of each of the parties to the marriage as contained the items recorded by reason of the occurrence of the marriage. These seemed to be, he said, the most complete documentary evidence that could be furnished as they contained a record, properly authenticated, of the fact that the registrar had received notification from or on behalf of the parties concerned and that the record of the marriage and therefore the marriage itself had been completed in accordance with Japanese law. He stated that the use of the expressions such as "picture brides", "photographic brides", "proxy marriages" might be abandoned since the explanations and assurances of the Japanese Government showed that the marriages in question were authorized and recognized by that Government, which fact had led to their full recognition by the United States Government so that the marriages involved were to be considered as in no sense distinguishable from marriages generally and the women could and ought to be referred to simply as wives. 

Ambassador Sato to Secretary Lansing, Apr. 28 and July 25, 1917, MS. 

Department of State, files 894.4054/12, 894.4054/19; the Secretary of Labor (Wilson) to Mr. Lansing, Aug. 20, 1917; ibid. file 894.4054/20. See also 

1917 For. Rel. 848-872.

MARRIAGE ON THE HIGH SEAS 

$165 The American Consul in Maracaibo, Venezuela, reported to the Department of State that an unmarried American citizen was contemplating marriage to a woman then in the United States, the ceremony to be performed by the master of an American vessel at a point outside of Curaçao upon the high seas, in order to avoid a delay of 30 days required under the laws of Venezuela to render a marriage ceremony legal. The Department of State replied: 

The legality of a marriage ceremony performed under the circumstances indicated would be questionable. Moreover, the 

Department would be constrained to look with disfavor upon an attempt to defeat the provisions of Venezuelan law, which in the present case do not appear to impose an unreasonable burden upon persons desirous of entering the marital status. 

It may be observed that the persons concerned may wish to consider whether a marriage ceremony so performed would be recognized as legal in Venezuela, where it is assumed they intend to reside, at least temporarily. 

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Sanders, Oct. 5, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 811.4054/110.

The chairman of the United States Shipping Board wrote to the Department of State as follows in regard to the authority of a master of a merchant vessel of the United States to perform a marriage ceremony on board a vessel when upon the high seas: 

It seems clear, therefore, that the master of a merchant vessel of the United States has no authority to perform a marriage ceremony. No opinion is expressed, however, on the validity of the marriages which have been performed by such masters. 

These may be valid as common law marriages under the laws of the states in which the vessels were documented at the time. 

The fact that the master performed the ceremony would not give it any greater validity than if it had been performed by any ordinary passenger on board the vessel. 

Chairman O'Connor to Secretary Kellogg, July 15, 1926, MS. Department of State, file 133/2463.

The Department of State instructed the Vice Consul in Bremerhaven, Germany, that an American consular officer would not be justified in issuing a certificate of marriage unless he had actually been present in the capacity of witness in the case of a marriage performed on the high seas on an American vessel. The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Vice 

Consul Hurst, Oct. 27, 1926, ibid. 133/2467.

The Department has given very careful consideration to the matter of the validity of a marriage entered into on an American vessel on the high seas between an American man residing

in Venezuela and an American woman en route to that country. 

While the question presented in this case is made difficult by the fact that there seem to have been very few decisions of courts having a direct bearing upon the question, the Department is of the opinion that it is justified in advising you that the marriage between Carl E. Patterson and Dayne E. Murphy should be recognized as valid for reasons which are hereinafter discussed. 

It is the well-established practice of the courts of this country, based upon public policy, to recognize, wherever it is possible to do So, the validity of a marital union which appears to have been entered into and maintained in good faith. In the case under consideration the vessel on which the marriage was contracted was American; both parties to the marriage were and are American citizens; a formal ceremony of marriage was performed by a minister of the gospel and the marriage was formally recorded on the log of the vessel. In view of these circumstances, attention is called to the fact that the recording of the marriage in the log of the vessel appears to have been made in accordance with the provisions of Section 4290 of the Revised Statutes of the 

United States which reads in part as follows: 

"Every vessel making voyages from a port in the United

States to any foreign port, or, being of the burden of seventy-five tons or upward, from a port on the Atlantic to a port on the Pacific, or vice versa, shall have an official log-book; and every master of such vessel shall make, or cause to be made therein, entries of the following matters, that is to say: "Paragraph 8. Every marriage taking place on board, with the names and ages of the parties.' 

The fact that a statute of the United States makes specific provision for the recording of marriages taking place on vessels sailing from ports of the United States to foreign ports and on certain vessels sailing from Atlantic ports of the United States to Pacific ports of this country, shows that such marriages are recognized by the chief legislative body of this country and would seem to involve the assumption that such marriages are to be regarded by administrative officials at least as valid. It is the opinion of the Department that Congress would hardly have provided for the recording of marriages which it considered to be invalid.

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to the Consul at Maracaibo, 

Venezuela (Sloan), Jan. 9, 1928, MS. Department of State, file 133/2515.

See also a similar instruction to the Consul General in Amsterdam, the Netherlands, Mar. 20, 1936, in respect to a case in which the marriage ceremony was performed by the captain of the vessel. The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Patton, Mar. 20, 1936, ibid. 133/2795. 

In 1929 the New York Court of Appeals held that the laws which follow a ship on the high seas are the laws of the State where the owner resides, not the laws of the State within which the ship is registered. In that case the marriage had been performed by the cap-

tain of the Leviathan, a ship registered in the State of New York but owned by the United States represented by the United States Shipping Board, at a time when the ship was 40 miles out of New York. In upholding the marriage the court declared that Congress by providing that every master of a vessel voyaging from an American port shall make an entry in his official logbook of every marriage taking place on board (46 U.S.C. §201), had recognized that there was a law of marriage on board a ship at sea. 

Fisher v. Fisher, 250 N.Y. (1929) 313, 165 N.E. 460. To the same effect, see Bolmer v. Edsall, 90 N.J. Eq. (1919) 299, 106 Atl. 646.

The plaintiff and John W. Johnson were married on September 

19, 1929 on the high seas, about fifteen miles off the mouth of the 

Columbia River by the captain of the gasoline boat Crescent. The

Supreme Court of Oregon affirmed a judgment of the circuit court directing the payment of a pension to the plaintiff as the widow of John W. Johnson. The court said that it was reasonable to infer from the evidence that the captain of the Crescent was the owner thereof and that he resided in Oregon. The court also said: 

Therefore, it follows that a marriage thus solemnized on the high seas is to be tested by the law of this state. It is a well established rule that a vessel upon the high seas is followed by the law of the nation or state in which its owner resides: 

Fisher v. Fisher, 250 N.Y. 313 (165 N.E. 460, 61 A.L.R. 1523); 

Bolmer v. Edsall, 90 N.J. Eq. 299 (106 Atl. 646). If the domocile of the parties to a marriage on the high seas is the deciding factor in determining the law applicable thereto, as apparently held in Norman v. Norman, 121 Cal. 620 (54 P. 143, 42 L.R.A. 

343, 66 Am. St. Rep. 74), and in Holmes v. Holmes, Fed. Cas.

No. 6638, the marriage in question would still be tested by the law of Oregon.

The court pointed out that this was not a case where the parties went on the high seas to evade the marriage laws of the State of their domicil, that the parties in the case were capable of contracting marriage and were laboring under no legal impediment, and that they were married in good faith. It declared that it was therefore its duty to invoke every presumption known to law to sustain the marriage. 

Johnson v. Baker et al., 142 Ore. (1933) 404, 407, 20 Pac. (2d) 407, 408.

The case of Maynard v. Maynard was an action to annul a marriage celebrated on board the American steamship President Roosevelt, owned by the United States Shipping Board, on the high seas by the captain of the vessel. Neither of the parties had obtained a marriage license. The parties to the marriage thereafter lived together as hus-

band and wife for about six months. The Superior Court of Cook 

County, Illinois, stated that the law of the domicil of the vessel governed and that domicil was the District of Columbia; that the requirement in the District of Columbia Code of a marriage license was merely directory and that the failure to procure such a license would not render the marriage absolutely void; and that the enumeration in the code of persons authorized to perform marriage ceremonies in the District, which did not include the captain of a vessel, was not to be taken to mean that ceremonies performed by other persons were absolutely void, but merely voidable. The court concluded that it did not hold the marriage void but was of the opinion that on the request of one of the parties to a ceremony performed without the license required by the District, by a person not authorized by the District court to perform marriage ceremonies, it should annul the marriage, since no common-law marriage could result under the laws of the 

District of Columbia. 

No. 469400, Superior Court of Cook County, Ill., Apr. 1928, unreported (enclosure to circular instruction 731 to American diplomatic and consular officers, June 22, 1928, MS. Department of State, file 133/2557).

MARRIAGE IN EMBASSIES, LEGATIONS, OR CONSULATES 

§166 It is stated in the Foreign Service Regulations that there is no objection to compliance with requests of Americans abroad to have marriage ceremonies performed in Embassies or Legations or Consulates but that there is no obligation to accede to such requests. It is also stated that when such an application is made it is the duty of the diplomatic or consular representative to inquire whether the parties may lawfully marry according to the laws of the country in which the Embassy or Legation or Consulate is situated and whether the proper steps have been taken to legalize the performance of the marriage ceremony in such country, and that it is their duty to refuse the request if either of these questions is answered in the negative. 

For. Ser. Reg. U.S. XIII-1, n. 1, June 1939. 

On May 2, 1914 the American Ambassador in Spain informed the Department of State that the Spanish Minister of State had informed him that a ceremony of civil marriage between two American citizens might be performed in the American Embassy provided the "extraterritoriality" thereof could be temporarily waived. The Department instructed the Ambassador that "extraterritoriality" is immunity from local jurisdiction accorded by the custom of nations and that if the validity under Spanish law of a civil marriage was dependent upon a

waiver of the right of "extraterritoriality" of the American Embassy it did not consider it advisable for the marriage to be performed in this manner. The suggestion was made that a religious ceremony might be performed in the Embassy by a clergyman in the presence of the Consul and that a civil ceremony might be performed with the formalities required by Spanish law within the regular jurisdiction of the appropriate official authorized by Spanish law to perform the civil act and also with the Consul as witness. 

Secretary Bryan to Ambassador Willard, May 6, 1914 (telegram), MS. 

Department of State, file 133/41.

In 1920 the Department of State wrote to the American Chargé d'Affaires in Cubayou are requested to refrain from permitting the use of your Legation for the performance of marriage ceremonies under the circumstances related in the despatch above referred to, as the Department cannot sanction your aiding or appearing to aid in the evasion or violation of the Cuban law, which requires foreigners to publish the bans fifteen days before the celebration of the marriage ceremony.

There is no law of the United States requiring its diplomatic and consular officers to permit the use of their legations or consulates for the performance of marriage ceremonies. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Adee) to the Chargé d'Affaires in 

Cuba (White), no. 101, May 22, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 133/1449. 

On August 6, 1927 the Department of State instructed the American Consul General in charge in Tampico, Mexico, as follows: 

The Secretary of State does not disapprove of marriage ceremonies being performed in American Consulates in those cases where one or both of the contracting parties are American citizens; provided, that in the judgment of the consular officer in charge, the parties to the marriage fully understand that this privilege is a courtesy extended to them which adds nothing to the validity of the marriage.

The Department of State to the American Consul General in charge at 

Tampico, Mexico, Aug. 6, 1927, MS. Department of State, file 133/2495.

In response to an inquiry as to whether, in view of the requirement of Cuban law that persons desiring to enter the contract of marriage must reside in Cuba six months, it would not be possible for two American citizens to be married at the American Embassy in Cuba without six months' residence, the Department of State expressed the opinion that if the proposed marriage was not permissible under Cuban law, the performance of the ceremony in the American Em-

bassy in Habana would not validate the marriage so far as concerned its effect in places where there was not a statute validating it, and that therefore the Department would not desire to have the ceremony performed there.

The Acting Secretary of State (Carr) to Representative Lindsay C. 

Warren, Nov. 29, 1929 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 133/2610.

MARRIAGE IN PRESENCE OF CONSULS 

$167 Section 4082 of the Revised Statutes of the United States provides: 

Marriages in presence of any consular officer of the United States in a foreign country, between persons who would be authorized to marry if residing in the District of Columbia, shall be valid to all intents and purposes, and shall have the same effect as if solemnized within the United States. 

Sections XIII-1, XIII-2, and XIII-3 of the Foreign Service Reg ulations of the United States (Ex. Or., Apr. 11, 1939) relates to the lack of power of Foreign Service officers to celebrate marriages, to the ability of consular officers to act as official witnesses of a marriage ceremony where one of the parties is an American citizen, and to the issuance by consular officers of certificates as to such marriages as they have witnessed.

A diplomatic representative is not empowered to act as an official witness at a marriage ceremony. 

For. Ser. Reg. U.S. XIII-2(a), June 1939. 

In a letter written by Secretary Bayard on July 2, 1888, in response to a communication inquiring whether American citizens can be validly married in foreign countries, and whether validity would attach to such marriages solemnized at the house of the 

American Legation at Antwerp or Berlin "according to home form", Mr. Bayard said: "In reply I have to say that it is a settled rule of international law that the solemnization of marriages, to have ubiquitous validity, must be in conformity with the law of the place of celebration if the place be in a civilized land, and unless the law of such place prescribe conditions repugnant to conscience. "It is also, I apprehend, settled law that a marriage not solemnized in conformity with the law of the place of celebration is not validated, so far as concerns its effect in places where there is not a statute validating it by the mere fact of its having been solemnized at the legation of the country to which the parties belong and in conformity with the form held valid in such latter country."

Whether a marriage solemnized abroad in the presence of a consular officer of the United States is validated so far as concerns this country, under the Act of Congress of June 22, 1860 [Rev. 

Stat., sec. 4082], by the fact of the presence of the Consul, depends, first, upon whether the parties are domiciled in the District of Columbia or in one of the territories of the United States, and second, as to whether the Act of Congress in question is applicable and constitutional to give validity to such marriages within the various States of the Union in the case of parties domiciled in such States; as to which the Department expresses no opinion. So far as concerns foreign countries, as Mr. Bayard remarks, "The question of the validity of the solemnization would depend upon their own law and that law is understood to incorporate the general principles above stated that a solemnization of marriage to be valid must be in conformity with the law of the place of celebration."

Whether a marriage solemnized in an American Embassy or Legation abroad, not in the presence of a consular officer of the United States, would be recognized as valid in the States of New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Rhode Island, is a question which the Department must respectfully decline to answer for the reasons given by Secretary Bayard, in the letter above referred to, when he said: "I have, however, now to add that the question you propose is one ultimately to be determined by courts of justice under the circumstances of each particular case; and that my duty is not to predict what would be the action of such courts, but to give in response to inquiries such cautions as may induce American citizens proposing to be married abroad to take every step which may be necessary to give validity to an act whose invalidity would be fraught with consequences serious both to themselves and to the community." 

The Acting Secretary of State (Bacon) to Mr. Roemat, Nov. 19, 1906, MS. Department of State, file 2531/1.

The Department of State instructed the Minister in Peking, China, in connection with section 4082 of the Revised Statutes, that it was of the opinion that in the absence of contrary indications the assurances of persons performing marriage ceremonies that they were qualified to render such services might be accepted by consular officers. 

Counselor Polk to Minister Reinsch, no. 523, Nov. 23, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 133/449.

With reference to section 4082 of the Revised Statutes of the United States, the Department of State made the following comments:

This provision does not exclude, however, modes of solemnization other than in the presence of a consular officer.

Marriages abroad, when not in the presence of a consular officer, if otherwise valid, are not invalidated by the above statute. It should be observed that this statute does not authorize a consular officer to perform the ceremony, but merely prescribes the legal effect which will be given to a marriage celebrated in his presence. In view of the exclusive authority of the states in such matters, it is probable that the statute referred to would not be operative outside of the District of Columbia and the territories of the United States. The law of each particular state should, therefore, be consulted in order to determine whether the marriage to which you refer would be considered valid. 

The Solicitor for the Department of State (Hackworth) to Mr. Arthur 

O. Kleemann, July 28, 1930, MS. Department of State, file 133/2633.

The Department of State instructed the Consul General in Shanghai that since the validity of a marriage for which an application for a consular witness had been filed seemed to depend on the validity of a decree of divorce granted to one of the parties and since he was legally incompetent to express an authoritative opinion on that question, the issuance by him of the certificate authorized by section 4082 of the Revised Statutes would merely indicate that he had witnessed the ceremony in the belief that the parties to the marriage "would be authorized to marry if residing in the District of Columbia". 

The Department stated that while such certificate would be evidence that a presumably valid marriage had been witnessed by him it would give no validity to the marriage if it were in fact invalid and that this fact should be made clear to the parties in interest. 

Secretary Hull to Consul General Cunningham, telegram 22, Jan. 31, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Murray, Annie T.

In 1906 the American Consul at Santiago de Cuba refused to issue a certificate in respect to a marriage of an American Army officer to an American citizen performed in his presence by an Army chaplain, on the ground that the chaplain was not authorized under the law of Cuba to perform such a marriage ceremony. The Department of State informed the Consul thatyour action in cautioning the parties to comply with the local laws respecting the solemnization of marriage is commended. 

You are correct in holding that as a rule the law of the place of solemnization of a marriage determines the mode of solemnization, and it would appear that the parties in this instance should have complied with the requirements of the laws of Cuba. It is not the function of the Department or of the Consul, however, to declare the marriage invalid because of the non-observance of the local laws, nor is it desirable to withhold the Consul's certificate to the mere fact that the ceremony took place in his presence. That certificate has no effect upon the validity of the

marriage and may prove useful in affording proof that a ceremony, though perhaps not according to the local laws, was actually performed. In issuing the certificate care should be taken to indicate the country and State authorizing Chaplain 

Stull to solemnize marriages, and in delivering the certificate the parties should be informed that your view of the marriage has received the Department's approval. 

The Third Assistant Secretary of State (Wilson) to Mr. Holaday, no. 145, Apr. 9, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 3047/1.

The certificate which a Consul is to issue when he consents to witness a marriage simply attests the fact of marriage in accordance with the laws of the country of its celebration, and he is not called upon, certainly in any civilized country, to concern himself with the consideration of the question whether such laws are different from or inferior to those of the United States. 

When, however, a marriage is manifestly wrong or would place the foreigner in a class prohibited by our immigration laws, as where, for example, there is reason to believe that the American is marrying a foreigner for the purpose of importing her for prostitution, the Consul should certainly decline to be a witness or in any way to further the marriage. In such a case he should immediately notify the Department of the marriage and of facts which caused him to decline to witness it. This Department would thereupon bring the matter to the attention of the Department of Commerce and Labor, which would thus be in a position to enforce the regulations. 

The Chief Clerk (Carr) to Consul General Miller, no. 173, Dec. 18, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 8112/1.

In 1918 a representative of the American Consulate at Bordeaux, France, witnessed the marriage of a Belgian who was a soldier in the American Army in France. The Department of State instructed the Consul:

As the presence of a consular officer as official witness is not essential to the validity of a marriage, it is not thought that any inconvenience to foreigners serving in the forces of the United States will result from the provision of the Consular Regulations which limits the extension of this privilege to American citizens. 

The Department cannot approve of your action in witnessing the marriage of a person who is not an American citizen, even though he may have declared his intention to apply for naturalization. 

The Acting Chief of the Consular Bureau (Hengstler) to Consul Buck lin, no. 348, Aug. 27, 1919, MS. Department of State, file 133/866.

The American Consul at Port-au-Prince, Haiti, inquired whether a chaplain in the United States Navy might celebrate at Cap Haitien a marriage, valid in the District of Columbia, between an American 

---

woman and a medical officer of the United States Navy attached to the Haitian Constabulary, in pursuance of the convention of September 16, 1915 between the United States and Haiti. The Consul inquired further whether, if the chaplain were not entitled to perform the marriage, it would be valid if celebrated aboard an American merchant vessel or an American naval vessel in a Haitian port. He also inquired whether he was authorized to witness the ceremony. 

The Department of State informed him that if the persons referred to would be authorized to marry in the District of Columbia if resident there, a marriage performed in the Consul's presence at Cape Haitien by a United States Naval chaplain would presumably be valid in the District of Columbia under the provisions of section 4082 of the Revised Statutes. It stated, however, that in order to have a ceremony which would be recognized as valid everywhere, the persons in question should apparently be married in accordance with the requirements of the law of Haiti. The marriage would apparently have no better standing, it was said, so far as the validity in the United States or elsewhere was concerned, if the ceremony were performed on an American merchant vessel in a Haitian port. There might be an advantage, the Department continued, in performing the ceremony on board an American naval vessel in a Haitian port, so far as its standing in the United States was concerned, but it might well be doubted whether such a marriage would be regarded as valid in foreign countries. The Consul was informed that the Department considered it preferable for him not to witness the ceremony or furnish a consular certificate if it was performed at Cape Haitien or on board a merchant vessel in a Haitian port, but left his course of action to his discretion if the ceremony was performed on board an 

American naval vessel in a Haitian port. 

Secretary Hughes to Consul Woods, May 23, 1923 (telegram), MS. 

Department of State, file 133/2398.

In February 1915, at which time the interests of Swiss citizens were under American protection in Turkey, the American Consul General in Constantinople inquired of the Department of State whether he was authorized to perform the ceremony of a marriage to which a Swiss citizen was a party. It appeared that under Swiss law a religious ceremony of the marriage to which a Swiss citizen was a party could not take place until after the civil rite, which, outside of Switzerland, was performed by the Swiss consular officer or the consular officer charged with the protection of Swiss interests, or by a competent foreign official. The Consul General stated that he was informed that the laws of Switzerland would fully sanction his performing the marriage in question. The Department in-

structed him that it considered that a marriage ceremony performed by him for Swiss citizens would at least be of doubtful validity and was therefore inadvisable. 

Secretary Bryan to Consul General Ravndal, Mar. 31, 1915 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 854.4054/2.

The American Embassy in Moscow inquired of the Department of State whether there was any objection to the issuance of a consular certificate as to a marriage based on the presence of a consular witness at the religious ceremony of a marriage which had been registered with ZAGS (inscription of acts of civil status) but at which registration no consular witness was present; also whether the Department approved the issuance of the consular certificate as to a marriage based on the presence of a consular witness at a church marriage not régistered at ZAGS. The Department replied that consular officers were not authorized to issue such certificates unless they had witnessed the performance of the marriage rites required by the law of the foreign country and that since a church marriage had no legal effect in the Soviet Union it was necessary that a consular certificate be issued on the basis of registration with zaGs. A consular officer, it was said, might witness the religious ceremony and make an appropriate notation of attendance at such ceremony on the certificate. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Moore) to the Embassy in Moscow, telegram 205, Dec. 11, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 133/2818.

The American Consul General in Tokyo informed the Department of State on November 7, 1924 that a written notification of marriage, under Japanese law, after being signed by the contracting parties had no validity until it had been properly witnessed, presented to the registrar, accepted, and filed by him as required by article 775 of the Japanese Civil Code. The Department of State informed the

withhold the certificate until they have received satisfactory evidence that the notification has been accepted by the registrar.
