DIVORCE 

$168 In an instruction to the Consul General in Beirut, Syria, the Department of State said that- according to the American theory of the conflict of laws, jurisdiction for rendering a decree of divorce is based upon domicile. 

It, therefore, follows that Mr. Sadak cannot, while domiciled in the United States, obtain a decree of divorce in Syria which would be recognized as valid in the United States. 

The Department of State to the Consul General at Beirut, Syria, Feb. 

14, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 130 Sadak, Farris.

The point upon which the validity of foreign divorces rests in the United States is that of jurisdiction. It is more or less accepted that if the court of the forum has jurisdiction of the subject matter and of at least one of the parties (the latter hinging to a certain extent upon domicile, i. e., actual presence within the jurisdiction with an intention to remain there, in the sense of making one's home), the decree would be valid elsewhere. If the defendant resided in the state or country of the forum it would not be necessary for the plaintiff to, and vice versa, for the purposes of jurisdiction alone.

The courts of New York, with regard to foreign nations, have not gone beyond the view that if they see fit to do so they are guided by principles of comity in the matter of the recognition of such decrees. 

Attorney General Bennett (State of New York) to Secretary Stimson, Feb. 4, 1931, MS. Department of State, file 854.4054/23.

As to national jurisdiction in matters of divorce, see the following 

American cases:

Whether a New York court will recognize a Norwegian decree of divorce depends upon New York law, irrespective of the validity of the divorce under Norwegian law. In a case arising in 1916 the court acknowledged the findings of a Norwegian court that the defendant in divorce proceedings was domiciled in Norway, concluded that the Norwegian court had jurisdiction, and recognized the decree of divorce on grounds of comity. Lie v. Lie, 96 Misc. (1916) 3, 159 N.Y. Supp. 748.

Where the French courts granted a decree of divorce to Americans resident in France but domiciled in New York, the New York Court of

Appeals held that it was not required (in an action for absolute divorce)

because of the absence of domicile of the parties in France to give effect to the French decree but that it might on grounds of comity recognize the decree where recognition thereof did not offend public policy, it appearing that the French courts had applied the law of New York. 

Gould v. Gould, 235 N.Y. (1923) 14, 138 N.E. 490.

Where a second husband sought the annulment of his marriage on the ground that a divorce obtained by his wife from her first husband was invalid, the Supreme Court of New York, Appellate Division (2d Dept.), in denying the petition, held that the wife's domicil was in Denmark at the time of the Danish divorce decree and that the rules of comity and private international law required a recognition of the validity of that decree; the court also held that the second husband could not attack the validity of the divorce decree as he was not a party to it and had full cognizance of it. Sorensen v. Sorensen, 219 App. Div. (1927) 344, 220 N.Y. 

Supp. 242.

Plaintiff who voluntarily appeared in a divorce action begun by her husband in France was held estopped from obtaining a declaratory judgment that the divorce was invalid; the court also held that the plaintiff must abide by the decision of the French court that it had jurisdiction in the divorce proceeding. Schneider v. Schneider et al., 232 App. Div. (1931) 71, 249 N.Y. Supp. 131.

In connection with an application for a visa as the wife of an American citizen by a woman who had submitted evidence of her divorce from her first husband in the Soviet Union, the Department of State expressed the opinion thatsuch divorce may properly be recognized as valid if, at the time when it was obtained, one of the spouses was domiciled in Russia and the petition was filed in the proper tribunal in Russia. 

If, on the other hand, it appears that neither spouse was domiciled in Russia at the time when the divorce was obtained, or if it appears that the petition was filed in a Russian consulate in some other country, the facts should be reported to the Department, so that the matter may be given further consideration. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Dumont, Habana, Cuba, Oct. 21, 1931, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Simon, Helen P.

Since the alien was in the Soviet Union and applied in person for his divorce, and since the divorce is apparently valid under Soviet law, the Department considers that its validity for the purposes of the immigration laws may not properly be questioned in the absence of a decree of a court of competent jurisdiction declaring it invalid. You should, therefore, proceed with the consideration of the alien's application for an immigration visa upon the presumption that the marriage in England subsequent to the divorce in the Soviet Union is valid. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Erhardt, 

Jan. 21, 1937, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Hohlstein, Paul O. divorces

Mexican divorces

It may be stated that a foreign decree of divorce is presumed prima facie to be valid and that, in general, the one who obtains the divorce is estopped to deny its validity. It is well established that a marriage valid by the law covering both parties when made will be recognized everywhere if valid by the law in force where it was performed, and it has been judicially stated that "a marriage which is valid under the laws of the present government of Russia is quite universally regarded as valid in this country."

The Department of State to the American Consul at Helsingfors, Finland, Apr. 2, 1934, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Parssinen, Martha H.

A naturalized American citizen obtained a divorce in the State of Morelos, Mexico, in 1932 from a woman whom he had married and lived with in the United States. Subsequently he was married to another woman in Calcutta, India, and thereafter executed a petition to obtain non-quota status for his second wife under the immigration laws of the United States. It appeared from the Mexican court record that the first wife was duly summoned in the divorce proceedings according to the local law but that she did not appear or make any defense. The Mexican court stated that it assumed jurisdiction over the case on the basis of a certificate of legal domicil issued by the Citizen 

Municipal President of Cuautla, Morelos, the certificate being made conclusive evidence of such domicil under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure in the State of Morelos. The Department of State instructed the Consul General at Calcutta, India, "that if neither party to the divorce was actually domiciled within the jurisdiction of the court issuing the decree, it should not be recognized as valid". The 

Department also stated that if the divorce was found invalid the second marriage would also be invalid.

The Acting Secretary of State to the Consul General at Calcutta, India, June 27, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Langer, Phyllis B. W.

The Department of State instructed the Consul in Montreal, Canada, as follows, regarding an application for a non-preference visa by a woman who had married an American citizen after having been divorced from her first husband by decree obtained in Mexico when neither of them was domiciled there and when she herself was actually resident in the Dominican Republic:

The Department has held, in accord with a number of decisions by state courts in this country refusing to recognize so-called Mexican "mail order" divorces [as valid, that such divorces,] obtained without either party appearing in the jurisdiction of the court

issuing the decree, are not to be regarded as valid for the purposes of the immigration laws. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Byington, Nov. 

18, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Dillenberg, Clarita K. At the same time, the Department instructed the Consul General that persons who remarried in good faith, in reliance upon a divorce obtained in Mexico either while sojourning there or by mail without appearing in the jurisdiction in which the decree was issued, and who admitted these facts and the fact of the remarriage, should not be considered to have admitted the commission of a crime involving moral turpitude and that, although remarriage under such circumstances might constitute the crime of bigamy under the laws of many States, in the absence of decisions of courts of competent jurisdiction to the contrary, it considered that a person who had acted in good faith in reliance upon a divorce which he believed gave him a legal right to remarry, might not properly be held to have committed a crime involving moral turpitude.

The Department of State in 1937 informed the American Consul in Mexico City in connection with an immigration case that in the absence of contest Mexican divorce decrees might generally be considered as valid when one or both parties were physically present within the jurisdiction of the court issuing the decree. 

Secretary Hull to Consul Stewart, Nov. 27, 1937 (telegram), MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Podolsky, Bertha E. G.

The Department of State made the following comment in regard to the Mexican "mail-order" divorce of an applicant for an immigration visa at the American Consulate at Hamilton, Ontario, Canada: 

The Department does not concur in the views you express regarding the validity of the Mexican mail order divorce which Mrs. obtained before she entered into a marriage ceremony with Mr.

It appears that the view expressed by the Attorney General of the State of New Jersey, in which State the alleged marriage occurred, is the proper one, namely, that while a decree of divorce obtained abroad is presumed to be valid, and a state officer who is requested to issue a marriage license after the exhibition of a foreign divorce decree is not required to inquire into the validity of the divorce, the presumption of validity in favor of the divorce nevertheless would be overcome by a showing that neither of the parties actually acquired a bona fide residence within the jurisdiction of the foreign court issuing the divorce decree. 

It appears that the Opinion of the Attorney General of New Jersey is even more restrictive, for he quotes with apparent approval a statement made by Chancellor Walker in the case of 

Feichert v. Feichert, 98 N.J. Equity, at page 451, as follows: "Of course if a resident of this State goes into another State to obtain a divorce and does not acquire a bona fide

residence there, such divorce will be null here, but its nullity will have to be proved here."

Under the view expressed by Chancellor Walker, it appears that if a plaintiff residing in New Jersey proceeds beyond the borders of that State and obtains a divorce without acquiring a bona fide residence within the jurisdiction of the court issuing the decree, such decree would not be recognized as valid in the State of New Jersey, upon proof submitted in that State that the foreign residence was not bona fide. Since Mrs. has admitted that she was not present in Mexico, where the mail order divorce decree was issued, it is assumed that there could be no question in New Jersey of the mala fides of her alleged residence within the jurisdiction of the Mexican court. 

The Chief of the Visa Division (Simmons) to Mr. 

7, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 A- Luigi. Feb.

A Mexican citizen resident in the United States obtained a decree of divorce from his wife in a court in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. His wife accompanied him to that city and submitted herself to the jurisdiction of the Mexican court. Thereafter he returned to the United 

States and married a Mexican citizen in El Paso, Texas. The second wife later applied to the American Consulate in Ciudad Juárez for a non-quota immigration visa. The Department of State instructed the Consul as follows: 

It is believed that a distinction should be drawn between a Mexican divorce obtained by mail, without the actual presence of the parties, or one of them, within the jurisdiction of the Mexican court issuing the decree, and the case of a divorce which has been issued after one or both of the parties appeared in person before the court concerned. In the absence of a showing that [the husband's] second marriage was not entered into in good faith in reliance upon the validity of his Mexican divorce, which was obtained after he and his first wife had appeared personally before the Mexican court issuing the decree, and further, in the absence of a showing that the validity of his second marriage has been successfully contested, there is perceived no objection to the issuance of an immigration visa to his second wife, so far as the question of the validity of her marriage is concerned. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Shaw, July 20, 1937. 

MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Ulloa, Carmen S. de.

In April 1938 there was referred to the Department of State an objection to the authentication by an American Consul at Juarez, Mexico, of a divorce decree procured in Mexico by American citizens in which the Consul included the citation of certain decisions of the courts of the Republic of Mexico holding certain Mexican divorce decrees invalid. The action of the Consul in including such citations was based on the provisions of note 2 to section 82 of the Consular

Regulations of the United States in which it was stated that there appeared to be no objection to the inclusion in a consular certificate of a statement of his knowledge in regard to the matter in connection with which his notarial services were required. The Department said: 

The citations are included in the form of authentication with a view to the prevention of possible misapprehension regarding the value and legal effect of the consular certificate and to invite attention to the apparent possibility, in view of more or less pertinent decisions of Mexican courts, that the validity of decrees of divorce obtained by American citizens may not in general be upheld by the courts of Mexico.

It would appear that the decisions in question tend to support the belief that the Mexican courts would not generally look with favor upon purported divorces obtained in Mexico by persons not actually domiciled in the states where such decrees were granted. 

Of course American Consuls in using the present form of authentication are animated by the laudable purpose of protecting American citizens from the effect of action they might take which would perhaps have unfortunate consequences, Secretary Hull to Representative Lea, May 4, 1938, MS. Department of 

State, file 812.04611/188.

In the following cases the courts of New York have held that a divorce obtained in Mexico by persons not resident or domiciled in Mexico is invalid: Alzmann v. Maher, 231 App. Div. (1930) 139, 246 N.Y. Supp. 60; 

Greenberg v. Greenberg, 218 App. Div. (1926) 104, 218 N.Y. Supp. 87; Coakley v. Coakley, 161 Misc. (1937) 867, 293 N.Y. Supp. 421; In the Matter of the Estate of Ruth Morrison Shuff, 151 Misc. (1934) 754, 272 N.Y. Supp. 

418; May v. May, 251 App. Div. (1937) 63, 295 N.Y. Supp. 599 (defendant appeared by written consent and submitted to the jurisdiction of the Mexican court). Contra: Fisher v. Fisher, 162 Misc. (1937) 775, 295 N.Y. Supp. 

451 (plaintiff estopped from attacking validity of decree obtained by her in Mexico).

The Supreme Court of New York, the court of appeals concurring, found (a declaratory judgment) that a Mexican divorce wherein the party procuring it went to Yucatán, Mexico, to obtain it, was void, no notice of the proceeding having been given to the other party to the divorce, a resident of New York who had not appeared in the action. Baumann v. Baumann, 132 Misc. (1928) 217, 228 N.Y. Supp. 539; 224 App. Div. (1928) 719, 229 N.Y. 

Supp. 833; 250 N.Y. (1929) 382, 165 N.E. 819.

But the Supreme Court of New York has held that a plaintiff in an action for an absolute divorce who had appeared in a Mexican court in a proceeding for divorce brought by the defendant and had accepted benefits under the decree granted there, should not be permitted to come into a court of equity and endeavor to profit by his own wrong. Weber v. Weber, 135 Misc. (1929) 717, 238 N.Y. Supp. 333.

In the following cases the courts of New Jersey have held invalid divorces obtained in Mexico by persons who went to Mexico without intention of becoming permanent residents there, personal service of notice in the United States having been made upon the other party to the proceedings: Reik v. 157511-40-VOL. II-26

Reik, 109 N.J. Eq. (1932) 615, 158 Atl. 519; 112 N.J. Eq. (1933) 234, 163 

Atl. 907; Newton v. Newton, 13 N.J. Misc. (1935) 613, 179 Atl. 621. See also

Robins v. Robins, involving a question of fraud in obtaining a divorce in 

Mexico following a decree of limited divorce and maintenance obtained in the State of New York. 103 N.J. Eq. (1928) 26, 142 Atl. 168.

The validity of a divorce as well as of marriage depends upon the law of the state in which the husband and wife are domiciled, and in a case where neither party was within the jurisdiction of Mexico at the time of the divorce, regardless of whether the divorce was valid in Mexico, which was not established, such divorce cannot be recognized under the law of 

Massachusetts. Bergeron v. Bergeron, 287 Mass. (1934) 524, 192 N.E. 86.

A divorce obtained in another state (Mexico) through fraudulent residence may be attacked, but the fraud must be proved like any other fact. 

Galloway v. Galloway et al., 116 Cal. App. (1931) 478, 2 Pac. (2d) 842.

A divorce obtained in a jurisdiction (Mexico) in which neither of the parties is domiciled is not entitled to faith and credit, and the consent of the wife to the jurisdiction of a Mexican court cannot confer jurisdiction. 

Ryder v. Ryder, 2 Cal. App. (2d) (1934) 426, 37 Pac. (2d) 1069; People v. 

Harlow, 9 Cal. App. (2d) (1935) 643, 50 Pac. (2d) 1052; Du Quesnay v. 

Henderson, 24 Cal. App. (2d) (1937) 11, 74 Pac. (2d) 294.

Where it did not appear that the Mexican court acquired jurisdiction of either party or of the subject-matter of a divorce procured in the State of Sonora, and it was nowhere intimated that either party was a resident of Mexico, the Supreme Court of the State of Washington held that the decree of divorce was void. Dailey v. Dailey, 154 Wash. (1929) 

499, 282 Pac. 830.

The Supreme Court of Iowa has held that no court of any state has authority to render a decree of divorce which will be recognizable under Iowa law when neither spouse is domiciled within the jurisdiction of the state granting the divorce. Bonner v. Reandrew et al., 203 Iowa (1927) 1355, 214 N.W. 536.

In a case in Pennsylvania it was held that in order to invalidate a Mexican divorce decree it would have to be shown not only that the wife in divorce proceedings instituted by the husband in Mexico was not in Mexico at the time of the proceedings but that she was never properly served with process, was not represented by counsel, and that the cause of action did not arise in the foreign jurisdiction. Commonwealth ex rel. 

Thompson et al. v. Yarnell et ux., 313 Pa. (1933) 244, 169 Atl. 370.

The Supreme Court of Alabama declared void a Mexican divorce where the husband was not a resident of Mexico, but had gone to Mexico for the sole purpose of obtaining the divorce, and stated that a valid divorce could not be granted on constructive service by a court of a state in which neither party was domiciled unless there was personal appearance. 

Wells v. Wells, 230 Ala. (1935) 430, 161 So. 794.

The granting of a decree of divorce to residents of the District of Columbia, where both parties to the proceedings remain in the District and neither of them was ever in the State of Durango, Mexico, where the divorce was procured, is contrary to the policy of the law of the District of Columbia and an annulment of the subsequent marriage of one of the parties to the divorce will be granted. Cover v. Mattingly, 62 Wash. L.R. (1934) 967.

They had been married there in 1902, and in 1907 while Russian subjects and domiciled in that country they appeared before a Jewish rabbi and were divorced according to the Jewish and Russian laws. 

The Supreme Court of New York found that under Russian law Jewish rabbis had jurisdiction to grant such divorces and that the status of the parties became fixed by that divorce under the laws of their then domicil. The complaint was dismissed on the ground that nothing had been shown to impeach the finding of the rabbinical court either for fraud, mistake, or lack of jurisdiction.

In the case of Machransky v. Machransky, 31 Ohio App. 482 (1927), 166 N. E. 423, the Ohio Court of Appeals, in upholding such a divorce, stated that the presumption was that it did not violate the law of Russia where it was granted.

The New York Constitution of 1894 provided in article 1, section 

9, that no divorce should be granted "otherwise than by due judicial proceedings". The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of 

New York (1st Dept.) has held that a writing, purporting to be a divorce obtained from a rabbi in Brooklyn, cannot be recognized as having any effect in New York State or as having been validated in Russia. The court said:

Although a divorce may have been perfected in Russia, according to the law prevailing there, by the delivery of the alleged divorce granted by a rabbi in New York city, the act of the local rabbi in granting it was not thereby rendered consonant with the law prevailing here. The rabbinical divorce must be regarded as having had its inception in the paper issued by the Brooklyn rabbi, and although the Russian government may recognize it, the divorce is void in its inception under our law.

We cannot regard it as a divorce obtained in Russia. The record indicates that what was done in that country was intended merely to give effect there to the rabbinical divorce obtained in Brooklyn. 

Chertok v. Chertok, 208 App. Div. (1924) 161, 162-163, 203 N.Y. Supp.

Mrs. Pearl Cohen obtained a rabinnical divorce in Warsaw, Poland, in 1924. In 1928 she arrived in Cuba, accompanied by her son, Maya 

Yuta Cohen, and was married in that country to an American citizen.

In December 1928 the American Consulate General at Habana granted her a non-quota immigration visa as the wife of an American citizen, and she was subsequently admitted to the United States. In 1931 her son was an applicant for a second-preference immigration visa. Final action on his application was deferred on the ground that no evidence had been presented to establish that his mother's divorce was valid under Polish law and that if her second marriage should prove to be invalid she would be subject to deportation, thereby raising in the case of her son the question of the likelihood of his becoming a public charge in the United States. The Department of State informed the 

American Consul General in Habana that, while it did not wish to interfere with his responsibility under section 2(f) of the Immigration Act of 1924 to determine Maya Yuta Cohen's admissibility to the United States, it submitted certain observations for his assistance. 

The Department said, inter alia, thatit would appear that in the absence of evidence of fraud in the inception of the marriage, such as for example the concealment from the competent Cuban authorities of her prior marriage to and her rabinnical divorce from her first husband, it would not ordinarily be necessary to go behind the Cuban marriage to inquire into the validity of the divorce obtained in Poland. It might properly be considered, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the latter question was determined by the appropriate Cuban officials in connection with the formalities incident to the celebration of the marriage.

It is pertinent at this point to recall that it is the general policy of the courts of the United States to avoid making any decision which would result in voiding marriages which have been entered into and maintained in good faith and that, therefore, if, as above stated, there is no indication of fraud in the inception of [the] present marriage you would be justified in relying on the general legal presumption which exists in favor of the validity of the marriage.

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul General Dumont, Feb. 

28, 1931, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Cohen, Maya Yuta.

A prospective applicant for a non-quota immigration visa as the alien wife of an American citizen had been married by a religious ceremony performed by a rabbi in Bucovina in 1924 which was never recorded by the civil authorities or published in accordance with the formal requirements of the civil law in effect in the territory concerned and had subsequently obtained a rabbinical divorce decree terminating her marital relationship with her first husband. The 

Department of State informed the American Consul in Bucharest, Rumania, in answer to his inquiries, that in the light of its circular instruction of July 28, 1933 it was unable to conclude that the first

marriage was not valid, so far as the immigration laws were concerned, and thatmembers of the Hebrew faith, and various organizations representing such members, are repeatedly contending before the Department and American consular officers that marriages which have been celebrated only in accordance with the Hebrew _religion, and not in accordance with the civil laws of the place where such marriages were celebrated, should be recognized as valid marriages. Marriage being a matter of common right, and the validity of all marriages being presumed by law, a ruling was embodied in the Department's circular instruction mentioned above to the effect that the formal requirements of local laws need not be complied with in order to establish the validity of a marriage. No reason is perceived why a departure should now be made from such ruling.

In this connection it may be pointed out that, unlike marriage, divorce is not a matter of common right, and that the validity of a divorce depends upon the law of the place where the divorce was obtained, with this exception, that a divorce obtained by a person who did not have an actual residence within the jurisdiction of the court or tribunal issuing the divorce decree, will not be recognized as valid in the United States for the purposes of the immigration laws. Many courts of last resort in the States of the Union have held so-called "mail order" divorces to be invalid under their laws. 

It was pointed out that if the applicant should obtain a valid divorce from her first husband, and thereafter lawfully be married to the second, he might then file a new petition for non-quota status in his wife's behalf. 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Hibbard, Apr. 19, 1937, MS. Department of State, file 811.111 Barsky, Sally R.

CHAPTER VII EXEMPTIONS FROM TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION  GENERAL PRINCIPLE OF EXEMPTION 

$169 The principle that, generally speaking, each sovereign state is supreme within its own territory and that its jurisdiction extends to all persons and things within that territory is, under certain circumstances, subject to exceptions in favor particularly of foreign friendly sovereigns, their accredited diplomatic representatives, their organized armed forces when entering or crossing territory of the state with the consent of the territorial sovereign, and their public vessels and public property in the possession of and devoted to the service of the state. These exemptions from the local jurisdiction are theoretically based upon the consent, express or implied, of the local state, upon the principle of equality of states in the eyes of international law, and upon the necessity of yielding the local jurisdiction in these respects as an indispensable factor in the conduct of friendly intercourse between members of the family of nations. 

While it is sometimes stated that they are based upon international comity or courtesy, and while they doubtless find their origin therein, they may now be said to be based upon generally accepted custom and usage, i.e. international law. 

In an action brought against the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet 

Republic, the Court of Appeals of New York (in 1923) said:

The government itself is sued for an exercise of sovereignty within its own territories on the theory that such an act, if committed by an individual here, would be a tort under our system of municipal law. It is said that, because of nonrecognition by the United States, such an action may be maintained.

The result we reach depends upon more basic considerations than recognition or nonrecognition by the United States. ...

Here We have an existing government, sovereign within its own territories. There necessarily its jurisdiction is exclusive and absolute. It is susceptible of no limitation not imposed by itself. This is the result of its independence. It 393

CHAPTER VII—EXEMPTIONS FROM TERRITORIAL JURISDICTION Extinction of govern- ment may be conceded that its actions should accord with natural justice and equity. If they do not, however, our courts are not competent to review them. They may not bring a foreign sovereign before our bar, not because of comity, but because he has not submitted himself to our laws. Without his consent he is not subject to them. Concededly that is so as to a foreign government that has received recognition. 

In But, whether recognized or not, the evil of such an attempt would be the same. "To cite a foreign potentate into a municipal court for any complaint against him in his public capacity is contrary to the law of nations, and an insult which he is entitled to resent." De Haber v. Queen of Portugal, 17 Q.B. 171.

In either case, to do so would "vex the peace of nations." either case the hands of the state department would be tied. 

Unwillingly it would find itself involved in disputes it might think unwise. Such is not the proper method of redress, if a citizen of the United States is wronged. The question is a political one, not confided to the courts, but to another department of government. Whenever an act done by a sovereign in his sovereign character is questioned, it becomes a matter of negotiation, or of reprisals, or of war. 

Wulfsohn v. Russian Socialist Federated Soviet Republic, 234 N.Y. (1923) 

372, 375-376, 138 N.E. 24, 25, 26. See also Nankivel et al. v. Omsk All- 

Russian Government et al., 237 N.Y. (1923) 150, 142 N.E. 569.

In subsequent actions to recover on claims against defunct Russian governments, the New York courts held in accordance with the above case that such governments were immune even though they had never been recognized by the Government of the United States, and furthermore that upon their extinction no better claims to their funds than previously existed were acquired. 

The property of such a government belongs to the state, as sovereign, and, upon the overthrow of the de facto government, another government replacing it would succeed to the representative right of such de facto government in all of its property. 

Voevodine v. Government of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed 

Forces in the South of Russia et al., 249 N.Y. Supp. (1931) 644, 649; affirmed, 257 N.Y. (1931) 557, 178 N.E. 793. Nankivel et al. v. Omsk All- 

Russian Government et al., 237 N.Y. (1923) 150, 142 N.E. 569. 

On April 16, 1931 the Mexican Ambassador in Washington informed the Department of State that the Mexican Consulate General in New York city had been served with summons in a suit brought in the courts of New York against an international committee of bankers and the United States of Mexico. The Department, in a letter dated April 27, 1931 to the Governor of New York, stated that: 

It hardly seems necessary to point out that a foreign government may not be sued in the United States in the absence of

an applicable treaty without the expressed consent of that government. It is assumed from the Ambassador's note of April 

16, 1931, that the Mexican Government does not consent to be sued in the present case. Moreover, it seems to be well established that neither the Ambassador nor the Consular Officer of the country concerned has any authority to accept service on behalf of their Government.

The Governor was requested to take appropriate action looking to the dismissal of the suit against the Mexican Government. He replied on May 15, 1931, enclosing a letter from the office of the Attorney General of the State expressing the view that, although the Mexican Government could not be made a party without its consent, as to property within the court's jurisdiction the court could adjudicate as to the parties before it and that such adjudication, while not legally binding upon the Government of Mexico, might affect the property in a manner which the Government of Mexico could never overcome without becoming a party to the suit. The 

Supreme Court of New York proceeded to appoint receivers for part of the fund held by the committee. An appeal having been taken to the appellate division, the Mexican Ambassador, on June 26, 1931, requested the Department of State to inform the court that the funds in question were the property of the Government of Mexico and therefore not subject to seizure. The Department, on June 29, 1931, requested the Attorney General of the United

States to cause the appropriate district attorney to acquaint the court with the position of the Mexican Government. The court held that "the Government of Mexico is a necessary party in interest in the fund proposed to be impounded by this receivership order; and since it is a sovereign state and cannot be made a party without its consent, there was no jurisdiction to appoint receivers of its funds or to issue an injunction against the disposition thereof". 

Ambassador Téllez to Secretary Stimson, Apr. 16, 1931, and Mr. Stimson to Governor Lehman, Apr. 27, 1931, MS. Department of State, file 

812.51/1715; Mr. Lehman to Mr. Stimson, May 15, 1931, with enclosure, ibiá. 

812.51/1721; Señor Téllez to Mr. Stimson, June 26, 1931, and the Acting

Secretary of State (Castle) to the Attorney General of the United States (Mitchell), June 29, 1931, ibid. 812.51/1734; Gallopin v. Winsor, 251 N.Y. 

Supp. (1931) 448, 449. 

To similar effect, see Ezra v. Lamont, 268 N.Y. Supp. (1933) 222; 271 

N.Y. Supp. (1934) 951; 265 N.Y. (1934) 635, 193 N.E. 421; certiorari denied, 295 U. S. (1935) 766.

In a suit brought in the New York courts in connection with the same financial arrangements involved in the cases of Gallopin v. 

Winsor and Ezra v. Lamont, the American bondholders' committee (Thomas W. Lamont and others, individually and as the International Committee of Bankers on Mexico) petitioned for a volun- State cannot be sued without its consent

Juridical aspect tary accounting of moneys received by the committee of bankers.

The plea of the Mexican Government, which intervened in the case, that it was the owner of the funds and that the court was without jurisdiction, was sustained by the Supreme Court, New York County, and affirmed by the Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Department, 254 App. Div. (1938) 511, 5 N.Y. Supp. (2d) 295, on the same ground as the two decisions just referred to, namely, that the Government of Mexico was a necessary party in interest and that the court could not determine the validity of that Government's contentions when it declined to submit to the jurisdiction. The New 

York Court of Appeals reversed the decision of the lower courts stating: 

The mere assertion by the Government of Mexico that the committee holds the moneys not as trustee for the bondholders but as agents of the Government for distribution among the bondholders does not, we think, preclude the court from determining whether, under the contracts, the committee has acted and is acting solely as agent and trustee of the bondholders and not as agent of the government. 

The court referred to the decision in Compania Espanola de Navegacion 

Maritima, S.A. v. The Navemar, 303 U.S. (1937) 68 (post, p. 453), and stated that the court held that such a suggestion, made by a foreign government to the court, constitutes merely the statement of a claim by the foreign government, and is not proof of the allegations contained therein. The right of the foreign government to demand the return of its property or to demand that the court shall recognize that the property is immune from judicial control is, then "[an] appropriate [subject] for judicial inquiry upon proof of the matters alleged;" but the assertion of the claim gives to the foreign government only the right to intervene and prove its allegation that it owns the property. If, in this case, the allegations of the pleadings are sustained, that the plaintiffs hold moneys received from the Mexican Government in trust for the depositing bondholders, then the court can direct distribution of the fund without invading the sovereign immunity of the foreign government, without sitting in judgment on the acts of the government done within its own territory, and without interference with any property which belongs to the government or is in its own possession or in the possession of its agents. The foreign government does not become a necessary party to the action, unless the issues raised in the action by the pleadings of the parties in the action cannot be decided without the presence of the foreign government. No issue is raised merely by suggestion of a government which refuses to intervene and to present proof to sustain its allegations; and immunity from suit exists only where the object of the suit is to enforce a claim or right against the foreign government or its

property. The mere assertion by a foreign government, without proof, that property which is the subject of controversy between the parties here belongs to the government, does not constrain the court to refuse jurisdiction of that property. 

It is true, of course, as the court pointed out in Compania 

Espanola De Navegacion Maritima, S.A. v. The Navemar, supra 303 U.S. page 74, 58 S. Ct. page 434, 82 L. Ed. 667, that a foreign government may claim immunity from suit either in the court or through diplomatic channels, and "if the claim is recognized and allowed by the Executive Branch of the government, it is then the duty of the courts to [accept the claim of immunity] upon appropriate suggestion by the Attorney General of the United States, or other officer acting under his direction." Here, as the United States Attorney states, he has done no more than to "present" the suggestion of immunity, "at the request of the Secretary of State of the United States, through the Attorney General, following diplomatic representations made to the Secretary of State in behalf of the Government of Mexico," and the United States Attorney adds. significantly: "In bringing this matter to the attention of the 

Court I respectfully inform it that the United States does not intervene as an interested party and that I do not appear either for the United States or for the Government of Mexico, but I present this suggestion as a matter of comity between the Government of Mexico and the United States Government for such consideration as the Court may deem necessary and proper." 

It seems plain that such a presentation of a "suggestion" does not indicate that the executive branch of our government has recognized and allowed the claim of the Government of Mexico, and the court remains free to give to the claim of immunity "such consideration as the Court may deem necessary and proper." 

We hold only that the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to pass upon the issues raised in the pleadings in this action and to render appropriate judgment, unless it shall appear at the trial that the Government of Mexico has, in fact, retained some right or interest in the property which is the subject of the accounting, and is a necessary party to any adjudication. 

The orders should be reversed, without costs, and the motion to dismiss denied.

Lamont et al. v. Travelers Ins. Co. et al., 24 N.E. (2d) 81, 85-86 (1939) 

281 N.Y. 362.

In 1937 a Spanish vessel, registered at the port of Bilbao, was requisitioned by the Republican Government of Spain and, subsequently, in 1938 by the Nationalist Government of Spain. At no date material to the case under discussion was the vessel in Spanish waters. The vessel having subsequently come into British territorial waters, the Republican Government caused a writ in rem to be issued against it with the object of obtaining possession. The judge of the 

Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty Division caused a letter to be written to the British Foreign Office asking whether the British Govern-

ment recognized the Nationalist Government of Spain as a foreign sovereign state. In reply it was stated that the Nationalist Government was recognized as a government exercising de facto administrative control over the larger portion of Spain including the Basque Provinces and that it was not a government subordinate to any other government in Spain. The House of Lords, in affirming decisions of the lower courts setting aside the writ, said:

There is ample authority for the proposition that there is no difference for the present purposes between a recognition of a State de facto as opposed to de jure. All the reasons for immunity which are the basis of the doctrine in international law as incorporated into our law exist. There is the same necessity for reciprocal rights of immunity, the same feeling of injured pride if jurisdiction is sought to be exercised, the same risk of belligerent action if Government property is seized or injured. The non-belligerent State which recognizes two Governments, one de jure and the other de facto, will not allow them to transfer their quarrels to the area of the jurisdiction of its municipal Courts.

For these reasons I think that it was established by the Foreign Office letter that the Nationalist Government of Spain at the date of the writ was a foreign sovereign State and could not be impleaded.

Government of the Republic of Spain and S. S. "Arantzazu Mendi”, [1939] A.C. 256, 265. 

In actions brought in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York by the Banque de France against two New York banks, it appeared that in 1917 the plaintiff had entrusted a quantity of gold to the State Bank of the Russian Empire for safekeeping, that this gold had been seized by the Soviet Government, and that the plaintiff now sought to recover, as the rightful owner, certain gold placed on deposit with the defendants by order and for the account of the State Bank of the U.S.S.R., even though it was not necessarily the identical gold which had been seized by the Soviet Government. Defendants set up certain matters as separate defenses, two of which alleged that the gold was immune from judicial process in these actions and that the determination of the actions would involve an examination of the acts of the Soviet Government within its own territory. At the time of the proceedings, the Soviet 

Government had not received the recognition of the Government of the United States. In denying motions to strike these defenses, the court, on March 21, 1929, said:

It is to be noted that the answer sets up that the shipments of gold in question were shipped by the State Bank of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and that it appears from the pleadings of the plaintiff that its gold was seized by the Government of

Immunity from process Russia and that the State Bank of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was a part of said government, so that the plaintiff is here asserting that the gold in question is claimed by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics in opposition to the plaintiff's rights, and the result is a suit brought in this jurisdiction which involves the title to property claimed by the Russian Government, and that leads to the consideration of the question: Who is the sovereign de facto or de jure in Russia? And this is not a judicial but is a political question, and it is immaterial whether the foreign sovereign has been recognized or not. Wulfsohn v. Russian 

Republic, supra; Jones v. United States, 137 U.S. 202, 11 S. Ct. 

80, 34 L. Ed. 691.

Furthermore, it is alleged by the plaintiff itself that the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is a foreign government, so that as in the Wulfsohn Case, it is unnecessary for that fact to be made known to the court by a formal "suggestion" through the State Department. Thus, it appears that this court is not in a position to pass upon the issue, not because of nonrecognition but simply for the reason, as stated by Judge Andrews in Wulfsohn v. Russian, etc., Republic, supra, at page 376 of 234 N.Y. (138 N.E. 

26): "They may not bring a foreign sovereign before our bar, not because of comity, but because he has not submitted himself to our laws. Without his consent he is not subject to them." 

Therefore, in my judgment both of these alleged defenses should be permitted to stand. 

Banque de France v. Equitable Trust Co. of New York, Same v. Chase 

Nat. Bank of City of New York, 33 F. (2d) 202, 207 (S.D.N.Y., 1929).

The holders of certain Ecuadoran railway bonds, to the payment of which the Ecuadoran Government had pledged certain customs receipts, brought suit in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York claiming that the defendants had been paid by the Government of Ecuador funds from the customs receipts to which the plaintiffs were entitled, and in disregard of the plaintiffs' prior lien thereon. The court refused to entertain jurisdiction of the suit and was sus tained by the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Second Cir cuit, which said that- "it is evident that the title of Speyer & Co. to the money herein involved is derived from the government of Ecuador and that the court cannot grant the relief invoked without sitting in judgment upon the sovereign acts of that nation. This very clearly it is not within the province of the court to do." Hewitt v. Speyer et al., 248 Fed. 590 (S.D.N.Y., 1917); 250 Fed. 

367, 370 (C.C.A. 2d, 1918). Compare The Luigi, 230 Fed. 493 (E.D. Pa., 

1916), and post, § 173; also The Jupiter (No. 2), [1925] P. 69, 78, post, § 173. 

On July 9, 1929 an action was instituted in the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia against the Government of Turkey. Summons was issued directed to the Government of the Republic of Turkey, which the United States Marshal on the advice of the district attorney refused to serve upon the Turkish Ambassador. At the instance of the Department of State, acting pursuant to a request of

the Turkish Ambassador, the Attorney General of the United States caused the court to be notified that the Turkish Government did not consent to be sued and that the Ambassador had no right to accept suit. The plaintiff then petitioned the court for a writ of mandamus requiring the appropriate officers to cause the Ambassador to be served with summons. Upon motion for an order to show cause why the mandamus should not issue the court held that a sovereign could not be sued without its consent, saying:

The court takes judicial notice of the fact that by no treaty has the Government of Turkey consented to be sued in this court or any other court in the United States. It also takes judicial notice of the fact that the Government of the United States has recognized the present Government of Turkey as a sovereignty, and that the President has recognized as its duly accredited 

Ambassador, His Excellency, Ahmed Mouhtar Bey. 

That a sovereignty may not be sued without its consent is settled law in the United States and the principle has been applied in attempted suits against both the State and the United States Governments. And with at least equal force the same principle has been recognized and applied in the field of international law, in cases where attempts have been made to sue foreign governments in courts other than those of their own countries. 

The motion was accordingly denied and the petition was dismissed. 

Secretary Stimson to Attorney General Mitchell, July 23, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 467.11 Cardashian, Vahan/5; the Assistant Attorney 

General (Farnum) to Mr. Stimson, Aug. 14, 1929, ibid. 467.11 Cardashian, Vahan/7; Cardashian v. Snyder, et al., 57 Wash. L. Rep. (1929) 738.

In a case involving the question whether the Territory of Hawaii could be joined as a defendant in a suit on a mortgage, it was held that- the doctrine [of sovereign immunity from suit] is not confined Organized to powers that are sovereign in the full sense of juridical theory, territories but naturally is extended to those that in actual administration originate and change at their will the law of contract and property, from which persons within the jurisdiction derive their rights. A suit presupposes that the defendants are subject to the law invoked. Of course it cannot be maintained unless they are so. But that is not the case with a territory of the United States, because the Territory itself is the fountain from which rights ordinarily flow. It is true that Congress might intervene, just as in the case of a State the Constitution does, and the power that can alter the Constitution might. But the rights that exist are not created by Congress or the Constitution, except to the extent of certain limitations of power.

Upon a motion by the Principality of Monaco to the Supreme Court of the United States for leave to bring suit against the State of Mississippi on certain State bonds, the Court denied the motion, saying: 

There is .. the postulate that States of the Union, still possessing attributes of sovereignty, shall be immune from suits, without their consent, save where there has been "a surrender of this immunity in the plan of the convention." The 

Federalist, No. 81.

The waiver or consent, on the part of a State, which inheres in the acceptance of the constitutional plan, runs to the other States who have likewise accepted that plan, and to the United States as the sovereign which the Constitution creates. We perceive no ground upon which it can be said that any waiver or consent by a State of the Union has run in favor of a foreign State. As to suits brought by a foreign 

State, we think that the States of the Union retain the same immunity that they enjoy with respect to suits by individuals whether citizens of the United States or citizens or subjects of a foreign State. 

Principality of Monaco v. Mississippi, 292 U.S. (1934) 313, 322-323, 330.

In a suit brought in New Jersey against a corporation "created by the State of Yucatan to carry out, or assist in carrying out certain policies of that government with reference to the growth and sale of sisal hemp", which was held not to be immune from suit, the court said:

I have thus far dealt with the case as if the state of Yucatan was one of the sovereign states which is immune from the jurisdiction of the courts of another state. That view is too favorable to the defendants. It is clear from the affidavits and the extracts from official documents, translations of which have been attached, that Yucatan is a member of the federated state of Mexico, and in external relations the United States of Mexico is alone sovereign. 

---

The members of a federal republic are universally treated as having no independent existence as states in their external relations. Lacking this independence, they lack the very foundation for the right to immunity from judicial process. 

Molina v. Comision Reguladora del Mercado de Henequen, 91 N.J.L. (1918) 382, 390-391, 103 Atl. 397, 400-401.

Ceara, In an appeal by the State of Ceara of Brazil to the Court of Cassation on the issue of its immunity from suit in the courts of France, the court held that the rule of immunity "is to be applied Brazil only when it is invoked by an entity which shows itself to have a personality of its own in its relations with other countries considered from the point of view of public international law" and that such was not the case with Ceara for "whatever may be its internal status in the sovereign confederation of the United States of Brazil of which it is a part it is deprived of diplomatic representation abroad and from the point of view of international political relations it does not enjoy a personality of its own". The appeal was rejected. État de Ceara c. Dorr et autres, Dalloz, Recueil periodique et critique (1933), 196; Hudson, Cases on International Law (2d ed., 1936) 510.

To similar effect, see the decision of the New York Supreme Court in

(Apr. 30, 1937) 2160. raised In an action in New York against a German company in which Immunity some of defendant's property was attached, one of the grounds of a properly motion to vacate the attachment was the alleged sovereign immunity of the defendant. In passing upon this question the court said: 

The claim of sovereign immunity will be instantly recognized, and operates as soon as interposed to end the proceedings. For a court to act on any other assumption would constitute an intolerable insult to a friendly government. However, such a claim must be properly and explicitly raised. 

The motion was denied principally on the ground that dependence was had upon an affidavit of a German consul general stating that he had been authorized by the Government of Germany to engage the attorneys to appear specially on behalf of the German Government.

$170 The Gaekwar of Baroda being named corespondent in a suit for divorce in England requested the court to dismiss the suit as to him on the ground that he was a reigning sovereign and by the rules of international law not amenable to the jurisdiction of the court. The court found him to be in fact an independent sovereign and ordered his name struck out, stating:

There is no doubt that an independent reigning sovereign cannot by the rules of international law be made against his will a party to proceedings in our Courts.

Statham v. Statham and His Highness the Gaekwar of Baroda, [1912]

MILITARY FORCES

Armed force

On December 5, 1924 military authorities in the Panama Canal Zone ordered a soldier to transport an injured man by ambulance into the city of Colón, Panama. While being driven in the city of Colón, pursuant to this order, the ambulance was involved in an accident, as a result of which a man was killed. Criminal proceedings were in foreign instituted against the soldier in the courts of Panama and the case territory was ultimately ruled upon by the Supreme Court of Justice of the Republic on August 11, 1925. The decision referred to the convention for the construction of a ship canal concluded by the United 

States and Panama on November 18, 1903 (2 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 

1910] 1349) and stated:

In accordance with the text of that treaty, the Canal Zone authorities may employ their forces, assigned for the protection of the Canal, to assure the security, operation and sanitation of the same, and in such case those forces, when acting in the name or on behalf of the Government of the United States, are subject to the authority and jurisdiction to which they belong, and not to our national authorities; nor to both simultaneously, because such a double jurisdiction is contrary to law. 

It is a principle of international law that the armed force of one state, when crossing the territory of another friendly country, with the acquiescence of the latter, is not subject to the jurisdiction of the territorial sovereign, but to that of the officers and superior authorities of its own command. 

In such case the government to which the army belongs is responsible for any damages that may be caused by the passage of the force, and for any violations of local law which it may commit. But individually its members remain subject to the jurisdiction of their own officers, and to the laws of the country to which they belong.

This exemption from the local jurisdiction is recognized by all civilized nations; and is not considered a diminution of their sovereignty or independence.

The court concluded that "since cognizance of the matter pertains to another jurisdiction, the judicial authorities of the Republic of Panama have no power to judge the accused". 

The Republic of Panama v. Wilbert L. Schwartzfiger, 24 Registro judicial (Panamá, 1926) 772; 21 A.J.I.L. (1927) 182, translation.

In 1918 the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals reviewed the decision of a lower court convicting and sentencing to death certain Mexican soldiers who had engaged in a skirmish on American soil as a result of which some American soldiers were killed. The incident took place in connection with border difficulties during which 

American soldiers under General Pershing invaded Mexico and

Mexican soldiers engaged in skirmishes on American soil. The court said that the soldiers under sentence were members of a "force organized at Monterey by the direction and under the authority of the Carranza de facto government". It decided that if at that time a state of actual war existed between the United States and Mexico, the question of defendants' guilt was an international or federal, rather than a state, matter. It pointed out that American soldiers similarly captured in Mexico were not tried by the Mexican courts but were turned over to the United States, that the Mexican soldiers were acting strictly under the compulsion of their superior officers, and that if the State court had jurisdiction, the conviction was erroneous. It concluded that from any viewpoint the judgment of the lower court should be reversed. 

Arce et al. v. State, 38 Tex. Cr. R. (1918) 292, 202 S.W. 951. 

By the act approved August 29, 1842 (Rev. Stat., sec. 753; 28 U.S.C. §453) it is provided that the writ of habeas corpus shall be withheld from prisoners in jail "unless being a subject or citizen of a foreign State, and domiciled therein, [he] is in custody for an act done or omitted under any alleged right, title, authority, privilege, protection, or exemption claimed under the commission, or order, or sanction of any foreign State, or under color thereof, the validity and effect whereof depend upon the law of nations . . ." 

A person imprisoned for illegal interstate transportation of explosives sought release by a writ of habeas corpus, contending that the above exception was applicable in as much as he was a German Army officer and the alleged criminal act was necessary to the destruction of a bridge in territory of the British Government, with which Germany was at war. The court held that even if the act were applicable, the petitioner had not come within the exception stipulated, in that it was not shown that he was domiciled in Germany or that he had acted pursuant to orders of German authorities. In affirming this decision, the United States Circuit Court of

Appeals for the First Circuit said that the fact that he was commissioned in the German Army did not constitute sufficient proof that he was authorized to act in this manner in the United States. 

Horn v. Mitchell, U.S. Marshal, 223 Fed. 549 (D.C. Mass., 1915); 232 

Fed. 819 (C.C.A. 1st, 1916). See I Hyde, International Law, etc. (1922) 

435, n. 1. See also United States v. Thierichens, post §172.

During the World War, the Department of State was in receipt of several communications from the British Embassy requesting that British military personnel and freight owned by the British Government be exempted from taxes imposed upon transportation by section 

500 of the War Revenue Act approved October 3, 1917 (40 Stat. 

314), and pointing out that personnel and supplies of the Government of the United States had been accorded preferential treatment in Great Britain. In a note of March 8, 1919 the Acting Secretary of State informed the British Ambassador on Special Mission that the replies received from the appropriate authorities indicated that the requested exemptions could not be granted; the note stated in part:

With regard to the exemption of British military personnel from the tax imposed on transportation by Section 500 of the Act approved October 3, 1917, you are informed that a communication has been received from the Treasury Department stating that the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, acting under the Secretary of the Treasury, is charged with the duty of administering the internal revenue laws of the United States; that after 

Congress has enacted a statute imposing a specific tax, the Treasury Department has no discretion in the administration of such a taxing measure, but is obliged to see to it that such taxes are collected, and under these circumstances the Secretary of the Treasury has no authority to take any steps with a view to according preferential treatment to British military personnel and stores on account of preferential privileges having been accorded United States troops and freight in Great Britain. ... no distinction will be made between imposition of the tax levied on passenger fares, provided for by Section 500 (c) of the Act of Congress approved October 3, 1917, and the imposition of the tax on freight charges, provided by Section 500 (a) of that Act.

In this relation it may be stated that it appears that the exemption of foreign Governments from the payment of the transportation tax was considered by Congress in connection with the recent revenue legislation. As the revenue bill, as passed by Congress, contains no provision for the exemption of any foreign Government from the transportation tax, it would appear that an adverse decision must have been reached by 

Congress with regard to this matter.

The Acting Secretary of State (Polk) to the Earl of Reading, Ambassador of Great Britain on Special Mission, no. 351, Mar. 8, 1919, MS. Department of State, file 811.512/162.

United States.

VESSELS OF WAR 

§172 The vessels of war of a foreign state, when under the command of responsible officers of and in the service of that state, are granted immunities from the jurisdiction of another friendly state in the ports, harbors, or roadsteads of the latter. They are organs or instrumentalities of the foreign state and when on friendly missions to ports open to them in another state are accorded immunity from the local jurisdiction of a character analogous to that accorded the foreign sovereign. This does not mean that a ship of war may freely enter the ports of a foreign state wholly in disregard of the wishes of that state or of regulations established by it for the entry and departure of such vessels. The practice generally observed in these respects is for the state whose vessel expects to make a call, to ascertain in advance whether such call would be agreeable to the state to be visited and for the vessel to make the visit only after a

favorable response has been received. This customary procedure does not of course apply to a ship of war that is driven into a port or the territory of a foreign state by reason of stress of weather or unseaworthiness.

The jurisdiction of the home state over the ship of war and over all persons and goods on board continues to attach even in foreign ports. The vessel is not subject to libel or other proceedings for debts, damages for collision, salvage service, or other causes. It may not be boarded by officials of the state visited without the permission of the commanding officer.

Oppenheim states with reference to vessels of war: 

The position of men-of-war in foreign waters is characterized by the fact that they are called "floating portions of the flag- State." For at the present time there is a customary rule of 

International Law, universally recognized, that the State owning the waters into which foreign men-of-war enter must treat them in every point as though they were floating portions of their flag-State. Consequently, a man-of-war, with all persons and goods on board, remains under the jurisdiction of her flag-State even during her stay in foreign waters. No legal proceedings can be taken against her either for recovery of possession or for damages for collision, or for a salvage reward, or for any other cause. No official of the littoral State is allowed to board the vessel without special permission of the commander. Crimes committed on board by persons in the service of the vessel are Criminal under the exclusive jurisdiction of the commander and the other jurisdiction home authorities. Individuals who are subjects of the littoral 

State, and are only temporarily on board, may, although they need not, be taken to the home country of the vessel, to be punished there, if they commit a crime on board. Even individuals who do not belong to the crew, and who, after having committed a crime on the territory of the littoral State, have taken refuge on board, cannot be forcibly taken off the vessel; if the commander refuses their surrender, it can be obtained only by diplomatic means from the home State. 

On the other hand, men-of-war cannot do what they like in foreign waters. They are expected to comply voluntarily with the laws of the littoral States with regard to order in the ports, the places for casting anchor, sanitation and quarantine, customs, and the like. A man-of-war which refuses to do so can be expelled, and, of [if] on such or other occasions she commits acts of violence against the officials of the littoral State or against other vessels, steps may be taken against her to prevent further acts of violence. But it must be emphasized that, even by committing acts of violence, a man-of-war does not fall under the jurisdiction of the littoral State. Only such measures are allowed against her as are necessary to prevent her from further acts of violence.

I Oppenheim's International Law (5th ed., by Lauterpacht, 1937) 666-668.

Theories of immunity A murder involving members of the crew of a Chinese armed public ship-the Chinese Maritime Customs cruiser Cheung Kengtook place in 1937 on board the vessel, at that time in British territorial waters. The vessel put in at Hong Kong where the accused, who was wounded, was taken to a hospital. The Chinese Government instituted extradition proceedings which failed because the accused was of British nationality. The accused was then tried, convicted, and sentenced to death in the courts of Hong Kong, whereupon he brought an appeal in the House of Lords, relying strongly upon the contention that the alleged crime occurred, in effect, upon Chinese soil. Lord Atkin, delivering the judgment of the House of Lords, said:

On the question of jurisdiction two theories have found favour with persons professing a knowledge of the principles of international law. One is that a public ship of a nation for all purposes either is, or is to be treated by other nations as, part of the territory of the nation to which she belongs. By this conception will be guided the domestic law of any country in whose territorial waters the ship finds herself. There will therefore be no jurisdiction in fact in any Court where jurisdiction depends upon the act in question, or the party to the proceedings, being done or found or resident in the local territory. The other theory is that a public ship in foreign waters is not, and is not treated as, territory of her own nation. The domestic Courts, in accordance with principles of international law, will accord to the ship and its crew and its contents certain immunities, some of which are well settled, though others are in dispute. In this view, the immunities do not depend upon an objective exterritoriality, but on implication of the domestic law. They are conditional, and can in any case be waived by the nation to which the public ship belongs.

Their Lordships entertain no doubt that the latter is the correct conclusion.

After discussing The Schooner Exchange v. M'Fadden & Others, 7 Cranch (1812) 116, and writings on both sides of the issue the court proceeded: 

Their Lordships have no hesitation in rejecting the doctrine of exterritoriality expressed in the words of Mr. Oppenheim, which regards the public ship "as a floating portion of the flag-State." [Quoted ante.] However the doctrine of exterritoriality is expressed, it is a fiction, and legal fictions have a tendency to pass beyond their appointed bounds and to harden into dangerous facts. The truth is that the enunciators of the floating island theory have failed to face very obvious possibilities that make the doctrine quite impracticable when tested by the actualities of life on board ship and ashore. Immunities may well be given in respect of the conduct of members of the crew to one another on board ship. If one member of the crew assault another on

board, it would be universally agreed that the local Courts would not seek to exercise jurisdiction, and would decline it unless, indeed, they were invited to exercise it by competent authority of the flag-nation. But if a resident in the receiving 

State visited the public ship and committed theft, and returned to shore, is it conceivable that, when he was arrested on shore, and shore witnesses were necessary to prove dealings with the stolen goods and identify the offender, the local Courts would have no jurisdiction? What is the captain of the public ship to do? Can he claim to have the local national surrendered to him? He would have no claim to the witnesses, or to compel their testimony in advance, or otherwise. He naturally would leave the case to the local Courts. But on this hypothesis the crime has been committed on a portion of foreign territory. 

The local Court then has no jurisdiction, and this fiction dismisses the offender untried and untriable. For it is a commonplace that a foreign country cannot give territorial jurisdiction by consent. Similarly, in the analogous case of an embassy. 

Is it possible that the doctrines of international law are so rigid that a local burglar who has broken and entered a foreign embassy and, having completed his crime, is arrested in his own country, cannot be tried in the Courts of the country? It is only necessary to test the proposition to assume that the foreign country has assented to the jurisdiction of the local Courts. 

Even so, objective exterritoriality would, for the reason given above, deprive our Courts at any rate of any jurisdiction in such a case. The result of any such doctrine would be not to promote the power and dignity of the foreign sovereign, but to lower them by allowing injuries committed in his public ships or embassies to go unpunished.

On this topic, their Lordships agree with the remarks made by 

Professor Brierly in The Law of Nations (1928), p. 110: "The term 'exterritoriality' is commonly used to describe the status of a person or thing physically present in a State's territory, but wholly or partly withdrawn from that State's jurisdiction by a rule of international law, but for many reasons it is an objectionable term. It introduces a fiction, for the person or thing is in fact within, and not outside, the territory: it implies that jurisdiction and territory always coincide, whereas they do so only generally; and it is misleading because we are tempted to forget that it is only a metaphor, and to deduce untrue legal consequences from it as though it were a literal truth. At most it means nothing more than that a person or thing has some immunity from the local jurisdiction; it does not help us to determine the only important question, namely, how far this immunity extends."

The true view is that, in accordance with the conventions of international law, the territorial sovereign grants to foreign sovereigns and their envoys, and public ships and the naval forces carried by such ships, certain immunities. Some are well settled; others are uncertain. When the local Court is faced with a case where such immunities come into question, it has to decide whether in the particular case the immunity exists or not. If it 

---

is clear that it does, the Court will of its own initiative give effect to it. The sovereign himself, his envoy, and his property, including his public armed ships, are not to be subjected to legal process. These immunities are well settled. In relation to the particular subject of the present dispute, the crew of a warship, it is evident that the immunities extend to internal disputes between the crew. Over offences committed on board ship by one member of the crew upon another, the local Courts would not exercise jurisdiction. The foreign sovereign could not be supposed to send his vessel abroad if its internal affairs were to be interfered with, and members of the crew withdrawn from its service, by local jurisdiction. What are the precise limits of the immunities it is not necessary to consider. Questions have arisen as to the exercise of jurisdiction over members of a foreign crew who commit offences on land. It is not necessary for their 

Lordships to consider these. In the present case, the question arises as to the murder of one officer, and the attempted murder of another, by a member of the crew. If nothing more arose, the Chinese Government could clearly have had jurisdiction over the offence; and, though the offender had, for reasons of humanity, been taken to a local hospital, a diplomatic request for his surrender would appear to have been in order. It is difficult to see why the fact that either the victim or the offender, or both, are local nationals, should make a difference if both are members of the crew. But this request was never made. The only request was for extradition, which is based upon treaty and statutory rights, and in the circumstances inevitably failed. But if the principles which their Lordships have been discussing are accepted, the immunities which the local Courts recognize flow from a waiver by the local sovereign of his full territorial jurisdiction, and can themselves be waived. The strongest instances of such waiver are the not infrequent cases where a sovereign has, as it is said, submitted to the jurisdiction of a foreign Court over his rights of property. Here is no question of saying you may treat an offence committed on my territory as committed on yours. Such a statement by a foreign sovereign would count for nothing in our jurisprudence. But a sovereign may say, you have waived your jurisdiction in certain cases, but I prefer in this case that you should exercise it. The original jurisdiction in such a case flows afresh. 

The court held that the Chinese Government had, "once the extradition proceedings were out of the way, consented to the British 

Court exercising jurisdiction", because it had "not only with full knowledge of the proceedings but at two different dates made no further claim, permitted four members of their service to give evidence before the British Court in aid of the prosecution". The appeal was accordingly dismissed.

Chung Chi Cheung v. The King, [1939] A.C. 160, 174–176.

In 1925 officials of Cherbourg, France, acting under a city ordinance, demanded the payment of certain local taxes on food and other Taxation of supplies supplies carried on board a United States naval vessel and consumed during a visit at that port. The American Ambassador was instructed: 

As it appears to be a recognized principle of international law that national ships of war when in a friendly foreign port are in general exempt from the jurisdiction of that port, the Embassy is requested to bring this case to the attention of the French Foreign Office, and to express the hope of this Government that no further attempts will be made to assess taxes against American ships of war in French ports. 

The French Foreign Office replied that it is as a customary courtesy, and not by exemption from jurisdiction, and under condition of reciprocity that foreign warships are exempt from all customs and octroi duties on articles destined for use on board during their stay in a port. 

The Ambassador was further instructed: 

It is the view of the Department that an effort to tax supplies of a war vessel, under circumstances obtaining in this case, is inconsistent with the courtesies usually extended to a foreign ship of war by the authorities of a port to which such ship may be paying a friendly visit. The assessment of a tax on supplies carried aboard such a vessel is in effect the assertion of jurisdiction over the vessel and, accordingly, is hardly reconcilable with the principle of public law that national ships of war entering the ports of a friendly power open for their reception are considered to be exempted by the consent of that power from its jurisdiction.

In connection with the question of reciprocity raised by the French Foreign Office, you should point out that Section 446 of the Tariff Act of 1922 [42 Stat. 953] provides that "vessels arriving in the United States from foreign ports may retain on board, without the payment of duty, all coal and other fuel supplies, ships' stores, sea stores, and the legitimate equipment of such vessels. Any such supplies, ships' stores, sea stores, or equipment landed and delivered from such vessel shall be considered and treated as imported merchandise This privilege is extended not only to vessels of war but also to merchant vessels. 

The Treasury Department has informed this Department that supplies used on board a French vessel in a United States port in the manner in which the supplies were used on the U.S.S. 

Pittsburgh would not have been treated as imported merchandise, and that no duty would have been assessed. 

You will inform the Foreign Office that this Government feels confident that the French Government on having brought to its

attention the facts herein set forth will agree that the attempt to assess octroi duties on the supplies of the U.S.S. Pittsburgh was not proper.
