On August 7, 1935 the Chargé d'Affaires of Ecuador, in Washington, informed the Department of State of the purchase by his Government of a vessel intended for use as a naval training vessel and requested exemption from the sales tax imposed upon the transaction by the city of New York, where the sale took place. The 

Chargé's request was communicated to authorities of the city of New York who replied on August 28, 1935 requesting the opinion of the Department as to whether, under the law, the Government of Ecuador should pay the tax or was exempt by treaty. The Department stated: 

The question as to whether the sale would be taxable would depend upon whether the tax is one imposed upon the Ecuadoran Government or upon the vendor of the property. It is well settled in international law that the public property of foreign governments is not amenable to the local jurisdiction for tax purposes. If, on the other hand, the tax is imposed upon the seller of the property and is merely passed on to the foreign government as part of the purchase price, immunity from the tax could hardly be claimed by the foreign government. Taxes imposed by the Federal Government on cables, telegrams, transportation tickets and similar services are not assessed against official messages of foreign governments and transportation tickets purchased by their diplomatic representatives in the 

United States.

While there is no treaty between the United States and Ecuador bearing on the subject it is hoped nevertheless that the City of New York may see its way clear to relieve the Ecuadoran 

Government of payment of the tax.

On August 7, 1934 the Portuguese Legation inquired of the Department of State with respect to the facilities which the United States was prepared to extend to naval vessels of Portugal visiting the United States, on a reciprocal basis. It was stated in reply that

foreign naval vessels are granted free naval wharfage and tugboat facilities, if available, when requested through the Department of State, it being "understood that the United States assumes no liability for damages incident to such use"; that naval officers arrange for a dock or anchorage, usually "assigned without charge by the local port authorities", and assist in other ways; that under section 309 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (46 Stat., pt. 1, p. 690) supplies (not including equipment) may be withdrawn from bonded warehouses free of duty or internal-revenue tax for certain classes of vessels, including naval vessels, of any nation reciprocating such privileges toward naval vessels of the United States in its ports; that foreign naval vessels are given the same privileged quarantine treatment as are naval vessels of the United States, without charge, and that necessary American consular bills of health are furnished by American consular officers without charge; that no entry fees, lighthouse dues, tonnage taxes, or port charges are collected in such cases; that towing and wharfage charges are not collected by the Government, but are made by private interests for services rendered on request of visiting war vessels; and that the Government of the United States was prepared to extend these facilities reciprocally to the Portuguese Government.

During the World War of 1914-18 the Appam, a British merchant vessel, was made captive by a German cruiser and placed in charge of an officer who, acting under instructions, brought it to the United States with the intention of laying it up. The vessel was libeled by the owners who sought to recover it upon the claim that holding and detaining the vessel in American waters was in violation of the law of nations and the laws of the United States and of the neutrality of the United States. 

The German Ambassador in Washington, on February 22, 1916, protested to the Department of State against the action of the United States District Court in taking jurisdiction of the libel, stating that "The sovereign whose officers have captured the vessel as a prize of war remains in possession of that vessel and has full power over her", and that the "neutral sovereign or its court can take no cognizance of the question of prize or no prize and cannot wrest from the possession of the captor a prize of war brought into its ports". 

After reviewing the facts of the case and concluding that neither by virtue of treaties nor by virtue of the rules of international law relating to prize did the German Government have the right to lay up the Appam indefinitely in an American port, the Department stated in its reply of March 2, 1916:

Whether in these circumstances the United States Court has properly or improperly assumed jurisdiction of the case and taken custody of the ship, is a legal question which, according to American practice, must now be decided by the municipal courts of this country. With the purpose, however, of having Your 

Excellency's views as to this matter brought to the attention of the court, I have transmitted your note of February 22d to the 

Attorney General with a request that he instruct the United

States District Attorney to appear in the case as amicus curiae and present to the court a copy of Your Excellency's note. 

Count von Bernstorff to Secretary Lansing, Feb. 22, 1916, and Mr. Lansing to Count von Bernstorff, Mar. 2, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 

763.72111 Ap. 4/108; 1916 For. Rel. Supp. 722–745.

The District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Virginia ordered the vessel restored to its owners. The Supreme 

Court of the United States, in affirming this decision, quoted from

the early decisions of Glass v. The Sloop Betsey, 3 Dall.

(1794) 6, and The Santissima Trinidad, 7 Wheat. (1822) 283, and continued: 

It is insisted that these cases involve illegal captures at sea, or violations of neutral obligation, not arising because of the use of a port by sending in a captured vessel and keeping her there in violation of our rights as a neutral. But we are at a loss to see any difference in principle between such cases and breaches of neutrality of the character here involved in undertaking to make of an American port a depository of captured vessels with a view to keeping them there indefinitely. 

Nor can we consent to the insistence of counsel for appellant that the Prize Court of the German Empire has exclusive jurisdiction to determine the fate of the Appam as lawful prize. 

The vessel was in an American port and under our practice within the jurisdiction and possession of the District Court which had assumed to determine the alleged violation of neutral rights, with power to dispose of the vessel accordingly. The foreign tribunal under such circumstances could not oust the jurisdiction of the local court and thereby defeat its judgment. 

The Santissima Trinidad, supra, p. 355.

Were the rule otherwise than this court has frequently declared it to be, our ports might be filled in case of a general war such as is now in progress between the European countries, with captured prizes of one or the other of the belligerents, in utter violation of the principles of neutral obligation which have controlled this country from the beginning. 

The violation of American neutrality is the basis of jurisdiction, and the admiralty courts may order restitution for a violation of such neutrality. In each case the jurisdiction and order rests upon the authority of the courts of the United States to make restitution to private owners for violations of neutrality where offending vessels are within our jurisdiction, thus vindicating our rights and obligations as a neutral people. 

The Appam, 234 Fed. 389 (E.D. Va., 1916); The Steamship Appam, 243 

U.S. (1917) 124, 155–156.

On April 9, 1914 a paymaster and boat's crew of the U.S.S. 

Dolphin, sent ashore at Tampico, Mexico, in a boat flying the American flag, to take aboard supplies, were arrested by an officer and squad of men of the army of General Huerta. The prisoners were compelled to march along one of the streets and were then taken back to the boat and released, the local Mexican general expressing his regrets. The admiral in command at once demanded of the 

Mexican military authorities formal disavowal and apologies, punishment of the officer in command of the squad, and a salute to the American flag. On April 11, 1914 the Department of State instructed the Chargé d'Affaires in Mexico City that the President had approved the admiral's demands. The government of General 

Huerta, while expressing regret and undertaking to investigate the responsibility of the officer, declined to consent to the latter part of the demand, claiming that the marines had landed at a place subject to military authority, that "The sovereignty of Mexico in accord with international practice was not limited in this respect because the city was subject to military operations", and that "the marines violated the military laws to which the city was then subject when they disembarked". It said that the offending officer was under orders to defend that particular place, that the disembarkation of the marines there was without previous advice or permission, and that the incident was the result of a misunderstanding. 

The Department of State, on April 14, 1914, instructed the Chargé d'Affaires to inform General Huerta that the American Government "cannot believe that the landing of the marines was really regarded in anything but its true light" and that the marines had not been warned that a landing at that place was contrary to regulations and that:

Even if they were acting contrary to the regulations governing that particular landing-place, the remedy should have been a request to them to withdraw and a notification to

their commanding officer of the real situation. In no conceivable circumstances, while peace between the two countries exists, could the arrest and even temporary detention of regularly commissioned officers and enlisted men of this Government by 

Mexican authorities have been excusable.

The refusal of General Huerta to comply with the expectations of the Government of the United States led ultimately to the occupation of Veracruz by forces of the United States on April 21, 1914.

On June 5, 1911 the Ambassador in Japan reported to the Department of State the murder of one United States naval enlisted man by another in a United States naval hospital ashore. The Ambassador stated that he had informally requested of the Japanese Foreign Office that American naval officials be allowed to take jurisdiction, but that the request had been refused. The Department, on June 7, 1911, instructed the Ambassador that "Unless the practice of other nations is contrary, you should concede jurisdiction to Japan, at the same time indicating that this Government would prefer by courtesy to try the prisoner." The man was later tried and convicted by a Japanese court.

The commander of a German naval vessel interned in a port of the United States during the World War, was indicted for smuggling certain goods into the port of Philadelphia. In dismissing defendant's motion to quash the indictments on grounds of immunity, the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of 

Pennsylvania said:

The well-settled rule that, under the comity existing between nations, the public armed ship of a friendly nation, acting under the immediate and direct command of the sovereign power, is not to be interfered with by the courts of a foreign state, is based upon the principle that, if the courts did attempt to assume jurisdiction over such vessel, it would require the sovereign of the nation to which the vessel belongs to be impleaded in the court from which the process issued, and, by common consent of nations, such situations could not arise without interference with the power and dignity of the foreign sovereign. Therefore the courts will not assume jurisdiction over such vessel or its officers, while acting as such, but leave controversies arising out of the acts of the vessel, and its officers, while acting in their official character, for settlement through diplomatic chanels.

Assuming that the doctrine applies to the commanding officer of the ship, as representative of the foreign power, while acting in conformance with his employment upon national objects, it is apparent that there is nothing in the bills of indictment or the bills of particulars to carry the application of the doctrine to the cases before the court. if the defendant is entitled to exemption from prosecution because the chronometers were carried ashore in furtherance of a national object of his sovereign, nothing appears upon the record to justify that inference, and if the fact is to be raised as a defense, its effect must be passed upon at the trial, if such fact then appears.

The court also held that the defense of extraterritoriality was inapplicable, as the act of smuggling was not complete until the goods were brought off the vessel and within the jurisdiction of the United States. 

United States v. Thierichens, 243 Fed. 419, 420-421 (E.D. Pa., 1917).

Compare Horn v. Mitchell, U.S. Marshal, ante §171. 

OTHER PUBLIC VESSELS 

$173 While in the port of Marseilles, France, in December 1915, the Luigi, an Italian merchant vessel under charter to an American firm, was requisitioned by the Italian Government, and thereafter proceeded to the United States under orders from that Government to obtain a cargo of grain for the account of the Royal Ministry of 

Agriculture, Industry, and Commerce. Thereupon, in January 1916, the charterers filed a libel for breach of charter party, in the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, and an attachment issued against the vessel. 

An oral suggestion of the public status of the vessel was made to the court by an attorney for the Italian Embassy appearing as amicus curiae, but the court was of the opinion that "inasmuch as the suggestion raised a question of international comity, it should come through official channels of the United States Government". The 

Department of State complied with a request of the Italian Ambassador to take the requisite steps to bring the matter officially to the attention of the court but pointed out to the Ambassador that under the American system of government the question as to the legal effect of the requisition of the ship was a question peculiarly appropriate for the decision of the court and that there did not appear to be any impediment to the bringing of the facts of the case to the attention of the court by the representative of the Italian Government.

Release on bond

Action by executive branch On February 15, 1916 the master of the vessel intervened for the owners and, by posting bond conditioned upon performance of any judgment or decree entered in the premises, obtained the release of the vessel.

The court said that it was "far more important to recognize the international rule of comity that an independent sovereign cannot be personally sued than it is to take cognizance of private rights, if, by so doing, that rule is violated". The question was said to be "whether, under the present circumstances, the authority of the court is so exercised as to be construed an attempt indirectly to bring within its authority the Italian Government". In holding that it was not, the court said that by entering bond and obtaining the release of the vessel, the owners had "accomplished for the vessel, and incidentally for the Italian Government, all that could have been accomplished through the Court refusing to allow the attachment to stand" and that:

The custody of the court, through the marshal, over the vessel, ceased at the moment of her release, and all that remains is the bond which has been substituted for the vessel. 

As the case now stands, therefore, the court possesses authority only over the obligors' bond, and none over the vessel. Nothing remains, therefore, through which, directly or indirectly, the court can exercise or attempt to exercise any authority to implead the Italian government in this suit the suit from now on is between private individuals. 

The attachment was allowed to stand. 

The Luigi, 230 Fed. 493, 494, 496-497 (E.D. Pa., 1916). Secretary 

Lansing to the Italian Ambassador (note verbale), Feb. 12, 1916, MS. 

Department of State, file 311.654L96/1; Counselor Polk to the Attorney 

General of the United States, Feb. 15, 1916, ibid. 311.654L96/-.

In September 1916 the Italian Embassy in Washington informed the Department of State that the Italian merchant vessel Attualita, which was under requisition by the Italian Government and was in the United States to load a cargo of grain and rails for Italy, had been libeled in an American port, and requested that the Department take steps looking to the release of the vessel. The Secretary of 

State informed the Attorney General of the notification and requested that he take the customary action. On September 16, 1916 the Department of Justice informed the Department of State that the appropriate United States attorney had been instructed to call to the attention of the court the fact of the requisition for such consideration as the court might deem necessary and competent and to make clear to the court that he did not intervene in the case but

presented the statement as a matter of comity between the Governments of the United States and Italy. 

The Counselor of the Italian Embassy (Brambilla) to Secretary Lans ing, Sept. 12, 1916, and Mr. Lansing to the Attorney General of the United

States, telegram of Sept. 14, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 

311.654At8/1; the Assistant Attorney General (Warren) to Mr. Lansing, Sept. 16, 1916, ibid. 311.654At8/3.

The decision of the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Virginia upholding the immunity of the Attualita, was reversed by the Circuit Court of Appeals, Fourth Circuit, which said: 

3. It is asserted that the steamship is immune to proceedings in any court. It is admitted that to give this immunity it will be necessary to take a step beyond that which has been taken in any decided case, although it is argued that the logic of some decisions heretofore made require that step. We are frankly reluctant to take it. There are many reasons which suggest the inexpediency and the impolicy of creating a class of vessels for which no one is in any way responsible. For actions of the public armed ships of a sovereign, and of those, whether armed or not, which are in the actual possession, custody, and control of the nation itself, and are operated by it, the nation would be morally responsible, although without her consent not answerable legally in her own or other courts. For the torts and contracts of an ordinary vessel, it and its owners are liable. But the ship in this case, and there are now apparently thousands like it, is operated by its owners, and for its actions no government is responsible, at law or in morals.

The persons in charge of the navigation of the ship remain the servants of the owners and are paid by them. The immunity granted to diplomatic representatives of a sovereignty, to its vessels of war, and under some circumstances to other property in its possession and control, can be safely accorded, because the limited numbers and the ordinarily responsible character of the diplomats or agents in charge of the property in question and the dignity and honor of the sovereignty in whose services they are, make abuse of such immunity rare. There will be no such guaranty for the conduct of the thousands of persons privately employed upon ships which at the time happen by contract or requisition to be under charter to sovereign governments. 

4. The steamship says that in any event her right to immunity is a political question, which has been passed upon by the executive branch of the government. A comparison of the suggestion which was filed in The Exchange, 7 Cranch, 116, 3 L. Ed. 287, with that in this case, shows quite clearly that, while in The Exchange the executive demanded the ship's release, it has in this case carefully refrained from doing anything of the kind. 

The Attualita, 238 Fed. 909, 911 (C.C.A. 4th, 1916). The decision of the district court is appended to this report at page 912. The vessel was 

Operated by owners

subsequently found liable in damages and sold. The Mina, The Attualita, 241 Fed. 530 (E.D. Va., 1917); the Deputy Clerk of the United States 

District Court (Kelsey) to Secretary Lansing, Aug. 13, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 311.654At8/24. To similar effect, see Maru Nav. Co.

V. Societa Commerciale Italiana Di Navigation, 271 Fed. 97 (D.C. Md., 1921). 

In reply to a protest from the Italian Embassy in Washington against the assumption by United States courts of jurisdiction over proceedings against the steamship Attualita, Secretary Lansing, after referring to the case of The Schooner Exchange v. M'Fadden & Others, 7 Cranch (1812) 116, said:

It appears that [Chief Justice Marshall] divided these cases [of immunity from territorial jurisdiction] into the following classes: (1) The immunities accorded the person of the sovereign in a foreign country; (2) The immunities granted by civilized nations to foreign diplomatic representatives; (3) The immunities allowed the troops of a foreign prince which are permitted to pass through his dominions; and (4) The immunities granted to public armed vessels.

In order to determine which, if any, of these rules is applicable, it is important to ascertain the exact status of the steamer in question. The only information on this point contained in the communication under acknowledgment is that the vessel has been "requisitioned" by the Italian Government. From the record of the court proceedings [238 Fed. at 910], however, it appears that under Italian law the owner of a steamer whose services are "requisitioned" by the Italian authorities is paid a compensation by the government calculated on a specifically prescribed basis; that the contract of the enrollment of the crew continues in force during the period of "requisition"; that the owner is obligated to pay the master and crew, as well as all expenses of operating the ship, and the cost of insurance against misfortunes; that the vessel must be returned to the owners at the termination of the period of requisition in a condition defined by the terms of the requisition, and that damages sustained by the vessel in consequence of the services performed must be determined by a technical commission and paid to the owners. 

It further appears that under the terms of the requisition of the Attualita, an arbitral procedure is provided for the adjustment of all controversies between the Italian Administration of War and the owner of the vessel in relation to the interpretation and fulfilment of the conditions of the contract of requisition as well as all other matters growing out of the requisition except the amount of compensation to be paid the owner; and that the Italian authorities hold the owners of the vessel responsible for the cargo from the time it is loaded until it is unloaded.

The Attualita therefore appears to be not only not an armed public vessel of the Italian Government, but not even a merchant vessel owned by that Government. She seems to be merely a merchant vessel-owned by private persons as heretofore, and fully equipped, insured, manned, and operated by and

at the expense of the owners, who are responsible for any damages sustained by the ship in the course of the services performed as well as for the cargo on board-whose services are purchased for a stated period by the Italian Government for a stipulated compensation. I do not perceive that this private character of the vessel is in any way impaired by the fact that the contract of employment is compulsory rather than voluntary. 

It seems obvious, therefore, that the Attualita cannot be regarded as entitled to any of the immunities under the rules pointed out by Chief Justice Marshall in the case of the Schooner Exchange. Nor do I perceive that there is any other rule of international law or comity granting this vessel immunity from the jurisdiction of the admiralty courts of this country in a case of this character. The object of the court in taking jurisdiction is, I presume, to determine whether the vessel or the owner is liable for the alleged marine tort on account of which the vessel was libelled. The courts are open to the owners of the vessel to defend their rights in the proceedings instituted against it and to endeavor through appropriate proceedings to have set aside by the court of last resort the decision holding the vessel for trial. 

It seems clear, therefore, that the action of the court in taking jurisdiction in the case on its merits does not necessarily result in directly or in indirectly impleading the Government of Italy. 

After quoting part of the opinion of the circuit court of appeals in the case of The Attualita, ante, the note continued: 

There are other practical reasons which impel me to my regret to disagree with the contentions advanced in the communications under acknowledgment. If those contentions were admitted, American tribunals might become impotent to determine even the rights of American citizens in cases of maritime torts, salvage, and contracts involving such vessels and that [sic] therefore no remedies would be open to American citizens in such cases except through diplomatic channels. Indeed, it would seem that, if your 

Excellency's contention is followed to its logical conclusion, the courts of this country would be precluded from the administration of criminal jurisprudence in cases where the arrest of any persons connected with such vessels for any offence committed within the territorial jurisdiction of this country might involve a delay in departure from port.

There is a further consideration to which I must call Your Excellency's attention. The steamer Attualita and other private merchant vessels whose services have been required by belligerent governments during the present war have freely entered and cleared in the ports of this country in conformity with the laws and regulations observed by other private merchantmen and have not claimed the immunities from local laws and regulations accorded to public vessels of war by the universal practice of nations.

Should this Government concede the contention which I understand you to make: namely, that vessels having the status of the steamer Attualita should be given in this country a treatment

Public nature of

Voyage assimilated to that accorded to vessels of war, and should not be subjected to the laws and regulations generally governing merchant vessels in foreign ports, a grave question might, in my judgment, be raised as to the propriety of this Government's permitting such vessels freely to enter, remain at will and leave the ports of this country and to transport therefrom merchandise of all kinds, including articles of contraband of war for the direct use of belligerent Governments.

Since it appears that the action of the Circuit Court of Appeals in refusing to deny the foreign libellant the opportunity to establish his rights in an admiralty court of this country was in conformity with the practice of the courts of the United States to take jurisdiction in controversies in admiralty between foreign vessels, and since it further appears that the proceedings in this case did not involve any attempt to exercise jurisdiction over the Italian Government or its property, I cannot bring myself to share the view of the Counselor of the Embassy in his note of October 13th, that the judicial proceedings which have taken place contravene "the rules of international courtesy which are universally observed when the Sovereign Rights of a foreign State are involved," or to admit that this procedure is "inconsistent with the dignity of a Sovereign State."

The district court, to which the suit had been remanded, on Mar. 17, 1917 rendered a decision finding the Attualita wholly at fault, and on Aug. 13, 1917 the Secretary of State was notified by the clerk of the court that the vessel had been sold under order of the court. (See ante, this section.) 

Replying, on Dec. 18, 1917, to an inquiry of the British Ambassador as to the exemption of the Derbent, a British requisitioned oil tanker, the Department of State substantially reaffirmed the views expressed in the case of The Attualita. Ambassador Spring Rice to Secretary Lansing, Nov. 

12, 1917, and Mr. Lansing to Mr. Spring Rice, Dec. 18, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 196/127.

The Pampa, a vessel of the Argentine Navy was libeled in a United States port for damages caused in a collision. At the time of the collision the vessel was carrying a commercial cargo, though it was shown that she was under orders to carry coal and munitions on her return voyage for the use of the Argentine Government. In ordering the release of the vessel from arrest, the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of New York adopted the following statement, made obiter dictum in the case of The 

Attualita, 238 Fed. 909 at 911 (C.C.A. 4th, 1916) (ante, this section) as controlling: 

For actions of the public armed ships of a sovereign, and of those, whether armed or not, which are in the actual possession,

custody, and control of the nation itself, and are operated by it, the nation would be morally responsible, although without her consent not answerable legally in her own or other courts. 

The Pampa, 245 Fed. 137, 139 (E.D.N.Y., 1917).

In the summer of 1918 the Italian Ambassador communicated to the Department of State the proposal of his Government that as a war measure the United States should grant immunity from seizure to vessels in the service of the other Allied Governments, on a basis of reciprocity. 

In its reply of Nov. 4, 1918 the Department referred to its position in the case of The Attualita (ante, this section) and stated that, although the United States was now a co-belligerent, no reason was perceived for modifying the views therein set forth. Ambassador di Cellere to Secretary Lansing, June 26, 1918, MS. Department of State, file 800.88/158;

Count di Cellere to Mr. Lansing, Aug. 29, 1918, and Mr. Lansing to Count di Cellere, Nov. 4, 1918, ibid. 800.88/179. 

Secretary Lansing, in a letter of November 8, 1918 to the Attorney

General of the United States expressed the view that "where [government-owned] vessels were engaged in commercial pursuits, they should be subject to the obligations and restrictions of trade, if they were to enjoy its benefits and profits" for the following reasons: (1) because of the soundness of the theory that "when a Sovereign enters into business, he submits himself to the conditions thereof"; (2) because "if merchant vessels owned and operated by foreign Governments are immune from process in United States Courts, added force would be given to the claim of neutral Governments who are taking over their merchant marine that they should be also immune from the operation of municipal regulations in United States Ports"; (3) because "if the claim of immunity were granted, American citizens as well as foreigners would be left without recourse in the Courts for such just claims as they might have against the vessels concerned", and "Their only means for obtaining satisfaction would be through political channels-either through Congress, or through diplomacy".

He was of the further view that "The questions involved are particularly suitable for determination by Courts, rather than by political departments of the Government". The purpose of the Secretary's letter was to suggest that a case involving the libeling of a government-owned vessel employed in commerce be brought before the Supreme Court of the United States and that the Department of Justice there present the doctrine of non-immunity.

Appearance by counsel for ambas- sador In refusing to adopt the suggestion of the Secretary the Attorney 

General said:

The Department of Justice is convinced that as the law now stands, these ships are immune. Its business is to deal with the law as it finds or believes it to be. It can not, in candor, urge upon the Supreme Court a position which it believes to be unsound If the sovereign's property can be made the subject of a libel in rem, the sovereign, for all substantial purposes, becomes a party defendant in a legal action. A concession that this may be done without express consent, seems to the Department the concession of the suability of the sovereign which you say you do not propose. At any rate, it is a concession which the Department is unwilling to make. Under all the circumstances, I am clear that pending a decision of the matter by the Supreme Court, which it is hoped may be speedily attained, the Department must continue to assert, in all appropriate cases, the immunity of merchant vessels which are the property of the United States. 

Secretary Lansing to Attorney General Gregory, Nov. 8, 1918, MS. Department of State, file 195/229a; Mr. Gregory to Mr. Lansing, Nov. 25, 1918, and Mr. Lansing to Mr. Gregory, Dec. 2, 1918, ibid. 195/230; Mr. 

Gregory to Mr. Lansing, Dec. 31, 1918, ibid. 195/236. The Supreme Court ultimately adopted the rule of immunity. See Berizzi Brothers Company v. Steamship Pesaro, post, this section.

The Roseric, a British merchant vessel, was libeled in the District Court of the United States for the District of New Jersey, having damaged libelant's barge in a collision. Counsel for the British Ambassador in Washington, appearing as amici curiae suggested to the court that the vessel was immune from its process since it was under requisition by the British Government and was in the service of that Government as an admiralty transport. In holding that the public status of the vessel was thus brought properly to its attention, the court said that the sources from which the suggestion might be received was a matter of judicial discretion and that each case should be governed by its own circumstances. In the present case no reasons were seen for rejecting the suggestion, while the co-belligerency of the United States and Great Britain at the time the Roseric was seized furnished so strong a reason for its acceptance that "in the absence of an intimation from the executive branch of this government that the public interests would be disserved by receiving such suggestion, its rejection would not be justified".

In holding the vessel immune, the court reviewed the case of The Exchange, 7 Cranch (1812) 116, and said that there was nothing in

the reasoning of that case limiting its application to vessels of war and that:

The privilege was based on the idea that the sovereign's property devoted to state purposes is free and exempt from all judicial process to enforce private claims. Such idea is as cogently applicable to an unarmed vessel employed by the sovereign in the public service as it is to one of his battleships. 

It was further said that "it is not the ownership or exclusive possession of the instrumentality by the sovereign, but its appropriation and devotion to such service, that exempts it from judicial process", Use in public requisitioned property therefore coming equally under the rule of service immunity. A decree was entered staying all proceedings so long as the vessel continued in the service of the British Government. 

The Roseric, 254 Fed. 154, 158, 161–162 (D.C.N.J., 1918).

Section 9 of the Shipping Act approved September 7, 1916 (39 

Stat. 728, 730) provided that vessels purchased, chartered, or leased from the board, while employed solely as merchant vessels, "shall be subject to all laws, regulations, and liabilities governing merchant vessels, whether the United States be interested therein as owner, in whole or in part, or hold any mortgage, lien, or other interest therein".

The Florence H., an American merchant vessel under requisition by the United States Government, was chartered by the United States Shipping Board to the French Government for the carriage of a cargo of food to France. While returning to the United States in ballast and still in the possession and under control of the French crew, she was involved in a collision with a British vessel. She was thereafter libeled in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York by the owners of the British vessel. 

The court held that even though the vessel was owned by the United States Government she was subject to libel and arrest under §9 of the act of September 7, 1916. It held further, under authority of The 

Siren, 7 Wall. (1868) 152, that a lien attached to the vessel at the time of the collision on the principle that "the ship is liable for the tortious acts of any one who lawfully comes in possession of her, and directs her navigation, be he charterer, agent, or crew". (See on this point The Western Maid, 257 U.S. (1922) 419, and post, this section.)

The fact that the vessel was in the hands of a French crew acting under authority of the French Government was held to present no obstacle to the determination of the cause since the collision took place on the high seas and the vessel was of American registry. The court expressed the opinion that it should not take cognizance of possible

The Maipo involved a vessel belonging to the Chilean Navy, the facts being substantially the same as those in the Pampa (ante), except that the proceeding was for breach of contract rather than for tort. 

A claim of immunity made to the court by the Chilean Chargé d'Affaires appearing specially through counsel was sustained, the court expressing the opinion that absence of any action by the Department of State merely indicated willingness that the matter should be adjudicated without executive interference. Immunity was upheld both upon authority and upon practical considerations of international comity. 

252 Fed. 627 (S.D.N.Y., 1918).

In the following year the Maipo was again before this court in circumstances presenting the same legal question. In sustaining the vessel's immunity, Judge Hough said that he felt that if a government engaged in trade it should be subject to the same liabilities as a private individual, but that, since this involved the Chilean Government's interpretation of what was a public function, it was a matter for diplomatic rather than judicial determination. 

259 Fed. 367 (S.D.N.Y., 1919).

In the case of The Adriatic, a British merchant vessel requisitioned by the British Government and subsequently libeled in a port of the United States, the British Ambassador appeared to claim immunity for the vessel, while the libelant claimed that the requisition was invalid as it took place while the vessel was on the high seas. The United States Circuit Court of Appeals, Third Circuit, decided that "it is not within the province of a court of this country to attempt to determine whether the requisition of the vessel was valid or invalid under the laws of Great Britain; it must here be accepted as legal", and accordingly affirmed the decree of the lower court dismissing the libel. 

258 Fed. 902, 904 (C.C.A. 3d, 1919). 

The Jupiter, a Russian merchant vessel, was on January 26, 1918 purportedly nationalized by decree of the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic. Subsequently it came into the possession and control of the Soviet Government; and while in this possession and control came into a port of Great Britain where it was made the

subject of proceedings in rem by its former owners who claimed possession. The Soviet Government intervened, claiming to be the sole owner, and moved to set aside the proceedings on the ground of sovereign immunity. The motion was granted in the Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty Division of the High Court of Justice and sustained by the Court of Appeal, which said that the suit had the effect of requiring the Russian Government to appear and defend Comity does what it claimed to be its property and that rules of international not permit impleading comity did not permit such steps to be taken against foreign of sovereign sovereigns.

Following the purported sale of the vessel by the Soviet Government to a private Italian company, the vessel still remaining within British jurisdiction, the former owners again issued a writ in rem against it, claiming possession. The Italian company moved to dismiss the writ upon the ground (among others) that since the ship had been sold by the Soviet Government free of incumbrances, to allow the action to proceed would be indirectly to implead a foreign state. The Court of Appeal sustained a decision refusing to set aside the writ, stating that the Soviet Government made no claim to ownership or possession of the vessel at the moment and that it seemed to be "a mere question of fact or of law as to whether or not the defendants, who are not a sovereign State, have in fact got a title to this ship, and no question, therefore, of impleading the foreign sovereign arises”.

Proceeding to the determination of the merits, the Probate, Divorce, and Admiralty Division of the High Court of Justice sustained the action and awarded possession to the plaintiffs. This position was sustained by the Court of Appeal, the principal ground being that at Cessation of the time of the nationalization decree, the vessel was not within the immunity territorial jurisdiction of the Government making the decree and was consequently not affected thereby, even though the owners were Russian nationals.

The Jupiter, [1924] P. 236; The Jupiter (No. 2), [1925] P. 69, 78; The 

Jupiter (No. 3), [1927] P. 122, 250. 

In a proceeding in rem against a vessel at the time "merely under charter to the French republic, not in its possession nor owned by it, though both facts changed within a few days", it was held that the vessel was not immune. The Beaverton; The Daisai Maru, 273 Fed. 539 (S.D.N.Y., 1919).

The Suits in Admiralty Act approved March 9, 1920 provides that vessels owned, possessed, or operated by the United States Government or a government-owned corporation, shall be exempt from arrest or seizure by judicial process in the United States and its possessions but that a libel in personam against the United States will lie in cases where such vessels would be amenable to process if Suits in Admiralty 

Act, 1920

Contested ownership privately owned. It also provides (section 7) that in case of the arrest or seizure of such vessels in foreign ports, the Secretary of State, on the request of the Attorney General, is authorized to direct the nearest consular officer to claim immunity for the vessel and to post such bond on behalf of the United States as may be necessary to obtain its release. 

41 Stat. 525; 46 U.S.C. §§ 741 et seq. 

In accordance with the above act the Department of State, on May 21, 1920, instructed American consular officers that they were "not to claim any vessel or cargo referred to therein, immune from arrest, attachment or other seizure nor to execute any stipulation or undertaking except upon instructions from the Department". Special instruction, consular, no. 722, May 21, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 195/283.

An action in rem was instituted in 1920 in the District Court of the United States for the Northern District of California by the 

"Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic" and Ludwig C. A. K. 

Martens, who claimed to be the duly authorized agent and representative of that government in the United States, against the steamship 

Rogdai. The "Russian Government" and Boris Bakhméteff appeared specially to move for an order dissolving the writ of attachment, Mr. 

Bakhméteff filing in support thereof a "suggestion" supported by a certificate of the Department of State certifying that he had been formally received by the President of the United States as the duly accredited Ambassador of Russia and had ever since been so recognized, and that the United States had not received or recognized Ludwig C. A. K. Martens in any representative capacity, nor had the

Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic been recognized by the Government of the United States. The suggestion further set forth that the vessel had been purchased by the Russian Government in July 1920 and was in its possession and under its control at the time of the seizure.

The court held that the entire question was whether the libelants or the claimants were to be regarded as the true representatives of Russia, that this was a question for the decision of the executive rather than the judiciary, and that the certificate of the Department of State recognizing Mr. Bakhméteff was to be considered as conclusive. It was also held that the public status of the vessel was properly brought to the attention of the court by the Ambassador's suggestion. The motion was allowed, and an order entered discharging the attachment. 

The Rogdai, 278 Fed. 294 (N.D. Cal., 1920). In a suit in the same court involving the same vessel, a suggestion by a Russian Consul, accompanied by the certificate of the Ambassador that he was entitled to recognition as Consul, together with the certificate of the Department of State

that the Ambassador was the duly recognized representative of his country, was held sufficient to bring the claim of immunity properly before the court. The Rogday [spelling varies], 279 Fed. 130 (N.D. Cal., 1920).

The case of Ex parte Muir involved the libeling in a United States District Court of the British vessel Gleneden. Private counsel, appearing for the British Embassy in Washington as amici curiae, presented to the court the written suggestion that the vessel was immune from process because it had been requisitioned by the British Government and was employed in its service as a grain carrier. In denying writs of prohibition and mandamus looking to the dismissal of the suit and release of the vessel, the United States Supreme Court held that, prima facie, the district court had jurisdiction and that it was incumbent upon those challenging the jurisdiction to furnish proof of immunity. The court said: 

As of right the British Government was entitled to appear in Method of the suit, to propound its claim to the vessel and to raise the claiming jurisdictional question. Or, with its sanction, its accredited immunity and recognized representative might have appeared and have taken the same steps in its interest. And, if there was objection to appearing as a suitor in a foreign court, it was open to that government to make the asserted public status and immunity of the vessel the subject of diplomatic representations to the end that, if that claim was recognized by the Executive Department of this government, it might be set forth and supported in an appropriate suggestion to the court by the Attorney General, or some law officer acting under his direction. 

But none of these courses was followed. The suggestion on behalf of the British Embassy was presented by private counsel appearing as amici curiae, and not through the usual official channels. This was a marked departure from what theretofore had been recognized as the correct practice ; and in our opinion the libelant's objection to it was well taken. The reasons underlying that practice are sufficiently indicated by observing that it makes for better international relations, conforms to diplomatic usage in other matters, accords to the Executive Department the respect rightly due to it, and tends to promote harmony of action and uniformity of decision. 

Of course, the suggestion as made could not be given the consideration and weight claimed for it. [Citations omitted.] 

Ex parte in the Matter of Muir, Master of the Gleneden, 254 U.S. (1921) 522, 532-533. 

The Carlo Poma, a merchant vessel owned by the Italian Government and engaged in commerce, was proceeded against in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York for damages to a cargo. A suggestion of immunity was made by the 

Italian Ambassador through counsel appearing specially. The vessel

was held to be immune, and the decision was sustained by the Circuit 

Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. With reference to the plea of libelants that the vessel lost its immunity through engaging in commerce, the court said:

The English courts go the whole way in refusing process against property of a foreign sovereign under any circumstances. 

This because of the international comity due from one sovereign to another

The law of the United States is the same, except that the immunity of property of a sovereign, whether the United States or a foreign sovereign, depends, not merely upon the ownership, but also upon the actual possession by the sovereign of the property at the time process is served. 

The Carlo Poma, 259 Fed. 369, 370 (C.C.A. 2d, 1919). The decree of the

Circuit Court of Appeals was vacated by the Supreme Court of the United States on the ground that the appeal should have been directly from the district court to the Supreme Court. The Carlo Poma, 255 U.S. (1921) 219. 

In August 1918 the owners of the American vessel St. Charles filed a libel in personam in the District Court of the United States for the District of Maryland, against the owners of the Italian vessel Tea to recover for salvage services rendered by the former vessel to the latter. The Tea was not within reach of the libelants and, under process of foreign attachment, the vessel Armando was attached as the only property of defendants within the jurisdiction of the court. 

Bond was posted and the vessel released. On October 23, 1918 the

Italian Ambassador in Washington informed the Department of State that at the time of the attachment the vessel was under requisition by the Italian Government and under its control, and requested that the Department take appropriate steps to release the attachment and vacate the bond. In its reply of January 16, 1919 the Department said that it appeared that "the appropriate representative of the Italian Government could bring, or through competent counsel appearing specially, cause to be brought to the attention of the Court the facts concerning the requisitioning of this vessel" and that this had in fact been done by the appropriate Italian Consul. It was further pointed out that:

The question of the immunity from legal proceedings in the Courts of the United States of ships requisitioned by the Italian Government was heard in argument of counsel and passed upon by a Court of competent jurisdiction in the Attualità case, and the attitude of this Government with respect to such immunity was indicated in the note of November 4, 1918 in reply to your note of June 26, 1918.

The Ambassador was therefore informed that the Department "regards it as inadvisable to interfere in any way in the legal proceedings to which your note refers".

It appears from the decision of the court, rendered February 28, 1921, that the Consul and the Ambassador both suggested to the court that the Armando was under requisition by the Italian Government and was therefore immune. The court held that in as much as these suggestions had not been made through the Department of State they could not be considered as evidence, citing for this view the case of 

Ex parte Muir, 254 U.S. (1921) 522 (ante, this section). The decision retaining jurisdiction was further based on the decision in The 

Attualita, 238 Fed. 909 (C.C.A. 4th, 1916) (ante, this section).

Ambassador di Cellere to Secretary Lansing, Oct. 23, 1918, and the Assistant Secretary of State (Phillips) to the Italian Chargé d'Affaires (di 

Valentino), Jan. 16, 1919, MS. Department of State, file 311.654Ar5/2; Maru

Nav. Co. v. Societa Commerciale Italiana Di Navigation, 271 Fed. 97 (D.C. 

Md., 1921); affirmed as to above rule in Societa Commerciale Italiana Di 

Navigazione v. Maru Nav. Co., 280 Fed. 334 (C.C.A. 4th, 1922).

The Department is of the opinion that vessels owned by a state and engaged in commerce are not entitled, within the terri- Department torial waters of another state, to the immunity accorded vessels of State, 1921 of war, and that notwithstanding such ownership these vessels are subject to the local jurisdiction to the same extent as other merchant vessels.

The purpose of the request was said to be "to avoid that private individuals or concerns may threaten to attach or actually attach a steamer owned, possessed and operated by a friendly Government, manned with officers and crew directly in the service of the said Government". by a foreign Government" and that it therefore declined to take the requested action.

Replying to an inquiry as to its policy and practice in the matter of claiming immunity for merchant vessels "owned through the 

Shipping Board or the Emergency Fleet Corporation", the Department of State, on August 2, 1921, said:

It is the view of the Department that government owned merchant vessels or vessels under requisition of governments whose flag they fly employed in commerce should not be regarded as entitled to the immunities accorded public vessels of war. The

Department has not claimed immunity for American vessels of this character. In cases of private litigation in American ports involving merchant vessels owned by foreign governments, the Department has made it a practice carefully to refrain from taking any action which might constitute an interference by the authorities of this Government in such litigation.

The Department of State, on January 11, 1923, instructed American diplomatic and consular officers as follows:

The Department does not regard Government owned or operated vessels when engaged in commercial work to be entitled to immunity as public vessels and when the Department has been requested by diplomatic representatives of foreign governments to inform our courts that such vessels were immune, it has declined to comply with the request. It accordingly has also declined to request foreign governments to grant immunity to Shipping Board vessels when arrested in foreign ports on judicial process. States vessels

Limitation 

This Government does not exempt foreign governments from the payment of customs duties on materials brought into the United States for use in repairing merchant vessels owned or operated by them. It accordingly declines to request foreign countries to exempt the Shipping Board from the payment of such customs duties on materials imported into such countries for repairing Shipping Board vessels.

Foreign governments are not taxed on incomes consisting of earnings derived in the United States from the operation of merchant vessels belonging to or operated by them and the Department has in the past endeavored to obtain an exemption, as a matter of comity, for the Shipping Board in certain foreign countries in which steps were taken to collect income taxes on the earnings of Shipping Board vessels. The matter was, however, not pressed as a matter of right.

On March 5, 1923 the Department instructed American diplomatic officers in maritime countries to inform the Governments to which they were accredited that this Government would not claim immunity for vessels operated commercially by or on behalf of the Shipping Board and that "Such ships, when so operated will be permitted to be subject to the laws of foreign countries which apply under otherwise like conditions to privately owned merchant ships foreign to such countries." 

Secretary Hughes to American diplomatic and consular officers, diplomatic serial 171, General Instructions, consular no. 871, Jan. 11, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 641.11241/28; Mr. Hughes to American diplomatic officers, diplomatic serial 178, Mar. 5, 1923, ibid. 195/474.

The above instruction further directed the diplomatic officers to say that the United States would, when occasion arose, continue to ask that foreign governments recognize the application of section 7 of the Suits in Admiralty Act approved March 9, 1920 (41 Stat. 525; see also ante, this section).

On April 18, 1923 the British Ambassador in Washington inquired of the Department of State as to whether the following interpretation of this section was correct:

If a suit is brought in the courts of a foreign country against a merchant vessel owned or operated by the United States Government, bail or its equivalent will be given on behalf of the United States Government and, if judgment is rendered against the vessel, payment will be made.

The Department replied on July 7, 1923 that this statement was correct as to the practice ordinarily followed, but pointed out that the statute merely authorized, without requiring, such practice. It was said that in cases where it was deemed undesirable to furnish bail

or its equivalent, it was expected that the vessel would be disposed of according to the usual practice in the country where the seizure took place. It was also pointed out that the statute did not apply to all merchant vessels but only to vessels when engaged in commercial pursuits. The note concluded as follows: 

All vessels in the charge of the United States Shipping Board are owned by the United States. When such vessels are seized or threatened with seizure in Admiralty proceedings abroad it has been the practice, particularly in Great Britain, to effect their release by the giving of a stipulation by the foreign representative of the Shipping Board. I am informed that judgments rendered in these cases are paid in the same manner as judgments in cases where the procedure provided in Section 7 of the Suits in Admiralty Act has been followed. 

Ambassador Geddes to Secretary Hughes, Apr. 18, 1923, MS. Department of State, file 195/482; Mr. Hughes to the British Chargé d'Affaires (Chilton), July 7, 1923, ibid. 195/503.

An act of Congress approved March 3, 1925 provides (sec. 1) that a libel in personam in admiralty may be brought against the United States, or a petition impleading the United States, for damages caused by a public vessel of the United States, and for compensation for towage and salvage services, including contract salvage, rendered to a public vessel of the United States, provided that the cause of action arose after April 6, 1920. It further provides (sec. 3) that in the event that the United States files a libel in rem or in personam in admiralty for damages caused by a privately owned vessel, the owner of such vessel, or his successors in interest, may file a cross libel in personam or claim a set-off or counter claim against the United States in such suit for and on account of any damages arising out of the same subject-matter or cause of action, provided that the respondent files security in the usual amount and form. 

However, it is provided (sec. 5) that no suit may be brought by a national of any foreign government, unless it is proved "that said

Diplomatic relations severed government, under similar circumstances, allows nationals of the 

United States to sue in its courts".

The Turkish merchant vessel Gul Djemal was arrested on December 2, 1920 by the United States Marshal for the Southern District of New York, pursuant to a libel filed by parties seeking to recover for advances made to the vessel. The Spanish Ambassador filed a suggestion with the court stating that he had charge of Turkish interests in the United States and that the Gul Djemal was owned, manned, and operated by the Turkish Government. This suggestion was later supplemented by a letter from the Department of State to the Ambassador, recognizing that he had charge of Turkish governmental interests in the United States during the suspension of diplomatic relations between the two countries. The court declined to release the vessel, holding that in as much as formal diplomatic relations between the United States and Turkey did not exist, any such action should be taken only upon a suggestion emanating from the Department of State and that "The adoption of a suggestion short of one originating in such department carries with it .. the possibility not only of confusion between co-ordinate branches of this government, but also the likelihood of embarrassment. If, in cases where diplomatic relations have been severed, such matters are left to the exclusive management of the executive, all such danger will be avoided." 

Ambassador Riaño to the Acting Secretary of State (Davis), Dec. 23, 1920, and Mr. Davis to Señor Riaño, Dec. 24, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 311.6753G951/1. The Gul Djemal, 296 Fed. 563, 567 (S.D.N.Y. 1920-21).

The Ambassador subsequently requested the Department of State to take appropriate steps to obtain the release of the vessel on the ground of its immunity as a public vessel of Turkey, to which the 

Department replied on January 25, 1921 that it was its practice "carefully to refrain from taking any action which might constitute an interference by the authorities of this Government in private litigation, even though such litigation may in some way involve merchant vessels owned by a foreign government". 

Señor Riaño to the Acting Secretary of State (Davis), Jan. 25, 1921, and

Mr. Davis to Señor Riaño, Feb. 14, 1921, MS. Department of State, file 311.6753G951/8. 

On June 6, 1921 the Supreme Court of the United States denied the motion of the master of the Gul Djemal for leave to file a petition for a writ of prohibition and a writ of mandamus looking to the termination of the proceedings and the release of the vessel. The Court

said that the questions presented were new and important and that it was well within the Court's discretion to refuse the writs. 

Ex parte in the matter of Hussein Lutfi Bey, Master of the Gul Djemal, Petitioner, 256 U.S. (1921) 616. 

In subsequent proceedings instituted by the special appearance of the master of the Gul Djemal to object to the jurisdiction of the district court, the parties entered into a stipulation of facts which showed that the vessel was owned by and in the possession of the Turkish Government, that she was exclusively engaged in commerce, and that diplomatic relations between the United States and Turkey were severed, although unofficial relations were maintained and the two countries were at peace. The court upheld its jurisdiction of the case in a decision of January 7, 1922 basing its decision upon the fact that diplomatic relations between the United States and Turkey were severed and that the suggestion should therefore come from the Department of State, and also upon the decision of Judge Mack in The Pesaro, 277 Fed. 473 (S.D.N.Y., 1921) (post, this section). Upon appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States this decision was affirmed Master not upon the ground that immunity of the vessel could not be successfully proper party set up by the master of the vessel who, although an officer of the Turkish immunity Navy, was performing no naval or military duty and was not shown to have any authority to represent his sovereign "other than can be inferred from his position as master and the circumstances specified in the stipulation of facts". Reference was made to Ex parte Muir, 254 U.S. (1921) 522 (ante, this section). 

The Gul Djemal, 296 Fed. 567 (S.D.N.Y., 1922); The "Gul Djemal”, 264 

U.S. (1924) 90, 95.

The São Vicente and several other vessels belonging to the Transportes Maritimos do Estado were, in 1921, made the subject of libel proceedings in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York. The owner claimed the São Vicente, and obtained its release by posting bond. Thereafter an answer was filed in which it was set forth that the owner was a department of the Government of Portugal. The answer was verified by the Portuguese Vice 

Consul General. The defense was held insufficient, and the court entered decrees against the vessels. Appeals to the Circuit Court of 

Appeals for the Second Circuit were dismissed (January 25, 1922) on motion, the grounds being that the defense did not allege that ownership of the department was the ownership of the Government, and that the answer was not supported by proper evidence so that "Even if it were to be held, notwithstanding The Pesaro, 255 U.S. 216, 41 Sup. Ct. 308, 65 L. Ed. 592 [post, this section] that the question of 

to assert

jurisdiction could be raised by the vice consul general, it is not properly raised upon this record." It was also held that immunity had been waived by general appearance (see post §176).

The São Vicente, The Murmugao, Rose v. Transportes Maritimos do 

Estado, 281 Fed. 111, 114 (C.C.A. 2d, 1922).

The Supreme Court issued writs of certiorari upon the petition of the Consul General of Portugal in the United States who raised the issue of jurisdiction. Upon consideration, the writs were ordered dismissed, the

Court stating that "The Consul General was not party to any of the proceedings below, and is not competent, merely by virtue of his office, to appear here for his Government and claim immunity from process in the manner attempted." The São Vicente, 260 U.S. (1922) 151, 154.

In July 1923 the Portuguese Minister in Washington filed in the above district court a formal suggestion stating that the vessel was owned and operated by a department of the Government of Portugal, protesting the court's assumption of jurisdiction and asking that the proceedings be dismissed. Upon motion the suggestion was stricken from the files and final judgment entered for the libelants. Upon petition of the Minister to the Supreme Court of the United States for writ of prohibition or mandamus to prevent further action in the proceedings, the Court dismissed the petition, holding that the trial court had jurisdiction of the res and that the Portuguese Government had not availed itself of its opportunity to present the claim of immunity in proper form. Reference was made to Ex parte

The Pesaro, a merchant vessel owned and operated by the Italian Government and engaged in carrying olive oil between Italy and the United States, was libeled in rem in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York. The vessel being arrested, the Italian Ambassador in Washington made a direct suggestion to the court that the vessel was owned and possessed by the Italian Government, and the court thereupon ordered the release of the vessel. The libelants appealed directly to the Supreme Court of the United States which reversed the decree, holding that the Ambassador's suggestion did not have the effect of placing him or the Italian Government in the position of a suitor and that in the circumstances, the libelants' objection that, to be entertained, the suggestion should should come through offi- come through official channels of the United States was well taken. cial channels Reference was made to Ex parte Muir (ante, this section). Suggestion

The Pesaro, 255 U.S. (1921) 216.

See also the case of the French vessel Secundus, wherein it was held that a suggestion from the French Consul General and a subsequent suggestion by the French Chargé d'Affaires, with a covering certificate by the Department of State that the latter was duly accredited to the United States, were inadequate as not constituting a suggestion made through the diplomatic channel. 13 F. (2d) 469 (E.D.N.Y., 1926); 15 F. (2d) 711 (E.D.N.Y., 1926). 

Upon consideration of the case in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York on an agreed statement of facts which showed the vessel to be owned and possessed by the Italian Government, and to be engaged solely in commerce, the court held the vessel not immune. Judge Mack, writing the opinion, said that the question was unsettled and that inquiry should be made "whether the public interests justify or require an extension of sovereign exemption from the usual processes of judicial justice". In his opinion "a government ship should not be immune from seizure as such, but only by reason of the nature of the service in which she is engaged". Also figuring in the decision were the facts that a United 

States vessel similarly situated would not be immune in Italian courts and that the Pesaro herself would enjoy no immunity in Italy. 

The Pesaro, 277 Fed. 473, 475, 482 (S.D.N.Y., 1921).

In the above case, in 1921, the matter was before the court on the claim and plea in abatement of the master of the Pesaro, who purported to speak for the Italian Government. When, in a separate case in 1924 (The “Gul Djemal”, 264 U.S. 90), it was held by the

Supreme Court of the United States that a valid claim of immunity could not be made in this way, the order of Judge Mack was vacated by consent of the parties.

The Italian Ambassador having filed a claim and answer, the matter again came before the District Court of the United States for the 

Southern District of New York, and in a decision written by Judge 

Augustus Hand in 1926 the immunity of the Pesaro was upheld. The court was of the opinion that the weight of authority supported this view and was opposed to that of Judge Mack. 

The Pesaro, 13 F. (2d) 468 (S. D. N. Y., 1926).

This decree was appealed to the Supreme Court of the United States, which stated the question involved to be "whether a ship owned and possessed by a foreign government, and operated by it in the carriage of merchandise for hire, is immune from arrest under process based on a libel in rem by a private suitor in a federal district court exercising admiralty jurisdiction". After reviewing the case of The

Engaged in trade- immunity upheld Exchange, 7 Cranch (1812) 116, holding that foreign naval vessels are immune from seizure, the Court held: 

We think the principles are applicable alike to all ships held and used by a government for a public purpose, and that when, for the purpose of advancing the trade of its people or providing revenue for its treasury, a government acquires, mans and operates ships in the carrying trade, they are public ships in the same sense that war ships are. We know of no international usage which regards the maintenance and advancement of the economic welfare of a people in time of peace as any less a public purpose than the maintenance and training of a naval force. 

It was concluded that the lower court rightly dismissed the libel for want of jurisdiction.

Berizzi Brothers Company v. Steamship Pesaro, 271 U.S. (1926) 562, 574. 

For similar rule see: The Jassy, [1906] P. 270; The Gagara, [1919] P. 95;

The Porto Alexandre, [1920] P. 30; Owners of S.S. Victoria v. Owners of the 

Quillwark, [1922] Scot. L. T., 68; The Ice King, 103 Entscheidungen des

Reichsgerichts in Zivilsachen (1921) 274. But see dicta expressed in the 

British House of Lords in Compania Naviera Vascongado and Steamship 

"Cristina" and Persons Claiming an Interest Therein, [1938] A.C. 485. And see Navires: Hungerford et Angers, 32 Revue internationale du droit mari time (1920-21) 345. 

On December 23, 1931 the Minister of the Dominican Republic informed the Department of State that the vessel Arminda, which had been libeled in a United States port, was a public vessel of the Dominican Republic under the command of a naval officer and engaged in public service, and asked that the Department take the necessary steps to bring this fact to the attention of the court. The Department of State transmitted to the Department of Justice the documentary evidence of the vessel's status submitted to it by the Minister and said: 

In accordance with the request made by the Legation, I ask you to instruct the appropriate United States attorney to file a suggestion with the Court of its lack of jurisdiction, because of the apparently public status of the Arminda, to entertain the suit in question and that you direct the Attorney to support that suggestion by filing with the Court the enclosures with this letter. 

The action was subsequently protested by the Norwegian and Canadian Legations on behalf of the libelants, the owners and charterers, respectively, of the steamship Norfold, claiming that the Norfold had undergone heavy expense in rescuing the Arminda and submitting that the Department of State should withdraw its suggestion and leave the adjudication in the hands of the court for its sole determination. In its replies the Department referred to the decision of the 

United States Supreme Court in The Pesaro, 255 U.S. (1921) 216 

(ante, this section) and stated that "In view of this position of the

Supreme Court, the Department considers that it was entirely warranted in asking that the suggestion above mentioned be made to the District Court in the instant case." It was added that libelants might submit to the court their views in opposition to the suggestion.

In dismissing a libel in rem against a public vessel owned by the United States Government, the Circuit Court of Appeals for the 

Fifth Circuit said:

It is a principle of force in admiralty law as well as common law, in fact, one of universal application, that public property in governmental possession is exempt from forced seizure.

It was held that no exception existed where the right of the Government to possession was the subject of dispute. The court also said: An admiralty court may not take a public vessel from the possession of the government in order to try out the claim of title to which that possession is referable. Immunity from seizure of public vessels in the government's possession is not dependent upon circumstances. It is not relative or variable. 

It is absolute and uniform. 

United States v. Jardine; The Cacoethes, 81 F. (2d) 745, 746-747 (C. C. A. 5th, 1935).

On October 10, 1936 the Compania Espanola de Navegacion Mari time, S.A., a corporation organized under the laws of Spain, was the owner and operator of the steamship Navemar plying between Spain, New York, and ports in South America. On that date, while she was in the port of Buenos Aires, Argentina, a decree was issued by the Spanish Government attaching the Navemar and declaring her to be in the service of the Spanish Government and subject to the management of the Ministry of Communication and Merchant Marine. The decree further provided that it was to be in force as a law of Spain upon its publication in the Gaceta de Madrid (which was done on October 11, 1936) and that a notation of the attachment should be made on the documents of the vessel and on the Consular Registries. 

The master of the Navemar received a cablegram from the Spanish authorities on October 16, 1936 informing him of the expropriation or attachment of the vessel and directing him to report and place

himself at the disposal of the Spanish Consul; he did so but not having received instructions, he sailed on the same day for Rosario, Argentina, where he loaded a cargo of linseed consigned to an American corporation. He deposited the ship's roll with the Spanish Consul at Rosario and was forced to leave without it because of a sudden notice of impending low water. He returned to Buenos Aires for additional cargo. There he received from the Spanish Consul the vessel's registry and roll that had been forwarded by the Consul at Rosario, each of which bore an endorsement to the effect that the vessel had become the property of the Spanish Government. No further instructions having been received from the Spanish Government, the Consul at Buenos Aires told him to continue his voyage and advised him to cable the Director of Navigation. The master cabled the latter that he was proceeding to New York as authorized by the 

Spanish Consul.

The vessel arrived in New York on November 25, 1936 and discharged her cargo. Upon arrival, the master deposited the ship's roll with the Spanish Consul General in New York who, on November 28, delivered a letter to him stating that "The ship of your command is from this date at the disposition of the Republic." He was requested to submit a detailed account of the expenses of the vessel. 

Meanwhile the Compania Espanola de Navegacion Maritima, S.A., ordered the master to prepare for another voyage to Buenos Aires and gave instructions that certain repairs be undertaken. Five members of the crew constituted themselves a committee and claimed authority to take charge of the provisions and pay of the crew and the Spanish Consul General stated that their activities met with his approval. 

The latter advanced $300 to the master to care for the expenses of the vessel and, on December 7, 1936, appointed a new master. 

A possessory libel was thereupon filed by the original owners of the vessel and process was served on the vessel and on each of the members of the committee. No appearance was entered by the Spanish 

Government and, on December 14, 1936, hearings having been held, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York entered a default decree holding that the Compania Espanola de Navegacion Maritima, S.A., was the owner of the vessel and entitled to its possession. (Decision unpublished.)

On December 10, 1936 the Spanish Ambassador in Washington had addressed a note to the Secretary of State, calling attention to the proceedings instituted against the Navemar and requesting that the public character of the vessel be called to the attention of the proper authorities to the end that the vessel be released. The Department of 

State replied on December 11, 1936 that it was its practice in such cases "to refrain from taking any action which might constitute an

Disputed facts interference by the executive authorities of this Government with regard to the merits of the controversy", and advised that the Spanish Government had the right to appear directly before the court in cases of this character. In a note of February 16, 1937 to the Secretary of State, the Ambassador protested this ruling and called attention to the cases of The Cucuta and The Attualita, in both of which, it was asserted, the Department of State requested the Attorney General to advise the court of the public nature of the vessels involved. The 

In those two cases there was no dispute concerning the facts embodied in the statements of the Ambassador or Minister concerning the ownership, possession, character, use, et cetera, of the particular vessel and the Department felt warranted, as a matter of courtesy in requesting the suggestion to be filed with the appropriate court. The situation is different in the case of the steamship Navemar. Here important facts having a direct bearing on the status of the vessels are in dispute. In the circumstances, the Department, following the course adopted by it in similar cases, considered that it was not in a position to make any representations to the court. Its position could not, however, in any way, prejudice the right of the Spanish Government to submit in a proper manner its claim respecting the vessel to the appropriate courts for adjudication. 

Ambassador de los Ríos to Secretary Hull, Dec. 10, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 352.1153 Garcia, Marcelino/3; the Acting Secretary of State (Moore) to Señor de los Ríos, Dec. 11, 1936, ibid. 352.1153 Garcia, Marcelino/5; Señor de los Ríos to Mr. Hull, Feb. 16, 1937, ibid. 352.1153
