On December 16, 1936 the Spanish Consul General, appearing specially, made an application to have the final decree vacated and to be permitted to file a suggestion, claiming immunity of the Navemar from the jurisdiction, and to intervene in the suit on behalf of the Spanish Ambassador, His Excellency Fernando de los Ríos. The application was denied, though leave to renew was granted. Thereafter, on January 8, 1937, a supplemental suggestion was filed by the Consul General appearing on behalf of the Spanish Ambassador and a final order was entered on February 3, 1937, denying the motion to intervene and to assert the claim of the Spanish Government. An appeal was taken by the Spanish Ambassador to the United States 

Circuit Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The circuit court reversed the order with directions to enter an order dismissing the libel on the ground that the court below had erred in refusing to act on the suggestion of the Spanish Ambassador and in assuming jurisdiction of the libel. In delivering the decision of the circuit court, Judge Manton stated with reference to the refusal of the lower court

to act on the suggestion of immunity filed by the Spanish Ambassador through the Spanish Consul: immunity; how filed

In filing the suggestion through the Consul as his agent and in seeking to intervene in the suit, the Ambassador followed a permissible and adequate procedure distinguishable from that which was held insufficient in United States v. Pesaro (255 U.S. 

216) and Ex parte Muir (254 U.S. 522). In the Pesaro case, a direct suggestion of immunity by the Italian Ambassador was Suggestion of deemed inadequate, the court pointing out that no intention was revealed by the Ambassador "to put himself or the Italian Government in the attitude of a suitor". In these circumstances mediation through the official channels of the United States was stated to be a proper method, though it was not held to be an exclusive one. Here the Consul, appearing as a duly appointed agent of his Government (compare, The Anne, 3 Wheat. 434; The Sao 

Vicente, 260 U.S. 146) filed the suggestion of immunity and the 

Ambassador had asked to intervene specially as a party to the proceedings, seeking, therefore, as a suitor to assert his Government's claim to the Navemar. Obviously, this is not merely a "respectful suggestion" inviting the court to give it effect-which was the court's description of the procedure followed in the 

Pesaro case. differences" 

Jurisdiction to entertain the suit was challenged (1) on the ground that under the terms of article XXIII of the treaty of friendship and general relations of July 3, 1902 between Spain and the United States matters relating to the "internal order of merchant vessels" Not and to "differences which may arise, either at sea or in port, between "Internal the captains, officers and crews", 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1701, 1708, are placed within the cognizance of the consuls of the respective nations; and (2) on the ground that the Navemar being a public vessel of the Spanish Government it was immune from judicial process. The first objection to the jurisdiction was dismissed with the observation that "the issue in this case is one of title or ownership to the Navemar and not the mere settlement or adjustment of internal differences on the vessel". As to the second objection to the jurisdiction, Judge Manton stated:

The claim of this public control is borne out by the Ambassador's suggestion and his desire to intervene. The allegations of the suggestion we are bound to accept as conclusive. Oetjen v. Central Leather Co., 246 U.S. 297; Ricaud v. Amer. Metal Co., supra; The Adriatic, 258 Fed. 902 (C.C.A. 3). It is not for us to examine the propriety or to determine the validity of the decree affecting property within the foreign sovereign's dominion. If by any misadventure the authorized representative of a foreign state should make an unfounded suggestion, the proper remedy would be through diplomatic channels between the two sovereigns and not by legal proceedings against an independent sovereign or its property. 

accept sug- gestion 

Bound to

Actually, as to a vessel possessed-though constructivelyand controlled by a foreign sovereign, the government is left by general public law at liberty to determine for itself what functions are of a governmental and what of a private nature; and the conclusions of the foreign sovereign or state in that regard are outside the scope of judicial determination in the courts of another state. The Adriatic, supra; The Roseric, 254 Fed. 154 (D.N.J.); The Parlement Belge, supra; See, Note, 31 Columbia 

Law Review, 660, 662.

Moreover, we have here as evidence of possession and control first that, while at Buenos Aires, the master placed himself "at the disposal of the Spanish Consul" pursuant to direct instructions by the Spanish Government; second, that the Consuls at 

Buenos Aires and Rosario made endorsements on the ship's registry and roll of which the master was aware and which claimed the Navemar as property of the Spanish Government; third, that the master on December 7, 1936, advised the former owners of the vessel that on October 28, 1936 the Spanish Government had obtained possession of the Navemar and that since that date he had been "generally under orders of the Spanish Government" as given him by the Consul at Buenos Aires; fourth, that on 

December 2, 1936, the master signed a receipt acknowledging that the Spanish Consul in New York had given him $300 as an advance to attend to the expenses of the vessel. 

It thus appears that the master and his vessel were acting under "compulsion of the sovereign"-subject to instructions of the Spanish Government or of its Consular representatives. The 

Roseric, supra.

In this view of the case, the court below erred in assuming jurisdiction of the libel and in refusing to act on the suggestion of the 

Spanish Ambassador.

After refusal of the Secretary of State to act upon the present claim, the Ambassador adopted the latter course. His application to be permitted to appear and present the claim was properly entertained by the district court. But it was not bound, as the 

Court of Appeals thought, to accept the allegations of the suggestion as conclusive. The Department of State having declined to act, the want of admiralty jurisdiction because of the alleged bound by public status of the vessel and the right of the Spanish Govern- suggestion of ment to demand possession of the vessel as owner if it so elected, ambassador were appropriate subjects for judicial inquiry upon proof of the matters alleged. 

Court not

But the filed suggestion, though sufficient as a statement of the contentions made, was not proof of its allegations. This Court has explicitly declined to give such a suggestion the force of proof or the status of a like suggestion coming from the executive department of our government. Ex Parte Muir, supra; The 

Pesaro, supra. Berizzi Bros. Co. v. S.S. Pesaro, supra, did not hold otherwise for there it was stipulated that the vessel, when arrested, was owned, possessed and controlled by a foreign gov- The Pesaro ernment and used by it in carrying merchandise for hire. The distinguished sole question was one of law, whether, upon the facts stipulated, the vessel was immune from suit.

The district court concluded, rightly we think, that the evidence at hand did not support the claim of the suggestion that

Actual pos- session or control necessary the "Navemar" had been in the possession of the Spanish Government. The decree of attachment, without more, did not operate to change the possession which, before the decree, was admittedly in petitioner. To accomplish that result, since the decree was in invitum, actual possession by some act of physical dominion or control in behalf of the Spanish Government, was needful, The Davis, 10 Wall. 15, 21; Long v. The Tampico, 16 Fed. 491, 493, 494; The Attualità, supra, The Carlo Poma, 259 Fed. 369, 370, reversed on other grounds, 255 U.S. 219, or at least some recognition on the part of the ship's officers that they were controlling the vessel and crew in behalf of their government. 

Both were lacking, as was support for any contention that the vessel was in fact employed in public service. See Long v. The 

Tampico, supra, 493, 494; cf. Berizzi Bros. Co. v. S.S. Pesaro, supra.

The district court rightly declined to treat the suggestion as conclusive or sufficient as proof to require the court to relinquish its jurisdiction. But as the suggestion was tendered in support of an application to appear as a claimant in the suit, and as it put forth a claim to title and right to possession of the vessel, the Ambassador should have been permitted to intervene and, if so advised, to litigate its claims in the suit. In Ex Parte Muir, supra, and in The Pesaro, supra, 219, the Ambassador of the intervening government challenged the jurisdiction of the court, but did not place himself or his Government in the attitude of a suitor. Here the application as construed by the trial court was for permission to intervene as a claimant. We think the applicant should be permitted to occupy that position if so advised." 

The decree of the Court of Appeals will be reversed. The respondent will be permitted to intervene for the purpose of asserting the Spanish Government's ownership and right to possession of the vessel Compania Espanola de Navegacion Maritima, S.A., Owner of the Spanish 

Steamship "Navemar", Petitioner v. Spanish Steamship "Navemar", Her 

Engines, etc., et al., 303 U.S. (1938) 68, 74–76.

The issues presented in the case were summarized by the Supreme Court in the above decision as follows: "Respondent's suggestion on the second application presented two contentions: one, a challenge to the jurisdiction on the ground that the 'Navemar' was a public vessel, immune from arrest and process of the court; the other, that the Spanish Government was owner of the vessel, and entitled to her possession by virtue of the decree of attachment." Ibid. 71-72.

The decision was appealed to the Circuit Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, which stated that the Supreme Court "referred back only the question of title and right to possession for determination at the new trial, and not the question whether the Navemar was immune from judicial process". It held that the decree of the President of the Spanish Republic

had the effect of vesting the ownership and right to possession of the vessel in that Government and, accordingly, it reversed the decision of the lower court, dismissed the libel and ordered the vessel released from arrest and delivered to the Acting Consul General of Spain in New York. 

Under the authority of Crapo v. Kelly, 16 Wall. (1872) 610, it held that if the decree did not take effect upon its promulgation, at which time the vessel was in an Argentine port, "nevertheless it was an instrumentality of expropriation that would become operative upon the vessel as soon as she reached the high seas".

A case involving the requisition by decree of the Mexican Government of the oil tanker San Ricardo while laid up for repairs in Mobile, Alabama, arose in 1938. The vessel flew the Mexican flag and was owned by a Mexican corporation in process of dissolution, the shares of which were owned by a British corporation. Subsequent to the vessel's requisition, the receiver for the Mexican corporation appointed by the Alabama court filed a possessory and petitory libel against the vessel in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of Alabama, and the United States Marshal took possession. The Department of State refused the Mexican Chargé d'Affaires' request that the court be notified of the requisition, stating that it was its policy in such cases to refrain from action which might be interpreted as an interference by the executive with regard to the merits of the controversy. Reference was made to Ex Parte 

Muir, 254 U.S. (1921) 522, Berizzi Brothers Company v. Steamship 

Pesaro, 271 U.S. (1926) 562, and The Navemar, 303 U.S. (1938) 68; and it was pointed out that in the last-named case it was specifically stated that the Ambassador might intervene for the purpose of asserting the Government's ownership and right to possession of the vessel.

In a note of May 19, 1938 the Chargé d'Affaires asked the Department to reconsider its position, to which the Department replied on June 2, 1938 again declining to take the requested action and setting forth its position as follows:

In those cases in which this Government is satisfied that a vessel, an object of litigation, is that of a foreign government, the Department is, of course, glad to bring the facts to the attention of the appropriate court. However, in those cases where title to the vessel is in question, the Department has properly taken the position that the matter is one for determination by the judicial rather than the executive branch of the Government. 

It was pointed out that doubt existed as to the ownership of the vessel by the Mexican Government, that the decree of requisition was being attacked in the courts of Mexico, and, particularly, that the vessel was within the territorial jurisdiction of the United States at the date of the requisition. 

The Mexican Chargé d'Affaires (Quintanilla) to Secretary Hull, Apr. 19, 1938, MS. Department of State, file 311.1253/6; the Acting Secretary of 

State (Welles) to Señor Quintanilla, Apr. 22, 1938, ibid. 311.1253/9; Señor

willingly came over, expressing their willingness to serve and serving the Republic on the vessel." The court said: 

We may assume, though The Jupiter, No. 1, 1924, Probate 231;

The Jupiter, No. 2, 1925, Probate 69 and The Cristina, 59 Lloyd's 

List L.R. 43; 107 L.J.P.

1, both cited with approval in Compania 

Espanola De Navegacion Maritima, S.A. v. The Navemar, 303 

U.S. 68, 58 S. Ct. 432, 82 L. This, if it still exists, is the only difference between the two jurisdictions. The difference appellant sees, that under American law, in order to [possess] immunity, possession for public use by a friendly foreign power must have begun before the ship entered our ports, though under English law this is not necessary, finds no support whatever in any decided case, English or American.

All that is here for decision is whether the Republic of Mexico may have immunity as to this ship, a Mexican ship owned by a 

Mexican company, documented in Mexico and flying the Mexican flag, when as here, she has taken peaceable possession of it in our waters through her lawful agents and representatives, and properly presents and presses her claim based upon that possession. 

We think the question is conclusively_answered in the affirmative, both upon reason and authority. In the last, and therefore the most authoritative statement of the Supreme Court in a case where the claim was very much like this, the Court said: [quoting the fifth paragraph in the above quotation from the opinion of the United States Supreme Court in the case of the 

Navemar, ante, pp. 453-454]

The point appellant makes is not only not decided in this case as he contends for it, it is not even discussed there. On the contrary, in the above quotation it is definitely declared that some recognition on the part of the ship's officers that they were controlling the ship in behalf of their government would be sufficient. Here there is not only full proof of this, but complete proof that they were working under and receiving their pay from the government, and that the drydock company, which had the ship for repairs, held it as in the possession of, and was working on it for and being paid by, the Mexican government.

A decree of the Spanish Government of June 28, 1937 requisitioning all vessels registered at the port of Bilbao included within its scope the merchant vessel Cristina. At the time of the decree the vessel was outside of the territorial jurisdiction of Spain. Coming on July 8, 1937 into the port of Cardiff, Wales, she was taken in charge by the

Spanish Consul and a new captain and crew were put aboard. 

Spanish company, claiming as sole owner of the vessel, then initiated an action by a writ in rem under which the vessel was arrested. The 

Government of the Republic of Spain entered a conditional appearance and moved to set aside the proceedings not on the ground that it was the owner of the vessel but on the ground that it was at all material times in de facto possession of the vessel and was therefore impleaded without its consent. The court of first instance and the court of appeal held that they were bound to decline jurisdiction, principally on the authority of The Jupiter, [1924] P. 236 (see ante, this section), and the decision was, on March 3, 1938, affirmed by the House of Lords. The holding was based on the rule "that the independent sovereign may not be directly or indirectly impleaded in the without its consent". The writ was held to implead the sovereign, notwithstanding that it was in rem, since it had the effect of requiring the sovereign state either to submit to the jurisdiction or lose the possession of the property. Strongly operative in this connection was the fact that the recognized Government was in actual and proved de facto possession of the vessel. The decision was also based on the ground that the writ claimed "to interfere with the property [rights] of the foreign sovereign". In this respect it was held unnecessary that the sovereign have actual ownership. 

Lord Atkin in discussing the bases of the decision said: courts The foundation for the application to set aside the writ and arrest of the ship is to be found in two propositions of international law engrafted into our domestic law which seem to me to be well established and to be beyond dispute. The first is that the courts of a country will not implead a foreign sovereign, that is, they will not by their process make him against his will a party to legal proceedings whether the proceedings involve process against his person or seek to recover from him specific property or damages. 

The second is that they will not by their process, whether the sovereign is a party to the proceedings or not, seize or detain property which is his or of which he is in possession or control. 

There has been some difference in the practice of nations as to possible limitations of this second principle as to whether it extends to property only used for the commercial purposes of the sovereign or to personal private property. In this country it is in my opinion well settled that it applies to both. 

Lord Wright in discussing the grounds of the decision said: 

But the grounds are separate and call for separate analysis, though both alike are based on the general principles of international law, according to which a sovereign State is held to be immune from the jurisdiction of another sovereign State. This is sometimes said to flow from international comity or courtesy, but may now more properly be regarded as a rule of international

law, accepted among the community of nations. It is binding on the municipal Courts of this country in the sense and to the extent International that it has been received and enforced by these Courts. It is true law that it involves a subtraction from the sovereignty of the State, which renounces pro tanto the competence of its Courts to exercise their jurisdiction even over matters occurring within its territorial limits, though to do so is prima facie an integral part of sovereignty. The rule may be said to be based on the principle "par in parem non habet imperium," no State can claim jurisdiction over another sovereign State. Or it may be rested on the circumstance that in general the judgment of a municipal Court could not be enforced against a foreign_sovereign State, or that the attempt to enforce might be regarded as an unfriendly act. Or it may be taken to flow from reciprocity, each sovereign State within the community of nations accepting some subtraction from its full sovereignty in return for similar concessions on the side of others. I need not discuss other possible explanations. . . . But the rule only applies as between sovereign States recognized as such by His Majesty's Government.

I may add that in the present case it is in my opinion sufficiently shown by the evidence before the Court that the Spanish Government had actually requisitioned, and taken possession and control of, the Cristina. That is all that is needed to justify the claim to immunity on the ground of "property." The question how far a mere claim or assertion by that Government would be conclusive on the Court, does not arise here.

The appellants attempted to distinguish this case from The Jupiter "because the requisition was there effected within the jurisdiction of the requisitioning State, whereas in the present case the Spanish Government seized the Cristina in British territorial waters"; and because "such seizure constituted a wrongful act which was a breach of international comity and excluded a right to claim the reciprocal comity of immunity". The judgment of Chief Justice Marshall in The Schooner 

Exchange, 7 Cranch (1812) 116, was also relied upon by the appellants, as resting the immunity on a license in favor of the sovereign state which brings its own property within the alien jurisdiction on the footing of the license, whereas no such license can be implied "when the vessel has entered the jurisdiction in the owner's possession and has then been wrongly seized". Discussing these aspects of the case, Lord

Wright said that the immunity of the sovereign was derived from his independent status in international law and that: 

I do not think Marshall C.J. had any such idea in mind. when he referred to an implied licence under which the foreign vessel entered the jurisdiction. His expressions were apt in regard to the facts before him, but were not intended to limit or define the immunity which follows not so much from the fiction of a licence, as from the independent status in international law of

Transports local regula- tions 

the foreign sovereign. This gives the sovereign, so far as concerns Courts of law, an immunity even in respect of conduct in breach of the municipal law. The remedy, if any, is prima facie by diplomatic representation or other action between the sovereign States, not by litigation in municipal Courts. as the relevant fact here is that the Spanish Government had in fact requisitioned her there is no need to consider whether in any sense, or to any extent, she was subject while in English territorial waters to the law of her flag, or to the operation of the Spanish decree. 

Nor is it necessary, even if it be competent, for the Court to debate whether the decree was validly made under Spanish law. I do not think that The Jupiter admits of any solid distinction because of the fact that The Jupiter was requisitioned within the territorial jurisdiction of the Soviet State. 

Compania Naviera Vascongado v. Steamship "Cristina" and Persons 

Claiming an Interest Therein, [1938] A.C. 485, 490, 602-503, 508-509, 513.

In 1918 the American Ambassador in Argentina transmitted to the Department of State a complaint of the Argentine Government that the steamer Chaco, when visiting American ports, was compelled to agree to certain regulations of the War Trade Board which were incompatible with her status as a national transport belonging to the Argentine Government. "These regulations", it was said, "perfectly logical when applied to merchant vessels cannot be accepted to [sic] the particular cases of our transport, which, while carrying on operations of a commercial nature, retain their character as transports of war by reason of the flag under which they sail, their crew, and finally by the character of their owner and outfitter, which is our Government." In reply the Department pointed out that the vessel was engaged in commerce and that it was the position of this Government that such vessels, even though owned or operated by a foreign government under a naval flag, should be subjected to the same restrictions as ordinary merchant vessels engaged in commerce. Otherwise, it was said, merchant vessels could avoid the regulations of this country with respect to exports and bunkers, adopted as a war measure and applied indiscriminately even to vessels of Allied Powers. 

Ambassador Stimson to Secretary Lansing, telegram of Apr. 9, 1918, MS. Department of State, file 635.119/331; Mr. Lansing to Mr. Stimson, telegram of May 3, 1918, ibid. 635.119/406.

In 1921 the United States filed petitions in the Supreme Court for writs of prohibition and mandamus, to the end of terminating proceedings in libel prosecuted in United States District Courts against three merchant vessels, to recover for damages alleged to have been inflicted by them in collisions in which they were involved while owned abso- Effect of lutely or pro hac vice by the United States and employed in the public sovereign immunity on service. The Supreme Court stated that the question involved was maritime "whether a liability attached to the ships which although dormant liens while the United States was in possession became enforcible as soon as the vessel came into hands that could be sued". In deciding the question in the negative, Justice Holmes, speaking for the majority of the Court, said:

The United States has not consented to be sued for torts, and therefore it cannot be said that in a legal sense the United States has been guilty of a tort. For a tort is a tort in a legal sense only because the law has made it so. If then we imagine the sovereign power announcing the system of its laws in a single voice it is hard to conceive it as declaring that while it does not recognize the possibility of its acts being a legal wrong and while its immunity from such an imputation of course extends to its property, at least when employed in carrying on the operations of the Government, yet if that property passes into other hands, perhaps of an innocent purchaser, it may be seized upon a claim that had no existence before. It may be said that the persons who actually did the act complained of may or might be sued and that the ship for this purpose is regarded as a person. But that is a fiction not a fact and as a fiction is the creation of the law. It would be a strange thing if the law created a fiction to accomplish the result supposed. It is totally immaterial that in dealing with private wrongs the fiction, however originated, is in force. But it is said that the decisions have recognized that an obligation is created in the case before us. Legal obligations that exist but cannot be enforced are ghosts that are seen in the law but that are elusive to the grasp

The Court therefore made a rule absolute for writs of prohibition.

It was held by the British Court of Appeal in 1916 that a requisitioned vessel remained the property of the owner but that it was not subject to arrest for such period as it was under requisition. The Broadmayne, [1916] P. 64.

It merely decides that you cannot arrest." 32 T.L.R. (1916) 519.

The steamship Sylvan Arrow, an American vessel, was requisitioned by the United States Government and while under its control was involved in a collision. The Sylvan Arrow, [1923] P. 220.

claim In 1918 the American vessel Ausable, which was under requisition by the Government of the United States and was being operated by the War Department in the Army Transport Service, ran into and damaged the Norwegian vessel Hassel while in a French port. Subse- Diplomatic quent to the return of the Ausable to its private owners, it was libeled by the owners of the Hassel in the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Virginia. On the basis of the decision of the United States Supreme Court in the Western Maid group of cases (ante), the proceedings were dismissed at the instance of the Department of Justice. Following the failure of the owners to obtain an adjudication of the case in the courts, the matter was presented to the Department of State through diplomatic channels. In a letter of 

February 21, 1924 to the President, the Secretary of State, after setting forth the facts of the case, said:

It seems to be generally recognized in international practice, that notwithstanding the immunity of public vessels from the judicial remedies usually obtaining with respect to other vessels, a Government should make reparation for the damages done the nationals of other countries by its public vessels. 

He explained that it appeared that the Ausable was at fault in the collision, and he accordingly recommended that Congress be asked to appropriate a sum of money to be paid to the Norwegian Government "as an act of grace and without reference to the question of the legal liability of the United States". Action having been taken in accordance with this request, the Department, on April 2, 1925, transmitted a check in the amount of $164,169.23 to the Norwegian Minister in settlement of the claim.

A convention for the unification of certain rules relating to the immunity of state-owned vessels was concluded at Brussels, April Brussels 10, 1926, among a number of maritime countries. The United States convention, was not a signatory, nor has it subsequently adhered to the conven tion. The first three articles of the convention provide as follows: 

ARTICLE 1. 

Seagoing vessels owned or operated by States, cargoes owned by them, and cargoes and passengers carried on Government vessels, and the States owning or operating such vessels, or owning such cargoes, are subject in respect of claims relating to the operation of such vessels or the carriage of such cargoes, to the same rules of liability and to the same obligations as those applicable to private vessels, cargoes and equipments. 1926

ARTICLE 2. 

For the enforcement of such liabilities and obligations there shall be the same rules concerning the jurisdiction of tribunals, the same legal actions, and the same procedure as in the case of privately owned merchant vessels and cargoes and of their owners. 

ARTICLE 3. 

§1. The provisions of the two preceding Articles shall not be applicable to ships of war, Government yachts, patrol vessels, hospital ships, auxiliary vessels, supply ships, and other craft owned or operated by a State, and used at the time a cause of action arises exclusively on Governmental and non-commercial service, and such vessels shall not be subject to seizure, attachment or detention by any legal process, nor to judicial proceedings in rem. 

Nevertheless, claimants shall have the right of taking proceedings in the competent tribunals of the State owning or operating the vessel, without that State being permitted to avail itself of its immunity: (1) In case of actions in respect of collision or other accidents of navigation; (2) In case of actions in respect of assistance, salvage and general average; (3) In case of actions in respect of repairs, supplies, or other contracts relating to the vessel. §2. The same rules shall apply to State-owned cargoes carried on board the vessels hereinabove mentioned. §3. State-owned cargoes carried on board merchant vessels for Governmental and non-commercial purposes shall not be subject to seizure, attachment, or detention, by any legal process, nor to judicial proceedings in rem.

Nevertheless, actions in respect of collision and accidents of navigation, assistance and salvage, and general average, and actions on a contract relating to such cargo may be brought before the tribunal having jurisdiction under Article 2. 

In explanation of the third article, the following provisions were included in a supplementary protocol, signed at Brussels on May 24, 1934: I. 

Doubts having arisen as to whether and how far the words "operated by a State" in Article 3 of the Convention apply to, or might be interpreted as applying to, vessels chartered by a State either for a given period or by the voyage, the following declaration is made in order to dispel those doubts: "Vessels chartered by States either for a given time or by the voyage, provided they are exclusively used on Governmental and non-commercial service, and the cargoes carried by such vessels, shall not be subject to seizure, attachment or detention of any kind, but this immunity shall not prejudicially affect any other rights or remedies open to the parties concerned. A certificate issued by the diplomatic representative of the State concerned,

in the manner laid down in Article 5 of the Convention, shall also afford in this case proof of the nature of the service on which the vessel is employed."

II. 

As regards the exception provided for in Article 3, paragraph 1, it is understood that the ownership, or the operation of the vessel by the State, at the time of the measures of seizure, attachment or detention, is placed on the same footing as ownership or operation at the time when a cause of action arose. 

Accordingly, this Article may be relied on by States in respect of vessels owned or operated by them at the time of seizure, attachment or detention if they are being used exclusively on governmental and non-commercial service.

The convention contained provisions that its benefits should not be extended to non-contracting states and their nationals (art. 6) and for exceptions in case of war (art. 7). In addition, the supplementary protocol provided in article 4: 

As the Convention does not in any respect affect the rights or obligations of belligerents and neutrals, Article 7 shall in no way restrict the jurisdiction of duly constituted prize courts. 

176 League of Nations Treaty Series (1937) 199, 201, 215. 

As of Nov.

1938 the following countries had deposited ratifications of the above convention in Brussels: Belgium (excluding the Belgian Congo and the mandated territories of Ruanda-Urundi), Brazil, Chile, Estonia, Hungary, Poland, Germany, Netherlands, Italy, Rumania, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

OTHER PUBLIC PROPERTY

On March 5, 1918 the Italian Ambassador in Washington informed the Department of State that the city of Louisville, Kentucky, had imposed a municipal tax on tobacco purchased by the agent of the Italian Government for the tobacco monopoly. In reply the Department said:

When it is considered that the purchase, ownership and disposal of property of this nature in the ordinary course of business by the Agency of a foreign government is generally regarded in the circumstances as a commercial transaction merely, I have no doubt that you will agree with me that the benefits of trade should also carry the obligations incident thereto and that no principle of international law would be violated should such property in these circumstances be subject to taxation to the same extent as other property located within the municipality. 

Ambassador di Cellere to Secretary Lansing, Mar. 5, 1918, and Mr. Lansing to Count di Cellere, Apr. 2, 1918, MS. Department of State, file 811.512/69.

In 1919 the board of supervisors of Jefferson County, Kentucky, assessed for taxation certain tobacco owned and held in that County by the French Government which exercised a monopoly of the sale of tobacco in territory under its jurisdiction. On an appeal of the assessment to the Court of Appeals of Kentucky it was contended by the County that under the Constitution of Kentucky only "public property used for a public purpose" was exempt from taxation and that this tobacco was held by France in a trading capacity. The court, in holding the property exempt, said that it was not competent to question the determination by a foreign government that it was holding property in a "public" capacity.

The court was also of the opinion that taxation is essentially an enforced contribution and therefore ordinarily applicable only to those amenable to legal process, whereas the property of a foreign sovereign is admittedly exempt from seizure; that the usual principle that the property owner should share in the expense of protecting his property should not be applicable in such cases, for international amity should require the full extension of such protection to the property of a foreign sovereign, even though not taxed. The court was further of the opinion that if one state went into another with its consent "for the purpose of mutual intercourse" it did not thereby impliedly submit to the local jurisdiction and that since, under the principles of international law, such property has always been considered exempt, the constitution should be interpreted in accordance with this view. 

French Republic v. Board of Supervisors of Jefferson County, 200 Ky. 

(1923) 18, 22, 252 S.W. 124, 125.

Attention is invited to the fact that neither the Government of Great Britain nor the Government of France taxed the public property purchased and possessed by this Government in those countries.

The case of The Johnson Lighterage Co. No. 24 involved a libel in rem against a vessel and cargo to recover for salvage services. The cargo was the public property of the Russian Government and, at the time the services were rendered, was in the hands of a lighterage company which (under contract with the representatives of the Russian Government) was engaged in transporting the goods from the shore to a vessel in New York harbor. The District Court of the 

United States for the District of New Jersey, after taking testimony on an order to show cause why the cargo should not be released from seizure and returned to its owner, discharged the order, saying thatas it the property in question, although it belonged to the Russian government and was destined to its public use, was subject to a lien for salvage services rendered in saving it, was not at that time, or at the time of its seizure by the marshal, in the actual possession of an officer of the Russian government, the lien may be enforced in this court by a proceeding in rem.

AGENCIES AND INSTRUMENTALITIES 

$175 In a suit against the Danish Consul in San Francisco for an accounting and a decree for the balance due plaintiff for legal services rendered the Danish Consulate, the Consul appeared specially and moved to dismiss the suit upon the ground that it was against him in his official capacity. The court, in discussing the question whether the suit could be considered as one against the sovereign, said thatin actions against the officials of a foreign state not clothed with diplomatic immunity, it can be said that suits based upon official authorized acts, performed within the scope of their duties on behalf of the foreign state, and for which the foreign state will have to respond directly or indirectly in the event of a judgment, are actions against the foreign state. Acts of such officials, beyond the scope of their authority or in connection with their private business, cannot be regarded as acts of the foreign state, and the official may be sued on account of any such acts. 

Applying this test to the present case, it appears that this is a case where the immunity from suit of the Kingdom of Denmark might be claimed, if the judgment will in fact affect the foreign sovereign.

It was pointed out, however, that the Kingdom of Denmark was not joined as a defendant in the suit and that it was not made clear whether, as between the Consul and the Kingdom, the acts sued upon would not be considered the private acts of the Consul. It was stated further "that the consul is not authorized merely on account of his

official status or his being named as defendant in the suit, to claim immunity from suit on behalf of the Kingdom of Denmark" (citing authorities, and particularly Ex parte Muir, 254 U.S. (1921) 522 

[ante §173] and The São Vicente, 260 U.S. (1922) 151 [ante §173]). 

The court denied the motion to dismiss and allowed 30 days in which to answer or further move. 

Lyders v. Lund, 32 F. (2d) 308, 309, 310 (N.D. Cal., 1929).

In a suit brought in the United States Federal courts by the Kingdom of Italy, involving a question of title to personal property, it was held by the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the 

Second Circuit: 

The plaintiff, being a sovereign power, will not be relieved of the consequences of the acts, stipulations, commissions, or omissions of its agents. It is only where the courts deem it necessary to uphold the sovereign power of the government that it yields to the political situation, and permits the government to be relieved of the consequences of the acts, omissions and agreements of its agents. In doing this, they have chosen the lesser of two evils, in order to strengthen the arm of the sovereign government. No such necessity or propriety exists where a foreign government's agents come to this country and enter into commercial contracts. They are obligated to the terms and conditions of such contracts, as are other persons and private corporations. It cannot be questioned that Gen. Tozzi's power as representative of the Italian government in the purchase of these necessary war supplies granted to him the power to make a particular interpretation of the contract, and by that interpretation and practice flowing therefrom to make known the intentions of the plaintiff as expressed in the contract. 

Royal Italian Government v. National Brass & Copper Tube Co., Inc., 

294 Fed. 23, 27 (C.C.A. 2d, 1923). See also Pilger v. United States Steel

Corporation et al., post §176. 

agencies On July 18, 1932 the Department of State was advised by the French 

Ambassador in Washington that the "American Battle Monuments

Commission" had been made defendant in a suit brought by a firm Government of architects and that certain of its funds had been attached. Replying to the Ambassador's request for information as to the status of the commission, the Department said that the commission was created by an act of Congress, that its functions were of a public nature, that its expenditures were appropriated for by Congress from public funds, and that "Under these circumstances it is believed that the American Battle Monuments Commission, as an agency of the United States Government, is entitled to immunity from suits in the French courts", as "A suit against the Commission would in substance be a suit against

the United States Government." The attachment against the funds was thereupon vacated. 

The French Ambassador to Secretary Stimson, July 18, 1932, and the

An action for damages brought in Massachusetts against a Canadian railway, the property of the English Crown, was dismissed on the ground that the action was in effect against a sovereign. 

Mason v. Intercolonial Ry. of Canada, 197 Mass. (1908) 349, 83 N.E. 876.

Here the suggestion of immunity was made by a member of the bar appearing as amicus curiae.

In a suit brought against the Government of Mexico and the National Railways of Mexico, in the State courts of New York, the Department of State requested the Governor of New York to ask a law officer of the State to appear before the court and make the following statement upon the authority of the Department of State: 

The Government of the United States has at present no official relations with the administration now functioning in Mexico. 

This fact, however, does not affect the recognition of the Mexican State itself, which for years has been recognized by the United States as an "international person", as that term is understood in international practice. The existing situation simply is that there is no official intercourse between the two States. 

The case having been subsequently transferred to the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York, the Department requested the Department of Justice to direct the appro-

priate United States attorney to bring the above facts to the attention of the court. 

Secretary Hughes to Governor Miller, telegram of Oct. 27, 1922, MS. 

Department of State, file 702.1211/1102; the Acting Secretary of State (Phillips) to the Attorney General of the State of New York, Oct. 31, 1922, ibid. 702.1211/1117a; Mr. Hughes to the Attorney General of the United 

States, Jan. 17, 1923, ibid. 702.1211/1102. See also 1922 For. Rel., vol. II, pp. 709-717; 1923 For. Rel., vol. II, pp. 574–577.

Subsequent to the removal of the cause to the United States court, the Government of Mexico was recognized by the Government of the United States. Thereafter the court vacated the attachment and any levy thereunder previously granted, refused to exercise further jurisdiction in the suit, and dismissed the action. 

The district court then certified this ruling to the Supreme Court of the United States under section 238 of the Judicial Code, which permitted appeal directly to the Supreme Court from district courts "in any case in which the jurisdiction of the court is in issue 36 Stat. 1157. The Supreme Court, however, held that the case was not properly before it and directed that it be transferred to the United 

States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, saying that a question of jurisdiction, such as is stipulated in the statute is not presented where the question of jurisdiction to be decided turns upon matters of general law, applicable alike to actions brought in other tribunals The question of sovereign immunity is such a question of general law, applicable as fully to suits in the state courts as to those prosecuted in the courts of the United States.

The circuit court of appeals held that the suit was in reality against the Government of Mexico alone, as the railways were owned by it and operated for national purposes. As to the assertion that the Mexican 

Government, in operating the railways was engaged in trade and in a non-governmental enterprise, it was stated: 

It is a fact, of which we take judicial notice, that in the leading countries of Europe, as well as in Canada, it is the practice of governments to own and operate railways. This is not regarded by them as engaging in trade, but as the performance of a fundamental governmental function. It evidently is so regarded in Mexico, and while in the United States the railways are not owned and operated by either the state or federal governments, we are not justified, on that account, in holding that the Mexican government is engaged in trade, and not performing a governmental function, in operating the National Railways of Mexico.

The court concluded that: 

the property involved was that of the government of Mexico, and was used by it in the performance of what it considers a governmental function. The property sought to be reached in this country is the public property of Mexico, and is movable property, which that government holds for public purposes, and, being such, it is entitled to the same immunity as a sovereign, or an ambassador, or a ship of war, and for the same reason. The exercise of such jurisdiction by the courts of this country is inconsistent with the independence and sovereignty of Mexico. 

The order vacating the attachment and dismissing the suit is affirmed.

The Nicaraguan Minister in Washington, in a note of April 11, 1922, informed the Department of State that his Government desired to obtain a refund of taxes paid to the United States by a corporation, the Ferrocarril del Pacifico de Nicaragua, created in the State of Maine for the purpose of taking over and operating the national railways and steamship lines of Nicaragua, as part of an arrangement between American bankers and the Nicaraguan Government in connection with a loan made by the bankers to that Government. The 

Nicaraguan Government owned all the stock of the corporation. 

The Minister's request was rejected by the Treasury Department in

a letter addressed to the Secretary of State on April 11, 1923, reading in part as follows: 

It is believed, however, that the claim has been made on the theory that there is such an identity of interest between the Republic of Nicaragua and the corporation as to constitute the latter merely an adjunct or part of the former and that consequently no tax whatever on the income of the corporation may properly be levied or collected, but, having been collected, it should be returned to the said Government as sole stockholder. 

This theory overlooks the elementary and fundamental principle, asserted repeatedly by the Supreme Court of the United States, that a corporation is an entity separate and distinct from its stockholders; that even a sole stockholder is not the corporation itself, and that its rights and powers are not those of the corporation but the limited rights and powers of a stockholder. 

The courts do not disregard the separate corporate status except to prevent fraud or the evasion of some statutory prohibition or requirement. Neither of these elements is involved in the present case and it is clear that the corporation is a separate legal entity from the Government of Nicaragua.

Thereafter, on June 26, 1924, Nicaragua renewed its claim, pointing out that the American corporation had acquired title to the railroad under an agreement of October 8, 1913, involving financial reorganization which had received the approval of the Secretary of State, that the revenues of the company were devoted wholly to the government expenses of Nicaragua, and that the company had no property in the 

United States.

In a communication addressed to the attorney for the corporation, dated June 20, 1925, the Secretary of State said:

Respecting your further arguments in support of the claim for a refund, I may state that I am of the opinion that, as a matter of international law, the Maine corporation in question is not exempt from taxation in the United States or entitled to a refund for taxes paid, and in this connection I desire to point out that this Government does not admit a duty to exempt from the local jurisdiction persons accredited to the United States in any diplomatic capacity who are American citizens, nor does it admit a duty to exempt from taxation salaries of consular or diplomatic officers of foreign governments who are American citizens. Finally, I am of the opinion that the American citizenship of the corporation in question is decisive of the freedom from a legal obligation not [sic] to grant immunity.

Tax in the tax is in effect a tax against the Nicaraguan Government since all the stock of the corporation is owned by that Government and effect on the earnings are used for Governmental expenses. In the light of government

With reference to an action brought in the New York courts against Kingdom of Roumania Monopolies Institute, in connection with which a warrant of attachment was issued against certain property of the Institute in the State of New York, the Rumanian Minister informed the Department of State that the action was in fact against the Government of Rumania, which declined to submit to the jurisdiction, and requested that the Department take steps to owned corpo- acquaint the court with the position of the Rumanian Government. 

At the request of the Department, the Attorney General instructed the appropriate United States attorney to present to the court, without argument or comment, the position of the Rumanian Government. 

The New York Supreme Court considering the motion of the defendant, appearing specially to plead immunity, held that it was shown that the Institute "was created by law of the Kingdom of Roumania whereby it became an agency and instrumentality of that government in the exercise of its sovereign capacity, that no private interests of any kind whatsoever are either directly or indirectly concerned with the administration of the Institute, that the securi-

ties referred to in the complaint are embraced in the public debt of Roumania, not only because of its guarantee of the funds and coupons but also by reason of its absolute ownership and control of the Institute, that the funds attached by the plaintiff are funds which have been deposited as assets of the Roumanian government in its sovereign capacity . . ." In dismissing the complaint, it held that the defendant in its character as an instrumentality of the Kingdom of Rumania was entitled to sovereign immunity and that the national interest of Rumania in the action "unalterably precludes" the court from taking jurisdiction, despite certain provisions in the law creating the Institute, designating its operations as commercial, and providing that it may sue and be sued. It said that "the national interest of the Kingdom of Roumania in the subject matter of the action compels the court to decline jurisdiction even though that sovereignty is not a defendant in the action" and that "Particularly universal is the rule obtaining in international law that when a question of the public debt of a sovereign nation is involved, the shield of immunity from suit in the courts of a foreign nation is impenetrable."

With reference to a suit brought by the United States in 1927 against the Deutsches Kalisyndikat Gesellschaft to enjoin violation of the anti-trust laws, the French Ambassador informed the Department of State that the defendant corporation was an organization "created and controlled by the French Republic" and that a suit instituted against it was, in fact, instituted against the French State. 

In response to an inquiry from the Attorney General of the United States as to the views of the Department of State regarding the matter, the Department stated thatit has long been the view of the Department of State that agencies of foreign governments engaged in ordinary commercial transactions in the United States enjoy no privileges or immunities not appertaining to other foreign corporations, agencies, and individuals doing business here, and should conform to the laws of this country governing such transactions. 

The Ambassador, being permitted to intervene in the suit on behalf of the Republic of France, asserted his Government's claim that the defendant was its instrumentality and therefore immune from process,

Government owned a part of stock 

Taxation of governmental agency and moved the court to set aside the service on the defendants. In denying the motion, the court said:

A suit against a corporation is not a suit against a government merely because it has been incorporated by direction of the government, and is used as a governmental agent, and its stock is owned solely by the government. 

The only difference between the defendants and other foreign corporations and their officers and agents doing business in the United States is that the French Republic owns a part of the stock of the defendant corporation, and that the defendant company and its agents are selling potash for the French government as well as for others. The defendant company being an entity distinct from its stockholders, immunity cannot be claimed by it or on its behalf on the ground that it and the government of France are identical in any respect. Private corporations in which a government has an interest, and instrumentalities in which there are private interests, are not departments of government. 

Neither principle nor precedent requires that this immunity, which, as a matter of comity, is extended to a foreign sovereign and his ambassador, should be extended to a foreign corporation merely because some of its stock is held by a foreign state, or because it is carrying on a commercial pursuit, which the foreign government regards governmental or public.

In 1933 the Department of State transmitted to the Treasury Department the request of the Chinese Legation that the Chinese Government Agency in New York be exempted from the Federal tax on cablegrams, telegrams, radiograms, telephone messages, bank checks and manufacturers' sales tax, and other taxes of like nature on the ground that these facilities were used in the official business of the agency, a representative of the Chinese Government. In refusing to grant the exemption, the Treasury Department distinguished the case of Ferrocarril del Pacifico de Nicaragua (ante, this section) to which the Department of State had referred, on the facts. Referring, how-

ever, to previous decisions in which exemptions had been granted in somewhat similar cases, the Treasury Department said:

Diplomatic representatives of foreign governments and those of the diplomatic class are the only agencies of foreign governments in the United States which are entitled to exemption from taxation as a matter of right under international law. As is expressly recognized in the ruling referred to, any tax exemption of an agency of a foreign government in the United States, other than that of a diplomatic character, must, in the absence of treaty provisions granting such exemption, be granted solely as a matter of policy. On this basis it was apparently assumed by this Department that as a matter of governmental policy such agencies should be exempted. But there is necessarily involved the fundamental question, which apparently was not given due consideration at the time the ruling was made, as to whether the Treasury Department is constitutionally authorized to determine such governmental policy. As is stated in the ruling, Congress has authorized no such exemption and in the absence of a treaty so providing there is no apparent constitutional authority on the part of this Department to establish such a policy for the government. Matters of foreign political policy are peculiarly the function of Congress and the treaty-making branches of the government to consider and determine; the function of the executive department is to administer the law as it finds it, that is, as enacted by Congress or as formulated by treaty, without regard to matters of policy or expediency.

(Morgenthau), Oct. 2, 1933, MS. Department of State, file 893.48/797; the 

Acting Secretary of the Treasury (Gibbons) to Secretary Hull, Mar. 5, 1934, ibid. 893.48/879.

The demurrer was overruled, and an answer was filed in which the claim of immunity was renewed and denials of the allegations of the complaint were set forth. Judgment was entered for the plaintiff. In the libeling of the steamship São Vicente in a United States District Court, the owner appeared and filed a claim in the usual form. A subsequent answer verified by the Portuguese Vice Consul 

General pleaded that the owner was a department of the Government of Portugal and was therefore immune from process in the courts of this country. The court held that by appearing generally the sovereign had waived its immunity.

The São Vicente; The Murmugao; Rose v. Transportes Maritimos do 

Estado, 281 Fed. 111 (C.C.A. 2d, 1922); 295 Fed. 829 (C.C.A. 3d, 1924).

See also L. Mundet & Son, Inc. v. Transportes Maritimos do Estado, 3 American Maritime Cases, pt. 2 (1925), pp. 1057, 1059.

In a suit in a court of the State of New York against the Transportes Maritimos do Estado for goods sold and delivered, the defendant appeared generally and among other defenses pleaded immunity as a department of the Government of Portugal. The court held that immunity was not thereby waived. On motion for rehearing, reference was made to The São 

Vicente, 281 Fed. 111 (C.C.A. 2d, 1922) (ante), which had been decided in the meantime. The court, however, adhered to its former position, summarizing its position as follows: 66 .. a voluntary general appearance of the defendant is equivalent to the personal service of the summons within the state (Code Civ. Proc. §424), and therefore waives the objection to the jurisdiction of the court in cases in which the court would acquire jurisdiction of the person if such service was made within the state. It follows from this that, where the person served is immune from suit in our courts, so that by personal service of the summons no jurisdiction could be obtained, his service of

an answer in which he protests against the assumption of jurisdiction, and pleads the want of jurisdiction as a defense, does not thereby waive the defense. 

De Simone v. Transportes Maritimos do Estado, 191 N.Y. 

Supp. (1922) 864; 192 idem 815, 819. 

Following the failure of the Government of France to establish its ownership of a vessel which had been seized under process issued out of the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of New York, it filed a libel against the vessel and moved the court for an order restraining its sale unless made subject to a mortgage lien which it claimed against the vessel. The court denied the motion, holding that by bringing the action the French Government had submitted to the court's jurisdiction, and that it was in the same position as any private litigant.

The Secundus, 15 F. (2d) 713 (E.D.N.Y., 1926). 

A contract entered into between the Government of Kelantan and the Duff Development Company in 1912 provided for the arbitration of disputes in accordance with the Arbitration Act of 1889 (52 & 53 Vict. c. 49). Certain matters of dispute having been arbitrated and the award having been in favor of the company, it applied, in accordance with the Arbitration Act, to the King's Bench Division of the 

High Court for leave to enforce the award. Upon appeal to the 

House of Lords it was said:

The Sultan's contract to arbitrate in accordance with the Arbitration Act is not, either in itself or in combination with anything else in this case, a submission to the jurisdiction of the High Court. It is not an undertaking given to the Court itself. It is an agreement inter partes, and no more. Sovereigns are not amenable except by their own consent, and there is no principle upon which such consent can be deemed to have been given short of action taken towards the Court itself, such as is commonly called a submission to the jurisdiction. It is, therefore, necessary to find something voluntarily done by the foreign sovereign in or towards the Court and to find in what is done something that really evinces an intention to submit. This seems to me to be beyond the limits of presumption or fiction, for the foundation of the jurisdiction is not any rule of municipal law but the action of an independent personage, who himself is beyond its reach.

Duff Development Company, Limited v. Government of Kelantan and 

Another, [1924] A.C. 797, 829. 

The city of Chattanooga, Tennessee, desired to condemn for street purposes certain land within its boundaries, owned by the State of Effect of arbitrate contract to

Real property Taxation of realty

Georgia and used as a railroad terminal. In dismissing the bill brought by the State of Georgia to restrain the proposed condemnation, the Supreme Court of the United States said: 

Having acquired land in another State for the purpose of using it in a private capacity, Georgia can claim no sovereign immunity or privilege in respect to its expropriation Land acquired by one State in another State is held subject to the laws of the latter and to all the incidents of private ownership. The proprietary right of the owning State does not restrict or modify the power of eminent domain of the State wherein the land is situated 

The sovereignty of Georgia was not extended into Tennessee. Its enterprise in Tennessee is a private undertaking. It occupies the same position there as does a private corporation authorized to own and operate a railroad; and, as to that property, it cannot claim sovereign privilege or immunity 

Georgia v. City of Chattanooga, Tennessee, 264 U.S. (1923) 472, 479-481.

In a suit brought by the Republic of France and the Newtown Creek Realty Corporation to remove the cloud of certain taxes on property in the city of New York, the complaint alleged that the corporation, owner of the property, was organized by the French Government for the purpose of holding title to the property; that it was an agent of the French Government which held all its stock; that the 

French Government paid for the property, was in actual possession of it, and used it for governmental purposes; and that the property was therefore exempt from taxation. The Supreme Court of New 

York in special term dismissed the suit, saying:

The cases cited by the plaintiff to the effect that a foreign. state cannot be sued or its property attached or seized have no application to the case before us, because the taxation of real property is entirely different from an attempt to sue a sovereign state or attach its property, or the seizure of its property by judicial process. It constitutes no interference with the sovereign use of such property as would an attachment or execution levied under judicial process.

In the case of French Republic vs. The 

Board of Supervisors [200 Ky. (1923) 18] the question there was as to the taxation of personal property, and not as to the taxation of real property. Several cases have been pointed out by the plaintiffs where exemptions were granted to the United States 

Shipping Board, to the United States Grain Corporation and to other so-called private corporations organized during the period of the war but all of those corporations were incorporated pursuant to a proclamation of the President of the United States and acts of Congress, and provision made for their operation and conduct and their exemption from taxation. In view of the fact that there is no statute or provisions of law authorizing the exemption claimed by the plaintiffs, I am of the opinion that the

plaintiffs are not entitled to the relief demanded in the complaint, and the complaint is therefore dismissed.

Republic of France and ano. v. City of New York, reported in 74 N.Y.L.J. (Dec. 30, 1925) 1279.

In a suit brought by the United States, under an assignment from the Soviet Government, against the National City Bank of New York to recover certain funds there on deposit, the defendant advanced as a Set-off set-off against this claim certain Treasury notes of the State of Russia which it held. In sustaining the defense, the court said: 

If a sovereign state goes into court seeking its assistance, it is in accord with the best principles of modern law that it should be obliged to submit to the jurisdiction in respect to a set-off or counter-claim properly assertable as a defense in a similar suit between private litigants. Where a sovereign voluntarily litigates, he must play the role of a litigant like any other suitor and abide by the consequences. It is now established that, where a sovereign comes into court, he is unarmed with immunity as against the rights of a defendant who has a proper set-off to his claim. 

United States v. National City Bank of New York, 83 F. (2d) 236, 238 (C.C.A. 2d, 1936). Certiorari denied, 299 U.S. (1936) 563. For case in lower court, see State of Russia v. Bankers' Trust Co., et al., 4 Fed. Supp. 

417 (S.D.N.Y., 1933). For decision granting motion to substitute the

United States as defendant, see State of Russia v. National City Bank of 

New York et al., 69 F. (2d) 44 (C.C.A. 2d, 1934).

In a suit commenced by the French Republic against an American company, in the District Court of the United States for the Eastern District of Missouri, the defendant interposed a counter claim for a sum in excess of that originally demanded by the plaintiff. In sus- Counter taining the plaintiff's motion to strike out the counter claim, the court claim said that in such a case "the defendant might, as a defense to the demand of the sovereign, set off a part, or the whole, of plaintiff's demand by pleading a demand which might otherwise form the subject-matter of a counterclaim" but that "no affirmative judgment can be sustained as upon a counterclaim against the sovereign, whereby the sovereign shall be compelled or adjudged to pay money or any other thing of value”.

French Republic v. Inland Navigation Co., 263 Fed. 410, 413 (E.D. Mo., 1920). 

See for similar rule: In re Patterson-MacDonald Shipbuilding Co., etc., 293 Fed. 192 (C.C.A. 9th, 1923); The Barendrecht, 286 Fed. 386 (S.D.N.Y., 1922); Republic of France v. Pittsburg Steel Export Co., Inc., 184 N.Y. Supp. (1920) 280. 

In July 1917 the Kingdom of Rumania commenced suit in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New

Substitution of parties

York for the purpose of recovering certain moneys deposited with the defendant bank. Previously, the bank had been sued in the State court by a person who, alleging breach of contract on the part of the Kingdom of Rumania, claimed a lien on the same moneys. This party was, on motion of the bank, substituted by the court as defendant in the suit brought by the Kingdom of Rumania. The circuit court of appeals reviewed the decision on writ of error on the petition of the Kingdom of Rumania, which claimed that it was a sovereign state and immune from suit in the courts of the United States and that the lower court did not have jurisdiction to make the order. 

This position was sustained by the circuit court of appeals. The court, after pointing out that there was no specific fund on deposit, but only a credit, said:

The relation between the Kingdom of Roumania and the Guaranty Trust Company being the usual one of debtor and creditor existing between banks and depositors, we are clear that the action by the Kingdom of Roumania to recover a debt owed it by the Guaranty Trust Company was not a waiver of its immunity as a sovereign to be sued by other parties. If this be not so, the immunity can be frittered away either by interpleader or attachment in any case where a foreign sovereign undertakes to collect a debt owed it. 

Kingdom of Roumania v. Guaranty Trust Co., 250 Fed. 341, 345 (C.C.A. 

2d, 1918). See also Union of Soviet Republics v. Belaiew, 134 L.T.R. (1925) 64. 

In a libel proceeding instituted in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York by the owners of the steamship F. J. Luckenbach against the Norwegian vessel Thekla to recover for damages sustained in a collision, the owners of the Thekla appeared as claimants and filed a cross-libel against the F. J. Luckenbach. The United 

States, as owner pro hac vice of the F. J. Luckenbach, became by its own motion party libelant of the Thekla and responded to the cross-libel by posting the bond necessary to prevent a stay of proceedings. The F. J. 

Luckenbach was found to be at fault, and full damages were decreed against the United States. In sustaining this decree, the United States 

Supreme Court said: 66 When the United States comes into Court to assert a claim it so far takes the position of a private suitor as to agree by implication that justice may be done with regard to the subject matter. The absence of legal liability in a case where but for its sovereignty it would be liable does not destroy the justice of the claim against it. 

"The reasons that have prevailed against creating a government liability in tort do not apply to a case like this, and on the other hand the reasons are strong for not obstructing the application of natural justice against the Government by technical formulas when justice can be done without endangering any public interest. As has been said in other cases the question of damages to the colliding vessel necessarily arose and it is reasonable for the Court to proceed to the determination of all the questions legitimately involved, even when it results in a judgment for damages

against the United States.

It is said that there is no statute by which the Government accepted this liability. It joined in the suit, and that carried with it the acceptance of whatever liability the courts may decide to be reasonably incident to that act." 

United States v. Norwegian Barque “Thekla”, Her Tackle, etc., 266 U.S. 

(1924) 328, 339-341. 

The opinion of Judge Mack in the above case in the lower court covered two other cases in which immunity was similarly denied sovereigns who, having commenced proceedings, claimed to be immune from counter claims. 

One of these cases was similar to the above. The other case was an action at law brought by the Kingdom of Norway against an American corporation to recover for an alleged breach of contract. The defendant interposed a counter claim demanding a sum in excess of that claimed by the plaintiff, which the plaintiff moved the court to restrict to such amount as might properly be pleaded as a set-off. The court was of opinion that while this might be correct under New York procedure, it was not necessary so to decide at that stage, and denied the motion. Speaking generally of the subject of immunity of sovereigns from counter claims, presented by all three cases, the court said: "A sovereign state, generally speaking, is not obliged to go into court; but, if it seeks the assistance of the court, it would seem to be in accord with the best principles of modern law that it should be obliged to submit to the jurisdiction of the court in respect of any set-off or counterclaim properly assertable as a defense in a similar suit between private litigants. 

Although, perhaps, the defendant should not be permitted to assert any counterclaim which would not be, in whole or part, a defense to the action brought by the state, yet, if it is necessary to examine a counterclaim for the purpose of determining whether there is a defense to the original action, it would seem inconsistent with the duty of a court of general jurisdiction to do complete justice for the court not to determine the whole nature and extent of the counterclaim, even though it involved incidentally a determination that a sovereign state was indebted or obligated to the defendant. "There is no principle of public law exempting a sovereign state from its obligations under the law. It should not be assumed that a state desires to deny or evade its obligations. There may be sound reasons of public policy why a state should be immune from the harassment of litigation in forums and under conditions not agreeable to the state. But, once the state has chosen its forum, there seems little reason in law or policy why it should not be subject to the substantive requirements of law and Justice."

Upon extending recognition to the Government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, on November 16, 1933, the Government of Statute of the United States took from that Government an assignment of all limitations "amounts admitted to be due or that may be found to be due it, as the

successor of prior Governments of Russia, or otherwise, from American nationals, including corporations . . ." On the basis of this assignment, the United States Government, in 1934, brought suit in the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York against the Guaranty Trust Company, a New York corporation, to recover a deposit made with that bank by the financial attaché of the Provisional Government of Russia, a predecessor of the Government of the Soviet Union. The defendant claimed that by virtue of certain prior transactions, including a repudiation of its indebtedness on the account in 1918, and the giving of due notice of the repudiation to the recognized Russian representatives, the statute of limitations of the State of New York applied, with the effect of barring the action. The district court sustained the defendant's plea, and this view was upheld by the United States Supreme Court which said:

It is true that upon the principle of comity foreign sovereigns and their public property are held not to be amenable to suit in our courts without their consent. See The Exchange, 7 Cranch 

116; Berizzi Bros. v. S. S. Pesaro, 271 U.S. 562; The Navemar, No. 242 this term, decided January 31, 1938. But very different considerations apply where the foreign sovereign avails itself of the privilege, likewise extended by comity, of suing in our courts. 

See The Sapphire, 11 Wall. 164, 167; Russian S.F.S. Republic v.

Cibrario, 235 N.Y. 255. By voluntarily appearing in the rôle of suitor it abandons its immunity from suit and subjects itself to the procedure and rules of decision governing the forum which it has sought. Even the domestic sovereign by joining in suit accepts whatever liabilities the court may decide to be a reasonable incident of that act. United States v. The Thekla, 266 U.S. 

328, 340, 341; United States v. Stinson, 197 U.S. 200, 205; The 

Davis, 10 Wall. 15; The Siren, 7 Wall. 152, 159. As in the case of the domestic sovereign in like situation, those rules, which must be assumed to be founded on principles of justice applicable to individuals, are to be relaxed only in response to some persuasive demand of public policy generated by the nature of the suitor or of the claim which it asserts. That this is the guiding principle sufficiently appears in the many instances in which courts have narrowly restricted the application of the rule nullum tempus in the case of the domestic sovereign. It likewise appears from those cases which justify the rule as applied to the United States suing in a state court, on the ground that it is sovereign within the state and that invocation of the rule nullum tempus protects the public interest there as well as in every other state. 

United States v. Beebe, 127 U.S. 338; . . . [Booth v. United 

States], 11 Gill. & J. 373; McNamee v. United States, 11 Ark. 148; cf. United States v. California, 297 U.S. 175, 186.

We are unable to discern in the case where a foreign sovereign, by suit, seeks justice according to the law of the forum, any of the considerations of public policy which support the application

of the rule nullum tempus to a domestic sovereign. The statute of limitations is a statute of repose, designed to protect the citizens from stale and vexatious claims, and to make an end to the possibility of litigation after the lapse of a reasonable time. It has long been regarded by this Court and by the courts of New York as a meritorious defense, in itself serving a public interest. 

Bell v. Morrison, 1 Pet. 351, 360; M'Cluny v. Silliman, 3 Pet. 

270, 278; Campbell v. Haverhill, 155 U.S. 610, 617; United States v. Oregon Lumber Co., 260 U.S. 290; Bank v. Barnaby, 197 N.Y. 

210, 227; Schmidt v. Merchants Despatch Transportation Co., 270 N.Y. 287, 302. Denial of its protection against the demand of the domestic sovereign in the interest of the domestic community of which the debtor is a part could hardly be thought to argue for a like surrender of the local interest in favor of a foreign sovereign and the community which it represents. We cannot say that the public interest of the forum goes so far. 

We lay aside questions not presented here which might arise if the national government, in the conduct of its foreign affairs, by treaty or other appropriate action, should undertake to restrict the application of local statutes of limitations against foreign governments, or if the states in enacting them should discriminate against suits brought by a foreign government. We decide only that in the absence of such action the limitation statutes of the forum run against a foreign government seeking a remedy afforded by the forum, as they run against private litigants. 

The case was remanded to the circuit court of appeals for further proceedings with reference to the Government's contention that the bank's repudiation of its indebtedness on the account was tentative and conditional. The circuit court held that the repudiation was "unequivocal" and that the bank's notice thereof to the recognized Russian representatives in the United States was sufficient.
