In an opinion of the Commissioners, General Claims Commission, United States and Mexico, on June 3, 1927, it was said: "There is, of course, no rule of international law putting a limitation of time on diplomatic action or upon the presentation of an international claim to an international tribunal" and it was held that "The Mexican Government could not by

Acts in excess of authority withholding payment for a period prescribed by a domestic statute of limitation relieve itself from an obligation under international law to make restitution of the value of the orders." It was added that "From a conclusion to this effect it does not follow that international tribunals must always disregard all statutes of limitation prescribing reasonable periods within which remedies may be enforced before domestic tribunals" and it was observed that, in view of the stipulations of article V of the convention of Sept. 8, 1923, "no question can arise in this case with respect to the exhaustion of local remedies". George W. Cook (United States v.

In a suit brought in the Court of Chancery of New Jersey against the Public Trustee, a corporation sole of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, the plaintiff, a German citizen, sought a decree requiring the defendant to surrender to him certain shares of stock which, he alleged, defendant had seized and was unlawfully withholding from him. The defendant's answer was in the nature of a plea to the jurisdiction of the court, setting up that he was the agent of the Government of Great Britain, that the suit against him was in effect a suit against a foreign sovereign, and that consequently the court did not have jurisdiction. Upon motion of the plaintiff, the court ordered the answer struck out, as being without legal merit. On appeal to the Court of Errors and Appeals of New Jersey, the order was affirmed, the court pointing out that while the trustee was a governmental agency and immune from process for acts performed within the scope of the powers vested in him, the bill in this case charged him with unlawful acts, and therefore of acts beyond and in violation of his authority, and that:

An instrumentality of government, whether corporate or not, although created for purposes of the very greatest importance, does not cease to be personally answerable for acts done under color of the authority conferred upon it, but, in fact, in excess of that authority and without legal justification. The immunity of a sovereign against suits arising out of the unlawful acts of its representatives does not extend to those who acted in its name, and cannot be set up by them as a bar to suits brought against them for the doing of such unlawful acts. 

Pilger v. United States Steel Corporation et al., 97 N.J. Eq. (1925) 102, 127 Atl. 103; on appeal, 98 N.J. Eq. (1925) 665, 667-668, 130 Atl. 523, 524.

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION GENERAL NATURE 

8177 The exercise of jurisdiction by the United States over its nationals in foreign countries to the exclusion of the customary jurisdiction of authorities of those countries-extraterritorial jurisdiction—is, at the' present time, confined to China, Morocco, and Egypt. Such jurisdiction was formerly exercised to a greater or less extent in a number of other countries. The right is derived from treaties between the 

United States and the other powers concerned, in some cases augmented by long-established custom and usage. The exercise of the right is provided for by acts of Congress designed to give effect to the treaties and to the practice that has developed pursuant thereto. Generally speaking, the treaties give the United States jurisdiction over disputes between its nationals as well as jurisdiction over all cases, criminal and civil, in which those nationals are defendants. In 

Morocco under treaties, custom, and usage, the United States has the right to extend protection also to certain categories of aliens referred to as "protected persons" engaged in the service of American diplomatic and consular establishments, as representatives of American merchants or appointed as such for signal services. Extraterritorial jurisdiction is exercised through American consular courts with certain appellate and special authority conferred upon American Ministers (Chiefs of Missions). In countries, other than China, in the absence of a Minister, appeal may be had to the Secretary of State. 

In China the jurisdiction formerly exercised by the American Minister and Consuls has, since 1906, been exercised by the United States Court for China with limited jurisdiction retained by the Consuls. The more recent developments with respect to the situation in the various countries will be set forth below. 

The principal statutes of the United States providing for the exercise of judicial functions by American officials in countries where the United States enjoys, or has enjoyed extraterritorial privileges, are compiled in Revised 

Statutes, secs. 4083-4130, 22 U.S.C., ch. 2; and the act of Congress approved June 30, 1906, 34 Stat. 814; 22 U.S.C., ch. 3.

For principal treaties, conventions, and other international acts pertaining to extraterritoriality, see post §§ 178-183 under appropriate countries. by treaty With reference to the trial of two American missionaries in the Congo by Belgian authorities, certain missionary organizations corre- Acquisition sponded with the Department of State, pointing out that the United States had not recognized the transfer of the Congo State from King Leopold to Belgium and inquiring whether, in these circumstances, the United States would not be justified in demanding that its na-

tionals be subjected to its own consular jurisdiction. The Department replied on October 22, 1909 thatinasmuch as it would not be possible for the United States to exercise in the Kongo power such as you suggest, unless such powers and rights had been expressly granted to the United States by treaty, and inasmuch as there is no treaty giving to this Government such rights in the Kongo, it would appear that it would not, under the rules of international law, be possible for this Government to assume to exercise in that region the jurisdiction which you desire to be invoked. 

Mr. S. H. Chester to Secretary Knox, July 22, 1909, and the Acting Secretary of State (Adee) to Mr. Chester, Oct. 22, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 12053/145.

On June 6, 1922 the Department of State instructed the Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Morocco to give his assent to the application to American citizens of a Shereefian Dahir of October 9, 1920 imposing a business tax within the French Zone, reserving all extraterritorial rights of the United States. The Diplomatic Agent inquired as to the date at which the tax could be considered as going into effect with respect to Americans. The Department, in an instruction of August 14, 1922, pointed out that "Under the most favored nation clause in the Treaty of 1836 between the United States and Morocco" and "Article IV of the Treaty of 1856 between Great Britain and Morocco, American citizens and protégés in Morocco could not be subjected to 'any taxes or impositions under any pretenses whatnation clause ever'" and stated that "In view of the express reservation of American extraterritorial rights, which, of course, include any rights accorded to the nationals of the most favored nation with respect to exemption from taxation, it is believed that American citizens and protégés may be regarded as liable to payment of the taxes ... only as from the date from which the nationals of the most favored nation were required to pay those taxes." The most-favored nation Most- favored- 

---

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

495 was in this case Great Britain, which had already assented to the tax and was the only country, aside from the United States, which at that time retained its extraterritorial privileges in Morocco. 

In a despatch of September 29, 1922 the American Diplomatic Agent in Morocco expressed the view that the employment of the mostfavored-nation principle in determining the date in question would be inconsistent with the fundamental principle that the United States is sovereign and independent in the exercise of its extraterritorial rights, which include the right to have American citizens and protégés exempted from all taxes except such as are assented to by the United States. The Department, in its instruction of December 22, 1922, concurred in this view. It pointed out that the tax in question was apparently that provided for in article 64 of the Act of Algeciras, 2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 2171, which required the consent of the diplomatic body before being applied to those under foreign jurisdiction and expressed the view that in as much as the United States and Great Britain were the only countries retaining extraterritorial rights in Morocco, assent by those two countries could be considered as equivalent to the consent of the diplomatic body. The 

Department concluded that in notifying the Shereefian Government of his assent to the taxes, the Diplomatic Agent could have specified the date at which they were to take effect as to American citizens and protégés but that, since this was not done, the date of notification should be considered as the date of taking effect.

With respect to the reported desire of certain American missionaries in China to relinquish their rights under extraterritoriality and all rights to protection, the Department stated:

American citizens are not entitled to waive rights of the character to which you refer. The treaties concluded between 

China and the United States are contracts between the two governments. They expressly provide that American citizens in 

China shall enjoy, with respect to their person and property, the protection of the local authorities of government, and that they shall be exempt from the processes of Chinese law. The observance of these provisions of the treaties this Government has a right to insist upon, and doubtless would insist upon, irrespective of the wishes of particular individuals who may be influenced by religious or other beliefs. It has been repeatedly held that a citizen cannot by his independent act control the right of his government to intervene or afford protection in an appropriate case. With reference to the exercise of extraterritorial rights, Congress has, furthermore, enacted legislation extending to American citizens in China the laws of the United States. No American citizen in China, so long as he remains such, can waive the application to his person or property of such laws by the claim of a preference to be subject to the laws of China.

PARTICULAR COUNTRIES 

CHINA $178 The extraterritorial rights of the United States in China were derived originally from the treaty of peace, amity, and commerce concluded between the United States and China on July 3, 1844.

Those rights were confirmed or supplemented by the following treaties between the two countries: treaty of peace, amity, and commerce, June 

18, 1858; the treaty of trade, consuls, and emigration, July 28, 1868; the treaty as to commercial intercourse and judicial procedure, November 17, 1880; and the treaty as to commercial relations, October 8, 1903. 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 196, 211, 234, 239, 261; 8 Stat. 592; 12 

Stat. 1023; 16 Stat. 739; 22 Stat. 828; 33 Stat. 2208.

Subsequent international acts affecting the extraterritorial position of the United States with reference to China are discussed infra. 

For the regulations governing the extraterritorial courts of the United States in China, together with forms, see Regulations for the United States Consular Courts in China, (Washington, Government Printing Office, 1918); 

Rules of Procedure for the United States Court for China (also containing 

Rules for American Consular Courts for China) (Shanghai, 1939). For

Tariff of Fees of Officers of United States Court for China, see Ex. Or. 

8062, Mar. 7, 1939, 4 Fed. Reg. 47, Mar. 10, 1939.

These treaties, in addition to providing that American citizens in China shall be subject to the laws of the United States and shall be tried only by the American authorities, also provide that representatives of the United States may participate in the proceedings of Chinese courts in cases where its nationals are parties plaintiff. This right, which is also possessed by other treaty powers, carries with it the corollary right of the Chinese Government to send representatives to the extraterritorial courts of treaty powers in similar circumstances. 

While this right has had an important development and subsequent decline on the side of the treaty powers, the corresponding privilege of the Chinese has never been exercised to an appreciable extent. So far as concerns the United States this right had its origin in the treaty of 1844 with China (1 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 196, 203) which provides in article XXIV that "if controversies arise between citizens of the United States and subjects of China which cannot be amicably settled otherwise, the same shall be examined and decided conformably to justice and equity by the public officers of the two nations acting in conjunction". This provision was given more specific application in article IV of the treaty of 1880 between the United 

States and China (1 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 239, 240) which provides that controversies between Chinese and American citizens shall be tried by the proper official of the defendant's nationality, and that a representative of the plaintiff's Government shall have the right to attend the trial, present and examine witnesses, and protest against irregularities. The Chinese courts in which proceedings of this nature take place are ordinarily those of the district magistrates. 

In the course of reorganizing its judicial system along western lines, the Chinese Government has in certain places created modern courts but, as foreign assessors are not permitted to appear in proceedings

499 in the modern courts, foreigners who desire to insist upon their treaty rights in this respect are obliged to bring their proceedings before the old courts of the district magistrates. In this connection, the Commission on Extraterritoriality established in 1926 pursuant to a resolution adopted on December 10, 1921 by the Washington Conference on the Limitation of Armament (3 Treaties, etc. [Redmond, 1923] 3131), recommended (in section 2 of article IV of the Recommenda tions) that "As a general rule mixed cases between nationals of the Powers concerned as plaintiffs and persons under Chinese jurisdiction as defendants should be tried before the modern Chinese courts (Shen Pan Ting) without the presence of a foreign assessor to watch the proceedings or otherwise participate". In accordance with this recommendation, the Department of State on February 23, 1927 directed the Minister in China to request the American Consuls to inform the local Chinese authorities that, pending a readjustment of treaty relations, the United States did not intend, except in unusual circumstances, to exercise its option of sending consular deputies to observe the proceedings in cases brought by American citizens against 

Chinese defendants.

Department of State, file 893.05/91. courts The special problems created by the congregation of large numbers Special mixed of foreigners in Shanghai from an early period led to the creation of the Mixed Court of the International Settlement, the primary function of which was to facilitate the fulfilment of the above-mentioned treaty obligations. 

The constitution of the Mixed Court of the International Settlement was originally based upon the Mixed Court Rules of 1869 [II Hertslet, China Treaties (1908) 662-664], although this court was actually functioning some years prior to that date. Since 

1869, however, various local practices and customs have arisen which have rendered these rules substantially obsolete. At the time of the Revolution in 1911, when the question arose as to whether the mixed court could continue to function, its position became anomalous in that the Chinese magistrates had to be confirmed in their position by the Shanghai Consular Body as an emergency measure to prevent the disintegration of the court and others have since been selected and appointed by that body without reference to the Chinese authorities 

Attention should be drawn to its very extensive jurisdiction in that it extends to all Chinese and non-extraterritorial nationals residing in the International Settlement and to the fact that under the present arrangement in all cases even purely Chinese civil cases, foreign assessors adjudicate conjointly with Chinese magistrates.

In an instruction to the Consul General of the United States in Shanghai, the Department of State, after expressing the view that a corporation organized in the United States was to be regarded as a citizen of the United States regardless of the American interest involved, said:

The question, however, as to the extent to which this Government should afford such a corporation assistance in a foreign country is one which may properly be governed in large measure by the nature and extent of the American interests involved. The Department considers the designation of an assessor to attend trials in Chinese courts in which the plaintiff is of American nationality as merely a permissible procedure intended as assistance to American litigants which may or may not be availed of by this Government in its discretion. Since it is not the purpose of this Government in the exercise of this right to promote other than bona fide American interests, you may decline to designate an assessor to sit at the hearing of the case brought by the United States Land and Investment Company, Limited, or any other similar case which may arise in the future.

Under a "Provisional Agreement for the Rendition of the Shanghai Mixed Court", signed August 31, 1926 by the Senior Consul and the Special Representative of the Kiangsu Provincial Government, the Shanghai Provisional Court was established by the Chinese Government, to take the place of the Mixed Court in Shanghai. 

The jurisdiction of the Provisional Court remained similar to that of the Mixed Court; but foreign assessors could sit as part of the court only when nationals of countries enjoying extraterritorial status were concerned in the proceedings as plaintiffs or complainants, though they were entitled to attend proceedings and record their objections thereto in criminal proceedings affecting the peace and order of the International Settlement or proceedings in which

On February 17, 1930 the diplomatic representatives in China of the 

United States, Brazil, France, Great Britain, Netherlands, and Norway, and the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs, on behalf of their respective Governments, entered into an agreement providing for the creation by the Chinese Government, in accordance with Chinese laws and regulations, of a District Court and a Branch High Court in Shanghai, superseding the Provisional Court. The practice of allowing foreign "assessors" to witness the proceedings or to sit jointly in the hearing of cases was discontinued in the courts established under this agreement.

Replying to an inquiry from the American Minister to China as to whether a protest should be made against the position of the Chinese Provincial Minister of Foreign Affairs at Tientsin, that, on the appeal of a case coming within the treaty of 1880, he should hear the case on the record alone without the appearance of the parties, the Department of State said:

Since 

Article IV [of the treaty] expressly pro vides that mixed cases shall be tried by the proper official of the nationality of the defendant, and that the law administered will be the law of the officer trying the case, it is not believed that the Consul General at Tientsin is in a position to protest against the decision of the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, that in rendering a decision in a case appealed from a Magistrate's Court the Commissioner would, in conformity with Chinese laws of procedure, consider the record alone, provided the Consul General is granted all proper facilities for watching the proceedings in

While Article 4 also provides that the officer of the nationality of the plaintiff shall have the right to present, to examine, and cross-examine witnesses, it is questionable, in the Department's opinion, whether such provision was intended to apply to hearings held before appellate courts particularly if, under the laws governing the procedure of such courts, neither party to a controversy is permitted to reopen the case for the purpose of offering additional testimony.

The Department therefore indicated its willingness to acquiesce in the proposed procedure.

Article XV of the treaty as to commercial relations between the United States and China, concluded on October 8, 1903, provides: 

The Government of China having expressed a strong desire to reform its judicial system and to bring it into accord with that of Western nations, the United States agrees to give every assistance to such reform and will also be prepared to relinquish extraterritorial rights when satisfied that the state of the Chinese laws, the arrangements for their administration, and other considerations warrant it in so doing. [1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 269.]

By authority of a "Resolution Regarding Extraterritoriality in 

China" adopted on December 10, 1921 by the Washington Conference on the Limitation of Armament, 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 

3131, referred to ante, a commission was constituted in 1926, the United States participating, which made a study of the system of extraterritoriality in China. Its report included findings of fact and recommendations as to steps to be taken preparatory to a general relinquishment by the powers of their extraterritorial rights in China. Report of the Commission on Extraterritoriality in China (Washington, 1926). 

In 1929 the Chinese Minister in Washington communicated to the Department of State a request of the Chinese Government that the United States agree to the initiation of steps looking toward a relin-

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

503 quishment of its extraterritorial rights in China. The Department replied that the Government of the United States was preparedto participate in negotiations which would have as their object the devising of a method for the gradual relinquishment of extraterritorial rights either as to designated territorial areas or as to particular kinds of jurisdiction, or as to both, provided that such gradual relinquishment proceeds at the same time as steps are taken and improvements are achieved by the Chinese Government in the enactment and effective enforcement of laws based on modern concepts of jurisprudence. 

Minister Wu to Secretary Stimson, May 2, 1929, and the Acting Secretary of State (Cotton) to Mr. Wu, Aug. 10, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 711.933/45. 

On December 28, 1929 the American Consul at Nanking informed the Department of State that the Chinese Nationalist Government had on that date issued a mandate stating:

For the purpose of restoring her inherent jurisdictional sovereignty, it is hereby decided and declared that on and after (January 1, 1930) all foreign nationals in the territory of

China who are now enjoying extraterritorial privileges shall abide by the laws, ordinances, and regulations duly promulgated by the central and local government of China. 

It ordered the appropriate Chinese officials to prepare a plan for carrying its provisions into effect. On December 30, 1929 the Consul transmitted the following additional statement by the Government:

The Chinese Government, relying on the sympathy already shown and the assurances given by the powers concerned, believes that there is no difference of opinion between those powers and China regarding the principle involved; and it is prepared to consider and discuss within a reasonable time any representations made with reference to the plan now under preparation in Nanking. In this respect the issuance of the Mandate on December 

28th should be regarded as a step towards removing the cause of constant conflict and at the same time promoting the relations between Chinese and foreigners.

Attempt at unilateral abrogation declaration On December 31, 1929 the Department of State informed the American Minister in China that it did not regard the declaration of the Chinese Government as having altered the "legal status quo", and in a further instruction of February 8, 1930 it expressed the desire that Effect of American officials should continue to exercise jurisdiction over all Americans in China and that in cases where arrests were made by Chinese authorities they should insist "that such citizens be handed over immediately to the consular officer concerned for appropriate action without preliminary trial of any sort by the Chinese authorities" and, when necessary, give "formal assurance to the Chinese

Franco- German convention, 1911 authorities that a complaint made against an American citizen will be dealt with promptly and strictly in accordance with the principles and procedure of American law".

While discussions have subsequently been undertaken by representatives of the two Governments, political developments in China have been of a nature to prevent further important progress toward the relinquishment by the United States of its extraterritorial rights in China.

$179 The conventional background of extraterritorial rights of the United States in Morocco is to be found in the treaties of peace and friendship between the United States and Morocco, 1786-87 and September 16, 1836; the convention as to protection between the United States, Germany, Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, France, Great Britain, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden and Norway, and Morocco, July 3, 1880; and the General Act of the International Conference at 

Algeciras of 1906.

The convention between Germany and France relative to Morocco, signed November 4, 1911 (see vol. I, §17), recognizing paramount

French interests in Morocco, contained provision in article 9 for the modification of judicial practices in that country and envisioned the eventual termination of extraterritoriality. In notes of November 3 

and December 6, 1911, the French Government expressed the hope that this convention would gain the adherence of the United States, to which the Department of State replied that so far as the article relating to the administration of justice was concerned such adherence "would involve a modification of our existing treaty rights with Morocco, which under our Constitution could only be done by and with the advice and consent of the United States Senate". The Department expressed its willingness to "undertake negotiations with a view to entering into such new treaty arrangements as may be appropriate for modifying our existing extraterritorial rights and the rights of American protégés in Morocco along the lines suggested in the Franco-German agreement and in general to agree in principle to the other articles of the agreement, provided that the commercial

Following the conclusion on July 29, 1937 of a convention between the British and French Governments terminating the rights of capitulation enjoyed theretofore by the British Government in French 

Morocco (Parliamentary Papers, Cmd. 5538), the United States was the only remaining country enjoying such rights. France suggested that the United States and France enter into an agreement providing for their termination and proposed that this renunciation take place either by a special convention or by an exchange of notes. The Department of State reiterated the position previously expressed by it that surrender of American capitulatory rights in Morocco could best be accomplished by the conclusion of an appropriate treaty and indicated its willingness "to consider the surrender of such rights through the conclusion of a convention along the lines of the Anglo- 

French Convention of July 29, 1937". The Department also expressed its desire simultaneously to enter into negotiations for a convention of commerce and navigation defining the commercial relations between the United States and Morocco. The French Government acquiesced in this proposal in a note of August 5, 1938 from its Chargé d'Affaires in Washington to the Department of State. 

Negotiations were accordingly undertaken with a view to the concurrent conclusion of the two instruments, but were suspended on the outbreak of war in Europe in 1939.

The Spanish Minister of State informed the American Embassy in Madrid on September 20, 1914 that a new judicial regime based Spanish upon modern principles of law had been organized in the Spanish Zone Zone of Morocco and that the Spanish Government would be gratified if the United States would "immediately place its subjects in the Spanish Zone of Morocco under this new jurisdiction, renouncing the exclusive jurisdiction of its consular agents".

On February 19, 1915 the Department of State informed the Spanish Embassy in Washington that before it could agree to surrender any capitulatory rights in Morocco it desired (1) settlement of American claims pending against Morocco, (2) satisfactory guaranties for the proper protection of legitimate American commercial interests in Morocco, and (3) the establishment of a satisfactory form of government for the International Zone of Tangier. 

In a note of July 25, 1917 the Spanish Ambassador in Washington informed the Department of State that Spanish courts of justice were functioning in the Spanish sphere of influence in Morocco. The note stated that The suppression of the capitulation régime must necessarily go with the existence and operation of the said Tribunals since 157511-40-VOL. II-33 507

the régime finds its excuse for being in those countries only where there are no courts acquainted with the European and 

American law and that the Spanish Government would be gratified if the United States would renounce the regime of capitulations in the Spanish sphere of influence and thereby recognize the Spanish Zone. The 

Department replied thatunder the provisions of the United States Constitution the American capitulatory rights in the Spanish sphere of influence in Morocco can only be renounced by a treaty between Spain and the United States, regularly ratified by the United States Senate.

On August 13, 1920 the Spanish Ambassador in Washington suggested that the two countries draw up a declaration which would provide for approval by the United States Senate, by which the United States would renounce its capitulatory rights in the Spanish sphere of influence. The Department, after some delay, in a reply of March 19, 1923, reiterated the position taken in its note of August 20, 1917, but went on to suggest that steps be taken toward the settlement of claims of American citizens and protégés in that Zone as a preliminary step to formal recognition of the Zone, renunciation of capitulations to be reserved for separate action at a later date. 

The claims here referred to subsequently became a subject of discussion between the Governments of the United States and Spain (see vol. I, §17), and, in a note of January 22, 1930 to the American Ambassador in Madrid, the Spanish Secretary General of Foreign Affairs said that the renunciation by the United States of the regime of capitulations in the Spanish Zone of Morocco was considered to be a condition precedent to the settlement of certain of them. The 

Department of State, on August 6, 1930, informed the American Ambassador in Spain thatwith respect to the capitulatory rights of the United States in Morocco, this Government's position is that the whole question must be considered integrally and not considered with respect to any one Zone, hence it can form no part of this particular question.

During ensuing negotiations the Department instructed the Embassy that the question of capitulations was considered entirely separate from the question of both recognition of the Spanish Zone and settlement of the claims. In January 1936 the American Ambassador in Spain forwarded to the Department a memorandum of the Spanish Foreign Office to the effect that settlement of the claims would be contingent upon both recognition of the Spanish Zone and an

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

509 agreement to relinquish capitulatory rights. The United States did not acquiesce in this position, and the negotiations were suspended.

The Statute of Tangier, concluded between France, Spain, and Tangier Great Britain on December 18, 1923 (see vol. I, §17) provided in article 13: 

As a result of the establishment at Tangier of the Mixed Court, as provided in Article 48, the capitulations shall be abrogated in the Zone. This abrogation shall entail the suppression of the system of protection

On May 29, 1924 the French, Spanish, and British Ambassadors in the United States advised the Department of State of the ratification of the statute by their respective governments and requested the adherence of the United States to that instrument. In its reply of July 

11 to the French Embassy, the Department of State said that the United States declined to assume any responsibility for the administration of the zone, but that after having had an opportunity to examine the regulations and codes referred to in articles 32 and 48 of the statute, it would consider the possibility of suspending the capitulatory rights of the United States in the zone to the extent that its rights appeared to be safeguarded, provided that— (1) more explicit guaranties of economic equality should be given; (2) the signatories to the convention should assume full responsibility for any act or omissions of the administrative authorities of the zone giving rise to a right of international reclamation; (3) the United States might select from the personnel of the American Consulate in Tangier the associate judges to sit in cases wherein American citizens might be parties; (4) existing rights with respect to semsars in other parts of 

Morocco should be preserved; and

(5) no future international agreements with respect to Tangier should affect the rights of American citizens without the consent of the United States.

In his reply of October 31, 1924 the French Ambassador gave assurances as to the first point (to which the Department of State, in a note of December 20, 1924, indicated its satisfaction). As to the second point, the French replied that the statute had continued the existing arrangement by which the French Resident Commissioner was the sole intermediary between the Sultan and foreign powers and that "the signatories to the Tangier Convention have thus confirmed in diplomatic matters and for that Zone the formal rights of France, the power which protects Morocco, and as a consequence the responsibility of France in such matters". The Department, in the note of 

December 20 above referred to, stated that it was not clear "whether it was intended that the French Government should assume this responsibility or whether that Government is merely to act as the intermediary of the Moroccan Government in such matters". In reply to the French objection to the third point, that it would be difficult to contravene the terms of the dahir establishing the Mixed Tribunals, providing that no person holding an official position should sit on the tribunal as an associate judge, the Department said that there was no likelihood of an American Consul participating in the administration of Tangier and consequently of holding public office and that the principle of separation of powers would therefore not be infringed. As to the French assurances fully endorsing the fourth and fifth points, the Department declared itself satisfied.

The Department asked to see the proposed regulations and codes for Tangier before steps were taken to put them into effect and inquired as to the method to be followed in maintaining diplomatic relations with the Shereefian Empire, following the conversion of the diplomatic agencies in Tangier to consulates, as provided in the statute. On May 31, 1925 the French Ambassador stated that the statute was being put into effect as of June 1, 1925 and expressed the hope that the United States would interpose no objection. The Department referred to its note of December 20, 1924 and stated that it considered satisfactory assurances on the points raised therein "to be essential to further consideration by this Government of the possibility of suspending extraterritorial rights in Tangier" and that in the absence of such assurances, it was considered necessary to make "full reservation of all rights of this Government and its nationals, whether by virtue of custom or of conventional arrangement, which may be affected by any effort to bring into force the provisions of the convention of December 18, 1923”.

On Mar. 20, 1928 representatives of France, Spain, Great Britain, and 

Italy met in Paris to discuss Moroccan affairs with a view to reaching an agreement as to the future administration of Tangier. Upon learning of the proposed conference, the United States communicated a memorandum to the Foreign Offices at Paris, Madrid, London, and Rome, reading in part as follows: "It will be recalled that prior to a similar Conference held in the autumn of 1923 by the French, Spanish and British Governments, this Government took occasion to remind the conferring Powers of its position as a party to the Act of Algeciras and ... stated that while it had no political interest in Morocco it had a fundamental interest in the maintenance of the Open Door and in the protection of the life, liberty and property of its citizens in Morocco. It further indicated that it presumed that nothing would be done by the conferring Powers to interfere with the principle of the Open Door or with the rights and interests of the United States. "The views of the United States regarding Tangier which were further set forth in its correspondence with the French, Spanish and British Governments regarding the possibility of its adherence to the Statute of Tangier, remain unaltered. EGYPT 

$180 The capitulatory rights enjoyed by the United States and other powers in Egypt are derived from treaties with the Ottoman Empire, of which Egypt was formerly a part, and from long-established custom and usage. These rights were restricted in 1876 by the inauguration of the Mixed Courts which assumed some of the jurisdiction formerly exercised by the consular tribunals. The courts were created by a statute the Règlement d'organisation judiciaire (66 Br. & 

For. St. Paps. 593)-which received the adherence of the principal capitulatory powers and has been regarded as in effect a treaty. 

See Salvatore Iscaki c. Mutual Life Insurance Cy. of New-York; 

Victoria de Berlin c. Hoirs Fabio Eminente, 23 Gazette des Tribunaux Mixtes d'Egypte (1932-33) 231. Pursuant to authority conferred by an act of Congress approved March 23, 1874 (18 Stat. 23), the President of the United States by proclamation of March 27, 1876 (19 Stat. 662) suspended the exercise of American extraterritorial jurisdiction in Egypt so far as such jurisdiction was embraced by that conferred upon the Mixed Courts. This jurisdiction included civil litigation between Egyptians and foreigners and between foreigners of different nationalities, except in matters of personal status. 

The criminal jurisdiction of the courts over foreigners, as agreed to by the powers, was limited to prosecutions for minor police offenses, for offenses against the officers and functionaries of the courts or those involving interference with the performance of their official duties, and for offenses involving fraudulent bankruptcies. The word foreigners within the meaning of the Règlement d'organisation has been defined as including nationals of all foreign states, irrespective of whether they are entitled to enjoy the regime of capitulations, but excepting nationals of Turkey and of countries separated from Turkey since the World War. Gouvernement Egyptien c.

513 

Mohamed bey Saadi and Georges Khayat c. Hoirs de feu Georges

Loutfallah Sursock, 21 Gazette des Tribunaux Mixtes d'Égypte, 

(1930-31) 87. 

The Mixed Courts consist of three District Courts of first instance (at Alexandria, Cairo, and Mansourah) and a Court of Appeals at Alexandria. The District Courts were originally composed of four foreign and three native judges and the Court of Appeals of four native and seven foreign justices. The personnel of the courts has been increased from time to time as provided in article 4 of the 

Règlement d'organisation.

For a detailed account of the Mixed Courts, see Brinton, The Mixed Courts of Egypt (Yale, 1930). The appendix of this volume (at p. 370) contains an English translation of the original Règlement d'organisation judiciaire pour les procès mixtes en Égypte. The Règlement d'organisation judiciaire was revised at the Montreux Conference in 1937. For the convention and protocol between the United States and other powers concerning the abolition of the capitulations in Egypt, signed on May 8, 1937, see 

Treaty Series 939. See also post, this section.

Judges of American nationality have consistently held places both on the Court of Appeals and on the District Courts of first instance since the inception of the Mixed Courts. Until the period of the World War the number of judges of the "principal" capitulatory powers sitting on the courts was generally equal. Because of the special position of Great Britain with respect to Egypt, particularly since this period, British judges on the Mixed Courts have thereafter outnumbered those of any other nationality. 

Also, since this period, the number of American judges on the bench has usually been fewer than those of the nationality of one or both of the other two "principal" capitulatory powers, France and Italy. The United States, while recognizing the special position of Great Britain, maintained, on the basis of the letter from Sir Henry Elliott to Nubar Pasha of May 26, 1873 (1873 For. Rel., pt. I, vol. II, p. 1118), that as a matter of principle it was entitled to equality. For illustrative correspondence on this subject, see Minister Gunther to the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs (Hafez Afifi Bey), Apr. 18, 1929 (enclosure to despatch 174), and Mr. Gunther to Secretary 

Stimson, Apr. 19, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 883.05/302; Mr. Stimson to Minister Jardine, telegram 15, Feb. 3, 1931, ibid. 883.05/375; Mr.

In a note of Feb. 21, 1911 the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs informed the Department of State that the Egyptian Government had chosen a certain American judge to fill a vacancy on one of the Mixed Courts and requested the acquiescence and permission of the United States in engaging this judge. On Apr. 19, 1911 the Department instructed the American 

Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Cairo to express to the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs the "acquiescence in and authorization of the appointment" and to state that the United States "hereby designates Mr.

Crabites for such appointment". In a note of Apr. 24, 1911 to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Department confirmed this instruction and added that in its opinion the proper procedure would be for the Egyptian Government to obtain the nominations of the United States before making such appointments. In his reply of May 27, 1911 the Egyptian Minister of 

Foreign Affairs objected to the Department's use of the word "designates" and to its theory as to the appointment of the judges, quoting article 5 of the Regulations on Judicial Organization, as follows: 

"The appointment and choice of the judges shall rest with the Egyptian Government; but, in order to obtain a satisfactory guarantee of the qualifications of the persons whom it shall choose, the Egyptian Government shall communicate unofficially with the Ministers of Justice abroad, and shall only appoint persons who have obtained the assent and authorization of their own Government."

In concluding his argument the Minister of Foreign Affairs said: "I will add that this right of choice belonging to the Egyptian Government seems to me all the more legitimate because its magistrates do not "represent" the foreign Government in the Mixed Courts, as Your Excellency appears to believe. They are Egyptian officials, sitting in Egyptian courts, who administer justice not in the name of the Powers but in the name of 

His Highness the Khedive."

In the case of George J. Salem (United States v. Egypt), one of the contentions of the United States was that a national, Salem, had suffered a denial of justice at the hands of the Egyptian Mixed Courts. In negotiations prior to the arbitration of the claim, the Egyptian Government took the position that: "The Egyptian Government's point of view is that its diplomatic responsibility cannot be involved by reason of judgments emanating from Mixed Tribunals which, in Egypt, exercise jurisdiction over foreigners; . . 

The Government of the United States contended that "the Egyptian Mixed Courts are for all intents and purposes municipal courts insofar as concerns actions by or against foreigners".

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

The principal legal basis of the Egyptian thesis, as developed before the arbitral tribunal, was that Egypt did not have freedom in the selection of Mixed Court judges, that foreign powers were more widely represented on the courts than was Egypt, and that the wrongs of the courts were the responsibility of the "States who participate in the working of that justice”. 

The United States pointed out that the institution of the Mixed Courts in Egypt did not involve concessions on the part of Egypt but, rather, was designed as a step toward the removal of concessions which had previously been made.

The arbitral tribunal, on June 8, 1932, held that the Mixed Courts involved a restriction of Egypt's sovereignty and therefore a corresponding restriction upon her responsibility, and that "Consequently the alleged denial of justice committed by the Mixed Courts cannot be brought forward against Egypt as a cause of complaint". The tribunal went further, for, while rejecting the Egyptian contention that the Mixed Courts were to be regarded as international tribunals, it held that the capitulatory powers, in concluding the Mixed Court arrangement, intended that resort to those courts should preclude further claims of a diplomatic nature on the part of their nationals, and that it was only because of doubt as to the meaning of the arbitration protocol of January 20, 1931 that the tribunal proceeded to an examination of the merits of this part of the case.

On May 8, 1937 representatives of Egypt and a number of other countries, including the United States, concluded, at Montreux, Switzerland, a convention regarding the abolition of the capitulations in Egypt. This convention provides that the parties "agree ... to the complete abolition in all respects of Capitulations in Egypt"; and that foreigners in Egypt shall be governed by Egyptian law which shall be in accord with modern concepts of legislation. Provision is made for the continuance of the Mixed Courts during a "transition period" until October 14, 1949, during which period they are to be governed by a Règlement d'organisation judiciaire of 58 articles, annexed to the convention, providing generally for the jurisdiction by the courts over foreigners in Egypt. The term "foreigners" is defined to mean nationals of states parties to the convention "together with nationals of any other State that may be specified by decree". Article 

9 provides that the high contracting parties who possessed consular courts in Egypt when the convention was signed may at their option retain such courts until October 14, 1949 "for the purposes of jurisdiction in matters of personal status in all cases in which the law applicable is the national law of the High Contracting Party concerned”. 

The convention became effective on October 15, 1937 as to the signatories which had deposited their ratifications prior to that date. It came into force as to the United States on August 29, 1938 by the deposit on that date of its instrument of ratification by the American Minister to Egypt who, at the same time under instructions from the Department of State, reserved the right to retain consular jurisdiction in matters relating to personal status as provided in article 9. 

Prior to the entry of the convention into force as to the United States, the President in fulfilment of an undertaking given to the Egyptian Government pursuant to authority conferred on him by the act approved March 23, 1874 (18 Stat. 23) issued a proclamation on October 9, 1937 suspending, effective from October 15, 1937 and during the pleasure of the President, "the judicial functions now exercised by the minister, consuls, or other functionaries of the

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

517 United States in Egypt, except as to cases actually commenced before October 15, 1937, and except as to matters involving the personal status of citizens of the United States as defined in article 28 of the Règlement d'organisation judiciaire annexed to the said convention of May 8, 1937" (51 Stat. 397). 

Treaty Series 939.

Under this convention, the court of appeals is to consist of 18 judges, 11 of whom must be foreigners. Provision is made for the possible increase of this number by two, one of whom must be a foreigner. Vacancies occurring among the foreign judges are to be filled by promotion of foreign judges of the tribunals of first instance. The three courts of first instance are to be composed of a total of 61 judges of whom 40 on Oct. 15, 1937 are to be foreigners. Vacancies among the foreign judges are to be filled by Egyptian judges. In Nov. 1938 there was one American judge on the Court of Appeals and two on the courts of first instance. Counselor Moore to Minister Fish, no. 329, July 18, 1938, MS. Department of 

State, file 783.003/347; the Second Secretary of Embassy (Merriam) to 

Secretary Hull, telegram 67, Sept. 15, 1938, ibid.

Paragraph II of the protocol to the Montreux Convention provides: 

‘... it is understood that the selection of foreign judges is a matter for the Royal Egyptian Government, but that, in order to satisfy itself regarding the suitability of the persons whom it may select, the Royal Egyptian Government will approach unofficially the Ministers of Justice of the foreign countries concerned and will appoint only persons of whom their respective Governments approve." Treaty Series 939.

On February 6, 1922 the Consul in Jerusalem informed the Department of State that he had concluded a provisional arrangement with the Legal Secretary for the Palestine Government, recognizing American capitulatory rights in Palestine. This modus vivendi was approved by the Department of State. However, in despatches of July 

20 and August 11, 1923, the Vice Consul informed the Department that the Palestine Court of Appeals had refused to recognize the above arrangement on the ground that American capitulations were not in accordance with the Palestine Order in Council. The Department, on 

October 4, 1923, informed the Chargé d'Affaires in London that the United States considered that "the capitulatory rights enjoyed by Americans in Palestine remain intact in the absence of an agreement concerning the formal recognition by the United States of the British Mandate over Palestine" and instructed him to express to the British Foreign Office the hope that appropriate instructions would be sent to the Palestine authorities "in order that any case now pending in the Palestine Courts involving American citizens may be treated in con- Council

formity with the agreement arrived at between the British Legal Secretary for Palestine and the American Consulate of Jerusalem". The reply of the British Foreign Office dated November 29, 1923 stated: 

The necessity of establishing the Legislative and Judicial Organisation of Palestine on a definite basis as soon as the terms of the mandate for Palestine were approved by the Council of the League of Nations, led to the framing of the Palestine Order in Council of 1922 which actually came into force on 1st September of that year. This instrument, in the prospect of an early entry into force of the terms of the mandate, on the one hand, and of the anticipated early conclusion of an agreement with the United States Government on the other, contained provisions for jurisdiction over foreigners in articles 58 and 59 to which you refer. 

Insofar as other foreigners previously enjoying capitulatory rights in Palestine were concerned, the request of the League of Nations that Great Britain should carry on the administration of Palestine in the spirit of the mandate, and subsequently the actual entry into force of the terms of that instrument on 29th September last, have had the effect, in accordance with article 8 of the mandate, of suspending the capitulatory privileges of all powers except the United States of America in that country for as long a period as Great 

Britain holds the Mandate.

His Majesty's Government recognize that the inclusion of nationals of American states in the category of those foreigners for whom judicial provisions were made in articles 58 and 59 of the Palestine Order in Council of 1922 was inconsistent with the assurances given to the American Vice-Consul in Jerusalem by the local administration. In these circumstances they admit that it has become necessary to reconcile the juridical position arising out of the Order in Council with those assurances, and are ready to consider what steps should be taken to regularize the position. 

The note continued by pointing out the constitutional and political difficulties in the way of correcting this situation and concluded by stating that the proposed American-British Palestine mandate convention "which allows United States nationals to pass under the jurisdiction of the Palestine Order in Council of 1922 without further difficulty would provide the most satisfactory way out of the present situation." • • • · •

525 A judicial agreement of March 25, 1924, made under article 9 of the treaty of alliance between Great Britain and Iraq of October 10, 1922, provided for the trial before British magistrates or courts presided over by British judges of legal proceedings involving nationals in Iraq of countries formerly enjoying capitulatory rights in Turkey and which had not renounced the same "and of any Asiatic State which is now permanently represented on the Council of the League of Nations". The Council of the League of Nations decided on September 27, 1924 that "the privileges and immunities, including the benefits of consular jurisdiction and protection formerly enjoyed by capitulation or usage in the Ottoman Empire, will not be required for the protection of foreigners in Iraq so long as the Treaty of Alliance is in force". The Anglo-Iraq treaty of January 13, 1926 extended the foregoing treaty, including the judicial agreement, for a period of 25 years.

TURKEY 

§182 Extraterritorial privileges of the United States in Turkey were based upon the treaty of commerce and navigation concluded between the two countries on May 7, 1830 (2 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 1318; 

8 Stat. 408) and upon custom and usage. See "The Origin of the

Capitulations and of the Consular Institution", by G. B. Ravndal, S. Doc. 34, 67th Cong., 1st sess. 1914 On September 10, 1914 the Turkish Ambassador in Washington Unilateral informed the Department of State that "by Imperial Iradé the Otto- abrogation, man Government has abrogated as from the first of October next the conventions known as the Capitulations". The Department replied that- the Government of the United States does not acquiesce in the endeavor of the Imperial Government to set aside the Capitulations, and does not recognize that the Ottoman Government has a right so to do, or that its action to this end, being unilateral, can have any effect upon the rights and privileges enjoyed by American citizens under the Capitulatory Conventions. 

The American Ambassador in Constantinople (Istanbul) also protested to the Turkish Government, as did representatives of other powers. Under instructions from the Department of State, the Embassy, on February 19, 1916, transmitted a note verbale to the Turkish 

Foreign Office, stating thatthe Department of State cannot agree with the position taken by the Imperial Government in this matter; but, on the contrary the 

Department holds that a convention by which one country gives the right to exercise certain rights of sovereignty within its territory to another country is absolute in its nature, and the grantor, having parted with the rights unconditionally, cannot resume their exercise except by a reconveyance or a formal consent on the part of the grantee who is entitled to exercise them. 

Extraterritoriality holds much the same relation to sovereignty over persons that international servitudes hold to sovereignty over territory. In both cases the unconditional grant of sovereign rights cannot be abrogated without the assent of the grantee, the owner.

The chief reason for obtaining the right of extraterritoriality is to insure protection for the life, liberty and interests of the nationals of one State while within the territory of the State granting the right. If the surrender of extraterritorial rights lessens such protection, a government cannot relinquish the right without violating its manifest duty. As to whether the surrender of the right will lessen the safety of its nationals within the foreign territory, their government alone is in a position to decide. Following the practice in similar cases with other countries in which the United States exercised extraterritorial rights under treaty, this Government will, upon the establishment of judicial and administrative reforms in Turkey, consider whether they are of such a character as to warrant the surrender of the extraterritorial rights of such American citizens in the Ottoman 

Empire. 

In conclusion, the American Embassy is further instructed to notify the Imperial Ottoman Government that the United States will hold it responsible for any injury which may be occasioned to the United States or to its citizens, through any interference on the part of the Ottoman authorities, with the extraterritorial rights possessed by the United States and its citizens in the 

Ottoman Empire. 

The Turkish Government maintained its position. The Embassy and the Foreign Office then agreed that, pending a solution of the matter, they would attempt to settle direct any cases that might arise.

OTHER COUNTRIES 

§183 American extraterritorial rights in Ethiopia were acquired by virtue of most-favored-nation clauses contained in treaties entered into between the United States and Ethiopia in 1903 and 1914, 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 466; 33 Stat. 2254; 3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 

2578; 41 Stat. 1711. Extraterritorial privileges were granted Great

Britain by Ethiopia in an early treaty, 37 Br. & For. St. Paps. 4, but the rights of the United States and other countries were generally considered to be based upon the treaty of friendship and commerce between Ethiopia and France concluded January 10, 1908, 101 idem 997. As a consequence of article VII of this treaty and of custom and usage, cases involving foreigners of the same nationality were subject to the jurisdiction of the consular court of that nationality. Cases involving foreigners of different nationalities were tried by the consular court of the defendant's nationality. Cases involving foreigners and Ethiopian subjects were under the jurisdiction of a special court consisting of an Ethiopian magistrate whose decision was required to be concurred in by the consul of the foreign litigant's nationality. In case of disagreement, the Emperor gave the final decision.

In 1913 the Minister to Bulgaria was instructed by the Department Bulgaria of State as follows: 

By reason of the fact that the United States possesses no capitulatory rights vis-à-vis Bulgaria, except by virtue of the Treaty of Berlin and through the operation of the most-favored-nation principle, which the Bulgarian Government recognizes as being applicable to this country as a matter of comity, there would seem to be no necessity for any formal negotiations on the subject of the relinquishment of American capitulatory rights in Bulgaria; it would seem feasible and advisable simply to define what is understood to be the existing situation by an exchange of views with the 

Bulgarian Government. To this end, you are authorized to bring to the knowledge of the Foreign Office, in whatever manner you may deem expedient, the fact that this Government, recognizing that it has no intrinsic right to the benefit of the Capitulations as established by the Treaty of Berlin, stands ready to facilitate the negotiations in which the Bulgarian Government is engaged, by assenting in advance to the relinquishment of such rights as it now enjoys in this respect, at such time as the signatory Powers shall all have consented to the discontinuance of the capitulatory régime Article 175 of the treaty of peace between the Allied and Associated 

Powers and Bulgaria, signed at Neuilly-sur-Seine on November 27, 1919, provides:

The immunities and privileges of foreigners as well as the rights of jurisdiction and of consular protection enjoyed by the Allied and Associated Powers in Bulgaria by virtue of the capitulations, usages and treaties, may form the subject of special conventions between each of the Allied and Associated Powers concerned and 

Bulgaria. [Gt. Br., Treaty Ser. no. 5 (1920), Cmd. 522.]

With respect to the status of American capitulatory rights in Bulgaria, the Department of State, on September 23, 1925, explained:

Inasmuch as the United States has not ratified the Treaty of Neuilly, it is of course not in a position to rely directly upon the provisions of that Treaty as a basis for any claim which it may care to assert in regard to the continued enjoyment of capitulatory rights in Bulgaria. On the other hand, it does not appear that this country has at any time relinquished its capitulatory rights in Bulgaria and, accordingly, those rights may be said to be still subsistent.

The Department added that it was principally interested in assuring to American nationals treatment equal to that accorded nationals of other countries and that it "would therefore, under present circumstances, be disposed to press for rights of a capitulatory character only 531

Iran Siam in the event that other Powers advance claims by virtue of the capitulations."

The extraterritorial rights enjoyed by the United States in Siam by virtue of the treaty of amity and commerce of 1856 (2 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 1629; 11 Stat. 683) were abolished in the treaty and protocol revising treaties hitherto existing, concluded between the two countries on December 16, 1920 (3 Treaties, etc. [Redmond, 

1923] 2829, 2835; 42 Stat., pt. 2, 1928, 1933), wherein it was provided that citizens of the United States should thereafter be subject to the jurisdiction of the Siamese courts. It was provided that until five years after the promulgation and putting into effect of all the Siamese codes, the United States would reserve the right to evoke any case in which an American was defendant or accused, from any Siamese court (except the Supreme or Dika Court) and try the case before American diplomatic or consular officials. It was further provided that cases evoked and tried by American officials should be tried according to the Siamese law when the subject-matter was covered by Siamese codes, regularly promulgated and in force. 

The United States also reserved the right to object to any of the new codes and the Siamese Government agreed to attempt to meet such objections. After having examined some of the Siamese Civil

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

533 and Commercial Codes, the Department of State, on December 17, 1925, instructed the Chargé d'Affaires at Bangkok thatthe Department takes the position that in changing from the extraterritorial regime to the present regime in Siam the vested rights of American nationals shall not be prejudiced, that American nationals shall be given full opportunity in the courts of Siam to protect not only their vested rights but such rights as they may acquire under Siamese law and that, with respect to the criminal jurisdiction of the Siamese Government over American nationals, they shall be subjected only to a just procedure and no cruel or unusual punishments shall be imposed. In general, the Department would be inclined to object only to such laws as would tend to bring about a reversion in Siam to the laws and procedure which were the basis for the establishment of extraterritorial jurisdiction. 

If American citizens in Siam are protected in the manner suggested above in civil and criminal affairs, the Department does not feel that it could object to the free exercise of Siamese sovereignty in enacting such laws as that Government deems to be necessary within its territory.

$184 With respect to the application to an American citizen of a Shanghai municipal bylaw regarding the carrying of arms, the United States 

Court for China held that- 535 it would create a condition of chaos for any one government to hold that it could not enforce these by-laws against its own citizens, and Municipal there seems to be some good reason for holding under the common bylaws and regulations law power which the Court possesses that the Court can enforce the rules and regulations of the municipality that is existing within its jurisdiction, especially in a municipality such as Shanghai where the by-laws have been passed and promulgated by and with the advice and consent of our Minister The court pointed out further that the bylaws had been conceded to be binding by courts of other nationalities and that the United States Commissioner and previously the consular officers had enforced the traffic regulations and other ordinances handed down by the Municipal Council after they had been sanctioned and approved by the consular body and the diplomatic corps in Peking. 

United States v. Fuller, 155 (n. s.) North-China Herald (Apr. 25, 1925) 158.

With reference to certain mining regulations promulgated by the Chinese Government in 1907, the Department of State instructed the Mining regu- Chargé d'Affaires in China to inform the appropriate Chinese official lations, 1907 as follows: 

Articles 49, 60, 61, and 62 are inconsistent with our extraterritorial rights in China. Article 49 places the foreigner under the control of the Chinese authorities and declares that the head office may order work stopped, and that any consequent loss must be sustained by the "mining merchants," but that "the foreign consuls and ministers can not be allowed to interfere."

Article 60 provides that when a foreigner has any monetary litigation with Chinese or other foreigners not members of the mining concern, the "matter must be settled in accordance with Chinese law without partiality, and if there is no precedent in Chinese records for any such case the usage and law of the countries concerned may be consulted and applied to assist the Chinese law."

Article 61 is offensively worded in the clause which threatens withdrawal of mining privileges as a penalty for any miscarriage of justice as administered by a consul and viewed from the standpoint of local authorities.

In article 62 appeal is allowed by foreigners, in matters pertaining to mines, to the head office, the provisional judge, the viceroy, or to the board of agriculture and commerce, "but the consul or minister must not interfere."

Press regulations, Egypt, 1909

On the whole, it seems to the department that the revised regulations are absolutely unreasonable and that their enforcement would interfere with our long-established treaty rights in China.

In May 1909 the British Embassy at Washington raised, with the Department of State, the question of the applicability to foreigners of the Press Law of 1881 which had been recently revived by the Egyptian Government with a view to checking the extreme license of the native press. The Department replied that, while the Government of the United States did not wish to be understood as approving the law as applicable to all American newspapers and while reserving all rights in the matter, it would not object to the application of the law to American newspapers supporting political propaganda threatening the peace and order of the Egyptian Government. 

Subsequently the Department made the following additional observations: 

1. The proposed press law would appear to enable the Egyptian Government entirely to control the press in Egypt, since, as the law provides that consent to publish must be obtained prior to publication, it would only be necessary to withhold consent in order to make it impossible for any paper, considered for any reason undesirable, to begin printing; or to withdraw consent in order to compel the suspension of any other publication already licensed and printed. Moreover, there appear to be no rules or regulations setting forth the causes which would justify either the withholding or the withdrawing of this consent, which would seem to leave the matter entirely within the arbitrary discretion of the officers whose duty it would be to enforce the law. It would therefore seem that before any general and unrestricted assent shall be given to this law, that at least the broad principles which are to govern the interpretation and enforcement of the law, should be fully set forth. 

Moreover, under the general theory of extraterritoriality, our citizens would, in Egypt, be subject to our own laws and entitled to certain constitutional privileges, one of the most highly prized of which is freedom of speech and of the press. Were this Government now unqualifiedly to consent to the proposed press law, it would seem that this freedom would be surrendered to a degree that would amount almost, if not quite, to abandonment. The propriety of such a course may well be questioned, particularly in view of the fact that the acquiescence of this Government as already suggested and communicated to the Government of Great Britain, would seem to be all that is actually necessary to

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

537 enable the Egyptian Government to meet the present untoward situation. 

Ambassador Bryce to Secretary Knox, May 14, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 19163/8-9; the Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Mr. 

Bryce, June 7, 1909, aide-mémoire, June 16, 1909, ibid. 19163/10.

In 1910 the Department of State informed the American Chargé d'Affaires in Siam that while it had no objection to compliance by American nationals with the Siamese automobile law and to the enforcement thereof, its authorization, which was to meet the wishes of the Siamese Government, was "not to be taken as indication that it desires to formulate and promulgate laws for American citizens in extraterritorial countries", adding:

Where the laws, extended by treaties and acts of Congress to extraterritorial countries, fail to furnish sufficient and appropriate Ministerial remedies, Congress has provided a method of supplying such regulations deficiencies by decrees and regulations which shall have the force of law until annulled or modified by act of Congress. (R.S. Section 4030 [4083] to 4130). The functions of the Secretary of 

State, in countries in which there is a Minister, is limited in this respect, merely to transmitting the regulations to Congress for revision. The Department, however, may comment and doubtless even criticise any such regulations and lay before Congress such comments or criticism, in connection with its transmission of the regulation.

In view of this condition of the law, the Department can merely state that it sees no objection to extending the Supplementary Law to the Law on Navigation in Siamese Waters to American citizens residing in Siam, reserving of course all treaty rights. 

As by statute [12 Stat. 73] our consular "jurisdiction [in those countries where the United States enjoys extraterritorial rights by treaties] in both criminal and civil matters shall, in all cases, be exercised and enforced in conformity with the laws of the United States which are hereby, so far as necessary to execute such treaties respectively, and so far as they are suitable to carry the same into effect, extended over all citizens of the United States in those countries ; but in all cases where such laws are not adapted to the object or are deficient in the provisions necessary to furnish suitable remedies, the common law and the Law of Equity and Admiralty shall be extended in like manner over such citizens and others in those countries," and if they fail to "furnish appropriate and sufficient remedies, the ministers in those countries, respectively, shall, by decrees and regulations, supply such defects and deficiencies," it is difficult to see how the consular courts can enforce local laws and regulations by assuming jurisdiction of offenses against the same, until such local laws and regulations have, in the manner authorized by Congress, been made a part of that body of American law, which has been extended to extraterritorial countries. In the opinion of the Department, it seems that this may be done where necessary, by incorporating the local laws or regulations into a decree or

Taxation

regulation of the Minister or other authorized agent which shall be promulgated by him in the manner provided in the Revised Statutes for the issuance and promulgation of regulations of ministers and other authorized agents. 

The Chargé d'Affaires at Bangkok (Tarler) to Secretary Knox, no. 581, Mar. 29, 1910, and the Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to Mr. Tarler, May 9, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 892.797; Mr. Tarler to Mr. Knox, no. 608, May 23, 1910, Mr. Wilson to Mr. Tarler, July 8, 1910, and the Acting

On December 14, 1922 the Minister of the United States in Peking reported the imposition by Chinese authorities of famine-relief surcharge tax stamps upon documents affecting the trade of treaty nationals. The reply of the Department of State, dated May 22, 1923, pointed out that "by Article IV of the Treaty of 1903 between this Government and China, (Malloy, Vol. I, page 261), .. the right of China to impose forms of taxation other than those specified in the article was specifically recognized". The Department referred to article XL of the treaty of 1858 between China and France (51 Br. and For. St. Paps. 637), to the benefits of which the United States is entitled by virtue of most-favored-nation treatment, which was interpreted as prohibiting all taxation of French nationals except as provided in the treaty, including, probably, the taxes here in question. 

It also said:

Apart from the possible legal sanction for foreigners, whether rightly or wrongly, to claim exemption from all forms of taxation in China, the Department suggests that, between the two extremes presented by the French Treaty of 1858 and our own treaty of 1903, an equitable medium might be found which would allow a reasonable exercise by China of the ordinary sovereign rights in fiscal matters, and at the same time prevent abuse of power through the imposition of undue burdens or vexatious restrictions upon foreigners residing or doing business in China.

It concluded that "there is no proper ground for protesting against the imposition of the Famine Relief Surcharge Stamps upon likin receipts".

In 1932 Chinese authorities threatened the withdrawal of postal facilities from foreign publications in China that did not register as provided in a Chinese law concerning publications. The Department of State considered that this law was of such a nature that companies could not register under it and at the same time retain their extraterritorial rights and status, and that: 

Although the American Government might be prepared in certain cases, when the circumstances so warrant, to acquiesce in a denial to American nationals of postal facilities by the Chinese authorities the American Government does not admit the right of the Chinese Government generally to deny postal facilities to American nationals in order to compel them to comply with a Chinese law which, under the extraterritorial system, is not applicable to them and which subjects them to penal provisions which the Chinese authorities have no right to impose. 

The application of the law was indefinitely postponed.

In 1927 a case arose in Morocco involving an American citizen who had entered into a contract purporting to give him title to a crop of hay. He had taken possession and was engaged in removing the hay when, at the instigation of certain French citizens who claimed to be the rightful owners, the hay was cut, removed, and sold under judicial order of the local French tribunal. The proceeds of the sale were held by the court; and the American citizen was advised to appear before it in order to obtain an adjudication of his claim. The American Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Morocco was instructed: 

As an American citizen, by virtue of a contract entered into in conformity with local law, Mr. Fink obtained a right to the hay in question. He was entitled by reason of privileges enjoyed by this Government and its citizens in Morocco to have any question as to rights of third parties in that hay decided only in the American Consular Court at Casablanca. The action of the French authorities in seizing a portion of the hay which Mr. Fink was gathering, at the request of third parties claiming an interest in

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

545 the hay, and the impounding of the money resulting from the judicial sale of the seized portion in the French court, deprived Mr. Fink of his right to have questions affecting his title tried by his Consular Court. The action of the French authorities, therefore, has resulted not only in a violation of Mr. Fink's privileges as an American citizen, but is an invasion of the American consular jurisdiction in Morocco established by treaty, custom and usage.
