In a suit brought in the United States Court for China, to quiet title to a piece of real property situated in the International Settlement of Shanghai, it appeared that plaintiff had a deed to the land and had occupied it for over 50 years and that the principal object of the suit was to extinguish any possible claims that might arise from Real property the fact that at an earlier date the land had been registered in the name of another in the American Consulate. The court held that under international law "prescription, like other incidents of land tenure, is governed by the lex rei sitae" which would in this case be the law of China, and that it had jurisdiction to apply this law in as much as international law is part of the "laws of the United States". It con-

Registration of deeds cluded that, in as much as China had no law of prescription, it would be impossible for it to give the decree asked for but that a sufficient showing had been made to justify a decree authorizing plaintiff to register his title.

Doong Nyi Benevolent Association v. Henry S. Grew et al., 2 Extraterr. 

Cas. (1921) 102, 103, 104. 

An earlier case, Laura Brown v. Robert W. Sexton, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1910) 211, involved suit on a mortgage to certain property owned by the plaintiff, a Spanish subject, of which the title deeds as well as the mortgage were registered in the Spanish Consulate. The court received proof as to the applicable law of Spain and, finding the mortgage invalid under that law, dismissed the petition.

In 1926 the United States Court for China considered a case wherein a Portuguese plaintiff who had leased real property to the defendant, an American citizen, sought to dispossess the latter, claiming that since he had not authenticated the lease as required by the District of Columbia Code, the lease was merely from month to month. The court referred to Brown v. 

Sexton (ante) and held in accordance therewith that the District of Columbia Code did not apply. Collaco v. Crawley, 158 (n. s.) North-China Herald (Mar. 13, 1926) 491. Although this rule was sufficient to decide the case at hand, the court raised the further question as to whether MacDonald v. 

Anderson (H.B.M. Supreme Court for China, 72 (n. s.) North-China Herald [Jan. 16, 1904] 247; 1 Extraterr. Cas. 77, n.) did not represent the correct law. In that case the two parties, both English, claimed title to a piece of land in Tientsin, and the defendant contended that the plaintiff's claim was barred by the British real-property-limitation act of 1874. The court applied the principle that land and its incidents are subject to the lex situs which was, in this case, the Chinese law, and held that the act in question was therefore not applicable. This case relied in turn upon The Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs v. Charlesworth, Pilling Co., et al., [1901] A.C. 

373, in which a similar rule was declared as to land in the extraterritorial jurisdiction of Zanzibar. 

With respect to the registration of deeds relating to estates in land, it is understood that the principle that title to realty is governed by the lex loci is not affected by the rights of extraterritoriality and, therefore, that the legal principles and forms under which foreigners acquire and hold land in China are governed by Chinese law and usage. Therefore, no reason is apparent why consular officers should decline to record deeds because they are not executed in accordance with the laws of the District of Columbia. They should, however, require such deeds to be executed in conformity with Chinese law.

The Director of the Consular Bureau (Carr) to Consul General Cun ningham, no. 37, Dec. 13, 1915, MS. Department of State, file 125.067/47.

An American citizen, since deceased, was the owner of the record title to a piece of real property in China, the document of title having been issued by the Taotai and placed on record in the American Consulate General at Shanghai. It appeared, however, that the

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

547 American citizen had held merely as trustee and that two Chinese nationals claimed to be the beneficiaries. In proceedings instituted in the United States Court for China by the petition of one of them to have the title made over to him, he introduced in evidence a judgment rendered by the Mixed Court of Shanghai in which his claim was recognized but in which it was said that the title deed was evidence of title in the Foreign Settlement and could not be canceled without creating diplomatic difficulties. This was held by the United 

States court to be a recognition by the mixed court "that it was without authority to enter any judgment affecting the integrity of any foreign deed which had received the chop [certification] of the Taotai" and that its decision therefore did not purport to announce a judgment that could be regarded by a foreign court as final and conclusive. The court, recognizing the matter as one for determination by Chinese authorities, left the matter in abeyance pending a request to the Consul General to submit the matter to the Shanghai 

Taotai for appropriate action. 

In re Barchet's Estate, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1911) 235, 239.

It had been pointed out by the Ambassador that the leased territory was to all intents and purposes a part of Japan proper and that the consul's exequatur was issued by Japan, by virtue of the treaty between the United States and Japan, and gave no authority for the exercise of extraterritorial powers.

In a criminal prosecution brought before the United States Court for China against an American citizen accused of having committed an offense in the Japanese leased territory of Kwantung, the court, in an oral opinion of Mar. 2, 1925, upheld a plea of abatement to the jurisdiction on the ground that the United States does not exercise extraterritorial jurisdiction in the leased territory. In a letter of Mar. 9, 1925 from the judge of the court to the American Consul General in Shanghai, the grounds of the decision were said to be that during the entire period of the lease of this territory, first to Russia, then to Japan, sole jurisdiction therein had been exercised by the lessee country and that this jurisdiction had been acquiesced in by the United States. 

Enclosure to despatch 2883 from Minister Schurman to Secretary Kellogg, Mar. 28, 1925, MS. Department of State, file 172.1/62. On Mar. 11, 1925 the

Department of State informed the United States District Attorney in China that it did not consider that the United States exercised extraterritorial rights in this territory. Secretary Kellogg to District Attorney Husar, telegram of Mar. 11, 1925, MS. Department of State, file 172.1/59.

However, it appearing to the Department that Japan had no legislation fixing the conditions of a valid marriage in the territory, it gave instructions, on Mar. 30, 1929, that "marriages of American citizens contracted in 

Kwantung Leased Territory should be performed in accordance with the law and procedure recognized as applicable to marriages of American citizens performed in other parts of the territory of China". The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Langdon, Mar. 30, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 133/2579.

PERSONS UNDER AMERICAN JURISDICTION 

$185 In April 1909 the Minister of the United States in China reported to the Department of State that the Chinese Foreign Office had decided that nationals of non-treaty nations, applying for permission to travel

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

549 in China, would henceforth be treated exactly as Chinese subjects. 

The Minister added that some treaty powers considered "that for occidentals in China, extraterritoriality is a natural right” and that they extended their protection to the nationals of nearly all European non-treaty powers. The Department said:

The contention of the Chinese Government that treaty powers have no jurisdiction over citizens of non-treaty nations, judged by the well established rules of international law, would seem to be valid, and the contention put forth by some of the treaty powers, that "extraterritoriality is a natural right", would seem to be groundless and supported by no recognized authority on international law

The view taken by the Chinese Government in this matter has on previous occasions been approved by the Department. In a report submitted to Congress by the Secretary of State in a letter dated December 18, 1906, it was stated that: "If it be asked what extraterritorial authority is exercised by the United States Government in any country, the answer must be found, first, in the treaty conferring extraterritoriality, and, second, in the statutes of the United States providing for the exercise of extraterritorial power by American Consular and Diplomatic officers. That is to say, the question concerns itself, first, with international law and treaty, and, second, with our own municipal law." [H. Rept. 326, 59th Cong., 2d sess., 200.]

In accordance, therefore, with the views above expressed, you will, if the matter is submitted to the Diplomatic Body for its consideration, assent to the Chinese Government's proposal; in such a way, however, as to avoid any inference of relinquishment of that jurisdiction indicated by Hinckley in the following passage on page 78 of his work entitled "American Consular Jurisdiction in the Orient": "So far as extraterritorial privileges are involved, American nationality includes all persons, whatever their civil status, who owe allegiance to the United States either as citizens by birth or by naturalization or as native inhabitants of the insular possessions or as seamen on American ships, or as assistants or guards in legations and consulates, or, to a limited extent, as employees of American citizens in oriental countries." 

Minister Rockhill to Secretary Knox, no. 1137, Apr. 13, 1909, and the

Acting Secretary of State (Wilson) to the Chargé d'Affaires at Peking (Fletcher), no. 616, July 30, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 19790/-2. 

See also 1909 For. Rel. 68-70.

In reply to a communication from the Russian Ambassador in Washington, in which he expressed his Government's dissent from the posi-

tion of the Chinese Government on the above subject and inquired as to the views of the United States, the Department of State said: 

The position uniformly taken by the Federal Government has been that by consenting to lend its good offices in behalf of subjects of other nations, it could not assume to assimilate such subjects to citizens of the United States and to invest them with extraterritorial rights which they did not enjoy as subjects of the country of their allegiance. The American Minister to China was informed in 1895 by the then Secretary of State, Mr. Gresham, that the consuls of the United States in China had never been invested with power to exercise jurisdiction over citizens or subjects of another nation, and that the Department of State had repeatedly so held even in respect to citizens of Switzerland who had, for many years, been under the protection of ministers and consuls of the United States. 

Moreover, the Supreme Court of the United States has held that the question of the jurisdiction of American consular courts in the Orient depends not merely upon international law and the provisions of the treaties but also upon the statutory law of the United States which plainly provides for the exercise of such jurisdiction in criminal cases over American citizens only. In civil cases, also, while the statute is not so clear, the law officers of the Department of State are of the opinion that the jurisdiction is doubtful.

Department of State to Russian Embassy, Oct. 11, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 393.00/3. See also 1910 For. Rel. 838-839.

When, in Sept. 1915, the Senior Consul at Shanghai, ostensibly acting in behalf of the consular body, assumed probate jurisdiction in the matter of the estate of an unrepresented foreigner who had not received the protection of any foreign government in China, the American Vice Consul informed him that in as much as this action was "directly opposite to the American views on the subject of jurisdiction over unrepresented foreigners" he was unable to acquiesce. The Legation in Peking brought the matter to the attention of the Department of State, which, in its reply of Nov. 12, 1915, referred to its acquiescence with the Chinese position set forth in the correspondence of 1909 (ante) and approved the action of the Vice Consul. The

551 In 1936 the Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Tangier, Mo- Activities rocco, requested the opinion of the Department of State as to whether prejudicial protection should be extended to certain American citizens who desired to the U. The memorandum stated:

Since the statute conferring jurisdiction on the United States Court for China, on which the ruling of the Circuit Court of Appeals was based, is also applicable to Morocco, it might be held that the Act of the District of Columbia cited herein, so far as it is necessary to execute the treaties of the United States with Morocco and so far as it is suitable to carry the treaties into effect, could be regarded as applicable to Americans in Morocco, certainly at least to the extent of warranting the American diplomatic and consular officers in Morocco in refusing to support the establishment of pawnbroking enterprises by American citizens and, if necessary, in cooperating with the local authorities to prevent their establishment until adequate provision should be made for their supervision in the interest of the public. 

The memorandum concluded by stating that, regardless of the applicability of the statute, there was no obligation on the part of the United States to give its protection to activities of its nationals in extraterritorial countries when there was reasonable ground for apprehension that such activities would be prejudicial to the interests of the United States and its relations with other governments. With reference to threatened judicial proceedings in Turkey against a Swiss citizen who had been placed under the protection of the United States upon his petition and with the consent of his Government, the question arose as to whether the consular courts of the United States in Turkey might take jurisdiction over him. The De- Nationals partment of State, with an instruction to the Minister in Turkey, of third enclosed a memorandum of the Solicitor for the Department on the subject, the conclusion of which, as to criminal jurisdiction, was as follows- it is clear that the Revised Statutes of the United States above quoted in detail, do not confer criminal jurisdiction upon the countries

consular courts in Turkey except in the cases of crimes and offences committed by citizens of the United States. It is further submitted that there is not the slightest suggestion to be found in any of the statutes above quoted that criminal jurisdiction is to be exercised except over American citizens. (See especially, sections 4084, 4087, and 4125 ). 

The consent of the individual foreigner and the consent of his Government, even though based on the consent of Turkey and the scope of the capitulations and treaties as they are interpreted in practice, all combined cannot confer criminal jurisdiction on the consular courts of the United States when such jurisdiction has been withheld from these courts by the statutes of the United States. The consent of the foreigner's Government and the treaty with Turkey may remove the international difficulties, but it requires a Federal statute to remove the constitutional difficulties. 

As to civil jurisdiction the Solicitor, after examining the Revised 

Statutes, sections 4086 and 4125 (12 Stat. 73, 76) said:

These blanket provisions would seem to confer jurisdiction in civil cases whenever such jurisdiction is permitted by the laws or customs of Turkey. If, as appears to be the case, it is a wellestablished custom in Turkey for the consuls of various nations to extend protection to persons not of their own nationality, and to entertain jurisdiction of civil suits against such persons if this custom is acquiesced in by Turkey as proper under the treaties, it would appear that such jurisdiction may be assumed by the Consular Courts of the United States under sections 4086 and 4125.

In 1913 the French Chargé d'Affaires in Washington requested Protected the Department of State to appoint a delegate in Tangier to assist persons the French authorities "in the revision of the protection list of people lying under the American jurisdiction". The Department replied that- the protection of native Moors in Morocco by this Government rests upon its treaty with Morocco of 1836 and the Madrid Convention of 1880. The relevant part of the treaty of 1836 is found in Article 15, which reads as follows: "Merchants of both countries shall employ only such interpreters, and such other persons to assist them in their business as they shall think proper."

The Convention of 1880 declares, in Article 1, that the protection of native Moors is based on the British and Spanish treaties with Morocco and on the Convention of 1863 between France, Morocco and other Powers, "with the modifications introduced by the present convention," and stipulates, in Article 16, that "the authorities of Morocco will recognize no protection of any kind whatever save such as is expressly provided for in this convention."

After a careful examination of the several articles of the Madrid Convention relative to the protection of American protégés, the Department is unable to reach the conclusion that the Moorish Government enjoys the right ultimately to decide upon the persons who may become protégés of this Government. On the contrary, Article 2 of the Convention provides that "foreign representatives at the head of a legation may select their interpreters and employees from among the subjects of Morocco or others"; and Article 3 provides that consular officers "shall be allowed to select" their employees. By Article 5 of the same 

Convention, "the Government of Morocco recognizes the right of Ministers, Chargés d'Affaires and other representatives, which is granted to them by treaties, to select the persons whom they employ." In regard to the lists of protected persons, the Convention is equally precise, as appears by Articles 7 and 8, Regarding the appointment of protégés for "signal services," the Convention provides (Article 16) that the "Minister of For-

eign Affairs at Tangier shall be previously informed of the nature of the services, and notified of the intention to award them, in order that he may, if need be, present his observations thereon; yet the final decision shall be reserved for the Government to which the service shall have been rendered.” 

Concerning the protection of the native employees of private persons, the treaty of 1836 appears to contain no stipulation; but, in Articles 9 and 10 of the convention of 1880, there are found the 

"Article 9. 

"Servants, farmers and other native employees of native secretaries and interpreters shall not enjoy protection. The same shall be the case with Moorish employees or servants of foreign subjects. "Nevertheless, the local authorities shall not arrest an employee or servant of a native officer in the service of a Legation or Consulate, or of a foreign subject or protected person, without having notified the authority upon which he is dependent. "If a subject of Morocco in the service of a foreign subject shall kill or wound any person, or violate his domicile, he shall be arrested immediately, but the diplomatic or consular authority under which he is shall be notified without delay. 

"Article 10. 

"Nothing is changed with regard to the situation of brokers, as established by the treaties and by the convention of 1863, except what is stipulated, relative to taxes, in the following articles." 

Inasmuch as the Madrid Convention refers, in Article 1, to the "Convention of 1863 between France, Morocco and other Powers" regarding the protection of native Moors, and to the British and Spanish treaties with Morocco on the same subject, it is appropriate to examine the provisions of these treaties on the subject. 

The provisions of the Convention of 1863 appear to be substantially the same as the "Regulations relative to protection adopted by common consent by the Legation of France and the 

Government of Morocco, August 19, 1863," reprinted in "Treaties in Force, 1904," at the end of the Madrid Convention. 

The British and Spanish Treaties mentioned in Article I of the Madrid Convention are presumably the General Treaty of December 9, 1856, between Great Britain and Morocco, and the 

Treaty of Commerce and Navigation of November 20, 1861, be tween Spain and Morocco. In the British treaty it is specifically provided that the Chargé d'Affaires and the consular officers of Great Britain "shall be at liberty to choose" their own employees, and that British subjects "shall be free" to commit their affairs "to the management of any persons whom they may appoint as their broker, factor, or agent; nor", says the treaty, "shall such

British subjects be restrained in their choice of persons to act in such capacities." The Spanish treaty provides that "the Chargé d'Affaires or Consul-General may choose his interpreters and servants from amongst the Mussulman subjects or amongst those

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

555 99 of any other country," that other consular officers "may name" employees "either Mussulmans or subjects of another country,' and that Spanish merchants may put their affairs "into the hands of brokers or agents appointed by themselves, and they shall not be interfered with, nor shall obstacles be raised to the free choice of the persons to fulfill this charge."

It would, therefore, seem that the choice of the protégés of the United States in Morocco rests, by right of treaty, ultimately with this Government. Such appears to be the view which this Department has always taken of the Convention of 1880, and which has been the basis of its action in carrying out the provisions of that convention.

In 1911 an American company requested that American semsar and mohalat certificates be issued to persons in various parts of Morocco on the request of its agent and semsar who was a native Moroccan. In its instruction on the subject the Department of State referred to article X of the Madrid convention of 1880 and to the convention of 1863 between Morocco and France referred to therein and said: 

According to the Department's understanding semsars are the persons included in the second class described in the convention of 1863. It is understood that the words, "French merchants," refer to merchants who are French citizens and not to native merchants who carry on trade with France. If this is true a similar construction must, of course, apply to American merchants. Accordingly, David Cabessa, who is apparently a native Moroccan and a semsar of the Varney and Puech Company, of Boston, cannot have semsar certificates issued to his factors, brokers or agents.

In 1929 an American company requested of the Department of State that certain persons, in Morocco, described as "clients" of the company, engaged in large-scale export and import business in Morocco, be appointed as its semsars. In declining to accede to the request, the Department said:

The right enjoyed by American citizens under the Convention as to protection, signed at Madrid in 1880 may be exercised by a "merchant" with respect to "native factors, brokers or agents employed by" such merchants "for their business affairs." It is the opinion of the Department that in the circumstances a semsar or protected person should be in the employ of an American citizen and one that is conducting a business entirely on his own individual capital and is not connected directly by employment with an American concern could not properly be considered in the class which has been described above.

The treaties and conventions would seem originally to have contemplated the granting of Semsar Certificates to native factors, brokers or agents employed only by foreign merchants who were established in Morocco. In connection with the sinking of the American merchant vessel Seamen Texas in Smyrna harbor in Turkey, in 1912, the master of the vessel, a Greek subject, was taken into custody by Turkish officials who denied the request of the American Consul General that the officer be turned over to him. In reply to an inquiry by the American Ambassador as to the course to be pursued, the Department of State, on May 29, 1912 said:

A seaman of whatsoever nationality serving under the American flag owes temporary allegiance to that flag and is therefore subject to its appropriate jurisdiction. 

American vessels and consequently their crews in the waters of countries in which the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction are subject to two sorts of consular juris-

diction: Firstly, that which (as to the internal government of the ship and members of its crew) would belong to the consul in any port not extraterritorial, either by virtue of the general principles of international law or by virtue of special treaty provisions; and, secondly, that which would accrue by virtue of extraterritorial rights, which the Department is strongly inclined to believe extends to jurisdiction in the case of crimes and misdemeanors committed in territorial waters by a citizen or member of the crew (other than subjects of the port country) against whatsoever parties.

Therefore, in accordance with the principles of extraterritorial jurisdiction which this Government has hitherto asserted, you are instructed, notwithstanding probability Ottoman Government may decline, again to make upon the Minister for Foreign Affairs, in such manner as you deem most appropriate, a specific request for the surrender of the captain to the jurisdiction of the American Consul-General at Smyrna, in addition to reserving in behalf of this Government all rights in connection with the case. 

Ambassador Rockhill to Secretary Knox, telegram of May 13, 1912, MS. 

Department of State, file 367.114M69/124; Mr. Knox to Mr. Rockhill, telegram of May 29, 1912, ibid. 367.114M69/131. From further correspondence it appears that the Turkish authorities declined to yield to the representations of the American Consul General. Secretary Bryan to Mr. Rockhill, telegram of May 26, 1913, ibid. 367.114M69/191. See also 1913 For. Rel. 1310-1339. 

The principles just stated with respect to the Texas were held by the Department of State also to be applicable to certain Greek subjects members of the crew of the American merchant vessel Indiana who were accused of assaulting and wounding Turkish soldiers on board the vessel in the harbor of Constantinople, and the American Consul General was instructed to assume jurisdiction in the case.

In 1920 the British Ambassador in Washington made inquiry of the Department of State as to the action of the American consular court in Alexandria, Egypt, in sentencing to imprisonment a British subject. The Department pointed out that at the time of the incident in question the man had the status of an American seaman and that it was of the opinion that the action of the consul was fully justified. 

In answer to an inquiry from the consul in connection with the case, the Department said thatin the opinion of the Department, "a seaman of foreign nationality shipped on an American vessel in a foreign port who comes upon a Consulate for relief and repatriation in an extraterritorial

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

561 country" is "amenable to the criminal jurisdiction of the American Consular Court functioning in that country" so long as he accepts the privileges offered him as a destitute seaman of the United States. In this connection reference is made to Sections 8317, 8368, 8369 and 8370 of the United States Compiled Statutes; to 

Sections 271 and 278 of the United States Consular Regulations; and to the cases of United States v. Sharp (27 Fed. Cas. 1041) the Bound Brook (146 Fed. 160), and In re Ross (140 U.S. 453).

In a note of January 18, 1922 the British Ambassador stated that while his Government did not desire to take further action with reference to this case, it was desired to obtain a further clarification of the issue involved for purposes of future reference. He also stated that the real question was whether an American consular tribunal in Egypt properly had jurisdiction to sentence a British subject to imprisonment. He expressed the opinion that the British subject in question was exempt from the local Egyptian jurisdiction only by virtue of the treaty of extraterritoriality between Great Britain and Egypt, that the treaty of extraterritoriality between the United States and Egypt could not give an American court jurisdiction over a British subject, and that "the Egyptian Tribunals have never recognised the special status claimed for American seamen as apart from the status of American citizens". In a note of June 23, 1926, the Department of State pointed out that the question raised by the British Ambassador was substantially identical with that which was discussed in a note addressed by Secretary Blaine to Sir Edward Thornton on

June 3, 1881 (MS. Department of State, XVIII Notes, Great Brit ain, 543; see also 2 Moore's Dig. 606–607) in which the position was maintained that the United States Consular Court in Kanagawa, Japan, had jurisdiction over a British subject who, while employed as an American seaman, had committed a murder. Extracts were quoted from the earlier note, as well as from the decision rendered by the Supreme Court of the United States when the same case was before it on appeal, and in which the jurisdiction of the consular court was sustained. In re Ross, 140 U.S. (1891) 453. The note continued: 

With respect to the remark made in the note of January 18, 1922, that there does not appear to be any recorded case where a Consular Tribunal has claimed or exercised jurisdiction over the nationals of another state, it may be stated that the Consular Courts of the United States in China and Japan have continued, when occasion arose, to exercise jurisdiction over American seamen of foreign nationality; and, by the converse of the proposition maintained by this Government in the discussion of the Ross case, those Courts have declined to assert jurisdiction over American members of foreign crews in China and Japan. Furthermore, the records of the Department indicate that in 1889, after an American Consul at Amoy, China, had declined to assume juris-

Nationality and protection diction over an American member of a British crew, a British court in China took jurisdiction.

The views expressed by Secretary Blaine and approved by the Supreme Court in the Ross case have been regarded by this Government as applicable in principle with respect to the situation of American seamen of foreign nationality charged with the commission of offences in the Ottoman Empire. In two cases which arose at Smyrna, one in 1912 affecting the captain of the American Steamship Texas and the other in 1913, affecting the captain of the American Steamship Nevada, this Government maintained the view that the masters and the enrolled seamen of an American vessel are assimilated to American nationality and are therefore amenable to American Consular jurisdiction in the 

Ottoman Empire. 

The action of the American Consular Court at Alexandria in the [instant] case... was consistent with the opinion expressed by the highest judicial authority in the United States, in the Ross case, with respect to the status of American seamen of foreign nationality and was consonant with the action of extraterritorial courts of His Majesty's Government in China. In view of the consideration which this subject has heretofore received in diplomatic correspondence between His Majesty's Government and the Government of the United States and in view also of the precedents cited above for the exercise by the courts of His Majesty's Government of jurisdiction over British seamen of American nationality, and for the exercise by the courts of the United States of jurisdiction over American seamen of British nationality, it would seem that the question of the propriety of the exercise by Consular Courts of the United States in Egypt over American seamen of British nationality on American vessels in Egyptian waters should be regarded as settled. 

I venture to express the hope, that on further consideration Your Excellency's Government will concur in the views of the 

Government of the United States. 

Ambassador Geddes to Secretary Colby, no. 634, Sept. 27, 1920, MS. Department of State, file 176.1/5; Secretary Hughes to Mr. Geddes, Apr. 20, 1921, and the Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to Consul Maynard, Apr. 21, 1921, ibid. 176.1/8; Mr. Geddes to Mr. Hughes, Jan. 18, 1922, ibid.

The American Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Tangier inquired, in 1935, as to the consonance of the ruling of February 15, 1934 (ante), with article 15 of the convention as to protection con-

Morocco- treaty of 1880 cluded July 3, 1880 between the United States, Morocco, and other powers, reading as follows: 

Any subject of Morocco who has been naturalized in a foreign country, and who shall return to Morocco, shall after having remained for a length of time equal to that which shall have been regularly necessary for him to obtain such naturalization, choose between entire submission to the laws of the Empire and the obligation to quit Morocco, unless it shall be proved that his naturalization in a foreign country was obtained with the consent of the 

Government of Morocco.

Foreign naturalization heretofore acquired by subjects of Morocco according to the rules established by the laws of each country, shall be continued to them as regards all its effects, without any restriction. [1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 1225.] 

The Department replied: 

After a careful study of this matter the Department has reached the conclusion that the provisions of Article 15 reasonably warrant, if they do not in fact require, a modification insofar as concerns American citizens of Moroccan origin residing in Morocco of the Department's general position respecting the jurisdictional status of American citizens in extraterritorial countries. 

That article apparently contemplates that subjects of Morocco who have been naturalized in a foreign country without the consent of the Government of Morocco shall, if they return to Morocco and continue to reside there after the end of the period equal to that which was required for obtaining naturalization abroad, submit themselves to the laws of Morocco, and this Government, by adhering to the Convention, would seem to have aquiesced in this provision, thereby recognizing the complete subjection of such persons to the laws and authorities of Morocco. 

The Government of the United States could not, therefore, claim the right to exercise any jurisdiction over them while they remain in Morocco, but since the treaty provision under reference does not operate to divest their American citizenship, they retain the legal status of American citizens so long as they have not expatriated themselves in the manner provided by the laws of the 

United States.

Naturalized American citizens of Moroccan origin who are unable to overcome the presumption established by Section 2 of the Act of March 2, 1907, but who have not resided in Morocco for five years following their naturalization, if there are any persons in this category, shall continue to be subject to the jurisdiction of American consular courts until the expiration of the fiveyear period mentioned, but shall not be accorded any other form of protection as American citizens while they continue to rest under the presumption established by the Act of 1907. Their continued residence in Morocco beyond the five-year period mentioned

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

565 would place them in the same category as the persons discussed in the preceding paragraphs.

The Diplomatic Agent and Consul General (Blake) to Secretary Hull, no. 1090, Aug. 31, 1935, and the Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to 

Mr. Blake, no. 897, Apr. 17, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 130 Laredo, Gabriel James.

The subject was further discussed by the Department of State in an instruction of December 17, 1936 in reply to a despatch of the 

American Consul at Casablanca, Morocco. The Department said that the question of the jurisdictional status of an American citizen in a country in which the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction is quite distinct from the question whether or not that citizen should be accorded diplomatic protection.

While the Department may properly refuse to accord diplomatic protection to any citizen of the United States in a foreign country for any of the reasons which have been or may be found sufficient for that purpose it clearly has no authority to deny the American citizenship of such persons so long as they have the status of American citizens or to acquiesce in the denial of any right to which they may be entitled by law or treaty. 

Since American citizens in Morocco are by treaty and law subject exclusively to the jurisdiction of American consular courts except those persons who are subject to the provisions of Article 15 of the Madrid Convention of 1880 and those persons having a dual citizenship status-any declaration by the Consulate that it had no objection to the assumption of jurisdiction over such persons by the protectorate authorities would appear to constitute official approval of the invasion by those authorities of the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the United States in Morocco. In addition to the fact that such a declaration appears to be beyond the authority of this Department or its representatives it may be doubted whether the attainment of the objective of such a declaration would, as a practical matter, be sufficiently important and desirable to warrant any impairment of the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the United States in Morocco. 

Consul Stanton to Secretary Hull, no. 134, Sept. 23, 1936, and the Assistant Secretary of State (Carr) to Consul Hopper, Dec. 17, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 130 Arcash, George Habib.

The American Minister to China, in July 1929, inquired as to the Dual attitude to be taken with reference to the case of one Char, an Amer- nationality ican-born citizen of Chinese parentage who had been arrested by Chinese authorities. The Department of State replied that it was of the opinion, first, that Char was a citizen both of the United States and of China, and second, that, in as much as the Chinese Provisional Court had first assumed jurisdiction over him as a Chinese citizen, no legal basis existed for questioning that jurisdiction. It indicated

that the fact that Char had so conducted himself as to emphasize his Chinese citizenship and had a close and official connection with the Chinese Government, furnished justification for refusal, on the part of the United States, to intervene in his behalf as an American citizen. 

Minister MacMurray to Secretary Stimson, telegram 652, July 30, 1929, and Mr. Stimson to Mr. MacMurray, telegram 272, Aug. 15, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 893.012/40.

With reference to proceedings instituted in Chinese courts in Shanghai against two American-born citizens of Chinese parentage who were residing in the International Settlement, the possibility being envisioned that one of these persons would be arrested by Chinese authorities if he went outside of the International Settlement, the Department of State instructed the Minister that if the persons involved were registered at the Shanghai Consulate General as American citizens and had not so conducted themselves as to emphasize their Chinese citizenship, all proper protection under the treaties of extraterritoriality between the United States and China was to be afforded them. 

Minister MacMurray to Secretary Stimson, telegram 853, Oct. 3, 1929, and Mr. Stimson to Mr. MacMurray, telegram 332, Oct. 11, 1929, MS. Department of State, file 893.012/43.

An opinion of the Solicitor for the Department of State, dated Oct. 10, 1929, prepared with reference to this situation, stated: "In so far as concerns the exercise of jurisdiction over these two men and others in a similar status, the rights of the two Governments are equal, that is, the persons are nationals of both countries and both countries are entitled to assume jurisdiction over them while they are in China. Therefore, the country first assuming jurisdiction in a given case is entitled to have that jurisdiction respected by the other country. Since the nationals are in China, the rights of the Chinese Government would be paramount to those of the United States, except for our extraterritorial privileges. As long as the persons remain in one of the International Settlements, we should undoubtedly claim exclusive jurisdiction. If, however, they leave the Settlement and the Chinese Government undertakes to exercise jurisdiction over them, I do not feel that this Government can complain in the absence of evidence that they are being accorded inhumane treatment or are being discriminated against in some way because of their American nationality. In either event we would be warranted in interposing in their behalf." MS. Department of State, file 893.012/43.

The Consul of the United States at Amoy having inquired of the Department of State as to the extent to which he was to extend protection to a corporation organized in the Philippine Islands and owned Corporations partially by Philippine and partially by Chinese subjects, the Department expressed the opinion thatit appears to the Department that, as a legal proposition, our Consular Courts and the United States Court for China will, under the present state of the law, have no option but to recognize as American citizens all American corporations irrespective of the nationality of the stockholders; and to consider all American corporations as entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of the respective courts. This would appear to follow from the fact that our general statutes conferring extraterritorial jurisdiction as well as the statute organizing and conferring jurisdiction upon the United States Court for China, all speak of a jurisdiction over citizens of the United States, or (as the Act for the United States Court for China specifies) any citizen of any territory belonging to the United States. It is assumed that for purposes of jurisdiction, a corporation organized under the laws of the Philippine Islands would be a citizen of the United States within the meaning of those sections of the Revised Statutes which confer jurisdiction upon our Consular Courts. It seems to be the established law of this country that so far as the question of the taking of jurisdiction by our Federal Courts is concerned, a corporation is to be regarded as a citizen within the meaning of the Constitutional provision governing these matters. It would appear not unreasonable to assume that the same rule would and should be applied by our courts in China. Therefore, as a judicial question affecting the jurisdiction of our various courts in China, it would seem that all American corporations must be regarded as American citizens. 

Consul Arnold to the Assistant Secretary of State, no. 96, June 22, 1909, MS. Department of State, file 20930; Secretary Knox to Mr. Arnold, no. 80, Apr. 7, 1910, ibid. 20930/1.

In an instruction in 1936 to the American Consul General at Casablanca, Morocco, the Department of State said:

As stated in the Department's instruction of December 17, 1936 [to Casablanca, see ante, this section], the question of the extension or withholding of diplomatic protection in the case of natural

persons who are citizens of the United States is quite distinct from the question of the jurisdictional status of such persons in countries where the United States exercises extraterritorial jurisdiction. While the Department has held that the same distinction applies in the case of companies having the legal status of American corporations, you are informed that the United States Court for China has recently refused to assume jurisdiction of two American corporations in China in which there was no substantial American interest.

In the case of the Far Eastern Recreation Grounds, Limited, versus Metropolitan Sporting Association, Incorporated, brought before the United States Court for China on June 14, 1935, based on a lease agreement, it was testified that the defendant company, an American corporation organized under the laws of Delaware, had a paid-in capital of more than $250,000 Chinese currency of which only approximately $5,000 appeared to be owned by American citizens, and that the company was actually controlled by aliens. At the conclusion of testimony and argument of counsel the court rendered the following opinion: "The case has some very interesting angles and although the court is not prepared at this time to state his reasons or an exhaustive opinion on this subject, nor to lay down a precedent, still the court feels that it should not entertain this action but that it should dismiss the same without prejudice to any of the parties to seek whatever remedies and reliefs may be available to them elsewhere and accordingly such will be the order of the court." [195 (n. s.) North-China Herald (June 19, 1935) 492.]

While the quoted opinion does not specify the ground on which jurisdiction was refused, the Judge for the United States Court for China subsequently informed the American Ambassador to China that lack of substantial American interest in the corporation was the basis of the court's decision. 

In October 1935 the Judge of the United States Court for China informally advised counsel for the Thrift and Investment Finance and Trust Company, a corporation organized under the laws of Nevada, that since no American interest in the corporation had been shown, and since registration of the corporation at the American Consulate had been refused, he saw no reason for the assumption by the United States Court for China of jurisdiction of the corporation for the purpose of liquidating its business. 

The corporation mentioned was controlled by aliens and the Department's records indicate doubt whether any of the corporation's shares were actually owned and controlled by American citizens. [Ambassador Johnson to Secretary Hull, telegrams 42 and 45, Oct. 10, 1935, MS. Department of State, files 811.5034 (China) Thrift Corporation/40 and /41.]

Whether the action of the United States Court for China would be upheld on appeal in the event that anyone having a proper interest should challenge it is a judicial question with respect to which the Department expresses no opinion. The Department is of the opinion, however, that, in the absence of an authoritative

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

569 judicial opinion contrary to the position taken by the United States Court for China in the two cases mentioned, it would appear to be within the judicial discretion of American consular courts to determine whether they should assume jurisdiction of any corporation known to be predominately owned and controlled by aliens and therefore lacking in substantial American interest. 

The Acting Secretary of State (Moore) to Consul Hopper, Dec. 29, 1936, ibid. 381.1141 Tarum Company/2.

The City Court of New York, in deciding an action brought on a Courts of judgment of a United States Consular Court in China found it neces- record sary to determine whether or not a consular court is a court of record.

Full faith and credit

Arrest by consular officer The court decided that although such courts are not designated by statute as courts of record, yet Because of the importance of its litigation, its long-continued exercise of jurisdiction in all matters of civil and criminal conception, its enrollment of pleadings and determinations, so that by bare inspection the record establishes itself, I conclude that its characteristics do establish it as a court of record within the legal sense, the time during which its judgments may be presumed to be satisfied or discharged extending to 20 years after rendition. 

Newman v. Basch, 89 Misc. (1915) 622, 630-631, 152 N.Y. Supp. 456, 461.

In the case just referred to, the court, after discussing the origin and nature of extraterritorial jurisdiction, said:

Since the statutes of the United States are extended over and apply to the enforcements of the capitulations of the treaties conferring jurisdiction, as well as grant the imposition of judicial authority, the judgments or determinations called judgments are subject to and have the same force and effect and are entitled to the same enforcing remedies within any state as judgments of federal courts outside of the state of their territorial location. 

By analogy with the rules pertaining to Federal courts, it was concluded that:

The determination or judgment of the Consular Court having been made with jurisdiction of the parties and the subject-matter, it seems to me that it is entitled equally with judgments throughout the United Sates to full faith and credit in the courts of every state in the Union, in like case with judgments of state courts under our federal Constitution. 

89 Misc. (1915) 622, 626, 627, 152 N.Y. Supp. 456, 458-459.

8, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 483.11Sa3/3. "An Act Creating a United States court for China and prescribing the jurisdiction thereof" was approved by the President on June 30, 1906. Section 1 provides that— 

Court for China a court is hereby established, to be called the United States court United States for China, which shall have exclusive jurisdiction in all cases and judicial proceedings whereof jurisdiction may now be exercised by United States consuls and ministers by law and by virtue of treaties between the United States and China, except in so far as the said jurisdiction is qualified by section two of this Act. 

Section 2 provides: 

The consuls of the United States in the cities of China to which they are respectively accredited shall have the same jurisdiction as 

---

they now possess in civil cases where the sum or value of the property involved in the controversy does not exceed five hundred dollars United States money and in criminal cases where the punishment for the offense charged cannot exceed by law one hundred dollars fine or sixty days' imprisonment, or both, and shall have power to arrest, examine, and discharge accused persons or commit them to the said court. From all final judgments of the consular court either party shall have the right of appeal to the United States court for China This section also confers on the court "supervisory control" over the discharge, by consular officers, of their duties with reference to decedents' estates. Consuls are required to file with the court inventories and schedules of debts of such estates, and to pay claims only on order of the court and the court can require the filing of reports or the posting of bonds by the consuls when deemed advisable. 

Section 3 allows appeals to be taken from final judgments or decrees of the United States Court for China to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Judicial Circuit, and thence to the Supreme Court of the United States, all such proceedings being "regulated by the procedure governing appeals within the United States from the district courts to the circuit courts of appeal, and from the circuit courts of appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States, respectively, so far as the same shall be applicable; and said courts are hereby empowered to hear and determine appeals and writs of error so taken".

Section 4 provides: 

The jurisdiction of said United States court, both original and on appeal, in civil and criminal matters, and also the jurisdiction of the consular courts in China, shall in all cases be exercised in conformity with said treaties and the laws of the United States now in force in reference to the American consular courts in China, and all judgments and decisions of said consular courts, and all decisions, judgments, and decrees of said United States court, shall be enforced in accordance with said treaties and laws. 

But in all such cases when such laws are deficient in the provisions necessary to give jurisdiction or to furnish suitable remedies, the common law and the law as established by the decisions of the courts of the United States shall be applied by said court in its decisions and shall govern the same subject to the terms of any treaties between the United States and China. 

Section 5 provides that the procedure of the court shall be in accordance, so far as practicable, with the procedure prescribed for consular courts, but the judge is authorized from time to time to modify and supplement the rules of procedure.

A defendant, charged in the United States Court for China with having allowed a prisoner to escape, demurred on the ground that the act of which he was accused took place outside of the territory of China and was therefore not within the jurisdiction of the court. In finding Scope of jurisdiction

that it had jurisdiction to entertain the action the court held that the treaties and statutes creating its jurisdiction did not necessarily confine that jurisdiction to the territorial boundaries of China. The court also held that it had jurisdiction conferred by Congress in certain cases in its capacity as a "Court of the United States" and aside from its extraterritorial status, referring to its decision in United States v. 

Thompson, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1912) 261 (post §188), and said thatthe criminal jurisdiction of this court is dual; i. e., over offenses committed in China (by which is meant, however, more than its precise territorial limits) and offenses committed elsewhere. The former is derived entirely from the treaties with China by which the latter's jurisdiction has been surrendered. Jurisdiction over offenses of the second class is derived not from the treaties but from the Acts of Congress which has unlimited power to confer upon this court jurisdiction over outside offenses; for this can in no way affect the sovereign rights of China nor enlarge the jurisdiction surrendered by the treaties. And this court's power to take cognizance of crimes committed outside of Chinese territory may arise not only from the Acts of Congress passed since the establishment of the court but by pertinent acts previously passed which according to a well settled doctrine came into force as to this court upon its organization. 

United States v. Willis B. Kilgore, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1914) 395, 403-404.

The court held in 1919 that it had jurisdiction "over offences committed on an American ship 'on the high seas'", citing the above case and In re Ross, 140 U.S. (1891) 453. United States v. William Dommer, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1919) 914, 915. 

By Act of Congress approved June 24, 1936, the jurisdiction of the

United States Court for China was extended concurrently to "all offenses committed on the high seas in cases in which the person or persons charged with such offenses shall be found in or brought first into China". 

49 Stat. 1909; 22 U.S.C., Supp. IV, §191. 

The conviction of an American citizen in the United States Court for China was, in 1928, reviewed by the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The appellant contended that the information under which he was convicted did not show that he was a citizen of the United States at the time of the commission of the alleged offense, as he claimed was required under article 21 of the treaty of peace, amity, and commerce of 1844 between the United States and China, 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 202. The court said:

The first question is of the sufficiency of the record to disclose jurisdiction in the trial court, which, like that of other United States courts, is limited, and must affirmatively appear.

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

575 The court found, on the basis of In re Ross, 140 U.S. (1891) 453, that the averment in the information that the defendant was at all material times the duly appointed, qualified and acting United States district attorney for China constituted an adequate jurisdictional charge. The decision was affirmed. 

Husar v. United States, 26 F. (2d) 847, 848 (C.C.A. 9th, 1928).

In passing upon the appeal of the case of the United States v. C. A. 

Biddle in 1907, the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit said, with reference to the criminal jurisdiction of the Criminal 

United States in China:

The object of the treaty and the intention of Congress, in creating the United States Court for China, in so far as that court is given criminal jurisdiction, was to throw around American citizens residing or sojourning in China, and there charged with crime, the beneficent principles of the laws of the United States relating to the trial of persons charged with crime-the rules of evidence, the presumption of innocence, the degree of proof necessary to convict, the right of the accused to be confronted with witnesses against him, exemption from being compelled to criminate himself, etc. But, while securing to them these privileges, the statute at the same time, made them subject to punishment for acts made criminal by any law of the United States, or for acts recognized as crimes under the common law. 

Biddle v. On March 3, 1932 the American Consul at Cairo, Egypt, reported to the Department of State that an Egyptian woman had obtained a Personal decree of divorce and property settlement against her American hus- status band in a rabbinical court in Cairo and that the Legal Advisor to the Egyptian Government was of the opinion that "no Egyptian Court, which would include the Rabbinical Courts, may assume jurisdiction in a case of personal status in which the defendant is the national of a capitulatory power". The Consul pointed out:

President Grant's proclamation of March 27, 1876 [19 

Stat. 662] suspended the jurisdiction of the Consular Courts only "so far as" the jurisdiction of the new courts [the Mixed Courts] embraced matters theretofore within the jurisdiction of the Con sular Courts. By Article 9 of the Charter of the Mixed Courts personal status is expressly excluded from their jurisdiction. It therefore follows that the American Consular Court still retains exclusive jurisdiction to entertain a case of this nature in which the defendant is an American citizen.

The Consul consequently felt that if the decree were brought into the consular court for execution, the court should decline to take cognizance of it. The Department expressed its agreement with the position taken by the Consul. 

Consul Merriam to Secretary Stimson, no. 40, Mar. 3, 1932, MS. Department of State, file 383.1141 Robinot, David H./1; the Acting Secretary of

In an action in the United States Court for China brought by an American citizen to recover damages for allegedly tortious acts of a British company acting as the agent of the defendant, an American corporation, the defendant demurred to the jurisdiction of the court, claiming that it had no office, branch, or place of business in China, and no agent in China over which the court had jurisdiction. The court quoted section 3 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (12 Stat. 73), providing that consular jurisdiction in China should embrace "all controversies between citizens of the United States, or others, provided for by such treaties, respectively" and concluded that there was "nothing in this, or in any legislation of Congress, which limits the jurisdiction of the Court to parties resident in China". The court said: "On the contrary, the American courts here are expressly given jurisdiction of 'all controversies between citizens of the United States' without reservation as to residence." It rejected the defendant's contention that the English law should be applied since its agents in 

China were English. 

Leonard Everett v. Swayne & Hoyt, Incorporated, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1916) 600, 603. Affirmed, Swayne and Hoyt v. Everett, 255 Fed. 71 (C.C.A. 

9th, 1919). In the latter case, the circuit court, after quoting article 

27 of the treaty of 1858 between the United States and China, to the effect that "All questions in regard to rights, whether of property or person, arising between citizens of the United States in China, shall be subject to the jurisdiction and regulated by the authorities of their own government; and all controversies occurring in China between citizens of the 

United States and the subjects of any other government shall be regulated by the treaties existing between the United States and such governments, respectively, without interference on the part of China", stated: "It is the contention of the plaintiff in error that the words 'in China,' in the foregoing article, qualify the word 'citizens,' and not the word 'arising'; in other words, that a residence of the parties in China is essential to the existence of any jurisdiction in the court. We think it

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

579 

obvious that such a construction of the provision is wholly inadmissible, for the subject-matter thereby dealt with is controversies arising in China. 

As said by counsel for the defendant in error, the bare reading of its second clause is all that is necessary to show that the words 'in China,' there used, fixes, as the basis of the jurisdiction of the court, the place of the origin of the controversy, and not the residence of the parties thereto. No sound reason is suggested why a like construction should not be placed upon the first clause. To adopt the view urged by the plaintiff in error would be, in effect, to hold a consular court in China vested with jurisdiction of a controversy between American citizens arising in the United States if they happened to be residents of China." Ibid. 73-74. In this case, however, the cause of action arose in China. 

In the case discussed in the text above (Leonard Everett v. Swayne &

The court said that this statute applied particularly to United 

States district and circuit courts, and that, in any event, it was not "suitable" (referring to section 4, 12 Stat. 73) to be applied in China since it would have the practical effect of exempting corporations from service in China. An act of Congress (31 Stat. 1419) permitting service to be had on corporations in the District of Columbia through their agents, in cases where the corporation had no place of business in the District, was held more applicable to the situation in China. The motion was overruled.

In reviewing a decision of the United States Court for China in which the corporate defendant had been held properly served in accordance with the above rule, the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that the controlling rule was that of the United States 

Supreme Court: 

"A foreign corporation is amenable to process to enforce a personal liability, in the absence of consent, only if it is doing business within the state in such manner and to such extent as to warrant the inference that it is present there."" Quoting from Philadelphia and Reading Railway 

Company v. McKibbin, 243 U.S. (1917) 264, 265.

The Circuit Court of Appeals said: "This limitation of jurisdiction is pe culiarly applicable to the United States Court in China. It has no jurisdiction except that conferred by the laws of the United States, and a cause is presumed to be without its jurisdiction unless the contrary affirmatively appears." The court concluded that it did not appear that defendant was doing business in China to such an extent as to warrant the inference that it was present there and that "The plea to the jurisdiction should have been sustained, and the petition dismissed." The court also said: "The service of summons upon W. P. Hough did not bring the defendant within the jurisdiction of the court, for the reason that it appears from the evidence that Hough was not an authorized agent of the defendant, upon whom a service of summons, binding upon the defendant, could be made.

In March 1938 the Department of State was informed that an American citizen claimed ownership of a fund in the hands of his agent in Morocco and that the agent refused to deliver the fund for the reason that a third person claimed a portion of it. Inquiry was made as to the authority of the American Extraterritorial Court at Tangier to entertain jurisdiction of an action of interpleader brought by the agent to determine the ownership of the fund. The Department replied that- it should be observed that the jurisdiction of the American Extraterritorial Court is limited to cases in which all defendants are American citizens or American-protected persons. Accordingly, since a bill of interpleader would give to all claimants to the fund under reference the status of defendants the court could not allow the bill unless all claimants are either American citizens or American-protected persons. 

The Legal Adviser to Mr. Phineas Toby, Mar. 24, 1938, MS. Department of State, file 178/2.

In a divorce proceeding instituted in the United States Court for China by an American citizen, the court considered the jurisdictional question raised by the fact that the defendant, who was of Chinese nationality, was not a citizen of the United States. The court held that as this was a simple suit for divorce and as the plaintiff did not seek personal relief it was a proceeding in rem having as its purpose the determination of the plaintiff's marital status and was therefore

In dismissing a plea of set-off interposed by an American defendant Set-off in an action brought against him in the United States Court for against non- China by a plaintiff of foreign nationality, the court said: A set-off is a counterdemand, generally of a liquidated debt, growing out of a separate transaction, for which an action might be maintained by the defendant against the plaintiff to recover a judgment in his own favor. Such is the character of the cross action in this case. This Court has no jurisdiction to give a judgment in such a case, because it is without power to enforce a judgment against anyone other than an American citizen. It has been held by Attorney-General Speed [11 Op. Att. Gen. 474] that in cases between a foreign plaintiff and an American defendant, where the foreigner establishes his claim against the American, the latter may plead a counterdemand in an amount equal to or less than the amount of the claim of the foreigner and the Court will allow the same. But in no instance will the Court give affirmative judgment against a foreign litigant in any amount. 

Axel Hillebrandt v. S. Zimmerman & Co., 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1907) 88, 91.

APPLICABLE LAW 

$188 With reference to the proper law to be applied in an action brought by a foreign plaintiff against an American defendant in the United 

States Court for China, the court said:

The defendant being an American citizen the forum is a court of the United States. This follows the uniform rule that, in an extraterritorial jurisdiction, all disputes are referred for settlement to the court of the defendant's nationality and are adjudicated in that court in accordance with the law of the country of whose judicial system it forms a part. In China, extraterritorial jurisdiction is exercised by some seventeen foreign gov-

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

583 ernments. The right thus exercised by each government within 

Chinese territory rests upon substantially identical treaty provisions. Each foreign power possesses jurisdiction over its own nationals and each thus has its forum. 

Each country also prescribes its own body of law to be administered in such forum. It is equally true also that in the exercise of such jurisdiction, China represents a territorial locus to each of said countries, to which the rights of property and person of its own citizens respectively must relate and to which they must be referred whenever disputes arise. In these respects each country stands upon exactly the same ground. In view of these conditions the court is unable to discern that there is any novel rule or principle which can be invoked in this court by reason of the fact that the existing controversy is in an extraterritorial court and that the two parties are of different nationalities. The general principles determining the choice of law in any controversy in every American court must be the same. It may be that extraordinary difficulties will arise in determining the choice of law in a particular case in an extraterritorial court. But it is true also that similar, if not greater, difficulties may be met in a case in a home court into which some foreign element intrudes. 

G. I. Shekury v. F. M. Brooks, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1910) 225, 226–227.

For the law to be administered by American extraterritorial tribunals, see 9 Stat. 276 and 12 Stat. 73 (Rev. Stat. §4086; 22 U.S.C. §145). 

law Prior to the Biddle case (infra), decided in 1907, the laws of the Common United States rendered applicable in extraterritorial countries by the above statutes were believed to be few in number. Attorney General 

Cushing, in 1855, referred to the common law as furnishing the "code of laws for the great mass of civil or municipal duties, rights and relations of men" in such countries since "the law of the United States,that is, the federal legislation,-does not include these matters". 7 

Op. Att. Gen. (1856) 495, 503-504. Thus, in 1906 when the American consular officer at Tientsin, China, inquired as to the steps which he might take to suppress disorderly houses operated under American auspices, the Department referred to this opinion of the Attorney General and advised that, under the common law, consular officers could entertain bills for the abatement of nuisances and punish for contempt.

The Vice and Deputy Consul General (Pontius) to the Assistant Secretary of State, no. 208, Sept. 22, 1906, and Secretary Root to Minister Rockhill, no. 223, Dec. 21, 1906, MS. Department of State, file 1782.

In the case of United States v. C. A. Biddle a criminal proceeding alleging the offense of obtaining money under false pretenses had been instituted in the United States Court for China. The defendant demurred on the ground that there was no such offense at common law and that, since the United States had no statute on the subject, the 

The Biddle case

Federal enactments for other jurisdictions offense did not exist under the laws and treaties giving the United States jurisdiction in China. The court overruled the demurrer. On appeal the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth 

Circuit affirmed the opinion of the United States Court for China that the offense charged was an offense under the common law, stating that- we are of opinion that in making the common law applicable to offenses committed by American citizens in China, and the other countries with which we have similar treaties, Congress had reference to the common law in force in the several American colonies at the date of the separation from the mother country, and this included not only the ancient common law, the lex non scripta, but also statutes which had theretofore been passed amendatory of or in aid of the common law. 

However, the court also held that the United States Court for China had jurisdiction for the reason that "such an act is a crime under the laws of the United States", stating:

It is true, there is no general statute applicable to every state in the Union, making this an offense against the United States; nor could there be, in view of the fact that under our system of government the right to punish for such acts committed within the political jurisdiction of the state is reserved to the several states. 

But in legislating for territory over which the United States exercises exclusive legislative jurisdiction, Congress has made the act of obtaining money under false pretenses a crime. Thus, in section 54 of title 1, pt. 1, of the act passed March 3, 1899 (chapter 

429, 30 Stat. 1260), entitled, "An act to define and punish crimes in the district of Alaska and to provide a code of criminal procedure for said district," Congress has enacted that obtaining money or property from another by any false pretense shall constitute a crime The court also referred to the act approved March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 

1326), making such an act an offense in the District of Columbia, and to the act approved July 7, 1898 (30 Stat. 717), of which the court said: 

Under this statute, any act committed in any place under the jurisdiction of the United States, if made an offense by the laws of the state in which such place is situate, when committed elsewhere in the state, is an offense against the United States, and punishable as in the state law provided. Sharon v. Hill (C.C.) 

24 Fed. 731; U.S. v. Wright, Fed. Cas. No. 16,774; U.S. v. 

Pridgeon, 153 U.S. 48-53, 14 Sup. Ct. 746, 38 L. Ed. 631.

At the date of the passage of the act of July 7, 1898, just quoted, the act of obtaining money or goods by false pretenses was made a crime by the laws of most of the states of the Union, and is, therefore, under this statute, also made a crime against the United States, in all places over which the United States exercises ex-

585 clusive legislative jurisdiction, within the several states, having laws providing for the punishment of such an act as a crime. 

In view of the legislation of Congress to which we have referred (the acts relating to Alaska and the District of Columbia, and the statute of July 7, 1898), our conclusion is that obtaining money or goods under false pretenses is an offense against the laws of the United States, within the meaning of the statute conferring jurisdiction upon the United States Court for China, and that an American citizen guilty of the commission of such an act in China is subject to trial and punishment therefor by that court. 

United States v. C. A. Biddle, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1907) 84; Biddle v. United 

States, 156 Fed. 759, 762–763 (C. C. A. 9th, 1907).

The Supreme Court of the United States decided in the case of In re Ross, 140 U.S. (1891) 453, that the constitutional guaranties of indictment by grand jury and trial by jury did not extend to extraterritorial courts. In 1920 it was contended before the United States 

Court for China that that decision was no longer applicable because at the time that it was decided "the laws of the District of Columbia and the Territory of Alaska had not been extended to American citizens residing in China". As to this contention the Court said that- 

Federal laws "the laws of the District of Columbia and the territory of Alaska" Extension of as such have never "been extended to American citizens residing in China." The extension was of "laws of the United 

States" and it was effected as early as 1848 [9 Stat. 276] while "the Ross case" was not decided until 1891. Moreover the extension thus effected was of "the laws" only; not "the constitution and laws" as in the case of the territories. 

Of course the "Biddle Case" extended nothing. Laws are not extended by judicial decision. Such extension is as much a legislative process as the original enactment and can be effected only by a legislative body-in this instance, Congress. All that the Court of Appeals did in "the Biddle Case" was to recognize and apply the legislative extension effected nearly sixty years before. It, indeed, impliedly treated certain acts of Congress, though passed for the District of Columbia and Alaska, as "laws of the United States;" but that was merely the natural interpretation of the phraseology used in the extending act. 

The defendant's motion for a new trial was accordingly dismissed. 

United States v. Henry W. Furbush, 2 Extraterr. Cas. (1921) 74, 84–85.

In a criminal prosecution brought in the United States Court for China in 1923, it was charged that the defendants were guilty of conspiracy to commit an offense against the United States (in violation of Federal Penal Code, sec. 37, 35 Stat. 1096), in that they conspired to import arms and ammunition into China in violation of certain treaty provisions. The defendants demurred on the ground that the treaties in question did not have the force and effect of law. 

The court pointed out that the statutes defining the scope of extraterritorial jurisdiction to be exercised by the United States in China (9 Stat. 276; 12 Stat. 72), extended to the court by the act approved 

June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 814) empowered it "to arraign and try

All citizens of the United States, charged with offenses against law”, in China and that "this grant of jurisdiction is made for the express purpose of carrying 'into full effect the provisions of the treaties"". 

It held that, if the treaties required legislation to make them effective, this legislation was sufficient to do so, and overruled the demurrer. 

United States v. Lawrence D. Kearny, 2 Extraterr. Cas. (1923) 662, 670–671.

In a criminal prosecution brought in the United States Court for China, alleging the offense of aiding a prisoner to escape, the court found the accused guilty under an act approved by Congress making such an act an offense in Alaska (30 Stat. 1268). It did not invoke the section of that statute specifying a penalty of from 10 to 20 years' imprisonment since, in this respect, it stated that it was governed by section 4 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (12 Stat. 75) which made it the duty of judicial officers in extraterritorial countries "to award punishment according to the magnitude of the offense". 

United States v. Adolph Grimsinger, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1912) 282. See also United States v. Lawrence D. Kearney, 2 Extraterr. Cas. (1923) 662, 679.

In a criminal proceeding in the United States Court for China in 1918, the question arose as to which of several applicable Federal statutes should be applied. The court said that "as the Federal Penal Federal

Code is applicable we apply it in preference to any special law”. 

United States v. Jose A. Diaz, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1918) 784, 786. In a later civil case the court said that "In applying federal statutes in this jurisdiction the general have always prevailed over the special." Judah I. 

Ezra v. W. L. Merriman, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1918) 809, 810. To same effect, see same v. same, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1918) 890.

In a criminal proceeding brought in the United States Court for China wherein the offense charged was that of escaping from prison, the defendant demurred on the ground that he had escaped prior to conviction, whereas the only applicable statute made such an act an offense only when committed following conviction. The court took the position that the offense charged was an offense at common law and that in as much as the statute penalized but one phase of the offense it was "deficient" within the meaning of section 4 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (34 Stat. 815). Under authority of this act the court applied the common-law rule and overruled the demurrer. 

United States v. Ralph S. Boyd, 2 Extraterr. Cas. (1922) 253, 254.
