A defendant charged by information in the United States Court for China with violation of the White Slave Act (36 Stat. 825) moved to quash on the ground that "the facts alleged do not constitute in China an offense against the laws of the United States". The court held that this was a law extended to citizens of the United States in China by section 4 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (12 Stat. 73) and that since 

Congress had declared acts in "foreign commerce" to be violations thereof, it undoubtedly intended this court to have jurisdiction of violations commenced in the United States and consummated in China as charged against this defendant. 

United States v. W. H. Thompson, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1912) 261. 

The Department of State took the position that the Prohibition amendment and the Volstead act did not apply in Morocco, and the Consul at Casablanca was authorized to reply to inquiries on the subject by referring to the case of Cunard Steamship Company, Ltd., et al. v. 

Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, et al., 262 U.S. (1923) 100, in which the Court held that the Volstead law was not intended to apply to domestic vessels when outside of territorial waters of the United States and that the act was intended "only to enforce the Eighteenth Amendment and limits its field of operation, like that of the Amendment, to the territorial limits of the United States". The Consul was informed that the Secretary of the Treasury had held "that the endorsement by American Consuls of the applications of American citizens in China for licenses to sell liquors is not in contravention of the law in question". 

The Assistant Secretary of State (Olds) to Consul Russell, Feb. 19, 1927, MS. Department of State, file 811.114/4590; 262 U.S. (1923) 129.

The American Agent and Consul General in Tangier raised the question, in 1921, whether judgments rendered by Belgian courts against American defendants could be executed in Morocco. The Department of State referred him to the case of Hilton v. Guyot, decided by the 

United States Supreme Court in 1895, and quoted the following passage from the decision:

The reasonable, if not the necessary, conclusion appears to us to be that judgments rendered in France, or in any other foreign country, by the laws of which our own judgments are reviewable upon the merits, are not entitled to full credit and conclusive effect

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

589 1 when sued upon in this country, but are prima facie evidence only of the justice of the plaintiffs' claim. (159 U.S. 113, 227.)

In 1932 the American Consul at Casablanca requested the opinion of the Department as to the effect that should be given to a judgment entered in the French Court of Appeals at Rabat, Morocco, and affirmed by the French Court of Cassation, reversing an earlier judgment of the Court of First Instance at Casablanca obtained by an American protégé, and ordering him to return money obtained under that judgment. The Department expressed the view thatsince the judgment is directed against a person and property under the exclusive jurisdiction of the American Consular Courtdespite the appeal by the American ressortissant to the French Court of Cassation, and since it is understood that French courts are unable to give conclusive effect to judgments of courts of the United States, the rule of reciprocity established by the 

Supreme Court of the United States in the case of Hilton vs. Guyot is applicable to the case under discussion and accordingly the judgment of the French court is reviewable on the merits in the action for its enforcement filed in the American Consular Court.

In the Department's opinion, the application of the rule of reciprocity by the American Consular Court to the judgment of the Court of Cassation under reference cannot properly be interpreted as a denial of the judicial authority of the French court with respect to persons and property subject to its jurisdiction, but results from the recognition of the fact that the judgment of the Court of Cassation is legally ineffective to accomplish its purpose without the concurrence of the American Consular Court by virtue of (1) the extraterritorial judicial system in force in Morocco, and (2) the changed judicial status of the persons and property involved in the suit on which the judgment is based when the judgment was rendered.

So long as French courts refuse to give conclusive effect to judgments of the courts of the United States, there would not appear to be any proper basis for complaint against the attitude of American courts towards judgments of French courts, and it is not perceived that the application in the instant case of the rule of reciprocity laid down by the Supreme Court of the United States should tend to defeat the ends of justice. 

The Diplomatic Agent and Consul General (Blake) to Secretary Colby, no. 189, Feb. 8, 1921, and the Under Secretary of State (Fletcher) to Mr. 

Blake, Jan. 11, 1922, MS. Department of State, file 855.04681/-; Consul 

Buhrman to Secretary Stimson, no. 184, May 3, 1932, ibid. 178.1/8; the 

Assistant Secretary of State (Rogers) to Mr. Buhrman, Sept. 29, 1932, ibid. 178.1/9.

In 1913 certain persons filed petitions in the consular court at Smyrna, Turkey, against an American steamship company, to recover damages under the employers' liability act of the State of Maine, which was the State of the company's incorporation. With reference thereto, the Department of State said thatthe Department desires to invite your attention to the provisions of section 4086 of the United States Revised Statutes which in effect provides that the diplomatic and consular representatives of the United States in so-called extraterritorial countries shall exercise jurisdiction in both civil and criminal matters in conformity with the laws of the United States, the common law, the law of equity and admiralty, and that in cases where none of these furnish appropriate and sufficient remedies, the defects and deficiencies shall be supplied by decrees and regulations of the ministers in those countries. The enumeration of these applicable laws would seem to exclude by implication the application of other laws, such as State statutes. 

Consul General Horton to Secretary Bryan, no. 136, May 24, 1913, and the Director of the Consular Bureau (Carr) to Mr. Horton, no. 74, June 23, 1913, MS. Department of State, file 367.114M69/198.

In response to a request from the Consul General in Shanghai for instructions on the question whether he had authority to order prisoners at the American jail to submit to having photographs taken for the use of the police department, the Department of State furnished him with a copy of an opinion of the Solicitor for the Department in which the following conclusion was reached:

Since the common law would appear to give to the police authorities no right to use force or violence to compel a prisoner to be photographed, and since it does not appear that the United States Statutes or the regulations of the Minister, which supplement the common law, as enforced in our Consular Courts in China give any such right, it would appear inadvisable and indeed illegal for the Consul to order the taking of such photographs. 

Chief Clerk Carr to Consul General Denby, no. 154, Oct. 22, 1908, MS. 

Department of State, file 15935.

In a criminal proceeding instituted in the United States Court for China the defendant raised the question, by plea in abatement, whether the proceeding was barred by a three-year statute of limitation enacted by Congress on April 13, 1876 (19 Stat. 32, 33; Rev. Stat., sec. 1044)

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

591 or whether the matter was governed by a ministerial regulation barring proceedings for such an offense after a period of six years. The court found that the regulation was adopted pursuant to section 5 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (12 Stat. 73) authorizing the Minister to make rules of procedure for consular courts, and that section 5 of the act approved June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 816) relating to the procedure of the

United States Court for China provided that it should be "in accordance, so far as practicable, with the existing procedure prescribed for Consular Courts in China in accordance with the Revised Statutes of the United States". The court concluded that this statute "cannot be considered as anything less than an affirmative recognition and confirmation of such of these regulations, at least, as relates to procedure" and that the regulations "are now clearly and unquestionably made binding and obligatory on this Court by direct and specific enactment".

The decision was also placed upon the ground that the local regulation should apply in China irrespective of the statute in as much as Federal laws relating to procedure are generally applicable only "to those courts, considered as part of the Federal system and as invested with the judicial power of the United States expressly conferred by the Constitution" (quoted by the court from Hornbuckle v. Toombs, 18 Wall. (1873) 648, 655) and in as much as the general rule of the applicability of local rules for a particular locality should be of special force in a jurisdiction outside the boundaries of the United States. 

United States v. Charles A. Engelbracht, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1909) 169, 173, 177. 

In 1934 the United States Court for China held that the statute of limitations prescribed for actions on contract in the District of Columbia (31 Stat. 

1389) was to be applied in China in preference to the ministerial regulations. On appeal, however, the Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth 

Circuit reversed this decision and held, in accordance with the former rule, that the regulations were in force by virtue of the act approved June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 814). Chalaire v. Franklin, United States Court for China, 192 (n. s.) North-China Herald 437 (Sept. 19, 1934); 81 F. (2d) (C.C.A. 9th, 1936) 105. For similar rule, see Leonard Everett v. Swayne & Hoyt, 1

Extraterr. Cas. (1919) 867, relating to interest rates allowable on judgments. For application of the rule in a divorce case, see Roberts v. Roberts, ibid. 916 (post, this section).

State pointed out to him that these regulations appeared to be substantive in nature and that the question whether the Minister was empowered to make such regulations or whether he was confined to acts merely procedural, had never been settled.

Procedural rules-U.S.

United States, involving a prosecution for vagrancy, wherein it was held that the above regulation was in conflict with a statute of the United States (sec. 151 of the 

Alaska Criminal Code), rendered applicable in China by the rule of the Biddle case (ante, this section), and that the statute, having been in force at the time the court was created, took precedence over a ministerial regulation promulgated subsequently. 

Minister Rockhill to Secretary Root, no. 590, Apr. 17, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 552/157; Mr. Root to Mr. Rockhill, no. 312, June 15, 1907, ibid. 552/159; 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1909) 180.

With respect to the provisions of the Statutes giving authority to the Minister to make regulations regarding the rules of procedure applicable to the consular courts, you are advised that the Department is clearly of the opinion that Section 5 of the Act of June 30, 1906, should be construed as effecting a transfer of the authority to modify and supplement existing rules of procedure from the Minister to the United States Court for China. 

You are further informed that the Department considers that the power conferred upon the Minister by Section 4086 of the Revised Statutes, to make regulations concerning remedial rights, is not revoked or transferred by the provisions of the Act creating the United States Court or by other legislation. However, in view of the fact that, according to the Department's information, under the holdings and decisions of the United States Court for China in construction of the authority vested in it and in the consular courts, American citizens in China are supplied with remedial rights to an extent apparently quite ample and in view also of the narrow construction which has heretofore been placed upon the authority of the Minister, derived from the provisions of Section 4086 of the Revised Statutes, with respect to the making of regulations concerning remedial rights, it would seem that there would be little, if any occasion for the Minister to exercise such authority. It is further believed that as a matter of policy and to avoid possible friction, it would be well for the Minister to abstain from exercising that authority. 

Counselor Polk to Minister Reinsch, no. 580, Mar. 2, 1917, MS. Department of State, file 171.3/-.

On April 18, 1914 the United States Court for China overruled a demurrer interposed to an information charging the defendant with selling liquor without a license in violation of Federal statutes (37 Stat. 938, 997, 1002; 30 Stat. 1253, 1340) making such an act an offense if committed within the District of Columbia or Alaska. The court, in its opinion, referred to section 1 of the act approved June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 814), ante, p. 571, conferring upon the court "jurisdiction in all cases and judicial proceedings whereof jurisdiction may now be exercised by United States consuls and ministers by law

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

593 1 and by virtue of treaties between the United States and China".

Reference was made to article 21 of the treaty of 1844 (1 Treaties, etc. 

[Malloy, 1910] 202) and article 11 of the treaty of 1858 (ibid. 215) between the United States and China providing for the punishment by consuls in China of American citizens guilty of crimes (according to the first treaty) or improper acts (according to the second treaty). 

This was broad enough, the court stated, to cover acts malum prohibitum as well as acts malum in se. It referred to the act approved 

August 11, 1848 (9 Stat. 276) and that approved June 22, 1860 (12

Stat. 72) extending the laws of the United States over citizens of the 

United States in China so far as they are necessary to execute the treaties and suitable to carry them into effect, and held that the laws therein referred to were the acts of Congress then or subsequently in force, which were extended to American citizens in China independently of their original purposes, citing Biddle v. United States, 156

Fed. 759 (C.C.A. 9th, 1907), ante. It found that the extension of such laws to China in the case under consideration was "necessary" to execute the treaties of the United States with China, particularly as the United States had obligated itself to punish all "improper acts". It was pointed out that nowhere within its jurisdiction had Congress permitted the liquor traffic to be unregulated. It was explained that it was "necessary" to invoke the statutes, rather than the common-law charge of committing a nuisance, because "it would be in open disregard of the legislative intent to treat as sufficient here a prosecution for a common law offense when Congress has everywhere else provided a statutory one". The court found that the statutes in question were "suitable" to carry the treaties into effect. 

United States v. John T. Allen, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1914) 308, 315–316.

In a case decided in 1919 the jurisdiction of the United States Court for China to entertain petitions in bankruptcy was challenged by demurrer on the ground that the Federal bankruptcy law then in force (act approved July 1, 1898, 30 Stat. 544), enumerating the Federal courts upon which jurisdiction was conferred, did not name the United States Court for China. The court held (April 30, 1919) that it had jurisdiction, pointing out that the act in question was passed before the creation of the court and further thatthe test of jurisdiction under extraterritoriality is found not merely in the text of the particular act in question but in its provisions as a whole as interpreted in connection with the extending act. Nearly all American statute law in this jurisdiction is applied in a manner and over a territory different from what was in the legislative mind at the time of its enactment and the question always arises whether it is (1) one of "the laws of the United

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

States," (2) "necessary to execute the treaties" with China, and (3) "suitable to carry them into effect [citing 9 Stat. 276 and 12

Stat. 73]." If it meets these tests it is treated as "extended over all citizens of the United States in China," regardless of the original purpose or intent of its enactment.

In re Petition for Bankruptcy of the American Food Manufacturing Company, Ltd., 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1919) 896, 897. The voluntary assignment provisions of the District of Columbia Code (31 Stat. 1256) were applied in 

China in In re Assignment of A. S. Fobes, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1920) 950. tion act In an action to recover damages for the accidental death of plain- Compensatiff's husband, the United States Court for China considered the possibility of applying the compensation act for the District of Columbia; it held, however, that many of the details of the act were unsuitable to China and that in any case the defendant could not be held to compliance without notice. Therefore judgment was given in accordance with the common law, which required dismissal of the complaint.

In a memorandum of the Office of the Solicitor, Department of State, Depositions November 16, 1921, enclosed with an instruction to the Consul General de bene esse at Tientsin, China, it was said with reference to the right of a consular court to take a deposition de bene esse:

It must be admitted that in view of the reasoning adopted by the courts in construing Section 863 of the Revised Statutes [28 U.S.C. §639], namely, that it was not intended by Congress to have application in a foreign country, the question whether a Consular Court might take such a deposition is not entirely free from difficulty. So far as can be determined that question has not been passed upon by a Federal court. Inasmuch as the laws of the United States are made by statute applicable to China, when necessary to execute the treaties, it can logically be contended that

Letters rogatory Interest Juveniles Personal status: domicil

Section 863 R.S. being a law of the United States may have such application. In the absence of a judicial decision to the effect that 

Section 863 R.S. is inapplicable to China, it is believed that the 

Department should not instruct American Consular officers acting judicially to decline to take such depositions, especially since the question of the applicability of this Section must, in each case, be decided by the court before the deposition taken by the consular officer may be introduced in evidence. Moreover, generally before a deposition de bene esse is taken application is made to the court before which the action is pending and the court in granting leave to take such deposition before a consular officer must, of course, consider first the authority of such officer to perform that service. It is believed, therefore, that American Consular 

Courts in China should continue to take depositions de bene esse until a judicial decision is rendered to the contrary.

United States v. A Juvenile Offender, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1918) 687. 

The case of In re Allen's Will, decided by the United States Court for China in 1907, involved the question of the law to be applied in the administration of the personal estate of a decedent whose domicil of origin was the State of Georgia but who had lived during the last 47 years of his life in China and was known to have considered that country his permanent place of residence. The court held that the decedent had acquired an "extraterritorial domicil" in China and that the applicable law was therefore that which Congress had extended to Americans in China, rather than the laws of Georgia. It was of

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

597 the opinion that an American who had made his home in China and intended to remain there had naturally acquired a domicil in the community in that country which was under the jurisdiction of the United States, even though that community did not possess the sovereign territorial power. This extension of the idea of "territory" or "locality" as an element of domicil was believed to be justified by the development of the law of extraterritoriality and preferable to the fiction that a person was domiciled in a place where he did not reside and had no intention of residing in the future. Consideration was given to the practical advantage to the court of having but one law of probate to administer in China rather than those of the various jurisdictions within the United States. 

In re Young John Allen's Will, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1907) 92.

Although In re Allen's Will came to an opposite conclusion from that of the earlier leading English case, In re Tootal's Trusts, 23 Ch. D. (1883) 

532, it was nevertheless apparently influenced by that decision which was based upon the proposition that an Englishman was presumed not to have intended to acquire a domicil in China because of the immiscibility of the two races, and which held further that an Englishman could not acquire an "Anglo-Chinese" domicil, that is, a domicil in a community that was not governed by the laws of the territorial sovereign. 

Mather v. Cunningham, decided by the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine, 105 Me. (1909) 326, 74 Atl. 809, involved facts substantially similar to those in the case of In re Allen's Will, and held that the decedent had abandoned his domicil of origin in the State of Maine and acquired a domicil of choice in Shanghai, China, and that the courts of Maine, therefore, did not have jurisdiction of his estate. While thus agreeing with the conclusion of Judge Wilfley in In re Allen's Will, and referring with approval to his opinion in that case, the Maine court took exception to his use of the term "extraterritorial domicil", stating: "... It appears to be inconsistent with the fundamental idea of domicile, which is a relation between an individual and a particular locality or country. The fact that the law governing the particular locality is extraterritorial does not make the domicile extraterritorial, since it is immaterial upon the question of domicile from what source the law is proclaimed, Ibid. 346. 

The court agreed that domicil necessarily implies subjection to the local law but was of the opinion that "ownership of the soil controls the establishment of all local laws. whatever laws may have been extended by Congress to the province of Shanghai are operative, not upon American soil, but upon the territory of the Chinese Empire. How do these laws reach there? By treaty, permission of the Emperor." Ibid. 

337-338. The court expressed the opinion that the doctrine of immiscibility should be abolished.

This view of the matter was adopted by the House of Lords in Casdagli v. Casdagli, [1919] A.C. 145, which expressly overruled In re Tootal's 

Trusts. The Lord Chancellor said: 66 

The position of British subjects in such a country is not extraterritorial. The domicil is acquired and can be acquired only by residence

Probate matters in Egypt. The law applicable to the foreigner so residing is, by the consent of the Egyptian Government, partly Egyptian and partly English. 

This is the result of the Convention between the two Governments. Though the domicil is Egyptian, the law applicable to persons who have acquired such a domicil varies according to the nationality of the person. The foreigner does not become domiciled as a member of the English community in Egypt, but he acquires an Egyptian domicil because he, by his own choice, has made Egypt his permanent home, and you have then to consider by what code of law he and his estate are governed according to the law in force in Egypt. The domicil is purely territorial, and you go to the law in force in the territory to see what system of law it treats as applicable to resident foreigners and to what Courts they are subject.” (pp. 160-161.) 

For a similar holding, see In re Coppock's Estate, 72 Mont. (1925) 431, 234 Pac. 258.

The Department of State, on July 27, 1914, ruled that persons born in countries where the United States enjoyed extraterritorial privileges whose parents were American citizens but had never resided in the United States, "are not citizens of the United States, even though their fathers may have resided in American communities and submitted themselves to the extraterritorial jurisdiction of the United States". Secretary Bryan to the diplomatic and consular officers of the United States in China and Turkey, July 27, 1914, MS. Department of State, file 130/508a. 

In May 1907 the United States Court for China, in considering a petition to admit a will to probate, stated that "The petition raises the question whether this court has jurisdiction in the matter of the administration of estates of Americans decedent in China." It found that, although Congress had enacted no laws on the subject, jurisdiction had been conferred upon the consular courts by section 4 of the act approved June 22, 1860 (12 Stat. 73), empowering them to exercise jurisdiction in accordance with the common law where the statutes were not adapted, or were deficient to carry out the treaties. The court said that, although "American courts of probate may properly be said to be purely creatures of statute at the present time", the law administered by them was based upon the common law and that "there can be no question about the proposition that Congress meant to extend the law of the administration of estates to China under the term 'common law' as fully as it meant to extend the law of crimes ." Therefore, it was pointed out that the consular courts. had this jurisdiction and it was held that it was extended to the United States Court for China under section 4 of the act approved June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 815), as regards all estates of the value of $500 or over. 

In the matter of the Probate of the Will of John Pratt Roberts, MS. 

Department of State, file 552/173½; 83 (n.s.) North-China Herald (May 

17, 1907) 423.

In May 1907 a suit was brought in the United States Court for China by the administrator, appointed in Maine, of the estate of a person deceased

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

599 2 2 in China. The court referred to its decisions In re the Will of John Pratt 

Roberts and In re Young John Allen's Will, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1907) 92, and said: "The significance of the foregoing decisions is that under the treaties of extraterritoriality in force between the United States and China and the Acts of Congress passed pursuant thereto, and for the purpose of carrying the same into full force and effect, China, in so far as the administration of the estates of Americans decedent therein is concerned, is a separate, distinct and complete jurisdiction, similar to that of an unorganized territory belonging to the United States." 

The court sustained a plea in abatement on the ground that the plaintiff had been appointed administrator in Maine and that his authority to act in that capacity did not extend beyond the boundaries of that statė.

The American Consul General in Tientsin was requested in 1910 to act as official witness to a marriage between an American and a Russian subject. It appeared that the parties desired to be married according to Jewish forms and that as there was no rabbi in Tientsin they proposed resorting to a form considered valid by Jews in Russia, in which the parties mutually took vows in the presence of witnesses of their own faith. The Russian Consul had advised the parties that they "must apply to the official Rabbi in Harbin, if the marriage is desired to have validity in Russia". The Consul General explained: is, to all in The form of ceremony which is proposed tents and purposes, a common law marriage. He is a citizen of the State of New York, in which State it is averred common law marriages are permitted. And he raises the question whether a ceremony of marriage by contract shall not be witnessed by an American consular officer the same as any other form of ceremony, when the laws of his own state permit such marriages.

The Department of State instructed him as follows: 

it would appear that the marriage [ceremony] might be consummated in one of the three following ways:

In the first place, it would appear that there could be no doubt regarding the legality of the marriage if it were performed by the Jewish Rabbi at Harbin, as was suggested by the Russian Consul. A ceremony before and by that official would seem to place the validity of the marriage beyond question. 

In the second place, it may be that an American Consul might, in his judicial capacity, perform a marriage ceremony under the laws of the United States. Inasmuch, however, as the Department has forbidden consuls to solemnize marriages this procedure is not free from objection and the Department therefore doubts the advisability of following this course.

In the third place, it would appear, as suggested by you, that the ceremony proposed by the parties themselves would clearly constitute a common law marriage, which would be as legal and binding as any ceremony and, if performed in accordance with the New York Statutes, which require that the contract entered into between them shall be reduced to writing and signed before witnesses, it seems quite clear that it would be regarded as valid in New York, should it be, as the Department is inclined to doubt, that the laws of New York control upon this matter. 

It would, therefore, appear that the parties may suit their convenience in the matter of the manner in which the ceremony is performed, either by having the ceremony performed by the Jewish Rabbi at Harbin, or by entering into a common law marriage which shall meet the requirements of the New York Statutes. 

Consul General Knabenshue to Secretary Knox, no. 18, Apr. 6, 1910, and the Assistant Secretary of State (Hale) to Mr. Knabenshue, July 30, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 15617/1.

In a proceeding brought in the United States Court for China for the annulment of a marriage on the ground of duress, the defendant interposed a demurrer to the jurisdiction of the court. The court Annulment overruled the demurrer, concluding that it had jurisdiction to grant the relief sought and that this jurisdiction could be derived from any one of the following sources: (a) The treaties [of peace, amity and commerce of 1844, art. 

XXV, 1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 203; and of 1858, art. 

XXVII, ibid. 220, between the United States and China] which reserve and impliedly confer jurisdiction "in regard to rights, whether of person or property." 

(b) The acts of Congress [secs. 3 and 4 of the act of August 

11, 1848, 9 Stat. 276 and sec. 4 of the act of June 22, 1860, 12

Stat. 72] which invest this court with full judicial powers "in regard to civil rights" including "matters of contract" and which elsewhere expressly provide for the annulment of marriages where consent is obtained "by force or fraud." [i. e. particularly, act of 

June 6, 1900, 31 Stat. 408, relating to Alaska, and act of March 3, 1901, 31 Stat. 1391, relating to the District of Columbia.] (c) The inherent jurisdiction of equity which this court is expressly permitted to exercise where the laws "are deficient in the provisions necessary to furnish suitable remedies." (d) The reversionary jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical courts in matrimonial causes, to which chancery has fallen heir. 

Tahmi H. Cavanagh v. Salter D. Worden, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1914) 317, 325. To similar effect, see Harry Ross v. Kitty Ro88, 1 idem (1919) 924.

Divorce 

On consideration of the bill for annulment and the defendant's answer in the nature of a cross-bill seeking a divorce in the above case, the United States Court for China in June 1914 granted a divorce to the defendant. On the question of jurisdiction, the court pointed to several recorded instances of consular courts having granted divorces (citing III Moore's Dig. 459 and LXIX [n.s.] North- 

China Herald 1138, 1194) and to the fact that sections on divorce were included in Regulations for Consular Courts, citing Hinckley, American Consular Jurisdiction in the Orient (1906) 230. While these regulations did not expressly confer jurisdiction, the court felt that its exercise over a long period of time and the important questions of marital status and legitimacy therein involved made it inadvisable to question it. Referring to the decision in McDermid v. 

McDermid, the court said:

But the subsequent announcement of the Court of Appeals 

[citing Biddle v. United States, 156 Fed. 759 (C.C.A. 9th, 1907)] 

that Congressional legislation, tho enacted originally for another locality, is to be applied here when the subject is not otherwise provided for, supplies that defect. For Congress has prescribed "grounds" on which divorce or judicial separation shall be granted in both Alaska [31 Stat. 408] and the District of Columbia 

Attention was called to the fact that the later of these two statutes provided only for a divorce a mensa et thoro for the grounds alleged by the defendant and also that a regulation of the American Minister provided that "Divorce releases both parties, and they shall not be remarried to each other." The question whether this clause would authorize the court in a proper case to grant an absolute divorce on the grounds alleged was raised but not answered, as the court felt that decree of divorce a mensa et thoro was all that was justified in the circumstances of the case. 

Tahmi H. Cavanagh v. Salter D. Worden, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1914) 365, 

370. In a later case involving the same grounds for divorce, the court on the basis of the above-mentioned regulation, granted an absolute divorce, stating that "while the regulations do not provide the grounds they prescribe the effect and that effect must be given, until such regulations are modified in the proper mode, to any grounds which are extended here by the supplementary legislation of Congress". Roberts v. Roberts, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1919) 916, 918.

For other cases holding Congressional enactments relating to divorce applicable in China, see Mitchell v. Mitchell, ibid. (1918) 690; Neugent v. 

Neugent, 2 idem (1922) 347. 

McDermid v. McDermid, 2 A.J.I.L. (1908) 225, decided by the United

States Court for China in 1907, a few months before the Biddle case, held that extraterritorial tribunals did not have jurisdiction of "matrimonial causes".

insane 

In June 1909 the American Consul General at Constantinople Protection of 

(Istanbul) reported to the Department of State that he had committed to a hospital a destitute American citizen who had become insane, and asked to be instructed regarding the maintenance of this person. An opinion of the Solicitor for the Department of State referred to the extraterritorial status enjoyed by American citizens under article IV of the treaty of commerce and navigation of May 7, 1830 (2 Treaties, etc. [Malloy, 1910] 1319) and to the statutes (Rev. Stat. 

§4086; 12 Stat. 73; Rev. Stat. §4125) in which the exercise and enforcement of extraterritorial jurisdiction is made to conform to the laws of the United States, where applicable, and in other cases to the common law and the law of equity and admiralty. He was of the opinion that— • · there is no general statute of the United States regarding the question of insanity, so that we are forced to an interpretation of "the common law and the law of equity". Upon investigation it appears that at the common law there was a writ de idiota inquirendo of inquiry whether a man be an idiot or not (1 Blackstone, 302) and that the care, custody and control of lunatics and persons not able to maintain themselves, form a recognized branch of chancery practice (2 Story Eq. Jur. Sections 3262-65; Malin v. 

Malin, 2 Johns Ch. N.Y. 238). In view of these facts it would seem to be proper for the consular courts to assume jurisdiction.

Judicial function in lunacy cases

He stated that the only authorized fund from which payment of maintenance could be made was that appropriated for keeping prisoners in extraterritorial countries but that, by a liberal interpretation, maintenance of an insane person could be justified as "one deprived of his liberty by order of an appropriate court". The Comptroller of the 

Treasury concurred in these views, and the Consul General was instructed accordingly. 

Consul General Ozmun to the Assistant Secretary of State, no. 379, June

In 1921 in reply to an inquiry from an American consular officer in China as to his duties with reference to American citizens who become insane in China, the Department of State said that it appeared from procedure previously followed, as well as from the action of Congress in appropriating a lump sum for the maintenance and transportation of prisoners and insane persons, that "the United States Court for China has jurisdiction to pass upon insanity cases and to provide for the keeping, feeding and transportation of American citizens in China who may be declared insane".

Upon being informed that an American citizen in Spain appeared to be insane, the Department of State (in 1909) advised the American Consul at Gibraltar to take steps to have him "legally committed" to the care of his brother to be taken out of the country. Upon being subsequently informed that this person had gone to Morocco, the Department instructed the Consul General at Tangier to detain him "and judicially determine his mental condition". At the same time the 

Minister in Tangier was instructed to take no steps in restraint of his liberty as this could be properly done only by judicial process in the consular court. The Department instructed the Consul General that the procedure should be "in regular judicial form, keeping record of testimony and making decision in writing", and that if he found the man to be insane he should issue an order delivering him for safekeeping to a suitable person. On December 29, 1909 the Consul General reported that the inquiry had been completed and that he and his associates were convinced that the person was of unsound mind, but

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

607 not that he was incurably or violently insane.

The Department replied: 

Department not clear that you have rendered formal decision [this person] insane. This necessary if ... [he is] to be treated as insane. In this connection you will understand that [his] sanity is a judicial question for your exclusive determination in your judicial capacity in which you are uncontrolled except by a sound judicial discretion, therefore Department cannot direct decision.

The Vice and Deputy Consul General then reported that the man had been adjudged of unsound mind and was being sent to New York in the custody of a keeper.

Upon his arrival in New York, the custodian submitted a report to the Department in which he requested information as to his future movements and as to how he was to be reimbursed for his expenses and return passage. In explaining why it was unable to instruct him on these points, the Department said:

The proceedings in a Consular Court are strictly judicial and in exercising this function of his office, a Consul is entirely uncontrolled except by a sound judicial discretion, the Department of State having no authority whatsoever to direct the Consul in the exercise of these judicial powers. 

Your authority, therefore, is, in this matter, derived from [the consular officer] who, in conferring it upon you, acted in his judicial capacity. It seems quite clear, therefore, that this authority is not derived from the Department of State and that you are not, therefore, responsible to the Department for the proper performance of the duties to which you were commissioned by the Vice and Deputy Consul General.

Having these considerations in mind, it will be quite clear to you that it will be necessary for you to look to [the consular officer] or to the [insane person's] family for compensation for your services and the Department has no authority to direct or compel either party to meet them.

It was added that it was understood that arrangements had been made by the family with the Consul for the payment of expenses.

APPEALS 

$189 In an appeal to the United States Court for China from a conviction in a consular court on a charge of vagrancy, the appellant applied for trial of his case de novo. The court pointed out that section 5 of the act approved June 30, 1906 (ante §177) provided that procedure in the United States Court for China should be, so far as practicable, in accordance with the existing procedure in the consular courts and that the applicable rule empowered the Minister to decide finally any case brought before him on appeal from a consular court "upon the evidence which comes up with it, or to hear the parties further, if he thinks justice will be promoted thereby". 12 Stat. 75. The court was of the opinion that this authorization to hear new evidence on appeal marked a departure from the usual rule of Federal procedure, which should not be extended by implication, and laid down the following rule of construction:

A fair construction of the law requires that some strong showing must be made, substantially such a showing as, under familiar rules, would be sufficient to justify the granting of a new trial, in order to admit of the reception of evidence in addition to that in the record; and some even stronger showing will be insisted upon before the appellate court can possibly be justified in granting a trial de novo. The Court does not, therefore, undertake at this time to say that in no case on appeal will a trial de novo be granted but contents itself with saying that, in its judgment, such cases will rarely, if ever, arise. The request of the appellant for a trial de novo must be denied. 

Robert W. Sexton, Appellant, v. United States, 1 Extraterr. Cas. (1909) 

180, 183.

It is believed that the better construction is to hold that the general provisions of ... section [4107] limiting an appeal, in a case where the Consul sits with associates, to a decision in which any associate differs with the Consul, should control in the case of Turkey rather than the special provisions of Section 4092 R. On January 22, 1936 the United States ministerial court at Tangier, Writ of Morocco, issued a writ of certiorari requiring the United States consular court at Casablanca, Morocco, to send up to the ministerial court the certified record and judgment in the case of Marcos Toledano v. Haim Toledano for its review and determination. The case involved the dissolution of a partnership by the lower court, the petitioner claiming error in fixing the date at which the dissolution was to become effective. In its judgment of May 20, 1936 the ministerial court denied respondent's motion to quash the writ, decreed a later date as the effective date of dissolution of the partnership, and ordered an accounting between the parties as of that date. With reference to its right to issue the writ, the court first considered the appellant's contention that section 4107 of the Revised Statutes (12 Stat. 74), providing that the judgments of consular courts shall be final when associates concur in the judgment, did not apply, since this was a suit in equity rather than a demand for damages. The court stated: 

The Court is not aware of any judicial interpretation of Section Rev. Stat., 4107 of the Revised Statutes and while the Petitioner's contention $4107 as to the limited scope of the Section appears to be supported by the opinion of former Attorney General Cushing (7 Op. Atty. 

Gen. 495, 508) it does not appear that any action was taken to insure the uniform interpretation of the Section in conformity with the Attorney General's opinion, and it seems not improbable that the Section has generally been regarded as applicable to "all civil cases arising under" the extraterritorial treaties irrespective of whether they involve "demands for damages."

The Court is of the opinion, however, that disposition of the case may be made without raising the question of the application of Section 4107. 

As to its general right to issue the writ, the court said: 

As to the question of authority of American extraterri- General right torial courts of appeal to issue the writ, the Court has found no to issue writ precedent or authoritative discussion, but after careful consideration of all the laws applicable to Consular Court jurisdiction in Morocco and the purpose for which those laws were enacted, the Court inclines to the view that the issuance of such a writ may reasonably be regarded as included within the authority conferred 

---

Denial of due process "Reasonable time" for appeal upon Ministers in extraterritorial countries by the provisions of 

Sections 4086, 4091 and 4109 of the Revised Statutes.

Proceeding to discuss its warrant for issuing the writ in the instant case, the court found that, while the forms of due process of law were fulfilled in the lower court, there was in fact a denial of due process to appellant, which furnished ground for the issuance of the writ. 

On this point the court said:

While the Supreme Court of the United States has held that the Constitution of the United States does not, of its own force, operate in foreign countries and has expressly declared inapplicable to extraterritorial countries certain provisions of the Constitution, no Court of the United States has ever questioned the right of American citizens in extraterritorial countries to due process of law whether as a Constitutional provision or as a natural right under the system of laws administered by the United States. The right to due process is so fundamental in character and so inherently a part of the administration of justice by the Government of the United States that any question of the denial of the right without an appropriate remedy to any American citizen under the jurisdiction of this Government in accordance with the laws of the United States cannot seriously be entertained. The 

Court entertains no doubt, therefore, that the denial of due process of law in a Consular Court proceeding in Morocco would warrant the issuance of a writ of certiorari to review the record of the case in which such denial occurred.

Marcos Toledano v. Haim Toledano, judgment of the United States ministerial court in the city of Tangier, May 20, 1936, enclosed with despatch 

1164, from the Diplomatic Agent and Consul General (Blake) to Secretary 

Hull, May 23, 1936, MS. Department of State, file 178.2/48.

On August 21, 1935 the French Chargé d'Affaires in Washington inquired of the Department of State as to whether any right of appeal would lie from a decision of the United States consular court at 

Casablanca, Morocco, dated October 22, 1932. The Department replied on September 16, 1935:

The judgment of the American Consular Court could have been appealed to the American Diplomatic Agent and Consul General at Tangier, if the appeal had been filed within a reasonable time after the judgment was entered. [12 Stat. 75, 22 U.S.C. §165.] 

However, nearly three years have elapsed since the entry of the judgment, and the time for filing an appeal has passed. While the American Consular Courts in Morocco are not definitely limited to a prescribed period for the filing of appeals, they conform generally to the practice observed in the American Consular Courts in other extra-territorial jurisdictions in which the maximum period for filing appeals was fixed at five days.

613 governing In an appeal from a decision of the United States Court for China to the United States Circuit Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Rules in 1925, the court applied rules governing appeals from district courts, appeals pointing out that this procedure was provided for by section 3 of the act approved June 30, 1906 (34 Stat. 815) creating the United States 

Court for China and further that it involved no conflict with section 5 of that act, providing that "the procedure of the United States Court for China shall be in accordance, so far as practicable, with the procedure prescribed for consular courts in China". The court held that the absence of a jury did not affect the rule and that the finding of the court, in the absence of a request for a special finding, was of the same effect as that of a jury and did not authorize the court to determine whether the facts supported the verdict. 

China Press, Inc. v. Webb, 7 F. (2d) 581, 582 (C.C.A. 9th, 1925). For similar rule, see Wulfsohn et al. v. Russo-Asiatic Bank, 11 F. (2d) 715 (C.C.A. 9th, 1926).

Consul General Ozmun to Secretary Knox, no. 472, Apr. 12, 1910, and

A controversy involving the respective jurisdictions exercised in Casablanca, Morocco, by the consular officials of Germany, an extraterritorial power, and the military officers of French forces in actual military occupation, arose in 1908 out of the action of the German Consul in granting safe-conduct to six deserters from the French forces in occupation of Casablanca, three of whom were German subjects, and of the action of the French authorities in arresting the men and removing them forcibly from the protection of the German Consul against his protest. Protests having been made on both sides and diplomatic negotiations having failed, the matter was referred for arbitration to a tribunal selected from the panel of the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague. In its award, dated May 22, 1909, the tribunal said:

Whereas, under the extraterritorial jurisdiction in force in Morocco the German consular authority as a rule exercises exclusive jurisdiction over all German subjects in that country; and Whereas, on the other hand, a corps of occupation as a rule also exercises exclusive jurisdiction over all persons belonging to it; and

Whereas, this right of jurisdiction should be recognized as a rule even in countries granting extraterritorial jurisdiction; and 

Whereas, in case the subjects of a Power enjoying the rights of territorial jurisdiction in Morrocco belong to a corps of occupation sent to that country by another Power, there necessarily arises a conflict between the two jurisdictions mentioned; and 

Whereas, the conflict of jurisdictions mentioned above can not be decided by an absolute rule which would in a general manner accord the preference to either of the two concurrent jurisdictions; and

Whereas, in each particular case account must be taken of the actual circumstances which tend to determine the preference; and 

Whereas, the jurisdiction of the corps of occupation should have the preference in case of a conflict when the persons belonging to this corps have not left the territory which is under the immediate, lasting, and effective control of the armed force; and 

Whereas, at the period in question the fortified city of Casablanca was occupied and guarded by French military forces which constituted the garrison of that city and were stationed either in the city itself or in the surrounding camps The German consulate did not, under the circumstances of the case, have a right to grant its protection to the deserters of 

German nationality 

---

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

615 It was also held that "under these circumstances the deserters of German nationality who belonged to the military forces of one of these camps and were within the inclosure of the city, remained subject to the exclusive military jurisdiction" but that as "the question of the respective competency of the consular and military jurisdiction is very complicated and has never been settled in an express, distinct, and universally recognized manner" the German Consul did not incur blame for having granted the protection. It was further held that the French authorities, having found the German deserters in the actual custody of the German consular authority, should have respected this situation so far as possible. With reference to the non- 

German deserters, the consulate was held to have been in error in attempting to afford them protection.

The Casablanca Case (France v. Germany), May 22, 1909, Scott, Hague 

Court Reports (1916) 110, 114, 115, 117.

In August 1914 the commander of the French forces occupying Morocco issued an order instituting martial law and proclaiming a state of siege over the whole extent of the French Zone. When, in 

1915, the Department of State was apprised of a new order by the French authorities placing, "pending the duration of the state of siege", infractions of a dahir concerning military requisitions under the jurisdiction of the military courts, even if the offender were a ressortissant of a power retaining capitulatory rights, it instructed the

Ambassador in Paris to "protest against it in so far as it affects citizens of the United States". Replying to the protest, the French Foreign 

Minister, on February 4, 1916, referred to the original order of August 1914 to which, he said, the United States had made no protest, and went on to state thatin issuing the order in question, General Lyautey has not exceeded the rights which have, at all times and in all places, been conferred upon Commanders of armies in the field for the purpose of ensuring the safety of their troops.

The consequences of the state of siege instituted by the said martial law result, it is true, in divesting in favor of the military jurisdiction of the occupying army, all civil courts-either French or consular belonging to the Powers which still hold judicial privileges in the French zone in Morocco,-of the jurisdiction of certain crimes or attempts against the safety of the French troops, or of actions prejudicial to public order or safety, which it is the duty of the Resident General, Commander-in-chief, to assure in the very interest of the foreign colonies. But such a measure which is of a military character and quite exceptional and temporary, like the circumstances which require and justify it, does not affect in any way the fundamental principle of the privileges of jurisdiction still claimed by the Federal Government in the Sherifian Empire; it merely suspends its action pending the duration of the state of siege and in certain cases.

Department of State, file 881.00/608; enclosures to despatch 1989 from Mr. Sharp to Mr. Lansing, Feb. 11, 1916, ibid. 881.00/612.

The Under Secretary of State 

(Fletcher) to the Consul in charge (Knabenshue), Jan. 18, 1922, ibid. 390d.11/4. 19 On July 19, 1920 the American Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Tangier, Morocco, informed the Department of State that a French military court in the French Zone had condemned to imprisonment an American protégé on charges of having engaged in "banded pillage", which was an offense specified in the order of August 2, 1914 proclaiming a state of siege in the French Zone. The specific act of which the protégé was accused was participation in an effort forcibly to dispossess certain persons of a piece of land, title to which was a matter of dispute. The Department of State directed the Ambassador in Paris to inform the French Foreign Office that the consent of the United States to the order of August 2, 1914 had never been requested and had never been given, and said:

The proclamation of martial law by the French authorities of the Protectorate cannot, in the absence of an agreement to that effect with the Government of the United States, confer upon 

French military tribunals jurisdiction over American protégés, who, under the treaties in force and the existing usages, are liable to judicial proceedings only in the American Consular Courts, representing in Morocco not the dignity of His Shereefian Majesty but the sovereign authority of the United States. 

The Ambassador was also instructed to request the release and indemnification of the protégé. The request was refused in the reply

of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs dated February 5, 1921, which stated that one of the principles of the law of nations is that any army of occupation must provide for its own security, both by extending its jurisdiction over every person within the occupied territory and by the issuance through the General-in-Chief of special orders and regulations which none may evade without risking prosecution by that jurisdiction. When capitulatory jurisdiction thus gives way to military jurisdiction in the event of occupation the same must obtain in the event of proclamation of a state of siege, especially when as in the case of Morocco the military occupation under the Treaty of Protectorate (Treaty of March 30, 1912, Art. 

2) is combined with a subsequent proclamation of Martial Law (Order of the General of Division Commander-in-Chief of the troops of occupation, of August 2, 1914).

The absence of agreement on the part of the American Government cannot affect the application of martial law. By recognizing the French Protectorate in Morocco, the Federal Government has in advance acquiesced in all military measures necessary for the maintenance of order for which the Government of the Republic is responsible.

On December 29, 1921 the Department instructed the Ambassador again to demand the release of the protégé and to say: 

I am instructed to make it clear to the Government of the Republic that the existing treaties and usages are regarded by my Government as conferring upon the United States a right to maintain in Morocco courts of justice separate from the local administration for the exclusive cognizance of alleged offenses by American citizens and protégés. My Government cannot admit that a right given to it before the establishment of the French protectorate can be modified in any way without its consent either by the treaty of the protectorate or by the action of French military forces pursuant to that treaty. 

With respect to the Ministry's statement that the Commanderin-Chief of the forces occupying Morocco has under general rules of international law the right to exercise jurisdiction over all persons so far as may be necessary for the security of the occupying forces, I am instructed to point out that, apart from the question of any principles of international law applicable to a military occupation effected under the peculiar conditions prevailing in Morocco, there is the authority of the French Government itself to support the view that the military jurisdiction should be extended to foreigners only when the offenses with which they are charged threaten the safety of the army of occupation. This necessary limitation upon the military jurisdiction was recognized in a memorial presented by the agent of the French Government in the Casablanca Arbitration of 1909, which contained the following language:

EXTRATERRITORIAL JURISDICTION 

619 "Occupation, far from entirely destroying the regime established by the Capitulations in the occupied territory, affects territorial sovereignty, and as a consequence the fragments of such sovereignty gathered by the Christian States in the form of Capitulations, only in so far as the interests of the occupying powers imperatively require. Hence, whenever a dispute or contract brings as contestants only persons who are foreign to the corps of occupation, whenever the infringement that must be repressed does not in any way threaten the safety of the corps of occupation, foreign consuls and persons subject to their jurisdiction retain all their rights and prerogatives.' 

The offenses with which the American protégé, Allal Ben El- Mamoon, was charged were clearly not of a nature to threaten the security of the French army of occupation The Ambassador was then instructed to say that the only remaining question seemed to be whether American capitulatory rights in Morocco had been modified to the extent claimed, that it was obvious that such modification could take place only with the consent of the Government of the United States, and that the French Government appeared to believe that in recognizing the French protectorate over Morocco, the United States had impliedly acquiesced in all military measures deemed necessary for the maintenance of order. In this connection the Ambassador was instructed to quote to the French Foreign Office the pertinent portions of the correspondence between the United States and France concerning recognition by the United States of the French protectorate (vol. I, §17, and 1917 For. Rel. 1093-1094, 1096), and to state as a conclusion therefrom that "it is clear that the rights enjoyed by the United States under the capitulations were not relinquished”. 

The Ambassador was instructed to conclude his note as follows: [The United States] has in no way admitted that the responsibility which the French Government has assumed with respect to the maintenance of order in Morocco imports any diminution of the authority of the American courts established in pursuance of treaties with Morocco and exercised in conformity with the laws of the United States.

It is needless to add that my Government has no desire to interfere with the performance by the French Government of its proper undertakings in Morocco, but it cannot overlook contravention of American rights by the action of the French military authorities in Morocco in assuming jurisdiction over an American protégé charged with an offense that obviously did not threaten or in any way affect the security of the Army of Occupation. My Government is therefore obliged to insist that this American protégé be without further delay surrendered to the American consular authorities in Morocco for proceedings in accordance with the rights conferred upon the United States by treaties which are still in force.

On March 30, 1922 the Ambassador informed the Department that he had been advised by the Foreign Office in a note of March 28 that the President of the Republic had by decree remitted the unserved portion of the protégé's sentence. In reply to requests of the United 

States Government that its protégé be indemnified for his long imprisonment, the French Government indicated that it had not receded from its position as to the legal aspects of the case, that the remission of the sentence was an "exceptional act of good-will", and that under these circumstances the matter of an indemnity could not be considered.

ASYLUM GENERAL PRINCIPLES §191 

Foreign ambassadors, ministers, and other accredited diplomatic officers are entitled under international law to certain well-recognized immunities from the local jurisdiction, including, among others, immunity of their official residences and offices from invasion by local authorities. Such authorities may not enter an embassy or a legation for the purpose of serving legal process or of making an arrest. 

While foreign consular officers do not under international law share this diplomatic immunity, they are nevertheless, as representatives of their governments bearing commissions from their own government and recognized as such officials by the government of the state in which they serve, entitled to special respect and consideration by the local authorities. They may usually display on the buildings or offices used by them for official purposes the coat of arms and the national flag of their country. The consular archives and other official property of the consulate are exempt from search or other interference by the local authorities, and not infrequently the consular buildings or offices themselves are declared by treaty provisions to be inviolable. 

Such treaty provisions, however, are usually coupled with prohibitions against the use of the consular premises for purposes of asylum. 

So also and for reasons analogous to those appertaining to embassies and legations, the public vessels of a state while in the ports of a friendly foreign state enjoy certain immunities, under international law, from the local jurisdiction. (See ante, this chapter.) It therefore frequently happens, particularly in times of local political disorder, that persons desiring to evade the local jurisdiction or to escape from threatened danger seek refuge in these places.

The granting of asylum by these foreign governmental agencies was formerly recognized and practiced to a considerable extent but in more recent times it has been discontinued for the most part, except in a limited number of countries. It has never been recognized in the 

United States. On the contrary, the Government of the United 

States has strongly disapproved of the principle of asylum as such and has declined to recognize or subscribe to it as a part of international law. It has, however, on occasion sanctioned the granting of temporary refuge by American diplomatic and consular missions and by American public vessels when the affording of such refuge seemed to be necessary for the preservation of human life. Generally speaking, such refuge should never be granted, or if granted be continued, in opposition to the demands of an existing local government that is able and willing to guarantee to the refugee the customary safeguards of its legal institutions. It is only when the local government has become unable to assure the safety of the refugee and his life is consequently endangered through mob violence or other lawlessness that protection may be granted. The question as to whether in a given case the imminence of danger is such as to justify the affording of temporary shelter must of necessity be left in the first instance to the sound discretion of the responsible officer to whom application is made, to be determined by him in the light of the emergency. In no case should shelter be continued after the emergency has passed.

While questions of asylum usually arise in connection with political refugees, they at times arise in connection with fugitives from justice. 

Persons of the latter category, fleeing from the pursuit of legitimate agents of the local government who succeed in obtaining temporary shelter within an embassy, a legation, a consulate, or aboard a foreign public vessel, must be either surrendered on demand or removed. 

The principle of asylum is also involved in those cases where political or other refugees seek protection in the territory of a foreign state. Each sovereign state, being supreme within its own territory, is free to give such persons when found therein the protection of its sovereignty or to expel or to extradite them as its domestic policy or its international obligations may seem to dictate. There is therefore a broad distinction between territorial asylum and legation asylum or asylum on public vessels. Since the right of asylum in these latter cases can hardly be said to be recognized in international law, its practice wherever resorted to must of necessity be at the tolerance of the local state. (Incidents of territorial asylum will be discussed in later chapters covering "Immigration", "Deportation", "Extradition", and "Internment".)

ASYLUM 

623 1 

Section III-4 of the Foreign Service Regulations of the United States (July 1939) provides: 

Asylum. A diplomatic representative or consular officer may not extend asylum to persons outside of his official or personal household. (E. O. June 22, 1939.) Note 1. Involuntary refuge. The extension of refuge to persons outside the official or personal household of a diplomatic or consular officer can only be justified on humanitarian grounds. Diplomatic and consular officers may afford refuge to uninvited fugitives whose lives are in imminent danger from mob violence but only during the period active danger continues. Refuge must be refused to persons fleeing from the pursuit of the legitimate agents of the local government. In case such persons have been admitted, they must be either surrendered or dismissed from the mission or consulate.

On Oct. 2, 1930 there was sent to American diplomatic officers in 

Latin American countries a circular instruction regarding asylum (diplomatic serial 998, Oct. 2, 1930, MS. Department of State, file 311.0022/10) which, by Executive order of Dec. 1, 1932 was incorporated in the printed 

Instructions to Diplomatic Officers as §6 of chapter 7, reading as follows: 

"Recent political disturbances in certain countries, together with the resultant requests for shelter in diplomatic missions by individuals whose personal safety was believed to be in danger, suggests the advisability of again stating this Government's position with respect to the granting of asylum in American embassies and legations. "Immunity from local jurisdiction is granted foreign embassies and legations to enable the foreign representatives and their suites to enjoy the fullest opportunity to represent the interests of their states. The fundamental principle of legation is that it should yield entire respect to the exclusive jurisdiction of the territorial government in all matters not within the purposes of the mission. The affording of asylum is not within the purposes of a diplomatic mission. "The limited practice of legation asylum, which varies in the few states permitting it according to the nature of the emergency, the attitude of the government, the state of the public mind, the character of the fugitives, the nature of their offenses, and the legation in which asylum is sought, is in derogation of the local jurisdiction. It is but a permissive local custom practiced in a limited number of states where unstable political and social conditions are recurrent. "There is no law of asylum of general application in international law. 

Hence, where asylum is practiced, it is not a right of the legate state but rather a custom invoked or consented to by the territorial government in times of political instability. While the practice is recognized in most of the Latin American countries, and was the subject of a convention signed at Habana at the Sixth Pan American Conference in 1928, it has never existed in the United States and has never been recognized as a right which could be claimed by refugees or granted by diplomatic missions. The custom is justified publicly on humanitarian grounds, but in practice it is used primarily for the personal protection of conspirators planning a coup d'état or for the government fearing or experiencing one. "American diplomatic officers will be guided by these considerations and will bear in mind that the Government of the United States can not counte-

nance the affording of protection to other than uninvited fugitives whose lives are in imminent danger from mob violence; that such protection may continue only so long as such imminent danger continues; that asylum must be refused to persons fleeing from the pursuit of the legitimate agents of the local government, and in case such persons have been admitted they must be either surrendered or dismissed from the embassy or legation." 

The American Minister to Bolivia, in October 1932, informed the Department of State that the President and his family had requested asylum at the Legation and that he had consented to grant it in case of urgent need. 

The Department instructed the Minister that it expected him to be guided by the circular instruction of Oct. 2, 1930. 

Minister Feely to Secretary Stimson, telegram 108, Oct. 24, 1932, MS. 

Department of State, file 724.3415/2449; Mr. Stimson to Mr. Feely, telegram 45, Oct. 24, 1932, ibid. 324.0022/2.

For similar instruction to the Minister in the Dominican Republic, see the Acting Secretary of State (Castle) to Minister Curtis, telegram 22, July 2, 1931, ibid. 339.3922/5.

In reply to a despatch from the Embassy at Peiping reporting that a request had been made for asylum in case of sudden need and suggesting the presence of unusual circumstances, the Department of State, on Aug. 7, 1937, instructed the Embassy to abide by the instruction of Oct. 2, 1930, and that in the event of unusual circumstances arising, which in the opinion of Embassy officials warranted a departure from that instruction, to report the facts to the Department. The Embassy was told that if time did not warrant this procedure, it should act in its best judgment and report the facts.

In a despatch of March 18, 1912 the American Chargé d'Affaires in Ecuador reported to the Department of State that certain individuals had requested asylum in the Legation in the event of disturbances and that he had replied that "the Department of State deprecates the granting of asylum except where it is absolutely necessary from the point of view of humanity"; that he could not discuss a hypothetical question of future danger, but must decide each case on its merits as it arose; and that he strongly urged the individuals in question to adopt every other means of securing their safety, in case of trouble, instead of coming to the Legation as he desired to hold "absolutely aloof from all internal questions". The Department approved his action, but at the same time referred him to its instruction of January 30, 1912 in which the distinction between asylum and temporary refuge was discussed, and it was pointed out that, in cases of temporary refuge to preserve innocent human life, the Department had found it desirable to leave considerable latitude to the consular or diplomatic officer to act as, in his best judgment, the circumstances warranted.

Asylum to government officials On January 27, 1917 the American Minister to Costa Rica informed the Department of State that a revolution had overturned the Government of that country and that the president and other officials were under the protection of the American Legation. In a despatch of February 3, 1917 the Minister explained that they had come into the Legation while he was ill and that he had since fed and sheltered them. 

He pointed out that "condition appears reverse of that described in 'instructions to diplomatic officers'; it was the government which sought asylum". He further stated that an amnesty had been declared and that safe-conduct out of the country had been arranged for the refugees.

Following a coup d'état and the establishment of a dictatorship in Honduras in 1919, the American Minister in that country reported to the Department of State that during conditions approaching a reign of terror he had given refuge to certain persons in the Legation. In a despatch of July 21, after describing prevailing conditions, the Minister said: 

It was at this time and under these conditions, believing as I did, that these brutalities were purely political, that the parties were in great bodily danger and that at the outbreak of any form of disorder in the shape of resistance, they would be assassinated, I permitted five gentlemen, among them two congressmen, to remain in the Legation, after they had rushed here,

On January 25, 1925 the Minister in Chile requested instructions from the Department of State as to his conduct in certain contingencies involving threat to the personal safety of certain members of the recent regime in that country. The Department, in replying on January 27, 1925, said that the following was its position with regard to asylum: 

The Government of the United States respects the principle that a sovereign state enjoys the exclusive right to control and administer justice within its territory, and hence that it should not be resisted or thwarted by an American diplomatic officer when its authorities demand the surrender for purposes of prosecution of any person charged with crime who is not, by reason of some connection with the mission, to be deemed exempt from the local jurisdiction. Because the granting of shelter is oftentimes, if not commonly, accorded with a view to withholding an individual from that jurisdiction such action cannot be regarded with favor, save under very exceptional circumstances. As Secretary Root declared in a note to the American Minister to Haiti on April 11, 1908, "instructions have made it clear that this 

Government does not recognize a so-called right of asylum". 

[post §193] The Department of State does not countenance 

"any attempt knowingly to harbor offenders against the laws from the pursuit of the legitimate agents of justice. 

While the Department has at times approved of the yielding by an American diplomatic officer of temporary shelter to an individual when the safety of his life was threatened as by mob violence in a country where conditions of great disorder prevailed, the significance of such an exceptional situation should not be misconstrued. It is based on the theory that disorderly conditions productive of mob violence, for example, have so impaired the power or disposition of local authorities to administer justice as to render inapplicable for the time being the principle above set forth. An American diplomatic officer must therefore exercise utmost discretion in determining whether such extraordinary conditions exist and continue to exist throughout the period of [for] which shelter is sought or granted; or whether on the contrary any shelter which he is asked to accord is designed rather to thwart the common exercise of jurisdiction by the territorial sovereign. 

That a refugee should be sought by his political enemies for an essentially political offense would not necessarily bring the case within the exception noted, at least if such an offense were one made punishable by the local law, and if there was no reason to

H 

ASYLUM 

believe that the rights accorded an accused person for purposes of defense would not be respected. 

An individual fleeing before a mob might be given temporary refuge in an American mission, if he entered the same in the course of flight, until the mob dispersed or until the mission could turn him over to the authorities of the country, de facto or otherwise, who were in a position to protect him from similar outbreaks of mob violence. The fact that a person already in the custody of the local authorities is in danger of mob violence would not suffice to justify intervention by American diplomatic officers. Should the individual break away from the authorities in the face of a mob attack and seek refuge in an American mission he might be given refuge until the authorities were again in a position to resume custody of the fugitive and accord him protection from mob violence. 

The foregoing principles will guide you hereafter in the relevant situations with which you may be confronted.
