On December 12, 1930 the American Legation in Guatemala reported to the Department of State that soldiers and police had surrounded the home of a certain Guatemalan General who had thereupon betaken himself to the Legation where he was afforded asylum. The Legation said that it had taken up with the Foreign Office its promise not to molest persons who conducted themselves properly and that it had been assured that the General would receive protection. Owing to the enmity of certain persons in power, however, the Legation felt that the General's life was in danger, and furthermore, that if he were assassinated, a revolution would result. For these reasons temporary asylum was being granted. The Department replied that if the man's life was in danger, the Legation might keep him until such time as satisfactory assurances for his safety were obtained from the proper authorities, but it called attention to the fact that no disorders were taking place in Guatemala City and cautioned the Legation to see to it that the asylum terminated as soon as the conditions described had terminated. On the same day satisfactory assurances were received and the General left the Legation.

In August 1936, shortly after the outbreak of revolution in Spain, the American Chargé d'Affaires in Madrid, in connection with the subject of refugees seeking shelter from violence in the various diplomatic missions, stated that some of his colleagues maintained the "broadest possible interpretation" of asylum, namely, that "diplomatic missions could give asylum to any one not a fugitive from justice without advising Spanish Government", to which the Department of State replied:

In view of the fact that Americans now in the Embassy and outside are more than sufficient to tax the facilities of the Embassy, there is no alternative but to discourage requests for providing refuge to other than American nationals, and this is especially true in those cases where nationals of other countries have places of diplomatic refuge in Madrid. While we are of course anxious to render every possible help to nationals and diplomatic representatives of Latin American and other countries, we could not throw open the doors of the Embassy so as to further jeopardize the safety and means of protection for our own nationals. 

In extreme circumstances where the immediate question of life is at stake you should of course extend such protection as the limitations of the Embassy permit.

Subsequently the Chargé d'Affaires informed the Department that large numbers of Spaniards were receiving asylum in various embassies and legations and that in some cases this practice had given rise to friction between the Diplomatic Missions and the Spanish Government. The Spanish Minister of State, in a communication of October 13, 1936 to the Dean of the Diplomatic Corps, stated that Spain had respected the right of asylum "through a spirit of tolerance and not because it is obligated to do so" and that due to the "notorious abuses" to which the practice had given rise the Spanish Government "finds itself compelled to terminate the attitude of extraordinary tolerance adopted by it up to the present with respect to the practice of the right of asylum, reserving to itself the right to proceed against the abuses already committed as the high interests of the Republic may require in each case". With reference to the proposed joint reply of the Diplomatic Corps, which protested the stand of the Spanish Gov-

ernment, the American Chargé d'Affaires informed the Dean of the Corps that there was no justification for including the United States, in as much as no Spanish nationals had been given asylum in its Embassy. On October 19, 1936 the Department of State cabled its approval of this action by the Chargé d'Affaires.

ASYLUM IN CONSULATES 

$193 In 1907 the Consul in San Salvador reported to the Department of State that "Diplomatic agent Nicaragua here seeks asylum in this Consulate owing to continued threats, insults and denial of passport." 

The Department instructed the Consul: 

You may grant temporary protection to diplomatic agent of Nicaragua if he is in immediate danger from lawless violence. 

In any other case Salvador must assent to your offer of asylum and in any and all events agent must suspend diplomatic business and communication with outer world while under protection. The 

American Consulate should not be used as Nicaraguan Legation. 

Consul Jenkins to Secretary Root, telegram of Apr. 5, 1907, and Mr.

Root to Mr. Jenkins, telegram of Apr. 5, 1907, MS. Department of State, file 3691/299. 

Shortly after the outbreak of a revolution in Haiti in January 1908, the Department of State was informed that one of the revolutionary leaders had taken refuge in the American Consulate at St. 

Marc. The American Minister was instructed to inform the Haitian 

Government that the consular agent had been dismissed from service and his commission canceled. Later the Minister advised the Department that Haitian Government officials had taken refuge in the American Consulate at Port de Paix, that town being in the hands of the revolutionists. He had previously, on January 17, reported the presence of Government officials at the American Consulate at Gonaïves. On January 28, 1908 the Minister reported that "the revolutionists at St. Marc were at the United States consular agency when the agent was dismissed January 23, and although there has been no agency there since that time, the Minister for Foreign Affairs announces that the revolutionists are considered under the protection of the Government of the United States", and that Gonaïves had fallen to the Government and that revolutionary leaders had taken refuge in the French Consulate there. The Department instructed the Minister to "Assure the Minister for Foreign Affairs that the revolutionists are not to be considered under the protection of the United States." At the same time the consular agent at Gonaïves was instructed not to assist or give asylum to anyone participating in the revolution against Haiti and that if revolutionists were already in the consulate he should "decline to harbor them or facilitate their escape". 

Subsequently the Department informed the Minister that revolutionists at St. Marc were said to continue under the protection of the consular agent (a new agent having been appointed) and instructed

him to go to St. Marc to investigate and "see that Department's instructions are obeyed". As to British and Cuban refugees said to be at the 

Consulate at Gonaïves, the Department said that this situation was exceptional and that these persons "should be protected, pending full investigation and in the absence of consular representatives of their own nationality". The Minister reported that the Haitians taking refuge at St. Marc had been seized by the Haitian authorities and that five of them had been summarily shot and ten imprisoned; that the members of the Government had left the agency at Port de Paix and that a number of revolutionists had taken refuge there, some of whom would be summarily executed if expelled. To this the Department replied: 

As to Haitians at Gonaives and Port-au-Prince, you will notify Minister for Foreign Affairs that we deny sanctuary against due process of law but we will protect refugees against summary lawless slaughter such as now appears to have been meted out to the refugees at St. Marc. 

You will consult with the Commander of the "Eagle" as to the practicability of transferring all the refugees from Gonaives and Port de Paix to Port-au-Prince to be turned over to your protection for safe-keeping until their status, whatever their nationality, can be determined under international law and until absolute guarantee from the President and government of Haiti can be obtained for their trial according to the orderly operation of Haitian law.

The removal of the refugees to Port-au-Prince was impractical, and the Haitian Government agreed to regard the refugees in the Consulates as under the protection of the Legation. In telegrams of February 10 and March 9, 1908 the Minister reported that all refugees had left the American Consulates.

As to a later statement by the Minister that the idea had become prevalent that the Government of the United States had decreed that under no circumstances would it permit its Legation and Consulates to shelter Haitians, both citizens and officials, who were being pursued for political purposes, the Department said thatprevious instructions have made it clear that this Government does not recognize the so-called right of asylum. Recent conditions prevented that policy from being carried out with regard to refugees who were then actually under shelter. 

Now that the American Legation and consulates have been cleared of refugees, you will make it distinctly known that no more Haitian refugees will be admitted to shelter by you or your subordinates and that no pretext will be afforded for reawakening the question of asylum so far as the Government of the United 

States is concerned.

During a revolutionary outbreak in Persia in 1908 the American Consul at Tabriz reported that he had offered a Moslem subject of Persia temporary asylum from assault at the hands of two Moslem outlaws who had been members of a set of lawbreakers which had previously attacked the Consulate, to which the Department replied: 

This is obviously not an instance of so-called "asylum" from the operation of the laws of the land, but merely a charitable shelter for the time being, from imminent lawless danger. The Department does not recognize any right on the part of the Consulate to assume to give "asylum" in such a way as to withdraw any accused person from the rightful jurisdiction. As for shelter, as in this case, the utmost prudence must be exerted. 

On July 20, 1908 the Consul reported that anarchy reigned in Tabriz and inquired whether American missionaries might receive refugees. 

The Department replied that neither the Consul nor missionaries should extend any asylum whatever.

Following the capture in 1911 of the city of Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, by revolutionary forces, the American Consul at that place afforded refuge in the Consulate to a number of civil officials of the city. The Department disapproved the action stating: 

This Government has remained an impartial spectator of the recent internecine conflict in Mexico, except in so far as this Government's interests or the interests of its citizens have been concerned, and the Department is of opinion that, in accordance with this attitude, you should have avoided taking any action which might have the appearance of interference with the political controversies of the Mexican Government, and that, accordingly, you should have declined to afford temporary refuge to the paroled officials of the city, especially in view of the fact that it does not appear that there was any urgent need of such action in order to preserve innocent human life.

The information before the Department indicates that this case should be distinguished from that based upon what is technically known as the right of asylum in the strict sense, which you are undoubtedly aware is not claimed by this Government.

On April 7, 1913 the Consul at Matamoros, Mexico, reported to the Department of State that he had afforded protection in the Consulate to an officer of the Mexican Army who was believed to be in danger of his life by reason of the fact that the force under his command had revolted and joined a revolutionary party. The Department replied:

While the Department is not inclined to disapprove your action, under the circumstances as you explain them, it is not entirely clear that it was necessary for such protection to be extended over so long a period of time, especially in view of the proximity of the international border.

In this connection, it seems pertinent to invite your attention to the Department's standing instructions that, while indisposed to direct its representatives to deny temporary shelter to any person whose life may be immediately threatened, this Government does not sanction the usage of asylum and enjoins upon its representatives the avoidance of all pretexts for its exercise.

ASYLUM 639 Your action therefore in similar cases, which may arise in future, should be limited to the affording of protection only when it appears to be absolutely necessary for the preservation of life and should be in the nature of temporary refuge. It should be distinctly understood that the protection extended should be strictly limited as indicated, and that no promise of shelter should be given in advance of an emergency seeming to call therefor.

$194 

On March 2, 1910 the Secretary of the Navy transmitted to the

Secretary of State a telegram received from the commander of the 

Nicaraguan Expeditionary Squadron stating that a man claiming to be an American citizen was smuggled aboard an American naval vessel and was there given asylum on his statement that his life was in danger, that he was an escaped prisoner, and that he was a colonel on Chamorro's staff. He had thereafter left the vessel although warned that he thereby forfeited protection, stating that he voluntarily relinquished asylum, and had delivered himself as a prisoner of war. The Commander inquired whether he should assume responsibility to deliver him in the United States if asked to do so by the de facto authorities. The man had also described himself as a 

French citizen. In reply to the Secretary of the Navy, the Department of State said:

It seems to me that the fact that Cannon has made contradictory statements as to his citizenship is not decisive. Under par-

allel circumstances the instructions of this Department to a Minister would be to ascertain the real citizenship of the party claiming protection and to act accordingly.

The fact, however, that Cannon, after having once been granted asylum, left the ship voluntarily and on his own responsibility and on so doing was warned that he thereby forfeited protection, is one which would permit the Rear-Admiral to exercise a wide discretion if again asked to give such protection. 

If on independent investigation it appears that Cannon is an American citizen, and the Nicaraguan authorities de facto offer to deliver him to Rear-Admiral Kimball, the latter might, in spite of his having been on board before, convey him to a place of safety just as a Minister might grant him asylum a second time. But a United States official would still have the right to exercise his discretion in extending or refusing him protection and in view of the particular facts and under the general rules applicable in such cases, one of which is that American citizens may forfeit their right to protection, though this Government does not forfeit its right to protect them, when they engage in hostilities within a friendly country. 

Department of the Navy to Secretary Knox, Mar. 2, 1910, MS. Department of State, file 6369/794; the Assistant Secretary of State (Wilson) to the Secretary of the Navy (Meyer), Mar. 8, 1910, ibid. 6369/803. 

On October 28, 1913 the Acting Secretary of the Navy informed the Department of State that General Díaz, two Mexican friends, and an American newspaper correspondent had boarded the U.S.S. 

Wheeling, then in the harbor of Veracruz, Mexico, and had asked for protection. In reply, the Secretary of State said thatwhile the rule governing such cases is that it is the duty of American men-of-war to protect American citizens, it is, as a general rule, against the policy of this Government to grant asylum in its ships to the citizens of foreign countries engaged in political activity, especially when such asylum is for the purpose of furthering their political plans. Temporary shelter to such persons, when they are seeking to leave their country, has sometimes been conceded on grounds of humanity, but even this is done with great circumspection lest advantage be taken of it to further the political fortunes of individuals with the result of involving us in the domestic politics of foreign countries. 

In this case you will please direct the Commander of the Wheeling to furnish Williams, the American Correspondent of the New York Herald who, we take it for granted, is not a citizen of Mexico, asylum on the American ship until he can secure passage to the United States. In the case of General Diaz and his two friends, you will give them temporary asylum until they can find a ship to take them away from Mexico, it being taken for granted that they do not desire to remain in Mexico. They will, of course, understand that while they are on an American ship they cannot use it as a basis for political activity.

ASYLUM 641 In acknowledging the above letter, the Acting Secretary of the 

Navy said:

As General Diaz and his two friends had previously been granted asylum at the American Consulate, and as the specific instructions from the Division Commander, under which the Commanding Officer of the Wheeling was acting, accord with the Naval Regulations on the subject, which are approved by the President, this Department approves the actions of its representatives at Vera Cruz in this matter. 

Appropriate instructions to the Division Commander were at once issued by cable regarding the disposition of General Diaz, his two Mexican companions, and Williams, the American correspondent of the New York Herald, as suggested by the Department of State.

During a revolutionary outbreak in La Ceiba, Honduras, an arrangement was entered into between the Government and the revolutionary leader by which the latter consented to surrender the town on condition that he might be allowed to take refuge in the American Consulate pending the receipt of information as to the attitude of the Honduran Government toward the revolutionists. At the request of the local Governor, the American Consul took this person under his protection. The following day the Mayor de Plaza with 100 soldiers came to the Consulate and demanded the surrender of the refugee, accompanying the demand by a show of force. During this incident the refugee in the Consulate committed suicide. The American Minister at Tegucigalpa, upon instructions from the Department of State, lodged a strong and formal protest with the Government of Honduras, as a result of which the latter apologized and promised to punish the offending persons. 

Consul Evans to Secretary Kellogg, telegram of Oct. 28, 1926, and Mr. 

Kellogg to Minister Summerlin, telegram of Oct. 29, 1926, MS. Department of State, file 815.00/3998; Mr. Evans to Mr. Kellogg, telegram of Nov. 6, 1926, ibid. 815.00/4015; Mr. Kellogg to Mr. Evans, telegram of Nov. 10, 1926, ibid. 815.00/4014.

Article XVIII of the treaty of peace, amity, and commerce concluded between the United States and China in 1858 provides that "if criminals, subjects of China, take refuge in the houses or on board

ASYLUM 643 the vessels of citizens of the United States, they shall not be harbored or concealed, but shall be delivered up to justice on due requisition by the Chinese local officers, addressed to those of the United States". 

1 Treaties, etc. (Malloy 1910) 217. In 1915 the Minister to China. requested an interpretation of this provision. The question was raised in a case in which the fugitive appeared to be a political offender. The Department said:

In view of the practice which has grown up in China of recognizing asylum for political offenders aboard merchant vessels, and in view also of the fact that, generally speaking, extradition treaties between the governments of the world expressly provide against the surrender of political offenders, the Department considers that American consular officers in China should decline to deliver up from American vessels persons accused of political offenses.

The practice referred to above as having grown up in China, was instanced during the insurrection in 1913 when the Diplomatic Corps declined to accede to the request of the Chinese Government to agree to certain regulations authorizing the search by Chinese authorities of foreign residences and foreign vessels in order that insurrectionists might be located and arrested. In this connection attention is invited to the despatches from the Legation, no. 939 of July 25, 1913, and no. 947 of July 29, 1913, with their enclosures. [MS. Department of State, files 893.00/1828 and /1832.] 

Moreover, the Department understands that in 1903, the authorities of the International Settlement at Shanghai, directed by the diplomatic and consular officers concerned, declined to hand over to Chinese authorities certain Chinese resident in the Settlement who were charged with sedition. 

The Secretary of Legation (MacMurray) to Secretary Lansing, no. 733, Aug. 23, 1915, and Mr. Lansing to Minister Reinsch, no. 349, Oct. 30, 1915.

Women and children In that case you will endeavor to secure for Chang safe passage from the country if majority of Diplomatic Body approves and is willing to co-operate. In 1920 the Minister to China informed the Department of State that he had addressed the following letter to American residents of the diplomatic quarter in Peking:

Owing to the present confused political situation I have decided that refuge should not be given to Chinese men seeking to hide themselves in the Legation Quarter. All Americans, therefore, who reside in the Quarter are requested not to allow Chinese men from outside to reside in their business offices or dwelling houses. As to Chinese women and children, American residents in the Legation Quarter may use their own discretion. 

In reply, the Department said:

Article 7 of the final protocol concluded between China and various foreign governments on September 7, 1901 [2 Treaties, etc. (Malloy, 1910) 2010], provides, as the Legation is aware, that the quarter occupied by the legations shall be considered as one specially reserved for their use and placed under their exclusive control, in which Chinese shall not have the right to reside, and which may be made defensible. Whatever may have been the original intention with respect to the quarter being reserved for the residence of foreign legations to the exclusion of private persons and interests, the Department is aware that from time to time private individuals of various nationalities, including a number of American citizens, have been permitted to reside in the Legation quarter. In view of this situation, the Department, in approving the Legation's instruction of July 28, 1920, to American residents of the quarter, considers it advisable to instruct the Legation, and through it the American residents of the quarter, in regard to the granting of asylum to Chinese refugees. 

It has been the universal practice of this Government to discountenance the granting of asylum by its representatives in foreign countries, as indicated in paragraphs 50 and 51 of the De partment's Instructions to Diplomatic Officers of the United 

States, with which the Legation is doubtless familiar. The Department considers that the paragraphs mentioned, although

ASYLUM 645 originally intended only for the guidance of American representatives in foreign countries, should also govern the action of American residents within the Legation quarter at Peking, since the quarter is under the exclusive control of the legations, and the harboring of Chinese refugees within it, whether by the Legation or American residents thereof, would be in contravention of the provision of Article 7 of the Protocol of 1901 that Chinese shall not be permitted to reside within the quarter. 

The Legation is particularly cautioned against the giving of assurances in advance to Chinese officials or others that they may be afforded protection within the quarter, should their lives become endangered. The Department desires also to state that whatever may be the practice of the legations of other nations in China with respect to the granting of protection to Chinese refugees, the Department can neither approve nor sanction the extension of this so-called right to such refugees when to do so would result in harboring offenders against the laws of China from the pursuit of the legitimate agents of justice. 

The American Legation at Peking to Secretary Colby, no. 66, Aug. 2, 1920, and the Assistant Secretary of State (Adee) to the Minister to 

China (Crane), no. 142, Mar. 10, 1921, MS. Department of State, file 

893.00/3498. See also 1920 For. Rel., vol. I, pp. 457-458; 1921 For. Rel., vol. I, pp. 342-346.

It may be said, however, that in cases of temporary shelter for women and children, the Department would not look too narrowly into the question of native or acquired citizenship of the country in which the Consul is situated; but the first duty is to 

Americans and the extension of asylum to persons engaged in political activities is to be avoided.

The Director of the Consular Service (Carr) to the Vice Consul at 

Saltillo, Mexico (Silliman), no. 47, Sept. 24, 1913, MS. Department of

$196 Article VIII of the consular convention concluded between the United States and Cuba in 1926 provides: 

Consular offices shall not be used as places of asylum. On February 20, 1928 the Sixth International Conference of Amervention, 1928 ican States in session at Habana adopted a convention on asylum. 

Article 1 of the convention prohibits the granting of asylum in legations, warships, military camps, or military aircraft, to persons accused or condemned for common crimes or to deserters from the army or navy and provides that when such persons take refuge in any of the places mentioned they shall be surrendered upon request of the local government. As to such persons taking refuge in foreign territory it is provided that surrender shall be brought about through extradition according to treaties and the constitution and laws of the country of refuge. Article 2 provides: shall be respected 

Asylum granted to political offenders to the extent in which allowed, as a right or through humanitarian toleration, by the usages, the conventions, or the laws of

ASYLUM 647 the country in which granted and in accordance with the following provisions: 

1. Asylum may not be granted except in urgent cases and for the period of time strictly indispensable for the person who has sought asylum to ensure in some other way his safety. 

2. Immediately upon granting asylum, the diplomatic agent... shall report the fact to the Minister for Foreign 

Relations of the State of the person who has secured asylum, or to the local administrative authority, if the act occurred outside the capital. 

3. The government of the state may require that the refugee be sent out of the national territory within the shortest time possible; and the diplomatic agent of the country who has granted asylum may in turn require the guaranties necessary for the departure of the refugee with due regard to the inviolability of his person, from the country. 

4. Refugees shall not be landed in any point of the national territory nor in any place too near thereto. 

5. While enjoying asylum, refugees shall not be allowed to perform acts contrary to the public peace. 

6. States are under no obligation to defray expenses incurred by one granting asylum.

Charles Evans Hughes, chairman of the delegation of the United States, explained that the delegation refrained from participating in the discussion of the project for the reasons that asylum was "contrary to the practice of the United States, and, in the opinion of the Government of the United States, was not a part of general international law". 

In signing the final act of the conference, containing the motions, agreements, resolutions, and conventions, the delegation made the following reservation with reference to the convention on asylum incorporated in the final act: 

The United States of America, in signing the present Convention, establishes an explicit reservation, placing on record that the United States does not recognize or subscribe to as part of international law, the so-called doctrine of asylum. 

Report of the Delegates of the United States of America to the Sixth

A convention on political asylum was adopted on December 26, 1933 at the Seventh International Conference of American States held at Montevideo, Uruguay. By article 1 thereof the corresponding article in the Habana convention of February 20, 1928 was superseded. The new article provides that it shall not be lawful for states to grant asylum in legations, warships and military camps, or airships, to those accused of common offenses who may have been duly prosecuted or who may have been sentenced by ordinary courts of justice, or to "deserters of land or sea forces", and that such persons who find refuge in any of the places mentioned shall be surrendered upon request by the local government. Article 3 states that political asylum "as an institution of humanitarian character, is not subject to reciprocity"; that any "man may resort to its protection, whatever his nationality, without prejudice to the obligations accepted by the State to which he belongs"; and that the states which do not recognize political asylum "except with limitations and peculiarities", can exercise it in foreign countries "only in the manner and within the limits recognized by said countries". Article 5 recites that the "present Convention shall not affect obligations previously entered into by the High Contracting 

Parties by virtue of international agreements".

CHAPTER VIII THE HIGH SEAS AND INTEROCEANIC CANALS HIGH SEAS LEGAL CONCEPT 

§197 The term "high seas" is used in international law in contradistinction to "territorial waters", "marginal seas", etc., to designate that portion of the ocean generally regarded as the common highway of all nations. (The extension of the national police power beyond the traditional marginal sea for certain purposes has been discussed in ch. V, vol. I.) 

In municipal law the term "high seas" is used with varying meanings but frequently for purposes of admiralty jurisdiction to denote that portion of the ocean lying beyond tidewaters. 

The term "high seas" may be said to refer, in international law, to those waters which are outside of the exclusive control of any State or any group of States, and hence not regarded as belonging to the territory of any of them. The ocean until it envelops the shores of a littoral State and constitutes its maritime belt, is not a part of the domain of any territorial sovereign. No State possesses, therefore, the right to determine the lawfulness of acts there committed unless taking place on board of one of its own ships, or unless the society of maritime States unites to confer upon it authority to do so. 

I Hyde, International Law, etc. (1922) 405-406.

Article 4 of the draft convention on The Law of Territorial Waters of the 

Research in International Law of the Harvard Law School (1929, p. 243) states that "The high sea is that part of the sea outside marginal seas." 

See also art. I, par. 4, of the draft on Piracy. Research in International 

Law (Harvard Law School, 1932) 743.

FREEDOM OF THE SEAS IN GENERAL 

$198 

In discussing "The Freedom of the Sea" Thomas Callander Wade states that, while there has been "no well-established principle of International Law which has been so keenly contested as that of the Freedom of the Sea", the fact that "the high sea is free to the commerce and navigation of all nations would not now [1920] be disputed". In reviewing the early history of the doctrine, he points out that Venice at one time levied tribute on all vessels navigating the Adriatic; that, in 1493, Pope Alexander VI conferred on Spain and 

Portugal "the whole undiscovered regions of the world" in the grant of which "a line was drawn from pole to pole 100 miles west of the History Azores, and all undiscovered land and sea to the west were given to Spain, and to the east to Portugal"; that over "the whole of the western Atlantic Spain declared herself to be sovereign, and a similar claim was made by Portugal in the East Indian seas"; and that Queen 

Elizabeth contested the claim of Spain to the Western Atlantic but that shortly thereafter England asserted claim to the North Sea, the

English Channel, and the Bay of Biscay as far south as the coast of Spain. He states that the Netherland Government disagreed with 

England as to the rights of Dutch fishermen to fish in the North Sea, and with Spain when the latter, as successor to Portugal, insisted that the Netherlands should give up her East Indian trade. This resulted, he explains, in the publication by Grotius, a Dutch subject, of the twelfth chapter of his treatise on the Law of Prize, written in 1605, under the title Mare Liberum, attacking the "whole principle of maritime dominion" on broad principles of equity, which Selden, a 

British subject, in turn endeavored to answer. Wade concludes:

Throughout the writings of the later jurists of all countries we find a steady progress towards the principle of the absolute freedom of the sea. By the nineteenth century this freedom had become axiomatic. The controversy had come to be of only historical interest, as an illustration of an obsolete theory and an example of the evolution of legal thought and international practice. The high sea, therefore, is now free to all. Even though a state were powerful enough to possess it, the claim to exercise rights of sovereignty over it would not now be recognised as just, not so much by reason of the difficulty of effective possession, as because no good reason for its possession could be put forward. Any vessel has therefore now "the right to come and go on the high sea without let or hindrance, and to take therefrom at will and pleasure the produce of the sea." This is the principle of the freedom of the sea as defined in the British case in the Behring Sea Arbi tration,¹ (1 Parliamentary Blue Book, 1893 (Behring Sea), No. 4. 

The American reply, Blue Book No. 8, admits the general principle of the freedom of the sea, but argues that it is not free when an important and just national interest is put in peril for the sake of individual profit. The arbiters, however, decided against the 

American contention.) and as now established by the unanimous consent of international lawyers and the universal practice of nations.

Wade's Introduction to Sir John Boroughs' Sovereignty of the British 

Seas (1920 ed.) 1-29. 

For a more detailed history of "the claims to the sovereignty of the sea", see Fulton, Sovereignty of the Sea (1911) 25 et seq.; see also Potter, Freedom of the Seas in History, Law, and Politics (1924). 

Oppenheim states: 

The term "Freedom of the Open Sea" indicates the rule of the Law of Nations that the open sea is not, and never can be, under the sovereignty of any State whatever. 

It is in the interest of free intercourse between States that the principle of the freedom of the open sea has become universally recognised and will always be upheld. 

I Oppenheim's International Law (5th ed., by Lauterpacht, 1937) 468, 472-473.

In the case of The Vinces, a vessel of British registry, a libel had been filed against the schooner and her cargo of intoxicating liquors, apprehended within the 12-mile limit of the United States. In that case, District Judge Cochran said:

The high seas, however, are the common property of all nations. The authority of a nation within its own territory is, of course, absolute and exclusive. The authority of a nation over the high seas is not exclusive, but must be exercised with due regard to the rights of other nations therein. Every nation has the inherent right to protect itself and to provide for the enforcement of its laws and the security of its territorial jurisdiction. 

For the purpose of self-protection and the due execution of its laws, and for the prevention of frauds on its revenue, it may exercise an authority on the high seas beyond the 3-mile limit. 

20 F. (2d) 164, 172 (E.D.S.C., 1927).

In its judgment in the case of the S.S. "Lotus" the Permanent 

Court of International Justice said: In virtue of the principle of the freedom of the seas, that is to say, the absence of any territorial sovereignty upon the high

HIGH SEAS 

657 "Lotus" seas, no State may exercise any kind of jurisdiction over foreign The S. S. vessels upon them. Thus, if a war vessel, happening to be at the spot where a collision occurs between a vessel flying its flag and a foreign vessel, were to send on board the latter an officer to make investigations or to take evidence, such an act would undoubtedly be contrary to international law. 

But it by no means follows that a State can never in its own territory exercise jurisdiction over acts which have occurred on board a foreign ship on the high seas. A corollary of the principle of the freedom of the seas is that a ship on the high seas is assimilated to the territory of the State the flag of which it flies, for, just as in its own territory, that State exercises its authority upon it, and no other State may do so. All that can be said is that by virtue of the principle of the freedom of the seas, a ship is placed in the same position as national territory; but there is nothing to support the claim according to which the rights of the State under whose flag the vessel sails may go farther than the rights which it exercises within its territory properly so called. It follows that what occurs on board a vessel on the high seas must be regarded as if it occurred on the territory of the State whose flag the ship flies. If, therefore, a guilty act committed on the high seas produces its effects on a vessel flying another flag or in foreign territory, the same principles must be applied as if the territories of two different States were concerned, and the conclusion must therefore be drawn that there is no rule of international law prohibiting the State to which the ship on which the effects of the offence have taken place belongs, from regarding the offence as having been committed in its territory and prosecuting, accordingly, the delinquent.

This conclusion could only be overcome if it were shown that there was a rule of customary international law which, going further than the principle stated above, established the exclusive jurisdiction of the State whose flag was flown. The French 

Government has endeavoured to prove the existence of such a rule, having recourse for this purpose to the teachings of publicists, to decisions of municipal and international tribunals, and especially to conventions which, whilst creating exceptions to the principle of the freedom of the seas by permitting the war and police vessels of a State to exercise a more or less extensive control over the merchant vessels of another State, reserve jurisdiction to the courts of the country whose flag is flown by the vessel proceeded against.

In the Court's opinion, the existence of such a rule has not been conclusively proved.

Judge Moore, in his dissenting opinion, stated: 

In conformity with the principle of the equality of independent States, all nations have an equal right to the uninterrupted use of the unappropriated parts of the ocean for their navigation, and no State is authorized to interfere with the navigation of other States on the high seas in the time of peace except in the

Hovering of warships case of piracy by law of nations or in extraordinary cases of self-defence (Le Louis (1817), 2 Dodson, 210, 243–244). 

Per. Ct. Int. Jus., Judgment 9, Sept. 7, 1927, Ser. A, No. 10, pp. 25-26, 69; II Hudson, World Court Reports (1935) 40, 68.

In notes to the British Government of December 16 and 22, 1915, the United States protested against the practice of British cruisers' hovering off the American coast. The British note in reply, dated 

March 20, 1916, stated in part:

My Government has carefully studied the contents of your notes. They are impressed by the fact that no suggestion seems to be made in either of them that British cruisers enter at all within the territorial waters of the United States and they note that, on the contrary, the effect of the notes is to take exception to proceedings of these vessels when navigating admittedly on the high seas. The objection appears indeed to rest upon a claim to distinguish between different parts of the high seas, a claim which causes surprise to His Majesty's Government who are unaware of the existence of any rules or principles of international law which render belligerent operations, which are legitimate in one part of the high seas, illegitimate in another. 

The position of the United States was clarified in Secretary Lansing's note of April 26, 1916, in which he stated:

In reply it may be stated that the Government of the United States advances no claim that British vessels which have been and are cruising off American ports beyond the three-mile limit have not in so doing been within their strict legal rights under international law. The grounds for the objection of the Government of the United States to the continued presence of belligerent vessels of war cruising in close proximity to American ports are based, not upon the illegality of such action, but upon the irritation which it naturally causes to a neutral country. 

Further reasons, if necessary, may be adduced to oppose the British practice. In time of peace the mobilization of an army, particularly if near the frontier, has often been regarded as a ground for serious offense and been made the subject of protest by the Government of a neighboring country. In the present war it has even been the ground for a declaration of war and the beginning of hostilities. Upon the same principle the constant and menacing presence of cruisers on the high seas near the ports of a neutral country may be regarded according to the canons of international courtesy as a just ground for offense, although it may be strictly legal. 

Sir Cecil Spring Rice to Secretary Lansing, no. 82, Mar. 20, 1916, and Mr. 

Lansing to Sir Cecil Spring Rice, no. 1152, Apr. 26, 1916, MS. Department of State, file 763.72111V76/10. See also 1916 For. Rel. Supp. 759-764.

VISIT AND SEARCH 

$199 An historical résumé of the subject of "visit and search", with particular reference to discussions between the United States and Great Britain during the latter part of the eighteenth and the first half of the nineteenth centuries, embodied in a memorandum prepared by the Office of the Solicitor for the Department of State on December 19, 1908, as one of a series of memoranda discussing important policies of the United States, reads as follows: 

The question of the right claimed by Great Britain to visit and search our vessels on the high seas and to impress alleged British Historical seamen who might be aboard, early became a source of vexatious résumé controversy between the two Governments. In 1792 Secretary of State Jefferson, protested to the British Government against this claim and in 1794 Mr. Jay sought to secure a relinquishment thereof. The omission of any provision on this point led Mr. 

Jefferson, become President, to refuse to send to the Senate the treaty negotiated with Great Britain by Monroe and Pinkney in 1806.

The practice of Great Britain in carrying out this claim in the first years of the nineteenth century was very harsh, due largely to the great demand for sailors in the British navy because of the Napoleonic wars. It took no notice of American naturalization of British subjects, and resulted in even the impressment of many native-born Americans. It culminated in the outrageous Impressment attack of the British man-of-war Leopard upon the frigate Chesapeake in 1807, the diplomatic discussion over which, together with that upon the general allied subjects of visitation, search and impressment, were the leading causes of the war of 1812. Of the period between the Chesapeake outrage and the beginning of the war, Foster, in his "History of American Diplomacy" (page 239) says: "For the next five years our Government devoted its energies unceasingly to securing a relaxation on the part of Great Britain of the offensive practice of visitation and impressment."

The question which so largely brought on the war singularly enough was not mentioned in the concluding treaty of peace. 

The status which existed prior to the war was accepted by both parties. However, in spite of the fact that Great Britain refused to admit the wrongfulness of her contention, she tacitly abandoned the practice in question after the conclusion of the war. 

The matter then apparently ceased to be of political moment until its discussion was revived in a somewhat modified form in connection with the various efforts to crush the African Slave trade. On March 13, 1824, a treaty was concluded between the 

United States and Great Britain for the suppression of this trade, by Article I, of which, the cruisers of the respective parties were to have the right, in order to carry out the provisions of the treaty, to visit and search each other's vessels "on the coast of 

Slave trade

Africa, of America, and of the West Indies." On May 22, 1824, the United States Senate amended the treaty by striking out of the said words of Article I the words "of America". (American 

State Papers; Foreign Relations_V, pp. 319-322, 344, 361-362, 489, 585; Moore's International Law Digest, vol. II, p. 924),

This action of the Senate was thus explained in a despatch dated 

May 29, 1824, from the Secretary of State Adams to Mr. Rush,

Minister to England: 

"The exception of the coast of America from the seas upon which the mutual power of capturing the vessels under the flag of either party may be exercised, had reference, in views of the Senate, doubtless, to the coast of the United States. On no part of that coast, unless within the Gulf of Mexico, is there any probability that slave-trading vessels will ever be found. The necessity for the exercise of the authority to capture is, therefore, no greater than it would be upon the coast of Europe. In South 

America, the only coast to which slave traders may be hereafter expected to resort, is that of Brazil, from which it is to be hoped they will shortly be expelled by the laws of the country. [Ameri can State Papers; Foreign Relations V, p. 362].” 

In reply Mr. Rush advised the Department that Mr. Secretary 

Canning stated that the alteration in question formed an insuperable bar to the ratification of the treaty by Great Britain. [Id. 

In 1834 the State Department informed the British and French Ministers that the United States could not give adhesion to the conventions between Great Britain and France of November 30, 1831, and March 22, 1833, for the suppression of the slave-trade, because of the statement of the British Minister, in a note of December 25, 1833, that in the act of accession it would be necessary that "the right of search should be extended to the coasts of the United States." (Notes to French Legation V, p. 91, March 

24, 1834; Notes to French Legation, VI, p. 3, Oct. 4, 1834.)

On July 8, 1840, in an instruction to Mr. Stevenson, Minister to 

England, Secretary of State Forsyth declared that the President, "having now directed the establishment of a competent naval force to cruise along those parts of the African coast which American vessels are in the habit of visiting in the pursuit of their lawful commerce, and where it is alleged that the slave trade has been carried on under an illegal use of the flag of the United States, has a right to expect that positive instructions will be given to all 

Her Majesty's officers to forbear from boarding or visiting vessels under the American flag." (House Ex. Doc. 115, 26th Congress, 2d Sess. p. 39-40).

The discussion of the question between the two governments continued intermittently and formed the subject of a pamphlet written by General Cass, then Minister to France, on February 1, 1842, and approved by the President through the State Department on April 5, 1842. (Instructions to France, XIV, p. 272).

The American position was reaffirmed by President Tyler in his message of August 11, 1842, transmitting to the Senate the Webster-Ashburton treaty of August 9, 1842, providing in part for

HIGH SEAS 

661 measures to suppress the slave-trade, which was silent upon the question of the right of search and which was assailed in the Senate for that reason and defended by President Tyler and Secretary

Webster. (6 Webster's Works, 353, 369, 381-388; House Ex. Doc. 

192, 27th Congress, 3d Sess.)

Commenting upon the terms of the treaty Secretary Webster instructed Mr. Everett, Minister to England, on March 28, 1843, that the stipulations therein, relative to the suppression of the slave trade amounted to no more than this: "Great Britain had claimed as a right that which this Government could not admit to be a right, and, in the exercise of a just and proper spirit of amity, a mode was resorted to which might render unnecessary both the assertion and the denial of such claim."

Continuing, Mr. Webster denied the British claim that a distinction existed between the "right of visit" and the "right of search" and said that the first, if exercised, must necessarily lead to the second. (6 Webster's Works, 331-342). 

Mr. Everett, in reply, notified Secretary Webster on April 27, 1843, that Lord Aberdeen concurred as to such lack of distinction between these two "rights". Formal renunciation of the claim to such "rights" did not come, however, until 1858. On April 10, of that year Secretary Cass, in a note to the British Minister, said: "The United States deny the right of the cruisers of any other power whatever, for any purpose whatever, to enter their vessels by force in time of peace. No change of name can change the illegal character of the assumption. Search, or visit, it is equally an assault upon the independence of nations." 

Ex. Doc. 49, 35th Congress, 1st Sess. pp. 42; 47–48.) (Senate Upon bringing this note to the attention of his Government the 

British Minister was instructed on June 11, 1858, that: "Her Majesty's Government recognize as sound those principles of international law which have been laid down by General Cass in his note of the 10th of April to your lordship, principles which Abandonment he supports by the authority of Lord Stowell and the Duke of of British Wellington, and Her Majesty's Government are also aware that claim nothing in their treaty of 1842 with the United States supersedes that law." (50 British and Foreign State Papers, 737-739).

The reply of this Government was in part as follows: "The President desires you would express to Lord Malmesbury his gratification at this satisfactory termination of the controversy which has given so much trouble to our respective Governments, concerning the claim of a right in behalf of a British cruiser in time of peace to search or visit American merchant vessels upon the ocean. Her Britannic Majesty's Government had disclaimed that pretension and recognized the principles of international law laid down in the letter from this Department to Lord Napier of the 

10th of April last, and which had been maintained by distin-

guished British statesmen and especially by that eminent Lord 

Stowell, who said emphatically, while deciding a case judicially before him, that 'no nation can exercise a right of visitation and search upon the common and unappropriated parts of the ocean, except from the belligerent claim.' (Instructions to Great Britain, XVII, p. 115, June 30, 1858.)

Lord Malmesbury is reported in the London Times of June 18, 1858, as having explained, in the House of Lords, his recognition of the American position on this long controverted question by stating that "He had admitted the international law as laid down by the American minister for foreign affairs, though not, of course, without being fortified by the opinions of the law officers of the Crown." (H. Ex. Doc. 7, 36 Cong., 2d Sess. 104, 105). Upon another occasion, in the same place, Lord Malmesbury, referring to the renunciation, said: "We frankly confessed that we have no legal claim to the right of visit and of search which has hitherto been assumed." (Fur 

Seal Arbitration, Vol. XIII, 326–329.) 

Mr. Dallas, Minister to England, thus commented upon the 

British renunciation on July 4, 1858, at a dinner of Americans in 

London: 

"Visit and search in regard to American vessels on the high seas in time of peace is finally ended." 

Lord Lyndhurst referred to this statement, in the House of 

Lords on July 26, 1858, saying: "Many persons we have appear to think that surrendered a most valuable and important right. The answer which I make to that is, that we have surrendered no right, for that, in point of fact, no right such as that which is contended for has ever existed. We have, my lords, abandoned the assumption of a right, and in doing so we have, I think, acted justly, prudently and wisely." (Fur Seal Arbitration, Vol. XIII, 326329).

President Buchanan, in his annual message of December 6, 1858, referred to the British renunciation thus: "I am gratified to inform you that the long-pending controversy between the two Governments in relation to the question of visitation and search has been amicably adjusted.” *(Richardson's Messages of the Presidents, V. 507).

International law limits the sovereignty of a country to three miles from low-water mark, and although Mexican sovereignty follows Mexican vessels upon the high seas until they put into a foreign port, international law does not recognize Mexican Sovereignty over a foreign vessel, or any right on the part of Mexico to assume the incidents of sovereignty upon a foreign vessel, beyond the three-mile limit. 

---

HIGH SEAS 

663 If, therefore, Mexican sovereignty beyond the three-mile limit is not recognized by international law, it follows that the Mexicans have no right to visit or inspect vessels beyond that line, unless there is a local law of Mexico permitting visit and search under such circumstances. The absence of such a law would make any inspection of foreign vessels beyond the three-mile limit clearly illegal. The existence of such a law does not change the nature of the transaction so far as the foreigner is concerned, but legalizes the action according to the municipal law of Mexico. In such a case the municipal law would be a defense to an action if brought, but Mexico itself would be liable for any damages sustained by reason of the exercise of a right unrecognized or forbidden by international law, inasmuch as Mexico expressly or tacitly recognizes the binding effect of international law.

Opinion of the Solicitor for the Department of State, Oct. 2, 1906, MS. 

Department of State, file 779/3. 

The right to visit and search a foreign vessel on the high seas has been regarded as pertaining to a belligerent as such, and hence a privilege which, in time of peace, a State may not exercise. That the existence of this right depends upon the existence also of a state of war does not seem to be due to the belief that a State is deterred by some rule of law from defending itself in times of peace by the methods which it might employ when a belligerent, but rather because what has proved to be the frequent need of a belligerent has rarely become a necessary mode of safeguarding the vessels of a State not at war. Obviously, there are distinct disadvantages to maritime trade in relaxing a rule generally forbidding interference with vessels on the high seas by foreign authorities. It is believed, however, that if circumstances warrant the boarding or arrest of a foreign vessel by authorities of the State whose laws persons controlling the vessel are attempting from the high seas to infringe, search may be fairly made. Conduct on the part of such vessel justifying visit might also be deemed to justify search. If this is true, it is not apparent why evidence derived from search and confirming previous suspicion should not be made use of in justification of seizure and ultimate adjudication.

Opinion of the Solicitor for the Department of State, Jan. 9, 1924, MS. 

Department of State, file 311.0053/5.

In rendering an award in favor of Great Britain against the United States, the Anglo-American tribunal established under the special agreement of August 18, 1910 stated in part: 

It is admitted that the Jessie, the Thomas F. Bayard, and the 

Pescawha, all of them British schooners, cleared at Port Victoria, B.C., for sealing and sea otter hunting and were in June, 1909, actually engaged in hunting sea otters in the North Pacific Ocean; that on June 23, 1909, while on the high seas near the north end of Cherikof Islands they were boarded by an officer from the United States Revenue Cutter Bear who, having searched them for seal skins and found none, had the firearms found on board placed under seal, entered his search in the ship's log, and ordered that the seals should not be broken while the vessels remained north of 35° north latitude, and east of 

180° west longitude.

It is a fundamental principle of international maritime law that, except by special convention or in time of war, interference by a cruiser with a foreign vessel pursuing a lawful avocation on the high seas is unwarranted and illegal, and constitutes a violation of the sovereignty of the country whose flag the vessel flies. 

It is not contested that at the date and place of interference by the United States naval authorities there was no agreement authorizing those authorities to interfere as they did with the British schooners, and, therefore, a legal liability on the United States Government was created by the acts of its officers now complained of.

It is unquestionable that the United States naval authorities acted bona fide, but though their bona fides might be invoked by the officers in explanation of their conduct to their own Government, its effect is merely to show that their conduct constituted an error in judgment, and any government is responsible to other governments for errors in judgment of its officials purporting to act within the scope of their duties and vested with power to enforce their demands.

The case of Maul v. United States involved the forfeiture of a domestic vessel, the Underwriter, seized upon the high seas for violation of the revenue laws. The District Court of the United States sustained the claimant's exception to the court's jurisdiction on the theory that Coast Guard officers lacked authority to seize the vessel at sea more than twelve miles from the coast. The Circuit Court of 

Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed the decree dismissing the

Seizure of domestic vessels libel and sustained the forfeiture. The action was affirmed by the 

Supreme Court which stated in the course of its opinion: 

The remaining question relates to the meaning of the clause indicating where the officers may seize. It says "as well without as within their respective districts." Two constructions are suggested-one restricting the natural sense and treating the clause as if saying "as well within other customs districts as within their own"; and the other accepting the natural sense. The difference is that one excludes and the other includes the sea outside customs districts. In actual practice the latter construction has been adopted and it appears to be right. Besides giving effect to the natural import of the clause, it is better adapted to the attainment of the purpose of the section. If vessels violating the revenue laws and thereby incurring liability to forfeiture could escape seizure by departing from or avoiding waters within customs districts the liability to forfeiture would be of little practical effect in checking violations; and it is most improbable that Congress intended to leave the avenues of escape thus unguarded. The terms it has used are easily broad enough to meet the situation effectively, United States v. Bowman, 260 U.S. 94, 98-100, and no reason is suggested or perceived for cutting them down as respects domestic vessels. If Congress were without power to provide for the seizure of such vessels on the high sea, a restrictive construction might be justified. But there is no want of power in this regard. 

The high sea is common to all nations and foreign to none; and every nation having vessels there has power to regulate them and also to seize them for a violation of its laws. The Apollon, 9 

Wheat. 362, 371; Wilson v. McNamee, 102 U.S. 572, 574; Lord v. 

Steamship Co., 102 U.S. 541, 544; The Hamilton, 207 U.S. 398, 403; American Banana Co. v. United Fruit Co., 213 U.S. 347, 355;

Cunard S.S. Co. v. Mellon, 262 U.S. 100, 123, 129; 3 Opinions A.G. 

405; 1 Kent's Com. *26; Hall's International Law, 7th ed., §77; 1 

Hyde International Law, $227.

Some distinctions have been recognized in respect of seizing domestic vessels when in foreign waters and of seizing foreign vessels on the high sea, Cunard S.S. Co. v. Mellon, supra, 123-124; 

The Apollon, supra, 370-371; Church v. Hubbart, 2 Cr. 187, 234235; The Marianna Flora, 11 Wheat. 1, 42; Manchester v. Massachusetts, 139 U.S. 240, 258; 1 Hyde International Law, $236;

Westlake Int. Law, p. 177; but the extent and application of these distinctions are not involved in this case. 

The concurring opinion of Justice Brandeis, in which Justice 

Holmes joined, dealt with this problem as follows:

There is no limitation upon the right of the sovereign to seize without a warrant vessels registered under its laws, similar to that imposed by the common law and the Constitution upon the arrest of persons and upon the seizure of "papers and effects." See Carroll v. United States, 267 U.S. 132, 151-153. Smuggling is commonly attended by violation of the navigation laws. From the beginning of our Government officers of revenue cutters have, for

HIGH SEAS 

667 the purpose of enforcing the customs laws, been expressly authorized to board and search inbound vessels on the high seas within twelve miles of our coast. It is not to be lightly assumed that 

Congress intended to deny to revenue cutters so engaged authority to seize American vessels found to be violating our navigation laws. Nor is it lightly to be assumed that Congress intended to deny to officers of revenue cutters engaged in enforcing other laws of the United States beyond the twelve-mile limit, the authority to seize American vessels found to be violating our navigation laws beyond those limits.

From the beginning of our government, it has been the practice of revenue cutters to make such seizures. The official records and judicial decisions show that revenue cutters were employed early in our history, and that they have been employed continuously since, in enforcing our navigation laws upon the high seas regardless of distance from the coast; and that, whether operating within the United States or without, they have, regardless of distance from the coast, seized American vessels found violating our laws, without regard to whether the laws violated related to the revenue. Congress has by its action sanctioned this exertion of power. It supported the activities of the service by ever increasing appropriations. It equipped the Coast Guard, before the Tariff Act of 1922, with able cruising cutters, many of which were engaged largely in patrol beyond the twelve-mile limit. To seize anywhere on the high seas American vessels found violating our laws was thus, I think, within the implied authority of its officers before the Act of 1922. It remains to consider whether that Act abridged the authority theretofore possessed. 274 U.S. (1927) 501, 510-512, 524-527.

TRAFFIC IN ARMS AND AMMUNITION 

§201 The convention for the control of the trade in arms and ammuni- Convention of Saint-Ger- tion, signed at Saint-Germain-en-Laye and Paris, September 10, 1919, main, 1919 authorizes the warships of the high contracting parties to exercise certain jurisdiction over small native vessels suspected of illicit conveyance of arms or ammunition outside of territorial waters in a maritime zone "including the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman, and bounded by a line drawn from Cape 

Guardafui, following the latitude of that cape to its intersection with longitude 57° east of Greenwich, and proceeding thence direct to the eastern frontier of Persia in the Gulf of Oman" (art. 6). 

The native vessels subject to the provisions of the convention are those of less than 500 tons' burden not engaged exclusively in the coasting trade as therein defined (art. 12). An officer of a warship of one of the high contracting parties is authorized to visit a native vessel flying the flag of one of the parties and to verify its nationality by examining the document authorizing the flying of the flag. 

If authorization to fly the flag cannot be produced, the vessel is to be conducted to the nearest port in the zone where there is a competent authority of the power whose flag is flown and turned over to that authority. Certain provisions are made with respect to cases in which the competent authority representing the power whose flag the vessel has flown is remote from the point of arrest. 

The convention was not submitted to the United States Senate and was never ratified on the part of the United States. According to the records of the Department of State it was in force in respect to the following countries as of March 31, 1939: Greece, Siam, Rumania,

Convention on trade in arms, 1925 

Portugal, Ethiopia, Chile, Muscat, Finland, Venezuela, Uruguay, Bulgaria, and Iran. 

3 Treaties, etc. (Redmond, 1923) 3752, 3757-3767.

A convention for the supervision of the international trade in arms and ammunition and in implements of war was signed at Geneva on June 17, 1925. It contains provision that when a warship belonging to one of the high contracting parties encounters within a specified maritime zone (stated to include the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Persian Gulf, and the Gulf of Oman) but outside of territorial waters, a presumed native vessel of under 500 tons' burden, flying the flag of one of the high contracting parties or flying no flag, and the commanding officer of the warship has good reason to believe that the vessel is flying the flag of a high contracting party without being entitled to do so or is illicitly conveying articles covered by the convention, he may stop the vessel and conduct her to the nearest port, certain procedure in these respects being required. If the authority subsequently entrusted with the inquiry into the matter decides that the detention and diversion of the vessel or other measures imposed upon her were irregular, he is to assess the amount of compensation which he considers to be due.

Although the convention was submitted to the Senate of the United 

States by President Coolidge on January 12, 1926, that body did not finally give its advice and consent thereto until June 6, 1935, when it did so subject to a reservation that the convention should not come into force as to the United States until it should come into force as to Belgium, the British Empire, Czechoslovakia, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Sweden, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

In addition to the United States, the British Empire, Denmark, France, and Sweden have ratified with reservations. Ratifications without reservations have been deposited by Latvia, Canada, Bulgaria, Spain, Egypt, Poland, Netherlands, Venezuela, and China. 

Since article 41 of the convention requires ratification by fourteen powers, and since only nine of the ratifications were without reservation, the convention was not in force on March 31, 1939.

UTILIZATION OF MARINE RESOURCES 

$202 The United States contended before the tribunal established by the United States and Great Britain pursuant to the terms of the con-

HIGH SEAS 

673 vention signed January 27, 1909 for the arbitration of the North 

Atlantic Coast Fisheries case thatwhile a State may renounce the treaty right to fish in foreign territorial waters, it cannot renounce the natural right to fish on the High Seas.

The tribunal held that it wasgranted unable to agree with this contention. Because though a State Rights cannot grant rights on the High Seas it certainly can abandon abandoned the exercise of its right to fish on the High Seas within certain but not definite limits. Such an abandonment was made with respect to their fishing rights in the waters in question by France and 

Spain in 1763. By a convention between the United Kingdom and the United States in 1846, the two countries assumed ownership over waters in Fuca Straits at distances from the shore as great as 17 miles.

For regulation of sponges by the State of Florida beyond the three-mile limit but within a belt of marginal waters of three leagues as fixed in the State constitution, see Pope et al. v. Blanton, 10 F. Supp. 18 (N.D. Fla., 

1935); Lipscomb, Sheriff v. Gialourakis, 101 Fla. 1130, 133 So. 104 (1931).

The principle enunciated by Hall is that the true key to the development of the law is to be sought in the principle that maritime occupation must be effective in order to be valid. If it is disuse and disuse alone which has led to a restriction of the rights of the Sovereign in the bed of the sea, it follows that in cases where there has been effective occupation of a portion of the bed of the sea within the meaning of the principle enunciated by Hall, and such occupation still continues, there has been no abandoning of the rights of ownership, and consequently the ownership still continues. Assuming that this proposition is sound, it removes a difficulty which has found expression in writings on international law as regards sedentary fisheries occurring outside the three-mile limit. Vattel's statement: "Who can doubt that the pearl fisheries of Bahrein and Ceylon may lawfully become property?" ceases to cause any difficulty to even the stoutest upholders of the principle that the limits of the territorial belt are not more than three miles if it is realised that the exclusive right to the pearls to be obtained from the banks flowed from the ownership of the bed of the sea where the banks were situated, and not from any claim to maritime jurisdiction over the waters. Wherever it can be shown that particular oyster beds, pearl banks, chank fisheries, sponge fisheries or whatever may be the particular form of sedentary fishery in question outside the three-mile limit have always been kept in occupation by the Sovereign of the adjacent land, ownership of the soil of the bed of the sea where the fishery was situated may be presumed, and the exclusive right to the produce to be obtained from these fisheries may be based on their being a produce of the soil. Ownership of the soil by the Sovereign of the country under such circumstances must carry with it the right to legislate for the soil so owned and for the protection of the wealth to be derived from it, and no doubt need be felt as to the binding force of the various enactments which have been issued for the protection of these sedentary fisheries outside the three-mile limit. 

The instances where ancient usage justifies a claim to sedentary fisheries outside the three-mile limit do not seem to be numerous, and of those which are known some appear to be situated in bays or gulfs which are claimed as part of the national territory by the State contiguous to whose shore they lie. For instance, the chank fisheries and the pearl fisheries in the Gulf of Manaar have been the subject of regulation by local ordinances, etc., throughout the nineteenth century. The pearl and chank

HIGH SEAS 

675 fisheries in the Gulf of Manaar were claimed from early times by the successive Portuguese, Dutch and British masters of the neighbouring territory, and there can be little doubt but that a good title to the ownership of these beds can be made out, based on long-continued occupation. Both the Gulf of Manaar and 

Palk's Bay, the two great bays which divide India from Ceylon and are separated from each other by the long stretch of islets known as Adam's Bridge, would probably be claimed as part of the national territory, and not part of the high seas at all. Palk's 

Bay at any rate has now been held by the Madras Courts to be an integral portion of the British Dominions, and if the question arose a similar decision might possibly be given as to the Gulf of Manaar. Even if it were not, however, the claim to the ownership of the pearl and chank beds in that gulf could be based on long usage and uncontested enjoyment; and the right to legislate with regard to these beds could be rested on the ground of their ownership.

Another instance which can be cited, and one where there is no doubt that the site forms part of the high seas, is that of the oyster beds off the east coast of Ireland. By the Sea Fisheries 

Act of 1868 power was taken to issue an Order in Council enabling the Irish Commissioners to regulate the dredging for oysters on any oyster beds within a distance of twenty miles seawards from a straight line between Lambay Island and Carnsore Point. Some of these banks were between ten and twenty miles beyond the three-mile limit. 

The above are instances where the State interested formed part of the British Empire. The same principle must of necessity apply also to sedentary fisheries on banks claimed by foreign Governments. The Bey of Tunis has, for instance, claimed the exclusive right to the sponges on a bank outside the three-mile limit off the coast of Tunis by the continuous and unquestioned enjoyment of the fructus of these banks. Such enjoyment would constitute a title to the bank which foreign States would no doubt recognise and would oblige their nationals to recognise. Similarly, Mexico is said to have legislated for regulating pearl fisheries off the Mexican coast though outside the three-mile limit.

The maintenance of a State's property rights in special areas outside the three-mile limit when more extensive general claims to sovereignty, jurisdiction and property were abandoned is in no way inconsistent with the principles laid down by Oppenheim, that the sub-soil beneath the bed of the open sea outside the marginal belt of territorial waters is a no man's land, property in which can be acquired on the part of the littoral State through occupation starting from the sub-soil beneath the bed of the territorial maritime belt. Tunnelling in the sub-soil for purposes of mining or communications seems to be the only aspect of the problem which Oppenheim had in mind, but the principles he lays down are in no way inconsistent with the recognition of a right of exclusive ownership arising from long and undisputed occupation of sedentary fisheries lying on the surface of the bed of the sea. 

---

Submarine cables Subsoil property rights- navigation 

The International Convention for the Protection of Submarine 

Cables (Paris, March 14, 1884) does not run counter to this theory of the bed of the sea being a no man's land in which property can be and is acquired by occupation. The effect of the convention is to place submarine cables under a kind of common protection, as all the parties to the convention accept the view that wilful injury to a cable outside territorial waters is an offence to be punished in the courts of the country of the vessel doing the damage. There is nothing exclusive in character about the occupation of the sea bed occasioned by the laying of a submarine cable. The mere fact that one cable is there already does not prevent another from being laid across it; hence there is no need for the application of the principle that sovereignty and property of the sea bed are acquired by the occupation which the first comer achieves by the laying of his cable. There is no call for the recognition of exclusive rights. All that is necessary for safeguarding the position of the cable owner and for the maintenance and encouragement of cable communications is some method of protection of the cable by the recognition of its right to be there and by ensuring the punishment of those who injure it. It is not so with a submarine tunnel or with a mine driven out into the sub-soil beneath the high seas. Unless the rights created by such operations were exclusive the works would be valueless, for at any moment they would stand the risk of destruction through contact with similar works carried out by some other party.

It cannot be too strongly emphasised that the recognition of special property rights in particular areas of the bed of the sea outside the marginal belt for the purpose of sedentary fisheries does not conflict in any way with the common enjoyment by all mankind of the right of navigation of the waters lying over those beds or banks. Nor does it entail the recognition of any special or exclusive right to the capture of swimming fish over or around these beds or banks. 

To sum up: so far as Great Britain at any rate is concerned, the ownership of the bed of the sea within the three-mile limit is the survival of more extensive claims to the ownership of and sovereignty over the bed of the sea. The claims have become restricted by the silent abandonment of the more extended claims. 

Consequently, where effective occupation has been long maintained of portions of the bed of the sea outside the three-mile limit, those claims are valid and subsisting claims, entitled to recognition by other States.

The claim to the exclusive ownership of a portion of the bed of the sea and to the wealth which it produces in the form of pearl oysters, chanks, coral, sponges or other fructus of the soil is not inconsistent with the universal right of navigation in the open sea or with the common right of the public to fish in the high seas. 

Hurst, "Whose is the Bed of the Sea?", in the British Year Book of 

International Law (1923-24) 39-43.

HIGH SEAS 

677 It is stated in the last edition of Oppenheim's treatise on Interna tional Law: 

Since the open sea is free, no part of it can be the object of Occupation, nor can rocks or banks in the open sea, although lighthouses may be built on them. Likewise the bed of the sea cannot be an object of occupation, but the subsoil of the bed of the open sea may become the object of occupation through driving mines and piercing tunnels from the coast. 

Although it is traditional to base some of these cases on the ground of prescription, it is submitted that it would be not inconsistent with principle, and would be more in accord with practice, to recognise frankly that, as a matter of law, a State may by strictly local occupation acquire, for sedentary fisheries and for other purposes, sovereignty and property in the surface of the sea-bed, provided that in so doing it in no way interferes with freedom of navigation and, perhaps we should add, with the breeding of free-swimming fish.

The rationale of the open sea being free and for ever excluded from occupation on the part of any State is that it is an international highway, which connects distant lands, and thereby secures freedom of communication, and especially of commerce, between States separated by the sea. There is no reason whatever for extending this freedom of the open sea to the subsoil beneath its bed. On the contrary, there are practical reasons-taking into consideration the building of mines, tunnels, and the like-which compel recognition of the fact that this subsoil can be acquired through occupation.
